body:
[Definition def:standard-twostream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$
and a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$.
Let $Z=(Z^A,Z^B)$ be the two-stream process with birth rate~$\lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and start time~$0$  
where for all $D\in \{A,B\}$ and all
positive integers~$k$,
$\mathbf{arr}_k^{Z^D}(\tau) = \emptyset$. 
Let $X$ be the backoff process with birth distribution~$\mathsf{Po}(\lambda)$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and cohort set $\mathcal{C}=\{A,B\}$ (Definition~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)).
The standard coupling of~$Z$ and~$X$ has the following invariants for every $i\geq 1$ and $t\geq 1$.
\begin{description}  
\item  [Inv-$b_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{b}_i^{Z^D}(t-1) \subseteq \mathbf{b}_i^{X^D}(t-1)$.
\item  [Inv-$B_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\item [Inv-$s_i(t)$:] 
For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\end{description}
Initially, Inv-$b_i(1)$ holds for every $i\geq 1$ since all of these sets are empty.

For any $t$ assuming Inv-$b_i(t)$, the coupling at step~$t$ proceeds as follows.
For each $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{n}^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t)$, so for all $i\geq 1$, 
Inv-$B_i(t)$ holds.
For every   
$D\in \{A,B\}$ and
$i\geq 1$, $\mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t)$ is formed by including each ball in 
$\mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t) \setminus \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t)$ 
independently with probability~$p_i$.
Then $\mathbf{s}^{X^D}_i(t) = \mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^D}_i(t)$, establishing Inv-$s_i(t)$.

 
  

  
The assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t)$ follow deterministically, using  Definition~(def:backoffasgen of the paper)
and the assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$  are chosen  following Definition~(def:two-stream of the paper).

Since $\mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, Inv-$b_i(t+1)$  follows from  
$ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, which holds:
If a ball~$\beta$ is in $ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) $ then
$\mathbf{s}^{X^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{X^B}(t)= \{\beta\}$ so
$\mathbf{s}^{Z^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^B}(t) = \{\beta\}$ so 
$\mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t) = \{\beta\}$.
title: Definition def:standard-twostream of arXiv:2602.21315

[Lemma le:good_scales_merging of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Suppose that $h$ is a GFF on $D$ with some bounded boundary values. For any $b>0$ and $q \in (0,1)$ there exist $M,p>0$ so that the following is true. 
Let $z \in D$ and $r>0$ such that $B(z,r) \subseteq D$. Let $\widetilde{h}_{z,r}$ be as defined in Section~(se:gff of the paper) with the same boundary values as $\widetilde{h}$ above (after scaling and translation). Let $G_{z,r}$ be the event that
\begin{itemize}
 \item the scale $(z,r)$ is $M$-good for $h$, and
 \item the event $G$ above occurs for the (scaled and translated) field $\widetilde{h}_{z,r}$.
\end{itemize}
For $k\in\mathbf{N}$ let $E$ be the event that the fraction of $1 \leq j \leq k$ so that $G_{z,2^{-j}r}$ occurs is at least $q$. Then $\mathbf{P}[E^c] = O(e^{-bk})$.

body: Fermat's Last Theorem: There are no three positive integers a, b, c satisfying a^n + b^n = c^n for any integer exponent n > 2. (By contrast, for n = 1 and n = 2 the equation has infinitely many positive integer solutions; for n = 2 these are the Pythagorean triples, e.g. 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2.) The statement was conjectured by Pierre de Fermat in 1637 and proved by Andrew Wiles in 1994, using a result obtained jointly with Richard Taylor, via the modularity of semistable elliptic curves.
title: Fermat's Last Theorem

[Lemma lem:pathbound of arXiv:2608.30888, 'Three-term asymptotics for discrete\\ Hardy--Rellich constants in high dimension'] Fix $J$ and two finite sets of partitions.  Uniformly for $0\leq j\leq J$ and
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$ in those sets or reachable from them in at
most $J$ steps,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\ip{A_N^j\psi_\lambda}{\psi_\mu}\right|
 \leq C_J N^{a_j(\lambda,\mu)/2},
\end{equation}
where $a_j(\lambda,\mu)$ is the largest number of dimensional edges among
length-$j$ paths from $\lambda$ to $\mu$; the left side is zero if no such path
exists.  Consequently, for fixed $\ell$ and bounded $s_\lambda,s_\mu$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\ip{K_{\ell,N}\psi_\lambda}{\psi_\mu}\right|
 \leq C_\ell N^{\ell-d_*(\lambda,\mu)}.
\end{equation}

[Definition def:openpath of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $\lambda\in(0,\infty]$, $\mu\in(0,\infty]$ and $\mathfrak r\in\{\mathrm{u},\mathrm{i}\}$. An \emph{open
path} from $(u_0,t_0)$ to $(u_n,t_{n+1})$ consists of particles $u_0,\dots,u_n$, such that
consecutive particles are distinct, and times $t_0<t_1<\dots<t_{n+1}$, such that
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item for $1\le j\le n$ there is an active transmission mark from $u_{j-1}$ to $u_j$ at time
  $t_j$; when $\lambda=\infty$ this says that $u_{j-1}$ and $u_j$ are in contact at $t_j$;
\item for $0\le j\le n$ there is no effective recovery mark of $u_j$ in $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$.
\end{enumerate}
Its \emph{trace} is the c\`adl\`ag path $\gamma$ on $[t_0,t_{n+1}]$ given by $\gamma(t)=X_{u_j}(t)$
for $t\in[t_j,t_{j+1})$ and $0\le j\le n-1$, and by $\gamma(t)=X_{u_n}(t)$ for
$t\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. Its jumps have size at most $2r$. The path is \emph{contained} in a
space-time region $D$ if $(\gamma(t),t)\in D$ for every $t\in[t_0,t_{n+1}]$.
title: Open path

body: [Definition Pareto optimality of arXiv:2608.22945, 'A Momentum-Based Variance-Reduced Algorithm for Federated Multiobjective Optimization'] For any two solutions $x, y\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, we say $x$ \emph{dominates} $y$ if and only if $f_s(x)\leq f_s(y), \forall s\in[S]$ and $f_s(x)<f_s(y), \exists s\in[S]$. A solution $x\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ is \emph{Pareto optimal} if it is not dominated by any other solution. A solution $x\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ is \emph{weakly Pareto optimal} if there does not exist a solution $y$ such that $f_s(y)< f_s(x), \forall s\in[S]$.
title: Pareto optimality

[Definition 4 (Size-biased law) of arXiv:2606.18458, 'Stable size-biasing and the positive scale-mixture order of generalized Gaussian laws'] Let $Y\ge0$ satisfy $0<\E Y<\infty$. The $Y$-size-biased version $Y^*$ of $Y$ is the positive random variable whose law is defined by
\[
\Prob(Y^*\in A)=\frac{\E[Y\mathbf{1}_{\{Y\in A\}}]}{\E Y},
\]
for Borel sets $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$. Equivalently,
\[
\E h(Y^*)=\frac{\E[Yh(Y)]}{\E Y}
\]
for all bounded measurable $h$.
title: Size-biased law

[Corollary 33 (Phase transition for Poisson-Voronoi percolation) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a non-compact connected semisimple real Lie group and $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space. Fix $\lambda>0$. Then 
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\rm (1)}] for every $p\in [0,p_c(\lambda))$, $\omega_p^{(\lambda)}$ does not have an unbounded cluster a.s.
\item[{\rm (2)}] for every $p\in (p_c(\lambda),p_u(\lambda))$, $\omega_p^{(\lambda)}$ has infinitely many unbounded clusters a.s.
\item[{\rm (3)}] for every $p\in (p_u(\lambda),1]$, $\omega_p^{(\lambda)}$ has a unique unbounded clusters a.s.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Phase transition for Poisson-Voronoi percolation

body: [Definition of arXiv:2412.04579, 'Solvable Families of Random Block Tridiagonal Matrices'] Let $\mathbf{Y}$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with i.i.d.~${\mathbb{F}} N(0,1)$ entries, and set \smash{$\mathbf{X}=\frac1{\sqrt{2}} \bigl(\mathbf{Y}+\mathbf{Y}^{\dag}\bigr)$}. The distribution of $\mathbf{X}$ is called the ${\mathbb{F}}$-valued Gaussian ensemble, or G${\mathbb{F}}$E$(n)$. For $\beta=1$, this is the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE), and for $\beta=2$, this is the Gaussian unitary ensemble (GOE).

[Lemma 18 (Differentiation formula for a finite-intensity Poisson process) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Let \((\mathsf X,\nu)\) be a finite measure space, and for \(t\ge 0\) let \(\Pi_t\) be
a Poisson point process on \(\mathsf X\) with intensity measure \(t\nu\). Then, for
every finite counting measures, the map
\(t\mapsto \Ebb[F(\Pi_t)]\) is differentiable on \((0,\infty)\), and its right
derivative at \(t=0\) is given by
\[
\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\Ebb[F(\Pi_t)]
=
\int_{\mathsf X}\Ebb\!\left[F(\Pi_t+\delta_z)-F(\Pi_t)\right]\nu(\dd z).
\]

body:
Let (M,tau) be a finite von Neumann algebra with faithful normal tracial state tau(1)=1. Let X=(X_1,...,X_n) be an algebraically free tuple of bounded selfadjoint elements, with n a fixed positive integer. On noncommutative polynomials in X, define the free difference quotient partial_j by partial_j X_i=delta_ij*(1 tensor 1) and the Leibniz rule, with the usual bimodule action on the tensor product. The conjugate variable J_j belongs to the L2(tau) closure of the polynomial algebra and, if it exists, satisfies tau(J_j P(X))=(tau tensor tau)(partial_j P(X)) for every polynomial P. Equivalently J_j is the adjoint of partial_j applied to 1 tensor 1. Define Phi_star(X)=sum_{j=1}^n ||J_j||_2^2 when all conjugate variables exist, and Phi_star(X)=+infinity otherwise. This is conjugate-variable, non-microstates free Fisher information relative to the scalar algebra C. It is not the Fisher information of a classical parametric likelihood.
Normalized faithful normal tracial state on a finite von Neumann algebra.
Fixed finite algebraically free bounded selfadjoint tuple, so the difference quotients on its polynomial algebra are well-defined.
Conjugate variables, when present, lie in the L2 closure of that polynomial algebra.

body:
Every separable real Banach space X is isometrically isomorphic to a closed linear subspace of C[0, 1], the space of continuous real functions on [0, 1] with the supremum norm. (The complex version holds with complex-valued C[0,1].) Consequently C[0,1] is universal for the class of separable Banach spaces up to isometry, and every separable metric space embeds isometrically into C[0,1] as well (Banach-Mazur, via the Kuratowski embedding x -> d(x, .) - d(x_0, .)). In contrast, no separable Banach space is isomorphically universal for the class of separable REFLEXIVE spaces with a separable dual of the same kind (Szlenk), and the universality fails in an essential way for spaces of continuous functions on countable compacta (Bessaga-Pelczynski, Milutin: C(K) for uncountable metrizable compact K is isomorphic to C[0,1], while C(K) for countable K is not).
X separable (the separability is essential: a non-separable space cannot embed into the separable space C[0,1])
real scalars in the statement; the complex case is identical with complex-valued functions

body:
[Proposition BBSTAB of arXiv:2411.04590, 'Singular stochastic delay equations driven by fractional Brownian motion: Dynamics, longti'] Assume that \( A \) and \( \pi \) satisfy the same conditions as in Lemma (PII of the paper), and let \( G \in {L}(\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n, {L}(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathbb{R}^n)) \). Consider the following linear stochastic differential equation:
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				\mathrm{d}y_t &= A\left( y_t, \int_{-r}^{0} y_{\theta+t} \, \pi(\mathrm{d}\theta) \right) \mathrm{d}t + \epsilon G(y_t, y_{t-r}) \, \mathrm{d}B_t(\omega), \\
				y_{\theta} &= \xi_{\theta} \quad \text{for} \quad \theta \in [-r, 0], \quad \xi \in C([-r, 0], \mathbb{R}^n),
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			where \( y^{\xi, \epsilon}_t \) denotes the solution. Let \( \lambda_1 \) be as defined in (equation TRFVV of the paper), and assume \( \lambda_1 < 0 \). Then, there exists \( \epsilon_0 > 0 \) such that for every \( 0 < \epsilon < \epsilon_0 \), there exists \( \lambda^\epsilon < 0 \) such that for any \( \xi \in C([-r, 0], \mathbb{R}^n) \), the following holds:
			\[
			\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{t} \log | y^{\xi, \epsilon}_t(\omega) |\leq \lambda^\epsilon, \quad \text{almost surely}.
			\]
			This yields in particular a pathwise stability result on $C([-r,0],\mathbb{R}^n)$
title: Proposition BBSTAB of arXiv:2411.04590

body: [Lemma le:random_scale of arXiv:2506.07158, 'The diffusivity of supercritical Bernoulli percolation is infinitely differentiable'] Suppose that $\mathcal{G}$ satisfies (equation e:local_dependence of the paper) and (equation e:rarely_bad of the paper). Given $t'>0$, there exists $C = C(K,s,t')$ and a random scale $\mathcal{M}_{S}\leqslant \mathcal{O}_{s/t'}(C)$, such that if $3^m \geqslant \mathcal{M}_S$, then for any $m/t' \leqslant k \leqslant m$, and $z \in 3^k \mathbb{Z}^d \cap {\scaleobj{1}{\square}}_m$, we have $z + {\scaleobj{1}{\square}}_k \in \mathcal{G}$.

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.03771, '\vspace{-5ex}\bfseries\scshape{Local law and delocalization for the Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev mo'] Let $q$ be even and fixed. We define the Fock space 
    \[
    \Fcal_{n} \coloneqq \left\{ \psi = (\psi_S)_{S\subset\unn{1}{n}}, \sum_{S\subset\unn{1}{n}}\vert \psi_S\vert^2<\infty\right\} \cong \Cbb^{D}.
    \]
    There exists $C_q>0$\footnote{The dependence of $C_q$ on $q$ is not explicit in \cite{visconti2026}, which is why we restrict this result to fixed $q$.} such that for $v,w\in\Fcal_n,$ we have
    \[
    \frac{1}{M}\sum_{\substack{A\subset\unn{1}{N}\\\vert A\vert=q}} \vert \langle v,\Gamma_Aw\rangle\vert^2 
    \leqslant C_q N^{-\frac{q}{2}}\Vert v\Vert^2\Vert w\Vert^2.
    \]
    The same bound holds after restriction to either parity sector. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.03771

[Definition def:prenosil-diamond of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] {simpson_proof_1994}}] 
  On an f-model $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$, consider the diamond clause
  \[
    x \Vdash^{\mathrm p}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \varphi
    \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;}
    \exists x', y \in W \,
      (x' \leq x \mathrel{\text{\&}} x' \sqsubset y \mathrel{\text{\&}} y \Vdash^{\mathrm p}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi).
  \]
  Thus $\Diamond \varphi$ holds at $x$ when $\varphi$ holds at an ${\sqsubset}$-successor
  of some ${\leq}$-predecessor of $x$.
  Simpson attributes this clause to unpublished work of Plotkin and Stirling.
  P\v{r}enosil later developed the corresponding operation on upsets [prenosil_duality_2014].

[Definition 43 ($\mathrm{RCD}(K, \infty)$ condition) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $(X,d,\mu)$ be a Polish measure space. We say that it is an $\operatorname{RCD}(K, \infty)$-space if it satisfies the $\mathrm{CD}(K, \infty)$-condition and if its Cheeger energy is quadratic, i.e., for all $f,g\in L^2(X,\mu)$ such that $0<\operatorname{Ch}_\mu(f)\operatorname{Ch}_\mu(g)<\infty$, one has
\[
\operatorname{Ch}_\mu(f+g) + \operatorname{Ch}_\mu(f-g)=2\operatorname{Ch}_\mu(f) + 2\operatorname{Ch}_\mu(g).
\]
title: $\mathrm{RCD}(K, \infty)$ condition

[Thm 41 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] For any real numbers $q_0>0, \delta > 0$, there exist constants $r = r(q_0) \in (0, 1)$ and $\mC = \mC(q_0, \delta) > 1$ such that the following holds. 
 Define
  \[
     i_{max}=\left\lfloor\frac 9{10}\frac{\log N}{\log(1/(1-r))}\right\rfloor
    \] and
  the sequence
\[
  N_i=\lfloor N (1-r)^i\rfloor,\quad 0\le i\le i_{max}\] that
decreases from $N_0=N$ to $N_{i_{max}}\asymp N^{1/10}$. Define also
the sequence \[
\epsilon_i=10^{-i}N^{-100},\quad 0\le i\le i_{max}
.\]
 For every $i\le i_{max}-1$, we have
   \begin{flalign}
     \tmix^{N_i}(\epsilon_i) \le \mC{N_i}^{2+\delta} + t_{\rm mix}^{N_{i+1}}(\epsilon_{i+1})+t^{\mq_0,N_i}_{\rm mix}\left(\frac   {\epsilon_i}4\right).
   \end{flalign} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 41 of arXiv:2605.26664

body:
[Lemma detect-pointed-presheaves of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let ${\mathcal{C}}$ be a cocomplete, pointed, and locally small $\infty$-category. Let ${\mathcal{I}}\subset{\mathcal{C}}$ be a small full subcategory containing the zero object and satisfying the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For any $I\in{\mathcal{I}}$, the unique lift ${\mathcal{C}}\to\Spc_*$ of ${\textup{Hom}}(I,-)$ is cocontinuous.
        \item The functors ${\textup{Hom}}(I,-)\colon{\mathcal{C}}\to\Spc$ are jointly conservative.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then ${\mathcal{I}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}$ extends to an equivalence $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\mathcal{C}}$.
    \begin{proof}
        As ${\mathcal{C}}$ is cocomplete and locally small, the inclusion extends to a functor $\Lambda\colon\PSh({\mathcal{I}})\to{\mathcal{C}}$ left adjoint to the restricted Yoneda embedding $\Upsilon$. By what it means to be a zero object, ${\textup{Hom}}(0,x)\simeq1$ for all $x\in{\mathcal{C}}$, i.e.\ $\Upsilon$ factors through $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})$, so we obtain a restricted adjunction $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})\rightleftarrows{\mathcal{C}}$. It remains to show that this is in fact an adjoint equivalence. As our second assumption guarantees that $\Upsilon$ is conservative, it will suffice for this that the unit $\eta\colon\textup{id}\to\Upsilon\Lambda$ is invertible. 

        Since ${\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}}$ has a zero object, postcomposing with the forgetful functor induces an equivalence ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc)$. Moreover, the full subcategory ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)\subset{\textup{Fun}}({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)$ is closed under colimits (as any colimit of initial objects is initial), so that colimits in ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)$ are computed pointwise. Thus, our first assumption guarantees that the right adjoint $\Upsilon$ is cocontinuous, so that the class of all pointed presheaves $X$ for which $\eta_X$ is invertible, is closed under colimits. It will therefore suffice to show that the unit $\eta_X$ is invertible whenever $X=\Upsilon(I)$ is representable. If we now let $Z\in{\mathcal{C}}$ arbitrary, then the composite
        \[
            {\textup{Hom}}(\Lambda(X),Z)\xrightarrow{\;\Upsilon\;}{\textup{Hom}}(\Upsilon\Lambda(X),\Upsilon(Z))\xrightarrow{\;{\textup{Hom}}(\eta,\Upsilon(Z))} {\textup{Hom}}(X,\Upsilon(Z))
        \]
        is invertible as it is just the adjunction equivalence. By assumption, $\Lambda(X)\simeq I\in{\mathcal{I}}$; if also $Z\in I$, then the first map is an equivalence by the Yoneda lemma, so that also the second map is an equivalence by $2$-out-of-$3$. We conclude that ${\textup{Hom}}(\eta_X,\Upsilon(Z))$ is an equivalence for every $Z\in I$. As $\eta_X\colon \Upsilon(I)=X\to \Upsilon\Lambda(X)\simeq\Upsilon(I)$ is a map in Yoneda image, this implies that $\eta_X$ is an equivalence.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma detect-pointed-presheaves of arXiv:2608.28504

Consider a sequence $\{Z_n\}$ defined as in (equation eq:defpolchaos of the paper) such that (equation e:can1 of the paper)--(equation e:can2 of the paper) are verified. If $\{Z_n\}$ is reducible, we will say that $\{{\ensuremath{\mathcal G}} _n\}$ {\em is reducible} or, more precisely, that $\{{\ensuremath{\mathcal G}} _n\}$ {\em generates a reducible CLT}.

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $k, n\in \mathbb{N}$, $n\ge k$, let $\nu_{k,n}$ be the normalized Haar measure on the Grassmannian
$Gr(k,n)$ of all $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb R^n$. Then there
exists a constant $C(k,n)>0$ such that, for every $k\times n$ matrix $J$,
one has
\[
\int_{Gr(k,n)}(\det J^H)^2\,\nu_{k,n}(dH)
=
C(k,n)\det(JJ^*),
\]
where $J^H:=JU_H$ and $U_H$ is the $n\times k$ matrix whose columns form an
orthonormal basis in $H$.

[Proposition prop:ik-proves-nnbb-to-bb of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] $\textbf{IK} \vdash \neg \neg \Box \bot \to \Box \bot$. Consequently, $\textbf{iK}_\Box \subsetneq \textbf{IK} \cap \mathscr{L}_\Box$.
  \begin{proof}
    By completeness, it suffices to show that $\neg \neg \Box \bot \to \Box \bot$ is valid in every IK-model.
    Take any $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$ and any $x_0, x_1$ such that $x_0 \leq x_1 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \Box \bot$,
    then we shall show that $x_1 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box \bot$.
    To do so, take any $x_2$ such that $x_1 \leq x_2$,
    then $x_1 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \Box \bot$ implies $x_2 \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \Box \bot$,
    so there is $x_3$ such that $x_2 \leq x_3 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box \bot$,
    which implies that, in paticular, there is no $y_3$ such that $x_3 \sqsubset y_3$.
    Now suppose, by way of contradiction, that there is $y_2$ such that $x_2 \sqsubset y_2$,
    then $x_3 \geq x_2 \sqsubset y_2$, so by the $\Diamond$-p condition, there must be some $y_3$ such that $x_3 \sqsubset y_3 \geq y_2$, which is a contradiction.
    Now that $\forall x_2\, (x_1 \leq x_2 \mathrel{\Rightarrow} \neg \exists y_2\, (x_2 \sqsubset y_2))$, then we obtain $x_1 \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Box \bot$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.16733, 'Concentration Inequalities for Sample Cross-Covariances'] Let \((X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^N\) be i.i.d. copies of a centered random vector
\((X,Y)\in\mathbb R^{d_X+d_Y}\). Assume that \(X\) and \(Y\) are
sub-Gaussian random vectors with covariance matrices \(\Sigma_X\) and
\(\Sigma_Y\), and sub-Gaussian constants \(K_X,K_Y\). Set
\[
r_{X}:=\frac{\tr(\Sigma_X)}{\|\Sigma_X\|},
\qquad
r_{Y}:=\frac{\tr(\Sigma_Y)}{\|\Sigma_Y\|}.
\]
For every \(u\ge 1\), it holds with probability at least \(1-\exp(-u)\) that
\[
\bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y_i^{\top}-\E X Y^{\top}\bigg\| \lesssim K_{X}K_{Y}(\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}+u}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{(r_{X}+u)(r_{Y}+u)}}{N}\bigg).
\]
As a corollary,
 \begin{align*}
\E \bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y^{\top}_i-\E X Y^{\top}\bigg\| \lesssim K_{X}K_{Y} (\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{r_{X}r_{Y}}}{N}\bigg).
 \end{align*}
Moreover, if $(X,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian, then
\begin{align*}
\E \bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y^{\top}_i-\E XY^{\top}\bigg\| \asymp (\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{r_{X}r_{Y}}}{N}\bigg).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.16733

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The following happen:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The rotation $R_t$ is not diagonalizable, unless at $t=0$ where it is the identity, $R_0=1$, and at $t=\pi$ where it is minus the identity, $R_\pi=-1$.

\item The symmetry $S_t$ is diagonalizable, with eigenvectors on the symmetry axis, and on its orthogonal, with respective eigenvalues $1,-1$.

\item The projection $P_t$ is diagonalizable, with the eigenvectors exactly as for the symmetry $S_t$, this time with respective eigenvalues $1,0$.

\item In fact, any projection is diagonalizable, with eigenvectors on it image, and on the orthogonal of its image, with respective eigenvalues $1,0$.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Defi The modified transition kernel $Q_{n,t}$ of arXiv:2607.19658, 'Hitting time mixing for random $k$-cycles'] For $t\ge t^*$, set
$$
C_t=(|M_t|-1)_{k-2},
\qquad
q_t=\frac{|M_t|}{|M_t|+1}
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}.
$$
If $k$ is odd, then the kernel $Q_{n,t}$ is defined by
\[
Q_{n,t}=\begin{cases}
(i\cdots i) & \text{with probability } C_tq_t \ \text{for } i\in S_t,\\[6pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } q_t\ \text{for } i_1\in S_t,\ i_2,\ldots,i_k\in M_t,\\[6pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } \left(\dfrac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}\ \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
If $k$ is even, then the kernel $Q_{n,t}$ is defined by
\[
Q_{n,t}=\begin{cases}
(ab)(i\cdots i) & \text{with probability } \dfrac{C_tq_t}{\binom{|M_t|}{2}}
\ \text{for } i\in S_t,\ \{a,b\}\subset M_t,\\[8pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } q_t\ \text{for } i_1\in S_t,\ i_2,\ldots,i_k\in M_t,\\[6pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } \left(\dfrac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}\ \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Here $(i\cdots i)$ is a labelled dummy move. In the odd case it acts as the identity. In the even case $(ab)(i\cdots i)$ acts on the permutation as the transposition $(ab)$ and carries the label $i$, which indicates the element to be marked. Throughout the marking argument we restrict to the event $|S_{t^*}|\leq \log n$, whose complement will be handled separately. Under both marking schemes the number of unmarked elements never increases, so for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $|M_t|\geq n-\log n$ for every $t\geq t^*$. Hence all quantities appearing in the definition of $Q_{n,t}$ are well-defined.

Let us check that $Q_{n,t}$ is indeed a probability kernel. The total mass assigned by the original uniform $k$-cycle kernel to cycles with exactly one element in $S_t$ is
$$
|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot(|M_t|-1)_{k-2}
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}=|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot C_t\cdot
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}.
$$
Under $Q_{n,t}$, this mass is replaced by two contributions. The ordinary one-unmarked $k$-cycles have total mass $|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot C_t q_t$,
while the dummy moves have total mass
$|S_t|\cdot C_t q_t$ in the odd case, and
$$
|S_t|\cdot \binom{|M_t|}{2}\cdot\frac{C_tq_t}{\binom{|M_t|}{2}}=|S_t|\cdot C_t q_t
$$
in the even case. Hence the total replacement mass is
$$
|S_t|\cdot (|M_t|+1)\cdot C_tq_t=|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot C_t
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1},
$$
by the definition of $q_t$. All other $k$-cycles retain their original mass. Therefore the total mass of $Q_{n,t}$ is indeed one.
title: The modified transition kernel $Q_{n,t}$

[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.09459, 'Multipoint connectivity in the branching interlacement process'] Let $X$ and $X^*$ be two independent random walks both indexed by infinite critical trees $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}^*$ respectively and independent from the branching interlacement. Let $\P_x$ denote the joint law of $X$ and $A^{(s_d)}(r,R)$, and $\P_z^*$ the law of $X^*$. Then there exist constants $c = c(u,d) > 0$, $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(u,d) > 0$ and $R' = R'(u,d)$, such that, for all $r$ and $R \geq R'$, satisfying $r^{d-4} \leq \varepsilon R$, and $r \geq \max(\|x\|,\|z\|)$,
  \[
    \P_z^* \otimes \P_x(\exists u \in \mathcal{T}^{*}_-:\, X^*_u \in A^{(s_d)}(r,R), n^*_u < \tau^*_{R^2}) \geq c,
  \]
  where the quantities with a * refer to $X^*$.

body: [Defipro def:made_markov of arXiv:2412.10001, 'On the Markov transformation of Gaussian processes'] Let $T \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a set, $E$ a Polish space, $P \in \mathcal{P}(E^T)$ a probability measure and $R = \{r_1 < \dots < r_m\} \subset T$ a finite set of times. For each finite set $S \subset T$, we write \[S \cup R = \{s_1^0 < \dots < s_{k_0}^0 < r_1 < s_1^1 < \cdots < s_{k_1}^1 < r_2< \cdots < s_1^{m-1} < \cdots < s_{k_{m-1}}^{m-1}< r_m < s_1^m < \cdots < s_{k_m}^m\}\] and \[\mu_S := \textnormal{proj}^S_{\#}[ P^{s_1^0,\dots,s^0_{k_0},r_1} \circ P^{r_1, s_1^1 , \dots, s^1_{k_1},r_2} \circ \dots \circ P^{r_m,s_1^m,\dots, s_{k_m}^m}].\] Denoting by $\mathcal{S}$ the class of finite subsets of $T$, it is readily verified that $(\mu_S)_{S \in \mathcal{S}}$ is a consistent family of measures. According to the Kolmogorov extension Theorem, there exists a unique probability $P_{[R]}$ on $E^T$ such that $\textnormal{proj}^S_\# P_{[R]} = \mu_S$ for every $S \in \mathcal{S}.$ We say that $P_{[R]} \in \mathcal{P}(E^T)$ is the measure $P$ made Markov at times $R.$ Given a process $X$ with law $P$, we say that $X^R$ is the\footnote{We speak about \emph{the} transformation, even if we just have uniqueness in law} transformation of $X$ made Markov at times $R$ if $X^R$ has law $P_{[R]}.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Measure made Markov at times $R$

The following schematic relations hold for scalar functions
($\alpha,\beta = 0,1,2,3$, $\kappa = 0,1,2,3,4$):
\begin{subequations} 
\begin{align}
\gfour_{\alpha \beta}, 
	\,
(\gfour^{-1})^{\alpha \beta}, 
	\,
\gtorus_{\alpha \beta}, 
	\,
(\gtorus^{-1})^{\alpha \beta}, 
	\,
G_{\alpha \beta}^{\kappa}, 
	\,
\smoothtorusproject_\beta^{\alpha}, 
	\,
\Lunit^{\alpha}, 
	\,
X^{\alpha}, 
	\,
\olduLunit^{\alpha}, 
	\,
\Yvf{2}^{\alpha}, 
	\,
\Yvf{3}^{\alpha}, 
& 
= \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity),  
	 
	\\
\left(\geop{t}\right)^{\alpha},
	\,
\left(\geop{x^2}\right)^{\alpha},
	\,
\left(\geop{x^3}\right)^{\alpha}
& 
= \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity),

	\\
\left(\geop{u}\right)^{\alpha}
& 
= \smoothfunction(\badcontrolvars,\LogDensity),
	 
		\\
G_{\Lunit \Lunit}^{\kappa}, 
	\,
G_{\Lunit X}^{\kappa}, 
	\,
G_{XX}^{\kappa} 
& = \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity), 
	 \\
\Xsmall^{\alpha}, 
	\,
\Yvfsmall{2}^{\alpha},
	\,
\Yvfsmall{3}^{\alpha}, 
	\,
\Yvfsmallcoeff{A}
& 
= \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity)(\controlvars,\LogDensity),
	 \\
\muX^{\alpha}
& = \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity)\upmu.
	
\end{align}
\end{subequations}Moreover, if $\varphi$ is a scalar function, then we have the following schematic relation for 
its $\angD$-Hessian (which is a symmetric type $\binom{0}{2}$-tangent tensorfield):
\begin{align} 
	\angDsquared \varphi
	& = \smoothfunction(\controlvars, \angrmd \vec{x} \, ) \tanderY^2 \varphi
			+
			\smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity, \angrmd \vec{x} \, ) \cdot \tanderY (\controlvars,\LogDensity) \cdot \tanderY \varphi.
\end{align}Finally, we have the following schematic relations for $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent tensorfields,
where $\angrmd \vec{x}$ is defined in \eqref{E:ANDGULARDIFFERENTIALOFCARTESIANSPATIALCOORDIANTES}:
\begin{subequations} 
\begin{align}
\gtorus, 
	\,
\angG_{\Lunit}, 
	\,
\angG_X,
	\,
\angG 
& = \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity, \angrmd \vec{x} \, ), 
	 
		\\
\Yvf{2}, 
	\,
\Yvf{3}, 
& = \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity, \gtorus^{-1}, \angrmd \vec{x} \, ), 
	 
		\\
\upchi 
& = \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity,  \angrmd \vec{x} \, ) \tander (\controlvars,\LogDensity), 
	 
		\\
\mytr_{\gtorus} \upchi 
& 
= 
\smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity, \gtorus^{-1}, \angrmd \vec{x} \, ) \tander  (\controlvars,\LogDensity), 
	  
		\\
\zetatan, 
	\,
\angktan 
& 
= \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity, \angrmd \vec{x} \, ) \tander \wavearray, 
	 
		\\
\zetatrans, 
	\,
\angktrans 
& = \smoothfunction(\controlvars,\LogDensity, \angrmd \vec{x} \, ) \muX \wavearray. 
\end{align}
\end{subequations}

[Thm summa of arXiv:2609.03033, 'An Overview of Einstein $4$-Manifolds'] Let $M$ be a compact oriented $4$-manifold with $b_+\geq 2$. 
Then any metric $g$ on $M$ satisfies the curvature estimates 
\begin{eqnarray}
\int_M s^2d\mu &\geq& 32\pi^2 \beta^2(M)\\
\int_M (s-\sqrt{6}|W_+|)^2d\mu &\geq& 72\pi^2 \beta^2(M)
\end{eqnarray}
where $s$ and $W_+$ respectively denote the scalar and Weyl curvatures of $g$. 
Moreover, if $M$ carries a non-zero monopole class, 
equality  occurs in either ((mocha of the paper)) or ((java of the paper))   
iff $g$ is K\"ahler-Einstein, with negative Einstein constant. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm summa of arXiv:2609.03033

body:
[Corollary 33 of arXiv:2609.03962, '$L^p$ isomorphisms for the fractional Laplacian on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their application'] Let $0<t\le\sigma<2$ and $p\in(1,\infty)$. For
    $T\in\Lambda^{t-\sigma,p}(\R^n)$ with
    $T\perp\mathcal P_{[\sigma-t-n/p']}$, define
    \[
      \big\langle(-\triangle)^{\tfrac{t}{2}}T,\,w\big\rangle
      :=\big\langle T,\,(-\triangle)^{\tfrac{t}{2}}w\big\rangle,
      \qquad w\in\Lambda^{\sigma,p'}(\R^n),
    \]
    the right-hand side being unambiguous because
    $(-\triangle)^{\frac{t}{2}}w$ is defined modulo
    $\mathcal P_{[\sigma-t-n/p']}$ (Proposition~\ref{scale_isom} with
    $(s,p)$ replaced by $(\sigma,p')$) and $T$ annihilates this space.
    Then
    \[
      (-\triangle)^{\tfrac{t}{2}}:\
      \Lambda^{t-\sigma,p}(\R^n)\perp\mathcal P_{[\sigma-t-n/p']}
      \longrightarrow
      \Lambda^{-\sigma,p}(\R^n)\perp\mathcal P_{[\sigma-n/p']}
    \]
    is an isomorphism, reducing to Theorem~\ref{dual_isom} when $t=\sigma$,
    and
    \begin{equation}
      (-\triangle)^{\tfrac{t}{2}}\circ(-\triangle)^{\tfrac{\sigma-t}{2}}
      =(-\triangle)^{\tfrac{\sigma}{2}}
      \qquad\text{on }L^p(\R^n),
    \end{equation}
    where $(-\triangle)^{\frac{\sigma-t}{2}}$ and
    $(-\triangle)^{\frac{\sigma}{2}}$ are the operators of
    Theorem~\ref{dual_isom} at orders $\sigma-t$ and $\sigma$.

body:
[Proposition 15 of arXiv:2604.07207, 'Mixing times of step-reinforced random walks'] Assume that $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $L \geq 120$. There exist positive constants $C_1=C_1(\alpha)$, $C_2=C_2(\alpha)$ and $H_0=H_0(\alpha)$ such that if $n\geq H_0 L^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}$, then for any $k= 1,2,\dots, \lfloor L/40 \rfloor$, one has
$$
\PP\left(  \left|\left\{1\leq j \leq n: \frac{L}{96k} \leq |\CalC_{j,n}|<\frac{L}{2k}\right\}\right| \leq \frac{  C_2 k^{\frac{1}{\alpha}} n}{L^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}} \right)  \leq 7\exp\left(- \frac{ C_1  k^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}n}{L^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}}\right).
$$
In the case $\alpha=1/2$, if $L/\sqrt{\log L} \geq 120$, then for any $n\geq  H_0 L^{2}/\log L$ and any integer $k \in [\sqrt{\log L}, \lfloor L/40 \rfloor]$, one has,  
$$
\PP\left(  \left|\left\{1\leq j \leq n: \frac{L}{96k} \leq |\CalC_{j,n}|<\frac{L}{k}\right\}\right| \leq \frac{  C_2 k^{2} n}{4 L^{2}} \right)  \leq 7\exp\left(- \frac{ C_1  k^{2}n}{4 L^{2}}\right).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 15 of arXiv:2604.07207

[Theorem Wallis 3 of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The polynomial integrals over the unit sphere $S^{N-1}_\mathbb R\subset\mathbb R^N$, with respect to the uniform mass $1$ measure, are given by the formula
$$\int_{S^{N-1}_\mathbb R}x_1^{k_1}\ldots x_N^{k_N}\,dx=\frac{(N-1)!!k_1!!\ldots k_N!!}{(N+\Sigma k_i-1)!!}$$
valid when all exponents $k_i$ are even. If an exponent is odd, the integral vanishes.
title: Wallis 3

\[
\sigma_0:= \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\xi_0^2] }<\infty.
\]
Define
$
M_n(t)
:=
\frac1{\sqrt n}
\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor nt\rfloor}\xi_k,$
 $t\in[0,1].$
Then,
$
M_n
\Rightarrow
\sigma_0 W$
in $\mathbf{D}([0,1])$,

[Definition def:back-transition of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$, a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, and a positive integer~$j_0$. Let $\tau_0$ be a non-negative integer. Let $\Psi_0$ be the  initialising high-level state with $\tau^{\Psi_0} = \tau_0$ and $j^{\Psi_0} = j_0$. 
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be the $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule from Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-rule of the paper).
Let $V$ be a volume process from $\Psi_0$ with transition rule $\mathrm{hls}$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$. 
For any $t>\tau_0$ 
the high-level state transition 
given by 
$\Psi(t) 
= \mathrm{hls}(\Psi(t-1), {\overline{b}}^{Y_{t-1}}_{[j^{\Psi(t-1)}]}(t), t)$ is a \emph{back transition} if 
$\textup{type}^{\Psi(t)} = \textup{refilling}$ and
one of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\textup{type}^{\Psi(t-1)} = \textup{refilling}$, and the transition is via (R(item:R5 of the paper))(i); or
\item $\textup{type}^{\Psi(t-1)} = \textup{stabilising}$, and the transition is via (R(item:R2 of the paper))(ii) or (R(item:R6 of the paper))(i).
\end{itemize}
title: Definition def:back-transition of arXiv:2602.21315

body:
[Definition of arXiv:2608.07042, 'Limit Points of Reflow with Minibatch Optimal Transport'] We call a set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d$ $N$-cyclically monotone for $N\geq 2$ if it holds for all $(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\in A$ and
$\tau\in\Sigma_N$ that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^N \|x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}\|^2\leq \sum_{i=1}^N \|x^{(i)}-y^{(\tau(i))}\|^2.
$$
Similarly, we call a transport plan $\gamma\in \mathcal P_2(\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d)$ $N$-cyclically monotone
if $\mathrm{supp}(\gamma)$ is $N$-cyclically monotone.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.07042, 'Limit Points of Reflow with Minibatch Optimal Transport'

[Proposition prop:mode of arXiv:2607.19844, 'Binomial probabilities at a fixed distance from the mode:\\ size-biasing and the complete '] The upper mode of $\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)$ is
	\[
		\lfloor(N+1)p\rfloor=\nu+\lfloor p-h\rfloor
		=\begin{cases}\nu, & h\le p,\\[2pt] \nu-1, & h>p,\end{cases}
	\]
	that is, $r_{\mathrm{mode}}=0$ if $h\le p$ and $r_{\mathrm{mode}}=-1$ if $h>p$.
	When $h=p$ (equivalently $(N+1)p\in\mathbb Z$), the lower adjacent point $\nu-1$ is also a mode.

[Definition 12 (Quantum triangles with  {possibly} thin vertices) of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] Fix $W_1, W_2, W_3>0$. Let $I:=\{i\in\{1,2,3\}:W_i<\frac{\gamma^2}{2}\}$. Let $\tilde W_i = W_i$ if $i \not \in I$ and $\tilde W_i = \gamma^2 - W_i$ if $i \in I$. Sample $(S_0, (S_i)_{i \in I})$ from 
 \[\QT(\tilde W_1, \tilde W_2, \tilde W_3) \times \prod_{i\in I } (1-\frac{2W_i}{\gamma^2}) \Md_2(W_i).  \]
 Embed $S_0$ as $(\tilde D, \phi, \tilde a_1, \tilde a_2, \tilde a_3)$, for each $i \not \in I$ let $a_i = \tilde a_i$, and for each $i \in I$ embed $S_i$ as $(\tilde D_i, \phi, \tilde a_i, a_i)$ in such a way that the $\tilde D_i$ are disjoint and $\tilde D_i \cap \tilde D = \tilde a_i$. Let $D = \tilde D \cup \bigcup_{i \in I} \tilde D_i$ and let $\QT(W_1, W_2, W_3)$ be the law of $(D, \phi, a_1, a_2, a_3)/{\sim_\gamma}$.
title: Quantum triangles with  {possibly} thin vertices

Given values of the first two moments of the exit time at some unknown point $(x,y)$ in $\mathcal T$, one can detect the location $(x,y)$ up to symmetry. Equivalently, given the mean exit time and the variance of the exit time at some unknown point $(x,y)$ in $\mathcal T$, one can detect the location $(x,y)$ up to symmetry. ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try a direct cluster-expansion (Mayer-type) argument for the susceptibility at fixed p (2d) in the d -> infinity limit. Result: At p = lambda/(2d) the expected cluster size chi(p) has, for fixed lambda < 1, a convergent expansion as d -> infinity in powers of 1/d obtained by comparing the cluster to a branching process with Poisson(lambda) offspring and counting cycles: the first correction is the non-backtracking one: an exploration with s - 1 = 2d - 1 new neighbours per vertex has critical point 1/(s-1) = s^-1 + s^-2 + s^-3 + ..., which already gives a_1 = a_2 = 1 with s = 2d; the cycles of Z^d first change the expansion at order s^-3, where the 4-cycles move the coefficient from 1 to the known 7/2. This direct route reproduces a_1, a_2 by hand; a_3 = 7/2 is the first coefficient the cycles change, and getting it requires the 4-cycle corrections together with the self-avoidance of the exploration; I did not complete it. Existence of the expansion to all orders without the lace expansion would need a general theorem that the non-backtracking cycle corrections form an asymptotic series, which is a version of the lace expansion in disguise (the lace expansion IS the systematic bookkeeping of these corrections); a Mayer-type expansion at fixed lambda < 1 converges for the subcritical susceptibility, and p_c is then the divergence point of the series in lambda, whose location in powers of 1/d is obtained by inverting the series, which is a purely algebraic step if the expansion of chi is known to all orders with uniform error terms. So: an alternative derivation exists in principle via the convergent subcritical cluster expansion plus inversion, but the uniformity of the subcritical expansion up to lambda near 1 is exactly the difficult point. Computing a_4 by hand would require the next order of cycle corrections; not done. Obstruction: Uniformity of the subcritical cluster expansion up to the critical point; a_4 requires third-order cycle corrections.

Let $D$ be a long virtual knot diagram. 
For each classical crossing $c$ of $D$, either one of  ``we reach $c$ along overarc first" or ``we reach $c$ along underarc first" holds. 
The set of crossings satisfying the former is denoted by EO, {\it early overarc}, and that of crossings satisfying the latter is denoted by EU, {\it earky underarc}.

[Lemma lem:hill-scc of arXiv:2608.08375, 'Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: ge'] Under the conditions stated previously, if $i \in \overline{Z}$, then $i \leadsto_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$, so that $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$ has one terminal SCC, which must include $u$.

\proof If $i = u$, then, by definition, $i \leadsto_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$. If $i \not= u$, then $i \leadsto_G z$ for some $z \in Z$. By Definition~(def:hill of the paper).2 and 3, the last edge on any path from $i$ to $z$ in $G$ is rerouted to $u$ in $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$, so that $i \leadsto_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$, as claimed. The final assertion follows in consequence. \hfill \qed (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem AnalyticStraightLine of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $\gamma:\left[0,K\right]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$
be a continuous BV path with unit speed parametrisation. Let $s$ be a point at which
$\gamma$ is differentiable. Let $T\in(s,K]$ be chosen such that \[
\big|\gamma_{t}-\gamma_{s}-\gamma'_{s}(t-s)\big|\leqslant\frac{1}{6}(t-s),\ \Big|\Big|\frac{\gamma_{t}-\gamma_{s}}{t-s}\Big|-1\Big|\leqslant\frac{1}{6}
\]for all $t\in(s,T]$ and
\[
\left|\gamma_{t}-\gamma_{s}\right|<\left|\gamma_{T}-\gamma_{s}\right|
\]for all $t\in(s,T)$. Suppose that $\log S\left(\gamma\right)$ has infinite R.O.C. on
the interval $\left[s,T\right]$. Then the following two statements hold true.

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (i) One has
\[
\eta\left(\tilde{\gamma},\left(x,y\right)\right)=0
\]for all $\left(x,y\right)\in\left(0,1\right)\times\mathbb{R}\backslash\tilde{\gamma}\left[s,T\right]$. Here $\tilde{\gamma}\triangleq\gamma|_{[s,T]}\sqcup(\gamma_{s}-\gamma_{T}).$

\vspace{2mm}\noindent (ii) Let $L$ be the line segment joining $\gamma_{s}$ to $\gamma_{T}$ (also parametrised on $[s,T]$).
Then for any smooth one-form $\Phi(x,y)=f(x,y)dx+g(x,y)dy$, one has 
\[
\int_{s}^{T}\Phi\left(d\gamma_{v}\right)=\int_{s}^{T}\Phi\left(dL_{v}\right).
\]

[Theorem theorem1 of arXiv:2607.01463, 'Two Multi--Draw Coupon Collector models with different retention rules'] Consider the  $d$ coupon collector's problem (d--CCP), where in each run we keep \textbf{all} the new observed coupons. Let $T_{N,d}$ be the number of trials until all $N$ different types of coupons, which are uniformly distributed, are collected (at least once). Then,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb {E}\left[T_{N,d}\right]=\binom{N}{d} \sum_{k=1}^{N}\left(-1\right)^{k+1}\binom{N}{k}\Bigg(\binom{N}{d}-\binom{N-k}{d}\Bigg)^{-1}.

\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Express the escape probability through the branching-process representation for the one-cookie deterministic case. Result: In the deterministic environment with one cookie of strength p at each site (M = 1, delta = 2p - 1... transient iff delta > 1 which needs more than one cookie; take M = 2 cookies of strength p each, delta = 2(2p - 1) > 1 iff p > 3/4). The event of never returning to 0 after the first step: the walk must never come back, which in the branching-process picture (right excursions counted by the number of down-crossings of each edge) means the branching process with migration started from the edge (0,1) never produces a down-crossing of (0,1) into 0... the escape probability equals the probability that the total number of down-crossings of the edge (0,1) is zero, which is P(the branching process with migration started at 1 individual at level 1 has zero descendants at level 0) - not directly a standard extinction probability but a hitting probability of the time-reversed process. For the source's example [Zer05, Th. 18] the closed form exists; for general bounded stacks the escape probability is the solution of a finite-dimensional fixed-point equation obtained by conditioning on the first cookie stack at sites 1, 2, ...: define q_k = P(never return to 0 | walk currently at k, all cookies at sites >= k intact, cookies at sites < k in their post-visit states); the states of the sites already visited matter only through the remaining cookie counts, which for M bounded is a finite vector, and the walk's returns to 0 require descending through all visited sites; the escape probability then equals the probability of survival of a Markov chain on finite cookie-count vectors, computable numerically for given (M, p) but with no closed form in general. Recorded: reduction to a finite-state escape problem; closed form only in special cases. Obstruction: No closed form beyond special cases; the reduction gives a numerical procedure only.

[Lemma lem-expinteraction of arXiv:2604.14318, '\large The free energy of the interacting Bose gas:\\\medskip a variational description \\'] Suppose that the interaction potential $v$ satisfies Assumption (V). Recall that $W=W_R=[-R,R]^d$ and $W'=W_{R+M}\setminus W_R$. For any $M\in(0,\infty)$, there is a constant $C\in(0,\infty)$ (only depending on $d$, $\beta$, $v$ and $M$) such that, for any $R\in(0,\infty)$, and for any $ y, y_1,y_2\in W',x, x_1,x_2\in (W')^{\rm c}$,
\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbb{E}_{y,x}^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({W'}})}}}\Big[\sum_{j_1,j_2=1}^{\ell(B)}\1_{\{j_1\not= j_2\}}V(B_{j_1},B_{j_2})\Big]
&\leq& C |y-x|,\\
\mathbb{E}_{y_1,x_1}^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({W'}})}}}\otimes \mathbb{E}_{y_2,x_2}^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({W'}})}}}\Big[\sum_{j_1=1}^{\ell(B^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({1}})}}})}\sum_{j_2=1}^{\ell(B^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({2}})}}})}V(B^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({1}})}}}_{j_1},B^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({2}})}}}_{j_2})\Big]
&\leq& C \Big(\big|[\underline y_1,\underline x_1]\cap [\underline x_2,\underline y_2]\big|+1\Big),\\
\mathbb{E}_{y,x}^{{{\scriptscriptstyle{({W'}})}}}\Big[\sum_{j_1=1}^{\ell(B)} V(B_{j_1},f)\Big]
&\leq& C g({\operatorname {dist}}(K_f,[y,x])),\qquad  f\in {\mathcal C }(W),
\end{eqnarray}
where $g$ is a function with $\lim_{r\to\infty}g(r)=0$, and we wrote $K_f$ for the $C_v$-neighbourhood of $ \{f(t)\colon t\in [0,\beta]\}$, where $C_v={\operatorname {supp}}\sup v$.

Source-derived ReLU negative-margin corollary, not asserted novel: there are universal K,C,W0 such that for w>=W0, n>=w/4, m>=w, and each fixed v in R^n with ||v||=sqrt(n), a standard independent Gaussian one-hidden-layer ReLU network H with hidden variance 1/n and output variance 1/m satisfies sign(H(v))*H(v-sign(H(v))*K*sqrt(log(w))*grad H(v))<=-1 with probability >=1-C*w^(-1/4). The coefficient is deterministic given w. Zero output is excluded as a failure event of probability 2^(-m).

A two-layer output margin from Montanari-Wu

Let H:R^n->R be a standard random one-hidden-layer ReLU network with hidden width m, hidden entries N(0,1/n), and output entries N(0,1/m). Let v be any fixed vector of norm sqrt(n). Write tau=sign(H(v)), with an arbitrary convention at zero. There are universal K,W1 such that for every w>=W1, n>=w/4, m>=w, the deterministic coefficient

    S=K sqrt(log w)

satisfies

    tau H(v-tau S grad H(v)) <= -1                         (M)

except on probability C w^(-1/4). This bound is uniform in the fixed direction of v and in n,m in the displayed range. It is pointwise in v, not a simultaneous all-input result.

Here is the derivation from the source estimates, rather than an inference from sign reversal. Montanari-Wu arXiv:2203.17209v2, Lemma 4.2 and Eqs.(19)-(25), PDF pp.10-12, give, for eta=1 and eta_1,eta_2>=1, an event on which

    |H(v-tau S grad H(v))-H(v)+tau S Q(mu,beta,gamma)|
       <=1+2S eta_2/sqrt(n),                              (2.1)

where

    Q(mu,beta,gamma)
      = E[1_(G>0) 1_((1-mu)G-beta Z 1_(G>0)-gamma U>0)],

for independent standard normal G,Z,U, and |mu|<=S eta_1/n. A conservative parameter-box radius, valid for either tau, is

    Delta = S eta_1/n + 2S eta_2/sqrt(nm)
                    + S/sqrt(m)+C S/sqrt(n).

The complement of this event has probability at most

    C[eta_1^(-2)+exp(-c eta_2)+exp(-cn)+m^(-1)+Delta].       (2.2)

This is Eq.(25) and its preceding probability bound, with the harmless larger box radius Delta replacing the maximum in Eq.(21). In particular the signed tau term in that equation is bounded in absolute value here; there is no assumption that tau is positive.

Choose eta_1=w^(1/8), eta_2=K2 log w with K2 sufficiently large. For n>=w/4 and large w, |mu|<1/2. Conditional on G>0, (1-mu)G is strictly positive and beta Z+gamma U is centered Gaussian (possibly zero). Its probability of being smaller than this positive threshold is at least 1/2. Consequently

    Q(mu,beta,gamma)>=1/4.                                (2.3)

This estimate is uniform in beta,gamma; no smallness or independence of the random parameters is asserted. It is an inequality for the deterministic expectation evaluated at their realized values.

With S=K sqrt(log w),

    Delta <= C sqrt(log w) [w^(-7/8)+(log w)/w+w^(-1/2)]
          <= C w^(-1/4)                                  (2.4)

for sufficiently large w. Lemma 4.4, PDF p.12, additionally gives |H(v)|<=M sqrt(log w), except on probability C w^(-1/4), for a universal M; increase M to make the Gaussian tail exponent at least 1/4. The exponential-in-m term is smaller. All constants are independent of the fixed input direction and of m.

For large w, 2 eta_2/sqrt(n)<=1/16. Combining (2.1)-(2.4) gives

    tau H(v-tau S grad H(v))
      <= M sqrt(log w)-S/4+1+S/16
      <= -1

after fixing K sufficiently large. This proves the margin assertion (M) from the source estimates. The zero-output event has probability 2^(-m): either every hidden preactivation is negative, or a nondegenerate Gaussian output equals zero, the latter having probability zero. It may be excluded explicitly and absorbed into the stated failure probability.

Its frozen overlap potential has a locally attracting latitude -a, unstable latitude -s, and exact positive barrier (1-p)BJ(a-s)^3/(d-1), with J=(d-1)(1+a^3)-3a(1-a^2), s=(1-a^2)/J, D=aJ+1-a^2, A=3D/(3D+2d(1-a^2)), B=1-A. B/A tends to zero as a tends to1. This gives neither uniform-initialization reachability nor a positive-temperature MFLD lower bound. [Lemma 3 of arXiv:2607.22374, 'Asymptotic properties of the heat equation driven by stochastic measure'] (Lemma 2.8~\cite{radbook})
Let $Z$ be an arbitrary set, and the function $q(z,x):
Z\times [j, j+1]\to\rr$ be such that all paths $q(z,\cdot)$ are continuous on $[j,j+1]$, $\aaa\subset(j,j+1]$ be a Borel set. Denote
\[
q_n(z,x)=\sum_{1\le k\le 2^n}q(z,{d}_{(k-1)n}^{(j)}){\bf 1}_{\Delta_{kn}^{(j)}}(x).
\]
Then the random function
\[
\eta(z)=\int_{\aaa}q(z, x)\,d\mu(x),\ z\in Z,
\]
has a version
\begin{equation}\begin{split}
\widetilde{\eta}(z)  = \int_{\aaa}q_0(z,x)\,d\mu(x)
+\sum_{n\ge 1}\Bigl(\int_{\aaa}q_n(z,x)\,d\mu(x)-\int_{\aaa}q_{n-1}(z,x)\,d\mu(x)\Bigr)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
such that for all $\beta>0$, $\omega\in\Omega$, $z\in Z$
\begin{equation} \begin{split}
|\widetilde{\eta}(z)| \le  |q(z,j)\mu(\aaa)|\\
  + \Bigl\{\sum_{n\ge 1}2^{n\beta}
\sum_{1\le k\le 2^{n}}|q(z,d_{kn}^{(j)})-q(z,d_{(k-1)n}^{(j)})|^2\Bigr\}^{1/2}\\
\times\Bigl\{\sum_{n\ge 1}2^{-n\beta}\sum_{1\le k\le 2^{n}}|\mu(\Delta_{kn}^{(j)}\cap\aaa)|^2\Bigr\}^{1/2}.
\end{split}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop alphgrndstateprop of arXiv:2411.00629, '\Large Transformation of Stochastic Recursions and Critical Phenomena in the Analysis of t'] Let $\alpha>1$. Consider the stochastic Picard ground state iterations $X_n(t)$ (equation X_n-eq of the paper) with constant 
ground states $X_0(t)\equiv \delta >0$. Denote $N_t=|\partial V(t)|$ as before.  Then, 
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $u_0\in[0,1]$ then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For $\delta\in(0,1)$, 
$$X_n\to\underline{X}=\begin{cases}
0 \ &\ \text{if}\ S<t\\
u_0^{N_t}, \ &\ \text{if}\ S\ge t.\end{cases}$$
In particular, the minimal solution $u(t) = \underline{u}(t)={\mathbb{E}}(\underline{X})$ is 
well-defined and $\underline{u}(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.
\item[(ii)] For $\delta=1$, $$X_n\to\overline{X}=\begin{cases}
1 \ &\ \text{if}\ L<t\\
u_0^{N_t}, \ &\ \text{if}\ L\ge t.\end{cases}$$
In particular, $u(t) = \overline{u}(t)={\mathbb{E}}(\overline{X})$ is well-defined and $\overline{u}(t)\to1$ as $t\to\infty$ 
\item[(iii)] For $\delta >1$, the limit 
$$X_\infty(t) = \lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(t) = \begin{cases}
\infty \ &\ \text{if}\ S<t\\
u_0^{N_t}, \ &\ \text{if}\ S\ge t.\end{cases}$$
In particular,  ${\mathbb{E}}(X_\infty(t))=\infty$ for all $t>0$ 
\end{enumerate}
\item Suppose that $u_0>1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For $\delta\in [0,1)$,
\[X_n\to\overline{X}=\begin{cases}
0 ,\ &\ \text{if}\ S<t\\
u_0^{N_t}, \ &\ \text{if}\ S\ge t.\end{cases}\]
In particular, for all $t>0$
$$\underline{u}(t) ={\mathbb{E}}(\underline{X}(t))
\ \begin{cases} <\infty, \ &\ \text{if}\ u_0<(2\alpha-1)/4,\\
                         =\infty, \ & \text{in finite time if}\  u_0>2\alpha-1,\\
                         \text{unknown} & \text{in other cases.}
                        \end{cases}
      $$
 If there is a locally integrable function $g$ such that $X_n\le g$ for all $n$, then
  $\underline{u}(t)={\mathbb{E}}\underline{X}(t)<\infty$.
\item[(ii)] For $\delta =1$, 
$$X_n(t)\to\overline{X}(t) =\begin{cases}
\infty & \text{on} \ [N_t=\infty]\\
u_0^{N_t} & \text{on} \ [N_t<\infty].
\end{cases}$$
In particular, if $\alpha\in(1,2)$, then $\mathbb{E}(\overline{X}(t)) = \infty$, and if $\alpha>2$ then 
$\overline{X}(t)\in\mathbb{R}$ is well-defined for all $t>0$, while
\[
\overline{u}(t) ={\mathbb{E}}(\overline{X}(t))
\ \begin{cases} <\infty, \ &\ \text{if}\ u_0<(2\alpha-1)/4-(6\alpha^2-15\alpha+4)/4(\alpha-1)(2\alpha-1),\\
                         =\infty, \ & \text{in finite time if}\  u_0>2\alpha-1\ \text{or}\ \alpha\in(0,2),\\
                         \text{unknown} & \text{in other cases}.
                        \end{cases}
\]
\item[(iii)] For $\delta>1$, 
$$X_n\to{X}_{\infty}=\begin{cases}
\infty \ &\ \text{if}\ S<t\\
u_0^{N_t} \ &\ \text{if}\  S\ge t.\end{cases}$$
$u(t) ={\mathbb{E}}({X}_\infty(t)) = \infty$ for all $t>0$.
\end{enumerate} 
\end{enumerate}

body: [Lem 2 (The limit of a martingale partition) of arXiv:2604.12853, 'Coupling Markov Chains \\with a Common Image Chain'] Let $I$ be a countable set and for each $i \in I$ let $(U_t^{(i)})_{t \ge 0}$ be a non-negative martingale, all with respect to the same filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ on a common probability space. Suppose that $ \sum_{i \in I} U^{(i)}_t   \le 1$ a.s. for every $t \ge 0$. Then almost surely \[\sum_{i \in I} \lim_{t \to \infty} U^{(i)}_t = \lim_{t \to \infty} \sum_{i \in I} U_t^{(i)}.\]

[Theorem thm:decompostion for all invariant upps of arXiv:2411.02030, 'Finite ergodic components for upper probabilities'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},V,T)$ be an UPPS, where $T$ is invertible.   Suppose that  $\mathcal{ M}^e(T)\cap\operatorname{core}(V)=\{Q_1,\ldots,Q_n\}$. Then for any $P\in\mathcal{ M}(T)\cap\operatorname{core}(V)$, there exist $0\le \alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{n+1}\le 1$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\alpha_i=1$ and $Q_{n+1}\in \mathcal{ M}(T)\cap\operatorname{core}(V)$, which is singular with respect to all $Q_i$, $i=1,2,\ldots,n$ such that 
	\[P=\alpha_1Q_1+\ldots+\alpha_nQ_n+\alpha_{n+1}Q_{n+1}.\]
	Moreover, the decomposition is unique.

[Proposition 2 (Classical scale in anchored local form) of arXiv:2606.07931, 'Pointwise Complexity for Gaussian Fields:\\Upper Envelopes, Algorithmic Lower Bounds, and '] There exist absolute constants \(0<c<C<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
c\,\Bigl(R_\ast+\inf_{\mu\in\Delta(T)}\Phi_{\mu,\ast}\Bigr)
\le
\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T}X_x
\le
C\,\Bigl(R_\ast+\inf_{\mu\in\Delta(T)}\Phi_{\mu,\ast}\Bigr).
\end{equation}
Moreover, since the process is centered and anchored,
\[
\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T}|X_x|
\asymp
\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T}X_x.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}
\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T}|X_x|
\asymp
R_\ast+\inf_{\mu\in\Delta(T)}\Phi_{\mu,\ast}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Classical scale in anchored local form

body:
[campaign status: unreviewed - author-checked against the source's exact wording; verification unreviewed] For a transversal Volterra quadratic stochastic operator the ITINERARY of a trajectory is the sequence of fixed-point neighbourhoods it visits; Rozikov (2009, p. 4) asks whether some trajectory has a periodic itinerary. CLAIM, in two halves. (i) YES at m = 3, by an example already in the literature: for the cyclic Volterra operator with a = b = c = 1, matrix A = [[0,1,-1],[-1,0,1],[1,-1,0]], whose leading 2x2 minor is 1 so the operator is transversal and whose fixed-point set - the three vertices and the centre - is finite, the itinerary of every non-fixed interior point is periodic, 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> ..., with sojourns 12, 51, 1073, ... growing geometrically by the heteroclinic-cycle mechanism of Ganikhodzhaev and Zanin (2004). (ii) NO in general: at m = 4, Ganikhodjaev and Zanin (arXiv:1205.3841, Theorem 5) show the trajectory moves along the routes 1-4-3-2-1, 1-4-2-1 or 1-4-3-1, and a simulated cyclic-type m = 4 map produces the MIXED itinerary 1,4,3,2,1,4,2,1 - so itineraries need not be periodic. THE SHARP OPEN QUESTION, which is what the source presumably meant: is every itinerary eventually periodic, or which matrices A force it? The 2012 route analysis is the starting point. A periodic ITINERARY is a symbol sequence, not a periodic ORBIT: periodic orbits are typically absent while periodic itineraries need not be.
transversal Volterra quadratic stochastic operator with a finite fixed-point set
the object asked for is a periodic ITINERARY, a symbol sequence, not a periodic orbit
m = 3 for the affirmative half; m = 4 for the negative half

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $a, \eta>0$, $k,d\in\mathbb N$, and $d\ge2$. There exists
a constant $C:=C(a,\eta,k,d)>0$ such that, for every $n\in\mathbb N$, every
log-concave measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^n$, and every polynomial mapping
$
f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in\mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)
$
satisfying
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f_j)\ge a
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge \eta,
\]
one has
\[
\mu(f\in A)
\le
C\bigl(\lambda_k(A)\bigr)^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+1}}
\]
for every Borel set $A\subset\mathbb R^k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.01516

body:
[Lem 89 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ and $\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$ as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip} and \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym}, and the symmetrization operation $\sym$ as defined by \eqref{e:symmetrize.set.of.measures}, we have \[\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha) = \sym(\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha))\,.\]
Similarly, for $\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0)$ and $\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0)$ as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.0.sym} and \eqref{e:sM.Lip.0.chaos}, we have
	\[\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0)
	=\sym(\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0))\,.\]

\begin{proof}
   By the definitions of these sets, we have
    \[
        \sym(\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha))
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip}}{=} 
        \sym\bigg(
            \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0}
            \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)
        \bigg)
        \subseteq 
        \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0}
        \sym\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym}}{=} \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)\,.
    \]
Similarly, we have
	\begin{align*}
	&\sym(\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0))
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip.0.chaos}}{=}\sym\bigg(

	&\qquad\subseteq

[Proposition 22 (Cross-regularity) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Assume \hyperref[ass:PJG]{\textup{(A1)}}--\hyperref[ass:D]{\textup{(A4)}}. There exist a constant \(C_{\mathrm{cross}}>0\) and a measurable function
\(b:\R^d\to[0,\infty)\) such that, for all \(x,y\in\R^d\) and all \(t\in(0,\lambda]\),
\[
  \KL\!\bigl(\delta_x \widehat P \,\big\|\, \delta_y P_t\bigr)
  \;\le\;
  \frac{C_{\mathrm{cross}}}{1-e^{-K't}}\,\|x-y\|^2
  \;+\;
  b(x)^2,
\]
where
\[
  b(x)^2 \le C\,\lambda^2\bigl(1+\|x\|^{2\ell+2}\bigr).
\]
In particular, taking \(t=\lambda\), one may take
\[
  c'=\frac{C_{\mathrm{cross}}}{\lambda}.
\]

[Proposition eq:sparse-profile-net-bound of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:sharp-profile-energy}
Suppose that the random field satisfies \(({\rm PT})_p\).
Put
\[
 \pi_N(a):=
 \sup_{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1)}
 \mathbb P\{\left\lverth_N^J(x)\right\rvert\ge a\}.
\]
Put
\[
 \mathcal S_{N,k}
 =\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
       \abs{\operatorname{supp}x}\le k\},
 \qquad
 \Lambda_p=\frac{p^{p+1}}{p!}.
\]
For \(1\le k\le N\), \(a>0\), and
\(0<\delta<\Lambda_p^{-1}\),
\begin{align}
 &\mathbb P\left\{
 \sup_{x\in\mathcal S_{N,k}}\left\lverth_N^J(x)\right\rvert\ge a
 \right\}\notag\\
 &\qquad\le
 \binom Nk\left(1+\frac2\delta\right)^k
 \pi_N\bigl((1-\Lambda_p\delta)a\bigr).
 
\end{align}
Consequently, if \(1\le k_N\le N\), \(k_N=o(N)\), and
\(a_N\to a>0\), then
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb P\left\{
 \sup_{x\in\mathcal S_{N,k_N}}\left\lverth_N^J(x)\right\rvert
 \ge a_N\right\}
 \le-\frac{a^2}{2}.
\end{equation}
The same conclusions hold for the standard symmetric-coordinate model
whenever its field satisfies \(({\rm PT})_p\); the profile MGF and
orbit-coordinate joint bounds described above are sufficient.

	\[

	\le
	1+\varepsilon
	\]
	and
	\[
	\norm{Q_T}_\infty
	\le
	3\sqrt{\frac{\log(d/\eta)}{d}}.
	\]

body:
[Proposition geoprop of arXiv:2412.08334, 'Maker-Breaker on Galton-Watson trees'] The probability of Breaker winning on an instantly revealed GW-tree with offspring distribution 
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item $\xi\sim\mathrm{Geo}_{\mathbb{N}}(s)$, i.e.\ $p_k=s\,(1-s)^{k-1}$ for $k\geq 1$, equals
		\[p=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4s}}{2\,(1-s)}\quad\text{and}\quad \bar{p}=\frac{1-2s-\sqrt{1-4s}}{2\,(1-s)}=p-\frac{s}{1-s}\]
		respectively (depending on who starts the game) for parameter $s\in(0,\frac14]$. Further it holds $p=\bar{p}=1$, for $s\in(\frac14,1]$.
		\item $\xi\sim\mathrm{Geo}_{\mathbb{N}_0}(s)$, i.e.\ $p_k=s\,(1-s)^{k}$ for $k\geq 0$, equals
		\[p=\frac{1+s-\sqrt{(1-s)\,(1-5s)}}{2\,(1-s)}\text{  and  }\  \bar{p}=\frac{1-s-\sqrt{(1-s)\,(1-5s)}}{2\,(1-s)}=p-q\]
		respectively (depending on who starts the game) for parameter $s\in(0,\frac15]$. Further it holds $p=\bar{p}=1$, for $s\in(\frac15,1]$.
	\end{enumerate}

body:
[Thm 16 of arXiv:2605.23308, 'Convergence rate estimates for semigroups and heat kernels associated with resistance form'] For $\calX_n=(X_n,d^{X_n},\rho_{X_n},\mu_{X_n}),\;\calX=(X,d^X,\rho_X,\mu_X)\in\frK_{\bullet}(\tau)$,
the following conditions are equivalent to each other.
\begin{itemize}
  \item [$\mathrm{(i)}$]There exist a compact metric space $(M,d^M,\rho_M)$ and root-preserving isometric embeddings $f_n:X_n\to M,\;f:X\to M$
  such that $f_n(X_n)\to f(X)$ in the Hausdorff topology, and $\mu_{X_n}\circ f_n^{-1}\to \mu_{X}\circ f^{-1}$ weakly.  
  \item [$\mathrm{(ii)}$]There exist a compact metric space $(M,d^M)$ and isometric embeddings $f_n:X_n\to M,\;f:X\to M$
  such that $f_n(X_n)\to f(X)$ in the Hausdorff topology, $f_n(\rho_{X_n})\to f(\rho_X)$ in $M$,
  and $\mu_{X_n}\circ f_n^{-1}\to \mu_{X}\circ f^{-1}$ weakly.
  \item [$\mathrm{(iii)}$]$d^{\tau,\BL^{\kappa}}_{\frK_{\bullet}}(\calX_n,\calX)\to 0$
\end{itemize}
In particular, $d^{\tau,\BL^{\kappa}}_{\frK_{\bullet}}$ induces the rooted compact Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov topology.

[Definition of arXiv:2411.17104, 'Two-barriers-reflected BSDE with Rank-based Data'] A function $v(\cdot,\cdot) \in C([0,T]\times \Gamma^{n})$ is called a viscosity subsolution (respectively, supersolution) to ($(4 of the paper)$) on condition that it satisfies for any $ x\in \Gamma^{n}$
\[
g(x)\geq v(T,x)\;\;(respectively,\;g(x) \leq v(T,x)),
\]
and for any  $\varphi(\cdot,\cdot) \in  C^{1,2}_{b}([0,T] \times \Gamma^{n})$, whenever $(t,x)\in[0,T)\times \Gamma^{n}$ is a local maximum (respectively, minimum) of $v(\cdot,\cdot) - \varphi(\cdot,\cdot)$, we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\min\Big\{v(t,x)-L(t,x), \max\Big\{v(t,x)-U(t,x),\\
\qquad \qquad \qquad\quad\;\qquad-\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t}(t,x)-
\mathcal{L}\varphi(t,x)-G(t,x,v(t,x),\sigma \triangledown \varphi(t,x))  \Big\}\Big\} \leq 0,\;x \in \Pi^{n},\\
\min\left\{\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_{k+1}}(t,x)-\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_{k}}(t,x), \min\Big\{v(t,x)-L(t,x),\max\Big\{v(t,x)-U(t,x),\right.\\
\left.\left.\left.
\qquad \qquad  \qquad \quad  -\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t}(t,x)-\mathcal{L}\varphi(t,x)-G(t,x,v(t,x),\sigma \triangledown \varphi(t,x))  \right\}\right\} \right\} \leq 0,\; x \in F_{k},\;k=1,\cdots,n.
\end{array}\right.
\end{eqnarray*}
(respectively,
\begin{eqnarray*}
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\min\Big\{v(t,x)-L(t,x), \max\Big\{v(t,x)-U(t,x),\\
\qquad \qquad \qquad\quad\;\qquad-\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t}(t,x)-
\mathcal{L}\varphi(t,x)-G(t,x,v(t,x),\sigma \triangledown \varphi(t,x))  \Big\}\Big\}\geq 0,\; x \in \Pi^{n},\\
\max\Big\{\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_{k+1}}(t,x)-\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_{k}}(t,x), \min\Big\{v(t,x)-L(t,x), \max\Big\{v(t,x)-U(t,x),\\
\qquad \qquad \qquad\quad\;\qquad-\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t}(t,x)-
\mathcal{L}\varphi(t,x)-G(t,x,v(t,x),\sigma \triangledown \varphi(t,x))  \Big\}\Big\}\Big\} \geq 0,\;x \in F_{k},\;k=1,\cdots,n.)
\end{array}\right.
\end{eqnarray*}

In all, if a function $v(\cdot,\cdot)\in C([0,T]\times \Gamma^{n})$ is both a viscosity supersolution and subsolution, it is called a viscosity solution to ($(4 of the paper)$).

STATUS: proof (unaudited), own-work draft. Exact normal linear-stability classification of every finite fixed point of joint-head factored-attention GD at every eta>0: the stationary curve v=0,kq=p_bar has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers 1-eta lambda_+/- with lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2(k^2+q^2)))/2. One normal direction is always repelling; the other attracts exactly when k^2+q^2<(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2, is neutral at equality, and repels beyond. Every positive fixed step loses the attracting normal direction at sufficiently unbalanced factorizations.

# Target 1: exact normal stability of the factored GD stationary curve

Version 1, proof unaudited. This is a linearized stability classification;
it does not claim a nonlinear flip bifurcation or a full-space GD basin theorem.

Assume precisely the n-example factored model of claim 010:
0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0, logistic average loss of
v h_i(kq), h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), and simultaneous Euclidean GD
with any fixed eta>0. Let p_bar<0 be the unique mean root and define

 A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
 B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0.

All finite stationary points, equivalently all GD fixed points, form the
curve E={v=0,kq=p_bar}. At such a point write S=k^2+q^2>=2|p_bar|.
The GD Jacobian has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers

 mu_-=1-eta lambda_-, mu_+=1-eta lambda_+,
 lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2 S))/2.

Here lambda_-<0<lambda_+, hence mu_->1 everywhere: no point of E is
linearly attracting in all normal directions. The other normal direction is

* strictly attracting in the linearization when eta lambda_+<2;
* neutral with multiplier -1 when eta lambda_+=2;
* strictly repelling with multiplier less than -1 when eta lambda_+>2.

Let
 J_eta=(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2.

The first case is EXACTLY S<J_eta, the middle case exactly S=J_eta,
and the last exactly S>J_eta. Equivalently, with C=k^2-q^2,
S=sqrt(C^2+4p_bar^2): there is an attracting normal direction only if
J_eta>2|p_bar|, and then precisely at

 |C|<sqrt(J_eta^2-4p_bar^2).

Equality gives neutral normal points when J_eta>=2|p_bar|. If J_eta
is smaller than 2|p_bar|, every point is repelling in both normal directions.
In particular, for EVERY eta>0, sufficiently unbalanced factorizations on
E are normally repelling in both directions. There is no positive constant
step that preserves the flow's one attracting normal direction uniformly
along the entire stationary curve. This does NOT imply an open basin of
cycles or disprove a full-space almost-everywhere GD endpoint theorem.

## Proof

The fixed-point condition is gradient L=0, classified in proof 008.
Its loss Hessian at E is
 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].
The tangent vector (0,k,-q) is in its kernel. In the orthonormal basis
e_v=(1,0,0), e_s=(0,q,k)/sqrt(S) of the normal plane, the Hessian is
 [[A,-B sqrt(S)],[-B sqrt(S),0]].
The quadratic characteristic polynomial is lambda^2-A lambda-B^2 S,
which yields lambda_+/- and their signs. The GD Jacobian is I-eta Hessian,
proving the multipliers and their linear classifications.

For equivalence with J_eta, consider the polynomial
f(z)=z^2-Az-B^2 S, whose positive zero is lambda_+ and negative zero
lambda_-. Since 2/eta>0, lambda_+<2/eta is equivalent to
f(2/eta)>0, or S<J_eta; equality and the reverse inequality follow likewise.
This avoids squaring a potentially negative expression 4/eta-A.
Finally S^2=C^2+4p_bar^2 by algebra, and S is unbounded along E by
taking k->infinity, q=p_bar/k. All asserted threshold statements follow.

## Scope of the obstruction

The obstruction is to a PARTICULAR transfer from flow to GD: retaining
one attracting normal direction uniformly on every imbalance leaf at fixed
step. It is not an obstruction to every possible discrete-time proof.
The imbalance leaves themselves are not invariant under GD:
C_+=(1-eta^2 v^2 G^2)C. Both facts must be accounted for in further work.
Normal multipliers on the unit circle require separate nonlinear analysis;
no attracting two-cycle is claimed. Scalar genuine self-attention embeddings
of this family are supplied in claim 008.
Coupled n>=2 scalar h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), 0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0; logistic average loss; simultaneous Euclidean GD. A=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4, B=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2, mean h_i(p_bar)=0. Linear normal stability only.

[Lemm 8 of arXiv:2605.23292, 'Second-order Poincaré inequalities and localization on the Poisson space'] (closeness in $d_{BL}$ implies closeness of mixed moments, bounded case)
Let $X_1,...X_4,X_1',...,X_4'$ be random variables such that
\[
d_{BL}\big( (X_1,...,X_4),\ (X_1',...,X_4') \big) \leq \alpha,
\]
where $\alpha \geq 0$. 
Assume that there exists $L \in [1,\infty)$ such that $|X_i|,|X_i'|\leq L$ for all $i=1,...4$. Then for all non-negative integers $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$ with $q=p_1+p_2+p_3+p_4 > 0$ it is the case that
\[
| \E \Pi_{i=1}^4 X_i^{p_i} - \E \Pi_{i=1}^4 X_i'^{p_i}| \leq 2q L^q \alpha.
\]

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: the Hoelder exponent satisfies 0 < alpha < 1 strictly, and the Lebesgue exponent satisfies 1 < p < infinity strictly. The reason is that the second derivatives of the Newtonian potential are given by a singular integral operator, which is bounded on C^{0,alpha} and on L^p only in the open ranges. Failure at alpha = 0 (continuous right-hand side does not give a C^2 solution): in the plane put u(x) = (x_1^2 - x_2^2) (log(1/r))^{1/2} for 0 < r = |x| < 1/2, u(0) = 0. A computation with u = p g, p = r^2 cos(2 theta) harmonic and g = (log(1/r))^{1/2}, using Laplacian(p g) = 4 p g'/r + p (g'' + g'/r), gives Laplacian u = -cos(2 theta) ( 2 (log(1/r))^{-1/2} + (1/4)(log(1/r))^{-3/2} ), which extends continuously by 0 at the origin, while D_{11}u = 2(log(1/r))^{1/2} + o(1) blows up. Since u is C^1 and C^infinity off the origin, it solves Laplacian u = f distributionally on the ball with f continuous; no C^2 solution of Laplacian v = f exists near 0, because v - u would be harmonic hence smooth. (Consistently, this f is continuous but not Dini continuous, and Dini continuity is the correct substitute hypothesis.) Failure at alpha = 1: with q = x_1^3 - 3 x_1 x_2^2 and g = log(1/r), the function u = q g has Laplacian u = -6 q/r^2 = -6 r cos(3 theta), which is Lipschitz, while D_{111}u = 6 log(1/r) + O(1) is unbounded, so u is not in C^{2,1}. Failure at p = infinity: u = (x_1^2 - x_2^2) log(1/r) has Laplacian u = -4 cos(2 theta) in L^infinity while D_{11}u = 2 log(1/r) + O(1) is not bounded, so Laplacian u in L^infinity does not give u in W^{2,infinity} = C^{1,1}; the correct endpoint statement is Laplacian u in L^infinity implies D^2 u in BMO. Failure at p = 1: let f_k = rho_{1/k} be standard mollifiers and u_k = Gamma convolved with f_k, so Laplacian u_k = f_k with ||f_k||_{L^1} = 1 and ||u_k||_{L^1(B_2)} bounded; on B_1 minus the origin D_{12}u_k converges pointwise to D_{12}Gamma, whose size is comparable to |x|^{-n} and hence not integrable near 0, so by Fatou ||D^2 u_k||_{L^1(B_1)} tends to infinity. No estimate of the form ||D^2u||_{L^1} <= C(||Laplacian u||_{L^1} + ||u||_{L^1}) can hold; the correct endpoint statements are weak-L^1 bounds and the Hardy space result Laplacian u in H^1 implies D^2u in L^1. Practical consequence: from f merely continuous (or bounded) one gets u in W^{2,p}_loc for every finite p and u in C^{1,alpha}_loc for every alpha < 1, but not, in general, u in C^2 - the first example above is exactly the obstruction (for particular right-hand sides, a smooth f say, the solution is of course C^2).
title: Pitfall: Schauder and Calderon-Zygmund Estimates Fail at the Endpoints (C^0, L^1, L^infinity)

For n servers, Poisson jobs of rate lambda*n/k routing to uniform k-subsets, and k tagged arrival streams observed exactly on [0,T], let H count tagged servers hit per job and beta=(lambda*n/k)*P(H>=2). Their joint path total variation from independent rate-lambda Poisson streams is at least 1-exp(-beta*T). If k tends to infinity with k=o(sqrt(n)), beta~lambda*k^3/(2*n). At k/n^(1/3)->c>0, the liminf is at least 1-exp(-lambda*T*c^3/2). Conversely k=o(n^(1/3)) gives path TV tending to zero by the delete-and-restore coupling. This proves a path-coupling obstruction, not a necessary threshold for a stationary queue vector at a single time.

lambda,T fixed and positive
Exact continuous arrival paths
For the asymptotic formula: k tends to infinity and k=o(sqrt(n))

body: Let (mu_eps) be probability measures on a topological space X satisfying a large deviation principle with good rate function I as eps -> 0+, and let phi: X -> R be bounded and continuous. Varadhan's lemma states that the limit as eps -> 0 of eps times the log of the integral over X of exp(phi(x)/eps) mu_eps(dx) equals sup_{x in X} (phi(x) - I(x)). The boundedness hypothesis on phi can be relaxed to a mild exponential tail (moment) condition. This is a Laplace-type asymptotic for LDP-obeying measures, generalizing Laplace's method for integrals. Due to S. R. S. Varadhan.
title: Varadhan's lemma

[Defi Def:W-cont-map of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] Suppose $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are
   weighted polyhedra of the same type. 
   A \emph{W-continuous map} from $(X,\lambda)$ to 
   $(X',\lambda')$ is a continuous map $f: X\rightarrow X'$   which satisfies: for all $x\in X$,
   $$ \begin{cases}
   \lambda'(f(x)) \mid \lambda(x),  &  \text{if  $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are of ascending type}; \\
   \lambda(x) \mid \lambda'(f(x)),  &  \text{if  $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are of descending type}.
 \end{cases}  
   $$  
    We also denote such a map by $f: (X,\lambda)\rightarrow (X',\lambda')$ to indicate its W-continuity
    since the definition of $f$ depends on the type of the weighted polyhedra involved.
   Moreover, $f$ is called \emph{weight-preserving} if 
$\lambda'(f(x))=\lambda(x)$ for all $x\in X$.\vskip 0.1cm

We say that $(X,\lambda)$ is \emph{isomorphic} to $(X',\lambda')$ if there exists a weight-preserving homeomorphism from $(X,\lambda)$ to $(X',\lambda')$.
title: W-continuous map

Consider binary classifiers obtained by thresholding the scalar output of feedforward ReLU networks with at most W scalar parameters, each encoded using at most B bits, where W,B are positive integers. Use the finite graph-description convention in the proof of Theorem 6.1: all edge endpoints can be indexed among U<=W named neurons, so the architecture is encoded by specifying the two endpoint indices for every parameter. No additional uncharged choice of input-coordinate names is allowed. Then the number of distinct classifiers is at most 2^{O(W B + W log(W+1))}, and their VC dimension is O(W B + W log(W+1)). For a fixed architecture the simpler bound VCdim <= W B follows. The variable-architecture term is the cost of describing the graph, not extra numerical precision.

[Definition 14 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] Let $(T, o) \ino \overline{\bbT}^\bullet$. Let $\lambda \ino (0, \infty)$ and let $p_{T, \lambda} (\cdot, \cdot)$ be the transition probabilities of $\lambda$-RWs on $T$ as defined in (\ref{deflambRW}).  
The transition kernel on $\obbT^\bullet\! $ 
of the $\lambda$-biased RW is then defined for all $\overline{x}\!:= \! (T,x) \ino \obbT^\bullet\! $ by 
\begin{equation}
 
\overline{\mathtt p}_{\lambda} ( \overline{x}, d\overline{x}^\prime  ) = \sum_{y\in T} p_{T, \lambda } (x, y) \delta_{(T, y)} ( d\overline{x}^\prime) \, .
\end{equation}
We then denote by $P_{T,o}$ the law of the $\lambda$-biased RW
on $(\obbT^\bullet\! )^\bbN$ (that is 
the space of the $\obbT^\bullet \! $-valued sequences equipped with the product topology, which makes it Polish) starting at $(T,o)$. 
Note that $P_{T,o}$ depends on $\lambda$ although it does not appear in the notation. \cq
title: Definition 14 of arXiv:2605.02430

[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Fix $\kappa>1$, and suppose $n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d^2\to\alpha\in(0,\infty)$.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

			mI_d\preceq R\preceq MI_d,

[Theorem 41 of arXiv:2609.02785, 'Characterization of Stanley-Reisner varieties by their automorphism group'] Let $\Delta$ and $\Delta'$ be fully exposed simplicial complexes on $[n]$ and $[n']$. If there is an isomorphism of ind-groups
$$
\theta\colon\Aut(X_\Delta)\longrightarrow\Aut(X_{\Delta'}),
$$
then $n=n'$ and there is a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$ with $\sigma\cdot\Delta=\Delta'$. In particular $\Delta\cong\Delta'$ as abstract simplicial complexes and $X_\Delta\cong X_{\Delta'}$ as algebraic varieties.
