[Dfn 204 (spatial rerandomization for spherical perceptron) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We use the buckets from Definition~\ref{d:buckets} to
 define a new process $\vY\equiv\vY^{\RomI:\RomIII}$, as follows. First let $a(q_0)$ be sampled uniformly at random from $[M]$. Then, conditional on $a(q_0), \ldots, a(q_d)$, we let $a(q_{d+1})$ be sampled from the measure $\bP$ conditional on the bucket at time $q_d$, that is,
    \[a(q_{d+1})
    \sim \bP
    \bigg( a = \cdot \,\bigg|\, 
    a\in B(q_d,a(q_d)) \bigg)\,.
    \]
We then let $\vY(q_d)$ be the average of $\vX^\trunc$ over all the particles in the bucket containing $a(q_d)$, 
    \beq
    \vY(q_d)
    =
    \sum_{a\in B(q_d,a(q_d))}
    \frac{\vX^\trunc(q_d,a)}{|B(q_d,a(q_d))|}
    \,.
    \eeq
Informally, $\vY$ is the process $\vX^\trunc$ with ``spatial rerandomization at scale $\eta$.'' It is easy to check (by induction) that each $a(q_d)$ is marginally uniform on $[M]$, which implies that $\vX^\trunc(q_d)$ and $\vY(q_d)$ are within $W_{\infty}$ distance $O(\eta/\delta)$ for each fixed $d$.  Likewise, we define $\vY^\frozen\equiv\vY^{\frozen,\RomI:\RomIII}$ to be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^\frozen$ at scale $\eta$, with random indices $a^\frozen(q_d) \in[M^\frozen]$
and buckets $\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$.
title: spatial rerandomization for spherical perceptron

$\mathcal F:=\supp(y)$ is a laminar family of cuts. Then there are a
weighted tree $(Q_y,\ell_{Q_y})$ and a map
$\alpha:V(G)\to V(Q_y)$ such that
\begin{equation}
 d_{Q_y}(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))
 =\sum_{\substack{F\in\mathcal F\\F\text{ separates }u\text{ and }v}}y_F
 \qquad(u,v\in V(G)).
\end{equation}
In particular, $d_{Q_y}(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))\le1$ whenever $uv\in E(G)$.

[Theorem 1 ($\delta\downarrow0$ stability of hitting laws for phase-space balls) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Suppose Assumptions~\ref{ass:U} and~\ref{ass:controlled-coefficients} hold,
and adopt the \hyperref[setup:domains]{bounded-domain setup}.  Then, for the
forward and adjoint processes in \eqref{eq:sde-delta}, the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item
    As $\delta\downarrow0$, 
    \[
        h_\delta^*\to h^*
        \qquad\text{in }L^1(\calD,\pi^\eps).
    \]

    \item 
     As $\delta\downarrow0$, 
    \[
        h_\delta^*F_{\delta,M}\to h^*F_M
        \qquad\text{in }L^1(\calD,\pi^\eps),
    \]
    where $F_{\delta,M},F_{M}$ are defined in \eqref{eq:F-defs} for $M<\infty$.

    \item 
     As $\delta\downarrow0$, 
    \[
        \sup_{z\in\partial A}|g_{\delta,M}(z)-g_M(z)|\to0,
    \]
    where $g_{\delta,M},g_{M}$ are defined in \eqref{eq:gF-defs} for $M<\infty$.
    Moreover $g_M\in C(\partial A)$.

    \item Let
    $\sigma^\delta=\tau_A^\delta\wedge\tau_\calC^\delta$ and
    $\sigma=\tau_A\wedge\tau_\calC$.  For $\pi^\eps$-almost every
    $z\in\Omega$ and every $M<\infty$,
    \[
        \sigma^\delta\wedge M
        \Longrightarrow
        \sigma\wedge M
    \]
    under $\Pbb_z$ as $\delta\downarrow0$, and the first-hit labels satisfy
    \[
        \bfone_{\{\tau_A^\delta<\tau_\calC^\delta\}}
        \Longrightarrow
        \bfone_{\{\tau_A<\tau_\calC\}} .
    \]
    Under the explicit SDE coupling of Theorem~\ref{thm:delta-coupling}, these
    convergences hold in
    probability at every starting point for which the limiting first killed hit
    is a non-characteristic crossing with a unique first-hit boundary component.

    \item The limiting killed process satisfies
    \[
        \Pbb_z(\tau_\calC<\infty)=1
        \qquad\text{for every }z\in\calD\setminus B.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
The analogous statements obtained by replacing each forward hitting functional
with its adjoint counterpart also hold. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b2b41f4304f2608b70619356bc93292adcdb2f917baeb238b2cbbf024e2b339b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b2/b2b41f4304f2608b70619356bc93292adcdb2f917baeb238b2cbbf024e2b339b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e5ef2edc6a2a6f3d1c5d6d828a2d52998c13cb4090f1de47795cb241700acbaa","bundle_entry_key":"relu-compact-generator","bundle_id":"population.t244-relu-angle-localization-001","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:gaussian-relu-reciprocal-angle-compact-generator","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Compact reciprocal-angle generator with an explicit regularized kernel

Status: independently checked proof; reviewer PASS on the listed claim version. Target 1, kind moved. The drift and variance coefficients were already predicted in the dossier; the result here is a finite-moment regularization and bounded-test-function argument. No entrance theorem or full weak path limit is claimed.

## Statement

Fix 0<d<K<infinity. Uniformly for u in [d,K], put theta=1/(nu). Let a,g be independent standard Gaussian vectors in R^n, X=a_+, and Y=(cos(theta)a+sin(theta)g)_+. An explicit event G below has probability at least 1-C exp(-c n), uniformly in u. Define U'=1/(n angle(X,Y)) on G and U'=u off G. For every bounded C^3 function f on [0,infinity) with bounded derivatives through order three,

    n E[f(U')-f(u)] = (2u+1/(3 pi)) f'(u) + u^2 f''(u) + O_{d,K,f}(n^-1/2).

The same assertion for the exact angle transition, killed at extinction or angle zero and with any bounded value for f at the cemetery state, follows by changing the generator by at most 2n||f||_infinity C exp(-cn). This is local generator convergence, not a compact-containment or entrance assertion.

## 1. Good event and quantitative elementary bounds

Write A={i:a_i>0}, k=|A|, S=sum_A a_i^2, C0=sum_A a_i g_i, V=sum_A g_i^2 and R=V-C0^2/S when S>0. Conditional on k>=2, S has chi-square k law; R has chi-square k-1 law and is independent of S. Indeed conditional on a, projection of g_A perpendicular to a_A is independent standard Gaussian on a (k-1)-dimensional subspace. Its squared norm has a law depending only on k, not on a.

Let J=sum_i g_i^2 1{|a_i|<=2 theta |g_i|}. Choose a fixed sufficiently small eta>0 (for example eta=10^-8), and let G be the intersection of

    n/3 <= k <= 2n/3; n/8 <= S,R <= 2n;
    ||a||^2 <= 2n; ||g||^2 <= 2n; J <= eta n.

For all sufficiently large n (depending on d), P(G^c)<=C_d exp(-c n). The binomial and chi-square bounds follow by applying Markov's inequality to their explicit moment-generating functions. For J, with any fixed 0<lambda<1/4,

    E exp(lambda g_i^2 1{|a_i|<=2 theta |g_i|})
    <= 1 + C theta E[|g_i| (exp(lambda g_i^2)-1)] <= 1+C_lambda theta.

Consequently E exp(lambda J)<=exp(C_lambda n theta)<=exp(C_lambda/d). Markov gives P(J>eta n)<=exp(C_lambda/d-lambda eta n). This also proves E[J^p]<=C_{p,d} for every fixed p, by integrating the exponential tail. Constants need not be efficient.

On k in [n/3,2n/3], all fixed positive and inverse moments of S/n and R/n are uniformly bounded for sufficiently large n. Their centered fluctuations have L^p size O_p(n^-1/2). Thus deleting the exponential-probability failures of the other conditions changes fixed such moments, including logarithmic moments, by exponentially small terms (Cauchy–Schwarz with a moment of twice the order). Small k is excluded before making this argument; no logarithm or inverse of a zero chi-square is taken.

## 2. Flip moments

Set b=cos(theta)a+sin(theta)g, Z=(b-a)1_A, r=Y-X-Z. The vector r is supported on sign flips. For theta sufficiently small, any flip satisfies |a_i|<=2 theta |g_i|. On that set,

    |r_i|+|Z_i| <= C theta |g_i|,  |X_i r_i| <= C theta^2 g_i^2.

Hence H=2<Z,r>+||r||^2 and B=<X,r> obey

    ||H||_p + ||B||_p <= C_{p,d} theta^2,  p fixed.

For the expectation of H use the exact Gaussian polar integral. A flip from a>0 to b<0 contributes 2ab-b^2; the opposite flip contributes b^2. Swapping a,b converts the latter contribution to a^2 on the first flip sector. In polar coordinates a=r0 sin(e), b=r0 sin(e-theta), 0<e<theta, with E r0^2=2 and uniform polar angle,

    E H_i = (1/pi) integral_0^theta [sin^2(e)+2 sin(e)sin(e-theta)-sin^2(e-theta)] de
          = (theta cos(theta)-sin(theta))/pi
          = -theta^3/(3 pi) + O(theta^5).

The last error follows from |sin x-x|<=|x|^3/6 on this interval, whose integrand error is O(theta^4) and length theta. Therefore EH=-n theta^3/(3 pi)+O(n theta^5). This recovers the dossier's settled coefficient and does not claim it as new.

## 3. Angular decomposition on G

Let P project perpendicular to X. Then PZ=sin(theta)Pg_A, and

    ||P Y||^2 = sin^2(theta) R + Htilde,
    Htilde = H - 2[(cos(theta)-1)+sin(theta) C0/S] B - B^2/S.

On G, S and R are of order n and |C0|<=sqrt(SV)<=2n. The J bound with eta small makes |Htilde|/(sin^2(theta)R)<=1/2. Also

    <X,Y>/S = Q = cos(theta)+sin(theta) C0/S+B/S

is bounded above and below by constants tending to 1 uniformly as n increases. In particular the angle is well-defined, positive and small on G. Set xi=Htilde/(sin^2(theta)R). The preceding moment bounds and chi-square inverse moments give

    E[xi 1_G] = -2 theta/(3 pi)+O_{d,K}(n^-3/2),
    E[|xi|^p 1_G] = O_{p,d,K}(n^-p), p=2,3.

For clarity, the denominator replacement uses ||H/theta^2||_2=O_d(1) and

    ||1/R-2/n||_2 = O(n^-3/2)

on the central-k region, including binomial variation of k. Thus replacing R by n/2 in the expectation costs O(n^-3/2); replacing sin^2(theta) by theta^2 costs O(n^-3). The projection corrections cost O(n^-5/2)+O(n^-3): use ||C0/S||_p=O(n^-1/2), ||B||_p=O(theta^2), and 1/S=O(1/n). Exponentially small deletions are controlled as in section 1. No untruncated inverse of the exact output angle is used.

From tan(theta')=||P Y||/(sqrt(S) Q), the logarithmic angular increment on G is

    z=log(theta'/theta)
      = (1/2)log(R/S)+(1/2)log(1+xi)-log Q+E0,

where |E0|<=C theta^2 on G. This uses sin(theta)/theta=1+O(theta^2) and arctan(v)/v=1+O(v^2); R/S and Q are bounded on G. Furthermore

    |E[log Q 1_G]|=O(n^-2),  ||log Q 1_G||_p=O(n^-3/2)+O(n^-2).

To see the expectation bound, E[C0/S; central k]=0 by Gaussian symmetry before the other restrictions; removing G^c changes it exponentially little by Cauchy–Schwarz. The remaining terms are O(theta^2), O(theta^2/n), and O(theta^2 E(C0/S)^2). These estimates hold uniformly on the fixed compact [d,K].

## 4. Baseline chi-square ratio and the generator

Define z=0 off G. For central k, the independent chi-square logarithms give

    E[(1/2)log(R/S)|k] = (1/2)[psi((k-1)/2)-psi(k/2)] = -1/(2k)+O(k^-2),
    Var[(1/2)log(R/S)|k] = (1/4)[psi1((k-1)/2)+psi1(k/2)] = 1/k+O(k^-2).

Here the expansions follow from the usual positive-real large-argument gamma logarithmic derivatives; they can equivalently be obtained by Taylor expansion of log(chi-square/k) on its central event and exponential tail bounds. Since E[1/k; central k]=2/n+O(n^-2), the mean is -1/n+O(n^-2) and variance 2/n+O(n^-2). Fixed centered third absolute moments are O(n^-3/2), from chi-square centered sixth moments and the same truncation. Deleting G^c is exponentially negligible as above.

Combining sections 2–3, and using Cauchy–Schwarz for the baseline/flip covariance, yields

    Ez = -1/n-theta/(3 pi)+O(n^-3/2),
    Ez^2 = 2/n+O(n^-3/2), E|z|^3=O(n^-3/2).

Moreover |z| is bounded on G by an n-independent constant. Thus Taylor's remainder for exp(-z) is bounded by C|z|^3. Since U'=u exp(-z), uniformly for u in [d,K],

    n E(U'-u)=2u+1/(3 pi)+O(n^-1/2),
    n E(U'-u)^2=2u^2+O(n^-1/2),
    n E|U'-u|^3=O(n^-1/2).

Taylor's theorem for f proves the stated generator formula. Bounded f makes comparison with the killed exact kernel immediate from P(G^c)<=Ce^-cn, even though the latter has infinite raw inverse-angle moments.

## What this does not settle

The argument is uniform only on fixed compact intervals [d,K] with d>0. It supplies no passage from fixed theta_0 to u>0 at time o(1), no compact-containment theorem, and no convergence rate for the final two-input outputs. Those remain the hardest target-1 requirements. The constants in the exponential deletion bound are inefficient; no numerical performance of that bound is asserted.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:c6924ed4fbeaf5d90fdf5114b0b93de31bd962d24a9c78646726cf7f392aec86","revision_digest":"sha256:853e9e56a5ede8d6cbc9d892220bc47974eee7136bb5ff5a8cad3399df3a4696","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C004:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1-reviewer-pass","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem.balanced_continuity_large of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let $K$ be a positive integer.
    Let $(X_i', i \in \{1, \dots, n\})$ and $(X_i, i \in \{1, \dots, n\})$ be
    sequences of independent random variables
    where $X_i$ is distributed unifomly on $\{-\frac{k_i-1} 2, \dots, \frac {k_i - 1} 2\}$
    while $X_i'$ is distributed uniformly on $\{-\frac {k_i+1} 2, \dots, \frac {k_i+1} 2\}$
    and $k_i$, $k_i \ge K$, are odd integers.

    Let $Y$ be a symmetric log-concave integer random variable, independent of both the sequences. 

    Then 
    \[
         \mathbb P(Y + \sum_{i=1}^n X_i + Y = 0)  \ge  \mathbb P(Y + \sum_{i=1}^n X_i' = 0)  \ge  
         \mathbb P(Y + \sum_{i=1}^n X_i = 0)  (1 -  14 
    K^{-\frac 1 5}).
    \]

[Lem tree-normalized-superquadratic of arXiv:2609.03856, 'Consensus time for asynchronous $\ell^p$ relaxation: graph dependence'] Let $p>2$, put $a=p-1$, and let $w_1,\ldots,w_k\ge1$, where $k\ge1$.  Set
\[
 w=\left(\sum_{i=1}^k(w_i+1)^a\right)^{1/a}.
\]
For signed numbers $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_k$, define
\[
 \mathfrak D_p(a)=\sum_{j=0}^k|a_j|^p
 -\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{j=0}^k|a_j-t|^p.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{|a_0|^p}{w}
 \le \sum_{i=1}^k\frac{|a_i|^p}{w_i}
 +C_p\mathfrak D_p(a).
\end{equation}

body: For alpha >= 1 let psi_alpha(x) = exp(x^alpha) - 1. The psi_alpha norm of a random variable X is ||X||_{psi_alpha} = inf{k in (0, infinity) : E[psi_alpha(|X|/k)] <= 1} = inf{k > 0 : E[exp((|X|/k)^alpha)] <= 2}. A random variable with finite psi_2 norm is sub-Gaussian and one with finite psi_1 norm is sub-exponential, and ||X||_{psi_p} < infinity if and only if P(|X| >= x) <= K exp(-K' x^p) for some constants K, K' > 0. (For 0 < alpha < 1 the same formula defines a quasi-norm, the 'sub-Weibull' case of later papers; the cited source covers alpha >= 1 only.)

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We have the generalized binomial formula
$$(1+t)^p=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\binom{p}{k}t^k$$
with the generalized binomial coefficients being given by
$$\binom{p}{k}=\frac{p(p-1)\ldots(p-k+1)}{k!}$$
for any $p\in\mathbb R$, and any $|t|<1$. With $p\in\mathbb N$, we recover the usual binomial formula.

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2609.01965, 'A logarithmic Bogomolov--Sommese vanishing theorem on compact K\"ahler manifolds'] Let $X$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold, $L$ a pseudo-effective line bundle over $X$ and $D$ a reduced simple normal crossing divisor on $X$. Then
    \begin{equation*}
        H^0(X,\Omega^p_X(\log D)\otimes L^{-1})=0 \quad \text{for every } p<\nd(L).
    \end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition modified-projection of arXiv:2512.10625, 'Bessel and Dunkl processes with drift'] Let $\lambda\in V$ be some drift vector, and $(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ a Brownian motion (without drift) on $V$ starting in $0\in V$ where, by definition,
  the distributions $d\mu_t(x)= \frac{1}{(2\pi t)^{n/2}} e^{-\|x\|^2/(2t)}dx$ of $B_t$ are $K$-invariant by construction.
  Then $(B_t+t\lambda)_{t\ge0}$ is a Brownian motion  on $V$ with drift $\lambda$ where, clearly,  $B_t+t\lambda$ has the distribution
  $\mu_t^\lambda:= e^{-\|\lambda\|^2 t/2} e_\lambda \> \mu_t$ for $t\ge0$. The projection $(p(B_t+t\lambda))_{t\ge0}$ of this Brownian motion
  with drift is a Feller diffusion on $V^K$. Moreover:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item[\rm{(1)}] The transition probabilities $p_t^\lambda(x,dy)$ and  $p_t^0(x,dy)$ of the projections of $(B_t+t\lambda)_{t\ge0}$ and of
    $(B_t=B_t+t\cdot 0)_{t\ge0}$ respectively with $t\ge 0$ and $x\in V^K$ are related by
    $$ dp_t^\lambda(x,dy)= \frac{e^{-\|\lambda\|^2 t/2}}{\alpha_\lambda(x) }\cdot \alpha_\lambda(y) dp_t^0(x,dy) \quad\quad(x\in V^K).$$
     \item[\rm{(2)}]  The generators $L^\lambda$ and $L^0$ of the transition semigroups of the projections of $(B_t+t\lambda)_{t\ge0}$ and of
  $(B_t=B_t+t\cdot 0)_{t\ge0}$ respectively are related by
\begin{equation}
  L^{\lambda}f(y)=  - \frac{\|\lambda\|^2}{2} f(y) +\frac{1}{\alpha_\lambda(y)} L^0(\alpha_\lambda f)(y)
\end{equation}
for all 
$f\in C_0(V^K)$ which are contained in  the domain $D(L^\lambda)$ of $L^\lambda$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition modified-projection of arXiv:2512.10625

Own-work draft C016 v1, proof (unaudited); no novelty or independent-review claim. Let f_theta(x)=m^(-1)sum_i a_i sigma(w_i dot x), d>=1, m>=28 and fixed finite total mean-field time T>=0. Assume sigma globally C2 with absolute values of sigma and its first two derivatives <=1, bounded data ||X||<=1, |Y|<=1, and population half-squared loss. Initialize two independent collections of iid pairs with common product law a~N(0,1), w~N(0,Gamma), Gamma PSD with trace <=1. Train BOTH layers simultaneously with mean-field SGD multiplier m, fresh samples or finite minibatch averages conditional on initialization and the JOINT past, and common deterministic nonnegative steps eta_n summing to <=T. Independent streams or common fresh samples are allowed; there is no teacher assumption. One joint initial permutation of (a,w) yields expected population loss-chord barrier <=2Lambda_T sqrt(3Astar_T)[2r_G(m)+2sqrt(2)G_T sqrt(sum eta_n^2)]^(beta_T/2)+49exp(2T)/sqrt(m), with explicit constants from proof statement and beta_T=exp(-kappa_T T)>0. Here r_G is the trace-bounded Gaussian covariance matching bound of C015 v1. If eta_max<=1/log(m+e), this gives O_T((log log m)^(beta_T/2)(log m)^(-beta_T/4)), uniformly over d,Gamma and bounded data laws. The proof uses population stability in D_Sigma=mean|delta a|+mean||Sigma^(1/2)delta w||, Sigma=E[XX^T], and accumulates fresh-data martingale noise in the full normalized Hilbert parameter norm. No arbitrary sample-path covariance Lipschitz bound or trained-neuron independence is assumed. Only the INITIAL matching estimate uses clipping; training is unclipped. C004/C015 matching and C010 boundary/Bihari arguments remain unaudited dependencies. This does not cover unscaled N(0,I_d) uniformly as d grows, ReLU, fixed independent-data steps, growing time or low-risk convergence; unrestricted permutation connectivity remains open.

body:
Let $x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^p$ be i.i.d. with mean zero, covariance $\Sigma$ and finite eighth moments, $S = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i x_i^T$, and let $\mu = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/p$, with the scaled Frobenius norm $\|A\|^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A A^T)/p$. Define $\alpha^2 = \|\Sigma - \mu I\|^2$, $\beta^2 = E\|S - \Sigma\|^2$, $\delta^2 = E\|S - \mu I\|^2 = \alpha^2 + \beta^2$. THEOREM (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004). Among all estimators of the form $\rho_1 I + \rho_2 S$ with nonrandom $\rho_1, \rho_2$, the expected loss $E\|\hat\Sigma - \Sigma\|^2$ is minimized by $$\Sigma^* = \frac{\beta^2}{\delta^2}\, \mu I + \frac{\alpha^2}{\delta^2}\, S,$$ a convex combination of the sample covariance and the scaled identity, with expected loss $\alpha^2 \beta^2 / \delta^2$. The constants have consistent plug-in estimates under general asymptotics $p/n \to \gamma \in (0, \infty)$: $\hat\mu = \operatorname{tr}(S)/p$, $\hat\delta^2 = \|S - \hat\mu I\|^2$, $\hat{\bar b}^2 = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i \|x_i x_i^T - S\|^2$, $\hat\beta^2 = \min(\hat{\bar b}^2, \hat\delta^2)$, $\hat\alpha^2 = \hat\delta^2 - \hat\beta^2$, and the resulting estimator $\hat\Sigma^* = \frac{\hat\beta^2}{\hat\delta^2}\hat\mu I + \frac{\hat\alpha^2}{\hat\delta^2} S$ has the same asymptotic loss as $\Sigma^*$, is always well conditioned and invertible, and is uniformly no worse than $S$. The shrinkage target is the scaled identity, so the estimator pulls all eigenvalues of $S$ toward their mean $\hat\mu$; when one eigenvalue of $\Sigma$ dominates the trace (a strong spike), $\hat\mu$ is dominated by that spike and the target is far from the small eigenvalues.
i.i.d. rows with finite eighth moments (mean zero, or centered)
p/n -> gamma in (0, infinity)
loss is the scaled Frobenius norm tr(A A^T)/p

body: In probability theory, a martingale is a stochastic process in which the expected value of the next observation, given all prior observations, is equal to the most recent value. In other words, the conditional expectation of the next value, given the past, is equal to the present value. Martingales are used to model fair games, where future expected winnings are equal to the current amount regardless of past outcomes.
title: Martingale (probability theory)

Let $L_{\max}(p)$ be the smallest integer $L$ such that there exist patterns $A,B,C$ with
$\max(|A|,|B|,|C|)\le L$ that form a non-transitive $3$-cycle under this common bias $p$.
Does $L_{\max}(p)$ exist for every $p\ne\tfrac12$?
Determine $L_{\max}(p)$ (or give meaningful bounds) and describe the length profiles that achieve it.
We exhibited cycles of profiles $(2,5,5)$ and $(3,6,6)$, and we classified all common-bias cycles with $\max(|A|,|B|,|C|)\le 8$. (Verbatim from the paper's TeX; symbols are the source paper's. [Lemma sylvester_solution_explicit of arXiv:2608.23765, '\texorpdfstring{Tight Majorizations and Convergence Rates\\ of Nuclear Norm Minimization I'] \mbox{}\\
    Let $\mathbf{Z} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ be an arbitrary matrix
    with SVD given by 
    $ \mathbf{Z} = \sum_{i=1}^d \sigma_i (\mathbf{Z}) \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^{\top} $,
    where $\sigma_1(\mathbf{Z}) \ge \sigma_2(\mathbf{Z}) \ge \ldots \ge \sigma_d(\mathbf{Z}) \ge 0$
    are the singular values of $\mathbf{Z}$.
    Here,
    $\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_{d_1} \} \subset \R^{d_1}$
    and
    $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_{d_2} \} \subset \R^{d_2}$
    are orthonormal bases of 
    $\R^{d_1}$ and $\R^{d_2}$,
    consisting
    of left and right singular vectors of $\mathbf{Z}$, respectively.
    Let $ \widetilde{\mathbf{L}}_{\mathbf{U}} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_1}, \widetilde{\mathbf{L}}_{\mathbf{V}} \in \R^{d_2 \times d_2}$
    be positive definite matrices
    which are diagonal in the bases $\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_{d_1} \}$
    and $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_{d_2} \}$, respectively.
    Then, the unique solution $\mathbf{W} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$
    of the Sylvester equation
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\mathbf{L}}_{\mathbf{U}} \mathbf{W} + \mathbf{W} \widetilde{\mathbf{L}}_{\mathbf{V}} = 2 \mathbf{Z}
    \end{equation*}
    is given by
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbf{W}
        =
        \sum_{k=1}^d
        \frac{2 \sigma_k (\mathbf{Z})}{
            \innerproduct{ \widetilde{ \mathbf{L}}_{\mathbf{U}}, \mathbf{u}_k \mathbf{u}_k^\top}
            +
            \innerproduct{\widetilde{\mathbf{L}}_{\mathbf{V}}, \mathbf{v}_k \mathbf{v}_k^\top}
        }
        \mathbf{u}_k \mathbf{v}_k^{\top}.
    \end{equation*}

body: Bounded-variation hub (bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture). For Q = 2 X_h (L + beta) + lambda V^2 + 2 L <q, X'> + sum_i phi_i(X_i) with L = <w, X'>, V = <v, X'>, (w, v) orthonormal, w_i^2 + v_i^2 <= 1/2, any q, any diagonal and linear terms, and a hub density of total variation V_h: |phi_Q(eta)| <= V_h |eta|^{-3/2} (A (1 + log_+(2 |eta|^{3/2}/V_h)) + 1/2) with A = 2 (4 pi/|lambda|)^{1/2}, and ||p_Q||_inf <= 14.9 V_h^{2/3} for |lambda| >= 1, for all light laws. Proof: |psi_h(zeta)| <= V_h/|zeta| by parts, paired with the slice bound |mu^_l(eta)| <= min(rho_L(l), A |eta|^{-1/2}) (valid for every cross term), split at |l + beta| = |eta|^{1/2}. Window hub laws U[0,1] * nu have V_h <= 2, so the open single hub needs a rough hub law as well as rough light laws.

[Proposition 8 (Complete-history covariance and context limit) of arXiv:2608.20998, 'Free-Probability Kernels for Zero-Rollout Hyperparameter Selection in Reservoir Computing'] Assume $\sigma_r<1$ and
$U=\sup_t\lVert u_t\rVert<\infty$. Define
\begin{equation}
Q_\theta^{(\infty)}(t,s)
:=
\alpha^2\frac{\sigma_{\rm in}^2}{d_{\rm in}}
\sum_{k,\ell\geq0}
\tau_{k,\ell}
u_{t-1-k}^\top u_{s-1-\ell}.

\end{equation}
The series converges absolutely. With
\[
r_\theta:=1-\alpha+\alpha\sigma_r^2<1,
\]
\begin{equation}
\left|
Q_\theta^{(\infty)}(t,s)
-
Q_\theta^{(L)}(t,s)
\right|
\leq
\frac{2\sigma_{\rm in}^2U^2}
{d_{\rm in}(1-\sigma_r^2)}
r_\theta^{L+1}.

\end{equation}
If $K_{\psi,\theta}^{(\infty)}$ is obtained from
$Q_\theta^{(\infty)}$ as in \eqref{eq:sm-deterministic-kernel}, then
\begin{equation}
\left|
K_{\psi,\theta}^{(\infty)}(t,s)
-
K_{\psi,\theta}^{(L)}(t,s)
\right|
\leq
C_\theta
r_\theta^{(L+1)/2}.

\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
K_{\psi,\theta}^{(L)}(t,s)
\longrightarrow
K_{\psi,\theta}^{(\infty)}(t,s)
\qquad (L\to\infty).

\end{equation}

Let (P, <=) be a partially ordered set (poset). A subset C of P is called a chain if any two elements in C are comparable: for all x, y in C, either x <= y or y <= x. A subset A of P is called an antichain if no two distinct elements in A are comparable: for all distinct x, y in A, neither x <= y nor y <= x.
(P, <=) is a partially ordered set

$$

\end{aligned}
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem Tauberianthm of arXiv:2603.24499, 'A central limit theorem for connected components of random coverings of manifolds with nil'] Let $b(t)$ be a measurable function $[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ which is bounded on finite intervals, and such that
\[
G(s):=\int_0^{\infty}b(t)e^{-st}{\rm d}t
\]
converges (in Lebesgue sense, i.e., absolutely) for all $s\in\mathbb{C}$ with ${{\rm Re}(s)}>0$. Suppose also that there exists an integer $m\ge 1$ and there exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that
\[
\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}tb(t)
\int_{0}^{\varepsilon_0}u^{m-1}e^{-tu}{\rm d}u=1\ .
\]
Let $a(t)$ be a nondecreasing function $[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$. Suppose there is some $\alpha>0$ such that
\[
f(s):=\int_0^{\infty}a(t)e^{-st}{\rm d}t
\]
converges (absolutely) for all $s\in\mathbb{C}$ with ${{\rm Re}(s)}>\alpha$.

Suppose that for some constant $c_0>0$, the function 
\[
F(s):=f(s)-c_0 G(s-\alpha)
\]
can be rewritten as
\[
F(s)=\frac{g(s)}{(s-\alpha)^{m-1}}+h(s)\ ,
\]
where $g(s)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m-2$ if $m\ge 2$, or identically zero if $m=1$, and where $h(s)$ is a function which is continuous on ${\rm Re}(s)\ge \alpha$
and holomorphic on the domain ${\rm Re}(s)>\alpha$.

Then, the previous hypotheses imply the asymptotics
\[
a(t)=(c_0+o(1))\ e^{\alpha t}\ b(t)\ ,
\]
as $t\rightarrow\infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem Tauberianthm of arXiv:2603.24499

For every $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, the law semiflow $\varphi_P^\epsilon$ has a unique invariant law $\mu_\epsilon^*\in P$. Moreover,
	\begin{align}
		\mathcal W_2\big(
		\varphi_P^\epsilon(t)\mu,
		\mu_\epsilon^*
		\big)
		\leq
		e^{-\kappa_0t/2}
		\mathcal W_2(\mu,\mu_\epsilon^*),

	\end{align}

[Lemma 10 (Stochastic Davie-Gronwall lemma) of arXiv:2607.18862, 'Tamed Euler Schemes for Singular SDEs with Multiplicative L\'{e}vy Noise'] Let $\epsilon_j>0$, $j=1,\cdots,5$; $\Gamma_i\geq 0$, $i=1,2,3$; $C_1,C_2,C_3,u,S,T\geq 0$ be fixed numbers such that $0\leq u<S<T$. Let $\sW$ be a determinstic control on $\Delta([S,T])$ which is continuous. Let $J$
  	be a $L_p$-integrable adapted process indexed by $\Delta([S,T])$ such that 
  	\be 
  	&&\|J_{s,t}\|_{L_p(\Omega|\sF_u)}\leq C_1\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_1},~~ \|\mE_s J_{s,t}\|_{L_p(\Omega|\sF_u)}\leq C_2\sW(s,t)^{1+\epsilon_2},\\
  	&&\|\delta J_{s,v,t}\|_{L_p(\Omega|\sF_u)}\leq \Gamma_1\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}}+\Gamma_2(\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_3}+C_3\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_4}),\\
  	&&\|\mE_s\delta J_{s,v,t}\|_{L_p(\Omega|\sF_u)}\leq \Gamma_3\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_5} 
  	\ee 
  	for every $(s,v,t)\in \Delta_2([S,T])$. Then there exists a constant $N=N(p,\epsilon)$ such that for every $(s,t)\in \Delta([S,T])$ and every integer $m\geq 1$
  	\be 
  	\|J_{s,t}\|_{L_p(\Omega|\sF_u)}&\leq& N[C_12^{-m\epsilon_1}\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_1}+C_22^{-m\epsilon_2}\sW(s,t)^{1+\epsilon_2}+ m\Gamma_1\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}}\no\\
  	&&+\Gamma_2(\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_3}+\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_4})+\Gamma_3\sW(s,t)^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_5}].
  	\ee (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stochastic Davie-Gronwall lemma

[Prop 2 of arXiv:2603.26228, 'A local limit theorem for nonlattice multidimensional random walks in cones'] \cite[Theorems 1 \& 3]{DW2015}  Under hypotheses {\bf C},  {\bf M} and {\bf N},  there exists  a positive constant  $\mathrm{K}$ such that,  for any ${\bf x} \in \cC$, 
	\[
	\mathbb P (\tau({\bf x}) >n) \leq K  {1+ \vert x\vert^p\over n^{p/2}}.
	\]
	Furthermore,  
 there exists an universal  constant $\kappa_0>0$  such that
 	\[
 	\mathbb P  (\tau({\bf x}) >n) \sim \kappa_0 V({\bf x})n^{-p/2}\quad\mbox{as} \quad\,  n \to +\infty 
 	\]
 and   
	\[ \bP\Bigl({{\bf x} +S(n)\over \sqrt{n}}\in  \cdot  \Big\vert \tau({\bf x}) >n\Bigr)\longrightarrow \mu(\cdot) \quad  weakly, 
	\]
	where  $\mu$ is the probability measure on $\cC$ having density $  H_0 u({\bf y})   e^{-\vert{\bf y}\vert^2/2} $  with respect to the Lebesgue measure with    $H_0= \displaystyle\left( \int_{\mathcal C}u({\bf y})  \ e^{-\vert{\bf y}\vert^2/2} {\rm d}{\bf y}\right)^{-1}.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 2 of arXiv:2603.26228

SCOPED KEEP AUDITS by w544 and w545; different-login provenance unverified; retained as a draft concept pending coordinator admission. Let T,Lambda,kappa,mu>0 and define C6_mu(x)=exp[-9T integral_(|k|<=Lambda)(1-cos(k.x))/(mu+kappa|k|^2) dk/(2*pi)^2] and C6_0(x)=exp[-(9T/kappa) integral_(|k|<=Lambda)(1-cos(k.x))/|k|^2 dk/(2*pi)^2]. For every R>0 and |x|<=R, 0<=log(C6_mu(x)/C6_0(x))<=9T*mu*R^2*log(1+kappa*Lambda^2/mu)/(8*pi*kappa^2). The bound tends to zero as mu->0, while each fixed mu>0 has the positive plateau (1+kappa Lambda^2/mu)^[-9T/(4*pi*kappa)]. Meanwhile log C6_0(rn)=-9T log r/(2*pi*kappa)+O(1). Thus arbitrarily good finite-window agreement with algebraic orientation is insufficient to prove the infinite-distance regime.

[Theorem 1 (Anisotropic halfspace theorem in $\R^3$) of arXiv:2609.03916, 'Halfspace Theorems for Anisotropic Minimal Surfaces and Perimeter Minimizers'] Let $\Phi:\R^3\to[0,\infty)$ satisfy
\eqref{old-eq:regularity-bounds}--\eqref{old-eq:ellipticity}, with $n=2$, and
be even.  Let
$\Sigma\subset\R^3$ be a connected smooth oriented proper surface without
boundary satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{tr}\bigl(D_T^2\Phi(\nu_\Sigma)\,\mathrm{II}_\Sigma\bigr)=0
 \qquad\text{on }\Sigma.
\end{equation}
If $\Sigma$ is contained in a closed halfspace, then $\Sigma$ is an affine
plane. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Anisotropic halfspace theorem in $\R^3$

body:
[Proposition Complexity of basic procedures of arXiv:2412.08400, '\vspace{-1.0cm} Characterization of Exponential Families of \\ Lumpable Stochastic Matrice'] We rely on the subroutines below.
\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
    \item[(i)\xspace] Determine whether $(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E})$ is strongly connected: $\mathcal{O}(\left| \mathcal{Y} \right| + \left| \mathcal{E} \right|)$.
    \item[(ii)\xspace] Determine whether $P \in \mathcal{W}(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E})$ is $\kappa$-lumpable: $\mathcal{O}(\left| \mathcal{X} \right|\left| \mathcal{Y} \right| + \left| \mathcal{E} \right|)$.
    \item[(iii)\xspace] Determine whether $\mathcal{W}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E})$ is non-vacuous: $\mathcal{O}(\left| \mathcal{X} \right|\left| \mathcal{Y} \right| + \left| \mathcal{E} \right|)$.
    \item[(iv)\xspace] Construct the lumped graph $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{D})$ (as adjacency lists) in $\mathcal{O}(\left| \mathcal{X} \right|^2 + \left| \mathcal{E} \right|)$.
    \item[(v)\xspace] List merging blocks of $(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E})$ with respect to $\kappa$: 
$\mathcal{O}(\left| \mathcal{X} \right|\left| \mathcal{Y} \right| + \left| \mathcal{E} \right|)$.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition prop:mu0 of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] A proof of Conjecture~(conj:CE of the paper) cannot restrict to selections with
$\mu=0$. Concretely, for the seventh-roots system
$t_j=\zeta^j,\ z_j=\zeta^{3j},\ p_j=\frac17$ ($\zeta=e^{2\pi i/7}$), every
$q$ with $\mu=0$ satisfies $C\ge\frac{7/k-1}2$ for support $k$ (a discrete
Parseval identity), i.e.\ $C\ge\frac38>\frac14$ at $k=4$ and
$C\ge\frac23>\frac58$ at $k=3$; yet unconstrained selections achieve
$C=\frac27$ at three points (the difference set $\{0,1,3\}$) and $C<\frac14$
at four consecutive points (an exact algebraic computation modulo
$x^3+x^2-2x-1$). Similarly, for the regular hexagon third-harmonic system
($t_j=e^{\pi ij/3}$, $z_j=(-1)^j$, $p_j=\frac16$) all $\mu=0$ selections of
support $\le3$ have $C=1$, while $\{0,1,2\}$ at weights $2{:}3{:}2$ attains
the exact three-point optimum $C=\frac12$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $\mu=0$ obstruction

body:
[Lemma lem:IBJ-kernel of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] We have
\[
\mathbb{P}_y\Bigl(\bigcap_{i=1}^m
\{Y_{n_i}(t) > a_i\}\Bigr)
= \det(I - K_{t, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}})
_{\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})},
\]
where
\[
K_{t, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}(x, x')
= \sum_{1 \le j \le i \le m}
  \sum_{r \le a_i} \sum_{r' \le a_j}
  \psi_{t, r, n_i}(x)
  \bigl[\delta_{ij}\delta_{r,r'}
  + [B_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}]_{ij}(r, r')\bigr]
  \phi_{t, r', n_j}(x').
\]
This identifies $K_{t, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}$ with
the kernel~(equation eq:K-def of the paper) on the product graph
$\mathcal{G}^m$, with $\psi, \phi$ as the seed data
and $B_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}}$ as the propagator.

[Proposition prop:Ergodic:InvariantMeasure of arXiv:2608.17031, 'A shape theorem for periodic branching diffusion'] [MR1326606]
    Let $(Z_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be the periodic diffusion (equation eq:Intro:Diffusion of the paper) with $\sigma$ and $b$ satisfying 	extbf{(AssumptionA:bSigmaRegularity of the paper)} and $	extbf{(AssumptionA:SigmaEllipticity of the paper)}$. Let $(\dot{Z}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be its projection into $\mathbb{T}^d$. There exists a unique invariant measure of $(\dot{Z}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ which has a strictly positive density $
u \in C^{2,\alpha}_p(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Furthermore, $
u$ satisfies the adjoint equation $\mathcal{L}^*
u=0$, and $
u$ is the unique periodic classical solution of the adjoint equation with the property that $\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}
u(x)dx=1$.

[Proposition 33 of arXiv:2604.00630, 'The contact process on a bipartite spatial network'] Assume that~$(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) \in \mathcal S$ and~$a > 0$.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[$\mathrm{(I)}$] If~$\gamma_2 \le \frac12$ (and consequently~$\gamma_1 > \frac12$), we have
		\[
			(\mu_\star,\nu_\star) = \begin{cases}
				(\mu_{\mathsf S}, \nu_{\mathsf B})&\text{if } a \le \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\Delta_2};\\[.2cm]
				(\mu_{\mathsf S}, \nu_{\mathsf S})&\text{if } a > \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\Delta_2}.
			\end{cases}
		\]
	\item[$\mathrm{(II)}$] If~$\gamma_1 \le \frac12$ (and consequently~$\gamma_2 > \frac12$), we have
		\[
			(\mu_\star,\nu_\star) = \begin{cases}
				(\mu_{\mathsf S}, \nu_{\mathsf S})&\text{if } a \le \frac{\Delta_1}{\bar{\gamma}_1};\\[.2cm]
				(\mu_{\mathsf B}, \nu_{\mathsf S})&\text{if } a > \frac{\Delta_1}{\bar{\gamma}_1}.
			\end{cases}
		\]

	\item[$\mathrm{(III)}$] If~$\gamma_1,\gamma_2 > \frac12$ and~$\frac{1}{\gamma_1}+\frac{1}{\gamma_2} > 3$, then
		\[
			(\mu_\star,\nu_\star) = \begin{cases}
				(\mu_{\mathsf S}, \nu_{\mathsf B})&\text{if } a \le \frac{\Delta_1}{\bar{\gamma}_1};\\[.2cm]
				(\mu_{\mathsf S}, \nu_{\mathsf S})&\text{if } \frac{\Delta_1}{\bar{\gamma}_1} < a \le \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\Delta_2};\\[.2cm]
				(\mu_{\mathsf B}, \nu_{\mathsf S})&\text{if } a > \frac{\bar{\gamma}_2}{\Delta_2}.
			\end{cases}
		\]
	\item[$\mathrm{(IV)}$] If~$\gamma_1, \gamma_2 > \frac12$ and~$\frac{1}{\gamma_1}+\frac{1}{\gamma_2} \le 3$, then
		\[
			(\mu_\star,\nu_\star) = \begin{cases}
				(\mu_{\mathsf S}, \nu_{\mathsf B})&\text{if } a \le \frac{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2}{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_2 - 1};\\[.2cm]
				(\mu_{\mathsf D}, \nu_{\mathsf D})&\text{if } \frac{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2}{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_2 - 1} < a \le \frac{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_1 - 1}{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2};\\[.2cm]
				(\mu_{\mathsf B}, \nu_{\mathsf S})&\text{if } a > \frac{\gamma_1\gamma_2 + \gamma_1 - 1}{\bar{\gamma}_1 \bar{\gamma}_2}.
			\end{cases}
		\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 33 of arXiv:2604.00630

body: [Definition of arXiv:2609.03755, 'The Scramble Number of Outerplanar Graphs'] A \emph{vertex coloring} is a map that assigns a color to each vertex such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color. The \emph{chromatic number} of a graph, $\chi(G)$, is the smallest number of colors required to give $G$ a vertex coloring.

[Lem 5 (Potter bounds; \cite{Bingham_1987}, Theorem~1.5.6(ii)) of arXiv:2607.27721, 'Asymptotic bias of the plug-in Shannon entropy estimator \\ under a regularly varying occu'] If $\ell: [0,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ is a slowly varying function at infinity that is bounded away from $0$ and $\infty$ on every compact subset of $[0,\infty)$, then for every $\delta>0$ there exists $A=A(\delta)>1$ such that 
    \[
    \frac{\ell(y)}{\ell(x)}\le A\max\left\{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^\delta,\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^{-\delta}\right\}\quad(x>0,y>0).
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a compact (hence closed) set F contained in E with |E \ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]

Converse (Lusin's criterion): let E be a Lebesgue measurable subset of R^d of finite measure and let f:E->C be a function. If for every eps>0 there is a closed F contained in E with |E\F|<eps such that f restricted to F is continuous, then f is Lebesgue measurable on E. Thus measurability of an a.e.-finite function on such E is equivalent to continuity of its restriction on closed subsets missing arbitrarily small measure. Applied on every bounded measurable piece, this gives the local criterion on R^d.
f measurable and a.e. finite
|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)
the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available

[Proposition prop:higher of arXiv:2608.30166, 'Square Functions and Rectifiability\\ under Monotone Transformations of the Density'] Let $\mu$ be $n$-AD-regular with constant $c_0$ and $\mu(\mathbb{R}^d)=\infty$, let $\phi$ be
as in Theorem~(thm:smooth of the paper), and let $k\ge1$. Let $F\in C^k(0,\infty)$ satisfy
\[
\lambda^{-1}\le|F'(s)|\le\lambda
\quad\text{and}\quad
|F^{(m)}(s)|\le\Lambda\ \ (2\le m\le k)
\qquad\text{for all } s\in J_\phi.
\]
Then $\mu$ is uniformly $n$-rectifiable if and only if there exists a constant $c$
such that, for any ball $B(x_0,R)$ centered at $\operatorname{supp}(\mu)$,
\begin{equation}
\int_0^R\!\!\int_{x\in B(x_0,R)}|\widetilde\Delta^{F,k}_{\mu,\phi}(x,t)|^2\,d\mu(x)\,\frac{dt}{t}
\;\le\;c\,R^n.
\end{equation}
The constants depend on $k$, $\lambda$, $\Lambda$, $\phi$, $n$ and $c_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:higher of arXiv:2608.30166

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2607.16954, 'Repeated differentiation of deterministic polynomials with asymptotically radial root dist'] Consider positive integers $k,l\leq n$  such that when $n\to\infty$ we have $1-k/n\to \alpha$ and $l/n\to t$. In the case $\Delta<0$, we assume
\[
\alpha>\alpha_{\min}=t\vert\Delta\vert. 
\]
Then 
\begin{equation}
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[\prod_{j=0}^{ml-1}\frac{\falling{mn-mk+j\Delta}{b}} {\falling{mn-mk+m+j\Delta}{b}}\right]^\frac{1}{m}=\begin{cases} e^{-\frac{ta}{\alpha}} & \text{if } \Delta=0, \\
\left(1+\frac{t\Delta}{\alpha}\right)^{-\frac{b}{\Delta}} & \text{if } \Delta\neq 0.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Here, it does not matter if $m$ is fixed or if it tends to $\infty$.

[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Let $(Y_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ denote the edge-field denoising process. Then its posterior distribution satisfies 
    $$
\operatorname{Law}(Y_1\mid Y_t)=(1-t)\otimes \mu^{Y_t},
    $$where we recall that $\mu^{Y_t}$ denotes the conditional law of $\mu$ conditioning on the event that for every edge $(u,v)\in E$ with $Y_t(u,v)=1$, then $A_{uv}$ occurs, so that $\sigma_u=\sigma_v=1$.

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2609.01114, 'Unbalanced spectral Tur\'an problem for color-critical graphs with prescribed large maximu'] Let $F$ be a color-critical graph with $\chi(F)=p+2\geq 4$.  With the cleaning tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ fixed in \Cref{sec:windows}, for sufficient large $n$,
\begin{align*}
&e(G^{\star}[A])+(n-D)D-e_{G^{\star}}(A,B)
  +\sum_{i=1}^{p} e(G^{\star}[V_i])
  \le 5\varepsilon^6D^2<5\varepsilon^2D^2,\\
&e(G^{\star}[B])\ge t(D,p)-\varepsilon^6D^2
  >t(D,p)-\varepsilon^2D^2,\\
&\sum_{i=1}^{p} e(G^{\star}[V_i])
  \le \varepsilon^6D^2<\varepsilon^2D^2,\\
&\max_{1\le i\le p}\left||V_i|-\frac Dp\right|
  \le 2\varepsilon^3D<2\varepsilon D.
\end{align*}

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2512.04297, 'Mixing at the Batchelor Scale for White-In-Time Flows'] Let $-\infty < s_1< s_2< s_3< \infty$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For every $f \in H^{s_3}_0$, we have
        $$\|f\|_{H^{s_2}} \leq \|f\|_{H^{s_1}}^{(s_3-s_2)/(s_3-s_1)}\,\|f\|_{H^{s_3}}^{{(s_2-s_1)/(s_3-s_1)}}.$$
    \item For every $f \in H^{s_2}_0$ and every $\epsilon>0$, there exists an $f^\epsilon \in H^{s_3}_0$, such that
    \begin{equation}
       \|f-f^\epsilon\|_{H^{s_1}} \leq \epsilon \|f\|_{H^{s_2}}, \quad  \|f^\epsilon\|_{H^{s_2}} \leq \|f\|_{H^{s_2}}, \quad \|f^\epsilon\|_{H^{s_3}} \leq \epsilon^{-(s_3-s_2)/(s_2-s_1)} \|f\|_{H^{s_2}}.
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 3 (Young integration) of arXiv:2607.04193, 'Onsager--Machlup Functionals for Generalized Newtonian Equations of Motion with Time-Varyi'] Let \(f\in C^\beta([0,T];\mathbb R)\) and
\(g\in C^\gamma([0,T];\mathbb R)\), where
\(\beta,\gamma\in(0,1)\) and \(\beta+\gamma>1\). Then the
Riemann--Stieltjes integral
\[
    \int_0^t f_s\,dg_s
\]
is well defined pathwise for all \(t\in[0,T]\). Moreover, there exists a
constant \(C_{\beta,\gamma,T}>0\) such that, for any
\(0\le s<t\le T\),
\begin{equation}
    \left|
        \int_s^t f_r\,dg_r
        -
        f_s(g_t-g_s)
    \right|
    \le
    C_{\beta,\gamma,T}
    [f]_{\beta}
    [g]_{\gamma}
    |t-s|^{\beta+\gamma}.
    
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Young integration

body:
[Proposition 9 (Consequences of delocalization and balance) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Under \eqref{eq:spike-package},
\begin{align}
 \max_i x_i^2&=o(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \sum_i x_i^4&=o(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \max_{i<j}|s_{ij}|&=o(1).
 
\end{align}
The linear profile satisfies
\begin{align}
 \max_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(1)}|&=o(1),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(1)}|&=O(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}(p_{ij}^{(1)})^2&=O(N^{-1}),
 \\
 N\left|\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}p_{ij}^{(1)}\right|&=o(1),
 \\
 \max_i\frac1N\sum_j|p_{ij}^{(1)}|&=o(N^{-1/4}).
 
\end{align}
The quadratic profile satisfies
\begin{align}
 \max_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(2)}|&=o(1),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(2)}|&=O(N^{-1}),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}(p_{ij}^{(2)})^2&=o(N^{-1}),
 \\
 \max_i\frac1N\sum_j|p_{ij}^{(2)}|&=o(N^{-1/2}).
 
\end{align}
No stronger polynomial rate follows from \eqref{eq:spike-package} alone.

DRAFT author proof, not a result about critical Z^3. On the finite path a-b-z_1-...-z_(m-1)-c-d with m>=1 bridge edges between b and c and uniform parameter t=beta J>0, sample independent random currents n1,n2,n3,n4 with sources {a,b},{c,d},empty,empty. Put p=tanh(t)^2. Then q=P(b connected to c in n1+n2)=p^m, while r=P(C_b(n1+n3) intersects C_c(n2+n4))=[1+m(1-p)]p^m. Thus q/r=1/[1+m(1-p)] tends to zero at fixed t, refuting a positive graph-uniform constant q>=c r. This does not refute a nonlinear comparison or a critical Z^3 comparison.
Finite path, zero field, uniform ferromagnetic t>0
Independent currents with the four specified source sets
The obstruction concerns linear graph-uniform comparisons only

[Corollary 32 (Associativity, filtration, and iterated products) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] The product $\star$ is associative for composable deterministic Hilbert
spaces.  For a fixed deterministic Hilbert space $\cC$, the classes are
nested in the radius and
\begin{equation}

 \mathscr A_r^{\mathrm{an}}(\cC)
 :=\bigcup_{B\ge0}\mathscr A_r(B;\cC,\cC)
\end{equation}
is an associative algebra filtered by
\[
 \mathscr A_r(C;\cC,\cC)\star
 \mathscr A_r(B;\cC,\cC)
 \subset \mathscr A_r(B+C;\cC,\cC).
\]
If
\[
 \mathbf K^{(j)}\in
 \mathscr A_r(B_j;\cC_{j-1},\cC_j),
 \qquad 1\le j\le N,
\]
then
\begin{align}

 &\norm{\mathbf K^{(N)}\star\cdots\star\mathbf K^{(1)}}
 _{\mathscr A_r(B_1+\cdots+B_N)}\notag\\
 &\qquad\le
 \exp\!\left(\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}B_iB_j\right)
 \prod_{j=1}^N\norm{\mathbf K^{(j)}}_{\mathscr A_r(B_j)}.
\end{align}
When $\Id_{\cC}\in\Sch_r(\cC)$, the order-zero sequence
$(\Id_{\cC},0,\ldots)$ is a unit.

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2609.02385, 'Kinetic Fokker--Planck Equations with Drifts in a Supercritical Range'] A function $u\in L^1(Q_2)$ belongs to the De Giorgi class $\cD\cG_{\sI}^+(Q)$ if there are $\bbp_i\in\sI$, $i=1,\ldots,m$, $1\leq j<m$, $\l,\, \cA\geq0$, such that for any $\bbp\in\sI$, there exists a constant $C_\bbp>0$ such that, for every $\bbp\in\sI$, $1\leq\tau<\s\leq2$, and $\k>0$,

Then the damped Sine--Gordon Markov cocycle \eqref{e.060402} has a unique stationary measure $\mu_\s^{\eps}$ that attracts transition probabilities exponentially under the Wasserstein metric $\mathbb{W}_{\|\cdot\|_X\wedge1}$.  
  
  Moreover, for $m$-a.e. $\s\in\Sigma$, the family $\{\mu_\s^{\eps}\}_{\eps\in(0,1]}$ obeys the upper bound Freidlin--Wentzell LDP with a good rate function.  If the pullback attractor of the limiting deterministic Sine--Gordon cocycle consists of a single random point, then the full LDP holds with the same rate function. [Lem 143 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $0\leq \ell\leq \ubl$ we have:
  \begin{align}
  
  \bbE[
  U^\ell-U^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,\cF^U(\ell-1)]
  &=0,
  \\
  
  \bbE[
  Y^\ell-Y^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell-1)]
  =
   \bbE[
  Y^\ell-Y^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^U(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0,
  \\
  
  \bbE[
  V^\ell-V^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^V(\ell-1)]
  &=0,
  \\
  
  \bbE[
  M^\ell-M^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^M(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[M^\ell-M^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^V(\ell-1)]
   &=
  0
  .
  \end{align}

\begin{proof}
We will show inductively that
\eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal}
implies
\eqref{eq:y-increments-orthogonal},
which implies
\eqref{eq:v-increments-orthogonal},
which implies 
\eqref{eq:m-increments-orthogonal},
which finally implies
\eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal}
with $\ell+1$ in place of $\ell$.
In the base case, \eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal} with $\ell=1$ is trivial, since $U^0=0$, $\mathcal{F}^U(0)$ is the $\sigma$-field generated by $Y[0]$, and $U^1$ is a centered gaussian random variable independent of $Y[0]$. We therefore proceed with the inductive argument:

\begin{itemize}
\item
\eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:y-increments-orthogonal}: from the definition
\eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments},
  \[
  \E\Big(Y^\ell-Y^{\ell-1} 
  \,\Big|\,
  \cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell-1)\Big)
  = \frac{w^{\ell-1}
  (\prxY^{\ell-1})}{\gamma(\ell-1,\delta)}
  \E \Big(U^\ell-U^{\ell-1} 
  \,\Big|\,
  \cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell-1)\Big)\,.
  \]
We also claim
that $\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell)$
is contained in 
$\cF^U(\ell)$ for all $\ell$: indeed, in the base case we have $\cF^{Y,\prxY}(0) =\cF^U(0)$, so if we suppose inductively that 
$\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell)$ is contained in $\cF^U(\ell)$, then
\eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments}  implies 
\[\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell+1)
\subseteq \sigma\Big(
\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell),
\cF^U(\ell+1)
\Big)
\subseteq \cF^U(\ell+1)
\,,\]
which verifies the inductive hypothesis. Thus \eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal} implies that the above equals zero, which in turn verifies \eqref{eq:y-increments-orthogonal}.

\item 
\eqref{eq:y-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:v-increments-orthogonal}: we apply the state evolution recursion \eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}, where
we recall from \eqref{e:h.l.k.explicit}
that $h_{\ell,k}=a_k Y^\ell$.  It follows that for $k\le s\le \ell -1$,
  \begin{align*}
  &\E\Big[(V^{\ell,k}-V^{\ell-1,k}) V^{s,k}\Big]\\
  &\qquad\stackrel{\eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup}}{=}
  \E\bigg[\Big( 
  h_{\ell,k}(U[[\ell]],
  	 Y[0] 
	)
  -h_{\ell-1,k}(U[[\ell-1]],
  	 Y[0] 
	\Big)
  h_{s,k}( U[[s]],
  	 Y[0] 
	)\bigg]
  \\
  &\qquad
  \stackrel{\eqref{e:h.l.k.explicit}}{=}
  (a_k)^2
  \E\Big[(Y^\ell-Y^{\ell-1})
  Y^s
  \Big]
  =0\,,
  \end{align*}
where the last step is by the inductive hypothesis \eqref{eq:y-increments-orthogonal}. Recall also from \eqref{eq:state-evolution-setup} that $V^{\ell_1,k_1}$ and $V^{\ell_2,k_2}$ are uncorrelated for $k_1\ne k_2$, so the above implies
  \[
  \E\Big[(V^\ell-V^{\ell-1}) 
  V^s\Big]=0
  \]
for $s\le \ell-1$. Since the $V^{\ell,k}$ are jointly gaussian, it follows that $V^\ell-V^{\ell-1}$ is independent of $V[[\ell-1]]$, thus yielding \eqref{eq:v-increments-orthogonal}.

	\sigma\Big(
	\cF^{X,\prxX}(\ell),

[Theorem teo:chfintpro of arXiv:2411.19192, 'Characteristic function and Esscher transform of a switching Levy model for the temperatur'] Let $(\xi_t)_{t \geq 0}$ be a two-regime switching Levy process starting at regime one, with  log-cumulant generating function $l_{\xi^l}$ when the process is at regime $l=1,2$. Then,
 \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber
  E [ exp( i \int_0^t f(s)\;d \xi_s) ]&=&  \left( \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}  M_1(k) [ p_{2k}(t)+ \lambda_{12} J_1  p_{2k+1}(t) ] \right)\\ \nonumber
   && \left( \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}   J_3(t,k)   p_{2k}(t) +  \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}   J_4(t,k) p_{2k+1}(t) \right) \\ 
  &&
\end{eqnarray}
where:
\begin{eqnarray*}
 J_1&=& \int_0^{+\infty} e^{I_{1}(x)}e^{-\lambda_{12}x}\; dx, \;\;J_2= \int_0^{+\infty} e^{I_{2}(x)}e^{-\lambda_{21}x}\; dx \\
 J_3(t,k)&=& D(k, -k, 2k) \sum_{l=0}^{+\infty}C(k,2k,l) G_1(t,2k+l)\lambda^l_{21} \\
 J_4(t,k) &=& D(k+1, -k, 2k+1) \sum_{l=0}^{+\infty}C(k+1,2k+1,l) G_2(t,2k+l+1) \lambda^l_{21} \\
G_j( t,m) &=& \int_0^{t} e^{I_j(t-z)}  z^{m-1}e^{-\lambda_{21}  z} \;dz,\; j=1,2 \\
 M_1(k) &=& \lambda^k_{12} \lambda^k_{21} J^k_1 J^k_2
\end{eqnarray*}
and
\begin{equation*}
  I_j(x)=\int_0^x l_{\xi^{j}}(-if(s))\;  ds, \;\;j=1,2
\end{equation*}
Expressions for $ p_{2k}(t)$ and  $ p_{2k+1}(t)$ are given in the  lemma (lemma:tausdistrib of the paper).

[Corollary 8 (Black--Scholes coefficients) of arXiv:2605.31471, 'Convergence Rates of Continuous-Time Random Walks to Time-Fractional Diffusions with Unbou'] Consider the componentwise geometric Brownian motion
    \[
        dX_t^i=\mu_iX_t^i\,dt+\sigma_iX_t^i\,dW_t^i,
        \qquad i=1,\dots,k,
    \]
    started from $x\in(0,\infty)^k$.  The natural state space is the
    invariant domain $(0,\infty)^k$, although the coefficients extend
    linearly to $\R^k$.  Put
    \[
        K_{\mathrm{GBM}}
        :=
        \max_{1\le i\le k}\{|\mu_i|,|\sigma_i|\}.
    \]
    Then Assumption~\ref{asm:classical} holds with
    $K=K_{\mathrm{GBM}}$ and $d=k$: first derivatives are bounded by
    $K_{\mathrm{GBM}}$ and all derivatives of order at least two vanish.
    For the quartic weight $W=1+|x|^4$, Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted_estim_tensor_poly}
    gives the explicit Lyapunov coefficient
    \[
        C_2=(8K_{\mathrm{GBM}}+24K_{\mathrm{GBM}}^2)d.
    \]
    If the random-walk and clock assumptions in
    Corollary~\ref{cor:frac-bounded-derivatives} also hold for the chosen
    discretization, then the bounded-derivative fractional estimate
    \eqref{eq:frac_main} applies to $f\in D_4$ whenever
    $c\ge\mu_4\ge\bar\mu_W$, where $\mu_4$ is the renormed $D_4$ growth
    bound from Corollary~\ref{coro:norm_estim} and $\bar\mu_W$ may be taken
    from the above Lyapunov coefficient.  In the scalar case
    $\mu=0.05$, $\sigma=0.2$, $K_{\mathrm{GBM}}=0.2$, and $d=1$, this gives
    $C_2=8(0.2)+24(0.2)^2=2.56$; the minimum killing condition in this
    theorem remains $c\ge\mu_4$.
    The estimate is stated for the linear extension of the coefficients to
    $\R^k$; the one-step increment $x+\eta_h(x)$ may leave the positivity
    domain $(0,\infty)^k$, so positivity-preserving discretizations are a
    separate matter not addressed here. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:61540c5a30665f23d715dfa877ed36851d4f5e6b8bcc57c61ae9d265cd7eb3e0","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/61/61540c5a30665f23d715dfa877ed36851d4f5e6b8bcc57c61ae9d265cd7eb3e0.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:7c673ab1f544f0e3955fcd92879e554a7907834c68728a34330c1cedd7cbda10","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-tangent-shared-quadratic-form","bundle_id":"population.t244-tanh-tangent-shared-wishart-noise-017","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_017.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-tangent-shared-quadratic-form","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Critical tanh: exact tangent kernel and its shared Wishart noise

20 October 2026. C050/C051; Target 3. Proof drafts, unaudited.
These are infinitesimal-angle one-step results, not a two-input tanh
diffusion theorem or an all-order cumulant expansion. No novelty asserted.

## C050: exact positive-variance kernel

Fix n>=2 and q>0. Let g,h be independent N(0,I_n) vectors. For two inputs
with equal preactivation variance q and angle theta, the next activated
vectors are exactly distributed as

    x = tanh(sqrt(q) g),
    y(theta) = tanh(sqrt(q)(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h)).

The independent Gaussian weight rows give these conditional marginals
given the present Gram matrix. The tanh critical weight variance is 1/n;
thus the next diagonal variance is K'=||x||^2/n and the radial multiplier
is M_q=||x||^2/(nq). There is no width-dependent shaping normalizer.

Set D=diag(sech^2(sqrt(q)g_i)), P_x=I-xx^T/||x||^2. Then the right-hand
derivative H_q of the angle between x and y(theta) at theta=0 is

    H_q^2 = q h^T D P_x D h / ||x||^2.

Proof: y(0)=x and y'(0)=sqrt(q)Dh. The derivative of y/||y|| is
sqrt(q)P_x Dh/||x||, whose norm is the nonnegative angular speed.
Almost surely x is nonzero and this speed is positive for n>=2.

Conditionally on g, Q_q=h^T D P_x D h is a sum of n-1 independent
chi-square_1 variables with positive weights equal to the nonzero
eigenvalues lambda_j of D P_x D. These satisfy

    d_min^2 <= lambda_j <= 1,
    d_min = min_i sech^2(sqrt(q)g_i).

Indeed these nonzero eigenvalues equal those of P_x D^2 P_x restricted
to x-perp, whose Rayleigh quotients lie in that interval. Both M_q and
the conditional weights depend on the same g. In particular the exact
positive-q model must retain this conditioning; replacing Q_q by an
independent chi-square is a different kernel. Even the radial sum
||x||^2/q is bounded above by n/q, unlike a chi-square variable.

For fixed n, q decreases to zero gives jointly, almost surely under the
original (g,h) coupling,

    M_q -> S/n,      H_q -> sqrt(R/S),
    S=||g||^2 ~ chi-square_n,
    R=h^T P_g h ~ chi-square_(n-1),  R independent of g and hence of S.

The independence follows because the conditional law of R given g is
the same chi-square_(n-1) law for every nonzero g. The SAME S appears in
the radial multiplier and angular denominator. For n=1 the tangent
speed is zero, so logarithmic angular statements below exclude n=1.

## C051: uniform leading noise at the critical variance scale

For every fixed C<infinity, uniformly over 0<q<=C/n, define

    A_q=log M_q,       B_q=log H_q.

As n increases,

    n Cov((A_q,B_q)) -> [[2,-1],[-1,1]].

Here Cov is centered covariance. Equivalently, replacing B_q by the
logarithmic reciprocal-angle multiplier -B_q changes both off-diagonal
entries to +1. This only identifies one-step noise, not a drift limit.

### Coupling and quantitative error

Draw g and, independently, eta_1,...,eta_(n-1) iid standard normals.
Use a measurable ordering of the eigenvalues above and put

    Q_q^* = sum_j lambda_j(g) eta_j^2,
    R^* = sum_j eta_j^2,       S=||g||^2.

The pair (M_q, sqrt(q Q_q^*/||x||^2)) has EXACTLY the required joint
law (M_q,H_q), by the conditional quadratic-form law. Also S and R^*
are independent chi-squares with the stated degrees of freedom.
Thus this construction verifies both coupled marginals. No pointwise
comparison with the original h projection is being asserted.

For z>=0, sech^2(z) <= tanh(z)/z <= 1, with the continuous value at zero.
Consequently, with Z=max_i |g_i|,

    d_min^2 <= ||x||^2/(qS) <= 1,
    d_min^2 <= Q_q^*/R^* <= 1.

Since log(cosh z)<=z^2/2, this yields the deterministic coupling bounds

    |A_q-log(S/n)| <= 2q Z^2,
    |B_q-(1/2)log(R^*/S)| <= q Z^2.

A Gaussian union bound P(Z^2>r)<=min(1,2n exp(-r/2)), integrated as
E Z^4=integral_0^infinity 2r P(Z^2>r)dr, gives
||Z^2||_2 <= C_0 log(2n). Hence each logarithmic error has L2 norm at
most C_1 q log(2n), without deleting any event or inverse tail.

### Covariance calculation

Let A_0=log(S/n), B_0=(log R^*-log S)/2. Gamma integration gives

    Var A_0 = psi_1(n/2),
    Cov(A_0,B_0) = -(1/2)psi_1(n/2),
    Var B_0 = (psi_1((n-1)/2)+psi_1(n/2))/4.

The trigamma series psi_1(z)=sum_(k>=0)(z+k)^(-2) and integral comparison
give psi_1(z)=1/z+O(z^-2). These identities can alternatively be obtained
by differentiating E S^t=2^t Gamma(n/2+t)/Gamma(n/2) at t=0.
The displayed baseline covariance therefore has the claimed limit
after multiplying by n, and its centered L2 norms are O(n^-1/2).

For centered random variables, covariance perturbation by L2 errors e
has size at most C(n^-1/2 ||e||_2 + ||e||_2^2); centering an error costs
no more than its L2 norm. After multiplying by n, our bound is

    O(sqrt(n) q log(2n) + n q^2 log(2n)^2)
       = O_C(log(2n)/sqrt(n) + log(2n)^2/n),

uniformly over 0<q<=C/n. This tends to zero and proves C051.

## Scope left open

The limits are: first the angle derivative at zero for fixed n,q,
then n -> infinity with q<=C/n. C051 does not justify exchanging the
infinitesimal-angle limit with a finite-angle network evolution, does
not give the order-1/n drift, and does not establish that actual tanh
input correlations approach one. The scalar critical-tanh diffusion
and cumulant-rate work remain separate claims C026-C027 and C044-C047.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:22c6d532d863fd81ef53240a00570657817f6c17e8e5fb0515c76a33cfbda523","revision_digest":"sha256:85f5ca6e4c11faf59b3859d20fd8b9c840a142c102084630954bf5c6cc79c24a","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C050:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T13:53:12.705197","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: Let X be a Banach space and (x_n) a sequence in X converging weakly to x. Then there exists a sequence (y_k) of finite convex combinations of the x_n, that is, each y_k = sum_i lambda_i^{(k)} x_i for finitely many indices i with lambda_i^{(k)} >= 0 and sum_i lambda_i^{(k)} = 1, such that y_k converges to x in norm. Equivalently, the norm-closed convex hull of {x_n : n >= 1} contains x and equals its weak closure. [standard, e.g. Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and PDEs]
title: Mazur's Theorem (Convex Combinations of a Weakly Convergent Sequence)

[Lemma of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $P(r_{j\wedge\tau}<r_{(j+1)\wedge\tau}\,|\,\tau>j)=1$ and, therefore, $K_{j\wedge\tau}$ is almost surely in descending order.
    \begin{proof}
        The first descent in the permutation of cards that appear is uniquely seen after card $n$ is shown. Prior to card $n$ being shown, the cards are in ascending order. After card $n$ is shown, the cards are in descending order. This is because card $n$ is the first card placed into the pile. Cards must be placed, from the bottom of the deck, on top or on the bottom of the pile. This preserves the relative order if placed on the top and reverses the relative order if placed on the bottom.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear (H(p)/|p| → ∞), let L = H* be its Legendre transform, and let g: R^n → R be Lipschitz. Define u(x,t) := min_{y ∈ R^n} ( t L((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) for t > 0, u(x,0) := g(x). Then: (i) the minimum is attained, u(·,t) is Lipschitz with constant at most Lip(g) for every t > 0, and |u(x,t) - g(x)| ≤ C t with C = max( |L(0)| , max_{|p| ≤ Lip(g)} |H(p)| ); hence u is Lipschitz on R^n × [0,∞) and attains the initial data continuously. (ii) u is differentiable almost everywhere in R^n × (0,∞), and at every point of differentiability u_t(x,t) + H(Du(x,t)) = 0. (iii) u is a viscosity solution of u_t + H(Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,∞) with u(·,0) = g. (iv) If in addition g is bounded, then for every T > 0, u is the unique viscosity solution of this Cauchy problem in the class of bounded Lipschitz functions on R^n × [0,T].
H: R^n → R finite, convex, superlinear (continuity is automatic from finiteness and convexity)
L = H* so that L is finite, convex and superlinear and L* = H
g: R^n → R Lipschitz continuous
for (iv): g in addition bounded, and uniqueness asserted only among bounded Lipschitz viscosity solutions
(ii) asserts the equation only at points of differentiability; a.e. solutions are not unique, so (ii) alone does not characterize u

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For f: {-1,1}^n -> R with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_S hat{f}(S) chi_S and the noise operator T_rho, which independently resamples each coordinate to a fresh uniform sign with probability 1-rho (equivalently, flips each coordinate with probability (1-rho)/2, so that each coordinate keeps correlation rho with the input), the Bonami-Beckner inequality states ||T_rho f||_q <= ||f||_p whenever 1 <= p <= q and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.
uniform (or explicitly known-bias) product measure on {-1,1}^n or {0,1}^n
f in the relevant L^p space, typically boolean or bounded
the noise parameter rho within the sharp Bonami-Beckner range 0<=rho<=sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))
a well-defined Fourier-Walsh expansion, i.e. finite n or a suitable limiting argument

[Theorem 15 (Matched-spectrum orientation dependence) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Let $X_0\sim\calN(0,\Sigma)$ with eigenvalues
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d>0$, let $1\le d_y\le d$, let
$A\in\R^{d_y\times d}$, and let $R_A=AX_0+\varepsilon$ with
$\varepsilon\sim\calN(0,\sigma_y^2\Id_{d_y})$.  Assume
$AA^\top=\Id_{d_y}$.  Thus every admissible $A$ has the same nonzero singular
values; isotropic measurement noise leaves orientation relative to \(\Sigma\)
as the only design variable.  Define
\[
C_\gamma=(\Sigma^{-1}+\gamma\Id_d)^{-1},
\qquad
\Sigma_A^{\rm post}
=
(\Sigma^{-1}+\sigma_y^{-2}A^\top A)^{-1},
\qquad
\psi_\gamma(\lambda)
=
\frac12\log
\frac{\sigma_y^2+\lambda}
{\sigma_y^2+\lambda/(1+\gamma\lambda)}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}

\mathcal M_\gamma(A)=\MI(R_A;Y_\gamma)
=
\frac12\log
\frac{\det(\sigma_y^2\Id_{d_y}+A\Sigma A^\top)}
{\det(\sigma_y^2\Id_{d_y}+AC_\gamma A^\top)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, among all row-orthonormal rank-$d_y$ measurements,
\begin{align}

\frac12\sum_{i=d-d_y+1}^{d}
\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lambda_i}{\sigma_y^2}\right)
&\le \MI(X_0;R_A)
\le
\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d_y}
\log\!\left(1+\frac{\lambda_i}{\sigma_y^2}\right),\\

2\MI(X_0;R_A)
&=
\log\frac{\det\Sigma}{\det\Sigma_A^{\rm post}},\\

\sum_{i=d-d_y+1}^{d}\psi_\gamma(\lambda_i)
&\le \mathcal M_\gamma(A)
\le
\sum_{i=1}^{d_y}\psi_\gamma(\lambda_i).
\end{align}
For every $\gamma>0$, $\psi_\gamma$ is strictly increasing.  Equality in the
upper (respectively, lower) bounds is attained by choosing the row space of
$A$ to be the span of the largest (respectively, smallest) $d_y$ prior
eigenvectors.  If the boundary eigenvalue is repeated, the extremizing row
space need not be unique: the required dimensions may be chosen arbitrarily
within that eigenspace.  Hence equal operator
singular values do not determine clean
measurement information, posterior covariance-volume contraction, or
reverse-path assimilation once the prior is anisotropic. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Matched-spectrum orientation dependence

The characteristic exponent \alpha \in (0, 2] of a stable distribution determines the decay rate of its tails. When \alpha = 2, the distribution is normal (Gaussian), all moments exist, and the tails decay exponentially. When 0 < \alpha < 2, the distribution has heavy tails: \mathbb{P}(|X| > x) \sim c x^{-\alpha} as x \to \infty, so \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] < \infty for all 0 < p < \alpha, but \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] = \infty for all p \ge \alpha.
\alpha \in (0, 2]

body: [Theorem 5 (Self-loop PageRank increase) of arXiv:2503.19927, 'Fully personalized PageRank and algebraic methods to distribute a random walker'] Let G = (V, E) be a strongly connected graph, with row-normalized adjacency matrix P. If we allow a node to establish an arbitrary number of self-loops onto itself (alternatively, a single self-loop with arbitrarily high weight), then for 1 −1/w ≤α ≤1 that node can always achieve the highest PageRank value.

body: Concept (campaign status: open, evidence strong): CONJECTURE - for every linear NAE triangle system, SOME choice of one pair per triangle yields a pair-sum span that is an admissible residual space (valid_R). Since c = k*beta - ell is intrinsic, every choice-graph shares one Z, so the choice is free on the Ising side, and the lemma would give d_cb <= |V| - b and hence Conjecture RC for ALL linear systems via cut-inflation. Evidence: on the single system where the fixed shared-pair rule failed, 725 of 729 pair-choices are admissible (min dim 5); a 60-system chosen-pair sweep found zero systems with no admissible choice, tight on trees (slack exactly 0). Structure of the obstruction: a signed extra like e_0 - e_1 + e_2 is covered exactly when the choice-graph places its two same-signed coordinates in one component on the same bipartition side (their difference then dies in R) or in a non-bipartite component (whose generator vanishes) - so the general lemma is a simultaneous matching problem over the 3^k choices.

[Lemma 15 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Let \((\Omega,\Fc,\P)\) be a probability space supporting two processes
\((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) and \((Z_t)_{t\ge0}\), jointly measurable in \((t,\omega)\).
Assume that, for every \(T>0\),
$
    \E [
    \int_0^T |Z_s|\,ds
    ]<\infty.
$
Then there exists a Borel-measurable function
$
    \hat z:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d
$
such that
\[
    \hat z(t,X_t)
    =
    \E[Z_t\mid X_t],
    \qquad
    \text{for a.e. }t\ge0,\ \P\text{-a.s.}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 15 of arXiv:2605.30560

[Defn hschwpop of arXiv:2601.09537, 'Gene genealogies in haploid populations evolving according to sweepstakes reproduction'] Consider a haploid, panmictic population evolving in discrete
(non-overlapping) generations.  In any given generation each of the
current individuals independently produces a random number of
potential offspring according to some given law.  If the total number
of potential offspring produced in this way is at least some given
number  \textcolor{black}{$M$},  then $M$ of them sampled uniformly at random without
replacement survive to maturity and replace the current individuals;
the remaining potential offspring perish.  Otherwise we will assume an
unchanged population over the generation (all the potential offspring
perish before reaching maturity).
title: Evolution of the population

[Lem 1 of arXiv:2605.03528, '\bf Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance and discrepancies {\em versus} Wasserstein distances'] $(a)$ Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ two probability measures on $([0,1]^d, {\cal B}or([0,1]^d),\lambda_d)$. Then
\[
D^{\infty}(\mu,\nu) \ge  \sup_{x,\, y\in [0,1]^d} \big| \mu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big) -  \nu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big)\big|.
\]
$(b)$ If furthermore, $\mu\big((0,1]^d\big)= \nu\big((0,1]^d\big) =1$, then 
\[
D^{\infty}(\mu,\nu) = \sup_{x,\, y\in [0,1]^d} \big| \mu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big) -  \nu\big(]\!]x,y]\!]\big)\big|.
\]
$(c)$ Without the additional assumption of $(b)$, we have:
\[
D^{\infty}(\mu,\nu) = \sup_{x,\, y\in [0,1]^d, x\preceq y} \big| \mu\big(]\![x,y]\!]\big) -  \nu\big(]\![x,y]\!]\big)\big|,
\]
where $]\![x,y]\!]$ is defined by 
$$]\![x,y]\!]=\begin{cases}
]\!]x,y]\!]\textnormal{ if $x^i>0,\,\forall \, i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$}\\
 \left\{u\in[0,1]^d, x^i<u^i\le y^i \textnormal{ if  $x^i>0$}, 0\le u^i\le  y^i \textnormal{ if  $x^i=0$}\right\}\textnormal{ otherwise.}
 \end{cases}
 $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.31300, 'Cone-Additive Functions for Random Walks on Free Products of Graphs'] Consider a function 
$$
f: \Pi\to\mathbb{R}, \pi \mapsto f(\pi).
$$
Then $f$ is called  \textit{cone-additive} w.r.t. $P$ if the following two properties hold:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item 
Additivity property: for all $n\in\N$,
$$
f\bigl([X_0,\ldots,X_n]\bigr)= \sum_{j=1}^{\mathbf{k}(n)} f(\pi_j) + f(\pi^\ast_{n}) \quad \textrm{ almost surely.}
$$
\item Shift invariance: for all $j\in\N$, 
\begin{equation}
f(\pi_j)=f\bigl(X_{\e_{j-1}}^{-1}\pi_j\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

Let p and q be probability mass functions on a nonempty finite set and p x q their independent coupling, whose disagreement probability is 1 - sum_x p(x) q(x). The following are equivalent: (i) p x q has the least disagreement d_TV(p, q) among couplings; (ii) it has the greatest, 1 - max_x (p(x) + q(x) - 1)_+; (iii) all couplings of p and q have the same disagreement probability; (iv) p and q have disjoint supports, or p or q is a point mass. Otherwise the independent coupling's disagreement lies strictly between the least and the greatest.

[Prop P:weighted-quadrangle of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Consider a weighted directed acyclic graph $G = (V, E, M)$, and let $H = (V, E, M')$ be another one with the same vertices and edges, but different weights satisfying $M' \le M$, with equality on a set $W \subset V$. Consider vertices $x_1 \prec y_1$ and $x_2 \prec y_2$ and suppose that we have the following {\bf path-crossing} property:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Let $\tau$ be any path from $x_1$ to $y_1$ and $\pi = (\pi_0, \dots, \pi_k)$ be any path from $x_2$ to $y_2$. Then if $\pi_i \notin W$ for some $i \in \llbracket1, k-1 \rrbracket$, there are indices $i^- < i < i^+$ such that the vertices $\pi(i^-), \pi(i^+)$ are on the path $\tau$.
\end{itemize}
Then
$$
H(x_1; y_1) + G(x_2 ; y_2)  \le G(x_1; y_1) + H(x_2 ; y_2).

body: In spectral graph theory, the Alon–Boppana bound provides a lower bound on the second-largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix of a -regular graph, meaning a graph in which every vertex has degree . The reason for the interest in the second-largest eigenvalue is that the largest eigenvalue is guaranteed to be due to -regularity, with the all-ones vector being the associated eigenvector. The graphs that come close to meeting this bound are Ramanujan graphs, which are examples of the best possible expander graphs.

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $m,n\in\Nsf$, $[S,T]\subseteq\Rsf$ be an interval, $p\in[1,3)$, and $\omega$ a control function on interval $[S,T]$. Let $X=(X^\tau)$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $M$ be an $m$-dimensional manifold and let $f: M\to R_n^2M$ be a rough velocity field. Let $Y:[S,T]\to M$ be a continuous function such that for every $r\in [S,T]$ there exists
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\itemsep0em
    \item an interval $[u,v] \subset [S,T]$ that contains $r$ in its relative interior and such that we either have $v = T$ or $\omega(r,v) > 0$,
    \item a chart $(U, x)$ whose domain contains the image of $[u,v]$ under $Y$, and
    \item a constant $C\in (0,\infty)$
\end{enumerate}
such that inequality~\eqref{eq:integral-curve}, where $(Y^i)$ is the representation of $Y$ in the chart $(U,x)$ and $(f^i_\tau)$ is the representation of $f$ in the induced chart $(\overline{U},\overline{x})$, holds for every $i\in \llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta [u,v]$. Then $Y$ is an integral curve of the rough velocity field $f$ driven by the rough path $X$.

body:
Let X be a real N-by-n design of rank q>=1 with q<n, Y an N-by-m response matrix, and hidden width h>=min(m,n). Consider continuous Euclidean gradient flow on L(U,V)=||Y-X U V^T||F^2/2, U n-by-h, V m-by-h. Choose an orthonormal basis Phi1 of the data row space, set U1=Phi1^T U, and let a=lambda_q(X^T X)>0 be the smallest positive design-covariance eigenvalue. The latent imbalance D=U1^T U1-V^T V is constant along the flow. Using decreasing eigenvalues with lambda_i=0 when i exceeds the matrix dimension, define delta_eff=max(lambda_q(D),0)+max(lambda_m(-D),0). If delta_eff>0 at initialization, the excess over the unrestricted linear-regression optimum obeys L(t)-L_star<=exp(-2a delta_eff t)(L(0)-L_star) for every t>=0. This is the sufficient-imbalance specialization of Min, Tarmoun, Vidal and Mallada, Convergence and Implicit Bias of Gradient Flow on Overparametrized Linear Networks, arXiv:2105.06351, Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 (printed pp.9-10), with the zero-padding convention on p.4 and delta_eff in equation (20), p.8. Positive definiteness of the h-by-h D alone is insufficient when q>h: its q-th eigenvalue is zero by convention, while all eigenvalues of -D are negative (or zero-padded). This is a continuous-time sufficient condition, not a discrete-GD or proper-bottleneck initialization theorem.
Real finite data with 1<=rank(X)=q<n; hidden width h>=min(m,n)
Euclidean continuous gradient flow; unrestricted linear-regression comparator
Effective imbalance delta_eff>0, with the precise zero-padded eigenvalue indices

body: [Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.30991, 'A block-Toeplitz approach to the spectrum of the Neumann-Poincaré operator on self-similar'] The scaled single layer operator $\widetilde{\mathbb{S}}_{\frac{d-1}{2}}$ is self-adjoint, negative definite, and injective in $\ell^2\big(\mathbb{N},L_0^2(\Gamma_0)\big)$. Furthermore, it extends to a coercive isomorphism from the weighted sequence space $D^{-1/2}\ell^2\big(\mathbb{N},H_0^{-1/2}(\Gamma_0)\big)$ onto its dual space $D^{1/2}\ell^2\big(\mathbb{N},H_0^{1/2}(\Gamma_0)\big)$, the duality being that of the $\ell^2$ pairing, for which the two weights are conjugate.

The formula 1-exp(-t^2/2-t) is not the exact distribution function of sqrt(n) times the least singular value of an n-by-n real Gaussian matrix at every finite n. For n=1 and t=1, the exact value is erf(1/sqrt(2))=0.6826894921, while the proposed formula gives 0.7768698399. Use the finite-n CDF F_n or a valid finite-n bound such as F_n(t)<=t instead.

[Lemma 20 (Exact symmetry of the finite chain) of arXiv:2608.30991, 'A block-Toeplitz approach to the spectrum of the Neumann-Poincaré operator on self-similar'] Write $\ell^2_N:=\ell^2\bigl(\{0,\dots,N-1\},H^{-1/2}_0(\Gamma_0)\bigr)$. For
	every $N\ge1$,
	\[
	T_N(\tau)\,\mathbb A_N=\mathbb A_N^*\,T_N(\tau),
	\]
	and there are constants $0<c\le C$ independent of $N$ with
	\[
	c\,\|u\|^2_{\ell^2_N}\le\langle T_N(\tau)u,u\rangle\le C\,\|u\|^2_{\ell^2_N},
	\qquad u\in\ell^2_N .
	\]
	Consequently $\mathbb A_N$ is compact and self-adjoint for the inner product
	$\langle T_N(\tau)\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ on $\ell^2_N$, with real eigenvalues.
