body:
[Definition def:walkbridge of arXiv:2411.12149, 'Airy limit for $\beta$-additions through Dunkl operators'] For $H_{1},H_{2}\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, $L\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$, $N\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$, $\mathcal{\tilde{W}}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)$ is the set of walk bridges of length $L$  from $H_{1}$ to $H_{2}$. 
    $\mathcal{W}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)$ is the set of walk bridges $W(t)$ of length $L$ from $H_{1}$ to $H_{2}$, such that $W(t)\ge0$ for all $t$ in its domain.
    
    For each element in $\mathcal{\tilde{W}}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)$ or $\mathcal{W}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)$, by viewing the increments of $W(t)$ as i.i.d. random variables with distribution $\mu(N)$, defined in Eqn.~((eq_rvx of the paper)), we assign a weight to each walk bridge as $$\text{weight}(W)=\prod_{l=-1}^{\infty}[P_{l}(N)V_{N}(z_{c}(N))]^{\# t:\ W(t)-W(t-)=l}.$$

    Let $$|\mathcal{\tilde{W}}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)|=\sum_{W\in \mathcal{\tilde{W}}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)}\text{weight}(W)$$
     be the \emph{partition function} of $\mathcal{\tilde{W}}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)$. The partition function of $\mathcal{W}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)$ is defined similarly.
title: Definition def:walkbridge of arXiv:2411.12149

[Definition 4 of arXiv:2609.00087, 'Translational tiles without spectra\\ in finite abelian $p$-groups'] A set $A\subset G$ is \emph{spectral} if there is a set
$\Lambda\subset\widehat G$ with $|\Lambda|=|A|$ such that the characters
in $\Lambda$, restricted to $A$, form an orthogonal basis of $\C^A$.
The set $\Lambda$ is then called a spectrum of $A$.

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2506.11918, 'Central limit theorems for the Euler characteristic in the Random Connection Model for hig'] For $F=\chi_a(\Delta_W)$ and pairwise different $x_1,x_2,x_3\in W$ it is true that
\begin{align*}
\E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_3,U_3),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^2 \left(\Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_3,U_3),(x_1,U_1)}^2 F\right)^2} \,&=\, \mathcal{O}\left(\beta^{4\alpha-4}\right), \\[10pt]
\E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^4 } \,&=\, \mathcal{O}\left(\beta^{4\alpha-4}\right), \\[10pt]
\E{ \left( \Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^1F \right)^2 \left( \Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_1,U_1)}^1F \right)^2} &= \mathcal{O}\left(\beta^{4\alpha}\right), \\[10pt]
\E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U)}F\right)^4 } \,=\, \mathcal{O}\left(\beta^{4\alpha}\right), \qquad\qquad
\E{ |\Lambda_{(x_1,U)}F|^3 } &= \mathcal{O}\left(\beta^{3\alpha}\right).
\end{align*}

body:
[Lem lem_app of arXiv:2603.29711, 'Strong Feller property, irreducibility,\\ and uniqueness of the invariant measure\\ for st'] The following properties hold.
        \begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]

For every $\varsigma\geq1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ 
it holds
that $m_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb R)$ and 
\[
  \norm{m_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}}_{L^\infty\left(\mathbb R\right)}
  \leq
\norm{m_\varsigma}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}+1,
\qquad
\norm{m'_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}\leq
\norm{m'_\varsigma}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}.
\]
\item[(ii)]

For every $\varsigma\geq1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ 
it holds
that 
\[
  \frac{1}{m_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}(r)}\le \frac{1}{\varepsilon^\varsigma} \quad \forall\, r \in \mathbb{R}.
\]
\item [(iii)]
 
For every $\varsigma\geq1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$
it holds that $\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}\in C^2(\mathbb R)$
is strictly convex, 
$\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}'$ is monotone increasing and $\frac{1}{\varepsilon^\varsigma}$-Lipschitz continuous,
with $\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}'(0)=0$, 
$m_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}''\equiv1$,
and 
\[
  \frac1{\norm{m_\varsigma}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}+1}\leq\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}''(r)\leq \frac1{\varepsilon^\varsigma}
  \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\]
\item [(iv)]

For every $\varsigma>1$, there exist $C_\varsigma, c_\varsigma>0$
such that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
it holds that 
\[
c_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma-1, \varepsilon}''(r)\leq 
|\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'(r)| 
\le C_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma-1, \varepsilon}''(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\]
\item [(v)]

For every $\varsigma\geq1$, there exist $C_\varsigma, c_\varsigma>0$
such that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
it holds that 
\begin{alignat*}{2}
c_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r) &\leq 
|\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'(r)| &&\le C_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R,\\
c_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+2, \varepsilon}(r) &\leq 
\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}''(r) &&\le C_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+2, \varepsilon}(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R,\\
c_\varsigma\Psi''_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r) &\leq 
|\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'''(r)| &&\le 
C_\varsigma\Psi''_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\end{alignat*}
\item [(viii)]

For every $\varsigma, \zeta \ge 1$, $\varsigma\le\zeta$,
there exists $C_{\varsigma,\zeta}>0$ such that,
for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, it holds that
\[
\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}(r)\leq C_{\varsigma,\zeta}
\Psi_\zeta(r) \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R, \qquad
\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}''(r)\leq C_{\varsigma,\zeta}
\Psi_\zeta''(r) \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\]
\item [(ix)]

For every $\varsigma, \zeta \geq 1$ with $\varsigma+\zeta>2$,
there is $K_{\varsigma,\zeta}>0$ such that,
for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, it holds 
    \[
    \Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'(r)
    \Psi_{\zeta, \varepsilon}'(r)
    \geq K_{\varsigma,\zeta}
    \Psi_{\varsigma+\zeta-2, \varepsilon}''(r) - K_{\varsigma,\zeta}^{-1} \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
    \]
   \end{itemize}

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] When flipping a coin, and with our winning function being
$$f:\big\{{\rm heads},\,{\rm tails}\big\}\to\mathbb R\quad,\quad f({\rm heads})=a\quad,\quad f({\rm tails})=b$$
with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, what we can expect to win, on average, is the quantity
$$E(f)=ap+b(1-p)$$
in the case of a biased coin. For a normal coin, this reads $E(f)=(a+b)/2$.
title: Unnumbered proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

[Def 11 of arXiv:2608.30990, 'Convergence of symmetries: nilpotency, dimension, and perfectness'] Given a metric  space $(X,d)$ and two subsets $A,B \subset X$, the \emph{Hausdorff distance} between them (denoted $d_H(A,B)$) is defined to be
\[    \max\{  \sup \{  \inf \{ d(a,b) \, \vert \, b \in B \} \, \vert \, a \in A \} ,    \sup \{  \inf \{ d(a,b) \, \vert \, a \in A \} \, \vert \, b \in B \}      \} .         \]
We say that a sequence of subsets $A_i \subset X$ \emph{converges in the Hausdorff topology} to a subset $A \subset X$ if $d_H(A_i , A) \to 0$ as $i \to \infty$.
title: Definition 11 of arXiv:2608.30990

[Lemma prob_cycles of arXiv:2603.28936, 'Composition of random functions and word reconstruction'] Let $\pi$ be a primitive word.
Let $Q\geq 1$,  $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_Q\geq 1$ and $\ell=\max_{q\in [Q]}\ell_q$.
Let $V_1,\dots,V_Q$ be independent uniform vertices in $[n]$.
	The probability that for all $q\in [Q]$,  $V_q$ belongs to a cycle of length $\ell_q$ of $\boldsymbol{\pi}$, and that these cycles are all distinct, is $\displaystyle n^{-Q}+O_{\ell}\bigl(n^{-(Q+1)}\bigr)$.

[Thm exist max slope of arXiv:2509.08659, 'Gap metrics for stationary point processes and quantitative convexity of the free energy'] Consider the metric space $( X^{a,b}_{p,p'},\mathscr W_p)$.
Every $\mathsf{P}\in X^{a,b}_{p,p'}$ with  $\mathcal F_{\beta}(\mathsf{P})<\infty$    is the starting point of a curve of maximal slope
for $\mathcal F_{\beta}$ with respect to the local slope $\abs{\partial \mathcal F_{\beta}}$, given by  \[
    \abs{\partial \mathcal F_{\beta}}(\mathsf{P}):=\limsup_{X^{a,b}_{p,p'}\ni \mathsf{P}'\to\mathsf{P}}\frac{(\mathcal F_{\beta}(\mathsf{P})-\mathcal F_{\beta}(\mathsf{P}'))^+}{\mathscr W_p(\mathsf{P}',\mathsf{P})}.
    \] Moreover, such a curve $(\mathsf{P}_t)_{t>0}$ satisfies the energy identity\begin{align}
    \frac{1}{2}\int_0^T\abs{\mathsf{P}'}^2(t)+\frac{1}{2}\int_0^T\abs{\partial \mathcal F_{\beta}}^2(\mathsf{P}(t))dt+\mathcal F_{\beta}(\mathsf{P}(T))=\mathcal F_{\beta}(\mathsf{P}(0)),\quad T>0.
\end{align}
title: Thm exist max slope of arXiv:2509.08659

Author-proved draft; w376 scoped KEEP, designated referee pending. For iid nonnegative nearest-neighbor edge weights on Z^d, d>=2, suppose disjoint positive-mass support sets satisfy I_low subset [ell,a] and I_high subset [b,infinity), with 0<=ell<=a<b. Let p_low and p_high be their probabilities. If integer k>=1 satisfies k*(b+ell-2*a)>2*a, then with probability at least p_high^(2*k^2+k)*p_low^(2*k+2), unrestricted passage time from 0 to k*(e1+e2) is strictly smaller than the minimum over all coordinate-monotone paths between those endpoints. The event puts all horizontal edges of [0,k]^2 and all its vertical edges with x<k in I_high, the right boundary column in I_low, and a bottom detour at y=-1 with two vertical connectors in I_low. Every monotone competitor costs at least k*b+k*ell; the detour costs at most (2*k+2)*a. The event uses disjoint deterministic edge sets. It is a finite event, not an asymptotic diagonal gap or a typical wandering bound.

body: In topology and related areas of mathematics, the quotient space of a topological space under a given equivalence relation is a new topological space constructed by endowing the quotient set of the original topological space with the quotient topology, that is, with the finest topology that makes continuous the canonical projection map. In other words, a subset of a quotient space is open if and only if its preimage under the canonical projection map is open in the original topological space.
title: Quotient space (topology)

[Definition 17 (normalized Horn pair) of arXiv:2609.03736, '2609.03736'] A pair $(K,L)$ satisfying Definition~\ref{def:Hamming-tensor-pair} is a
\emph{normalized Horn pair}.
Write $G=K+L$, and let $k,l,g\in\RR_{\geq0}^m$ be the decreasing eigenvalue
lists of $K,L,G$, padded by zeros when necessary.  We call $(k,l,g)$ its
\emph{additive spectral data}.  Its \emph{Hamming overlap} and
\emph{entropy cost} are
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma(K,L)=2\tr(K^{1/2}L^{1/2}),\qquad
 \Phi(K,L)=\Ent(K)+\Ent(L)-\Ent(G).
 
\end{equation}
Here $\Ent(A)=-\tr(A\log_2A)$, with the usual continuous value at zero.
title: normalized Horn pair

body:
[Proposition pr:apriori of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Let $(A(t))_{t \geq 0}$ be an IDLA process on $V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} $ starting from $A(0) = R_0$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Fix $C \in (0, \infty)$ and $\b > \max(1, e^2 C)$. Then, for every integer $T \leq C N \log N$ and every $N$ large enough (depending on $C$ and $\b$),
	\[ {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}}  \big( A(T) \nsubseteq R_{\b \log N} \big) \leq N^{-(\b - 1)}\,. \]
\item[(b)] Fix $\b > e^2$. Then there exists $K_0 = K_0(\b) < \infty$ such that, for every integer $T \geq K_0\, N\log N$ and every $N$ large enough,
	\[ {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}}  \big( A(T) \nsubseteq R_{\b T/N} \big) \leq \exp\!\Big( -\b\, \frac{T}{N}\Big)\,. \]
\end{itemize}

Owner campaign draft w726-T332-C5 v1, proof (unaudited). Assumptions: n>=1, 0<=c<=n, d>=1; G(n,c/n) with iid standard-Borel marks independent of edges; common measurable permutation-invariant local rule F_(t,degree)(own mark; own state and neighbor states), independent of graph size and remote structure; initial state depends only on own mark; all iterates on full graphs and induced subgraphs lie in the same fixed Borel K subset R^d of diameter D<infinity; maximum-input Lipschitz constant <=rho in (0,1), uniformly over degree, marks and layers; nu_L is the root-output law of a similarly iid-marked PGW(c) tree with the same update rules; depth can depend arbitrarily on n. Under the bounded invariant Euclidean-state and degree-uniform contraction hypotheses below, for every depth L and radius r put a=1+c and q=a^(2r+2)/n. Expected empirical output Wasserstein distance to the PGW(c) root law is at most D times 2rho^r plus: 18sqrt(q) when d=1; 2sqrt(2)[4+(3/2)log_2^+(1/q)]sqrt(q) when d=2; 32sqrt(d)q^(1/d) when d>=3. For fixed c>=0 and rho in (0,1), let b=log(1/rho), m=max(d,2), k=b/[2log(a)+mb], r=floor(log(n)/[2log(a)+mb]). Uniformly over all finite depths, the bound is D[2/rho+18a]n^(-k) for d=1, D[2/rho+2sqrt(2)a(4+(3/2)log_2(n))]n^(-k) for d=2, and D[2/rho+32sqrt(d)a^(2/d)]n^(-k) for d>=3. D=0 gives exact equality. This is a classical dyadic transport application with graph dependence controlled by the audited categorical second moment; no novelty or optimality claim.

body: For a weighted sum S = sum a_i x_i of independent Rademacher signs with all |a_i| >= 1, the probability that S lands in any interval of length 2 is at most C n^{-1/2} (Erdos's sharpening via Sperner's theorem: the middle binomial coefficient over 2^n). Inverse Littlewood-Offord theory (Tao-Vu, Nguyen-Vu) characterizes when the concentration probability is large - the weights must have rich additive structure (generalized arithmetic progressions) - and powers the least-singular-value and universality results for discrete random matrices.
title: Littlewood-Offord Anti-Concentration

body:
[Prop separation-intro-permutations of arXiv:2512.20338, 'Up-down chains and scaling limits: \\ application to permuton- and graphon-valued diffusio'] Let $  \mathbb S  _n$ be the set of permutations or graphs of size $n$
	and $  X _n $ the up-down chain defined above on $   \mathbb S  _n $.
	Let $ \Delta _n(m)$ denote the separation distance between $  X _n( m ) $ and the stationary distribution $  M _n $ (for the worst initial distribution).
	Then we have the identity
  \begin{equation}
  
   \Delta _n(m)
  	= 
		\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} 
			(-1)^{j-1} 
			(2j+1) 
			\frac{(n-1)!n!}{(n-1-j)!(n+j)!} 
			\bigg(1-\frac{j(j+1)}{n(n+1)}\bigg)^m
  	,
		\qquad
		n \ge 2,
		\,
		m \ge 0
	.
  \end{equation}

    \noindent
    Let now $  \Delta _ F  $ be the separation distance associated with the limiting diffusion of the $  X _n $.
    Then {$ \Delta _ F $ is given by the following monotonic limit and series}:
	
    
     \begin{equation}
      
        \Delta _n(\lfloor t n ( n + 1 ) \rfloor)
    		\underset{ n \to \infty}{{\nearrow}}
    	 \Delta _ F ( t )
    		=
    			\sum_{ j = 1 }^\infty 
					( -1 )^{ j - 1 } ( 2j + 1 ) 
    				e^{ -t j ( j + 1 ) }
    		,
				\qquad
				t > 0
			.
         \end{equation}
    
    \noindent
    Moreover, $  \Delta _ F  $ exhibits the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}[ label = (\roman*)]
    
    \item
    
    $
    	 \Delta _ F (t)
    		=
    			1
    			-
    			\prod_{ j = 1 }^\infty
    				( 1 - e^{ - 2 j t } )^3
    		=
    			1
    			-
    			e^{ t/4} 
				\eta^3( i t/\pi )
    $
    for $ t > 0 $,
  \item 
	$
		1 -  \Delta _ F ( t )
			=	
				\exp\big( -\frac{ \pi^2 }{ 4 t } + \frac{ t }{ 4 } \big)
				\left(
					\frac{ \pi }{ t }
				\right)^{ 3/2 }
				\big( 1 -  \Delta _ F \big( \frac{ \pi^2 }{ t } \big) \big)
	$
	for $ t > 0 $,

  \item 
    $  \Delta _ F ( t ) \sim 3 e^{ - 2 t } $ as $ t \to \infty $,
    
    \item 
	$
		1 -  \Delta _ F ( t )
			\sim	
				e^{ -\frac{ \pi^2 }{ 4 t } }
				\left(
					\frac{ \pi }{ t }
				\right)^{ 3/2 }
	$
    as $ t \to 0 $,
    and

  \item 
      $ \Delta _ F $ is in $C^\infty[0, \infty )$ and its successive derivatives
    satisfy
    $ 
    	\orange{
		 \Delta _ F ^{(k)}( t ) = 0 
		}
	$ for $ k \ge 1 $.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 17 (Nested exponential-spacing coupling) of arXiv:2606.29635, 'Extremality and Limit Laws for the Siblings of the Coupon Collector'] Fix $j\ge2$. Let $\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots$ be independent random variables with
\[
        \xi_r\sim\Exp(r),
\]
and let $G_{1,j},G_{2,j},\ldots$ be iid $\GammaDist(j-1,1)$ random variables, independent of the $\xi_r$'s. Define
\[
        \widetilde U_j^N=1+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N-1}\ind{G_{\ell,j}>\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_\ell}.
\]
Then $\widetilde U_j^N$ has the same distribution as $U_j^N$ in the equal-probability $N$-coupon model. Consequently,
\[
        \widetilde U_j^2\le \widetilde U_j^3\le \widetilde U_j^4\le\cdots\qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]

Step 1. We show that $T$ is bounded from $L^\infty_\sigma (\Omega)$ to $L^\infty(\Omega; \mathbb{C}^d)$.

Let $u \in L^\infty_\sigma(\Omega)$. 
There exists a sequence $\{ u_k \}\subset C_{0, \sigma}^\infty(\Omega)$ such that
$u_k \to u$ a.e. in $\Omega$ and
$\| u_k \|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} \le C \| u\|_{L^\infty (\Omega)}$ [AG-2013].
As $\Omega$ is bounded, we also have $u_k \to u$ in $L^2_\sigma(\Omega)$.
Since $T$ is bounded from $L^2_\sigma (\Omega)$ to $L^2(\Omega; \mathbb{C}^d)$,
it follows that $Tu_k \to Tu $ in $L^2(\Omega; \mathbb{C}^d)$.

[Lem 32 of arXiv:2608.13976, 'Boundary Harnack principle for diffusion with jumps on metric measure spaces'] For each $R>0,$
 there is a constant  $C=C(d, R)>0$  such that for
  each ball $B$ with radius $R$,
  any $r\in (0, R/4)$ and $t>0,$
\begin{equation}
\P_x\big(\wh\tau^{b, B}_{B(x,r)}< t\wedge\wh\tau^{b, B}_{2^{-1}B}\big)\leq  C  t/r^2
\quad \hbox{for }  x\in \tfrac{1}{2} B.
\end{equation}
Consequently, ${\bf (\wh{EP})} _{\leq, R, \gamma}$   holds   with  $\gamma=2.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:harris of arXiv:2608.15344, 'A Harris recurrent continuous-time Markov process without wide-sense regenerative structur'] The process $X$ is said to be \textit{Harris recurrent} if there exists a non-trivial $\sigma$-finite measure $\eta$ on $\mathcal{S}$ for which $\eta(A)>0$ implies that
\[
\int_0^\infty I(X(t)\in A)dt=\infty,\;\;\;\;P_x\text{-a.s.},
\]
for each $x\in\mathcal{S}$.

[Lem 20 of arXiv:2605.05986, '\bf Convergence rate of the occupation measure of { classes of ergodic processes toward th'] Let $(U,V)$ be an $\ER^2$-valued centered Gaussian variable such that $\sigma_U=\sigma_V$. Then, if $|{\rm Cov}(U,V)|\le 1/2$, we have for every Borel functions $f:\ER\mapsto\ER$ and $g:\ER\mapsto\ER$ such that $\E[f^2(U) ]\vee\E[g^2(U)]<+\infty$,
$$|{\rm Cov}(f(U),g(V))|\le 2 \sqrt{{\rm Var}(f(U)){\rm Var}(g(U))} \sigma_U^{-2} |{\rm Cov}(U,V)|.$$

not weakly $q$-summable.

Necessity: relative compactness gives total boundedness in sup norm, from which uniform boundedness is immediate and equicontinuity follows by approximating within eps by one of finitely many functions and using their (uniform) continuity.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a6be95bbb4662305a643f630ae8d990a4bfb7564c1967f16e55d282cc7b6946b","revision_digest":"sha256:8b6dd2c481303014c48761fef0392a2013a1708e7e3f7db6dd0e9983d543134f","source_id":"proofwiki:Arzela-Ascoli Theorem","source_revision":"as-known-2026-08-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
[Definition Threshold selector of arXiv:2608.09368, 'A proof of Ross's conjecture for two-site moving-target search'] A deterministic stationary selector $\mu:[0,1]\to\{1,2\}$ is a
threshold selector if there is $p^*\in[0,1]$ such that
\[
 p<p^*\Longrightarrow\mu(p)=2,
 \qquad
 p>p^*\Longrightarrow\mu(p)=1.
\]
At $p=p^*$ either action is permitted.  More generally, if an interval
of beliefs consists entirely of ties, a threshold may be placed at any
point of that interval and the ties resolved monotonically.
title: Threshold selector

body:
[Prop maypoletwist of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $C^0$-foliation on $M$ with a $\mathbb{T}^3$-type planar exceptional minimal set $\Lambda$. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, and after an arbitrarily $C^0$-small isotopy of $\mathcal{F}$ whose size is independent on $\varepsilon$, there exists a maypole green $\mathfrak{G} = (N, \gamma, P)$ for $\Lambda$ of size $\leq \varepsilon$ (with a smooth framing of $P$) such that for every $\delta > 0$, there exist two $C^0$-foliations $\mathcal{F}^\pm_\delta$ on $M \setminus \interior P$ such that
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mathcal{F}^\pm_\delta$ coincide with $\mathcal{F}$ away from $N$ and near $\partial M$,
    \item $T\mathcal{F}^\pm_\delta$ is $\varepsilon$-close to $T\mathcal{F}$ everywhere, and $\delta$-close to it near $\partial P$,
    \item $\mathcal{F}^\pm_\delta$ has \emph{positive} (resp.~\emph{negative}) slope along $\partial P$ in the chosen smooth framing.
\end{itemize}
In particular, for $\varepsilon$ small enough, the minimal sets of $\mathcal{F}^\pm_\delta$ disjoint from $P$ correspond to minimal sets of $\mathcal{F}$, and $\mathcal{F}^\pm_\delta$ coincide with $\mathcal{F}$ near those.
title: Prop maypoletwist of arXiv:2608.30031

body:
[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2607.24533, 'Colored Markov-Modulated Brownian Motion for Preemptive Workload Stacks'] {Suppose that Assumptions~\ref{assump:intensity} and~\ref{assump:stability} hold, and fix a depleting color $\ell$.} Then $\vect U_\ell$ solves
\eqref{eq:layer-qme}, has a simple zero eigenvalue with right
eigenvector $\e$, and has all remaining eigenvalues in the open left
half-plane.
Let $\vect V_\ell$ denote the complementary solution of
\begin{equation}

\tfrac12(\vect\Delta_\sigma^{(\ell)})^2\vect V_\ell^2
+\vect\Delta_\mu^{(\ell)}\vect V_\ell
+\widetilde{\vect T}^{(\ell)}
=\vect 0,
\end{equation}
whose eigenvalues lie in the open right half-plane. Standard MMBM
Wiener--Hopf theory gives this complementary solution and the
nonsingularity of $\vect V_\ell-\vect U_\ell$
\citep{Asmussen1995,AhnMeini2020}. Define
\begin{equation}

\vect W_\ell
:=2\big[(\vect\Delta_\sigma^{(\ell)})^2
(\vect V_\ell-\vect U_\ell)\big]^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Then, the Green kernel appearing in \eqref{eq:launch-op-correct} is
\begin{equation}

\vect G_\ell(y,x)=
\begin{cases}
\big(e^{\vect V_\ell y}-e^{\vect U_\ell y}\big)
e^{-\vect V_\ell x}\,\vect W_\ell,
& 0\le y\le x,\\[4pt]
\big(e^{\vect U_\ell(y-x)}
-e^{\vect U_\ell y}e^{-\vect V_\ell x}\big)\vect W_\ell,
& y\ge x>0.
\end{cases}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 3 of arXiv:2607.24533

[Thm 3 of arXiv:2608.23450, 'The Oldest Allele in a Moran Model'] Let $\alpha_n = (n+\theta)(n+1)$.  If $(X_n^{(0,\theta)}(k))_{k\geq{0}}$ is running in stationarity then 
\[
\left( \frac{1}{n} Z_n^{(0,\theta)}(\lfloor \alpha_n t \rfloor), t \ge 0\right) \Rightarrow Z^{(0,\theta)}
\] 
in the Skorokhod topology where $Z^{(0,\theta)}$ is a diffusion on $[0,1]$ jumping in from the boundary at $0$ with generator $\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{D}\subseteq C[0,1]\xrightarrow{}C[0,1]$ given by
       $$\mathcal{L}f(x)=x(1-x)f''(x)-\theta xf'(x)$$
       for $x\in (0,1),$ where $\mathcal{D}$ forms a core for the true infinitesimal generator and consists of functions $f \in C^2([0,1])$ satisfying 
       \begin{enumerate}
           \item $\int_{0}^{1} (f(x)-f(0))\theta(1-x)^{\theta-1} \,dx=0,$ and
           \item $\lim_{x\rightarrow1}f'(x)(1-x)^\theta = 0$ if $\theta < 1$.
       \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 3 of arXiv:2608.23450

body:
[Corollary 2 (Asymptotic consequence) of arXiv:2606.21137, 'A Sudakov--Fernique proof of Lehner-type edge bounds for matrix-valued GUE sums'] Let \(n\) be fixed.  For each \(M\), let
	\(A_{0,M},A_{1,M},\ldots,A_{n,M}\in M_{N_M}(\C)\) be Hermitian matrices with
	\(A_{i,M}\succeq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), and assume \(N_M=o(M)\).  Suppose
	there is a constant \(K\) such that
	\[
		\max_{1\le i\le n}\|A_{i,M}\|_{\op}\le K
	\]
	for all \(M\).  Let \(\rho_{+,M}\), \(\rho_{-,M}\) be the free right and left
	edges defined in \eqref{eq:rho-plus}--\eqref{eq:rho-minus} for the coefficient
	family \(A_{0,M},A_{1,M},\ldots,A_{n,M}\), and set
	\[
		\rho_{*,M}=\max\{\rho_{+,M},-\rho_{-,M}\}.
	\]
	Let \(H_M\) be formed from these coefficients as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
	Then, for all sufficiently large \(M\) (for which \(N_M=o(M)\) ensures
	\(M\ge N_M\)),
	\[
		\E\|H_M\|_{\op}\le \rho_{*,M}+o(1).
	\]
	In particular, if \(\rho_{*,M}\to\rho\), then
	\[
		\limsup_{M\to\infty}\E\|H_M\|_{\op}\le\rho .
	\]
title: Asymptotic consequence

[Corollary cor:compact-block of arXiv:2608.28330, 'Realising atomless laws as distance distributions on metric measure spaces'] Let $R,\zeta,\varepsilon,b,\rho$ be as in
	Lemma~(lem:local of the paper), and fix $J,\eta,\beta$ satisfying the
	conditions in its conclusion. Then there exist a compact metric probability space
	$(X,d_X,\mu)$ and a $1$-Lipschitz map $\phi:X\to J$ such that
	\[
	\phi_\#\mu=\eta,\qquad
	\operatorname{diam} X<\varepsilon,\qquad
	\beta\,\operatorname{Law}(d_X(U,V))\le\zeta.
	\]
	Here $U$ and $V$ are independent with common law $\mu$.

body:
[Thm Loewner coordinate change in H of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] Let $\gamma = \gamma(t)$ be a continuous, non-self-crossing curve in the closed upper half-plane $\overline{\mathbb{H}}$, with $\gamma(0) = x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\gamma((0, t]) \subset \mathbb{H}$. Assume that $\gamma$ is generated by the Loewner chain
\[
\partial_t g_t(z) = \frac{2}{g_t(z) - W_t}, \quad \dot{W}_t = b(W_t, g_t(z_1), \ldots, g_t(z_m)), \quad g_0(z) = z, \quad W_0 = x,
\]
for some function $b : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{C}^m \to \mathbb{R}$. To simplify notation, we write $\dot{W}_t = b(W_t)$, with the understanding that $b$ may depend implicitly on the evolution of marked points $g_t(z_j)$.

Let $\Psi : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{H}$ be a conformal map defined on a neighborhood $\mathcal{N}$ of $x$, such that $\gamma([0,T]) \subset \mathcal{N}$ for some $T > 0$, and $\Psi$ maps $\partial \mathcal{N} \cap \mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{R}$. Define the image curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t) := \Psi \circ \gamma(t)$.

Let $\widetilde{g}_t$ be the conformal map from $\mathbb{H} \setminus \widetilde{\gamma}([0,t])$ onto $\mathbb{H}$ normalized at infinity by $\widetilde{g}_t(z) = z + o(1)$ as $z \to \infty$. Define
\[
\Psi_t := \widetilde{g}_t \circ \Psi \circ g_t^{-1}.
\]
Then the Loewner chain $\widetilde{g}_t$ satisfies
\[
\partial_t \widetilde{g}_t(z) = \frac{2 \Psi_t'(W_t)^2}{\widetilde{g}_t(z) - \widetilde{W}_t}, \quad \widetilde{g}_0(z) = z, \quad \widetilde{W}_0 = \Psi(x),
\]
where the new driving function is given by
\[
\widetilde{W}_t = \widetilde{g}_t \circ \Psi \circ \gamma(t) = \Psi_t(W_t).
\]

The image curve $\widetilde{\gamma}$ is parameterized such that its half-plane capacity satisfies
\[
\operatorname{hcap}(\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]) = 2 \sigma(t), \quad \text{where} \quad \sigma(t) := \int_0^t \Psi_s'(W_s)^2 \, ds.
\]

Moreover, assuming the evolution of $W_t$ is sufficiently smooth, the driving function $\widetilde{W}_t$ evolves according to
\begin{equation}
\dot{\widetilde{W}}_t = \partial_t \Psi_t(W_t) + \Psi_t'(W_t) \dot{W}_t = -3 \Psi_t''(W_t) + \Psi_t'(W_t) b(W_t),
\end{equation}
where the identity $\partial_t \Psi_t(W_t) = -3 \Psi_t''(W_t)$ follows from Equation (4.35) in [Lawler:book].
title: Loewner coordinate change in $\mathbb{H}$

[Lemma improved-m-steps of arXiv:2607.05054, 'Root Dynamics of Differentiated Polynomials with Rotationally Invariant Structure'] For integers $m, n \geq 1$ and nondecreasing sequences of positive radii
$(r_j^{(n)})_{1 \leq j \leq n}$, 
we consider the polynomial $P_{n,m}(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(z^{m}-(r_j^{(n)})^{m}\bigr)$. 
Then, the $m$-th derivative of $P_{n,m}$ can be written as 
$$P_{n,m}^{(m)} (z) = \frac{(nm)!}{((n-1)m)!} \prod_{j = 1}^{n-1} (z^m - (R_j^{(n)})^m) $$
for a nondecreasing sequence of  $(R_j^{(n)})_{1\le j\le n-1}$ of positive numbers. Let $(r_j)_{1 \leq j \leq n}$ be an increasing sequence of positive real numbers, and let $\alpha$ be larger than or equal to the maximum of $r_j/r_{j+1}$
for $1 \leq j \leq n-1$. If $r_j^{(n)} \leq r_j$ for $1 \leq j \leq n$, 
then for $1 \leq j \leq n-1$, 
$$ R_j^{(n)} \leq \left(1 - \frac{\alpha^m}{j + 3 + 2 y_m} \right)
r_{j+1}$$
where
\[
y_m=\frac{2+\log_{-}{(m\log(\alpha^{-1}))}}{m\log(\alpha^{-1})}.
\]
On the other hand, if $r_j^{(n)} \geq r_j$ for $1 \leq j \leq n$, then for $1 \leq j \leq n-1$, 
$$ R_j^{(n)} \geq \left(1 - \frac{1}{\max(1, j-1 -  y_m)} \right)
r_{j+1}.$$

body: Let X have independent coordinates with densities at most 1, and let u, v be orthonormal with u_i^2 + v_i^2 <= 1/2 for every coordinate. Then the density of <u, X> + c <v, X>^2 is at most 8 |c|^{-1/2} for every real c != 0 and all laws. Proof: the Fresnel identity in V (with Gaussian damping) gives |E e^{i eta (U + cV^2)}| <= (4 pi |eta c|)^{-1/2} g(eta) with g(eta) = int |prod_i psi_i(eta u_i + xi v_i)| d xi; Hoelder along the line with p_i = 1/v_i^2 >= 2 and int |psi|^p <= 4 pi p^{-1/2} give g(eta) <= 4 pi for EVERY eta, and the two-dimensional Brascamp-Lieb bound gives int g <= (4 pi)^2; split the frequency integral at |eta| = pi. Using the Fresnel bound at all frequencies, not only above |eta| = 1, is what removes the constant term. Consequence for a single hub: given X_h = x the form 2 X_h (L + beta) + lambda V^2 has density at most 4 sqrt 2 (|lambda| |x|)^{-1/2}, which is integrable in x, so its density is at most 16 |lambda|^{-1/2} for every hub law and every hub diagonal; a small c is a large hub value.

[Theorem 109 (Localized first Picard smoothing) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Fix an admissible spectral family and interpret $\Lambda\to\infty$ along
an arbitrary admissible cofinal sequence in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:admissible-cutoff}.  Let $T<\infty$,
$a\in\mathfrak C$, $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)$,
$\kappa>0$, and $2\le p<\infty$.  Then there are cutoff-independent random
distributions $V_a$ and $\partial_tV_a$ such that
\begin{align}
  \chi V_{a,\Lambda}&\longrightarrow \chi V_a
  &&\text{in }L^p\!\left(\Omega;
  C_T\cC^{\frac12-\betasum-\kappa}
  \cap L_T^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{\frac12-\betasum-\kappa}\right),
  \\
  \chi\partial_tV_{a,\Lambda}&\longrightarrow \chi\partial_tV_a
  &&\text{in }L^p\!\left(\Omega;
  C_T\cC^{-\frac12-\betasum-\kappa}
  \cap L_T^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{-\frac12-\betasum-\kappa}\right).
  
\end{align}
The same limits are obtained from $V^{\mathrm{out}}_{a,\Lambda}$.  If
the family is fixed-profile and $\Lambda=2^j$, the convergence holds almost
surely along the entire dyadic sequence on one event, simultaneously for any
prescribed countable family of compactly supported cutoffs, rational time
horizons, rational losses $\kappa>0$, and integer probability moments.  In
particular, one may use the predetermined localizers attached to the compact
exhaustion in Proposition~\ref{prop:measurable-lifetimes}.  Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  V_a\in C_T\cC_{\loc}^{\frac12-\betasum-},
  \qquad
  \partial_tV_a\in C_T\cC_{\loc}^{-\frac12-\betasum-},
\end{equation}
and both objects possess the corresponding local $B_{2,\infty}$ shell envelopes. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Localized first Picard smoothing

[Defini 10 of arXiv:2608.27934, 'An example of biquandle and an invariant of long virtual knots defined through it'] (Pointed Gauss diagram)\\
Take a counterclockwise oriented circle $S^{1}$ with one specified point $p$ on it. 
For a long virtual knot diagram $D$, fix an orientation preserving immersion $\phi$ from $S^{1}\setminus \{p\}$ to the image of $D$. 
For each classical crossing $c$ of $D$, the preimage $\phi^{-1}(c)$ of $c$ consists of two points of $S^{1}\setminus \{p\}$. 
Let $c_{O}$ and $c_{U}$ be the points of $\phi^{-1}(c)$ corresponding to for the points being on  the overarc and the under arc, respectively. 
Connect $c_{O}$ and $c_{U}$ by a dashed arrow oriented from $c_{O}$ to $c_{U}$ for each classical crossing of $D$. 
Assign this dashed arrow the symbol $+$ or $-$ according to the sign of the crossing $c$. 
The obtained pointed circle with dashed arrows is called {\it the pointed Gauss diagram of} $D$, denoted by $G(D)$. 
An example of a pointed Gauss diagram of a long virtual knot is presented in Figure~\ref{gaussdiagram_k3(4)}.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d86de94316bdcb0f9c2774df16ccd6ecb01559c5bd9b186023902dc90f306cc4","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d8/d86de94316bdcb0f9c2774df16ccd6ecb01559c5bd9b186023902dc90f306cc4.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:84af1934cacea267a5b9c9f12a49446cbbb34b6cb06e6a52248be4cd29ac0816","bundle_entry_key":"stein-companion-log-regularity","bundle_id":"population.w722-t311-logarithmic-regularity-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"analysis","draft":"w722/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:analysis.stein:w722-t311-stein-companion-logarithmic-hermite-regularity","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Target 2: logarithmic regularity and companion semigroup decay

Status: proof (unaudited), conditional on the operator comparisons explicitly stated below. This is an application of classical resolvent and fractional-power order methods; novelty is not claimed. It concerns the symmetric companion, not a nonlinear SVGD law or a density-profile decay theorem.

## Statement

Let (psi_j)_(j>=0) be an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space. Fix q>=1 and 0<B<1. Put

    Q psi_j=(j+1)psi_j,
    R psi_j=d_j psi_j,       d_j=(j+1)(1-B)B^j.

Let S be a bounded positive self-adjoint operator satisfying, as bounded forms,

    q^(-1) R <= S <= q R.                                      (A)

Let H be positive self-adjoint and suppose, as closed quadratic forms,

    q^(-1) Q <= H <= q Q.                                      (B)

In the Gaussian/RBF application these are exactly the S, R, Q and H of proofs/spectral_order.md. Here H is the ordinary Gaussian number operator plus identity, transported to flat space, whereas Q is the squeezed oscillator plus identity.

Set kappa=e*q/(1-B), and define the positive self-adjoint operator L=log(kappa/S) by spectral calculus. Then, for 0<r<=1/2,

    Dom(L^r)=Dom(Q^r)=Dom(H^r),                                (C)

with equivalent norms. Moreover, there are positive constants a_r,b_r depending only on q,B,r such that for every t>=1,

    a_r [log(1+t)]^(-2r)
      <= sup_{u in Dom(H^r), ||H^r u||<=1} ||exp(-tS)u||^2
      <= b_r [log(1+t)]^(-2r).                                (D)

The supremum allows u to depend on t. The lower bound is not a decay assertion for one fixed initial law.

## 1. Logarithms of the compact sandwich

The scalar sequence d_j is positive and summable, with sum_j d_j=1/(1-B). Thus R is injective, trace class and bounded by I/(1-B). Assumption (A) makes S injective: <u,Su>=0 forces sum_j d_j |<u,psi_j>|^2=0, hence u=0. Also ||S||<=q/(1-B), so L>=I by the choice of kappa. Compactness is not needed for the logarithm argument, but follows from (A), for example by summing diagonal forms to bound the trace of S.

We first justify the logarithm comparison, including its domains. For bounded positive operators X,Y that are bounded below by a positive scalar, X<=Y implies (X+tI)^(-1)>=(Y+tI)^(-1). To see inverse order, conjugate X<=Y by Y^(-1/2), invert the resulting positive operator bounded by I, and conjugate back. Apply the same argument to X+tI and Y+tI.

The scalar identity

    log x = integral_0^infinity [1/(1+t)-1/(x+t)] dt

holds for x>0 by integration of the two fractions. On a compact positive spectral interval the truncated integrals converge in operator norm to log X. The inverse order above therefore proves log X<=log Y in the bounded, bounded-below case. Scalar multiplication commutes with spectral calculus: log(aX)=log(a)I+log X for a>0.

For epsilon>0, (A) implies

    q^(-1)(R+q epsilon I) <= S+epsilon I
                            <= q(R+epsilon I/q).

The bounded logarithm comparison consequently gives

    log(kappa/(R+epsilon I/q))-log q I
      <= log(kappa/(S+epsilon I))
      <= log(kappa/(R+q epsilon I))+log q I.                    (1)

Let epsilon decrease to zero. For each of the three spectral calculi, the scalar logarithms increase to log(kappa/x). For 0<epsilon<=1 these functions have a common finite lower bound; subtracting that bound makes the functions nonnegative. Monotone convergence of their spectral integrals applies to every vector and permits the value +infinity. Thus the central limit is finite exactly when the diagonal logarithm form is finite. In particular

    Dom(L^(1/2))=Dom(log(kappa/R)^(1/2)),
    log(kappa/R)-log q I <= L <= log(kappa/R)+log q I           (2)

as closed forms on that common domain. This limiting argument does not assume that the logarithms commute.

## 2. Comparison with the number operator and its fractional powers

Write b=-log B>0 and

    ell_j=log(kappa/d_j)
         =b*j-log(j+1)+log(kappa/(1-B)).

Since d_j<=sum_k d_k=1/(1-B), ell_j-log q>=1. Also both sequences

    (ell_j-log q)/(j+1),       (ell_j+log q)/(j+1)

converge to b. Therefore the constants

    c=inf_{j>=0} (ell_j-log q)/(j+1)>0,
    C=sup_{j>=0} (ell_j+log q)/(j+1)<infinity                 (3)

are well defined. Positivity of c follows by separating a tail where the ratio is at least b/2 from the remaining finite collection of positive terms. Equations (2)-(3) give

    c Q <= L <= C Q                                          (4)

as closed forms, with common form domain Dom(Q^(1/2)). By (B), also

    (c/q) H <= L <= Cq H.                                    (5)

For completeness, the fractional-power order step used next can be derived by resolvents. If positive self-adjoint E<=F in form order, the variational identity

    <u,(E+tI)^(-1)u>
      =sup_v [2 Re<u,v>-||E^(1/2)v||^2-t||v||^2],

where v runs through Dom(E^(1/2)), gives (E+tI)^(-1)>=(F+tI)^(-1). The inclusion of form domains in the definition of E<=F gives the correct direction of the two suprema. Hence

    E(E+tI)^(-1)<=F(F+tI)^(-1).

For 0<theta<1 the scalar formula

    x^theta=(sin(pi theta)/pi)
              integral_0^infinity t^(theta-1) x/(x+t) dt

follows by substituting t=xs in the convergent beta integral. Spectral calculus and Tonelli's theorem express the corresponding quadratic forms as integrals of the positive resolvents above. Therefore E^theta<=F^theta in form order, including the relevant domain inclusions. The endpoint theta=1 is the original form order.

Apply this fact to both sides of (5) with theta=2r in (0,1]. The result is

    (c/q)^(2r)||H^r u||^2 <= ||L^r u||^2
                              <= (Cq)^(2r)||H^r u||^2,        (6)

with equality of the domains of these norms. Applying the same argument to (4), or to (B), proves the remaining equality with Dom(Q^r) in (C). No assertion for r>1/2 follows from this power-order argument.

## 3. Upper semigroup bound

For t>=1 put T=log(kappa*t). Since kappa>=e, T>=1. A spectral value lambda of S corresponds to m=log(kappa/lambda)>=1, and

    exp(-2t lambda)=exp(-2 kappa*t*exp(-m)).

For m>=T/2, the product exp(-2 kappa*t*exp(-m))*m^(-2r) is at most (2/T)^(2r). For 1<=m<T/2 it is at most exp(-2 exp(T/2)). The elementary inequality exp(T/2)>=T for T>=1 and exp(2x)>=2x give

    exp(-2 exp(T/2)) <= 1/(2T) <= (1/2)T^(-2r),

where the last step uses 2r<=1 and T>=1. Thus

    sup_{m>=1} exp(-2 kappa*t*exp(-m))*m^(-2r)
      <= 2^(2r) [log(kappa*t)]^(-2r).

Spectral calculus and (6) now yield

    ||exp(-tS)u||^2
      <= (2Cq)^(2r)[log(kappa*t)]^(-2r)||H^r u||^2.

For t>=1, kappa*t>=1+t, so this proves the upper bound in (D) with b_r=(2Cq)^(2r).

## 4. Matching lower bound on the Sobolev ball

For t>=1 choose n=ceil((2/b)log(1+t)). Then B^n<=(1+t)^(-2), and

    t*q*d_n <= q(1-B)(n+1)/(1+t)
              <= q(1-B)(2/b+2)=K.                            (7)

Here ceil(x)<=x+1 and log(1+t)/(1+t)<=1 were used. Also

    n+1 <= M log(1+t),       M=2/b+2/log 2.                   (8)

From (B) and fractional-power order, ||H^r psi_n||<=q^r(n+1)^r. Hence

    u_t=q^(-r)(n+1)^(-r)psi_n

belongs to the H^r unit ball. The spectral measure of S at the unit vector psi_n is a probability measure. Convexity of x -> exp(-2tx), Jensen's inequality, and (A) give

    <psi_n,exp(-2tS)psi_n>
      >= exp(-2t<psi_n,S psi_n>) >= exp(-2tq d_n).

Combining with (7)-(8),

    ||exp(-tS)u_t||^2
      >= q^(-2r) M^(-2r) exp(-2K) [log(1+t)]^(-2r).

This proves (D), with the displayed positive constant as a_r.

## 5. Exact remaining transfer gap

In the Gaussian application H=DD* has ordinary normalized Hermite eigenfunctions and eigenvalues j+1. Thus the class in (D) is an ordinary Hermite Sobolev class for the companion initial variable u. If those coefficients are bounded by a constant times (j+1)^(-s), then u belongs to Dom(H^r) whenever r<s-1/2. This is just convergence of sum_j (j+1)^(2r-2s), not identification of Stein eigenvectors with Hermite functions.

The density generator is A=CC*, where C=D*T^(1/2), whereas S=C*C. Let V be the polar unitary from the companion Hilbert space to the mean-zero density space, so A=VSV*. Transporting (D) to a density perturbation f requires control of ||H^r V*f|| by the ordinary density norm ||H^r f||. The boundedness of H^r V*H^(-r) on the appropriate mean-zero space is NOT established by this proof. Equality of spectra and unitarity in L2 alone do not supply it.

This leaves a precise linear transfer question, and leaves all nonlinear regularity propagation questions open. No statement here identifies a fixed positive initial probability law achieving the Sobolev-ball lower bound.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:559b2d4a17cda971141e8b93f8b6fa97539dc237743f2691a7ac21016844fd7f","revision_digest":"sha256:8ba5546065d6a545db7e2706544d5288f35652cb1836c9935703dcfd3f7bd11b","source_id":"own-work:w722:T311:w722-log-regularity-bridge-v2","source_revision":"w722-log-regularity-bridge-v2","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary 4 of arXiv:2506.09592, 'Extremal process of the local time of simple\\random walk on a regular tree'] Given~$n\ge1$ and a sample~$\ell_{\tau_\varrho}$ on~$\T_n$ under~$P^\zero$, let~$Y_n$ denote the a.s.-unique maximizer of~$x\mapsto\ell_{\tau_\varrho}(x)$ on~$\BbbL_n$. Then~$\theta_n(Y_n)$ converges in law to a random variable~$U$ on~$[0,1]$ described as follows: Given a sample~$\{Z_{T_k}\}_{k\ge1}$ of the measures in Corollary~\ref{cor-1.3}, let~$K$ be the smallest~$k\ge1$ maximizing
\begin{equation}

k\mapsto \log Z_{T_k}\bigl([b^{-1},1]\bigr)-2k\log b+G_k
\end{equation}
where~$\log0:=-\infty$ and $\{G_k\}_{k\ge1}$ are i.i.d.\ standard Gumbel 
independent of $\{Z_{T_k}\colon k\ge1\}$.
Then $K<\infty$ a.s.\ and $U$ is uniform on~$[b^{-k-1},b^{-k})$ conditional on~$\{K=k\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 4 of arXiv:2506.09592

body:
[Definition 43 (Finite Peter--Weyl block family) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $J_v$ be a finite ordered leg set.  For every $h\in J_v$, fix a
countable label set $\mathscr L_{v,h}$, finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces
$Z_{v,h}(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\in\mathscr L_{v,h}$, and a sign
$\sigma_{v,h}\in\{+,-\}$.  Put
\[
 E_{v,h}(\lambda)
 :=
 \begin{cases}
  Z_{v,h}(\lambda),&\sigma_{v,h}=+,\\
  \conj{Z_{v,h}(\lambda)},&\sigma_{v,h}=-.
 \end{cases}
\]
A finite Peter--Weyl block family at $v$ is a specified tensor
\begin{equation}

 \mathbf v_{\boldsymbol\lambda_v}
 \in\bigotimes_{h\in J_v}E_{v,h}(\lambda_h)
\end{equation}
for every
$\boldsymbol\lambda_v\in\prod_{h\in J_v}\mathscr L_{v,h}$; zero tensors
are allowed.  All tensor products over subsets of $J_v$ use the inherited
order.  For $I\subset J_v$, let
\[
 \Flat_I^{\mathrm{str}}(\mathbf v_{\boldsymbol\lambda_v}):
 \conj{\bigotimes_{h\in I}E_{v,h}(\lambda_h)}
 \longrightarrow
 \bigotimes_{h\in J_v\setminus I}E_{v,h}(\lambda_h)
\]
be the canonical Hilbert-space linearization and define
\begin{equation}

 \mathfrak f_{v,r,I}(\boldsymbol\lambda_v)
 :=
 \norm{\Flat_I^{\mathrm{str}}
        (\mathbf v_{\boldsymbol\lambda_v})}_{\Sch_r}.
\end{equation}
Singleton label sets encode fixed auxiliary legs.  A dyadic Peter--Weyl leg
has label set $\Dya$ and space $H_L$; conjugating the leg changes its sign.
title: Finite Peter--Weyl block family

For independent Bernoulli trials with probabilities p_1,...,p_M followed by fair trials, let F_m count failures before the m-th success. For m>=M and m>=1, s=sum p_i, t=sum p_i(1-p_i), and delta=sum(2p_i-1), E F_m=m-delta and Var F_m=2(m-s)+4t. This is a quenched single-stack identity; it assumes no independence between stacks. It does not settle the stationary-ergodic excited-walk recurrence criterion.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Fix a cookie stack of length M, with independent Bernoulli success probabilities p_1,...,p_M in its first M trials and probability 1/2 thereafter. Let F_m count failures before the m-th success. For every integer m>=M with m>=1, set s=sum p_i, t=sum p_i(1-p_i), and delta=sum(2*p_i-1). Then

    E[F_m]=m-delta,
    Var(F_m)=2(m-s)+4t.

Proof: sample all M prefix trials and let S be their number of successes. When m>=M, the stopping time processes the whole prefix, except that it may finish precisely at its end when m=M=S; that exception has zero tail and satisfies the same representation. Conditional on S,

    F_m = M-S + NB(m-S,1/2),

where NB(k,1/2) counts failures before k fair-coin successes, with mean k and variance 2k (and NB(0)=0). Conditional expectation is m+M-2S, whose variance is 4t. The total-variance identity gives the formulas. They hold quenched, without any independence between stacks at different sites.

[Prop lem:triangular of arXiv:2606.08325, 'Digit Mixing under Polynomial Maps'] Fix an integer \(q\ge1\) and a real number \(0<\rho<1/2\). There exist constants $c=c(q,\rho)>0$ and $C=C(q,\rho)<\infty$ with the following property.
			Let \(A(k_1,\ldots,k_q)\), \(1\le k_1,\ldots,k_q\le L\), be real coefficients satisfying
			\begin{align}
				&\left\|A(k,k,\ldots,k)\right\|\ge\rho \qquad(1\le k\le L) , \\
				\text{and} \quad &A(k_1,\ldots,k_q)=0
				\quad\text{if}\quad (k_1,\ldots,k_{q-1})\succ(k_q,\ldots,k_q).
				
			\end{align}
				Let \(U_{j,k}\) be as in Lemma~(lem:GCS of the paper). Then
			\begin{equation}
				\left|\mathbb E e\!\left(\sum_{k_1,\ldots,k_q=1}^{L} A(k_1,\ldots,k_q) \prod_{j=1}^{q}U_{j,k_j}\right)\right|
				\leq C e^{-cL}.
			\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop lem:triangular of arXiv:2606.08325

body:
[Definition def: ConditionW of arXiv:2603.26932, 'On the satisfaction frequency of spectral characterization conditions'] Fix a prime $p$. 
    Then, a $\widehat{R}$-module $\sM$ is said to satisfy \emph{condition $\cW_p$} if one of the following two events is satisfied:
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = 2.8em]
        \item[(W1)] It holds that $\sM\otimes_{\widehat{R}} R_{p,\beta} \cong 0$ for every monic $\beta(x) \in \bbZ[x]$ with irreducible reduction in $\bbF_p[x]$.
        \item[(W2)] Or, there exists $a\in \bbZ$ such that $\sM \otimes_{\widehat{R}} R_{p,x-a} \cong \bbF_{p}[x]/(x-a)\bbF_{p}[x]$ 
        and $\sM\otimes_{\widehat{R}} R_{p,\beta} \cong 0$ for every $\beta \not\equiv x-a \bmod p$.     
    \end{enumerate}
title: Definition def: ConditionW of arXiv:2603.26932

body:
[Theorem Offset reconstruction of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] There exist
constants \(\varepsilon_{rec} > 0\), \(C_{low} > 0\),
\(C_{up} > 0\), depending only on the positive-reach
reconstruction constants of \(M\), such that the following holds.
Let \(S \subset M\) be compact with
\(d_{H}(S,M) \leq \varepsilon\) and
\(0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_{rec}\). Then, for every
reconstruction radius \(r\) with

\[C_{low}\,\varepsilon \leq r \leq C_{up}\, \operatorname{reach}(M),\]

the offset \(S^{r}\) is homotopy equivalent to
\(M\); in particular \(H_{q}\left( S^{r} \right) \cong H_{q}(M)\)
for every \(q = 0,\ldots,d\).

[Corollary 2 of arXiv:2609.03954, 'Galois representations ramified at one prime via relative deformation theory'] Let $p$ be any odd prime and let $n>1$. Then there exist infinitely
many continuous representations $\rho:G_{\{p\}}\longrightarrow\GL_n(\Zp)$
unramified outside $\{p,\infty\}$ whose images contain a principal
congruence subgroup of $\SL_n(\Zp)$. The determinant may be chosen to
have open image, and hence the resulting representations have open
image in $\GL_n(\Zp)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 2 of arXiv:2609.03954

[Lemma (q)cof-resolution of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The inclusions induce equivalences of global $\infty$-categories 
    \[
        \ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl},*}^\textup{qcof}\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl},*}
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        \ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_*^\textup{cof}\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_*.
    \]
    \begin{proof}
        If we fix a compact Lie group $G$, then an inverse is induced by cofibrant replacement in the $G$-global and $G$-equivariant model structure, respectively.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma (q)cof-resolution of arXiv:2608.28504

[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] Let $\nu$ be a supercritical offspring distribution whose mean is denoted by $\ttm_\nu$. 
We assume that $\ttm_\nu (2)\eqo \sum_{k\in \bbN} k^{2} \nu(k) \leko \infty$. 
Let $(\bT, \boo)$ be an infinite tree GW($\nu$)-tree as in Definition \ref{GWptdef} 
or an invariant GW($\nu$)-tree as in Definition \ref{definvRW}. Let the r.v.s $U_x, S_x$, $x\ino \bT$, be as in (\ref{welldefcoo}) and  (\ref{defSx}). Recall from (\ref{spinedfbis}) the notation $\partial \Loo$ and $\boo (p)$, $p\ino \bbN$. 
Then the following holds true. 

  

\smallskip

\begin{compactenum}
\item[$(i)$] For all $p\ino \bbN^*$ we set $\fbeta_p \eqo \mnu^{-1}\sum_{x\in \partial \Loo: \overleftarrow{x}= \boo (p)} U_x$. 
Then $\fbeta_p \eqo  U_{\boo (p)} \! - \! \mnu^{-1}U_{\boo (p-1)}$. Moreover, the r.v.s $(\fbeta_p)_{p\in \bbN^*}$ are 
i.i.d.~such that $\bE [\fbeta_1]\eqo \mnu^{-2} (\mnu (2) \! -\! \mnu)$. If $\ttb\ino (1, \infty)$ is such that 
$\ttm_{\nu} (\ttb +1)\! :=\! \sum_{k\in \bbN} k^{\ttb+1} \nu(k) \leko \infty$, then $\bE [\fbeta_1^\ttb] \leko \infty$.    

\smallskip

\item[$(ii)$] Recall $\sigma_\nu$ from (\ref{vutchi}) and assume that there exists $\ttb\ino (1, \infty)$ such that 
$\ttm_\nu (2\ttb+1)\eqo $ $\sum_{k\in \bbN} $ $k^{2\ttb+1}\nu(k)$ $\leko \infty$. Then, there is a constant $c\ino (0, \infty)$ that only depends on $\nu$ and $\ttb$ such that for all $p\ino \bbN$, 
$\bE \big[ \big| \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2_\nu} S_{\boo (p)}\!  -\! \bbn \boo (p) \bbn  \big|^{2\ttb}\big] \leqo 
c\, p^\ttb $. 
Moreover, for all $\beta\ino (\tfrac{1}{2} +\tfrac{1}{2\ttb} , 1)$, we set 
\begin{equation}

R_\beta= \sup_{p\in \bbN} \, \frac{\big| \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2_\nu} S_{\boo (p)} \!-\! \bbn \boo (p) \bbn  \big|}{1+ p^\beta} .
\end{equation} 
Then, there exists a constant $c'\ino (0, \infty)$ that only depends on $\nu$, $\ttb$ and $\beta$ such that for all $\lambda \ino (0, \infty)$, we get $\bP \big( R_\beta \geq \lambda \big)\leqo c' \lambda^{-2\ttb}$. 
\end{compactenum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 39 of arXiv:2605.02430

[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2606.09022, 'Steady-State Approximation Error of Heterogeneous Mean-Field Models'] Consider the heterogeneous \(M\)-agent system introduced in the previous section and the corresponding quenched and annealed mean-field models. Assume that A1-A3 and the following additional conditions hold.

\begin{itemize}
\item
\textbf{A4 - Occupancy stability.}
There exists a constant \(C_0>0\), independent of \(M\), \(\nu_M\), and \(\hat w\), such that
\[
\int_0^\infty
\|x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)-x_{\nu_M}^*\|^2\,dt
\le C_0,
\] where $x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)=\frac1M \sum_m w_{\nu_M,m}(t;\hat w)$. 

\item
\textbf{A5 - Occupancy robustness.}
Let \(\Delta\) denote the change in the full state vector  $w$ resulting from a single transition of the CTMC.
There exists a constant \(C_1>0\), independent of \(M\), \(\nu_M\), \(\hat w\), and \(\Delta\), such that
\[
\int_0^\infty
\left\|
\nabla_{\hat w}x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)[\Delta]
\right\|^2dt
\le
\frac{C_1}{M^2},
\]
and
\[
\int_0^\infty
\left\|
\nabla_{\hat w}^2x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)[\Delta,\Delta]
\right\|dt
\le
\frac{C_1}{M^2}.
\]
\end{itemize}

Then the steady-state approximation error with respect to the quenched mean-field equilibrium satisfies
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
\left\|
X_{\nu_M}(\infty)-x_{\nu_M}^*
\right\|^2
\,\middle|\,\nu_M
\right]
=
O\left(\frac1M\right).
\]

Furthermore, if the following condition also holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
\textbf{A6 - Equilibrium regularity.}
There exists a distance measure \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\) on probability measures over \(\Theta\) such that
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
\|\nu_M-\nu\|_{\mathcal D}^2
\right]
=
O\left(\frac1M\right),
\]
and the equilibrium map is Lipschitz continuous with respect to \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\), i.e.,
\[
\|x_{\nu_M}^*-x^*\|
\le
L\|\nu_M-\nu\|_{\mathcal D},
\]
\end{itemize}
then the steady-state approximation error with respect to the annealed mean-field equilibrium satisfies
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
\left\|
X_{\nu_M}(\infty) - x^*
\right\|^2
\right]
=
O\left(\frac1M\right).
\]

Let (X, d) be a complete metric space and let U_1, U_2, U_3, ... be countably many dense open subsets of X. Then their intersection is dense in X; in particular, if X is nonempty the intersection is nonempty. Equivalent formulation: a nonempty complete metric space is not the union of countably many nowhere dense sets (sets whose closures have empty interior); such spaces are Baire spaces.

[Df inf_tube of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] Let $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$.
  A continuous map $\gamma\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times[0,\infty)\to X$ is called an \emph{infinite $k$-tube} in $X$ if the following conditions hold:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item (\emph{Local self-avoidance}).
    For every $t\in[0,\infty)$, there exists a neighborhood $U\subset[0,\infty)$ of $t$ such that the restriction $\gamma|_{\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times U}$ is injective.
    \item (\emph{Finite width}).
    The \emph{width}
    \[
    \width(\gamma):=\sup_{t\in[0,\infty)}\diam\gamma(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times\{t\})<\infty.
    \]
    \item (\emph{Escape to infinity}).
    It holds that
    \[
    \lim_{t\to\infty}d_\infty(o,\gamma(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times\{t\}))=\infty,
    \]
    where $d_\infty(o,S):=\inf_{x\in S}\|x\|_\infty$ denotes the $\ell^\infty$-distance from the origin $o\in\mathbb{R}^d$ to $S$.
  \end{itemize}
  If $\gamma$ itself is injective, then $\gamma$ is said to be \emph{self-avoiding}.
  The topological $(k-1)$-sphere $S=\gamma(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times\{0\})$ is called the \emph{initial sphere} of $\gamma$ (the \emph{initial loop} of $\gamma$ when $k=2$).
  In this case, we further say that $S$ is \emph{joined to infinity} in $X$, and denote this by $S\overset X{\approx}\infty$.
title: Infinite $k$-tube

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). On a product probability space (Omega_1 x ... x Omega_n, mu), define the convex distance d_T(x,A) = sup_{alpha>=0, |alpha|=1} inf_{y in A} sum_i alpha_i 1_{x_i != y_i}, a weighted Hamming-type distance from x to a set A, maximized over convex combinations of nonnegative unit-norm weight vectors. Talagrand's inequality states integral exp(d_T(x,A)^2/4) dmu(x) <= 1/mu(A), which implies mu(A) mu({x : d_T(x,A) >= t}) <= exp(-t^2/4), a strong concentration of any set A around itself in convex distance. Applied to a function f that is certifiable, meaning any difference f(x) - f(y) can be witnessed by a bounded number of coordinates with bounded weight, this yields subgaussian concentration of f around its median without requiring f to be linear or even close to it, making the method far more flexible than Azuma-Hoeffding for combinatorial optimization functionals such as the longest increasing subsequence, bin-packing cost, or chromatic number. It does not directly give concentration around the mean, only the median, so a separate median-to-mean gap argument is needed, and it requires exhibiting an explicit certificate structure for f, which can be technically demanding to construct. Typical failure: Applying Talagrand concentration by treating f as ordinary Hamming-Lipschitz (uniform weight 1 per coordinate change) when the natural certificate for f actually requires nonuniform or superlinear weighting, since changing one coordinate can move f by an amount depending on many other coordinates; using the wrong or absent certificate yields either the wrong concentration scale or, more commonly, no valid proof at all, since the convex-distance formulation is easy to state and easy to misapply. Canonical reference: Talagrand, 1995, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.

the function or event of interest admits a certifiable Lipschitz-type structure with bounded, possibly nonuniform, weights

[Proposition prop:intertwine of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] For $f \in \mathcal{D}_{+}$, a kernel $w \in C^{1}([0,1])$, and any
		perturbation $h$ with
		$\int h = 0$, the G\^ateaux derivative of $\rho_{w}$ at $f$ is an
		exact derivative:
		\begin{equation}
			D\rho_{w}[f]\,h
			\;=\; \frac{d}{dx}\Big[\, w\big(F(x)\big)\int_{-\infty}^{x}h \,\Big].
			
		\end{equation}
		Consequently, under the primitive map
		$h \mapsto \int_{-\infty}^{\cdot}h$, which identifies mean-zero
		perturbations with functions vanishing at $\pm\infty$, the
		linearization is conjugate to multiplication by $w\circ F$; realized
		on primitives in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R})$, its spectrum is the essential
		range of $w\circ F$, which coincides with the closure of the range
		of $w$ on $(0,1)$ because $F$ maps the support onto $(0,1)$, and is
		the interval $[0,2]$ for the canonical kernel,
		and, by
		the composition law, the linearization of $\rho_{w}^{\,n}$ has
		spectrum the range of $(A_{w}^{\circ n})'$, so that the sharp
		Lipschitz constant of $\rho_{w_{\mathrm{III}}}^{\,n}$ in $d_{K}$ and
		$W_{1}$ equals $\sup(A_{w_{\mathrm{III}}}^{\circ n})' = 2^{n}$.
title: Intertwining of the linearization

body: Uniform L^3 integrability of each direction (bounded-density conjecture for quadratic forms). Let X have a density f<=1 and g(s)=E e^{isX^2}. Then ||g||_{L^3} <= (2pi)^{1/3} (E|X|^{-1/2})^{2/3} <= (2pi)^{1/3} 5^{2/3}, uniformly over the class. Proof: the density h of X^2 satisfies h(w)<=w^{-1/2}, so int h^{3/2} <= E|X|^{-1/2} = int f|x|^{-1/2} <= 4+1 = 5 (f<=1 near 0, mass 1 in the tail); Hausdorff-Young with p=3/2, p'=3. [Definition 13 of arXiv:2609.01574, 'A linear bound for Fujita's freeness conjecture'] Let $(R,\m)$ be a $d$-dimensional analytically unramified local ring with $d\geq1$. For $k\gg0$, write
\[
 \ell_R(R/\overline{\m^k})
 =\sum_{i=0}^{d}(-1)^i\overline{e}_i(\m)
  \binom{k+d-1-i}{d-i}.
\]
The integers $\overline{e}_i(\m)$ are the \emph{normal Hilbert coefficients} of $\m$.

body: The condition number of an invertible matrix A in the spectral norm is kappa(A) = ||A|| ||A^{-1}|| = s_max(A) / s_min(A) >= 1. It bounds the relative-error amplification of solving A x = b: relative perturbations of the data can be magnified by up to kappa(A) in the solution, and log10 kappa estimates the decimal digits lost. Matrices with large kappa are ill-conditioned; kappa is infinite exactly at singular matrices.
title: Condition Number

body: [Theorem thm:single of arXiv:2602.18784, 'A note on the cooperative two-type SIR processes on Galton-Watson trees'] Let the infection rate be $\alpha$ and the recovery rate be $\mu$ for a single-type SIR process on $GW (p)$. At time 0, only the root is infected. The probability of survival is greater than 0 if and only if   $   \alpha/\mu > 1/{(m-1)}   $, where $m$ is the mean of $p$. Thus, if $\mu$ is fixed, then the critical value for $\alpha$ is  $\mu/(m-1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:poisson-noisy of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence $\overline{p}$. Fix real numbers $c>0$ and $W\geq 1$. Let $S$ be a set of positive integers such that, for every $k\in S$, $W_k \geq W$. Let $\{ P_k : k\in S\}$ be a set of   independent Poisson variables 
such that, for each $k\in S$,
$\mathbb{E}(P_k) \ge cW_k$.   Then for all $\delta \in (0,1)$,
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(\sum_{x \in S} P_xp_x < (1-\delta)c|S|\big) \le \exp(-\delta^2 c |S| W/2).
\]
title: Lemma lem:poisson-noisy of arXiv:2602.21315

[Definition of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] A norm on a representation $(E,\rho)$ of $Q$ over $K$ is \textbf{non-expansive} if each $\rho(a)$, $a\in Q_1$, is a non-expansive map with respect to this norm.
If a non-expansive norm exists on $E$, we say that $(E,\rho)$ itself is non-expansive.
Denote by $\mathbf{Rep}^{\mathrm{ne}}(Q,K)\subseteq\mathbf{Rep}(Q,K)$ the full subcategory of non-expansive representations.
This subcategory is closed under subobjects, quotients, and extensions, in particular itself abelian.

[Lemma lem:division of arXiv:2608.28330, 'Realising atomless laws as distance distributions on metric measure spaces'] Let $\nu$ be an atomless finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
			\item If $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ and $0\le a\le\nu(E)$, there is a Borel set
			$E_a\subseteq E$ with $\nu(E_a)=a$.
			\item If $\mathcal R$ is a finite Borel partition of a full-$\nu$-measure
			Borel set into cells of positive measure and $\delta>0$, then there is a
			finite Borel partition $\mathcal P$ of a full-$\nu$-measure Borel set
			such that every cell of $\mathcal P$ has positive measure, every cell of
			$\mathcal P$ is contained in a cell of $\mathcal R$, and
			$\max_{C\in\mathcal P}\nu(C)\le\delta$.  If $\nu$ is a probability
			measure, then
			$\sum_{C\in\mathcal P}\nu(C)^2\le\delta$.
			\item Every finite Borel measure $\lambda$ satisfying $0\le\lambda\le\nu$
			is atomless.
		\end{enumerate}

[Prop 7. prop: effective resistance comparison for fused electrical networks of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $G$ be an electrical network with finite vertex set $V_{G}$.
  Fix two distinct vertices $a, b \in V_{G}$ such that $\mu(a,b) > 0$.
  Write $\tilde{G}$ for the electrical network $G$ fused over $V_{0} \coloneqq \{a, b\}$.
  Let $\pi: V_{G} \to V_{\tilde{G}}$ be the canonical map.
  Then, it holds that, for any $x, y \in V_{G}$,
  \begin{equation} 
    R_{\tilde{G}}(\pi(x), \pi(y)) 
    \leq 
    R_{G}(x,y) 
    \leq 
    R_{\tilde{G}}(\pi(x), \pi(y)) + \mu_{G}(a, b)^{-1}.
  \end{equation}

[Lemma lem:distribution of cumulative arrivals of arXiv:2412.06452, 'Time-dependent queue length distribution in queues fed by $K$ customers in a finite interv'] For $(t,k) \in (0,T) \times \{0,1,\ldots,K\} \cup [T,\infty) \times \{K\}$,
$m \in \{1, 2, \ldots\}$, 
$t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_m \in [0, t]$, and 
$k_1, k_2, \ldots$, $k_m \in \{0, 1, \ldots, k\}$, 

\begin{align}
\lefteqn{
\Pr\bigl[A(t_1) = k_1, A(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, A(t_m) = k_m \mid A(t) = k\bigr]
}\qquad
\notag 
\\
&= 
\Pr\bigl[
\widehat{A}(t_1) = k_1, \widehat{A}(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, \widehat{A}(t_m) = k_m 
\mid \widehat{A}(t) = k
\bigr].

\end{align}

In particular, for $t \geq T$

\begin{align}
\lefteqn{
\Pr\bigl[A(t_1) = k_1, A(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, A(t_m) = k_m\bigr]
}\qquad
\nonumber
\\
&
=
\Pr\bigl[\widehat{A}(t_1) = k_1, 
\widehat{A}(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, \widehat{A}(t_m) = k_m 
\mid \widehat{A}(t) = K\bigr]
\nonumber
\\
&=
\Pr\bigl[\widehat{A}(t_1) = k_1, 
\widehat{A}(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, \widehat{A}(t_m) = k_m 
\mid \widehat{A}(T) = K\bigr].

\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop 32 of arXiv:2608.06576, 'The Resultant Distribution Method: Universality for $p$-adic Random Matrices and Polynomia'] Let $Z_1,Z_2,Z_3\in\Z_p[x]$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\Res(Z_1,Z_2)=(-1)^{\deg Z_1\deg Z_2}\Res(Z_2,Z_1)$.

\item
$\Res(Z_1,Z_2)=0$ if and only if $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ have a common root.

\item
We have
$$
\Res(Z_1Z_2,Z_3)=\Res(Z_1,Z_3)\Res(Z_2,Z_3),
$$
and
$$
\Res(Z_1,Z_2Z_3)=\Res(Z_1,Z_2)\Res(Z_1,Z_3).
$$

\item
If $Z_1$ is monic, then
$$
\Res(Z_1,Z_3)
=
\Res(Z_1,Z_3-Z_1Z_2).
$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 32 of arXiv:2608.06576

[Theorem 11 (Corollary 2.2 in~\cite{IP10}) of arXiv:2607.17396, '2607.17396'] Let $\beta: [0,\infty)\times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\gamma: [0,\infty)\times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous functions.
Assume that uniqueness in the sense of probability law holds for the SDE
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{d}\mathcal{U}_{t}=\beta\left(t, \mathcal{U}_{t}\right)\mathrm{d}t+\gamma\left(t, \mathcal{U}_{t}\right)\mathrm{d}W\left(t\right), \ \ t \geq 0,
\end{equation}
with initial condition $\mathcal{U}_{0}=u_{0}$ for all $u_{0}\in \mathbb{R}$, where $W\left(t\right)$ is a standard Wiener
process. Let $\left\{\mathcal{U}_{t}, t \geq 0 \right\}$ be a solution of \eqref{eq35} with initial value $\mathcal{U}_{0}=0$.

For each $n \geq 1$, let $\left\{U_{k}^{\left(n\right)} \right\}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables adapted to
a filtration $\left\{\mathfrak{F}_{k}^{\left(n\right)}, k \geq 0 \right\}$ such that $\mathbf{E}\left(U_{k}^{\left(n\right)} \right)^{2}<\infty$ for each $n,k \geq 1$. Let
$$ \mathcal{U}_{t}^{\left(n\right)}=\sum_{k=0}^{\left[nt \right]}U_{k}^{\left(n\right)}, \ \ t \geq 0,\ \ n \geq 1. $$
Suppose that as $n\to \infty$,
\begin{align*}
\text{(a)}\quad
&\sup_{t\in [0,T]} \left| \sum_{k=1}^{[nt]} \mathbf{E}\Bigl(U_{k}^{(n)} \big|\ \mathfrak{F}_{k-1}^{(n)} \Bigr)
- \int_{0}^{t} \beta\bigl(s, \mathcal{U}_{s}^{(n)}\bigr) \, \mathrm{d}s \right|
\xrightarrow{\mathbf{P}} 0, \\[6pt]
\text{(b)}\quad
&\sup_{t\in [0,T]} \left| \sum_{k=1}^{[nt]} \operatorname{Var}\Bigl(U_k^{(n)} \big|\ \mathfrak{F}_{k-1}^{(n)} \Bigr)
- \int_{0}^{t} \bigl(\gamma\bigl(s, \mathcal{U}_s^{(n)}\bigr)\bigr)^{2} \, \mathrm{d}s \right|
\xrightarrow{\mathbf{P}} 0, \\[8pt]
\text{(c)}\quad
&\sum_{k=1}^{[nT]} \mathbf{E} \Biggl((U_{k}^{(n)})^{2} \mathbf{1}{\{|U_{k}^{(n)}| > \varepsilon\}}
\Bigg|\ \mathfrak{F}_{k-1}^{(n)} \Biggr)
\xrightarrow{\mathbf{P}} 0.
\end{align*}
Then
$$ \mathcal{U}^{\left(n\right)} \mathop{\to}\limits^{\mathcal{D}} \mathcal{U}, \ \ n\to \infty. $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 2.2 in~\cite{IP10}

[Lemma lem:v not orthogonal to reactions of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] In the setting of Theorem (thm:fast-switching-transience of the paper), suppose we are given a finite collection $\Xi\subset\mathbb R^d$ with the property that for all $\xi\in\Xi$ we have $\operatorname{supp}(v)\cap\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\ne\varnothing$. Then without loss of generality we may assume that $v\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$.

Explicitly, the claim is that in the setting of Theorem (thm:fast-switching-transience of the paper) there exists a vector $v^\varepsilon$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $v^\varepsilon\in\mathbb R^d_{\ge0}$.
    
    \item $(v^\varepsilon M)_m>0$ for each $m$ such that $v^\varepsilon_m>0$.

    \item $\operatorname{supp}(v^\varepsilon)=\operatorname{supp}(v)$ (and hence in particular $\operatorname{supp}(v^\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{supp}(x)=\operatorname{supp}(v)\cap\operatorname{supp}(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb Z^d_{\ge0}$).

    \item $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$.
\end{itemize}
\begin{proof}
Let $v\in\mathbb R^d_{\ge0}$ be the vector given by the statement of the theorem, and consider the subspace $A$ of $\mathbb R^d$ defined by
\[
    A:=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{supp}(z)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(v)\}=\operatorname{span}\{e^m:v_m>0\},
\]
where $e^m$ is the unit vector in direction $m$. For each $\xi\in\Xi$, the space $\{z\in A:z\cdot\xi=0\}$ is a subspace of $A$ of dimension at most one less than that of $A$. Since the union of finitely many lower-dimensional sets is not the whole space, there exists some $z\in\mathbb R^d$ such that $z\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$ and also $\operatorname{supp}(z)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(v)$.

Let $z$ be such. For $\varepsilon>0$, consider the vector $v^\varepsilon:=v+\varepsilon z$. Notice that as long as $\varepsilon$ is small enough, $v^\varepsilon$ will be a non-negative vector with $\operatorname{supp}(v^\varepsilon)=\operatorname{supp}(v)$ (here it is important that $v$ is non-negative and $\operatorname{supp}(z)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(v)$). Furthermore, notice that
\begin{align*}
    (v^\varepsilon M)_m
    &=(vM)_m+\varepsilon (zM)_m.
\end{align*}
From this it follows that if $\varepsilon$ is small enough, $(v^\varepsilon M)_m$ will be positive whenever $(vM)_m$ is.

Lastly, we claim that $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$ as long as $\varepsilon$ is small enough. Toward this end, notice that $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi=v\cdot\xi+\varepsilon z\cdot\xi$; since $z\cdot\xi\ne0$ this quantity is a linear function of $\varepsilon$ (with non-zero slope). It follows that for each $\xi$ there is exactly one value of $\varepsilon$ for which $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi=0$. The desired result follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 22 (Weyl integration formula for Hermitian matrices; see {\cite[Sec.~3.1) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] {Mehta}}]\lab{lem:Weyl}
Let $ \Herm_n$ denote the real vector space of $n\times n$
complex Hermitian matrices, equipped with Lebesgue measure
\[
  dH
  = \prod_{i=1}^n dH_{ii}
    \prod_{1\leq i<j\leq n}
    d(\operatorname{Re}H_{ij})\,d(\operatorname{Im}H_{ij}).
\]
Let $dU$ be normalized Haar probability measure on $\mathrm U(n)$.
We equip \(\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one\) with the induced \(n\)-dimensional
Lebesgue measure \(d\lambda\).
Then, for every nonnegative measurable function
$F\colon\mathcal H_n\to[0,\infty]$ (and hence for every integrable
function $F$),
\[
	  \int_{\Herm_n} F(H)\,dH
	  =
	  \frac{\pi^{n(n-1)/2}}{V_n(\tau_n)}
	  \int_{\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one}\int_{\mathrm U(n)}
	  F\!\left(U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^*\right)
	  V_n(\lambda)^2\,dU\,d\lambda,
	\]
	where \(V_n\) is the sorted Vandermonde defined above.  Since
	\(\lambda\in\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one\), this is simply
	\(\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq n}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)\).

In particular, if $F$ is invariant under unitary conjugation, then
\[
	  \int_{\Herm_n} F(H)\,dH
	  =
	  \frac{\pi^{n(n-1)/2}}{V_n(\tau_n)}
	  \int_{\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one}
	  F\!\left(\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\right)
	  V_n(\lambda)^2\,d\lambda.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem.variance of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let $Y_\alpha \sim \nu_{\alpha}$. Then
    \[
       {\mathrm{Var}}\, Y_\alpha 
= \frac 1 {12} \left(-3 \alpha^2 k^2 (k+1)^2 + 2\alpha k (k+1) (2k+1) \right), \quad  k = \lfloor \alpha^{-1} \rfloor.
    \]
    In particular, if $\alpha = \frac 1 k$ for a positive integer $k$ then
    \[
         {\mathrm{Var}}\, Y_\alpha = \frac {k^2 - 1} {12}.
    \]
    If $\alpha \ge \frac 1 2$ then
    \[
        {\mathrm{Var}}\, Y_\alpha = \alpha (1-\alpha).
    \]
    Furthermore, let $f$ be defined by $f(\alpha) = {\mathrm{Var}}\, Y_\alpha$. 
    Then $f$ is continuous and non-increasing for $\alpha \in (0,1)$.
    If $k$ is a positive integer, then in the interval $(\frac 1 {k+1}, \frac 1 k)$
    
    $f$ is differentiable and for $\alpha$ in this interval $f''(\alpha)<0$ and
    \[
        
        -\frac 1 6 k (k+1)(k +2)  \le  f'(\alpha) \le - \frac 1 6  k (k^2-1) \le 0.
    \]
    Finally, if $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, $k \ge 2$ then
    \[
        
        \partial_+ f(\frac 1 {k+1}) = 
    \sup_{\alpha \in (\frac 1 {k+1}, \frac 1 {k})} f'(\alpha)
=
 - \frac 1 6  k (k^2-1) =
    \inf_{\alpha \in (\frac 1 {k}, \frac 1 {k-1})} f'(\alpha)
        
     = \partial_- f(\frac 1 {k-1}), 
    \]
    where $\partial_+ f(\alpha)$, $\partial_- f(\alpha)$ denote the right and left derivatives of $f$ at $\alpha$ respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 1 of arXiv:2608.26698, 'Mapping class groups of simply connected closed spin 5-manifolds with no 2- and 3-torsion '] Let $M$ be a simply connected closed spin 5-manifold.
        	\begin{itemize}
        		\item[(1)] There is a short exact sequence \[0 \rightarrow \mathcal{I}(M) \rightarrow \mathrm{MCG}(M) \xrightarrow{\phi} \mathrm{Aut}(H_2(M), L_M) \rightarrow 1,\] where $\mathrm{Aut}(H_2(M), L_M)$ denotes the group of automorphisms of $H_2(M)$ that preserve the linking form $L_M$, and $\phi$ maps an isotopy class of diffeomorphisms to its induced automorphism of $H_2(M)$.
        		
        		\item[(2)] Suppose $H_2(M)$ has no 2-torsion elements. There is an isomorphism of abelian groups \[\mathcal{I}(M) \cong {\Omega}^{\mathrm{Spin}}_6(K(H_2(M), 2)).\] The generators of $\mathcal{I}(M)$ are given in \ref{5.3}.

[Lemma l:trunc of arXiv:2605.20587, 'Persistence and entropic repulsion of stationary Gaussian fields with spectral singularity'] Let $\mu = \mu_1 + \mu_2$, let $f'$ be an SGF with spectral measure $\mu_1 + \phi_s^2 \mu_2$. Then for every $0 < s <T$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[  \mathbb{P} \Big[ \inf_{x \in B(T)} f(x) \ge \ell \Big]  \le  \mathbb{P} \Big[ \inf_{x \in B(T-s)} f'(x) \ge \ell  \Big] .\]
 Moreover, if $\eta \in \mathcal{M}$, then for every $0 < s <T$, $\ell,\ell' \in \mathbb{R}$, and $\delta > 0$,
\begin{align*}
& \mathbb{P} \Big[\inf_{x \in B(T)} f(x) \ge \ell , \langle 
 f,\eta \rangle \ge \ell' \Big] \\
& \qquad \le  \mathbb{P} \Big[ \inf_{x \in B(T-s)} f'(x) \ge \ell , \langle f',\eta \rangle \ge \ell' -\delta \big]  + \mathbb{P} \big[ \sup_{u \in B(s/2)} | \langle f, \eta - \eta_u \rangle | \ge \delta  \Big],
\end{align*}
where $\eta_u(\cdot) = \eta(\cdot - u)$ is the translation of $\eta$. The same result holds in the discrete case after replacing $\phi_s$ with $\tilde{\phi}_s$.
title: Smoothing for the persistence

body:
[Thm matrixperp of arXiv:2605.31054, 'On the empirical spectral distribution of matrix perpetuities'] Let $({\mathbf A}_n,{\mathbf B}_n)_{n\geq 1}$ be iid copies of $({\mathbf A},{\mathbf B})$. If 
\begin{align}
{\mathbb E}\left[ \log^+\left(\lambda_{\max}({\mathbf A}{\mathbf A}^\top)\right)\right]<+\infty\quad\mbox{and}\quad {\mathbb E}\left[ \log^+\left(\lambda_{\max}({\mathbf B}{\mathbf B}^\top)\right)\right]<+\infty 
\intertext{and}
\gamma=\inf_{n\geq 1} \frac{1}{n}{\mathbb E}\left[ \log( \lambda_{\max}\left({\mathbf A}_1{\mathbf A}_2\ldots{\mathbf A}_n {\mathbf A}_n^\top\ldots{\mathbf A}_{2}^\top{\mathbf A}_1^\top\right))\right] <0, 
\end{align}
then there exists a unique solution to (equation eq:matperp of the paper). 

Moreover, this solution has a series representation
\begin{align}
{\mathbf X}\stackrel{d}{=} \sum_{n=1}^\infty {\mathbf A}_1\ldots {\mathbf A}_{n-1}{\mathbf B}_n{\mathbf A}_{n-1}^\top\ldots{\mathbf A}_1^\top,
\end{align}
where the series on the right-hand side above converges almost surely, with $({\mathbf A}_n,{\mathbf B}_n)_{n\ge1}$  iid copies of $({\mathbf A},{\mathbf B})$. 

Finally, letting
\[
{\mathbf X}_n={\mathbf A}_n {\mathbf X}_{n-1}{\mathbf A}_n^\top+{\mathbf B}_n,\qquad n\ge1,
\]
where ${\mathbf X}_0$ is independent of $({\mathbf A}_n,{\mathbf B}_n)_{n\ge1}$, we have 
\[
{\mathbf X}_n \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow} {\mathbf X}.
\]
title: Thm matrixperp of arXiv:2605.31054

diffeomorphism $A$ of $\mathbb{T}^3$, isotopic to the identity, with
\[
  \norm{\mathbb{E}\nabla A}_{C^\alpha}=1,\qquad
  \mathbb{E}\left\lVert \nabla A\right\rVert_{C^\alpha}\ge c_\alpha N .
\]
Moreover, volume preservation places no lower bound on the smallest singular value of a
mean: the four rotations
$R_0=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1)$, $R_1=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, $R_2=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,-1)$,
$R_3=\mathrm{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ all lie in $SO(3)$, yet $\tfrac14\sum_jR_j=0$.

body:
[Definition 1 of arXiv:2511.14740, 'Marking and re-marking'] Let $n \in \mathbb N$ and $p \in [0,1]$. A one-dimensional random variable $Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N$ with probability mass function
\[ p(y) = \binom{n}{y} p^{y} (1-p)^{n-y}  \]
is said to be a \emph{binomial distribution} with parameters $n$ and $p$. We write $Y \sim \Bin(n, p)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb N$ and $\mathbf p \in [0,1]^c$ with $|\mathbf p| \leq 1$. A $c$-dimensional random variable $\mathbf Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N^c$ with probability mass function
\[ p(\mathbf y) = \binom{n}{\mathbf y} \prod_{i=1}^c p_i^{y_i} \, \big(1 - |\mathbf p|\big)^{n-| \mathbf y|}  \]
is said to be a \emph{multinomial distribution} with parameters $n$ and $\mathbf p$. We write $\mathbf Y \sim \Multi(n, \mathbf p)$.

Let $X$ be a random variable taking values in $\mathbb N$ and $a \in [0,1]$. Consider the one-dimensional random variable $Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N$ whose conditional distribution given $X$ is $\Bin(X,a)$, so its probability mass function is
\[ p(y) = \mathbb E \left(\binom{X}{y} a^{y} (1-a)^{X-y}\right) . \]
We call $Y$ the \emph{binomial thinning} (or just \emph{thinning}) of $X$ with parameter $a$, and write $Y = a \circ X$.

Let $X$ be a random variable taking values in $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbf a \in [0,1]^c$ with $|\mathbf a| \leq 1$.  Consider the $c$-dimensional random variable $\mathbf Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N^c$ whose conditional distribution given $X$ is $\Multi(X,\mathbf a)$, so its probability mass function is
\[ p(\mathbf y) = \mathbb E \left(\binom{X}{\mathbf y} \prod_{i=1}^c a_i^{y_i} \, \big(1 - |\mathbf a|\big)^{X-| \mathbf y|} \right) . \]
We call $\mathbf Y$ the \emph{multinomial marking} (or just \emph{marking}) of $X$ with parameters $\mathbf a = (a_i)$, and write $\mathbf Y = \mathbf a \circ X$.
title: Definition 1 of arXiv:2511.14740

[Definition 23 (Finite-scale flexibility) of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] For \(r\ge1\), let
\[
  \cS_r=\{\sigma\in\cS:\cC_r(\sigma)\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
Given an integer \(h\ge1\), the graph is
\emph{\(h\)-flexible at scale \(r\)} if, for every
\(\sigma\in\cS_r\), there are forests
\[
  \Gamma_\sigma^-,\Gamma_\sigma^+\in\cC_r(\sigma)
  \quad\text{such that}\quad
  \#E(\Gamma_\sigma^+)=\#E(\Gamma_\sigma^-)+h.
\]
Thus every realizable way of connecting the boundary of an \(r\)-cell
has two internal realizations whose lengths differ by exactly \(h\).
The graph is \emph{\(h\)-flexible} if it is \(h\)-flexible at some
finite scale; such an \(h\) is called a \emph{flexibility step}.
title: Finite-scale flexibility
