[Definition 6 of arXiv:2608.19065, 'Boundedly exchangeable graphs'] A random adjacency measure $\xi$ on $S$ is a graph process on $S$ if it admits a representation \eqref{EqRandomAdjacencyMeasure} in which, for some connection kernel $W$ on $S$,
    \begin{equation*}
        A_{ii} = 0, \qquad
        A_{ij}\mid \bigl( N,(S_k) \bigr) \;\overset{\textnormal{ind.}}{\sim}\; \mathrm{Bernoulli}\bigl(W(S_i,S_j)\bigr), \qquad 
        i < j,
    \end{equation*}
    the remaining entries being given by symmetry, $A_{ji}=A_{ij}$. We call \eqref{EqRandomAdjacencyMeasure} an i.i.d.\ representation of $\xi$ if, in addition, the $(S_k)$ are i.i.d.\ according to some probability measure $\hat\mu$ on $S$ and $N\indep(S_k)$.

body:
Let f be an orientation-preserving C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle with irrational rotation number alpha, and suppose log f' has BOUNDED VARIATION (in particular this holds if f is C^2). Then f is topologically conjugate to the rigid rotation R_alpha; in particular f is minimal and has no wandering intervals. The engine is Denjoy's inequality: for every n the distortion is controlled, exp(-V) <= (f^n)'(x) / (f^n)'(y) <= exp(V) where V is the total variation of log f', valid whenever the intermediate iterates of the interval between x and y are disjoint - which the combinatorics of closest returns to an irrational rotation number supplies. Regularity is sharp: Denjoy also constructed C^1 examples with irrational rotation number and a wandering interval, so the bounded-variation hypothesis cannot be dropped.
Orientation-preserving, irrational rotation number, and log f' of bounded variation (C^2 suffices, C^1 does not).
The conjugacy produced is a homeomorphism;
its smoothness requires Diophantine conditions on alpha and much more regularity (Herman-Yoccoz theory).

[Proposition prop1 of arXiv:2609.03988, 'A $p$-summability approach to the weak maximizing property'] Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces such that $(X, Y)$ has the $\mathrm{SMP}_p$ for some $1 \leq p < \infty$. \\
{\rm (1)} If $F$ is a closed subspace of $Y$, then $(X,F)$ has the $\mathrm{SMP}_p$. \\
{\rm (2)} If $E$ is a $1$-complemented subspace of $X$, then $(E,Y)$ has the $\mathrm{SMP}_p$. \\
{\rm (3)} If $q > p$, then $(X, Y)$ has the $\mathrm{SMP}_q$. \\
{\rm (4)} The pair $(X, Y)$ has the $\mathrm{WMP}$.
title: Proposition prop1 of arXiv:2609.03988

[Definition def:relations of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] A binary relation $R$ is said to be
  \emph{serial} if $\forall x\, \exists y\, (x R y)$,
  \emph{reflexive} if $\forall x\, (x R x)$,
  \emph{symmetric} if $\forall x,y\, (x R y \mathrel{\Rightarrow} y R x)$,
  \emph{transitive} if $\forall x,y,z\, (x R y \mathrel{\text{\&}} y R z \mathrel{\Rightarrow} x R z)$,
  and \emph{Euclidean} if $\forall x,y,z\, (x R y \mathrel{\text{\&}} x R z \mathrel{\Rightarrow} y R z)$.
  We also say $R$ is \emph{preordered} if $R$ is both reflexive and transitive.
title: Definition def:relations of arXiv:2608.29708

[Lemma lem:cone-invariance of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Let \(L_t\), \(0\le t\le T\), be a continuous family of matrices indexed by a
finite set \(\Omega\).  Assume
\[
        L_t(\omega,\eta)\ge0\quad(\omega\ne\eta),
        \qquad
        \sum_{\omega\in\Omega}L_t(\omega,\eta)=0 .
\]
Then \(\dot x_t=L_tx_t\) preserves the nonnegative cone and the total mass.
If \(\Omega_0\subset\Omega\) satisfies
\(L_t(\omega,\eta)=0\) for \(\eta\in\Omega_0\), \(\omega\notin\Omega_0\),
then support in \(\Omega_0\) is preserved.

Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: when every F_n is a proper distribution function (F_n(x) -> 0 as x -> -infinity and F_n(x) -> 1 as x -> +infinity), the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R (without properness the 'if' fails: a single improper F_1 makes the family non-tight while every subsequential limit can be proper). For the selection itself nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]
each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]

body:
[Theorem thm:twistbc of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] The twist field two-point correlation 
$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_{1}, z_{2})$ for constant boundary condition $v \in \mathbb{R}$ can be defined in the following equivalent ways.
\begin{enumerate}[i)]

\item
As $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\to 0$, we consider the limit of
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\pi/2}{(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/8}\sqrt{|\log \varepsilon_1|\,|\log \varepsilon_2|}} 
\exp\Bigg[
-\mu^{\rm loop}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}
\bigl(\indx_\gamma(z_1)+\indx_\gamma(z_2)\text{ odd}\bigr) \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad
-v^2\mu^{\rm exc}_{D}
\Bigl(
\indx_\gamma(z_1)+\indx_\gamma(z_2)\text{ odd },\,
\gamma\subset D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)
\Bigr)
\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\item
Consider
$\mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}$
the Brownian loop soup in
$D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)$
with intensity
$\frac{1}{2}\mu^{\rm loop}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}$.
For $v\geq 0$, denote by
$\Xi^{v^2/2}_{D, D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}$
the Poisson point process of boundary excursions in
$D$ with intensity
\[
\dfrac{v^2}{2}\,
\1_{\{\gamma\subset D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)\}}
\mu^{\rm exc}_{D}(d\gamma).
\]
As $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\to 0$, we consider the limit of
\begin{equation}
\frac{\pi/2}{(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/8}\sqrt{|\log \varepsilon_1|\,|\log \varepsilon_2|}}
\mathbb{P}\Big(
\text{No cluster of }
\mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}
\cup
\Xi^{v^2/2}_{D, D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}
\text{ disconnects } z_1 \text{ from } z_2
\Big).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\noindent Moreover, for all $v\in\mathbb{R}$, its value is equal to
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_1,z_2)
=
\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D}(z_1,z_2)
\exp\bigl(-v^2 \mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2)\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2) = \mu^{\rm exc}_{D}
\bigl(\indx_\gamma(z_1)+\indx_\gamma(z_2)\text{ odd}\bigr)$.
Further, $\exp(-\frac{\pi}{4}\mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2)) = \hat q$,

where $\hat q$ is the complementary nome to nome $q$ (i.e. $\log q \log \hat q = \pi^2$), that in turn is by Lemma (lem:parametr of the paper) uniquely defined via 
$$\exp\Big(\pi G_D(z_1,z_2)\Big) 
= \dfrac{\theta_3(q^{1/2})}{\theta_2(q^{1/2})}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Two-point correlation of twist field with boundary data

body:
[Theorem 35 of arXiv:2512.07202, 'Hitting Probabilities for Hypoelliptic Differential Equations Driven by Fractional Brownia'] Suppose that the vector fields $\{V_\alpha\}_{\alpha=1}^d$ satisfy Hypothesis \ref{h1} and Hypothesis \ref{1.2}. Let $p_{s,t}(x,y)$ be the joint density of the random vector $(Y_s,Y_t)$ defined by the RDE (\ref{density1}). For any $\delta>0$, there exist constants $C_1,C_2,\tau>0$ depending only on $\delta,H,N$ and the vector fields $\{V_\alpha\}_{\alpha=1}^d$ such that
\begin{equation}
p_{s,t}(x,y)\leqslant \frac{C_1}{|B_d(x,(t-s)^H)|_{\mathrm{Vol}}}\exp\left(-\frac{d(x,y)^2}{C_1(t-s)^{2H}}\right)+C_2|t-s|
\end{equation}
for all $(s,t,x,y)\in(\delta,T]\times \mathbb{R}^N\times \mathbb{R}^N$. Moreover, if one restricts to the cone region
$$
d(x,y)\leqslant (t-s)^H~~\text{and}~~(t-s)<\tau,
$$
then $C_2$ can be taken to be $0$.
title: Theorem 35 of arXiv:2512.07202

	is  a $p$-dimensional space-time white noise on $(\Omega\,, \sF_T, \rQ)$, 
	where
	\[
		\d\rQ/\d\P = \exp\left(-M_T-\tfrac12\<M\>_T\right),
	\]
	for $M_t=\int_{[0, t]\times \T}  Z \cdot \d\xi$ for every $t\in[0\,,T]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary 62 (Sharp Fourier--Galerkin approximation rates) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Under the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:torus-singular-wick-multipliers}, let
$a,b>\beta_m$ and define
\[
 A_m^{a,b}:=\lim_{N\to\infty}J^{-a}M_{V_{m,N}}J^{-b}
 \quad\text{in }L^2(\Omega;\cL(L^2(\mathbb T^D))).
\]
For $R\in\Dya$, $R\ge2$, let
\[
 \Pi_Re^{\mathrm iq\cdot\theta}
 :=\mathbf1_{\{\langle q\rangle<R\}}e^{\mathrm iq\cdot\theta},
 \qquad q\in\mathbb Z^D,
\]
and put
\[
 \cE_R^{a,b}:=A_m^{a,b}-\Pi_RA_m^{a,b}\Pi_R,
 \qquad
 \delta_{a,b}:=\min\{a-\beta_m,b-\beta_m\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}

 \norm{\cE_R^{a,b}}_{L^2(\Omega;\cL)}\asymp
 \begin{cases}
  R^{-\delta_{a,b}},&\sigma<D/2,\\
  R^{-\delta_{a,b}}\log(e+R)^{(m-1)/2},&\sigma=D/2.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The implicit constants are independent of $R$.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}

 \rank(\Pi_RA_m^{a,b}\Pi_R)\lesssim R^D.
\end{equation}

body:
Let H and K be Hilbert spaces (not necessarily separable) and let T: H -> K be compact. Then there exist finite-rank bounded operators T_N with ||T - T_N|| -> 0. Explicitly, if T = sum_n s_n <., e_n> f_n is a Schmidt decomposition, the truncations T_N = sum_{n <= N} s_n <., e_n> f_n satisfy ||T - T_N|| = s_{N+1}(T) -> 0. Combining with the closedness of K(H,K) in operator norm: a bounded operator between Hilbert spaces is compact if and only if it is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators. (This equivalence uses the Hilbert structure; in a general Banach space it can fail, see the approximation-property pitfall.)

[Defn def:local-weak of arXiv:2510.18856, 'Evolution of recursive trees with limited memory'] Fix a probability measure $\varpi$ on $\mathbb{T}$.
	\begin{enumeratea}
 \item  Say that a sequence of trees $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n\right\}_{n\geqslant 1}$ converges in {\bf expectation}, in the fringe sense, to $\varpi$, if \[\E[\mathfrak{P}_n^{0}] \to \varpi, \quad \text{ as } n\to\infty. \]
 Denote this convergence by $\mathcal{T}_n\stackrel{\mbox{$\E$-\bf fr}}{\longrightarrow} \varpi$ as $n\to\infty$.
	    \item   Say that a sequence of trees $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n\right\}_{n\geqslant 1}$ converges in the probability sense, in the fringe sense, to $\varpi$, if \[\mathfrak{P}_n^{0} \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\longrightarrow} \varpi, \quad \text{ as } n\to\infty. \]
	Denote this convergence by $\mathcal{T}_n\stackrel{\mbox{$\operatorname{P}$-\bf fr}}{\longrightarrow} \varpi$ as $n\to\infty$.
	    \item  Say that a sequence of trees $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n\right\}_{n\geqslant 1}$ converges in probability, in the {\bf extended fringe sense}, to a limiting infinite random {\tt sin}-tree $\mathcal{T}_{\infty}$ if for all $k\geqslant 0$ one has
	  \[\mathfrak{P}_n^k \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\longrightarrow} \mathbb{P}\left(F_k(0,\mathcal{T}_{\infty}) \in \cdot \right), \qquad \text{ as } n\to\infty. \]
	Denote this convergence by $\mathcal{T}_n\stackrel{\mbox{$\operatorname{P}$-\bf efr}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{T}_{\infty}$ as $n\to\infty$.
	\end{enumeratea}
title: Local weak convergence

Author-derived explicit counterexample, awaiting designated referee review: in the rooted tree T whose depth-(n-1) vertices have four children when n is a positive perfect square and two children otherwise, maximum degree is five, p_c(T)=1/2, and P_{1/2}(o connects to infinity)>=2/7. The uniform-ray common-edge energy at r=1/2 is 7/2. The unique degree-four root fixes infinitely many distance orbits, so T is not quasi-transitive. This refutes removing quasi-transitivity from P0043 and does not refute P0043.

[Propn cdfPdfEquiv of arXiv:2605.04860, 'Branching Brownian motion with rank-based selection and reaction-diffusion equations'] Suppose that $(\mu_t)_{t\geq 0}$ satisfies ((muinfLimit of the paper)); that is
    \begin{align*} \langle \mu_t, f(\cdot,t)\rangle = \langle \rho ,f(\cdot,0)\rangle + \int_0^t \langle \mu_s,\frac12 f_{xx}(\cdot,s)+f_t(\cdot,s) + r(s)f(\cdot,s)\rangle - \left\langle \mu_s,f(\cdot,s)r(s)\psi((H\star\mu_s)(\cdot)\right\rangle ds, 
    \end{align*}
    for every $f\in \mathcal{BC}^{2,1}(\mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty),\mathbb{R})$. 
    Define $F(x,t):=(\tilde{H}\star \mu_t)(x)$. Then $\langle \mu_t,1\rangle=1$ for all $t\geq 0$ and $F$ 
    satisfies
    \begin{align}
        \langle F(\cdot,t),f(\cdot,t)\rangle - \langle \tilde{H}\star \rho, f(\cdot,0)\rangle = \int_0^t \langle F(\cdot,s),\frac12 f_{xx}(\cdot,s) &+ f_t(\cdot,s) + r(s)f(\cdot,s)\rangle \\
        &- r(s)\left\langle f(\cdot,s),\int_{1-F(\cdot,s)}^1 \psi(u)du\right\rangle ds. \notag
    \end{align}
    for all test functions $f$ such that $(H\star f(\cdot,t))(x)\in \mathcal{BC}^{2,1}(\mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty),\mathbb{R})$.

[Theo 3 of arXiv:2510.26207, 'A combinatorial perspective on the Kemeny constant and more'] \begin{itemize}
  \item[$(i)$] The power series $\l(\bK_u^{\geq 0}(x), u \in V\r)$ are all equal on $\bar{B}(0,R_t)$.

[Lemma talagrand-bousquet of arXiv:2608.12056, 'Deviation inequalities for U-processes of growing order, with applications to half-space d'] [boucheron2013concentration]
Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of measurable real-valued functions and let $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ be i.i.d. Assume that $\mathbb{E}f(X_1)=0$ for all $f\in \mathcal F$ and that $\sup_{f\in \mathcal F} |f(X_1)|\leq U$ with probability $1$. Denote $Z=\sup _{f \in \mathcal{F}} \sum_{k=1}^N f\left(X_k\right)$.
Assume that $\sigma_\ast^2\geq N\sup_{f\in \mathcal F} \mathbb{E}f^2(X_1)$ and set $v = \sigma_\ast^2 + 2U\mathbb{E}[Z]$. Then for all $t\geq 0$, 
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{P}\left(Z \geq \mathbb{E} Z + \sqrt{2 t v}+\frac{tU}{3}\right) \leq e^{-t}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 8 (A div--curl concentration example) of arXiv:2608.30715, 'Endpoint Energy Atoms Force Local Pressure Concentration in Three-Dimensional Navier--Stok'] There exist a divergence-free field
\(V\in C^\infty(\T^3;\R^3)\), a divergence-free field
\(Y\in C^\infty(\T^3;\R^3)\), a gradient field
\(G\in C^\infty(\T^3;\R^3)\), a scalar \(\eta\in L^1(0,1)\), and, for every
\(\tau\in(0,1)\), a smooth \(b_\tau\) supported in \((\tau,1)\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \norm{b_\tau}_2\le1,
 \qquad
 \left(\int_\tau^1 \eta(t)b_\tau(t)\dd t\right)
 \left(\int_{\T^3}V\cdot[(Y\cdot\nabla)G]\dd x\right)=1.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently, \(u(t,x)=\eta(t)V(x)\) has vanishing
\(L^1((\tau,1);\BMO)\) tails, the fields
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak k_\tau(t,x)=b_\tau(t)(Y\cdot\nabla)G(x)
 
\end{equation}
are uniformly bounded in \(L^2((\tau,1);\Hh^1)\), and yet their
Hardy--BMO pairings equal one for every \(\tau\).

[Theorem 9 (Random environment: simple sufficient conditions) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Consider the Poissonian growth with binomial survival of Example~\ref{ex:poisson-binomial}.  Let $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary ergodic random environment whose marginal distribution is that of the random vector $\mathcal E=(\theta,\lambda,p,d)$ with $\theta>\lambda$\ a.s.\ and $d\in\mathbb N$, $d\ge2$.  Assume
\[
\E[|\log p|]<\infty,\qquad
\E[|\log(1+\lambda/\theta)|]<\infty,
\]
and that $\E\bigl[\bigl|\log\bigl(\p(\xi_{1,0}>0\mid\mathcal E_0)\bigr)\bigr|\bigr]<+\infty$ (which is automatically satisfied for this model under the previous hypotheses).  Then, for every dispersion mechanism $\Delta^{(j)}$, $j=1,2,3,4$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item if
  $\displaystyle \E[\log p] < \E\!\left[\log\frac{\theta}{\theta+\lambda}\right]$,
  the process becomes extinct almost surely;
  \item if almost surely
  \[
  p > \frac1d \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\lambda}{\theta} > \frac1{(d-1)p},
  \]
  the process survives with positive probability.
\end{itemize}

\(u\in\ell^p(\N,x^{-2})\). Then there exists a sequence

\]
as \(j\to\infty\). The limits are understood in \([0,\infty]\).

[Theorem 5 (Sudakov--Fernique with deterministic drift) of arXiv:2606.21137, 'A Sudakov--Fernique proof of Lehner-type edge bounds for matrix-valued GUE sums'] Let $T$ be a compact metric space. Let $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ and
	$(Y_t)_{t\in T}$ be centered Gaussian processes whose sample paths are
	almost surely continuous. Suppose that for every $s,t\in T$,
	\[
		\E\bigl[(X_s-X_t)^2\bigr]
		\le
		\E\bigl[(Y_s-Y_t)^2\bigr].
	\]
	Then, for every continuous deterministic function $a:T\to\mathbb R$,
	\[
		\E \sup_{t\in T}\{a(t)+X_t\}
		\le
		\E \sup_{t\in T}\{a(t)+Y_t\}.
	\]
title: Sudakov--Fernique with deterministic drift

[Corollary cor:polytope-learning-examples of arXiv:2606.19763, 'Optimal Sparsification of Gaussian Processes'] Let $r\geq1$, let $0<\eps<1/2$, and let $f:\R^n\to\zo$ be an unknown Boolean function. 
	There is an algorithm which, given access to independent labeled examples
	$(\bx,f(\bx))$ with $\bx\sim N(0,I_n)$, runs in time
	\[
		n^{
			O\pbra{
				\log(\alpha(r,\eps/2))/\eps^4
			}
		}
		=
		n^{\wt{O}(r^4/\eps^6)}
	\]
	and, with probability $9/10$, outputs a hypothesis $h:\R^n\to\zo$ satisfying 
	\[
		\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{G}}(f,h)
		\leq
		\mathrm{OPT}_r(f)+\eps\,.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let sum_n a_n be a series of REAL numbers that converges but not absolutely (a conditionally convergent series). Then for every alpha in the extended reals [-infinity, +infinity] there is a permutation sigma of the indices with sum_n a_{sigma(n)} = alpha, and there are permutations for which the partial sums have any prescribed pair liminf <= limsup in the extended reals. Consequently a real series is unconditionally convergent (every rearrangement converges to the same sum) if and only if it is absolutely convergent. In R^d with d >= 2 the analogous statement is FALSE and is replaced by the Levy-Steinitz theorem: the set of sums achievable by rearranging a convergent series in R^d is an AFFINE SUBSPACE of R^d, that is a translate of a linear subspace, so it can be a single point, a line, a plane, or all of R^d, but never for instance a disc or two isolated points. In infinite-dimensional Banach spaces unconditional and absolute convergence differ (Dvoretzky-Rogers), so the equivalence in the first sentence is a strictly finite-dimensional phenomenon. [Riemann (1854); Levy (1905) and Steinitz (1913); Dvoretzky and Rogers (1950)]
the series is real-valued and conditionally convergent
for the affine-subspace conclusion: finite-dimensional target R^d and a convergent (not necessarily conditionally convergent) series

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $b\in\{0,1\}$. Then there exists a mutually independent family of smooth, centered, autonomous, Gaussian fields $\{u^j\}_{j\geq 0}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $U^{\alpha,b}$ is equal to $\sum_{j= 0}^\infty u^j$ in law,
    \item for each $j\geq 1$, $u^j$ has a finite spatial range of dependence $2^{-j}$,
    \item and there exists $C(d,\alpha)>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$, $p\geq 1$, and $n\in\{0,1,2\}$,
    \[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_x}\leq  C (p^{1/2}+j^{1/2})2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if $b=1$ and $d\geq 2$, then
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $\nabla\cdot U^{\alpha,b}=0$,
    \item[(ii)] and almost surely, letting $Z_\eps$ be defined as in~\eqref{eq:zero sets}, for all $0 \leq \alpha'<\alpha$,
    \[\lim_{\eps\rightarrow 0} \eps^{-\alpha'd}|Z_\eps|=0.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem thm:semi of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] Assume that $\mathbf{f}$ and $g$ satisfy~(equation eq:g1 of the paper),~(equation eq:g2 of the paper),~(equation eq:g5 of the paper),~(equation eq:g3 of the paper)~and~(equation eq:g4 of the paper) and assume that $B\in L_2(U,W_0^{1,2}({\mathcal O}))$. Assume that Hypotheses~(hyp:quant of the paper)~and~(hyp:mixing of the paper) hold. Then the Markovian Feller semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of the stochastic semilinear equations of the form~(equation eq:semi of the paper) for $d=1,2$, with degenerate additive Wiener noise is exponentially mixing and exponentially ergodic and possesses a unique invariant measure $\mu_\ast$ with finite second $V$-moments. In particular, this holds for the stochastic Burgers equation in 1D for $f_1(x)=x$.

body: Lagrange's four-square theorem, also known as Bachet's conjecture, states that every nonnegative integer can be represented as a sum of four non-negative integer squares. That is, the squares form an additive basis of order four: $p=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2},$ where the four numbers $a,b,c,d$ are integers. For illustration, 3, 31, and 310 can be represented as the sum of four squares as follows: ${\begin{aligned}3&=1^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}+0^{2}\\[3pt]31&=5^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}\\[3pt]310&=17^{2}+4^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}\\[3pt]&=16^{2}+7^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}\\[3pt]&=15^{2}+9^{2}+2^{2}+0^{2}\\[3pt]&=12^{2}+11^{2}+6^{2}+3^{2}.\end{aligned}}$

body:
[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Let \(Y\) have a centred, possibly singular, Gaussian law on
\(\mathbb R^d\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be Borel and convex with
\(\PP(Y\in C)>0\), and let
\(b=\EE(Y\mid Y\in C)\).  For every nonnegative convex Borel function
\(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)\),
\begin{equation}
  \EE\left[\varphi(Y-b)\,\middle|\,Y\in C\right]
  \leq \EE\varphi(Y),
  
\end{equation}
whenever the right-hand side is finite.  In particular, for every linear
functional \(\ell\) and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\),
\begin{equation}
  \EE\left[
    e^{\lambda\ell(Y-b)}\,\middle|\,Y\in C
  \right]
  \leq
  \exp\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2}
  \operatorname{Var}(\ell(Y))\right).
  
\end{equation}
title: Lemma 14 of arXiv:2607.21374

[Defi Def:Product-Wt-Complexes of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] Let $(K,\mu)$ and $(K',\mu')$ be weighted simplicial complexes of the same type. 
  The \emph{Cartesian product} of $(K,\mu)$ and $(K',\mu')$ with respect to some total orderings of the vertices of $K$ and $K'$
   is a weighted simplicial complex $(K\times K',\mu\times \mu')$, where for a simplex
  $\{(v_{i_1},v'_{j_1}),\cdots, (v_{i_s},v'_{j_s})\}$ of
  $K\times K'$,
  \begin{equation} 
   \mu\times \mu'\big( \{(v_{i_1},v'_{j_1}),\cdots, (v_{i_s},v'_{j_s})\} \big):= \mu(\{v_{i_1},\cdots, v_{i_s}\})\cdot \mu'(\{v'_{j_1},\cdots, v'_{j_s}\}).  
   \end{equation}
   It is easy to see that
  $(K\times K',\mu\times \mu')$ has the same type as $(K,\mu)$ and $(K',\mu')$.
title: Cartesian product of weighted simplicial complexes

[Lemma 43 of arXiv:2609.01473, 'Keller sequences of exact $\infty$-categories'] Let 
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        \cal{A} & \cal{C} \ar[l, shift right=.6ex, bend right=2ex, "j"', "\rotatebox{90}{$\vdash$}", hookleftarrow] \ar[l, shift left=.6ex, bend left=2ex, "q"] \ar[r, bend right=2ex, shift right=.6ex, "i"', hookleftarrow] \ar[r, shift left=.6ex, bend left=2ex, "p", "\rotatebox{90}{$\vdash$}"'] & \cal{B}.
    \end{tikzcd}\]
be a semi-orthogonal decomposition.
Then a $p$-cartesian inclusion in $\cal{C}$ is also a $\Span^{\dagger}(p)$-cartesian arrow in $\Span^{\dagger}(\cal{C})$ when viewed as a purely forward span and a $p$-cartesian projection is also a $\Span^{\dagger}(p)$-cocartesian arrow in $\Span^{\dagger}(\cal{C})$ when viewed as a purely backward span.

Dually, any $q$-cocartesian inclusion in $\cal{C}$ is also $\Span^{\dagger}(q)$-cocartesian when viewed as a purely forward span and any $q$-cocartesian projection is $\Span^{\dagger}(q)$-cartesian when viewed as a purely backward span.

body:
[Mainthm c of arXiv:2608.26564, 'Real ideal points, Conway spheres, and left-orderable Dehn fillings'] Let $K$ be an $(n, m)$ torus-torus, twist-torus, or twist-twist knot in either the base or the flipped-pair class, and let $M$ be its exterior.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Theorem (mainthm:a of the paper) applies to exactly $nm$, $m$, and $1$ admissible real limiting data respectively, producing that number of distinct real ideal points of $X(M)$ detecting the Conway sphere, each with a two-sided real analytic branch of irreducible $SL_2(\mathbb R)$-characters.
	\item Along every such branch, $\operatorname{tr}\rho_u(\mu) > 2$ while $|\operatorname{tr}\rho_u(\lambda)| \to \infty$; in particular the meridian-normalized lifts define a pair of unbounded augmented holonomy arcs.
	\item Theorem (mainthm:b of the paper) applies to exactly $\min(n, m)$, $1$, and $1$ of these branches respectively; the corresponding arcs lie in $H_{0,0}(M)$ and are unbounded with vertical asymptotes on opposite sides. Consequently, there exist $R^- < R^+$ such that $\pi_1(M(r))$ is left-orderable for every rational $r \notin [R^-, R^+]$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Mainthm c of arXiv:2608.26564

    C\sqrt{D/s}\,B_\infty^S\right)
  \le \exp(O(s)).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma idempotent-restrict of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $i\colon S\hookrightarrow T$ be a cleft, let ${\mathcal{C}}\in\CAT_T^\textup{$S$-cc}$, and let $X$ be a global section. Then $({\mathcal{C}},X)$ is an idempotent in $\CAT_T^\textup{$S$-cc}$ if and only if the restriction $(i^*{\mathcal{C}},i^*X)$ is an idempotent in $\CAT^\textup{$S$-cc}_S$. Moreover, in this case a ${\mathcal{D}}\in\CAT_T^\textup{$S$-cc}$ is a ${\mathcal{C}}$-module if and only if $i^*{\mathcal{D}}$ is an $i^*{\mathcal{C}}$-module.
    \begin{proof}
        This follows at once from Lemma~(lemma:restr-cleft-sym-mon of the paper) since the restriction functor $i^*\colon\CAT_T\to\CAT_S$ is conservative.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[campaign status: proved - the campaign's own proof, author-checked, unrefereed; the prior-art search was not completed] Let B_{m,n} be the balls-in-boxes model with a weight sequence (w_j), partition function Z(m,n), radius of convergence rho > 0 and w_0, w_1 > 0, and let Y(1) be the largest box occupancy. CLAIM (Janson, Conjecture 18.4): if m = o(n) then Y(1) = o_p(log n). Quantitatively, for m <= n/4, with gamma = min(1, w_1/w_0) and any r < rho such that gamma r n / (2m) > 1 (true for all large n when m = o(n) and r is fixed; otherwise the logarithm is not positive and the bound says nothing), Y(1) <= (1 + delta) log n / log(gamma r n / (2m)) with high probability, i.e. Y(1) = O_p(log n / log(n/m)). The case w_1 = 0 (span 1) follows by the same comparison, writing j as a fixed sum of parts from a finite allowed set F by Frobenius, with constant max F / log(gamma_F r^{max F} n / (2m)), again once that logarithm is positive; span d > 1 reduces to span 1 by dividing box counts by d. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the finer multinomial asymptotics log n / log(n log n / m) of Gonnet and of Raab and Steger have no general-weight analogue here.
weights w_j >= 0 with w_0 > 0, w_1 > 0 and radius of convergence rho > 0 (w_1 = 0 handled separately)
m = o(n); the quantitative bound assumes m <= n/4
r < rho with gamma r n/(2m) > 1, and gamma = min(1, w_1/w_0)

[Lemma dco of arXiv:2608.30747, 'Compact homogeneous complex manifolds'] For any Hermitian C-space, the only possibly nonzero components of $d\omega$ are given by 
$$
d\omega(E_\alpha,E_\beta,E_\gamma)= -\im N_{\alpha,\beta}(\epsilon_\alpha x_\alpha+\epsilon_\beta x_\beta+\epsilon_\gamma x_\gamma),  \qquad \alpha+\beta+\gamma=0, 
$$
$$
d\omega(A,E_\alpha,E_{-\alpha}) =\omega_\ag(A,A_\alpha)=g_\ag(J_\ag A,A_\alpha), \qquad \forall A\in\ag^c, \;\alpha\in\Delta_\qg,  
$$
and for the $3$-form $d^c\omega=-d\omega(J\cdot,J\cdot,J\cdot)$,  
$$
d^c\omega(E_\alpha,E_\beta,E_\gamma)= \epsilon_\alpha\epsilon_\beta\epsilon_\gamma N_{\alpha,\beta}(\epsilon_\alpha x_\alpha+\epsilon_\beta x_\beta+\epsilon_\gamma x_\gamma), \qquad \alpha+\beta+\gamma=0, 
$$
$$
d^c\omega(A,E_\alpha,E_{-\alpha}) =g_\ag(A,A_\alpha),  \qquad \forall A\in\ag^c,\;\alpha\in\Delta_\qg.  
$$
On the other hand, 
$$
d\omega(A,e_\alpha,f_\alpha) = \omega_\ag(A,\im A_\alpha) 
= g_\ag(J_\ag A, \im A_\alpha), \qquad\forall A\in\ag, \;\alpha\in\Delta_\qg^+.  
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma untied-approximate-integral-equation of arXiv:2609.03858, 'High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics of \\ Attention-Indexed Models'] Under the conditions of Theorem (theo:untied-SGD of the paper), let \(J\) be a
stopping time satisfying (equation eq:stopping-time of the paper), and fix \(T>0\). Set $\tau_d:=\frac{\alpha_d}{d}$ and $N_T:=\left\lfloor\frac{Td}{\alpha_d}\right\rfloor$.
Then, for every \(\alpha\), there exists
\(\mathcal E_\alpha^{(d)}:[0,T]\to\mathbb R\) such that
\begin{equation}
\tilde\mu_{\alpha,J}^{(d)}(\tau)=\mu_\alpha^{(0)}+\int_0^\tau
[\widetilde{\mathcal V}_{\mathrm{eff},J}^{(d)}(s)]_\alpha\,ds+\mathcal E_\alpha^{(d)}(\tau),
\qquad
0\le\tau\le T,

\end{equation}
and $\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}|\mathcal E_\alpha^{(d)}(\tau)|\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0$.

body:
[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] (Asymptotic Quota Stabilization for Nonexceptional $\tau$) Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the exceptional set of finite $\tau \in (-\frac 13,\frac 13)$ such that Theorem \ref{tau_limit_thm1} fails. Fix $\tau \notin \mathcal{E}$. Then there exists some $x_\tau$ such that for all $x \geq x_\tau$, $A(1,x,y(x,\tau))$ is always a lower quota violation caused by nonzero allocation or always not a violation, with this behavior determined by $\tau$. 

Specifically, let state $i \in \{2,3\}$ be the state that receives the last seat when apportioning $M$ seats among only states $2$ and $3$ from $A(\tilde{q}_2, \tilde{q}_3)$. 
Then: 
\begin{enumerate}
 \item If $A(\tilde{q}_2, \tilde{q}_3)$ assigns state $i$ its lower quota 
 $\lfloor \tilde{q}_i \rfloor$, then for all $x \geq x_\tau$, the apportionment 
 $A(1, x, y(x,\tau))$ is a lower quota violation caused by nonzero allocations, 
 with state $i$ receiving $\lfloor \tilde{q}_i \rfloor - 1$ seats.
 \item If $A(\tilde{q}_2, \tilde{q}_3)$ assigns state $i$ its upper quota 
 $\lceil \tilde{q}_i \rceil$, then for all $x \geq x_\tau$, the apportionment 
 $A(1, x, y(x,\tau))$ is not a quota violation.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Thm 1 of arXiv:2607.17576, 'How much randomness is needed to symmetrize a random variable?'] For an exponential random variable $X$, every absolutely continuous independent symmetrizer $Y$ of $X$ satisfies
$$
\Var(Y)\geq \Var(X)
$$
and for every $\alpha>0$,
$$
h_\alpha (Y)\ge h_\alpha(X),\quad
T_\alpha (Y)\ge T_\alpha(X),
$$
where $h_\alpha(\cdot)$ and $T_\alpha(\cdot)$ are  R\'enyi and Tsallis entropies, respectively. Equality holds in all inequalities if and only if $Y$ is an independent copy of $-X$. Analogous results hold for geometric random variables. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 1 of arXiv:2607.17576

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.00449, 'First-order phase transitions in the hard-core model'] \label[lemma]{lem:bifpoint} The map $g$ has a unique critical fixed point $(r_c, \lambda_c)$. It satisfies
    \[\frac{1}{ab-1}<r_c<\frac{1}{b-1}\]
    and is determined by the following equations:
     \begin{enumerate}
        \item $(1+r_c)^{b+1}(abr_c - (1+r_c))^{a-1} = (ab)^ar_c^{a+1}$, and
        \item $\lambda_c = \frac{(1+r_c)^{b+1}}{abr_c - (1+r_c)}$.
    \end{enumerate}

body: [Theorem 1.3 of arXiv:2607.29403, 'Strong invariants and Tverberg numbers in convexity spaces'] Let $(X,\mathcal{C})$ be an $S_{3}$ -separable convexity space with Helly number $h$, and let $\mathcal{B}$ be its family of halfspaces. If $\textup{VC}(\mathcal{B})\leq d$, then $r_{t}=O\bigl(dh\log h\bigr)t.$ In particular, if the Radon number is $r$, then $r_{t}=O(r^{2}\log r)t.$

body: Let X be a square-integrable function of independent coordinates and X^L its value after an independent resampling of a block L, and suppose the pair (X, X^L) is exchangeable (automatic for independent block resampling). Then E[((X^L - X)^+)^2] = Var(X) - Cov(X, X^L). Proof in two lines from facts that hold separately: exchangeability gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 Var(X) - 2 Cov(X, X^L), and the symmetry of X^L - X gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 E[((X^L - X)^+)^2]; equate. Consequences: Cov(X, X^L) <= Var(X) always; summing over a partition of blocks turns Efron-Stein into the exact statement Sum_L E[((X^L - X)^+)^2] = Sum_L (Var(X) - Cov(X, X^L)), so bounding the positive-part functionals a resampling engine consumes is EXACTLY the problem of lower-bounding the block covariances. Numerically checked on a nonlinear functional (relative difference 0.008 at 200,000 samples).

body:
[Proposition 6 (A mixed example with all three coefficient distances) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, let $0<\lambda<1$, let $\varpi>0$, and let $b_0,a_0\in\R$. Let $\beta\in L^1(0,T)$ and $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)\equiv b_0,
  \qquad
  \wt b(t,x)=b_0+\beta(t),
\]
\[
  a(t,x)\equiv a_0,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=a_0+r(t),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr),
  \qquad
  \wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\varpi+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then both stable coefficients are bounded, bounded away from zero, and H\"older while failing to be Lipschitz at the origin. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions}, the coefficient distances satisfy
\[
  B=\|\beta\|_{L^1(0,T)},
  \qquad
  A=\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)},
  \qquad
  S=\varpi T^{1/\alpha}.
\]
Consequently, if $x_0=\wt x_0$ and these three quantities are smaller than one, then Theorem~\ref{thm:noncritical} gives
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
\le C\max\left\{
\|\beta\|_{L^1(0,T)}^{\frac{\alpha\wt\eta-1}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+1}},
\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}},
(\varpi T^{1/\alpha})^{\alpha-1/\wt\eta}
\right\}.
\]

[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2607.09246, 'Scaling limit of 1+1 dimensional directed polymer with power-law tail and spatial correlat'] Assume conditions \((A)\) and \((B)\), and suppose that the right tail of
\(\xi\) satisfies
\[
        \mathbb Q(\xi>x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x),
        \qquad \alpha>2.
\]
For fixed \(q>0\), denote log-cumulant generating function by
\[
        \Lambda_N(q)
        :=
        \log\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}
        \left[
        \exp\{q\beta_N\bar\omega(i,x)\}
        \right].
\]
Let \(\theta\in(2,\alpha)\) satisfy \(r\theta>1\), and put
\(p:=\lfloor\theta\rfloor\).  Assume \(\beta_N\to0\), \(k_N\beta_N\) is
bounded away from zero, and that for some
\(\varepsilon\in(0,\alpha-\theta)\),
\[
        \left(
        \beta_N^{p+1-\theta}
        +
        \beta_N^{\alpha-\theta-\varepsilon}
        \right)
        \exp\{q\beta_Nk_N\sup_y\psi_y\}
        \longrightarrow0 .
\]
Then, as \(N\to\infty\),
\[
        \frac1{\beta_N^\theta}
        \left|
        \Lambda_N(q)
        -
        \sum_{y\in\mathbb Z}
        \log\left(
        1+
        \sum_{j=1}^p
        \frac{(q\beta_N\psi_y)^j}{j!}
        \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[\bar\xi^j]
        \right)
        \right|
        \longrightarrow0 .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Carleson's theorem: the Fourier series of every L^2 function on the circle converges pointwise almost everywhere (extended by Hunt to L^p for p > 1). By contrast Kolmogorov constructed an L^1 function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere, so the integrability threshold is sharp in this sense. The proof is one of the deepest in classical analysis, via time-frequency decomposition of the Carleson operator.

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let $\beta\ge0$. We define
		\[
		\mathbb B^\beta
		\triangleq
		\left\{
		\mathcal B:\
		\text{there exist }\mathcal J\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S_0^\beta
		\text{ and }\mathcal V\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S_0^0\text{ such that }
		\mathcal B=\mathcal J+\mathcal V
		\text{ and }
		\mathcal J+\mathcal J^*\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S_0^0
		\right\}.
		\]
		Such a pair $(\mathcal J,\mathcal V)$ is called an admissible decomposition
		of $\mathcal B$. A family $\mathscr N\subset\mathbb B^\beta$ is called
		bounded if one can choose an admissible decomposition
		$\mathcal B=\mathcal J_{\mathcal B}+\mathcal V_{\mathcal B}$ for every
		$\mathcal B\in\mathscr N$ such that
		\[
		\{\mathcal J_{\mathcal B}:\mathcal B\in\mathscr N\}
		\text{ is bounded in }\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S_0^\beta,
		\]
		and both
		\[
		\{\mathcal J_{\mathcal B}+\mathcal J_{\mathcal B}^*:
		\mathcal B\in\mathscr N\},
		\quad
		\{\mathcal V_{\mathcal B}:\mathcal B\in\mathscr N\}
		\]
		are bounded in $\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S_0^0$.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2609.03098, 'Standing waves for Schr\"odinger equations with Kato class potentials and $L^\infty$-bound'] Let $f$ satisfy the conditions $(f1)$\,--\,$(f3)$ with $f(x,0)=0$ for a.e.\
$x\in\R^N$, and let $\alpha, \omega\in L^{\infty}(\R^{N})$ be such that
$$\lim_{u\to 0} \frac{f(x,u)}{u} = \alpha(x) \quad \text{for a.e. }
x\in\R^N, \leqno{(L_0)}$$
and
$$\lim_{|u|\to \infty} \frac{f(x,u)}{u} = \omega(x) \quad \text{for a.e. }
x\in\R^N. \leqno{(L_\infty)}$$
Assume that $\lambda$ belongs to the resolvent set of both $-\Delta+V-\alpha$
and $-\Delta+V-\omega$, and that
\begin{equation}
\max\{\hat\varrho(|\alpha|), \hat\varrho(|\omega|)\} < \inf \sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}
(-\Delta+V)-\lambda \quad\text{and}\quad d^{-}(V-\alpha, \lambda)\neq
d^{-}(V-\omega, \lambda).
\end{equation}
Then there exist a nonzero solution $\bar u \in H^2(\R^N)$ of $(E)_\lambda$
and a bounded solution $u : \R \to H^1(\R^N)$ of $(P)_\lambda$ such that
either $\bar u$ belongs to the $\alpha$-limit set of $u$ and $u(t) \to 0$ in
$H^1(\R^N)$ as $t \to +\infty$, or $\bar u$ belongs to the $\omega$-limit set
of $u$ and $u(t) \to 0$ in $H^1(\R^N)$ as $t \to -\infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), w730-T355-C003 version 2. Not independently checked. Let d,q>=1 be finite integers. Let u in R^d, v,z in R^q, and
A in C^4(R^d,R^{q x q}). Put H=A^T A and assume globally

    0<m I<=H(u)<=M I,
    (sum_{i=1}^d ||partial_i A(u)||^2)^(1/2)<=D,
    ||D^j H(u)[e_1,...,e_j]||<=B_j product_l |e_l|, j=1,...,4.

All vector norms are Euclidean; matrix norms are operator norms. The bounds
on the derivatives of H are multilinear operator bounds, not coordinatewise
bounds. No common eigenbasis or commutation assumption is made. Let sigma>=0,
0<eta<=min(1,1/M). Let z_k be iid, independent of the past, centrally
symmetric with E z_k z_k^T=I_q, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity;
mu_4=E|z_k|^4. Start at deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. The full-gradient
label-noise recursion for residual A(u)v is

    u' = u + h,
    h_i = -eta v^T (partial_i H)v/2
          -eta sigma z^T (partial_i A)v, i=1,...,d,
    v'=(I-eta H)v-eta sigma A^T z.

Define the global ODE

    U'=b(U), b=-(sigma^2/4) grad tr H, U(0)=u_0.

For bounded C^3 observables F with bounded derivatives put f(u)=F(u,0),
F_j=sup ||D^j f||, j=1,2,3, and F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||.
For T>=0 define the following finite nonnegative constants:

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2+sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4+15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        +sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2,
    beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4, j=0,1,2,3,
    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                    +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2,
    S0=B_1/(2m), S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2, C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2, Ct=Gtu S0/2,
    Qg=G2 J2/2+Gtu sqrt(J2)+Gtt/2,
    Qc_d=C0 M^2 c2+C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
         +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(d M) D c2+2 C2 Jcv+Ct c2,
    C_d(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2+T(Qg+Qc_d).

Then

    sup_{0<=k<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C_d(T) eta.       (1)

The supremum is over integer k. Thus a=1, with an explicit constant for
all finite tangential and normal dimensions. The dependence on dimension
is displayed or contained in the stated derivative and noise norm bounds;
no dimension-free rate constant is asserted.

This extends the saved C002 v2 proof; it does not assume scalar projection
cancellation for multiple outputs. The known limiting vector field remains
Li-Wang-Arora's Corollary 5.2, arXiv:2110.06914v4, pp.8-9,33.

## Statement and explicit constants

Let d,q>=1 be finite integers. Let u in R^d, v,z in R^q, and
A in C^4(R^d,R^{q x q}). Put H=A^T A and assume globally

    0<m I<=H(u)<=M I,
    (sum_{i=1}^d ||partial_i A(u)||^2)^(1/2)<=D,

All vector norms are Euclidean; matrix norms are operator norms. The bounds
on the derivatives of H are multilinear operator bounds, not coordinatewise
bounds. No common eigenbasis or commutation assumption is made. Let sigma>=0,
0<eta<=min(1,1/M). Let z_k be iid, independent of the past, centrally
symmetric with E z_k z_k^T=I_q, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity;
mu_4=E|z_k|^4. Start at deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. The full-gradient
label-noise recursion for residual A(u)v is

    u' = u + h,
    h_i = -eta v^T (partial_i H)v/2
          -eta sigma z^T (partial_i A)v, i=1,...,d,
    v'=(I-eta H)v-eta sigma A^T z.

Define the global ODE

    U'=b(U), b=-(sigma^2/4) grad tr H, U(0)=u_0.

For bounded C^3 observables F with bounded derivatives put f(u)=F(u,0),
F_j=sup ||D^j f||, j=1,2,3, and F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||.
For T>=0 define the following finite nonnegative constants:

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2+sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4+15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        +sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2,
    beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4, j=0,1,2,3,
    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                    +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2,
    S0=B_1/(2m), S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2, C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2, Ct=Gtu S0/2,
    Qg=G2 J2/2+Gtu sqrt(J2)+Gtt/2,
    Qc_d=C0 M^2 c2+C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
         +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(d M) D c2+2 C2 Jcv+Ct c2,
    C_d(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2+T(Qg+Qc_d).

Then

    sup_{0<=k<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C_d(T) eta.       (1)

The supremum is over integer k. Thus a=1, with an explicit constant for
all finite tangential and normal dimensions. The dependence on dimension
is displayed or contained in the stated derivative and noise norm bounds;
no dimension-free rate constant is asserted.

## 1. Normal moments and increments

The second, fourth and sixth normal recurrences in C002 v2 section 2
condition on (u_k,v_k), so changing the dimension of u does not change
any of their terms. In detail with r=|v|, w=(I-eta H)v and
n=-eta sigma A^T z, symmetry gives

    E[|v'|^2|past]<=(1-eta m)r^2+eta^2 sigma^2 qM,
    E[|v'|^4|past]<=(1-eta m)r^4
       +eta^2 sigma^2 M(2q+4)r^2+eta^4 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4,
    E[|v'|^6|past]<=(1-eta m)r^6
       +eta^2 sigma^2 M(3q+12)r^4
       +15 eta^4 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 r^2+eta^6 sigma^6 M^3 mu_6.

These follow by expanding (|w|^2+2w.n+|n|^2)^j, j=1,2,3;
odd powers of n vanish. The contraction uses eta m in [0,1]. Starting
at r=0, induction gives E r^2<=c2 eta, E r^4<=c4 eta^2,
E r^6<=c6 eta^3. All expectations used below are consequently finite.

The deterministic part of h is bounded in Euclidean norm by
eta B_1 r^2/2, by testing its inner product with an arbitrary unit
vector e and using v^T DH[e]v. For its noise part,

    E|h_noise|^2=eta^2 sigma^2 sum_i |partial_i A v|^2
              <=eta^2 sigma^2 D^2 r^2,
    |h_noise|<=eta sigma D |z| r.

Consequently E|h|^2<=J2 eta^3 and E|h|<=sqrt(J2)eta, using eta<=1.
The same product estimate as in C002 v2, with |h| replacing |d|, gives

    E[|h|^2 |v'|^2]<=4 Jcv eta^3.                     (2)

Indeed |h|^2<=2 eta^2[B_1^2 r^4/4+sigma^2 D^2 |z|^2 r^2]
and |v'|^2<=2r^2+2eta^2 sigma^2 M |z|^2. Multiplying these inequalities
and conditioning on the past gives exactly the four terms in Jcv, since
E|z|^2=q. The powers of eta in those four terms are respectively
5,6,4,5, all bounded above by eta^3 for 0<eta<=1. No sum over d
is omitted: it is absorbed by the specified square-sum bound D.

## 2. Vector backward flow

For every j=0,1,2,3, ||D^j b||<=beta_j. To see this, for unit vectors
e_0,...,e_j, take the inner product of D^j b[e_1,...,e_j] with e_0:
its absolute value is sigma^2/4 times
|tr D^{j+1}H[e_0,...,e_j]|<=q sigma^2 B_{j+1}/4.
Thus b is bounded and globally Lipschitz. For a terminal integer K with
tau=K eta^2<=T, let g(t,u)=f(S_{tau-t}u), where S is its global flow.
The vector variational equations for J=DS, K2=D^2S, K3=D^3S are

    J'=Db J,
    K2'=Db K2+D^2b[J,J],
    K3'=Db K3+sum_of_three D^2b[J,K2]+D^3b[J,J,J].

The operator norm inequalities are precisely the scalar inequalities
used in C002 v2. Variation of constants gives
||J_s||<=exp(beta_1 s), ||K2_s||<=beta_2 s exp(2 beta_1 s),
||K3_s||<=(beta_3 s+3 beta_2^2 s^2/2)exp(3 beta_1 s).
This remains valid at beta_1=0, without division by beta_1.
The chain rule gives the displayed G1,G2,G3 for the first three spatial
derivatives of g. The backward equation is g_t+b.grad g=0;
its derivatives give ||D g_t||<=Gtu and |g_tt|<=Gtt.

## 3. Matrix-valued one-form corrector

For each u define a linear map S_u:R^d->Sym_q by

    H S_u[e]+S_u[e] H=DH(u)[e].

The inverse Lyapunov operator on symmetric matrices has norm <=1/(2m),
as shown by its exponentially convergent integral in C002 v2 section 3.
Thus ||S_u[e]||<=S0|e|. Differentiating in a direction a gives

    H (D_a S)[e]+(D_a S)[e] H
       =D^2H[a,e]-DH[a]S[e]-S[e]DH[a].

A second derivative gives the B_3 term, two B_2 S0 terms, and four
B_1 S1 terms. Therefore the first two u derivatives of this one-form
have multilinear norms <=S1,S2 respectively. Define

    C(t,u)=-S_u[grad g(t,u)]/2,
    G(t,u,v)=g(t,u)+v^T C(t,u)v.

The chain rule gives ||C||<=C0, ||DC||<=C1, ||D^2C||<=C2,
||C_t||<=Ct, with the constants stated above. In particular

    HC+CH=-DH[grad g]/2,
    sigma^2 tr(CH)=-(sigma^2/4) tr DH[grad g]=b.grad g. (3)

These are identities without a commutation hypothesis. The frozen
quadratic increment is exactly

    E[v'^T C v'-v^T C v|past]
       =-eta v^T(HC+CH)v+eta^2 v^T HCH v
        +eta^2 sigma^2 tr(CH).                       (4)

The first term cancels the deterministic normal-quadratic term in the
increment of g; (3) cancels its eta^2 g_t term.

## 4. Shared-noise tensor contraction

The coefficient expansion is C(t,u+h)=C+DC[h]+R,
||R||<=C2 |h|^2/2. Equation (2) bounds its expected contribution by
2 C2 Jcv eta^3. The time coefficient change costs Ct c2 eta^3.
The drift part of DC[h] costs at most
C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 qM c2)eta^3/2, as in C002 v2.

For the noise part write A_i=partial_i A, C_i=partial_i C,
a_i=A_i v, and w=(I-eta H)v. Conditional on the past, symmetry and
E zz^T=I imply the exact identity

    E[(z^T a_i)(w-eta sigma A^Tz)^T C_i(w-eta sigma A^Tz)]
       =-2 eta sigma w^T C_i A^T A_i v.

Summing over i and multiplying by -eta sigma gives

    E[v'^T DC[h_noise]v'|past]
       =2 eta^2 sigma^2 sum_i w^T C_i A^T A_i v.       (5)

The index sum cannot be discarded or replaced by its scalar version.
For every u, each ||C_i||<=C1, and sum_i ||A_i||^2<=D^2.
Cauchy-Schwarz in the i index yields

    sum_i ||C_i|| ||A_i||<=sqrt(d) C1 D.

Using |w|<=r, ||A||<=sqrt(M), and E r^2<=c2 eta, the absolute
expectation in (5) is <=2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(d M) D c2 eta^3.
This is the only new explicit dimension factor relative to C002 v2.

The g Taylor remainder is bounded by Qg eta^3, since its spatial
second derivative is bounded by G2, its mixed derivative by Gtu,
and its time second derivative by Gtt. The HCH term in (4) costs
C0 M^2 c2 eta^3. Combining all terms gives

    |E[G(t+eta^2,u',v')-G(t,u,v)]|<=(Qg+Qc_d)eta^3.   (6)

## 5. Endpoints and full observables

Telescope (6) for K steps. The initial quadratic correction is zero;
the final correction has expectation bounded by C0 c2 eta. Hence
|E f(u_K)-f(U(tau))|<=[C0 c2+T(Qg+Qc_d)]eta.
The law of (u_k,v_k) is invariant under (u,v)->(u,-v): applying
(v,z)->(-v,-z) leaves every component of u' fixed and reverses v'.
Induction starts from v_0=0 and uses the central symmetry of each fresh
z_k. The linear normal term in Taylor expansion of F(u,v) at v=0
therefore has mean zero. Its quadratic remainder is bounded in
expectation by F_vv c2 eta/2. This proves (1) for arbitrary K and
the same constants for all K eta^2<=T, including K=0.

## Boundary of this result

This treats arbitrary finite d,q in the repaired quadratic-normal model.
It does not prove the general curved-manifold problem, handle fixed
off-manifold starts in a uniform supremum including zero, or establish
priority over all later literature. Symmetry of labels is used explicitly;
no nonsymmetric-label result is claimed. All proof claims remain unaudited.
The next unpaid model extension is nonsymmetric finite-moment labels or
an explicitly corrected off-manifold initial layer.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:187fcaa1123ef86d82609c8874d3b3e63fce8e93ce7a1a85148d5aa8311216e5","revision_digest":"sha256:8d156243bb4b38cd384035c284eb21cb9225cfd962d41818e04245168d977da0","source_id":"own-work:w730:T355:w730-T355-C003:v2","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v2-unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem:uniform-moving-cubic of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $C\geq1$.  There is $C_1=C_1(C)$ such that, uniformly for $N\geq3$,
integers $L$ satisfying $|L|\leq CN^2$, and arbitrary sets
$E\subset[-CN,CN]\cap\mathbb Z$, one has
\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1\left|
  \sum_{x\in E}\exp\bigl(2\pi i\alpha(x^3+Lx)\bigr)
 \right|^8d\alpha
 \ll_C N|E|^4\Delta_3(C_1N^3).
\end{equation}
In particular, when $|E|\ll_C N$, the right side is
\begin{equation}
 N^5\exp\!\left(O_C\!\left(
  \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\right)\right).
\end{equation}

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ which follows the exponential law of parameter $\lambda>0$, its cumulative distribution function (CDF) is given by
$$F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$$
with the picture of this CDF being as follows,
\vskip-5mm
$$\xymatrix@R=12pt@C=25pt{
&&&&&\\
&&&&&\\
&&1\ar@.[uu]&&&&&\\
\ar@{-}[rr]&&0\ar@/^/@{-}[urrrr]\ar@{.}[u]\ar@.[rrrrr]&&&&&}$$
and the converse holds too, in the sense that having this CDF means that our variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ must follow the exponential law of parameter $\lambda>0$.
title: Unnumbered proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

REPLICA-SYMMETRIC PREDICTION, not a proved storage threshold. Consider the spherical treelike committee machine with N inputs divided into K disjoint groups of size N/K. For input group x_j in {-1,+1}^(N/K), each hidden weight w_j has ||w_j||^2=N/K and local field h_j=sqrt(K/N)*w_j dot x_j. The output preactivation is s=K^(-1/2)*sum_(j=1)^K v_j*g(h_j)-theta, with fixed balanced signs v_j in {-1,+1} (K even and sum v_j=0), hence theta=K^(-1/2)*E[g(Z)]*sum v_j=0. There are P=alpha*N patterns with independent fair-sign input coordinates and independent fair-sign labels y; storage requires y*s>=kappa for every pattern. Take N,P to infinity at fixed K and alpha, then K to infinity. Let kappa>=0 and g be nonconstant in H^1(gamma), where gamma is standard normal; write sigma^2=Var_gamma(g)>0 and D=E_gamma[(g_prime)^2]<infinity. Under the paper's formal replica analytic continuation, interchange of limits, self-averaging, and replica- and hidden-unit-symmetric saddle ansatz, its equations8-9 give alpha_RS(kappa)=(D/sigma^2)*alpha_G(kappa/sigma), where alpha_G(u)=[integral_(-u)^infinity (u+z)^2*gamma(dz)]^(-1). Thus alpha_RS(0)=2*D/sigma^2 is finite. The analytic input is sigma^2-C_g(q)=D*(1-q)+o(1-q) as q increases to1. The source explicitly identifies a non-rigorous limit interchange and generally expects replica symmetry breaking for nonlinear activations. The formula does not establish existence of storing weights, a sharp threshold, or equality of the true capacity with alpha_RS. The source uses fair-sign inputs; no rigorous Gaussian-input universality conclusion is included.
The stated spherical treelike architecture, balanced readout, iid fair-sign data, nonnegative margin, and sequential limit.
Nonconstant Gaussian H^1 activation; finite positive activation variance and finite weak-derivative energy.
Formal replica analytic continuation and limit interchange; replica- and hidden-unit-symmetric ansatz.

Let U ⊂ C be open and let F be a family of holomorphic functions on U that is locally uniformly bounded: for every compact K ⊂ U there is M_K < ∞ with |f(z)| ≤ M_K for all f in F and all z in K (equivalently, every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is uniformly bounded). Then F is a normal family: every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U, and the limit is holomorphic on U (it need not belong to F). Conversely, a family of holomorphic functions in which every sequence has a locally uniformly convergent subsequence with finite limit is locally uniformly bounded. Pointwise boundedness alone is not sufficient.
U ⊂ C is open
every member of F is holomorphic on U
F is uniformly bounded on each compact subset of U

[Definition 33 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $\alpha\in\R$ and fix a linear splitting rule $\mathsf s$. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $0<\gamma<1$, a {\bf subcritical admissible selection domain} is a linear subspace $\D^{\mathsf s}_{\gamma}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)\subset Z\hat C^{\gamma}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$ such that, for every $H\in\D^{\mathsf s}_{\gamma}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$, the dyadic recursion
is well defined, \eqref{eq:scale-splitting-identity} holds at each splitting step, and \eqref{eq:subcritical-scale-splitting-estimate} holds with $\theta<2^{-\gamma}$ and
$C_H\le C_{\mathsf s}\norm{H}_{\gamma,\alpha}$.

\item At $\gamma=1$, a {\bf critical admissible selection domain} is a linear subspace $$\D^{\mathsf s}_{1}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)\subset Z\hC^{1}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$$
such that, for every $H\in\D^{\mathsf s}_{1}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$, the dyadic recursion is well defined, \eqref{eq:scale-splitting-identity} holds at each splitting step,
and \eqref{eq:critical-scale-splitting-estimate} holds with fixed $C_\ast,\eta>0$ and $C_H\le C_{\mathsf s}\norm{H}_{1,\alpha}$.
\end{enumerate}
In both cases we require the residual continuity criterion
\begin{equation}

\lim_{h\downarrow0}\sup_{\substack{s\le t,\ s,t\in\D\\ t+h\le T}}\norm{(S_h-\mathrm{Id})R^{\mathsf s}_{ts}}_{B_\alpha}=0
\end{equation}
for every $H$ in the corresponding domain.
title: Definition 33 of arXiv:2606.16164

body:
[Theorem 56 (Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{Z}},\Prb)$ be a probability space and let
$\vartheta : \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{Z}$ be measurable and preserve $\Prb$. Then for
every $F \in L^{1}(\Prb)$,
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} F \circ \vartheta^{k}
  \;\longrightarrow\; \Ex_{\Prb}\bigl[ F \mid \mathcal{I} \bigr]
  \qquad \Prb\text{-almost surely and in } L^{1}(\Prb) .
\]
If $\vartheta$ is ergodic for $\Prb$, the limit is the constant $\Ex_{\Prb}[F]$.

If moreover $F \in L^{r}(\Prb)$ for some number $r \in [1,\infty)$, then the
convergence holds in $L^{r}(\Prb)$ as well. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem

[Dfn 20 of arXiv:2608.30763, 'Ultracontractivity of heat semigroups with non-local Robin boundary conditions via two-sid'] We define the operator associated with the form $\tilde{a}(A,B)$ as follows.
\begin{align*}
& D ( \tilde{L}(A, B) ) = & \\
& \left\{ u \in D \left( \tilde{a}(A, B) \right) \ | \ \exists v \in \mathrm{L}^{2}\left( \Omega \right) : 
\tilde{a}(A, B) (u, \varphi) = \langle v, \varphi \rangle_{\mathrm{L}^{2}\left( \Omega \right)} \ \text{ for every } 
\varphi \in D \left( \tilde{a}(A, B) \right) \right\} & 
\end{align*}
as the domain of 
$\tilde{L}(A, B) \colon D ( \tilde{L}(A, B) ) \subset \mathrm{L}^{2}\left( \Omega \right) \to \mathrm{L}^{2}\left( \Omega \right)$ 
which is characterized by the equation
$$
\tilde{a}(A, B)(u, \varphi) =  \langle \tilde{L}(A, B)u, \varphi \rangle_{\mathrm{L}^{2}\left( \Omega \right)}
$$
for $u \in D ( \tilde{L}(A, B) )$ and every $\varphi \in D \left( \tilde{a}(A, B) \right)$.

body: [Definition 9 (Majorization) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] For $a,b\in\R^d_{\ge0}$ with equal sums, $a$ \emph{majorizes} $b$ ($a\succeq b$) if $\sum_{i=1}^k a_{[i]}\ge\sum_{i=1}^k b_{[i]}$ for all $k$, where $x_{[1]}\ge\cdots\ge x_{[d]}$ are the sorted entries. Intuitively $a$ is ``more concentrated'' than $b$.\footnote{A terminology caution held throughout the survey: we use \emph{concentration} in the transform-coding sense: energy packed onto few coordinates. Part of the quantization literature uses the word in the \emph{opposite} sense, for low distributional spread, so that a Hadamard, which we call \emph{flattening}, \emph{increases} their ``concentration'' \citep{federici2026dissecting}. The two senses are inverses; we always mean the former.} A function $f$ is \emph{Schur-convex} if $a\succeq b\Rightarrow f(a)\ge f(b)$, and \emph{Schur-concave} if the inequality reverses. Fixing the partition of the coordinates into scale groups, we write $a\succeq_G b$ ($a$ majorizes $b$ \emph{within groups}) when the two agree on every group's sum and the restriction of $a$ to each group majorizes the restriction of $b$. A block-diagonal doubly stochastic map is doubly stochastic, so $a\succeq_G b$ implies $a\succeq b$, and every Schur-concave function is therefore monotone along $\succeq_G$ as well. The converse fails, and that failure is what matters below: a sum of per-group maxima depends on the grouping, so it is not a functional of $\succeq$ at all, and the opposition of \Cref{prop:schur} is stated along $\succeq_G$.
title: Majorization

1-

\frac12,

\[
k\ge T_{\rm rigid}(\delta^*),
\]
the covariance satisfies
\[
\mathrm{Cov}_{p_k}
(\lambda^2,\log(1/p_k))
<0,

\[
S_{\rm spec}(k+1)
<
S_{\rm spec}(k).
\]

[Definition Convergence in distribution (game-theoretic) of arXiv:2512.21026, 'Minimax Duality in Game-Theoretic Probability\thanks{Work in progress: mistakes are likely'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{Z})$ be a gamble space and $\{X_n:\Omega\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\}_n$ a sequence of variables.
  We say the $X_n$ \emph{converge in distribution} to some $P\in\Delta(\mathbb{R})$ with CDF $F$, written $X_n \xrightarrow{D} P$, if for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $F$ is continuous at $x$ we have $\lim_{n\to\infty} \overline{\textsf{\textbf{P}}}[X_n \leq x] = \lim_{n\to\infty} \underline{\textsf{\textbf{P}}}[X_n \leq x] = F(x)$.

body:
[Theorem thm:U_process of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Suppose $z=0$ and $\widehat{\delta}>0$. For all $r>0$, $\frac{r}{U(r)}$ has distribution $\mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\widehat \delta+\delta}{2},\frac{\widehat \delta}{2})$. 
\item The family $(P^z,z\ge 0)$ defines a time-homogeneous Feller process. For each $z\ge 0$, the process  $\left(U(r)-r\right)_{r\ge 0}$ is a time-homogeneous $(\mathscr{W}^+_r)_{r\ge 0}$-adapted Feller process starting from $z$. 
\item Suppose $z>0$ and write $\mathrm{x}:=\inf\{r\ge 0\,:\, U(r)>z\}$, $\mathfrak{U}:=\lim_{r\downarrow \mathrm{x}} U(r)$. We have $\frac{\mathrm x}{z}\sim\mathcal{B}(1,\frac{\delta}{2})$ and conditionally on  $\{{\mathrm{x}}=x\}$, $\frac{z-x}{\mathfrak{U}-x}\sim \mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\widehat{\delta}+\delta}{2},1)$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Theorem thm:U_process of arXiv:2411.04773

body: Let X be a Banach space with continuous dual X*. A sequence (f_n) in X* converges weak-star to f in X*, written f_n converges to f weak-star, if f_n(x) converges to f(x) for every x in X. Weak-star convergence is implied by, but does not imply, weak convergence of (f_n) in X*; the two notions coincide when X is reflexive. [standard, e.g. Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis]
title: Weak-Star Convergence in a Dual Banach Space
Step A in theorem~\ref{SWLOG}

body:
[Defn def:uncovered-general of arXiv:2411.14336, 'Finding the root in random nearest neighbor trees'] For each edge $(p_1, p_2)$ in the graph, if a vertex $x$ with parent $p_1$ lands in the region such that $d(x, p_1) < d(p_1, p_2) \text{ and } d(x, p_2) < d(p_1, p_2)$, a direction can be assigned to the edge $(x,p_1)$. Particularly, orient the edge from $x$ to $p_1$ to indicate that the arrival time of $p_1$ must be earlier than that of $x$. We can similarly orient all of the vertices in the subtree of $x$. We consider $x$ and its subtree \textit{covered}. Denote by $\mathcal{C}_n = [n] \setminus \mathcal{U}_n$ the set of covered vertices. 

A vertex is called \textit{uncovered} if it is not a covered vertex. An edge is called \textit{uncovered} if both of its endpoints are uncovered vertices.
title: Uncovered vertex and edge

[Lemma lem:finite-comparison of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Let $\Omega\subseteq X$ be finite and let $\eta_1,\eta_2 \colon [0,T]\times(X\setminus\Omega)\to\mathbb R$ be exterior data such that
$\eta_i(t,\cdot)$ is $(\phi,\Omega)$-admissible for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$i=1,2$.  Let $u_1,u_2 \colon [0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ satisfy
\[
    u_i(\cdot,x)\in C([0,T])\cap C^1((0,T))
    \qquad \text{for } x\in\Omega,\ i=1,2
\]
and
\[
    \left(\partial_t +\Delta_\Omega^{\eta_1(t,\cdot)}\Phi\right) u_1
    \le
    \left(\partial_t +\Delta_\Omega^{\eta_2(t,\cdot)}\Phi\right) u_2
    \qquad\text{on }(0,T)\times\Omega .
\]
If $u_1(0,\cdot)\le u_2(0,\cdot)$ on $\Omega$ and $\eta_1\le\eta_2$ on $[0,T]\times\partial_e\Omega$, then
\[
    u_1\le u_2\qquad\text{on }[0,T]\times\Omega .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:finite-comparison of arXiv:2608.11931

body: [Definition of arXiv:2411.16103, 'Non-commutative Stein's Method: Applications to Free Probability and Sums of Non-commutati'] For a given $\rho\in\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$, the moment matching rank $q[\rho]$ associated to $\rho$ is the maximum of the set of natural numbers $\ell$ satisfying $m_{j}[\mu_{k,n}]=m_{j}[\mathfrak{g}[\mu_{k,n}]]$. The matching rank of a sequence of probability measures ${\rho}=\{\rho_{i}\ ;\ i\in I\}$, with $I$ being an arbitrary index is defined as the maximum rank in the components of ${\rho}.$

[Lem 14 of arXiv:2512.03884, '2512.03884'] Let $d>1$ be a squarefree integer, and let
\[ Z_{d'}(s) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \zeta(s) & \textrm{if } d'=1, \\ \zeta_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d'})} (s) / \zeta(s) & \textrm{if } d'>1 \textrm{ squarefree}. \end{array} \right. \]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If $d \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ and $h(d)=2^{\omega(d)-1}$, then
\[ \begin{split} c_1 \bigg( \frac{1+\sqrt{d}}{2} \bigg) &=\frac{d}{4 \pi^4 h(d) \log \varepsilon} \sum_{\substack{d' \mid d \\ d' \equiv 1 \pmod{4}}} Z_{d'}(2) Z_{d/d'}(2), \\  c_2 \bigg( \frac{1+\sqrt{d}}{2} \bigg) &=\frac{d^2}{8 \pi^8 h(d) \log \varepsilon} \sum_{\substack{d' \mid d \\ d' \equiv 1 \pmod{4}}} Z_{d'}(4) Z_{d/d'}(4) . \end{split} \]
\item[(ii)] If $d \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ and $h(4d)=2^{\omega(d)}$, then
\[ \begin{split} c_1 (\sqrt{d}) &=\frac{d}{\pi^4 h(4d) \log \varepsilon} \sum_{d' \mid d} Z_{d'}(2) Z_{d/d'}(2), \\  c_2 (\sqrt{d}) &=\frac{2 d^2}{\pi^8 h(4d) \log \varepsilon} \sum_{d' \mid d} Z_{d'}(4) Z_{d/d'}(4) . \end{split} \]
\item[(iii)] If $d$ is even and $h(4d) = 2^{\omega(d)-1}$, then
\[ \begin{split} c_1 (\sqrt{d}) &=\frac{d}{\pi^4 h(4d) \log \varepsilon} \sum_{\substack{d' \mid d \\ d' \equiv 1, 5 \textrm{ or } d \pmod{8}}} Z_{d'}(2) Z_{d/d'}(2), \\  c_2 (\sqrt{d}) &=\frac{2 d^2}{\pi^8 h(4d) \log \varepsilon} \sum_{\substack{d' \mid d \\ d' \equiv 1, 5 \textrm{ or } d \pmod{8}}} Z_{d'}(4) Z_{d/d'}(4) . \end{split} \]
\end{enumerate}

 \mathcal T_E(C,D)(x,y)
 =\tr\bigl(K_C(x,y)K_D(y,x)\bigr).
 
\end{equation}
The reverse arrows close to an endomorphism of $E_x$, so this trace is
intrinsic and unchanged by unitary changes of frame in the fibers.

[Definition def:reach of arXiv:2609.00889, 'Dominant-Degree Conditions for Ramsey--Tur\'an Factors of Non-Directed Cycle Orientations'] {Let $H$ be a fixed oriented graph on $h$ vertices. Distinct vertices $x,y\in V(D)$ are \textbf{$(H,m,t)$-reachable} if for every set
$W\subseteq V(D)\setminus\{x,y\}$ with $|W|\le m$, there is a set $Q\subseteq V(D)\setminus(W\cup\{x,y\})$ with $|Q|\le th-1$ such that both $D[Q\cup\{x\}]$ and $D[Q\cup\{y\}]$ have $H$-factors. [Thm 2 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] For each $n$ and corresponding $d$, set $p = \binom{n}{d}$ and consider i.i.d.\ samples \[\mathbf x_p^{(1)},\dotsc,\mathbf x_p^{(m)} \sim \PrincipalT(n,d,\nu).\] Let $K = K_p = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^m \mathbf x_p^{(k)}{\mathbf x_p^{(k)}}^\trp$ be the sample covariance matrix, and assume $\binom{n}{d} / m \to c$. Let ``$\wkconv$'' denote weak convergence of probability measures.

    For all $n$, let $\mathbf X^{(n)} = \mathbf X = (X_1,\dotsc,X_n)$ have independent components with zero mean, unit variance, and $\sup_n \max_{1\leq \alpha\leq n} \E X_\alpha^4 < \infty$. If $d = o(\sqrt n)$, then $\ESD(K) \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}$ with probability $1$.

    Furthermore, for base vectors with i.i.d.\ components, we have the following complete characterization:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item  For all $n$, let $\mathbf X^{(n)}$ have components independent and identically distributed as the same random variable $X$, which satisfy $\E X = 0$, $\E X^2 = 1$, $\E X^4 < \infty$, and also $\Pr(\abs{X} = 1) < 1$. Then $\ESD(K) \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}$ with probability $1$ if and only if $d = o(\sqrt n)$.
        \item  If $\mathbf X \sim \Unif\{-1,1\}^n$, then $\ESD(K) \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}$ with probability $1$ if $\min\{d,n-d\} = o(n)$. 
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 2 of arXiv:2607.21759

[Corollary 42 (A nonconvex target covered by the theory) of arXiv:2608.28827, 'Quantitative Target Convergence and Uniform-in-Time\\ Propagation of Chaos for Langevin-Re'] Let \(m,A,\omega>0\) satisfy \(A\omega^2>m\), and set
\[
    V(x)=\frac m2\|x\|^2+A\cos(\omega x_1).
\]
Let \(k(x,y)=\Psi(x-y)\), where
\(\Psi\in C_b^4(\mathbb R^d)\) is even and \(k\) is positive definite.
Suppose that \(\mu_0\) has a smooth positive density and satisfies
\[
    \KL(\mu_0\|\pi)<\infty,
    \qquad
    \int e^{a_0\|x\|^2}\,\mu_0(dx)<\infty
\]
for some \(a_0>0\).  Then Assumptions~\ref{ass:core-target} and
\ref{ass:concentration} hold, as do both kernel assumptions.
Consequently, all main propagation of chaos and uniform-in-time conclusions
apply to this nonconvex target.

Method: Feasible length and stretch statistics of scale-invariant networks structural attempt Result: The feasible set is convex under the source axioms. Choose one of two entire SIRSN laws once using an independent Bernoulli variable, and use that law for all routes. Every realization retains compatibility and all required distributional invariances. Each of Delta,ell,p(1) is an expectation or monotone limit of expectations, hence is the same convex combination of the corresponding statistics. Taking near-minimizers shows ell_*(lambda*Delta1+(1-lambda)*Delta2)<=lambda*ell_*(Delta1)+(1-lambda)*ell_*(Delta2). Check: The random choice is global, so routes from the two networks are never spliced together. No ergodicity assumption appears in the cited definition; imposing one would invalidate this mixture argument. Finite expected statistics remain finite for a two-law mixture. Obstruction: Convexity does not locate the feasible region or give its sharp boundary. It also does not guarantee an extremal law exists; a convex set need not be closed.

[Proposition free cumulants of mu_w of arXiv:2411.13062, 'Graphon-Theoretic Approach to Central Limit Theorems for $\epsilon$-Independence'] The $p$-th free cumulant of $\mu_{w}$ is vanishing if $p$ is odd and is equal to
$$\kappa^{\operatorname{free}}_p(\mu_{w})=\sum_{\pi \in P_2^{con}(p)}\rho(f_\pi,w)$$
if $p$ is even, where $P_2^{con}(k)$ is the set of connected pair partitions of $P_2(p)$ (the partition for which the intersection graph has only one connected component). More generally, the $p$-th free cumulant of $\mu_{w,h}$ is vanishing if $p$ is odd and is equal to
$$\kappa^{\operatorname{free}}_p(\mu_{w,h})=\sum_{\pi \in P_2^{con}(p)}\int_{[0,1]^{V(f_\pi)}}\prod_{u\in V(f_\pi)}|h(x_u)|^2\prod_{(u,v) \in E(f_\pi)} w(x_u,x_v) \, \text{d}x$$
if $p$ is even.

[Theorem thm:rank-diversity-frequency of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq3$. For every $0\leq r\leq k-2$,
\begin{equation}
 \tau_{k,r}(h)
 =\Theta_{k,r}\!\left(h^{(k-1)r}\right)
 \qquad(h\to\infty).
\end{equation}
For $r=0$ one has, more precisely, $\tau_{k,0}(h)=1$ for every $h$.
More locally, let $U$ be any nonempty relatively compact open subset of
$\Delta_{k-1}^{\circ}$. There is a constant $c_{k,U}>0$ such that, for all
sufficiently large $h$, at least
\[
 c_{k,U} h^{(k-1)(k-2)}
\]
maximal-rank types have a representative
$A=\{0=a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_k\}$ for which
\[
 \frac{(a_2-a_1,\ldots,a_k-a_{k-1})}{a_k-a_1}\in U,
 \qquad a_k\leq h^{k-2}.
\]

For each fixed $h$ and each $\mathsf T\in\mathfrak T_{h,k}$ of rank $r$,
the exact frequency law is
\begin{equation}
 F^{(k)}_{h,\mathsf T}(q)
 =c_{h,k,\mathsf T}q^{k-r}
  +O_{h,k,\mathsf T}(q^{k-r-1}),
 \qquad c_{h,k,\mathsf T}\in\mathbb Q_{>0},
\end{equation}
and this function is a quasipolynomial in $q-1$ for every positive integer
$q$. Consequently, whenever $\tau_{k,r}(h)>0$,
$G^{(k)}_{h,r}(q)$ is an exact quasipolynomial in $q-1$ of degree $k-r$,
with
\begin{equation}
 G^{(k)}_{h,r}(q)
 =C_{h,k,r}q^{k-r}+O_{h,k,r}(q^{k-r-1}),\qquad
 C_{h,k,r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathsf T\in\mathfrak T_{h,k}\\
                            r(\mathsf T)=r}}
                    c_{h,k,\mathsf T}\in\mathbb Q_{>0}.
\end{equation}

[Lemma 39 (Monotonicity) of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Let $V,V' \in \metregions$, $V \subseteq V'$, and suppose that $V \setminus V_{(\rmvdeadends{\epsilon})} \subseteq V' \setminus V'_{(\rmvdeadends{\epsilon})}$. Let $x,y \in \ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$ and suppose one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item For every $u \in V' \setminus V$ there is a point $z \in \ol{V}$ that separates $u$ from $x,y$ in $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$.
 \item There exist $z_1,z_2,\ldots \in \ol{V}$ with $\abs{z_i-z_{i'}} \ge 5\epsilon$ for $i\neq i'$ such that no \emph{simple} admissible path in $\ol{V}$ from $x$ to $y$ intersects $\{z_1,z_2,\ldots\}$, and the set $\{z_1,z_2,\ldots\}$ separates $x,y$ from $V' \setminus V$ in $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$.
\end{enumerate}
Then there are points $x',y' \in \ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_\Gamma$ with $\dpathY[\ol{V}](x',x) \le \epsilon$, $\dpathY[\ol{V}](y',y) \le \epsilon$ such that
\[
 \rmetapproxres{\epsilon}{V'}{x'}{y'}{\Gamma} \le \rmetapproxres{\epsilon}{V}{x}{y}{\Gamma} .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Monotonicity

    Define $\Delta_n = M_n - M_{n-1}$ and 
$\Gamma_n := \sum_{k=n+1}^\infty \mathbb{E}[\Delta_k \Delta_k^\top]$.
Assume that $\Gamma_n$ is is positive definite for all sufficiently large and that for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
\begin{align}
   &\Gamma_n^{-1/2} \sum_{k=n+1}^\infty \mathbb{E}\Bigl[ \Delta_k \Delta_k^\top  \,

   \Gamma_n^{-1/2} \xrightarrow{p} 0,\\
& \Gamma_n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=n+1}^\infty \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\Delta_k \Delta_k^\top  \,\Big|\, \mathcal{F}_{k-1} \Bigr] \Gamma_n^{-1/2}
    \xrightarrow{p} I_d.
\end{align}
Then $
\Gamma_n^{-1/2}(M_\infty - M_{n}) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}_d(0, I_d).$

[Theoalph Theorem_B of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] Let $\lambda(n)$ denote the random partition distributed according to $M^{\mathcal A,\mathcal B}_n$, let $\lambda'(n)$ denote the transpose partition, and $s$ denote the number of $i$ such that $\beta_i=1$. Then $\lambda(n)'_1=\dots=\lambda(n)'_s=n$ almost surely and as $n\to\infty$
$$
\left(\frac{\lambda(n)_1-\alpha_1n}{\sqrt{n\alpha_1(1+\alpha_1)}},\dots, \frac{\lambda(n)_k-\alpha_kn}{\sqrt{n\alpha_k(1+\alpha_k)}} \right) \to \mathbf x^{GUE}_{\mathcal A},
$$
$$
\left(\frac{\lambda(n)'_{s+1}-\beta_{s+1}n}{\sqrt{n\beta_{s+1}(1-\beta_{s+1})}},\dots, \frac{\lambda(n)'_l-\beta_ln}{\sqrt{n\beta_l(1-\beta_l)}} \right) \to \mathbf y^{GUE}_{\mathcal B},
$$
where both convergences are in distribution and $\mathbf x^{GUE}_{\mathcal A}, \mathbf y^{GUE}_{\mathcal B}$ denote random vectors defined in Section (finitesect of the paper) in terms of GUE eigenvalue distributions. In particular, in probability, $\frac{\lambda(n)_i}{n}\to \alpha_i$ for $i\in [1,k]$ and $\frac{\lambda(n)'_i}{n}\to \beta_i$ for $i\in [1,l]$. The condition k ≥m + 1 can be weakened as follows. For i ∈[m −1] such that σ(i) < i, we define the set Ii = {u ∈N : σ(i) < u ≤i}.

[Lemma lem:log-sum of arXiv:2412.02777, 'How to quantify the coherence of a set of beliefs'] Let $(V, \boldsymbol p)$ and $(V, \boldsymbol q)$ be coherent credence bases and suppose that $V^T \boldsymbol 1=k\boldsymbol 1$ for some $k\in \mathbb N$. Then,
    $$\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \ln \frac{p_i}{q_i}\ge 0$$
    with equality if and only if $\boldsymbol p = \boldsymbol q$.

Let Omega in R^n be open and let Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + sum b^i D_i u + c u be uniformly elliptic in Omega with bounded coefficients: lambda|xi|^2 <= sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j, a^{ij} = a^{ji}, and |a^{ij}|, |b^i|, |c| <= K, with lambda > 0 and K finite. Let u be in C^2(Omega) with Lu >= 0 in Omega, and let x0 be a boundary point of Omega such that (i) u is continuous at x0; (ii) u(x0) > u(x) for every x in Omega; (iii) Omega satisfies an interior sphere condition at x0, i.e. there is an open ball B contained in Omega with x0 on its boundary. Assume in addition that c = 0, or that c <= 0 and u(x0) >= 0, or that u(x0) = 0 (then c may have any sign). Then, with nu the outward unit normal of B at x0, liminf as t decreases to 0 of (u(x0) - u(x0 - t nu))/t > 0; in particular, if the outward normal derivative of u at x0 exists, it is strictly positive. Consequently u cannot have vanishing gradient at such a boundary maximum point.

body:
Nishimori matched-posterior identity. Let Theta_star and Y take values in standard Borel spaces with their actual joint probability law, and let pi_y be a regular conditional law of Theta_star given Y=y. On an extension of this probability space, draw replicas Theta_1,...,Theta_{k+1}, for integer k>=0, conditionally iid from pi_Y and conditionally independent of Theta_star given Y. Conditional on Y, the planted latent variable and all replicas are iid with the same posterior law. Therefore E f(Y,Theta_star,Theta_1,...,Theta_k)=E f(Y,Theta_{k+1},Theta_1,...,Theta_k) for every measurable f for which the expectations are absolutely finite. In particular E E[h(Theta_1)|Y]=E h(Theta_star) for integrable h. The posterior must be the actual conditional law under the planted joint model. If Theta is a pair of coupled latent matrices, each replica is sampled as a whole pair; the identity supplies no independence between the two components within that pair. This is the standard Bayes exchangeability principle used as Nishimori in Pourkamali-Macris AppendixD.2, not a new frontier result.
Standard Borel latent and observation spaces with the actual joint law and its regular conditional posterior.
Replica draws are conditionally iid from that posterior and independent of the planted variable conditional on Y.
The displayed test functions are absolutely integrable; coupled latent components are kept together.

[Corollary 43 (Ordinary-sequence Gaussian stratum) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] In the setting of Theorem~\ref{bridge:thm:physical-fourth-moment}, assume that
$\Sigma_n\to\Sigma$.  Then the following are equivalent as
$n\to\infty$:
\[
 \sum_a\kappa_{n,a}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,a}}\longrightarrow0
 \quad(a\le d,\ 1\le r<q)
\]
\[
 \Longleftrightarrow\quad
 X_n\Longrightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).
\]
For a fixed represented subsequence,
\begin{equation}
 \Ulim\sum_a\kappa_{n,a}=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 P_{\cD_q}\xi=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 A^{\phys}=0.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently, the ordinary conditions above are equivalent to
$P_{\cD_q}\xi=0$ (equivalently, $A^{\phys}=0$) for every
represented subsequence.  Hence the fourth moment theorem of \cite{NualartPeccati} and its vector
form \cite{PeccatiTudor} are exactly the one-particle stratum of the
primitive--Fock terminal.

body: In the theory of abelian groups, the torsion subgroup $A_{T}$ of an abelian group $A$ is the subgroup of $A$ consisting of all elements that have finite order (the torsion elements of $A$). An abelian group $A$ is called a torsion group (or periodic group) if every element of $A$ has finite order and is called torsion-free if every element of $A$ except the identity is of infinite order.
