ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Variance scale and Gaussian fluctuations of NUV lengths structural calculation Result: The variance decomposes exactly as Var(L)=Var(E[L|G])+E Var(L|G), separating graph disorder from random-start disorder. This implies a lower bound from either term but gives no additivity across mandatory local edges. Even if two vertices force an edge into every NUV walk, its random contribution can covary negatively with the remainder; the scalar example U+(1-U)=1 shows why mandatory participation alone cannot prove a variance lower bound. Check: The law of total variance is applied with the entire weighted graph fixed and the starting vertex random. Conditional independence of local edge contributions is not asserted: the chosen trajectory depends on the full configuration. A Gaussian limit further needs a Lindeberg or stabilization estimate for the actual greedy functional; neither has been proved.

[Thm finitelypresented of arXiv:2507.09120, 'Chemical distance in graphs of polynomial growth'] For each $D, \Delta \le \infty$, there exists $\tilde{p} = \tilde{p}(D, \Delta) < 1$ such that the following holds.
   Let $G = (V,E)$ be the Cayley graph of a finitely presented group $\langle S | R \rangle$
   with respect to the generating set $S$. Suppose that $|S| \le D$ and
   suppose that every relator in $R$ has word length at most $\Delta$.
   Then, for every $p_0 > \tilde{p}$, there exist $c(p_0) >0$ and $K(p_0) < \infty$
   such that for all $x,y \in G$, for all $t \ge d_G(x,y)$, and for all $p \in [p_0,1]$ we have
   \[
      \mathbb{P} \left( d_{G_p}(x,y) \ge K t , x \xleftrightarrow{G_p} y \right) \le \exp(- c t).
   \]
   In particular, if in addition $p > p_u$ (where $p_u$ is the uniqueness threshold for $G$),
   then for some $C(p) < \infty$,
   \[
      \mathbb{P} \left( d_{G_p}(x,y) \ge K t \middle| x \xleftrightarrow{G_p} y \right) \le C \exp(- c t).
   \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm finitelypresented of arXiv:2507.09120

body:
Own work, proof draft UNAUDITED; novelty unestablished. U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M) and standard Gaussian Z in R^(N by P)
are mutually independent. Entries are iid within each factor array,
from fixed real laws satisfying

 E u=E v=0, E u^2=E v^2=1,
 H=E|u|^p<infinity for some real p>34,
 E v^3=0, m8=E|v|^8<infinity.

Assume positive integer dimensions, P/N<=alpha_*, M/N<=beta_*,
with fixed alpha_*,beta_*>0. Put beta_N=M/N and
i_N(s)=I(UV^T/sqrt(N);sqrt(s)UV^T/sqrt(N)+Z)/(NP).

Define

 a=6/(p+14),             r=4-48/(p+14)=3+(p-34)/(p+14),
 R0=(8H)^(1/(p-2)),      ell=32 sqrt(1+beta_*),
 d0=ell^2+beta_*,
 c0=min{1/(2d0),1/sqrt(128 alpha_* d0)},
 s0=min{1,(c0/R0^2)^(1/(1-2a))},
 C0=d0^4/3+10240 alpha_* beta_* d0^2
       +240 beta_* m8 ell^8,
 B0=C0 R0^8+2 beta_* sqrt(H) R0^(-(p-2)/2).

Here H>=1, so R0>=1; 0<a<1/8 and 3<r<4. For 0<s<=s0, let
R=R0 s^(-a), K_R=4R. Let E_(N,R)(s) be the explicit finite-size
error E_N(s) in035/034, evaluated with this K_R and the same aspect
upper bounds. In particular it is completely specified by

 q_N=2 exp(-5N), J_R=sqrt(beta_*^2+16 K_R^4 beta_*),
 delta_(N,R)=sqrt(2 J_R sqrt(q_N)+4 beta_* q_N),
 E_(N,R)(s)=2q_N/(NP)+sqrt(s)delta_(N,R)
       +s[beta_*q_N+J_R sqrt(q_N)]/(1+s beta_N).

Then the explicit finite-size bound is

 0<=log(1+s beta_N)/2-i_N(s)
 <=B0 s^r+E_(N,R0 s^(-a))(s).                        (1)

At each fixed positive s<=s0 the last error tends to zero
exponentially with N. Uniformity of this error at s=0 is NOT
asserted: the truncation radius diverges there. If beta_N->beta>0,
each subsequential limiting information function therefore satisfies

 0<=log(1+beta s)/2-i(s)<=B0 s^r,
 i(s)=beta s/2-beta^2 s^2/4+beta^3 s^3/6+O(s^r),

with explicit remainder bound (B0+beta_*^4/8)s^r for 0<s<=s0.
Subsequential functions exist by the uniform I-MMSE Lipschitz bound;
a unique full information limit is not asserted.
Independent iid factor arrays and standard Gaussian noise; fixed real prior laws
E u=E v=0, E u^2=E v^2=1; E|u|^p finite for p>34
E v^3=0 and E|v|^8 finite
P/N<=alpha_*, M/N<=beta_*; explicit 0<s<=s0
Limiting expansion assumes beta_N converges positively; full unique limit not asserted

Define

 a=6/(p+14),             r=4-48/(p+14)=3+(p-34)/(p+14),
 R0=(8H)^(1/(p-2)),      ell=32 sqrt(1+beta_*),
 d0=ell^2+beta_*,
 c0=min{1/(2d0),1/sqrt(128 alpha_* d0)},
 s0=min{1,(c0/R0^2)^(1/(1-2a))},
 C0=d0^4/3+10240 alpha_* beta_* d0^2
       +240 beta_* m8 ell^8,
 B0=C0 R0^8+2 beta_* sqrt(H) R0^(-(p-2)/2).

Here H>=1, so R0>=1; 0<a<1/8 and 3<r<4. For 0<s<=s0, let
R=R0 s^(-a), K_R=4R. Let E_(N,R)(s) be the explicit finite-size
error E_N(s) in035/034, evaluated with this K_R and the same aspect
upper bounds. In particular it is completely specified by

 q_N=2 exp(-5N), J_R=sqrt(beta_*^2+16 K_R^4 beta_*),
 delta_(N,R)=sqrt(2 J_R sqrt(q_N)+4 beta_* q_N),
 E_(N,R)(s)=2q_N/(NP)+sqrt(s)delta_(N,R)
       +s[beta_*q_N+J_R sqrt(q_N)]/(1+s beta_N).

Then the explicit finite-size bound is

 0<=log(1+s beta_N)/2-i_N(s)
 <=B0 s^r+E_(N,R0 s^(-a))(s).                        (1)

At each fixed positive s<=s0 the last error tends to zero
exponentially with N. Uniformity of this error at s=0 is NOT
asserted: the truncation radius diverges there. If beta_N->beta>0,
each subsequential limiting information function therefore satisfies

 0<=log(1+beta s)/2-i(s)<=B0 s^r,
 i(s)=beta s/2-beta^2 s^2/4+beta^3 s^3/6+O(s^r),

with explicit remainder bound (B0+beta_*^4/8)s^r for 0<s<=s0.
Subsequential functions exist by the uniform I-MMSE Lipschitz bound;
a unique full information limit is not asserted.

## 1. Normalize truncations without changing the energy

For R>=R0 let w=u 1_(|u|<=R), mu=E w, sigma^2=Var(w), and
u_R=(w-mu)/sigma. Set eps^2=H R^(2-p)<=1/8. Since E u=0,

 E[u^2 1_(|u|>R)]<=eps^2,
 mu=-E[u 1_(|u|>R)],  mu^2<=eps^2,
 sigma^2=1-E[u^2 1_(|u|>R)]-mu^2>=1-2eps^2>=3/4.

Consequently sigma is positive and u_R is centered with variance
exactly one. Under its natural coupling with u,

 ||u-(w-mu)||_2<=eps,
 ||(w-mu)-(w-mu)/sigma||_2=|sigma-1|<=2eps^2<=eps,
 ||u-u_R||_2<=2eps=2sqrt(H) R^(-(p-2)/2).             (2)

Because R>=1, |mu|<=E|u|<=1, and sigma>=1/2, we have
|u_R|<=4R. Hoeffding's lemma for a centered variable in [-4R,4R]
gives the sub-Gaussian proxy K_R=4R. This use of the standard
bounded-variable MGF inequality is not a novelty claim.

## 2. Apply035 at each SNR, with its radius paid explicitly

For this normalized truncated prior, the constants of035 satisfy

 L_R=ell R,
 D_R=L_R^2+beta_*<=d0 R^2,
 s_*(K_R)>=c0 R^(-2),
 A_two(K_R)<=C0 R^8.                                 (3)

For example, the second radius term is
1/sqrt(8 alpha_* K_R^2 D_R)>=R^(-2)/sqrt(128 alpha_* d0).
The term 40 K_R^4 alpha_* beta_* D_R^2 is bounded by
10240 alpha_* beta_* d0^2 R^8, explaining its constant.

With R=R0 s^(-a), the restriction s<=s0 guarantees
s^(1-2a)<=c0/R0^2, hence s<=s_*(K_R). For each fixed s this
truncated law is fixed as N varies; we are not applying035 to a
dimension-dependent prior. Its bound consequently reads

 0<=log(1+s beta_N)/2-i_(R,N)(s)
 <=C0 R^8 s^4+E_(N,R)(s).                            (4)

## 3. Pay the information cost of truncation

Use036's equal-energy product transport bound (3). Both original
and truncated priors are centered with variance one, so (2) yields

 |i_N(s)-i_(R,N)(s)|
 <=2s beta_* sqrt(H) R^(-(p-2)/2).                    (5)

The powers agree exactly under the chosen a:

 4-8a=1+a(p-2)/2=r.

Insert R=R0 s^(-a) in (4)-(5) to obtain the upper bound in (1).
Its lower bound follows directly from the original product's
covariance beta_N I and Gaussian maximum entropy. Pass to any
limiting information function at fixed s and then let s approach
zero; r>3 proves the claimed cubic Peano expansion. The Gaussian
logarithm's cubic Taylor remainder is at most beta_*^4 s^4/8,
which is at most beta_*^4 s^r/8 because s<=1 and r<4.

## Scope, remaining gap, and audit dependencies

This proves a cubic limiting expansion with an explicit remainder
for priors that can have no exponential moments, rather than just
bounded/sub-Gaussian factors. It still requires p>34 on U, zero
third moment and finite eighth moment on V. It neither covers all
finite-moment hypotheses contemplated by Target1 nor gives a
quartic coefficient or a first prior-dependent limiting term.

The threshold34 is a sufficient condition of this truncation bound,
not an optimal threshold or a conjectured phase transition. No
claim of a sharper constant is being used as frontier progress:
the new part is the whole finite-high-moment prior class.

Dependencies requiring independent review:035v1 (including its
inherited scalar Taylor and Gaussian-V second moment bounds),036v1
(equal-energy transport), and the standard Hoeffding MGF inequality.
Least trusted new step is keeping the SNR-dependent truncation
radius admissible while taking N to infinity at each fixed SNR.
Finite rational exponent checks cannot certify the analytic inputs.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:d651fa62524049184cc5f89ae46469092d9505452ee8fa5c9f3ad64a9afe0295","revision_digest":"sha256:8d9d94c834d876781bb8a7f7474f8cea1c41c28cf273d31c2d34f0b4b966f8f7","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:finite-high-moment-cubic-information-expansion-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 8 (Subcritical Galton--Watson moments) of arXiv:2607.13183, '2607.13183'] Let $0<\mu<1$, put $\delta=1-\mu$, and let $(Z_j)_{j\ge0}$ be a
$\PGW(\mu)$ process started from one particle. Set
\[
        T:=\sum_{j\ge0}Z_j,
        \qquad
        A:=\sum_{j\ge1} jZ_j,
\]
where $A$ is the total depth of the tree, equivalently the area under its
generation-size profile.
There is an absolute constant $C<\infty$ such that, uniformly in $\mu$,
\[
        \E T=\delta^{-1},\qquad
        \Var(T)\le C\delta^{-3},\qquad
        \E[(T-\E T)^4]\le C\delta^{-7},
\]
and
\[
        \E A\le C\delta^{-2},\qquad \E A^2\le C\delta^{-5}.
\]
Accordingly, if a $\PGW(\mu)$ tree is attached to a core vertex $z$, and
$W_z$ is the degree mass of the resulting rooted component as in
\eqref{eq:Wnu}, then, conditionally on the core,
\[
\begin{aligned}
        \Egr[W_z\mid\Core]&\le C(\delta^{-1}+d_{\Core}(z)),\qquad
        \Vargr(W_z\mid\Core)\le C\delta^{-3},\\
        \Egr[(W_z-\Egr W_z)^4\mid\Core]&\le C\delta^{-7}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Own-work draft. Status: proof (unaudited), T326-w697-C13 v1. No independent reviewer PASS. Let d>=1, M>=1, n=d+1, J=[I_d,0], R=diag(I_d/d,1), rho>=0 and W=[w_1,...,w_M]. Set s_i=||w_i||^2/d+rho, X=[W/d;s^T], C=XX^T/M, T=dJ and G=W^TW. Train A in R^(d by n), B in R^(n by n), v in R by Euclidean negative-gradient flow of L=tr((vAB-T)C(vAB-T)^T)/2, retaining the extra feature column and holding v21=0. Write E=vAB-T, let e be the last unit vector, P the orthogonal range projector of C and N=I-P. The effective map is Gamma=vABR. For the C07 source-augmented flow with 1<=M<=d, full-column-rank task matrix W, fixed rho>=0 and exact isotropic initialization with 0<g0=alpha^3/sqrt(d)<1, entry at a finite time t0 into sqrt(2M L(t0))<sigma_min(W) implies exponential zero-loss convergence of the factors. With delta=sigma_min(W)-sqrt(2M L(t0)) and the C07 bound ||A||op^2<=Zmax, L prime<=-2delta^2 L/(M Zmax) thereafter. The set U of pools satisfying this trigger is exactly the zero-loss basin, is open in task-pool space, and has a continuous limiting selector. It contains every C09 structured pool and open neighborhoods of all orthogonal equal-norm full-column-rank pools, including nonsymmetric pools with Gs not parallel to s. Thus Gaussian pools have positive probability of belonging to U at each fixed d,M. No probability-one or dimension-uniform probability bound is proved. On U, Gamma_infinity=TPR+alpha v_infinity A_infinity N R. For fixed M deterministic sequences in these basins with W_d^T W_d/d -> I_M and alpha=epsilon/sqrt(d), fixed 0<epsilon<1, fresh Gaussian-task risk tends to 1+1/M, worse than zero prediction. Such nonsymmetric sequences exist. The proof uses a strict singular-value margin. Fresh risk means E[||Gamma z-w||^2]/d for independent w~N(0,I_d), z=(w,||w||^2/d+rho).
Source augmented K^TQ model with v21 held zero and m21 trained; exact initialization A0=alpha J, B0=alpha I_(d+1), v0=alpha sqrt(d)
1<=M<=d; rank W=M; rho>=0 fixed; alpha>0; 0<alpha^3/sqrt(d)<1; training time tends to infinity first
The trigger uses a finite uniform bound ||A(t)||op^2<=Zmax, supplied by C07 under the stated initialization; C09 supplies convergence of structured pools
U is defined by a certified strict finite-time inequality, not a floating-point observed trigger; C07 bounds are uniform locally in full-column-rank pools
Fixed-M risk limit uses deterministic Gram convergence W_d^T W_d/d -> I_M and alpha_d=epsilon/sqrt(d), with each W_d in its corresponding basin

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:cc7987dedf7bd8506e2cfa015cde8994e7769293d880caa1fea1e1a5561ddea4","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/cc/cc7987dedf7bd8506e2cfa015cde8994e7769293d880caa1fea1e1a5561ddea4.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:7429cd0460d732743a1028161c6daade984e4e6863e0d6b6dc26b8fe6ec7bb81","bundle_entry_key":"t326-c13","bundle_id":"population.t326-balanced-curves-open-pool-basins","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"in-context learning; linear matrix factorization; gradient flow","draft":"w697/bundle_007_r1.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.incontext:t326-deficiency-trigger-open-task-pool-basin","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# A finite-time convergence trigger and open nonsymmetric task-pool basins

Target 2(b). Status: proof (unaudited). This is a partial result, not probability-one convergence for iid Gaussian pools. The deficiency-margin method is known; no novelty is claimed for that method.

## Finite-time trigger for the exact source-augmented flow

Use all hypotheses of C07, with 1<=M<=d and full column rank W in R^(d by M), X=[W/d;s^T], Y=W, s_i=||w_i||^2/d+rho. Let residual F=vABX-Y, so L=||F||_F^2/(2M). Set sigma=sigma_min(Y)>0. C07 supplies a uniform upper bound ||A(t)||_op^2<=Zmax<infinity. Suppose at some finite t0

sqrt(2M L(t0))<sigma.

Put delta=sigma-sqrt(2M L(t0))>0. Loss is nonincreasing, so for every t>=t0 and every unit z in R^M,

||vABXz|| >= ||Yz||-||Fz|| >= delta.

Therefore, writing H=vBX, we have sigma_min(H)>=delta/||A||_op>=delta/sqrt(Zmax). This argument does not assume that A is square or invertible. The gradient in A is F H^T/M, so

||grad_A L||_F^2 >= (delta^2/Zmax)||F||_F^2/M^2
                 =2 delta^2 L/(M Zmax).

Consequently L(t)<=L(t0) exp[-2delta^2(t-t0)/(M Zmax)]. C07 bounds every factor, so every gradient component is bounded by a finite constant times sqrt(L); hence the parameter derivatives are integrable and the factors converge to a zero-loss limit. This is a deterministic certificate for an entire trajectory after t0. Floating integration can suggest its occurrence but does not certify this strict inequality.

The method is closely related to Arora, Cohen, Golowich and Hu, arXiv:1810.02281, Definition 2 and Claim 1 (printed p.4), and Theorem 1 (printed p.5): deficiency margin plus approximate balance gives linear convergence for freely trained matrix layers on whitened data. That theorem is not applied directly to the scalar-plus-two-factor, unwhitened augmented model here. The displayed direct gradient bound checks this parameterization and metric instead.

The strict trigger cannot be replaced by its boundary in the general bounded-trajectory argument: C11's critical witness has sigma_min(Y)^2=2/25 and M=2, hence L_*=1/50=sigma_min(Y)^2/(2M), while its loss is positive. This is a static boundary control, not evidence that the prescribed initialization reaches that witness.

## The zero-loss basin is open in task-pool space

Fix d,M,rho,alpha with 1<=M<=d, rho>=0, alpha>0 and g0=alpha^3/sqrt(d) in (0,1). For each full-column-rank pool W use the same prescribed initialization A0=alpha J, B0=alpha I, v0=alpha sqrt(d). Define the set U of pools whose initialized trajectory satisfies the finite-time strict trigger above at some t0.

Then U is open. Indeed, at a qualifying W0 choose its finite t0. The ODE coefficients are polynomial in W and the trained factors, and all nearby pools retain full column rank. Ordinary finite-time continuous dependence therefore makes both L_W(t0) and sigma_min(W) continuous at W0. The strict trigger persists in a neighborhood. C07 gives global solutions for each neighboring pool. No exchange of infinite-time and parameter limits is used.

Every structured full-column-rank pool from C09 lies in U: its loss tends to zero exponentially and sigma_min(W)>0, so it eventually meets the trigger. In particular, for every d,M in the stated range, U contains an open neighborhood of every orthogonal equal-norm pool W0 with W0^T W0=d I_M. Every pool in U, including pools with Gs not parallel to s, has factor convergence and zero training loss under the exact isotropic initialization. Conversely, zero limiting loss implies eventual entry into the strict trigger, so U is exactly the zero-loss basin within these full-column-rank pools.

The limiting factors, and hence Gamma_infinity, depend continuously on W within U. To see this, fix a trigger time at W0. On a small closed neighborhood the strict margin has a common positive lower bound, sigma_min(X) stays positive, and the C07 factor bounds have a common finite upper bound (the rank is M throughout). The displayed PL rate is then uniformly positive. The bounds on each parameter derivative by a constant times sqrt(L) are also uniform there. Integrating them gives a uniformly vanishing tail from each finite time to the parameter limit. Finite-time continuous dependence followed by this uniform-tail bound proves continuity of the limit. It does not assert a neighborhood size uniform in d.

For M>=2 these neighborhoods contain pools outside C09's structural condition. Perturb just the length of the first column of an orthogonal equal-norm W0 by a factor 1+h, leaving the other columns fixed. For nonzero sufficiently small h, all s_i>0 while G has two distinct diagonal eigenvalues; s is therefore not an eigenvector. This proves that the conclusion extends to nonsymmetric task-pool sets with nonempty interior. A standard iid Gaussian W has everywhere-positive density, so P(W in U)>0 for each fixed d,M. No lower probability uniform in d or M is provided, and P(W in U)=1 has not been proved.

## Selector on that open basin and a fixed-M deterministic limit

At each W in U, the zero-loss limit satisfies the exact selector identity

Gamma_infinity=TPR+alpha v_infinity A_infinity N R,

with the inherited-nullspace bound (A) of C07. Here P is the projector onto range X, N=I-P and R=diag(I_d/d,1). This identity includes the extra feature column.

Fix M, rho>=0 and 0<epsilon<1. For any deterministic sequence of pools W_d in U_d with W_d^T W_d/d -> I_M, use alpha_d=epsilon/sqrt(d). The deterministic versions of the C07 bounds give Zmax=O_M(d), q=e^TNe=O(1/d), and inherited-nullspace fresh-risk contribution h=O(1/d). The C04 projection formula with a_raw=0 gives B_d,M ->1+1/M; the fresh-task norm triangle inequality then implies Risk(Gamma_infinity)->1+1/M. The limit is worse than the zero predictor's risk 1, due to the extra feature column.

Such nonsymmetric sequences exist for each fixed M>=2: at each dimension choose a nonzero first-column length perturbation smaller than both the local open-neighborhood radius (converted to Frobenius distance) and 1/d in Frobenius norm. Their Gram matrices divided by d tend to I_M. This is an existence statement with potentially very small neighborhoods, not the iid Gaussian convergence theorem.

## Remaining gap

C07 and C10 alone do not establish finite-time entry into the trigger set for arbitrary iid Gaussian pools. Openness and positive Gaussian probability do not imply probability one, and the neighborhood radii may shrink too fast for high-dimensional concentration to help. Establishing that entry, or a quantitative neighborhood broad enough for the actual Gaussian fluctuation scale, remains the hardest open piece. No numerically observed inequality is used as a certified entry time here.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:61c886c6b487fb701e5ddf7cfc493b2cb628fa34624f154f809264727f128b00","revision_digest":"sha256:8da1b6078ad9af581ff4d657f28c58434091cc19c524fdcc64b64412c0bcb2ba","source_id":"own-work:w697:T326:C13:v1","source_revision":"C13 v1; proof sha256 1337da3c450477fc90c74511638e4b90df8b321c116fc32e5da09d9f4f4443be","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

\[
h(\mz_1,\ldots,\mz_m)=h(\mz_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,\mz_{\sigma(m)})

Open problem (current status UNKNOWN after bounded 2026-10-14 search; no settlement found): for every d>=0 and compact convex body C in R^d of positive intrinsic volume, is Unif(C) n-completely mixable for every integer n>=d+1? n-CM means there exist n random vectors each with law Unif(C), whose sum is the constant n times the centroid of C almost surely. The source states the universal conjecture is equivalent to just order d+1 in every dimension. Source: Ruodu Wang, Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability, arXiv:1411.6190v3, Section 2.5, Open Problem 5, p.16. The uniform-law formulation is understood only where normalized volume exists.

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2607.29327, 'Fractal Random Variables\\ Defined by Probability Distributions of Digits\\ of Their $G_2$'] Random variable $\xi$ has either pure discrete or pure continuous distribution.
  Moreover, it is discrete if and only if
  \begin{equation}
    
    M\equiv \prod_{n=1}^{\infty}\max\{p_{0n}, p_{1n}\}>0.
  \end{equation}
  In discrete case, point spectrum (set of atoms) of the random variable
  is a tail set whose representative is a point
  $x_0=\Delta^{G_2}_{c_1...c_m...}$
  such that
  $p_{c_nn}=\max\{p_{0n}, p_{1n}\}$,
  or its subset.

[Theorem 55 (Critical stability and projection convergence) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let \(X,Z\) be continuous square-integrable \(H\)-valued martingales with
\(X_0=Z_0=0\), and assume, almost surely,
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}\langle\!\langle X\rangle\!\rangle_T\leq E,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Tr}\langle\!\langle Z\rangle\!\rangle_T\leq\delta^2.
\]
For every finite \(r>0\),
\begin{align}
 \left\|\sup_{t\leq T}\|Z_t\|_H\right\|_{L^r}
 &\leq C_r\delta,
 \\
 \left\|\sup_{t\leq T}
 \|A_t^{X+Z}-A_t^X\|_{1,\infty}\right\|_{L^r}
 &\leq C_r(\sqrt E\,\delta+\delta^2),
 \\
 \sup_{t\leq T}
 \|\langle\!\langle X+Z\rangle\!\rangle_t
     -\langle\!\langle X\rangle\!\rangle_t\|_1
 &\leq2\sqrt E\,\delta+\delta^2.
 
\end{align}
The constants are independent of the Hilbert-space dimension.

If \(P_n\to I\) strongly are increasing finite-rank orthogonal
projections and \(M\) is any continuous square-integrable Hilbert
martingale with \(M_0=0\), then its split anchors
\[
 \mathbf M_t^{(n)}
 :=\bigl(P_nM_t,A_t^{P_nM},
        \langle\!\langle P_nM\rangle\!\rangle_t\bigr)
\]
converge to a continuous
\(\mathscr G^+_{\mathrm{crit}}(H)\)-valued anchor \(\mathbf M\), uniformly
on compact time intervals in probability for \(d_{\mathrm{crit}}\).
Moreover, on one event of probability one,
\begin{equation}
 A_t^M\in\mathcal S^0_{1,\infty}(H)_{\mathrm{skew}}
 \qquad\text{for every }t\leq T.
 
\end{equation}
Thus every individual continuous martingale realization belongs to the
little weak core; this is a samplewise assertion and does not give a
dimension-uniform decay modulus.

[Theorem thm:sc-Darboux of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] Let $K$ be dressing compatible with $(\Psi, \Phi)$, with
resolvent $R(u) = (I - zK(u))^{-1}$.  Define the dressed
observable and dressed waves by
\[
\mathcal{M}(u) \vcentcolon= I + z\Phi(u)R(u)\Psi(u),
\]
\[
\widehat\Psi(u) \vcentcolon= R(u)\Psi(u), \qquad
\widehat\Phi(u) \vcentcolon= \Phi(u)R(T^{-1}u).
\]
Then $\mathcal{M}(u)$ is invertible for every
$u \in \mathcal{V}$.  The dressed waves
$\widehat\Psi, \widehat\Phi$ satisfy the linear problem
(equation eq:sc-linear-1 of the paper)--(equation eq:sc-linear-j of the paper) and adjoint
linear problem
(equation eq:sc-adjoint-1 of the paper)--(equation eq:sc-adjoint-j of the paper)
respectively, with data $(\mathcal{M}_k, \Lambda_k)$: for each $j \geq 2$,
\begin{align*}
\partial_1\widehat\Psi(u)
  &= \widehat\Psi(Tu)\mathcal{M}_1(u)
     - \widehat\Psi(u)\Lambda_1(u), \\
\widehat\Psi(S_j u)
  &= \widehat\Psi(Tu)\mathcal{M}_j(u)
     - \widehat\Psi(u)\Lambda_j(u),
\shortintertext{and}
\partial_1\widehat\Phi(Tu)
  &= \Lambda_1(Tu)\widehat\Phi(Tu)
     - \mathcal{M}_1(u)\widehat\Phi(u), \\
\widehat\Phi(Tu)
  &= \mathcal{M}_j(u)\widehat\Phi(S_j u)
     - \Lambda_j(Tu)\widehat\Phi(TS_j u),
\end{align*}
where the dressed edge weights are given by
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{M}_1(u) \vcentcolon=
  \mathcal{M}(Tu)^{-1}C_1(u)\mathcal{M}(u),
\quad
\mathcal{M}_j(u) \vcentcolon=
  \mathcal{M}(Tu)^{-1}C_j(u)\mathcal{M}(S_j u),
\end{equation}
and $\widehat K(u) \vcentcolon= K(u)R(u)$ is dressing compatible
with $(\widehat\Psi, \widehat\Phi)$.
Moreover, the pair $(\mathcal{M}_k, \Lambda_k)$ satisfies the
semi-discrete diamond equations of Proposition~(prop:sc-diamond of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: for the global statement 'u in H^1_0(Omega), Laplacian u in L^2(Omega) implies u in H^2(Omega) with ||u||_{H^2} <= C ||Laplacian u||_{L^2}', the boundary must be C^{1,1} (C^2 in the usual textbook proof) or Omega must be convex. Lipschitz is not enough. Counterexample (reentrant corner): in the plane let Omega be the sector {0 < theta < beta, 0 < r < 1} with pi < beta < 2 pi (a nonconvex Lipschitz domain) and put v(r,theta) = r^{pi/beta} sin(pi theta/beta), which is harmonic and vanishes on the two straight edges. Let eta be a smooth cutoff equal to 1 near the vertex and supported in {r < 1/2}, and set u = eta v. Then u is in H^1_0(Omega) (grad v is comparable to r^{pi/beta - 1}, which is square integrable in the plane for every beta, since pi/beta > 0) and f = -Laplacian u = -(2 grad v . grad eta + v Laplacian eta) is smooth and bounded (it is supported in an annulus away from the vertex). But near the vertex |D^2 u| is comparable to r^{pi/beta - 2}, and integral of r^{2(pi/beta - 2)} r dr diverges precisely when pi/beta <= 1, i.e. when beta >= pi. So u is not in H^2(Omega) although the data are smooth: the singularity is created by the geometry, not by the coefficients or the right-hand side. Remarks an auditor should keep in mind: interior H^2 regularity is untouched (it needs only Lipschitz coefficients and no boundary hypothesis); on a convex domain, even a convex polygon, the H^2 estimate does hold (Kadlec/Grisvard), which is why finite-element arguments often assume convexity; on a general polygon the solution splits into an H^2 part plus explicit corner singularities r^{k pi/beta} sin(k pi theta/beta); and the analogous failure occurs for the W^{2,p} estimate, so a C^{1,1} (or convexity) hypothesis cannot be quietly weakened to Lipschitz.
title: Pitfall: Boundary H^2 Regularity Needs a C^{1,1} or Convex Boundary

[Conjecture 1 (K-polystable smooth fibres) of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Assume that every fibre \(F_y\) is K-polystable with respect to
\(-K_{F_y}\).  Then the finite-time K\"ahler--Ricci flow is Type I:
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{0\le t<T}\sup_{x\in X}
 (T-t)|\Rm(g(t))|_{g(t)}(x)<\infty.
\end{equation}
Moreover, fix \(q\in Y\), and let
\(\omega_{q,{\rm KE}}\in2\pi c_1(F_q)\) be a normalized
K\"ahler--Einstein metric,
\[
                 \Ric(\omega_{q,{\rm KE}})=\omega_{q,{\rm KE}}.
\]
Write \(g_{q,{\rm KE}}=2g_{\omega_{q,{\rm KE}}}\), so that
\(\Ric(g_{q,{\rm KE}})=\tfrac12g_{q,{\rm KE}}\).  After forgetting the
conjugate heat measures, every Type-I-scale blowup at \(\xi\) based at
\(F_q\) is isomorphic, as a K\"ahler metric flow, to
\begin{equation}
 \left(
   \C^m\times F_q,\,
   J_0\oplus J_{F_q},\,
   g_{\rm E}+(-s)g_{q,{\rm KE}}
 \right)_{s<0}.
\end{equation}
Thus the residual factor is the central fibre with its own complex
structure. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: K-polystable smooth fibres

The 2018 Bourgade survey studies the Anderson operator Delta + lambda V on Z^d, with iid centered variance-one site potentials. In dimension three at weak disorder it identifies two distinct open-at-publication questions: existence of absolutely continuous spectrum for the infinite-volume operator, and GOE microscopic eigenvalue statistics for periodic finite-volume restrictions. The survey does not prove either implication, and its 2018 open label is not a current-status certificate. The C0056 intake combined the two goals in one row.
Historical source statement as of 2018
Delta is the nearest-neighbor hopping operator with free spectrum [-2d,2d]
title: C0056 has separate spectral and GOE obligations

    \end{enumerate}

[Corollary cor:Lambda_spectral of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] By Lemma~(lem:quad_identity of the paper),
\begin{align}
  \Lambda^A(k)
  \equiv
  \sup\left\{
    \bigl\langle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_k^A f, f\bigr\rangle_{L^2(\mu)}
    |
    f \in D(\mathcal{L}_k^A), \|f\|_{L^2(\mu)} = 1
  \right\}.
  
\end{align}
Since $\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_k^A$
is self-adjoint in $L^2(\mu)$ by construction
(see Def.~(def:sym_tilted of the paper)),
the Rayleigh-Ritz theorem guarantees 
that the supremum of the quadratic form is precisely the principal (maximal) eigenvalue
of $\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_k^A$, i.e., 
\begin{align}
  \Lambda^A(k)
  =
  \lambda_{\max}\bigl(\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_k^A\bigr).
  
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Spectral interpretation of $\Lambda^A(k)$

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2506.20411, 'Maximal Counts in the Stopped Occupancy Problem'] Let  $(G_n)$ be a sequence in $S$ and let $\rho(n)$ be a sequence in $J$.
Then the following are equivalent.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]
For any subsequence $(n_j)$ and $\gax\in J$
such that   $\rho(n_j)\to\gax$ as $j\to\infty$,
we have $G_{n_j}\to H_\gax$.  
\item[(ii)]
As $n\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
d_{\rm }(G_n, H_{\rho(n)})\to0.
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}
Furthermore,
if these hold, then $(G_n)$ is relatively compact.

		f(z) = a_{k_{\lambda}} (z-\lambda)^{-k_\lambda} + \ldots + a_{1} (z-\lambda)^{-1} + h_1(z)
		\end{equation*}
		where $h_1: D \to \C$ is holomorphic in a neighborhood of $z=\lambda$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_{k_\lambda} \in \C$,
		$a_{k_\lambda} \not = 0$.
		Further, suppose that $f(z) = g(e^{-z})$ for $z \in D$.
		Then $e^{-\lambda}$ is a pole of $g$ of multiplicity $k_\lambda$ and 
		\begin{equation*}
		g(z) = b_{k_\lambda} (z-e^{-\lambda})^{-k} + \ldots + b_1 (z-e^{-\lambda})^{-1} + h_2(z)
		\end{equation*}
		for a function $h_2: D \to \C$ which is holomorphic in a neighborhood of $z = e^{-\lambda}$
		and for coefficients $b_1,\ldots,b_{k_\lambda}$ satisfying 
		\begin{equation}	
		\sum_{k=i}^{k_\lambda} \frac{(-1)^k}{(k-1)!} \stirfst{k}{i} b_k e^{\lambda k} = \frac1{(i-1)!} a_i.
		\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 15 of arXiv:2607.22414

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, split B, full calibration, paired). The two-vertex blend of the transductive covariance penalty keeps the simplex's gain on EMIT and closes three quarters of its deficit to the pool's hand-tuned heuristic on OCO-2 (-0.27 there); the heuristic is itself label-free, so it was added as a third vertex with barycentric weights chosen by the same criterion. P26 (a) REFUTED: on OCO-2 the three-vertex blend reads -0.09 vs the pool best and +0.18 vs the two-vertex blend; (b) HELD: on EMIT it reads +4.78 vs the pool best and +0.05 vs the two-vertex blend; (c) HELD: mean weights (simplex, least squares, pool) are (0.09, 0.44, 0.47) on OCO-2 and (0.59, 0.24, 0.17) on EMIT; falsifier (three-vertex worse than two-vertex by more than 0.5 on either corpus) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P27, split C, pre-registered before the split-B result was read): P27 (a) HELD: on split C OCO-2 the three-vertex blend reads -0.12 vs the pool best and +0.20 vs the two-vertex blend; (b) HELD: on EMIT +4.83 vs the pool best and +0.18 vs the two-vertex blend; (c) HELD: mean weights (simplex, least squares, pool) (0.11, 0.42, 0.48) on OCO-2 and (0.57, 0.26, 0.17) on EMIT; falsifier (three-vertex worse than two-vertex by more than 0.5 on either corpus) not triggered. A fourth vertex (P33, the CV-shrunk long-only stack that the calibration-only selector picks on most EMIT cells): P33 (a) REFUTED: on EMIT the four-vertex blend reads +0.06 vs the three-vertex blend and +4.84 vs the pool best (candidate B alone +5.23, the three-vertex blend +4.78); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 +0.00 vs the three-vertex blend (-0.09 vs the pool best); (c) REFUTED: mean weights (simplex, least squares, pool, B) are (0.48, 0.26, 0.14, 0.12) on EMIT and (0.01, 0.48, 0.40, 0.11) on OCO-2; falsifier (four-vertex worse than three-vertex by more than 0.3 on either corpus) not triggered.
the three bases are fitted on the calibration rows only (simplex = long-only relative-metric stack; least squares = per-output ridge 1e-6; pool heuristic = per-output ridge with a GCV lambda shrunk toward the pooled convex weights by a 5-fold-CV amount); barycentric weights on the 0.1 grid (66 points); the criterion is the 5-fold cross-validated squared relative error on the calibration rows plus the excess pairs-bootstrap variance (B = 8) of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows; the two-vertex blend is the face with zero pool weight, so its comparison is exact

[Thm RC of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] [{[Revuz_70_Mesures]; see also [Kajino_Noda_26_Kac]}] 
  
  There is a one-to-one correspondence between equivalence classes of PCAFs $(A_{t})_{t \geq 0}$
  and smooth measures $\nu$ characterized by the following relation:
  for any $\alpha > 0$ and non-negative Borel measurable function $f$ on $M$,
  \begin{equation} 
    E_x\!\left[
      \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\alpha t} f(X_t)\, dA_t
    \right]
    = 
    \int_M r_{\alpha}(x,y) f(y)\, \nu(dy),
    \quad 
    \forall x \in M.
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 36 (Finite expected degree) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a non-compact connected semisimple real Lie group and $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space.
Then there is $\alpha\ge 1$ such that if $Y$ is a Poisson point process on $X$ with intensity $\lambda \, {\rm vol}$ for some $\lambda>0$, $Y_0=Y \cup \{o\}$ and ${\rm Vor}(Y_0)$ is the associated Voronoi diagram, then $\mathbb E[{\rm deg}_{\mathcal G}(\rho)] = O(\lambda^{-\alpha})$ as $\lambda\to0$,
where $\mathcal G$ denote the Delaunay graph associated to ${\rm Vor}(Y_0)$. In particular, $\mathcal G$ is locally finite a.s. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Finite expected degree

[Lemma lem:nuclear-ricci-entrance of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be Hilbert spaces and let
\[
 Z:W\otimes\mathcal B\longrightarrow W\otimes\mathcal A
\]
be trace class.  Realign its Hilbert vectorization from the physical
grouping $(W\otimes\mathcal A)\mid(W\otimes\mathcal B)$ to the grouping
$(W\otimes W)\mid(\mathcal A\otimes\overline{\mathcal B})$, without
transposing a proper subsystem, and denote the resulting Hilbert vector
by $\mathfrak R(\operatorname{vec}Z)$.  If
\[
 P_{\mathcal R}=\frac1{n-2}XX^*
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12p}$}
\]
is the orthogonal projection of $S_2(W)$ onto the traceless-Ricci
summand, then
\[
 \boxed{
 \|(P_{\mathcal R}\otimes I)
       \mathfrak R(\operatorname{vec}Z)\|_2
 \le \frac2{\sqrt{n-2}}\|Z\|_1.}
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12p_1}$}
\]
The estimate remains true after the diagonal Haar projection.  At a
predeclared joint cut in the packetless aggregate-Ricci construction of
(lem:prior-low-cells of the paper), $Z$ may be the complete once-normalized port
state; (eq:3.3.1w-12p-1 of the paper) then uses no new circuit base.

On {-1, 1}^n (n >= 1) with the uniform probability measure mu, chi_S(x) = prod over i in S of x_i for S inside [n], and f^(S) = E[f chi_S] is the Walsh-Fourier coefficient of a real function f, so f = sum over S of f^(S) chi_S. A probability density is phi >= 0 with E phi = 1; it gives the law P(Y = y) = 2^(-n) phi(y), and then E[g(Y)] = E[phi g] for every real g. For nonempty A, phi_A = 1_A / mu(A) = (2^n/|A|) 1_A is a density whose law is uniform on A. The normalized convolution is (f * g)(x) = E_y[f(y) g(x y)] with y uniform and x y the coordinatewise product (addition on F_2^n written multiplicatively), and (f * g)^(S) = f^(S) g^(S) for every S. If phi is a density then (phi * g)(x) = E[g(x Y)] for Y with density phi, and if Y and Z are independent with densities phi and psi, then phi * psi is a density and it is the density of the coordinatewise product Y Z.

[Definition of arXiv:2609.00481, 'The frameset of the second-order B-spline along $ab=1/q$'] The \emph{Zak transform} of $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ with parameter $\lambda>0$ is
\[
    (Z_\lambda f)(x,\gamma) = \sqrt\lambda \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z} f(\lambda(x-k))\, e^{2\pi ik\gamma}, \qquad \text{a.e. } (x,\gamma)\in\mathbb R^2,
\]
with convergence in $L^2_{loc}(\mathbb R^2)$. This normalization makes $Z_\lambda$ a unitary map of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ onto $L^2([0,1)^2)$, satisfying
\[
    Z_\lambda f(x+1,\gamma) = e^{2\pi i\gamma}Z_\lambda f(x,\gamma), \qquad Z_\lambda f(x,\gamma+1) = Z_\lambda f(x,\gamma),
\]
so that $[0,1)^2$ is a fundamental domain for $|Z_\lambda f|$, independent of $\lambda$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:0e7bdb46d2f4a1d617e5cb6016d4f34e707c53c4a1b76a099c930f590249d9eb","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/0e/0e7bdb46d2f4a1d617e5cb6016d4f34e707c53c4a1b76a099c930f590249d9eb.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:91acd56335975a932539f4073e0edfa8458a1eb6dee249a431112ed253e3e53b","bundle_entry_key":"uniform-cayley-reset","bundle_id":"population.probability-critical-moments-two-end-kernels-and-dependence-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.markov:candidate-unweighted-abelian-cayley-product-condition-no-cutoff","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0276: unweighted Abelian Cayley graphs with the product condition and no cutoff

Status: complete author-checked counterexample candidate to the literal unrestricted statement of Salez Problem 2.4. A scoped independent review is recorded below; novelty remains unverified. This construction has unbounded degree. It does not address a bounded-degree or random-generator version of the question.

## Primary source and scope

Justin Salez, *Modern aspects of Markov chains: entropy, curvature and the cutoff phenomenon*, arXiv:2508.21055, Problem 2.4, PDF page 27; the definitions are on pages 25-26. Primary PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.21055 . Archived SHA256: 9b58f5e6c2b13103f9ca02ddd53b7890e259b2d93f632c25d3414dd87002e267.

The source defines the unweighted Cayley walk by uniform choice from a generating set. It asks whether cutoff is equivalent to the product condition for Abelian Cayley graphs, without a degree bound in that question. The subsequent paragraph separately introduces weighted increment laws. Therefore a weighted reset walk alone would not answer it. The construction below is a connected simple undirected unweighted Cayley graph and controls its entire state-space law.

The reset mechanism is classical prior art (often associated with Pak counterexamples); novelty, if any, would concern this exact unweighted realization and its application to the literal source statement. No novelty claim is made here. Earlier and later formulations may impose additional restrictions that this construction does not satisfy.

## The graph and its exact rates

For integers $d\ge8$, set

$$m_d=1+\left\lceil\frac{2^d\log d}{4}\right\rceil,
\qquad G_d=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^d\times(\mathbb Z/m_d\mathbb Z).$$

Write $H_d=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^d$, $K_d=\mathbb Z/m_d\mathbb Z$, and let $e_i$ be the cube basis vectors. The generating set is the disjoint union

$$S_d=\{(e_i,k):1\le i\le d,\ k\in K_d\setminus\{0\}\}
\ \cup\ \{(x,0):x\in H_d\setminus\{0\}\}.$$

It contains no identity and is inverse closed. The second part generates the cube factor, and adding $(e_1,0)$ to $(e_1,k)$ generates $(0,k)$, so it generates the full group. The Cayley graph is consequently simple, connected, undirected and vertex transitive. Every edge has the same transition weight. Its degree is

$$D_d=d(m_d-1)+2^d-1.$$

Use the rate-one continuization of simple random walk, whose generator is $P-I$. Split its jumps into local-type and global-type events. Their rates are

$$\alpha_d=\frac{d(m_d-1)}{D_d},\qquad
\theta_d=\frac{2^d-1}{D_d},\qquad
\beta_d=\frac{2^d}{D_d}.$$

On a local event the cube flips a uniformly chosen coordinate and the second coordinate receives an independent uniform nonzero increment. On a global event the cube receives a uniform nonzero increment and the second coordinate is unchanged.

## Exact projected semigroup

Let $L_d$ be the rate-one cube generator, and $\Pi_d$ the projection onto the uniform law on $H_d$. The transition operator for a uniform nonzero cube increment is

$$Q_d=\frac{2^d\Pi_d-I}{2^d-1}.$$

Therefore the cube projection has generator

$$\alpha_dL_d+\theta_d(Q_d-I)
=\alpha_dL_d+\beta_d(\Pi_d-I).$$

Since $\Pi_d$ commutes with the cube semigroup, if $q_d(t)$ is its total-variation distance from uniform when started at zero and $c_d(t)$ is the corresponding distance for rate-one cube walk, then

$$q_d(t)=e^{-\beta_dt}\,c_d(\alpha_dt).$$

This is exact; no replacement of a nonzero increment by an approximate reset is used.

## Control of the whole graph, not just its projection

Let $v_d(t)$ denote the total-variation distance of the full walk from the uniform law on $G_d$. Projection gives $v_d(t)\ge q_d(t)$. Let $N_t$ count local-type events, so $N_t$ is Poisson of mean $\alpha_dt$.

Conditional on the event types, their times, and all cube increments, the second coordinate is the sum of $N_t$ independent uniform nonzero $K_d$ increments. When $N_t\ge1$, its distance from uniform is at most $1/m_d$: the first increment has exactly that distance and subsequent convolution contracts total variation. When $N_t=0$, use the bound one. Coupling this conditional law to an independent uniform coordinate yields

$$0\le v_d(t)-q_d(t)\le e^{-\alpha_dt}+\frac1{m_d}.$$

Conditioning on the cube path is legitimate because local increments in the two factors are chosen independently given the event type. Their common jump count does not invalidate the conditional bound. Uniformity of an auxiliary coordinate is not silently assumed.

## A self-contained cube cutoff calculation

Define the comparison time

$$T_d=\frac{d\log d}{4\alpha_d}.$$

The rate-one cube coordinates flip independently at rate $1/d$. Their signs have means $e^{-2t/d}$ from the all-zero start. Hence

$$\chi^2(\mathcal L(X_t),\operatorname{Unif}(H_d))
=(1+e^{-4t/d})^d-1.$$

At $t=sd\log d/4$ this tends to zero for $s>1$, proving $c_d(t)\to0$. For $0<s<1$, the sum of coordinate signs has mean $d^{1-s/2}$ and variance at most $d$, while its stationary mean is zero and stationary variance is $d$. Chebyshev applied at half the former mean under both laws gives

$$c_d(sd\log d/4)\ge1-8d^{s-1}\longrightarrow1.$$

Also

$$\beta_dT_d=\frac{2^d\log d}{4(m_d-1)}\longrightarrow1.$$

Combining the exact projected formula with the whole-space error bound proves the limiting profile away from $s=1$:

$$\lim_{d\to\infty}v_d(sT_d)=
\begin{cases}e^{-s},&0<s<1,\\0,&s>1.\end{cases}$$

The large drop near $s=1$ does not constitute cutoff: a nonvanishing fraction of total-variation decay has already occurred gradually over a time proportional to $T_d$.

## Spectral gap and the product condition

Characters of $G_d$ are indexed by a subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ and a character $\psi$ of $K_d$. Put $a=|A|$. The eigenvalues of the discrete jump operator are

$$\lambda_{A,\psi}=\frac{(d-2a)c_\psi+b_A}{D_d},\qquad
c_\psi=\begin{cases}m_d-1,&\psi=1,\\-1,&\psi\ne1,\end{cases}
\quad b_A=\begin{cases}2^d-1,&A=\varnothing,\\-1,&A\ne\varnothing.\end{cases}$$

The three nonconstant sectors have gap candidates

$$\frac{2a(m_d-1)+2^d}{D_d}\quad(a\ge1,\psi=1),\qquad
\frac{dm_d}{D_d}\quad(A=\varnothing,\psi\ne1),\qquad
\frac{D_d+d-2a+1}{D_d}\quad(A\ne\varnothing,\psi\ne1).$$

For all sufficiently large $d$ the minimum is in the first sector at $a=1$. Thus

$$\gamma_d=\frac{2(m_d-1)+2^d}{D_d}
=\frac{2\alpha_d}{d}+\beta_d\sim\frac2d.$$

This also follows by noting that every nonconstant auxiliary-factor character is contracted at a rate bounded away from zero, while the first cube character has the displayed slow rate. The full character computation checks that a hidden auxiliary bottleneck has not been overlooked.

Write $t_d(\varepsilon)=\inf\{t:v_d(t)\le\varepsilon\}$. Monotonicity and the limiting profile imply

$$\frac{t_d(1/4)}{T_d}\longrightarrow1,\qquad
\frac{t_d(3/4)}{T_d}\longrightarrow\log(4/3).$$

For the first assertion, $e^{-s}>e^{-1}>1/4$ for every $s<1$, whereas the limit is zero for $s>1$. For the second, $e^{-s}$ crosses $3/4$ at the interior point $s=\log(4/3)$, so bracketing on either side gives the limit. Therefore

$$\gamma_d t_d(1/4)\sim\frac12\log d\longrightarrow\infty,
\qquad \frac{t_d(3/4)}{t_d(1/4)}\longrightarrow\log(4/3)<1.$$

The product condition holds and total-variation cutoff fails. By transitivity these are also the worst-start mixing times.

## Review limits

The potentially surprising assertion is that uniform generators can encode the rare-reset mechanism. Its load-bearing checks are disjointness and inverse closure of the generator set; exact projected reset rate $\beta_d$, which is different from the actual global jump rate $\theta_d$; conditional mixing of the auxiliary factor; the full character spectrum; and the distinction between a discontinuity in the limiting profile and cutoff. Each is derived above.

The construction has very large degree and specially chosen generators. It says nothing against the bounded-degree transitive-expander problem or almost-sure cutoff for uniformly random generating sets. Searches found both the literal Salez statement and related nilpotent-group conjecture formulations, but no verified prior disposition of this exact construction. The simple mechanism makes prior-art checking essential. This packet remains a candidate, with no promoted original solution count.

body: A commutative ring R is Noetherian if every ideal is finitely generated; equivalently every ascending chain of ideals I_1 <= I_2 <= ... stabilises, equivalently every nonempty set of ideals has a maximal element. Facts: fields, Z, and principal ideal domains are Noetherian; quotients and localisations of Noetherian rings are Noetherian; the Hilbert basis theorem says R[x] is Noetherian when R is, hence every finitely generated algebra over a field or over Z is Noetherian; a Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes and every ideal has a primary decomposition (Lasker-Noether); the power series ring R[[x]] over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian; a subring of a Noetherian ring need not be (the ring of all algebraic integers is not Noetherian). The KRULL DIMENSION dim R is the supremum of the lengths n of chains of prime ideals P_0 < P_1 < ... < P_n. Facts: a field has dimension 0, and a Noetherian ring has dimension 0 exactly when it is Artinian (Akizuki); Z and every principal ideal domain that is not a field have dimension 1, as does every Dedekind domain; dim k[x_1, ..., x_n] = n for a field k (Krull's principal ideal theorem and Noether normalisation), and more generally dim R[x] = dim R + 1 for Noetherian R; the dimension of a finitely generated k-algebra that is a domain equals the transcendence degree of its field of fractions over k; Krull's height theorem: in a Noetherian ring a minimal prime over an ideal generated by n elements has height at most n; a Noetherian LOCAL ring (R, m) has finite dimension, equal to the least number of generators of an m-primary ideal, and dim R <= dim_k (m / m^2) with equality exactly for regular local rings. Non-Noetherian rings can have infinite dimension, and there are Noetherian rings of infinite dimension (Nagata's example), though every Noetherian local ring has finite dimension.

body: Let (X, F, mu) be a measure space with mu(X) < infinity and let T: X -> X be measurable and measure-preserving, meaning mu(T^{-1}A) = mu(A) for every measurable A. The Poincare recurrence theorem states that for any measurable set A with mu(A) > 0, almost every point x in A satisfies T^n(x) in A for infinitely many n >= 1; equivalently, almost every point of A returns to A infinitely often under iterating T. It applies in particular to any Hamiltonian flow restricted to a bounded energy surface, via the invariant Liouville measure. Due to Henri Poincare.

[Corollary corol:bndtreewidth of arXiv:2609.00636, 'Forcing monochromatic subdivisions'] The family of graphs with bounded treewidth is $R_\Delta$-bounded.
  More precisely, for every integers $s \ge 2$,  $d \ge 1$ and $w \ge 0$ there exists an integer $D$, depending only on $s, d$ and $w$, such that for every graph $P$ with maximum degree at most $d$ and treewidth at most $w$, there is a graph $H$ with maximum degree at most $D$ such that every $s$-coloring of $E(H)$ yields a monochromatic copy of $P$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary corol:bndtreewidth of arXiv:2609.00636

[Lemma 25 (Uniform moments for tRLMC) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Assume \hyperref[ass:PJG]{\textup{(A1)}}, \hyperref[ass:PLC]{\textup{(A2)}}, and
\hyperref[ass:D]{\textup{(A4)}}. Let \((\bar Y_n)_{n\ge0}\) denote the tamed randomized
Langevin Monte Carlo scheme \eqref{eq:tamed-rLMC}, initialized at
\(\bar Y_0=x_0\in\R^d\). Then the following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item
There exist constants \(\lambda_{2,\max}^{tRLMC}>0\), \(\mu>0\), and \(M_2>0\),
depending only on \(a,b,L,L_0,\beta\), such that for every
\(\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{2,\max}^{tRLMC}]\),
\[
\E\|\bar Y_n\|^2
\le
e^{-\mu n\lambda}\,\E\|x_0\|^2 + M_2\,d,
\qquad n\in\mathbb N_0.
\]

\item
For every \(p\in[2,4\ell]\cap\mathbb N\), there exist constants
\(\lambda_{p,\max}^{tRLMC}>0\), \(c_p>0\), and \(\widetilde C_p>0\), depending only on
\(p,a,b,L,L_0,\beta\), such that for every
\(\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{p,\max}^{tRLMC}]\),
\[
\E\|\bar Y_n\|^{2p}
\le
(1-c_p\lambda)^n\,\E\|x_0\|^{2p}
+
\widetilde C_p(1+d^p),
\qquad n\in\mathbb N_0.
\]
In particular,
\[
\sup_{n\ge0}\E\|\bar Y_n\|^{2p}<\infty.
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 2 (Duflo (1997), Theorem 1.3.24) of arXiv:2606.21111, 'On Elephant Random Walk with Delayed Amnesia'] Let $\{\varepsilon_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a square-integrable random sequence which takes values in $\mathbb{C}^d$ and is adapted to some filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ such that $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_{n+1}|\mathcal{F}_n)=0$ and $\sup_{n\ge1}\mathbb{E}(\parallel\varepsilon_{n+1}\parallel^2|\mathcal{F}_n)\le C$ a.s., where $C$ is a finite random variable. Also, let $\{\Phi_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a sequence of complex $d$-dimensional random variables which is adapted to $\{\mathcal{F}_n\}_{n\ge 0}$, and $s_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\parallel\Phi_k\parallel^2$, $s_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}s_n$ and $M_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\langle \Phi_{k-1},\varepsilon_k\rangle$. Then, \vspace{.1cm}\\
\noindent{(i)}  $\{M_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ converges a.s. on the set $\{s_\infty <\infty\}$, and	\vspace{.1cm}\\
\noindent{(ii)} $\lim_{n\to\infty}M_n/s_{n-1}=0$ a.s. on the set $\{s_\infty =\infty\}$ (law of large numbers (LLN)).\vspace{.1cm}\\
Also, the rate of this LLN can be specified as follows: $|M_n|^2=O((\log s_{n-1})^{1+\gamma}s_{n-1})$ a.s. for all $\gamma>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Duflo (1997), Theorem 1.3.24

[Definition of arXiv:2608.00295, 'Quadratic Perturbations of Markov Systems'] A {\it probability vector} is a vector $v=(v^{(i)})_{1\leq i\leq d}\in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $v^{(i)}\geq 0$  for all $1\leq i\leq d$ and  ${\displaystyle \sum_{s=1}^dv^{(s)}=1}$. \\
A {\it null-sum vector} is a vector $v=(v^{(i)})_{1\leq i\leq d}\in \mathbb{R}^d$  such that  ${\displaystyle \sum_{s=1}^dv^{(s)}=0}$.\\
A {\it stochastic matrix} is a matrix $A=(a_{i,j})_{1\leq i,j\leq d}\in M_d(\mathbb{R})$ such that $a_{i,j}\geq 0$ for all $1\leq i, j\leq d$, and ${\displaystyle \sum_{s=1}^da_{s,j}=1}$  for all $1\leq j\leq d$. \\
The inner product of two vectors  $v_1=(v_1^{(i)})_{1\leq i\leq d}$ and $v_2=(v_2^{(i)})_{1\leq i\leq d}\in \mathbb{R}^d$  is defined as 
$$\langle v_1, v_2 \rangle={\displaystyle \sum_{s=1}^dv^{(s)}_1v^{(s)}_2}.$$
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.00295, 'Quadratic Perturbations of Markov Systems'

			+
			\min
			\bigl\{
				\mathscr{G}_{\mathbf{k}}(x,y,z_0-1\mid A),
				\mathscr{G}_{\mathbf{k}}(x,y,z_0+N-1\mid A)
			\bigr\}.
		\end{split}
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 20 (Mean and variance of inverse descents) of arXiv:2606.18047, 'Analysis of the asymmetric shelf shuffle'] Assume $n\geq 2, m\geq 1$ and $p\in (0, 1)$. Put $\dd=2p-1$. Then,
\[
\E[D_n^{\leftarrow}]=\frac{n-1}{2}-\frac{\dd(n-1)}{2m},
\]
and
\[
\Var(D_n^{\leftarrow})=\frac{n+1}{12}+\frac{n-2}{6m^2}-\frac{\dd^2(n-1)}{4m^2}.
\]
In particular, for $p=q=1/2$, this gives
\[
\E[D_n^{\leftarrow}]=\frac{n-1}{2},
\qquad
\Var(D_n^{\leftarrow})=\frac{n+1}{12}+\frac{n-2}{6m^2},
\]
which recovers~\cite[Corollary 3.11]{DiaconisFulmanHolmes2013}.

[Defn 27 of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] Let $f: X \rightarrow S$ be a projective surjective morphism of integral Noetherian schemes with $X$ normal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
For a Cartier divisor $D$ on $X$,
the base locus of $D$ over $S$ is defined as
\[\Bs|D/S| := \Supp \Coker (f^{*}f_{*} \sO_{X}(D) \rightarrow \sO_{X}(D)). \]
\item
For a $\Q$-Cartier $\Q$-divisor $D$ on $X$,
the stable base locus of $D$ over $S$ is defined as
\[\B (D/S) := \bigcap_{\substack{m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \\ \text{$mD$ Cartier}}} \Bs|mD/S|.\]
\item
For an $\R$-Cartier $\R$-divisor $D$ on $X$,
the augmented base locus of $D$ over $S$ is define as
\[\Bp (D/S) := \bigcap_{A}  \B (D-A/S), \]
where $A$ runs through all $f$-ample $\R$-Cartier $\R$-divisors such that $D-A$ is $\Q$-Cartier, and the restricted base locus of $D$ over $S$ is defined as
\[\Bm (D/S) := \bigcup_{A}  \B (D+A/S), \]
where $A$ runs through all $f$-ample $\R$-Cartier $\R$-divisors such that $D+A$ is $\Q$-Cartier.
\end{enumerate}

[Corollary 17 of arXiv:2607.27082, '2607.27082'] Let \(X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a Brownian motion started from zero with variance
parameter \(\sigma^2>0\), and define
\(\tau_1^+(X):=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\ge1\}\). Then, for every \(\theta>0\),
\begin{equation}
\E\!\left[(\tau_1^+(X))^{-\theta}\right]
=
\frac{2\,\Gamma(2\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)}
\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)^\theta.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
\E\!\left[(\tau_1^+(X))^{-\theta}\right]<\infty
\qquad\text{for every }\theta>0.
\]

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2608.29046, '2608.29046'] Let $\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\dots,\epsilon_{r-1})$ and define

$$
-\epsilon=(-\epsilon_1,\dots,-\epsilon_{r-1}),
\qquad
\epsilon^{\mathrm{rev}}
=
(\epsilon_{r-1},\dots,\epsilon_1).
$$

Then the following hold:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] (Mirror symmetry)
$$
S(r,s,-\epsilon)
\cong
\overline{S(r,s,\epsilon)},
$$
where $\overline{S(r,s,\epsilon)}$ denotes the mirror image of $S(r,s,\epsilon)$.

\item[(2)] (Reversal symmetry)
$$
S(r,s,\epsilon^{\mathrm{rev}})
\cong
S(r,s,\epsilon).
$$
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition prop.detailed_close_is_close of arXiv:2605.10911, 'The stochastic block model has the overlap graph property for modularity'] [\bf Partitions with near-optimal modularity are close to the planted] 

Fix $a>b>0$ and integer $k\ge 2$. Let $p=p(n)=\omega\; a / n$ and $q=q(n)=\omega \; b/n$. For any $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta<\frac{a-b}{a+(k-1)b} \cdot \frac{2}{k^2}$, there exists $c=c(\varepsilon)$ such that, if $\omega>c$, then the following holds with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ provided $n$ is large enough.

Let $G \in \mathcal{G}(n,k,p,q)$ with the planted partition $\mathcal{P}$. 

Then, $q_\mathcal{A}(G)>q^{\star}(G) - \delta $ for some $k$-part partition $\mathcal{A}$ implies $d(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}) < \delta' + \varepsilon$,
where $\delta' =\delta'(\delta) \in \big(0,\frac{1}{k(k-1)}\big)$.

In fact, $\delta'=\delta'(\delta)$ is the unique value in the interval $\big(0,\frac{1}{k(k-1)}\big)$ that satisfies 
$$
\frac {a-b}{a+(k-1)b} h(\delta') =  \frac {a-b}{a+(k-1)b} h(0)-\delta,
$$
which is equivalent to 
$$
\delta = \frac {a-b}{a+(k-1)b} \Big( 2 \delta' ( 1 - \delta'(k-1)) \Big).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop 3 of arXiv:2609.00719, 'On the Aleksandrov--Bakelman--Pucci estimates for the weighted $1$-Laplacian'] Let $u\in\operatorname{USC}(\R^n)$ be nonnegative with $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq\overline\Omega$. Set $M:=\sup_{\R^n}u$ and
\[
c_\epsilon:=2\epsilon+\sqrt{2\epsilon M}.
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\renewcommand{\labelenumi}{(\roman{enumi})}
\item $u^\epsilon$ is $1/\epsilon$-semiconvex, i.e.
$u^\epsilon(\cdot)+|\cdot|^2/(2\epsilon)$ is convex.
\item $u^\epsilon$ is globally Lipschitz in $\R^n$.
\item
\[
\operatorname{supp}u^\epsilon\subseteq\Omega_{c_\epsilon}.
\]
\item Suppose that $F\in C(\R^n\times\mathcal S^n)$ satisfies $F(x,0)=0$ for every $x\in\R^n$ and is uniformly elliptic with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, that $f\in C(\R^n)$, and that $u$ is a viscosity subsolution of \eqref{F} in $\{u>0\}$. Define, for $x\in\R^n$,
\begin{align*}
F_\epsilon(x,X)&:=\sup_{q\in B_{c_\epsilon}(x)}F(q,X),\\
f_\epsilon(x)&:=\inf_{q\in B_{c_\epsilon}(x)}f(q).
\end{align*}
Then $F_\epsilon\in C(\R^n\times\mathcal S^n)$, $f_\epsilon\in C(\R^n)$, $F_\epsilon(x,0)=0$, and $F_\epsilon$ is uniformly elliptic with the same constants $\lambda,\Lambda$. Moreover, $u^\epsilon$ is a viscosity subsolution of
\[
|\nabla u^\epsilon|^{(2-n)/(n-1)}
F_\epsilon\bigl(x,\widetilde D^2u^\epsilon\bigr)\geq f_\epsilon(x)
\qquad\text{in }\{u^\epsilon>0\}.
\]
\item For every sequence $x_\epsilon\to x$,
\[
\limsup_{\epsilon\to0}u^\epsilon(x_\epsilon)\leq u(x).
\]
\item For every $x\in\R^n$,
\[
u^\epsilon(x)\longrightarrow u(x)\qquad\text{as }\epsilon\to0.
\]
\end{enumerate}

and the stochastic maximal-regularity space
$$
\mathbb Y_\delta(T)\coloneqq
{_0H}^{\sigma/2,p}_{\beta_\delta}\left([0,T];H^{1,q}(\mathbb T^d)\right)
\cap
L^p_{\beta_\delta}\left([0,T];H^{1+\sigma,q}(\mathbb T^d)\right).
$$
We introduce the Banach spaces $\mathbb K_1$, $\mathbb S_\delta$ of progressively measurable random processes with values in $\mathbb X_1$ resp. $\mathbb Y_\delta$ through their norms
$$
\norm{{\bm u}}_{\mathbb K_1(T)}
\coloneqq
\norm{{\bm u}}_{L^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb X_1(T))}, \quad 
\norm{{\bm v}}_{\mathbb S_\delta(T)}
\coloneqq
\norm{{\bm v}}_{L^p(\Omega;\mathbb Y_\delta(T))}.
$$
The corresponding product space $\mathbb K_1(T) \oplus \mathbb S_\delta(T)$ will be the target space of our fixed-point iteration.
title: Coupled weighted solution space

[Definition Genocchi of arXiv:2512.19897, 'On the convoy of the ASEP speed process'] Denote $\Delta_q$ as the q-Hahn operator, which is a q-analogue of difference operator on the polynomials.
    \[
    \Delta_q f\left(x\right) := \frac{f\left(1 + qx\right) - f\left(x\right)}{\left(1+qx\right) - x}.
    \]
    The q-Gandhi polynomials $B_n\left(x,q\right)$ are defined by the following recurrence, with $B_1\left(x,q\right) = 1$, and for $n \geq 2$,
    \[
    B_n\left(x,q\right) := \Delta_q\left(x^2  B_{n-1}\left(x,q\right)\right).
    \]

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2606.24703, 'Scheduling jobs with unknown size distribution in a M/G/1 queue: the shifted empirical Git'] Consider a stable M/G/1 queue in which the scheduler does not observe individual
    job sizes. Assume that $f$ (the density of job size distributions) satisfies assumption \ref{ass:1}. Let $n$ be the number of samples, $\epsilon >0$, $1/2 > \alpha >0$ be two constants and let  $n \geq  \Delta^{2 +4\alpha} $.
     Define
      \[ \gamma_n  = \frac{1 + \frac{n^{-\alpha (1-2\alpha)}}{\ell}}{1 -
            \frac{n^{-\alpha (1-2\alpha)}}{L}} \frac{1 + \frac{L}{\Delta \epsilon
              \ell}}{1 - \frac{L}{\Delta \epsilon \ell}} \quad\mbox{ and }  \quad p_n = 2\Delta \exp(-2n\alpha),\]
              (note that $\gamma_n $ goes to 1  and $p_n$ goes to 0 when $\Delta$ goes  to $+\infty$).
              Let $\pi_{\textsc{shifted-samples}}$ be the priority policy using the  shifted empirical index function $\widehat{\nu_{n,\Delta}}$ and preemption set $\XP^{\Delta,\epsilon}$. Then, by denoting $K$ a bound on the expected response time of any work-conserving policy,
     $$   \mathbb{E}(T_{\textsc{shifted-samples}}) \leq \gamma_n^2
        \mathbb{E}(T_{\textsc{Gittins}}) + p_n K.$$

body: A family {e_i : i in I} in a Hilbert space H is orthonormal if <e_i, e_j> = 0 for i distinct from j and ||e_i|| = 1 for every i. An orthonormal basis (complete orthonormal system) of H is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is all of H. Equivalent characterizations: the family is a maximal orthonormal set; the only vector orthogonal to every e_i is 0; every x in H has the expansion x = sum over i of <x, e_i> e_i, where at most countably many coefficients <x, e_i> are nonzero and the series converges in norm regardless of ordering. Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis (by Zorn's lemma), any two orthonormal bases of H have the same cardinality, and H is separable exactly when it has a countable orthonormal basis. An orthonormal basis of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not a vector-space (Hamel) basis.
title: Orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space

body: For two probability distributions P and Q on the same discrete set X, with pmfs p and q respectively, the Kullback-Leibler divergence from Q to P is D(P||Q) = sum_{x in X} p(x) * log( p(x)/q(x) ), with the conventions 0*log(0/q) = 0 for any q >= 0, and D(P||Q) = +infinity if there exists x with p(x) > 0 and q(x) = 0. D(P||Q) is in general not symmetric (D(P||Q) need not equal D(Q||P)) and does not satisfy the triangle inequality, so it is not a metric, but it is the standard measure of how much one probability distribution P differs from a reference distribution Q.
title: Kullback-Leibler Divergence

Set H=diag(lambda_1^2,...,lambda_r^2,0,...,0), lambda in [mu,1]^r, and let G be r-by-p iid standard Gaussian. For full-row-rank G put C=(GG^T)^(-1), solve Vdot=C V H(I-V^T C V), V(0)=G, and define q_T=tr H-tr(V(T) H V(T)^T C). Assume the almost-everywhere reduced-flow convergence q_T->0 established in the unaudited C029 v2 dependency. A terminating exact rational interval-certificate search returns an integer T with E_G q_T<rho*mu^2/64 uniformly in lambda. It combines a Gaussian tail bound, a finite-cube Lebesgue integral upper bound, complete Gaussian/spectral partitions, interval Euler with bounded local Taylor remainder, universal residual bound r on uncertified Gram boxes, and a dovetail refining each fixed horizon indefinitely. Conditional on C029 v2, this makes its sufficiently-large-scale threshold and a conservative GD hitting-time bound computable for rational scale and accuracy inputs. Only the finite ODE kernel has been implemented and checked; no global partition certificate, numerical T, efficient complexity estimate or whole-target solution is asserted.
Integers p>=r>=1; rational 0<mu,rho<=1; target positive singular values in [mu,1]
C029 v2 reduced-flow almost-everywhere convergence, still unaudited
Exact outward rational intervals; complete finite partitions; bound r on every uncertified Gram box
Computability theorem, not a performed computer-assisted global bound; novelty and independent audit unresolved

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:08dfe55d5144298a67b2e6b4d50219fdfb3cabf77ad6588575bea71aa02ca20a","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/08/08dfe55d5144298a67b2e6b4d50219fdfb3cabf77ad6588575bea71aa02ca20a.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f87e479a6eda4865849fd7009feb966eda889ab6bb65cc919bd04d6ea103b88c","bundle_entry_key":"effective-entry-search","bundle_id":"population.t419-effective-entry-certificate-search-017","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"matrix factorization and gradient dynamics","draft":"w705/bundle_017.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-weighted-stiefel-effective-entry-certificate-search","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C031 v2 — a terminating rational search for the large-scale entry quantile

Kind: moved. Target1. Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unresolved. This is a computability refinement of C029 v2, whose reduced-flow convergence proof is an unaudited dependency. It is not a computed computer-assisted bound and does not give a useful complexity estimate or settle the intermediate-scale regime.

## Statement and hardest remaining piece

Fix integers p>=r>=1 and rational 0<mu,rho<=1. There is a terminating algorithm using finite rational interval operations which returns an integer T such that, for every lambda in [mu,1]^r, the C029 reduced squared residual q_T satisfies

    E_G q_T(G,lambda) < rho mu^2/64,

where G is r-by-p iid standard Gaussian. No persistent nonsingularity of the signal overlap is assumed. The algorithm below is specified mathematically; only its finite ODE interval kernel has been implemented and checked. No global partition certificate or numerical T has been produced. A practical complexity estimate for this search, and the general intermediate-scale population dynamics, remain open.

## 1. A rational reduced equation and an integrable bound

Write D=rp, tau=rho mu^2/64 and H=diag(lambda_1^2,...,lambda_r^2,0,...,0). For full-row-rank G let M=GG^T, C=M^(-1). The equivalent reduced equation from C029 is

    V'=C V H(I-V^T C V), V(0)=G,
    q=tr H-tr(V H V^T C).

It has VV^T=M: the derivative of VV^T is zero on this invariant manifold, since (I-V^T C V)V^T=0. Thus P=V^T C V is an orthogonal projection and 0<=q<=tr H<=r. Conservation also bounds ||V||_F=||G||_F. Smooth local existence and this bound give global existence for each full-rank G. Its parameters depend continuously on G and lambda away from singular M. On singular G define q_T=r; that algebraic set has Lebesgue and Gaussian measure zero.

Choose an integer b>=1 with rD/b^2<=tau/4. Outside Q=[-b,b]^D, Markov's inequality and E||G||_F^2=D give

    E[q_T 1_(G outside Q)] <= rD/b^2 <= tau/4.

The standard Gaussian density is at most1. Hence for every spectrum

    E q_T <= I_T(lambda)+tau/4,
    I_T(lambda)=integral_Q q_T(G,lambda) dG.

Using Lebesgue measure instead of Gaussian quadrature is deliberately wasteful, but avoids numerical transcendental density evaluation.

## 2. Existence of a strict-slack integer horizon

For every fixed lambda, C029 gives q_T->0 for almost every Gaussian G. Gaussian and Lebesgue null sets agree on Q, since the Gaussian density is strictly positive there. The integrand is bounded by r, so dominated convergence gives I_j(lambda)->0 at integer times j.

For each j, I_j is continuous on the spectral cube: pointwise continuous dependence holds at every full-rank G and the same domination applies. Along the reduced flow, with Y=M^(-1/2)V,

    q'=-2||M^(-1/2)Y H(I-Y^T Y)||_F^2<=0.

Consequently I_j is nonincreasing. Dini's theorem on the compact spectral cube gives uniform convergence to zero. In particular there exists an integer T with sup_lambda I_T(lambda)<tau/4. This existence result alone is nonconstructive; the next steps give a search which recognizes a suitable horizon with strict slack.

## 3. A sound fixed-horizon interval enclosure

Partition Q and the spectral cube into rational dyadic boxes. For each G box form outward interval enclosures of M and det M. If the lower determinant endpoint is not strictly positive, declare the box uncertified and use the universal q upper bound r. Otherwise M is positive definite for every actual G in the box: actual Gram matrices are positive semidefinite and have positive determinant. The adjugate formula, with outward interval division by the positive determinant interval, encloses C uniformly on that box.

For a certified G box and spectral box, integrate the polynomial vector field F(V)=C V H(I-V^T C V) by validated interval Euler. All endpoints are rational; every elementary operation rounds outward to a dyadic grid. Let B=Db and R=DB. Each true component of V has absolute value <=sqrt(D)b<=B. Intersect every endpoint enclosure with [-B,B] componentwise; this preserves inclusion. Every point in the resulting matrix boxes has Frobenius norm <=sqrt(D)B<=R.

Take a rational c>=||C||_op valid for the entire parameter box, for example r times the maximum absolute endpoint among its inverse-Gram entries. The true H has operator norm <=1. On ||V||_F<=R,

    ||F(V)||_F <= M_f=cR(1+cR^2),
    ||D_V F(V)||_(F->F) <= L=c+3c^2R^2.

The derivative bound follows by differentiating the linear term C V H and the cubic term C V H V^T C V; each of its three differentiated factors contributes at most c^2 R^2. Along the actual trajectory, ||V''||_F<=L M_f. For a step h=T/n the exact Taylor remainder in each component is therefore in [-h^2 L M_f/2,h^2 L M_f/2]. Adding this interval to the interval Euler update encloses all actual solutions in the parameter box. The true solution remains in the component bound throughout each step, so this remainder estimate is valid even if a numerical Euler prediction leaves that bound. Induction proves enclosure through time T. An empty intersection signals a failed implementation/check, never a successful certificate.

Evaluate tr H-tr(V H V^T C) by outward interval operations at T and intersect with [0,r]. Its upper endpoint u is a valid uniform integrand upper bound. Uncertified boxes instead use u=r. Every returned bound is rational.

## 4. Consistency including almost singular boxes

For fixed T and compact sets of full-rank G, inverse-Gram parameters are bounded, their natural interval enclosures converge uniformly as G boxes shrink, and the same holds for the polynomial field on bounded state sets. More explicitly, on any such compact set the width recurrence for the interval Euler boxes has the form

    w_(k+1) <= (1+h K)w_k + h K delta + K h^2 + K 2^(-P),

where delta bounds parameter-box widths, P is dyadic precision, and K is a finite constant uniform on that compact set and the spectral cube, at the fixed horizon. Initial widths are O(delta). This follows by bounding the finitely many sums/products/divisions in the natural interval expression; the sole denominators are uniformly bounded away from zero. Clipping does not increase width. Discrete Gronwall gives endpoint widths tending to zero when delta->0, h->0 and n 2^(-P)->0. The same argument controls excess upper bounds for the integrand. Choose, for example, mesh widths O(2^(-ell)), n=2^ell and P=80+4ell. No efficiency is asserted for these constants; increasing precision is essential.

To include near-singular G, let Z={G in Q: det(GG^T)=0}. This is a compact algebraic null set. For any epsilon>0 there is an open neighborhood U of Z in Q with volume below epsilon. Choose a smaller neighborhood of Z with closure in U. On its compact complement the Gram determinant is bounded below, so every sufficiently fine box outside U is certified and the preceding convergence is uniform. Boxes near Z eventually lie inside U; their total contribution is at most r volume(U). This bounds both uncertified cells and certified cells where inverse conditioning could spoil uniform enclosure convergence. Since epsilon is arbitrary, the upper integration certificates converge to the true integrals uniformly in lambda. This is an existence proof of convergence; finding U is not a required subroutine of the search.

For precision, the spectral cells also shrink. On the compact complement of the small singular neighborhood, uniform continuity in lambda and uniform interval consistency bound the difference between a cell's upper sum and I_T at every lambda in that cell. Inside the neighborhood both are bounded by r times its volume. Thus the maximum excess over all spectral cells tends to zero.

## 5. Complete certificates and terminating dovetail

At a pair (T,ell), enumerate every cell in both finite partitions. For each spectral cell J, sum vol(K)*u(K,J) over every G cell K, using the universal bound on every uncertified cell. Accept only if all these rational sums are <=tau/2. The checker must reconstruct the complete partitions from their global mesh parameters, check each cell exactly once and recompute every enclosure. An asserted row count, a sample of cells, or an omitted singular box is not a certificate. Streaming the finite sums is permitted; none of this requires a stored array of all cells.

Enumerate all pairs of positive integers (T,ell) by increasing T+ell. Each pair requires finitely many rational operations and produces either acceptance or rejection. Every fixed T is eventually tested at arbitrarily large ell. Choose the T with strict slack from section2; section4 implies that it is eventually accepted. The algorithm therefore terminates. A schedule which only tests T=ell would not be justified by fixed-horizon consistency.

For the accepted T, each spectrum belongs to a checked spectral cell, giving I_T<=tau/2. Section1 then gives E q_T<=3tau/4<tau as claimed. Good G sets need not be common to distinct spectra. No assertion is made that one draw works for every target orientation or spectrum simultaneously.

## 6. Computable large-scale GD corollary and its limits

C029's threshold and time-step expressions use this T and finitely many positive computable constants, square roots, exponentials and logarithms at known positive arguments. Outward rational approximations provide strict positive lower bounds for its epsilon_0 and step cap; searching for such bounds terminates. Exact equality comparisons with real constants are unnecessary. If 0<e0<=epsilon_0<=1 is rational, choose an integer S>=max(1,1/e0); then S^(-4)<=epsilon_0.

For each rational s>=S, physical entry time t*=s^2 T is rational. Given a rational positive h0 below C029's admissible step cap, choose an integer N>t*/h0 and eta=t*/N. These are finite rational calculations, with eta fixed independently of the requested accuracy. With a rational K0 above C029's global factor bound K, its tail estimate

    error_k <= sqrt(r) exp(-eta mu^2 (k-N)/(32K))

implies the conservative rational hitting count

    N+ceil(32 K0 r/(eta mu^2 epsilon))

for rational epsilon>0: use sqrt(r)<=r and exp(-x)<=1/x for x>0. The high-probability statement, normalizations and dependencies are exactly C029's; this supplies an algorithmically computable bound in its sufficiently-large-s regime. It gives neither a practical complexity bound nor coverage of the remaining middle scales. Positive-noise Target2 is untouched.

## Checks and provenance

scripts/entry_certificate_kernel.py implements only the finite interval enclosure in section3. logs/C031_interval_kernel_checks.json records exact Fraction arithmetic with outward dyadic endpoints, a stationary refinement check, containment of a nonstationary rank-one analytic bracket, and negative controls for an orthogonal stationary frame and singular Gram. Its finite runtime caps are prototype safeguards, not restrictions of the mathematical search. No whole-cube integration, search output or computed GD complexity has been checked. The proof above is a direct construction, relying on C029's reduced-flow theorem and the classical Dini/dominated-convergence arguments; independent review and prior-art assessment remain required.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:82de096e300ec8bdae9eb239d5aaf69e82061a7cddf1a1a992fdc73479616af7","revision_digest":"sha256:8e65bce50534c8ced47bd29efadb47765bf6e641851fcfb395750c92858d6831","source_id":"owner-work:w705:T419-C031:v2","source_revision":"as-read-2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem:transferral of arXiv:2609.00889, 'Dominant-Degree Conditions for Ramsey--Tur\'an Factors of Non-Directed Cycle Orientations'] Fix $\ell\ge3$ and a non-directed orientation $\widetilde C$ of $C_\ell$. For every $d>0$, $M\in\mathbb N$, and $0<\varepsilon\le d/8$, there exist constants $\nu,\gamma>0$ and $n_0\in\mathbb N$ such that the following holds. Let $D$ be an $n$-vertex oriented graph, $n\ge n_0$, with a partition $\mathcal P=(V_1,\dots,V_k)$. Suppose that for distinct $i,j\in[k]$ there are $X\subseteq V_i$ and $Y\subseteq V_j$ with $|X|,|Y|\ge n/M$ such that $(X,Y)$ is an $(\varepsilon , d)$-regular directed pair. If $\alpha(D)\le\gamma n$, then both
\[
\mathbf e_i+(\ell-1)\mathbf e_j\quad\text{and}\quad (\ell-1)\mathbf e_i+\mathbf e_j
\]
are $(\widetilde C,\nu)$-robust with respect to $\mathcal P$.

Let D>=1,N>=2 be integers, let phi_1,...,phi_D be real orthonormal functions in L2(Omega,tau), and draw theta_1,...,theta_N independently from tau. Write v_i=(phi_1(theta_i),...,phi_D(theta_i)) and S_N=(1/N)sum_i v_i v_i^T. Assume that for every integer q>=2, sup_(j<=D)||phi_j||_(L2q(tau))<=C(q). For every such q there is K(q), depending only on q and C(q), such that, with delta=K(q)D log(max(D,N))/N^(1-1/q), E||S_N-I_D||_op<=delta vee sqrt(delta). The square-root term is retained when delta is small. In an asymptotic sequence with N->infinity, constants C(q) uniform along the sequence, and D<=N^(1-eta) for a fixed eta>0, choose q>1/eta to obtain E||S_N-I_D||_op->0 and ||S_N-I_D||_op=o_P(1). These are uncentered second moments; the coordinates of v_i need not be independent or have zero means.
