[Proposition thm:N-moments-general of arXiv:2607.14266, 'The Swapping Mechanism for Interacting Diffusions: Framework, Comparison with Switching, a'] Assume affine drifts $\beta_i(x)=a_ix+b_i$, affine jump amplitudes
		$\chi_i(x,u)=\phi_i(u)x+\psi_i(u)$ with
		$\int(|\phi_i(u)|^2+|\psi_i(u)|)\nu_i(\mathrm{d} u)<\infty$, constant
		diffusion coefficients $\sigma_i>0$, and bounded swap rates
		$\gamma_{ij}\ge 0$. Then for every integer $k\ge 1$, the moments up to
		order $k$, $\{m_\alpha(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_t^\alpha]:|\alpha|\le k\}$,
		satisfy a closed linear ODE system of dimension
		$\binom{N+k}{k}=O(N^k/k!)$.
		
		By contrast, under the switching description the moments
		$\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_t^\alpha;\Lambda_t=\theta]$ for $|\alpha|\le k$
		and $\theta\in\mathfrak{S}_N$ form a system of dimension
		$N!\binom{N+k}{k}$, which does not close without tracking the full
		permutation state.

[Lemma 20 (Mixing times asymptotics for $0 < \gamma < 1$) of arXiv:2603.29473, '$\chi^2$--cut-off phenomenon for Galerkin projections of Fokker--Planck equations with mon'] \hfill

	\noindent
	Let $0 < \gamma < 1$, let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $\psi_{k,\varepsilon}$ be the $k$-th non-constant eigenfunction of $-\mathcal{L}_\varepsilon$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_{k,\varepsilon}=\lambda_k\varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma-1}{1+\gamma}}$, let $N$ be as in \cref{lem:general-shape}, and let $\alpha_{j,d}$ be as in \cref{eq:alpha_def}.
	If $x_0 \neq 0$, define
	\begin{equation*}
		S_{k}(x_0,\varepsilon)
		:=
		\sum_{d=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j=d+1}^{N}
		\lambda_k^{\,j-d}\, \hat A_{j,j-d}(\gamma)\,
		\varepsilon^{\frac{\alpha_{j,d}-1}{1+\gamma}}
		|x_0|^{\,1-\alpha_{j,d}},
	\end{equation*}
	where, in the resonant case $N=\frac{1+\gamma}{2\gamma}$, the term corresponding to $(j,d)=(N,0)$ is replaced by $\lambda_k^N A_{N,N}(\gamma)\left(\log|x_0| - \frac{1}{1+\gamma}\log\varepsilon\right)$.
	Let $t_\varepsilon$ be the (unique) time satisfying
	\begin{equation}
		e^{-2\lambda_k \varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma-1}{1+\gamma}} t_\varepsilon}
		\Big(\!\int \varrho_{\varepsilon,0}(x)\psi_{k,\varepsilon}(x)\dx\!\Big)^2
		=1.
	\end{equation}
	Then for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $C=C(\gamma,k)\geq 1$ such that
	\begin{equation}
		\frac{\varepsilon^{\frac{1-\gamma}{1+\gamma}}}{\lambda_k}\bigl(S_{k}(x_0,\varepsilon)-\log C\bigr)
		\le
		t_\varepsilon
		\le
		\frac{\varepsilon^{\frac{1-\gamma}{1+\gamma}}}{\lambda_k}\bigl(S_{k}(x_0,\varepsilon)+\log C\bigr).
	\end{equation}

	If $x_0=0$ and $\psi_k(0)\neq 0$, define

	\begin{equation*}
		S_k^{\mathrm{cen}}(\varepsilon)
		:=
		\frac{\gamma(1-\gamma)}{1+\gamma}\log\varepsilon
		+
		\sum_{d=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j=d+1}^{N}
		\lambda_k^{\,j-d}\, \hat A_{j,j-d}(\gamma)\,
		\varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma(\alpha_{j,d}-1)}{1+\gamma}},
	\end{equation*}
	where, in the resonant case $N=\frac{1+\gamma}{2\gamma}$, the term corresponding to $(j,d)=(N,0)$ is replaced by $-\lambda_k^{N}A_{N,N}(\gamma)\,\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma}\log\varepsilon$.
	Let $t_\varepsilon$ be the (unique) time satisfying \cref{eq:teps_def}. Then for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $C=C(\gamma,k)\geq 1$ such that
	\begin{equation}
		\frac{\varepsilon^{\frac{1-\gamma}{1+\gamma}}}{\lambda_k}\bigl(S_k^{\mathrm{cen}}(\varepsilon)-\log C\bigr)
		\le
		t_\varepsilon
		\le
		\frac{\varepsilon^{\frac{1-\gamma}{1+\gamma}}}{\lambda_k}\bigl(S_k^{\mathrm{cen}}(\varepsilon)+\log C\bigr).
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Mixing times asymptotics for $0 < \gamma < 1$

Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n and let f be locally Lipschitz with f and its gradient in L^2(gamma). Then Var_gamma(f) <= E_gamma[ |grad f|^2 ]. The constant 1 is SHARP and is attained exactly by the affine functions: for f(x) = a . x + b both sides equal |a|^2. The inequality is DIMENSION-FREE - the same constant 1 for every n - which is what makes it useful in high dimension, and it follows from the one-dimensional case by tensorization of the variance. It is strictly weaker than the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality, which implies it by applying the log-Sobolev inequality to 1 + eps f and expanding to second order in eps. Note the direction: the inequality bounds the variance by the gradient energy, so it gives concentration only at the level of variance, not exponential tails; exponential tails require the log-Sobolev inequality and the Herbst argument. [standard; e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.20]

Actual TASEP jump histories have blocking constraints and do not form that independent product. Check: The ratio follows by cancellation of adjacent factorials; the same conclusion follows from discrete concavity of -log(k!). The independent-particle calculation is explicitly a comparison model, not a TASEP formula. Obstruction: Blocking changes holding rates according to the configuration. The determinantal transition formula contains signed terms, and log concavity is not preserved under signed summation. [Lemma 13 of arXiv:2609.02779, '2609.02779'] Let $J\subset\T$ be a closed arc on which
$u_\lambda<0$, and identify $J$ with a compact interval in $\R$.  At every
differentiability point of $u_\lambda$ in $J$,
\[
 u_\lambda'(x)+a
 =\pm\sqrt{Q(x)^2-2\lambda u_\lambda(x)}.
\]
Moreover, the negative root cannot occur to the left of the positive root.
Thus there exists $\sigma\in J$ such that, up to a set of measure
zero,
\[
 u_\lambda'(x)+a=\sqrt{Q(x)^2-2\lambda u_\lambda(x)}
 \quad\text{for }x<\sigma,
\]
and
\[
 u_\lambda'(x)+a=-\sqrt{Q(x)^2-2\lambda u_\lambda(x)}
 \quad\text{for }x>\sigma.
\]
Here $\sigma=\inf J$ corresponds to the negative root almost everywhere on
$J$, and $\sigma=\sup J$ to the positive root almost everywhere on $J$.

[Proposition prop:projected.Stein.Wishart of arXiv:2606.04859, 'Stein's method for the Wishart distribution'] Suppose that the true scale matrix $\Sigma\in \mathcal{S}_{++}^d$ admits the linear representation
\[
\Sigma = \Sigma(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star}) = \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^{\star} B_j
\]
for some $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star}\in \mathbb{R}^p$ and fixed symmetric templates $\smash{\{B_j\}_{j=1}^p \subseteq \mathcal{S}^d}$. Let $\{U_m\}_{m = 1}^{M} \subseteq \mathcal{S}^{d}$ be given, and for the corresponding linear probes $f_{U_m}(S) \vcentcolon= \mathrm{tr}(U_m S)$, form the structured Stein moment equations
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{tr}\{\Sigma(\boldsymbol{\beta}) U_m\} = y_{n,m}, \qquad y_{n,m} \vcentcolon= \frac{1}{\alpha n} \sum_{k=1}^n \mathrm{tr}(\mathfrak{W}^{(k)} U_m), \qquad m\in \{1, \ldots,M\}.
\end{equation}
Let $C\in \mathbb{R}^{M\times p}$ be the design matrix with entries $C_{mj} \vcentcolon= \mathrm{tr}(B_j U_m)$, and let $\boldsymbol{y}_n \vcentcolon= (y_{n,1}, \ldots,y_{n,M})^{\top}$. If $C$ has full column rank, then the least-squares solution
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_n = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in \mathbb{R}^p} \|C \boldsymbol{\beta} - \boldsymbol{y}_n\|_2^2 = (C^{\top} C)^{-1} C^{\top} \boldsymbol{y}_n
\]
is strongly consistent for the true coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star}$, as $n\to\infty$. In particular, the structured estimator $\widehat{\Sigma}_n \vcentcolon= \Sigma(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_n) = \sum_{j=1}^p \hat{\beta}_{n,j} B_j$ converges almost surely to $\Sigma$ and solves the projected Stein moment equations (equation eq:structured.Wishart.moments of the paper) in the least-squares sense. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2607.12384, '2607.12384'] Under the assumptions \eqref{hyp:main}, let $\{u(t,x), (t,x)\in[0,T]\times\R\}$ be the mild solution to the SPDE~\eqref{eq:main equation} given by \eqref{eq:solution}. Denote
	\[
	\xi(s)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sigma(u(s,y))^2\right], \qquad s\geq 0.
	\]
	Then, for any $T>0$,
	\[
	\left(
	\frac{1}{\sqrt{R}}
	\left(
	\int_{-R}^{R} u(t,x)\,dx - 2R
	\right)
	\right)_{t\in[0,T]}
	\longrightarrow
	\left(
	\int_0^t \sqrt{2\xi(s)}\,dB_s
	\right)_{t\in[0,T]},
	\]
	 as $R$ tends to infinity, where $B$ is a standard Brownian motion and the convergence is in law on the space of continuous functions $C([0,T])$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary coro:sign_d_regular of arXiv:2508.17838, '\bf Edge Universality for Inhomogeneous Random Matrices'] Let $G_N$ be the adjacency matrix of a $d$-regular graph on $N$ vertices,   assume $d\gg N^{2/3+\tau}$ for some fixed $\tau>0$ and $|\lambda_2(G_N)|,|\lambda_N(G_N)|=o(d)$.  Then edge universality holds for the extreme eigenvalues of $\sigma\circ G_N$. In particular, the rescaled largest eigenvalue converges weakly to $\mathrm{TW}_1$ which  has  the Tracy-Widom $F_1$ distribution, that is, 
  \begin{equation}
    N^{\frac{2}{3}}\Bigl(\tfrac{\lambda_1(\sigma\circ G_N)}{\sqrt{d}} - 2\Bigr)  \longrightarrow   \mathrm{TW}_1.
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2607.17192, 'Geometric Regime--Switching Diffusions on Stratified Riemannian Spaces with an Application'] Suppose Assumptions~\assref{ass:diffusions} and~\assref{ass:jumps} hold.
		Then for every starting point $x\in E$ there exists a filtered
		probability space $(\Omega,\cl F_t^x,\P_x)$ and an
		$E$--valued càdlàg process $(X_t)_{t\ge 0}$ such that:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),ref=\roman*]
			\item $X_0=x$ $\P_x$--a.s.;
			\item between its jump times, the process remains in a single stratum:
			if $X_{t-}\in S_\alpha$ and $X_t=X_{t-}$, then $X_s\in S_\alpha$
			for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $t$; on each such interval,
			$X$ evolves as the diffusion with generator $L_\alpha$;
			\item the jumps of $X$ are governed by the structural kernels and rates:
			whenever $X_{t-}=x\in S_\alpha$, jumps of type $e\in\cl E$ with $\alpha(e)=\alpha$
			occur with conditional intensity $\lambda_e(x)$, and conditional on such a jump of type $e$,
			the post-jump location has law $K_e(x,\cdot)$;
			\item for every $f\in\cl D_0$, the process
			\[
			M_t^f=f(X_t)-f(X_0)-\int_0^t A f(X_s)\,ds
			\]
			is an $(\cl F_t^x)$--martingale. In particular, the law of $X$
			on $D([0,\infty);E)$ is a solution of the martingale problem for
			$(A,\cl D_0)$ with initial condition $x$.
		\end{enumerate}
		Moreover, $X$ is non-explosive and the map $ x \mapsto \P_x$ is Borel.

[Lemma lem:escape-stab-middle of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0 = 1$ and finitely many strongly-exposed bins, and fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$ with $\lambda$ sufficiently small. Let $\Psi = (g,\tau,j,\overline{z},\mathcal{S},\textup{stabilising})$ be a high-level state with $j$ sufficiently large. Let $E$ be an escape process with high-level state $\Psi$, send sequence $\overline{p}$, birth rate $\lambda$. Fix a tuple $\overline{a} \in (\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0})^j$, let $d$ and $\theta$ be real numbers with $0 \le d \le j^{\phi+51}$ and $0 \leq  \theta \leq  1/(64j^2)$, and suppose that $\overline{a}\in (\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0})^j$ is a $(d,j^{10},\theta,1)$-RS-good beginning. Fix $\tau' \ge \tau$
and let $T = \min\{\tau' + j^{\phi+70}, T_{\nu_j^\mathrm{lo}, \tau' + j^{19}}\}$.
Then, conditioned on $\overline{b}_{[j]}^E(\tau') = \overline{a}$, the following properties hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\tau' + j^{19} \le T \le \tau' + j^{\phi+70}$.
\item With probability at least $1-\exp(-350j/\lambda^2)$, for all $t$ in the range $\tau' \le t \le T$, $\overline{b}_{[j]}^E(t)$ is a $(d+6j^{22},j^{27},\theta+3/j^4,2)$-RS-good beginning.
\item With probability at least $1-\exp(-350j/\lambda^2)$, $\overline{b}_{[j]}^E(T)$ is a $(d+6j^{22},j^{10},\theta+3/j^4,1)$-RS-good beginning.
\item With probability at least $1-\exp(-(\log j)^2/2)$, $\overline{b}_{[j]}^E(T)$ is a $j^7$-AF-good beginning.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 53 of arXiv:2606.11758, '2606.11758'] Let \(W\ge0\) satisfy \(\mathbb E W=1\).  Let
\(
    (\widetilde\mu_n)_{n\ge0}
\)
be the dyadic scalar cascade on \([0,1]\) generated by the dyadic weights \((W_v)\), 
and suppose that
\(
    \widetilde\mu_n\weak\widetilde\mu.
\)
Set
\[
    g=f_{\mathbb T}\circ q,
    \qquad
    \mu_{\circ}=g_{\#}\widetilde\mu.
\]
Then \(\mu_{\circ}\) is the weak limit of the scalar dyadic circle cascade
constructed from the same weights, with level-\(n\) dyadic arcs
\[
    A_v=g(I_v)\subset\mathbb S^1,
    \qquad v\in\Sigma_n,
\]
using the endpoint convention inherited from the interval construction.  In
particular, \(\mu_{\circ}\) has the law of the scalar dyadic circle cascade
generated by \(W\).  Moreover,
\(
\mu_{\circ}(\mathbb S^1)=\widetilde\mu([0,1]).
\)

[Theorem thm:MO-service-Markovianity of arXiv:2606.24881, 'Queues with Correlated Service Times --- the $M/M_D/c$ Model'] Consider a time-homogeneous queueing system with finitely many servers
indexed by $\{1,\ldots,c\}$. Suppose that arrivals are generated by
Poisson processes and that service completions are governed by a
Marshall--Olkin shock system. That is, for each nonempty subset
$A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,c\}$, there is an independent Poisson process
\[
N_A(t),\qquad t\ge0,
\]
with rate $\mu_A$, and a jump of $N_A$ simultaneously completes the
services currently being processed at the busy servers in $A$.

Let $Y(t)$ denote a state descriptor containing all queueing variables
needed to determine the future evolution of the system, such as queue
lengths, busy-server indicators, customer locations, routing information,
and scheduling variables. Assume that all routing, scheduling,
service-allocation, and service-initiation rules are time-homogeneous and
depend only on the current state $Y(t)$.

Then $\{Y(t):t\ge0\}$ is a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain.

[Proposition 3 ({\cite[Th.~5.10, Th.~6.4) of arXiv:2609.03455, '2609.03455'] {KKtheta}}]
The map
\[
 \Theta_\tau:\C/(\Z+\tau\Z)\longrightarrow\P^6,
 \qquad
 z\longmapsto
 (\theta_0(z):\theta_1(z):\cdots:\theta_6(z))
\]
is an elliptic normal embedding of degree $7$.
Its image is cut out by fourteen quadrics.
If
\[
 S=\Theta_\tau(\tau/7),\qquad T=\Theta_\tau(1/7),
\]
then $S$ and $T$ are points of order $7$, and translation by them is
given respectively by cyclic permutation and diagonal multiplication
by powers of $\zeta_7=e^{2\pi i/7}$.
Moreover, $[-1]$ is given by \eqref{eq:minus-one-intro}.

Set
\begin{equation}
 a_i=\theta_i(0,\tau)\qquad (i=1,2,3).
\end{equation}
Then the universal elliptic curve is given by the fourteen quadrics
\begin{equation}
 \left\{
 \begin{aligned}
 a_1a_2x_i^2&=a_2^2x_{i+3}x_{i-3}-a_3^2x_{i+2}x_{i-2},\\
 a_2a_3x_i^2&=a_1^2x_{i+3}x_{i-3}-a_3^2x_{i+1}x_{i-1},
 \end{aligned}
 \right.
 \qquad i\in\Z/7\Z,
\end{equation}

[Definition def:meta-process of arXiv:2605.19835, 'Reemergence of the Epidemic Threshold in SIRS Infections on Connected Stars'] Let $k, \ell \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{\geq 1}$, and let~$G^\star$ be a \conStar{k}{\ell}.
    Moreover, let $\varepsilon \in \mathOrText{\mathds{R}}_{>0}$ be a constant, and let $C$ be an SIRS process on a super-graph of~$G^\star$ (over $n \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{\geq 1}$ vertices) with infection rate $\lambda \in (0, 1]$ such that $\lambda \in \bigOmega{\ell^{-1/2+\varepsilon}}$ and with constant deimmunization rate $\varrho \in \mathOrText{\mathds{R}}_{> 0}$. For each star $s$ of~$G^\star$ and each $t \in \mathOrText{\mathds{R}}_{\geq 0}$, let $A_{s,t}$ be the indicator random variable of the event that~$s$ is active at time $t$. We call the union of these indicator variables over all~$k$ stars the \emph{meta process} $A$ of $C$. Furthermore, for each $t \in \mathOrText{\mathds{R}}_{\geq 0}$, let~$X_t$ be the random variable of the number of active stars at time~$t$, and for each $i \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}$, let $\tau(i)$ be the $i$-th time point at which $(X_t)_{t \in \mathOrText{\mathds{R}}_{\geq 0}} \eqqcolon X$ changes its value, defining $\tau(0) = 0$. We call~$X$ the \emph{simplified meta process} of $C$, and $\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(X_{\tau(i)}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)_{i \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}}$ the \emph{discrete version} of $X_t$.

body:
[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] Denote
\[
\Delta_n:=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
f(\lambda)\,|g(\lambda)-g(\mu)|\,H_n^2(\lambda-\mu)\,\dd\lambda\,\dd\mu,
\]
where $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{-\alpha}L_f(\lambda)$ and $g(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{-\beta}L_g(\lambda)$ with $\alpha, \beta < 1$. Assume that $\alpha+\beta<1$, then
\[
\Delta_n\longrightarrow 0.
\]
In addition, if \(g\) satisfies \eqref{ass:meanvalue} and \(\alpha+\beta\ge 0\), then for every \(\eta>0\),
\[
\Delta_n\le C_\eta n^{\alpha+\beta+\eta-1}.
\]

[Proposition 14 of arXiv:2609.03171, 'Factorization patterns and fields of definition of $\ell$-torsion points on the Jacobians '] Let $p_1(x),\dots,p_n(x)$ be distinct irreducible polynomials of degrees 
$d_1,\dots,d_n$, respectively, and consider the  matrix $$M=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(
C[p_1^{e_{1,1}}],\dots,C[p_1^{e_{1,m_1}}],
\dots,
C[p_n^{e_{n,1}}],\dots,C[p_n^{e_{n,m_n}}]
\right).$$
For elements with nonzero components in blocks 
$C[p_{i_1}^{e_{i_1,j_1}}],\dots,C[p_{i_r}^{e_{i_r,j_r}}]$ 
at levels $k_1,\dots,k_r$, (i.e., with minimal 
polynomials exactly $p_{i_s}^{k_s}(x)$ respectively), the following statements hold:
\begin{itemize}
    \item [(i)] Their minimal polynomial is $\operatorname{lcm}\!\left(p_{i_1}^{k_1}(x),\dots,p_{i_r}^{k_r}(x)\right),$

\item [(ii)] They are defined over an extension of degree
$o\!\left(\operatorname{lcm}\!\left(p_{i_1}^{k_1}(x),
\dots,p_{i_r}^{k_r}(x)\right)\right)$. 

\item[(iii)] The total number of such elements is $\prod_{s=1}^{r}\ell^{d_{i_s}(k_s-1)}(\ell^{d_{i_s}}-1)$ .
\end{itemize}

\[

Then

\Lp(\cT_n,\Omega)\longrightarrow\Lp(\cT,\Omega).
\]
If the positive eigenfunctions are normalized at a fixed $x_0\in \Omega$, then they converge to the normalized limiting eigenfunction in $C^1(\overline \Omega)$.

body: In the program toward the first-passage percolation fluctuation exponent chi = 1/3, the obstruction that the variance-ratio induction does not start is two-sided rather than one-sided. The upper argument, (L1'), caps the block-increment fluctuation from above and needs alpha = chi through the ratio rho = Q^2/Var = O(1); rho = O(1) needs a variance lower bound that an upper-bound induction cannot supply about itself; and a second argument bounds the same fluctuation from below, reducing that lower bound to restricted-minimum anticoncentration. So the wall is a two-sided sandwich on the block-increment scale - a fixed-point equation whose solution is chi - and a one-directional induction cannot reach a fixed point, which is why it does not start. Proposed escape: carry a window [L, U] on the variance instead of a single value. The ratio R = U/L can contract (the upper leg lowers U given L, the lower leg raises L given U, neither proved about itself), which removes the circularity and reduces the difficulty to one missing ingredient: the lower leg as a per-scale contraction rate rho_L, a restricted-minimum anticoncentration statement weaker-looking than a full variance lower bound. Quantitative floor: the base window R(0) ~ n/log^2 n is polynomially large and only about log n scale steps are available, so the contraction must be at most about 1/2 at every step, not merely have a product below 1. Status: heuristic at the sandwich framing (the equivalence of the two sides holds at the level the block-sum argument needs, not as a formal if-and-only-if); the existence of rho_L and the bookkeeping by which the product beats the growth are open, chi = 1/3 is not proved, and a referee reading is owed.

body: In mathematics, the Fortuin–Kasteleyn–Ginibre (FKG) inequality is a correlation inequality, a fundamental tool in statistical mechanics and probabilistic combinatorics, due to Cees M. Fortuin, Pieter W. Kasteleyn, and Jean Ginibre. Informally, it says that in many random systems, increasing events are positively correlated, while an increasing and a decreasing event are negatively correlated. It was obtained by studying the random cluster model.

\[
    \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{(\log k)^{\alpha}}{k^{\beta}} \asymp

body: [Theorem thm: main right of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] The process $(U(-r)+r,\, r\ge 0)$ is a homogeneous Feller process starting from $0$. For any $r>0$, $\frac{r}{U(-r)+r}$ has distribution ${\mathcal B}(\frac{2-\delta+\widehat{\delta}}{2},\frac{\delta'}{2})$. Conditionally on $U(0)=z>0$, the process $U(-r)$ stays constant then jumps at time $\mathrm{x}$ where  $\frac{z}{z+{\mathrm x}}$ has distribution ${\mathcal B}(\frac{\delta'}{2},1)$. Conditionally on ${\mathrm x}=x$, $\frac{z+x}{U(-x)+x}\sim {\mathcal B}(\frac{2-\delta+\widehat{\delta}}{2},1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm: main right of arXiv:2411.04773

[Definition of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Fix a finite subset $J\subset \N_{\geqslant1}$. 
We denote by $\mathcal{P}(J)$ the set of all partitions of $J$. For $\rho\in \mathcal{P}(J)$, we write $|\rho|$ for the number of elements of $\rho$. We denote the elements of $\rho$ by $(\rho_q)_{q\in[|\rho|]}$: they are non-empty subsets of $J$, non-overlapping, and their union is $J$.
We adopt the convention of ordering these subsets by the order of their minima, writing $\rho=(\rho_q)_{q\in[|\rho|]}$ where $k<p\Rightarrow\min\rho_k<\min\rho_p$. 

Moreover, for two finite non-empty subsets $I,J \subset \N_{\geqslant1}$ we define 
\begin{equs}
    \mathcal{Q}(I,J)\eqdef\Big\{(\pi,\rho):\rho\in\mathcal{P}(J)\;\text{and}\;\pi:I\rightarrow[|\rho|]\Big\}\,,
\end{equs}

and we adopt the convention that if $I=\emptyset$, then we set $  \mathcal{Q}(I,J)=\mathcal{P}(J)$.

Finally, given $(\pi,\rho)\in\mathcal{Q}(I,J)$, for every $q\in[|\rho|]$, we use the shorthand $\pi_q\eqdef \pi^{-1}(q)$. The $\pi_q$'s are therefore some possibly empty subsets of $I$, non-overlapping, and whose union is $I$.

body: Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space, let p satisfy 1 <= p <= infinity, and let f, g be functions in L^p(mu). Then f + g is also in L^p(mu) and satisfies ||f + g||_p <= ||f||_p + ||g||_p, where ||f||_p = (integral |f|^p dmu)^(1/p) for p < infinity and the essential supremum of |f| for p = infinity. This is exactly the triangle inequality for the L^p norm, which is what makes L^p(mu) a normed vector space; the same inequality holds with sums replacing the integral for the sequence spaces l^p.
title: Minkowski inequality

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2606.10336, 'From Pitman's local times representation to the Gorin-Shkolnikov identity and beyond'] Let $\{\mathcal{F}_a\}_{a \ge 0}$ be the excursion filtrations\footnote{See \cite{Mc86, Wil79} for background on excursion filtrations.}.
Assume that $\phi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sufficiently smooth and $\int_0^1\phi(x)^2dx < \infty$.
We have:
\begin{equation}
\int_a^\infty \phi(I_x) dx - \frac{1}{4} \int_a^\infty \ell_x^2 \left( \frac{\phi(I_x)}{I_x} + \phi'(I_x) \right)dx \,\bigg|\, \mathcal{F}_a
\stackrel{d}{=} \mathcal{N}\left(-\frac{\ell_a \phi(I_x)}{4}, \frac{1}{4} \int_{I_x}^\infty \phi(y)^2dy \right).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:old of arXiv:2607.19844, 'Binomial probabilities at a fixed distance from the mode:\\ size-biasing and the complete '] Let $K\subset(0,1)$ and $H\subset\mathbb R$ be compact.  As $N\to\infty$, uniformly for admissible
	$p\in K$ and $t\in H$ with $Np+t\in\{0,1,\dots,N\}$,
	\begin{equation}
		\pi_N(t;p)\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi Npq}}\,
		\exp\Bigl(\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{A_k(t;p)}{N^{k}}\Bigr),
	\end{equation}
	with $A_k$ as in (equation eq:Ak of the paper).  For every $M$ the remainder after $M$ terms is
	$O(N^{-M-1})$ relative to the leading factor, with an implied constant depending only on
	$M$, $K$ and $H$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theo 7 of arXiv:2609.03188, 'Some generalizations of Oort's conjecture'] Let $w\in \tW$.
Assume that $\supp_\sigma(w)=\tS$ and there exists $v\in \LP(w)$ such that $v^{-1}p(w)v$ is a Coxeter element with $\supp(v^{-1}p(w)v)=\bS$.
Let $\tau\in\Omega$ be the unique element such that $w\in W_a\tau$.
Then $X_w(\tau)\neq \emptyset$.
Moreover, there exist elements $w=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_r\in \tW$ satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For each $0\leq k<r$, there exists $s\in \tS$ such that $w_{k+1}=sw_ks$ and $\ell(w_{k+1})\leq \ell(w_k)$.
Moreover, $\ell(w_r)<\ell(w_{r-1})$.
\item For each $0\leq k<r$ with $\ell(w_{k+1})=\ell(w_k)-2$, the element $s$ in (i) satisfies $X_{sw_k}(\tau)=\emptyset$ and $X_{sw_ks}(\tau)\neq \emptyset$. In particular, if $k=r-1$, then $s\notin\supp_\sigma(w_r)$.
\item The element $w_r$ is a $\sigma$-Coxeter element and $\J_\tau\cap P_{\supp_\sigma(w_r)}$ is a very special parahoric subgroup of $\J_\tau$.
In particular, $\supp_\sigma(w_r)\subsetneq\tS$ and $w_r$ is of minimal length in its conjugacy class.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, there are $\J_\tau$-equivariant morphisms
$$X_w(\tau)=X_{w_0}(\tau)\longrightarrow X_{w_1}(\tau)\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow X_{w_r}(\tau),$$
each of which is a universal homeomorphism or a Zariski-locally trivial $\A^1$-fibration up to a universal homeomorphism.

body: [campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Our result (id P0033, 2026-09-08): NO. Take Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 (mean 12/5) and an isomorphism-invariant colour in {0,1} defined by AND at two-child vertices and OR at three-child vertices; both preserve unanimity, so every vertex has at least one child of its own colour, and the flow chooses uniformly among those. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. The colour exists because F(p) = (3/5) p^2 + (2/5)[1 - (1-p)^3] fixes 1/2, and r_n = E[q_n^2] satisfies r_{n+1} = 3/10 + (3/5) r^2 + (2/5) r^3 whose increment factors as (r - 1/2)[(2/5) r^2 + (4/5) r - 3/5], driving r_n from r_0 = 1/4 up to 1/2 and giving E[q(1-q)] = 0. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. Prior art unchecked; the tree-automaton and factor-of-iid literature is where to look. Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 consistent equivariant flow rule choosing uniformly among same-coloured children

body:
[Corollary of arXiv:2412.08886, 'On domination for (non-symmetric) Dirichlet forms'] {Assume that both $({\mathscr E},{\mathscr F})$ and the active reflected Dirichlet form $({\mathscr E}^\mathrm{ref},{\mathscr F}^\mathrm{ref}_a)$ are quasi-regular on $L^2(E,m)$.}
The quasi-regular (not necessarily symmetric) Dirichlet form $({\mathscr A},\mathcal{D}({\mathscr A}))$ is sandwiched between $({\mathscr E},{\mathscr F})$ and $({\mathscr E}^\mathrm{ref},{\mathscr F}^\mathrm{ref}_a)$ if and only if there exists an ${\mathscr E}^\mathrm{ref}$-quasi-open set $G$ with $E_M\subset G$,  ${\mathscr E}^\mathrm{ref}$-q.e.,  and a smooth measure $\mu$ with respect to ${\mathscr E}^{\mathrm{ref},G}$ with $\mu(G\setminus E_M)=0$ such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
	&\mathcal{D}({\mathscr A})={\mathscr F}^{\mathrm{ref},G}_a\cap L^2(G,\mu),  \\
	&{\mathscr A}(f,g)={\mathscr E}^\mathrm{ref}(f,g)+\int_G \tilde{f}\tilde{g}d\mu,\quad f,g\in \mathcal{D}({\mathscr A}),
\end{aligned}\]
where $({\mathscr E}^{\mathrm{ref},G}, {\mathscr F}^{\mathrm{ref},G}_a)$ is the part Dirichlet form of $({\mathscr E}^\mathrm{ref},{\mathscr F}^\mathrm{ref}_a)$ on $G$.  Particularly,  $({\mathscr A},\mathcal{D}({\mathscr A}))$ is symmetric.

[Theorem permuton_convergence_thm of arXiv:2412.07258, 'Permuton limit of a generalization of the Mallows and $k$-card-minimum models'] Given $g$ and $\sigma_n \sim \mathrm{PERM}(g,n)$ as in Definition (def_gen_perm_model of the paper), let $F_{\sigma_n}$ denote the (random) c.d.f.\ of the (random) permuton corresponding to $\sigma_n$ (cf.\ Definition (def_permutation_permuton of the paper)).         F_{\sigma_n}(x,y) \stackrel{\mathbb{P}}{\longrightarrow} F_{g}(x,y), \quad n \to \infty, \quad x,y \in [0,1].
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma backward estimate of arXiv:2605.03151, 'Giants through Higher-Order paths in Random Simplicial Complexes'] Let $k \geq 0$ and $v$ be a vertex that can create a backward $d$-dimensional simplex a $(d-1)$-simplex $\sigma^k$ that is being explored at Step $k$. Then, the probability that $\sigma^k \cup \{v\}$ appears at Step $k$ is lower bounded by
\[  \tag{3.2.18}
p_k^B := \bigg( 1- \sum_{\ell = 1}^{d-1} \sum_{\substack{\rho \subseteq \sigma^k, \\ \dim(\rho) = \ell-1}} \deg_{\ell-1, d-1}^{\mathcal{X}_{k-1}}(\rho) p_{d, \ell} \bigg) \left( \frac{\lambda}{n} + o(1) \right).
\]
In particular, if the given MRSC model is the Linial-Meshulam model, the probability is exactly $\lambda/n + o(1)$.
title: Lemma backward estimate of arXiv:2605.03151

[Lemma lem:later-conflict of arXiv:2609.02845, 'Degeneracy bounds, stability, and a sharp gap for $B$-colorings'] Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, and let $G$ be a $d$-degenerate graph with degeneracy ordering $v_1,\ldots,v_n$.  Order $E(G)$ by increasing index of the earlier endpoint, breaking ties arbitrarily.  For an edge $e=v_i u_1$, where $u_1$ is later than $v_i$, let $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ be the later neighbors of $v_i$.  Then the number of edges following $e$ in this ordering that $B$-conflict with $e$ is at most
\[
  d_G(u_1)-1+
  \sum_{j=2}^{r}|N_G(u_1)\cap N_G(u_j)|.
\]
title: Lemma lem:later-conflict of arXiv:2609.02845

body:
[Definition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] We say $\mathfrak{F} = (W, \leq)$ is an \emph{intuitionistic frame (i-frame)} if $W$ is a non-empty set and $\leq$ is a preorder on $W$.
  We say $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ is an \emph{intuitionistic model (i-model)} if $\mathfrak{F}$ is an i-frame and $V: \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}} \to \mathcal{P}(W)$,
  where each $V(p)$ is upward closed with respect to $\leq$ (i.e. $\forall x, y\, (x \leq y \mathrel{\text{\&}} x \in V(p) \mathrel{\Rightarrow} y \in V(p))$).
  Such $\mathfrak{M}$ is said to be \emph{based on} $\mathfrak{F}$.
  For $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, V)$, we define a \emph{satisfaction relation} $\Vdash_\mathfrak{M}$ on $W \times \mathscr{L}_p$ by:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item $x \nVdash_\mathfrak{M} \bot$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} p \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} x \in V(p)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \land \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} (x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\text{\&}} x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \lor \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} (x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\text{or}} x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \to \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} \forall x' \geq x\, (x' \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\Rightarrow} x' \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
  \end{enumerate}
  We write $\mathfrak{M} \vDash \varphi$ (``$\varphi$ is \emph{valid in} $\mathfrak{M}$'') to mean $\forall x \in W\,(x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \varphi)$,
  and $\mathfrak{F} \vDash \varphi$ (``$\varphi$ is \emph{valid on} $\mathfrak{F}$'') to mean that $\mathfrak{M} \vDash \varphi$ for every $\mathfrak{M}$ based on $\mathfrak{F}$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical M'

For $k > 0$ the truncation at level $k$ is $T_k(s) = \max(-k, \min(k, s))$, $s \in \mathbb{R}$: it equals $s$ for $|s| \leq k$ and $\pm k$ outside. $T_k$ is Lipschitz with constant 1, odd, and $T_k(0) = 0$. Chain rule (Stampacchia): if $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ is open and $u \in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, then $T_k(u) \in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ with $
abla T_k(u) = 
abla u \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\{|u| < k\}}$ almost everywhere; if $u \in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ then $T_k(u) \in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, and $|T_k(u)| \leq \min(|u|, k)$. In particular $
abla u = 0$ a.e. on every level set $\{u = c\}$. Companion functions: the positive part $u^+ = \max(u,0)$ and $G_k(u) = u - T_k(u)$ (the part of $u$ beyond level $k$); all such compositions satisfy the same chain rule $
abla(\phi \circ u) = \phi'(u)
abla u$ a.e. for piecewise $C^1$ Lipschitz $\phi$ with finitely many corners (with $\phi(0) = 0$ to stay in $W_0^{1,p}$). The truncation method uses $T_k(u)$ (or $G_k(u)$) as a test function in a weak formulation; because it is bounded by $k$ it is admissible against $L^1$ right-hand sides, and $\int_\Omega |
abla T_k(u)|^p$ measures the energy of $u$ on the set where $|u| < k$. Sharp edges: the chain rule needs $\phi$ Lipschitz (a merely continuous or unbounded-derivative $\phi$ can leave $W^{1,p}$); for a function that is only in $L^1_{loc}$ with no Sobolev regularity, $T_k(u) \in W_0^{1,p}$ for all $k$ is a genuine extra hypothesis, and this is exactly the class in which entropy solutions of $L^1$-data problems live.

body:
[Lemma lem:plane-blind-ricci-packet of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a complete orthogonal-Weingarten atom $(p,q,r)$ before opening any
packet front.  Let $P$ be an external $q$-component assigned wholly to
one aggregate-Ricci root time, and suppose its $s$ coefficient
occurrences all carry
\[
 \mathsf C_i=|a_i\rangle\langle a_i|-N^{-1}I_W.
\]
The aggregate-Ricci passive boundary has no $q$-dart, so the coefficient
contraction of $P$ is a closed scalar, denoted $Z_{P,q}(i)$.  It satisfies
\[
 \boxed{Z_{P,q}(i)=z_{P,q}\quad\hbox{for every coordinate plane }i,
 \qquad |z_{P,q}|\le4^s.}
\tag{3.3.1w$_{6b}$}
\]
If $P$ has one occurrence, then $z_{P,q}=0$.  If it is nonzero and has
at least two occurrences, then $c=c^{\!*}(P)\ge2$, and replacing its bare
carrier $n^c$ by the closed scalar costs at most
\[
 A^s n^{-c}
\tag{3.3.1w$_{6c}$}
\]
relative to the bare Euler majorant.

[Lemma 14 (Normalized Gaussian scale mixture) of arXiv:2605.11451, '2605.11451'] Let $1\le p<2$, and let $Z$ have density $g_p(x)=e^{-|x|^p}/(2\Gamma(1+1/p))$. Then there is a positive non-degenerate random variable $V$ such that
\[
 Z\mid V\sim N(0,V).
\]
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 g_p(x)=\E\left[\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi V}}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2V}\right)\right].
\end{equation}

This classifies possible scalar curvature LIMITS. It does not assert that a

Let f(x)=lambda x^2/2, lambda,eta,epsilon>0, 0<b<1, 0<d<1. Use ordinary
uncorrected Adam or ordinary separate bias corrections, epsilon outside sqrt.
Let D_t=sqrt(v_(t+1))+epsilon (uncorrected) or sqrt(vhat_(t+1))+epsilon
(corrected), C_t=lambda/D_t. Suppose C_t->C_infinity exists and is positive.
Then one of the following holds:
 (i) C_infinity=lambda/epsilon and x_t,m_t,v_t ->0;
 (ii) eta*C_infinity=2(1+b)/(1-b), |x_t|->a>0, and signs eventually
      alternate. The state approaches the known two-cycle, with
      a=eta*(1-b)/(2(1+b))-epsilon/lambda.
For b=.9 the constant is 38. In case (ii), a>0 requires eta lambda/epsilon>38.

If equality holds, v_t->0, and v_(t+1)=d v_t+(1-d)lambda^2 x_t^2 forces
x_t^2->0. Then m_t->0 by a stable linear recursion.
Otherwise v_t tends to a strictly positive value lambda^2*a^2; subtracting
d v_t from v_(t+1) gives x_t^2->a^2, so x_t is nonzero eventually.

Write the actual x update as x_(t+1)=x_t-alpha_t*m_(t+1), where
alpha_t=eta/D_t (uncorrected) or eta/[(1-b^(t+1))*D_t] (corrected).
Then alpha_t->alpha=eta*C_infinity/lambda>0 and alpha_t/alpha_(t-1)->1.
Eliminating m_t using the preceding update gives exactly
 x_(t+1)=[1+b alpha_t/alpha_(t-1)-alpha_t(1-b)lambda]x_t
          -b alpha_t/alpha_(t-1)*x_(t-1).
Thus with s_t=sign(x_t), A=1+b-alpha(1-b)lambda<1+b,
 s_(t+1)=A s_t-b s_(t-1)+o(1).                                (1)
There are only finitely many sign quadruples (s0,s1,s2,s3) in {+1,-1}^4.
Any quadruple occurring arbitrarily late must satisfy BOTH limiting equations
 s2=A s1-b s0,  s3=A s2-b s1.
Eliminate A, using s_i^2=1:
 s1*s3=1-b+b*s0*s2.
If s0*s2=-1 the right side is 1-2b, strictly between -1 and 1, impossible.
So s0=s2 and s1=s3. The two remaining possibilities are constant signs, with A=1+b, and alternating signs, with A=-(1+b). The former contradicts
A<1+b. Since finitely many words can occur, every sufficiently late word
is alternating, and A=-(1+b). It follows that alpha(1-b)lambda=2(1+b),
so eta*C_infinity=2(1+b)/(1-b). The claimed a follows from D_limit=lambda*a+epsilon.

[Theorem thm:main1 of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $D$ be a simply-connected domain and $z_1 \neq z_2 \in D$. Let $E^{\rm nest}_\varepsilon(z_1,z_2)$ denote the event that there is a nested CLE$_4$ gasket that comes $\varepsilon_1$-close to both $z_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$-close to $z_2$. Then we have
$$\lim_{\max(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2) \to 0}\varepsilon_1^{-1/8}\varepsilon_2^{-1/8}\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm nest}_\varepsilon(z_1,z_2)) = C_0\CR(z_1,D)^{-1/8}\CR(z_2,D)^{-1/8}\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{2}G_D(z_1,z_2)\right),$$
where $C_0$ is an absolute constant \footnote{Both here and in the next statements these absolute constants are explicit up to a term depending on SLE$_4$ loop measure (that we think does not have an explicit expression). This term would disappeaer when using conformal radii instead of actual radii, or when normalising the two-point function by product of one-point functions. We prefer to keep this dependence and remark here that some duality arguments are nicer using the Euclidean normalisation, although the conformal radii one would also follow from the same techniques.}.
Further, this two-point function also equals,
up to an absolute constant,
$$\Big\langle:\exp\Big(i\sqrt\frac{\pi}{2}\Phi_D(z_1)\Big):~
:\exp\Big(-i\sqrt\frac{\pi}{2}\Phi_D(z_2)\Big):
\Big\rangle .$$
Here the GFF $\Phi_D$ in $D$ is normalized to have covariance $G_D$, and we consider the usual imaginary multiplicative chaos. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Two-point correlations of nested CLE$_4$

[Proposition prop: exact ruin brownian motion for collective model of arXiv:2606.28031, 'Insurance risk models in a heterogeneous time-dependent population: scaling limits and rui'] Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent arithmetic Brownian motions. We assume the existence of $\rho$ and $\eta$ defined in Assumptions~(A:hyp LLN for V of the paper) and (A:hyp CLT for V of the paper). Set $\alpha_*:=2\frac{\rho {\mathrm c}_X+(1-\rho){\mathrm c}_Y}{\sigma_X^2\eta^2+\sigma_Y^2\left(\eta^2+1-2\rho\right)}$. 

Under the net profit condition $\rho{\mathrm c}_X+(1-\rho){\mathrm c}_Y>0$, for any $\alpha>\alpha_*$,
\begin{equation}
p(u)=\frac{{\mathrm e}^{-\alpha u}}{\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathrm e}^{-k_{\alpha}(\tau(u))}\,\big|\,\tau(u)<\infty\right]}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, when $F$ is deterministic, the decay rate of $p(u)$ is $\alpha_*$:
\[
\lim_{u\to \infty}\frac{1}{u}\log p(u)= -\alpha_*.
\]

body:
[Lemma upper bound for s2 summand of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have
    \[\max_{1\leq j\leq\frac{n}{2}-m-1}\frac{\binom{2j-2}{n-j}}{2^{2j-2}}=\frac{\binom{n-2m-4}{\frac{n}{2}+m+1}}{2^{n-2m-4}}\]
    \begin{proof}
        Denote 
        \[a_j=\frac{\binom{2j-2}{n-j}}{2^{2j-2}}\]
        First notice that $a_j>0$ if and only if $j\geq\frac{n+2}{3}$. Fix $n\geq 5$. We will apply the ratioing method from the proof of Proposition $(middle terms strategy of the paper)$. We have
        \[\frac{a_{j+1}}{a_j}=\frac{(2j)(2j-1)(n-j)}{4(3j-n+1)(3j-n)(3j-n-1)}:=f_n(j)\]
        We sketch the rest of the proof. One can show by differentiation that when $n\geq 5$ is fixed, $f$ is decreasing on $j\geq\frac{n+2}{3}$, which is precisely in the nonzero terms of $S_2$. By direct computation, we have $f(\frac{n}{2})<1$ and $f(\frac{n}{2}-1)>1$. Since $f$ is decreasing, this implies 
        \begin{equation}
        
        f_n(j)>1\;\;\;\; \text{for all}\;\;\;\; \frac{n+2}{3}\leq j\leq\frac{n}{2}-1. 
        \end{equation}
        In particular, since $\frac{n}{2}-m-1<\frac{n}{2}-1$ when $n\geq 5$, equation $(s2 ratio equation of the paper)$ holds for all $\frac{n+2}{3}\leq j\leq\frac{n}{2}-m-1$. We deduce that $a_j$ is maximized at $j=\frac{n}{2}-m-1$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma upper bound for s2 summand of arXiv:2507.10294

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The lace expansion writes the two-point function of self-avoiding walk, Bernoulli percolation, oriented percolation or lattice trees as a renormalised random-walk Green function plus a correction series: for SAW, c_n(x) = sum_y D(y) c_{n-1}(x - y) + sum_{m=2}^{n} sum_y pi_m(y) c_{n-m}(x - y), with pi_m the alternating-sign lace coefficients obtained by inclusion-exclusion over self-intersections (for percolation the analogous expansion is in terms of pivotal bonds and sausages). The expansion is an exact identity; its use requires a bootstrap showing the coefficients are small in a norm controlled by a random-walk diagram: the bubble diagram for SAW (finite for d > 4), the triangle diagram for percolation (finite for d > 6) and the square diagram for lattice trees (d > 8). Proved regimes: nearest-neighbour SAW for d >= 5 (Hara-Slade), spread-out SAW for d > 4, nearest-neighbour percolation for d >= 11 (Fitzner-van der Hofstad) and spread-out percolation for d > 6 (Hara-Slade). Conclusions there: mean-field exponents (gamma = 1, eta = 0, beta = 1 and delta = 2 in bounded-ratio senses), Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limits, and asymptotic expansions of critical points. It gives nothing at or below the upper critical dimension, and for nearest-neighbour percolation in 7 <= d <= 10 there is no small parameter, so the expansion holds only as an identity, not as a bound. Typical failure: Applying the expansion's mean-field conclusions (eta=0, Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limit) to a model at or below its upper critical dimension without re-verifying the triangle or bubble condition; the coefficients pi_m are not shown small there, the bootstrap can fail to close, and the diagrammatic control silently assumed at the outset is exactly the open problem, which is why four-dimensional nearest-neighbor percolation mean-field behavior remains open despite the spread-out and high-dimension cases being resolved. Canonical reference: Hara and Slade, 1990, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Madras and Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk, 1993, Birkhauser.
A small parameter: bubble (SAW), triangle (percolation) or square (lattice trees) diagram small at criticality
Above the upper critical dimension: d > 4 (SAW), d > 6 (percolation), d > 8 (lattice trees)
Nearest-neighbour models need d >= 5 (SAW) or d >= 11 (percolation) with current methods
title: Technique: Lace Expansion

[Prop 26 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] Let \(N\geq1\) and \(S>0\), let
\(\left|c_0\right|,\left|c_1\right|\leq S\), and let
\(\mathbf{A}\) be a deterministic \(N\times N\) complex matrix.  For all
\(z,w\in\C\),
\begin{align}
 &\E\!\left[
 \left(
 \exp\!\left(-\frac{c_1-c_0}{2N}\partial_z^2\right)
 \det(z\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{Z}_N(S,c_0))
 \right)\right.\nonumber\\[-2mm]
 &\hspace{28mm}\left.
 \overline{
 \left(
 \exp\!\left(-\frac{c_1-c_0}{2N}\partial_w^2\right)
 \det(w\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{Z}_N(S,c_0))
 \right)}
 \right]\nonumber\\
 &\qquad=
 \E\!\left[
 \det(z\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{Z}_N(S,c_1))
 \overline{\det(w\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{Z}_N(S,c_1))}
 \right].
 
\end{align}
The same assertion holds conditionally when \(\mathbf{A}\) is random and
independent of the joint sigma-field generated by the two Gaussian
matrices, or by the two complete Gaussian sequences in a sequence-level

body: [Lemma 45 of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] Let $x\in C_0$ and $y\in C_\tau$.  Under the probability measure $\IG_\tau^*$, the conditional law of $\eta_y^\rmE$ given $\eta_x^\rmW$ and the conditional law of $\eta_x^\rmW$ given $\eta_y^\rmE$, agree with the description of the conditional laws of $\eta$ given $\wt\eta$ and $\wt\eta$ given $\eta$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:curve-resample}. Furthermore, let $\eta'$ be the counterclockwise space-filling $\SLE_{\kappa'}$ loop associated with $h^{\mathrm{A}}$ parameterized by Lebesgue area, and let $\tau_x$ be the time when $\eta'$ hits $x$. Then $((-i)x^{-1}\eta_x^\rmW,(-i)x^{-1}\eta'(\cdot+\tau_x))\overset{d}{=} (\eta_{-i}^\rmW,\eta')$ where we set $\eta'(t+\mathrm{area}(\cA_\tau)) = \eta'(t)$ for $t\in\bbR$.

Define F6(x) as the mean of ((q-p_x)/|q-p_x|)^6 over its Delaunay edge-neighbors. Put C6(x,y)=E[F6(x)conjugate(F6(y))]-E[F6(x)]E[conjugate(F6(y))], V(t)=P(Phi intersect B(0,t) is empty), and alpha(A,B)=sup |P(E intersect H)-P(E)P(H)| over events of the restrictions to A and B. Then for every r>0 and deterministic x,y, |C6(x,y)| <=16alpha(B(x,3r),B(y,3r))+28V(r/32). No independence of empty-disk events is needed.

[Lemma lem.aux2 of arXiv:2607.10105, 'The four-dimensional Anderson model: a case study for critical SPDEs'] For any $\theta>0$ and positive integers $m\leq n$, we have
\begin{equation} \sum_{1\leq z_1,\cdots,z_m\leq n}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}\min(1,2^{-\theta(z_j-z_{j+1})})\leq C^n,
\end{equation} where $C=C(\theta)>1$ is an absolute constant depending on $\theta$. Similarly, if $(P_1,\cdots,P_n)$ are distinct elements of $2^\mathbb N$, then
\begin{equation}\sum_{1\leq x(1),\cdots x(n)\leq n}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\min\bigg(1,\bigg(\frac{P_{x(j+1)}}{P_{x(j)}}\bigg)^{\theta}\bigg)\leq C^n.
\end{equation} 
The same result is true if the product in ((eq.aux6 of the paper)) is taken over $j\in\{1,\cdots,n-1\}\backslash E$ for any set $E$ with at most $100$ elements.
title: Lemma lem.aux2 of arXiv:2607.10105

[Theorem 20 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $\gamma\in(0,1]$, $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $h\in Z\hat C^{\gamma}(\Delta^3_T;B_\alpha)$.  Then, for every $\tau\in[0,T]$, if $\gamma\in(0,1)$, one has
\[
r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)\in C^{\gamma}(\Delta^2_\tau;B_\alpha), \quad \delta r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)=h^\tau
\]
and the uniform estimate $\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)\|_{\gamma,\alpha;\tau}\le C_\gamma M_{\alpha,T}\|h\|_{\gamma,\alpha}$; if $\gamma=1$, one has
\[
r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)\in C^{1}_{\mathrm{log}}(\Delta^2_\tau;B_\alpha), \quad \delta r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)=h^\tau
\]
and the uniform estimates $$\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)\|_{1,\log;\tau,\alpha}\le C_{1,T} M_{\alpha,T}\|h\|_{1,\alpha},$$ 
as well as, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $$\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha;\tau}\le C_{\varepsilon,T} M_{\alpha,T}\|h\|_{1,\alpha}.$$

[Definition def:bracketprod of arXiv:2411.06827, 'The Exponential Lie Series and a Chen--Strichartz Formula for L{\'e}vy Processes'] We define a commutative associative product $[\cdot , \cdot ]$  on the vector space over ${\mathbb R}$ generated by the alphabet ${\mathbb A}$ as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item if $i=0$ then $[i, j]:=\mathbf{0}$ for all $j\in {\mathbb A}$, 
\item 
$[i, i]:=i^{(2)}$ and $[i, i^{(2)}]:=\mathbf{0}$ for all $i=1, \ldots , d$, 
\item $[i^{(l)}, i^{(k)} ]:=i^{(l+k)}$ for all $l, k\ge 1$ and for all  $i=d+1, \ldots ,\ell$, and
\item $[i^{(l)}, j^{(k)} ]:=\mathbf{0}$ for $i\not=j$ and all $l, k\ge 1$.
\end{enumerate}
We extend this definition to the vector space generated by
 ${\mathbb A}$ linearily. Here $\mathbf{0}$ denotes
the zero in $\mathbb R$ to distinguish it from the letter $0$ in ${\mathbb A}$.
For  letters $a_i$ in ${\mathbb A}$, iterated products are denoted by 
$$
	[a_1,\dots,a_n]:=[a_1,[a_2,\dots,a_n]].
$$
title: Bracket product on $\Ab$

(Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:subcritical_one_arm_exponent of arXiv:2509.23496, 'Crossing probabilities in geometric inhomogeneous random graphs'] For $0\leq\gamma<\frac12$ and 
    $0< \lambda < \widehat{\lambda}_c,$ as $R\nearrow\infty$,
    $$\frac1{d\log R} \log \mathbb P^*((0, U) \longleftrightarrow B(0,R)^{\sf c})
\longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
{1-\delta} & \text{if $2 < \delta < 1/\gamma -1$,}\\
(1-\frac1\gamma)(1-\frac1\delta)
            & \text{if $1/\gamma - 1\leq \delta < 1/ \gamma$,}\\
(1-\frac1\gamma)(1-\gamma)
& \text{if $\delta \ge 1/ \gamma$ or $\delta = \infty$,}
\end{cases}
$$
where $\mathbb P^*$ is the Palm measure at the origin associated with the marked Poisson point process on which our graph is defined, and $(0,U)$ is the vertex located at the origin under $\mathbb P^*$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Subcritical one-arm exponents

body:
[Definition def:c4-witness-block of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] In this section a root, or candidate root, is a right vertex $j_\star\in J$.
Its first left layer is
\[
I_\star:=N_G(j_\star).
\]
For $i\in I_\star$, an $L$-\hyperref[def:c4-witness-block]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{reservoir}}}{} at $i$ is a set
\[
\mathcal R_i\subseteq N_G(i)\setminus\{j_\star\}
\]
of auxiliary right vertices with $|\mathcal R_i|\ge L$. 
After choosing, for each $i\in I_\star$, an $L$-\hyperref[def:c4-witness-block]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{reservoir}}}{} $\mathcal R_i$,
the associated $L$-\hyperref[def:c4-witness-block]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{witness block}}}{} at $j_\star$ is the subset of right vertices
\[
{\mathcal W}(j_\star):=\{j_\star\}\cup\bigcup_{i\in I_\star}\mathcal R_i.
\]
The \hyperref[def:c4-witness-block]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{reservoir}}}{}s $\mathcal R_i$, $i\in I_\star$, witness this block.
title: Roots, reservoirs, and witness blocks

[Theorem thm.Ber_Harris of arXiv:2605.17725, 'Limit theorems for random walks with spatio-temporal drift'] Assume that the SDE (equation eq:sde_appendix of the paper) has the strong Feller property and
is irreducible, that is, $P_t(x,U)>0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^d$, all nonempty
open sets $U\subset\mathbb R^d$, and all $t>0$. Assume moreover that there
exist a norm-like function $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R_+$, constants
$c_0,d_0>0$, a function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[1,\infty)$, and a compact set
$C\subset\mathbb R^d$ such that
\begin{equation}
(\mathcal L V)(x)
\le
-c_0 f(x)+d_0\mathbf 1_C(x),
\quad x\in\mathbb R^d.
\end{equation}
Then $(P_t)_{t\ge0}$ admits a unique invariant probability measure. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2609.02193, 'State-law dynamics of McKean-Vlasov stochastic reaction-diffusion equations on $\mathbb R^'] Assume \textnormal{(A1)-(A4)}. For every $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $t\geq0$ and $\mu,\nu\in P$,
	\begin{align}
		\mathcal W_2^2\big(
		\varphi_P^\epsilon(t)\mu,
		\varphi_P^0(t)\nu
		\big)
		\leq
		e^{(L_G-\bar\gamma)t}\mathcal W_2^2(\mu,\nu)
		+\epsilon^2\mathfrak J_{\bar\gamma-L_G}(t)
		\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|h_j\|^2.
	\end{align}
	Consequently, for every $T>0$,
	\begin{align}

		\mathcal W_2\big(
		\varphi_P^\epsilon(t)\mu,
		\varphi_P^0(t)\mu
		\big)

		\Big(

		\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|h_j\|^2
		\Big)^{1/2}.
	\end{align}
	If \textnormal{(A5)} also holds, then

		\big)

		\epsilon
		\Big(
		\frac1{\kappa_0}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|h_j\|^2
		\Big)^{1/2}.
	\end{align}

body:
[Lemma lemsimpole of arXiv:2605.01878, '\Large Random trade timing and power-law tails in realized prices'] Let $\mathbb{A}(z)$ be an $N\times N$ complex matrix-valued holomorphic function on an open connected set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C$. Suppose that $\mathbb{A}(z)$ is invertible for some $z \in \Omega$, and that $\mathbb{A}(z_0)$ has rank $r<N$ for some $z_0 \in \Omega$. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item  $\mathbb{A}(z)^{-1}$ has a simple pole at $z=z_0$.
    \item  There exist $N \times (N-r)$ matrices $x$ and $y$ of full column rank such that $\mathbb{A}(z_0)x = 0$, $y^\top \mathbb{A}(z_0) = 0$, and $y^\top \mathbb{A}^{(1)}(z_0)x$ is invertible.
\end{enumerate}
Under either condition, the residue of $\mathbb{A}(z)^{-1}$ at $z=z_0$ is
\[
x \left(y^\top \mathbb{A}^{(1)}(z_0) x\right)^{-1} y^\top.
\]
title: Simple-pole criterion

$B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and that $\mathbb P(X_i>0)=1$ for all $i$.

\right\},
\]

title: Marshall--Olkin characterization

Let (X, mu) and (Y, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces and K: X x Y -> C measurable for the product sigma-algebra. (a) Unweighted form: suppose A = sup_{x in X} int_Y |K(x,y)| dnu(y) < infinity and B = sup_{y in Y} int_X |K(x,y)| dmu(x) < infinity (suprema may be essential suprema). Then for every 1 <= p <= infinity and f in L^p(nu), (Tf)(x) = int_Y K(x,y) f(y) dnu(y) converges absolutely for mu-a.e. x and ||Tf||_{L^p(mu)} <= A^{1 - 1/p} B^{1/p} ||f||_{L^p(nu)}. In particular ||T|| <= sqrt(A B) on L^2. (b) Weighted form: let 1 < p < infinity, p' = p/(p-1), and suppose there exist measurable h_1 > 0 on X and h_2 > 0 on Y and constants C_1, C_2 with int_Y |K(x,y)| h_2(y)^{p'} dnu(y) <= C_1 h_1(x)^{p'} for a.e. x, and int_X |K(x,y)| h_1(x)^p dmu(x) <= C_2 h_2(y)^p for a.e. y. Then ||T||_{L^p(nu) -> L^p(mu)} <= C_1^{1/p'} C_2^{1/p}.
(X, mu), (Y, nu) sigma-finite (needed for Tonelli)
K measurable for the product sigma-algebra
both kernel bounds hold (one alone is not enough except at the endpoints p = 1, infinity)

[Theorem thm:CGLT of arXiv:2608.30166, 'Square Functions and Rectifiability\\ under Monotone Transformations of the Density'] {CGLT}}]
Let $\mu$ be an $n$-AD-regular measure in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Then $\mu$ is uniformly
$n$-rectifiable if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that, for any ball
$B(x_0,R)$ centered at $\operatorname{supp}(\mu)$,
\begin{equation}
\int_0^R\!\!\int_{x\in B(x_0,R)} |\Delta_\mu(x,r)|^2\, d\mu(x)\,\frac{dr}{r}
\;\le\; c\,R^n.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, a Dedekind domain or Dedekind ring, named after Richard Dedekind, is an integral domain in which every nonzero proper ideal factors into a product of prime ideals. It can be shown that such a factorization is then necessarily unique up to the order of the factors. There are at least three other characterizations of Dedekind domains that are sometimes taken as the definition: see below.

Let F:R^d->R be locally Lipschitz and admit the chain rule: for every locally absolutely continuous arc z, (F composed with z)'(t)=<h,z'(t)> for every h in partial^C F(z(t)), for almost every t. Suppose F(a x)=a^k F(x) for every x and every a>0, with fixed degree k. Then partial^C F(a x)=a^(k-1) partial^C F(x) for every a>0, and <x,h>=k F(x) for every x and every h in partial^C F(x). Here partial^C is the Clarke subdifferential, and multiplying a set means multiplying each element. This is a nonsmooth chain-rule result; no differentiability of F at x is assumed.
F locally Lipschitz on R^d
F admits the stated chain rule for all locally absolutely continuous arcs
Homogeneity F(a x)=a^k F(x) for all x and a>0

[Lemm l:abs12 of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] Fix $k\in\mathbb{N}$.
    Let $\{X_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\{Y_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be sequences of $k$-dimensional random vectors on the same probability space, such that the pair $(X_n,Y_n)$ jointly converges weakly to some $(X,Y)$ as $n\to\infty$.
    Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exist sequences of random vectors $\{W_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\{Z_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that $Z_n$ and $W_n$ are independent for every $n$, and such that
    \begin{align*}
        \limsup_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\left[
            \left\lVertX_n - Z_n\right\rVert_2^2
        \right] 
        \leqslant \varepsilon,
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        \left\lVertY_n - W_n\right\rVert_2
        \xrightarrow{\,p\,} 0
        \text{ as $n\to\infty$.}
    \end{align*}
    Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

[Ppn 22 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $F^{\rii}$ from \eqref{e:F.rii}
    and $F^{\riii}$ from \eqref{e:F.iii}. 
    For sufficiently large $N$, for all $t\in \R$,
    \[
        \P(F^{\rii}(k) \ge t)
        \le \P
        \bigg(
        F^{\riii}(k,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
         + \frac{\epsilon'}{5} \ge t
        \bigg) + e^{-cN} \,.
    \]
That is, $F^{\riii}(k)$ approximately stochastically dominates
$F^{\rii}(k)$.

\begin{proof} Condition on any realization of $\bG$. Recall that
$F^\rii(k)$ is defined by \eqref{e:F.rii}
as the average of $F^\ri$ over $k$ orthogonal replicas, maximized over $S_\perp(k)$. Recall moreover that $F^\ri$ is defined by summing \eqref{e:F.B}--\eqref{e:F.w}, where we rewrote \eqref{e:F.B} and \eqref{e:F.U} in \eqref{e:F.B.rewrite} and \eqref{e:F.U.rewrite} above.
\begin{itemize}
\item Considering \eqref{e:F.U.rewrite}, 
note that $\bXi^\ell \hat{\bx} / \sqrt{N}$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^M$, independent of the gaussian process $\{\bXi^\ell \by^\ell : (\hat{\bx}, \by^\ell) = 0\}$.
Thus, the quantity inside
the maximum defining $F^\rii(k)$
(see \eqref{e:F.rii}),
as a process indexed by $\by^{1:k}$, remains distributionally unchanged if we replace each $\bXi^\ell \hat{\bx} / \sqrt{N}$ with $\bz^\ell$, which corresponds to replacing $F_U$ with $\bar{F}_U$. 
\item Considering \eqref{e:F.B.rewrite}, we can set
     \[
        \tbmeta^j
        = \frac{1}{|B_j|^{1/2}}
        \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \bmeta^{\ell,a}\,,
    \]
and note that the $\tbmeta^j$ are i.i.d.\ standard gaussian vectors in $\R^N$.
\end{itemize}
This shows that
    \begin{align*}
    F^{\rii}(k)&
       \stackrel{d}{=}
       \sup\bigg\{
       \frac{1}{k} \sum_{\ell=1}^k
     \bigg[
       \bar{F}_B(\tbmeta^\ell,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
       +F_v(\bG,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)) \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad 
       +\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N}
       \bar{F}_U(\bG,\bz^\ell,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
       +F_w(\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)) \bigg]
        : \by^{1:k}
    \in S_\perp(k)
       \bigg\} \,.
    \end{align*}
Enlarging the domain from $S_\perp(k)$ to $S_+(k)$ can only decrease the above supremum. Finally, the difference between the quantity inside the above supremum, versus the quantity inside the supremum \eqref{e:F.iii} (with $\cB = \hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)$),
is upper bounded by
    \baln
        &\lt|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \rt|
        \frac{1}{k}
        \sum_{\ell=1}^k
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hU_j}{MN|B_j|}
        \bigg(
            \sum_{a\in B_j}
            (\bz^\ell)_a \barbg^a,
            \by^\ell
        \bigg)^2 \\
        &\le \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \bigg|
        \frac{1}{k}
        \sum_{\ell=1}^k
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hU_j}{MN|B_j|}
        \|\bz^\ell(B_j)\|^2
        \|\bG^{B_j}\|_{\op}^2
        \|\by^\ell\|^2\,.
    \ealn
    By standard estimates, we have $\|{\bz^\ell(B_j)}\|^2 \le 2|B_j|$ with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$.
    Combined with the estimate $\|\bG^{B_j}\|_{\op} \le C\sqrt{N}$ from \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, and $\|\by^\ell\| = \sqrt{N}$, we find that the last display is
        \[
    \le O(1)
    \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \bigg|
    \le \frac{\epsilon'}{5}\,,
    \]
where the last inequality holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ by
 Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem disintegrated deviation bds of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] Let $(Y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a random walk started at $o$ with step distribution $\mu$. For any $D\geq 0$ and $n\geq 0$ sufficiently large, there exists $C_D>1$ such that for all $\xi\in \partial G$
\[ C_D^{-1} {\rm e} ^{-D} \leq \mathbb{P}_{o}\big[d_{{\mathcal G}}\big(Y_n, [o,\xi)\big)\geq D\big \vert \xi \big]\leq C_D {\rm e} ^{-D}.\]
The constants $C_D$ are bounded in $D$ and do not depend on $\xi$.

[Lemma lem.peakednessl2 of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let $\epsilon \in (0, \frac 1 2)$ and define $V_0 = V_0(\epsilon) := \frac{320 \cdot 2^{\frac{1}{3}}}{\epsilon^{2}}$. 
    Let $X \sim \mu_X$, $Y \sim \mu_Y$ be indepedent random variables on integers.
    Let $X' \sim \mu_X'$ and $Y' \sim \mu_Y'$ be independent symmetric log-concave integer random variables. 
    
    If
    \[
        \mu_X \preccurlyeq_\epsilon \mu_X', \quad \mu_Y \preccurlyeq_\epsilon \mu_Y', \quad {\mathrm{Var}}\, X' \ge V_0 \quad\mbox{and}\quad {\mathrm{Var}}\, Y' \ge V_0
    \]
    then
    \[
        \mathcal{Q}(X+Y) \le (1+20\epsilon)\mathcal{Q}(X'+Y').
    \]

Own-work draft: proof (unaudited); no independent C009 PASS. Instance and hypotheses: n>=2; K>=1; T=nK; 0<mu<=L; f_i(x,y)=mu*x^2/2+L*y^2/2+b_i*x+c_i*y; sum b_i=sum c_i=0; s_mu=mean b_i^2, s_L=mean c_i^2; deterministic x0!=0,y0; s_mu+s_L>0; fresh independent uniform permutations each epoch; shared permutation across coordinates allowed; all parameters fixed as K tends to infinity; global step minimization over eta>=0 or a fixed positive capped interval. Natural logarithms; all global minimizers intended.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:da704187e683c75687c34cba5425d7b2187b3aa1316235bc6bfddc8a4981bc63","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/da/da704187e683c75687c34cba5425d7b2187b3aa1316235bc6bfddc8a4981bc63.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9afa88a3c3a646433088a5648a4f7494552195796931a76422c1e2673e285e46","bundle_entry_key":"second-order-optimal-step-common-hessian","bundle_id":"population.t362-second-order-optimal-step-008","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"optimization; random reshuffling; optimal constant step; second-order asymptotic","draft":"w732/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.randomreshuffling:common-hessian-random-reshuffling-second-order-optimal-constant-step","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C009 v2: second-order optimal step, fixed instance

Kind: special. Target: 1, reviewer-requested refinement of C001.
Status: proof (unaudited). This does not alter the approved C001/C002 proof files.
Prior campaign work is credited in PRIOR_WORK_ATTRIBUTION.md. No novelty is asserted.

Use exactly the instance and fixed-parameter asymptotic hypotheses of C001:
n>=2, 0<mu<=L, x0!=0, s_mu+s_L>0, fresh independent uniform
epoch permutations, deterministic initialization, and T=nK tending to infinity.
Let eta_T be ANY global minimizing constant step, either unrestricted over
eta>=0 or subject to a fixed cap H>0. Put

    t_T = mu*T*eta_T,
    D = n*(n+1)*(mu^2*s_mu+L^2*s_L)/(48*mu^3),
    A0 = mu*x0^2/2                       if L>mu,
    A0 = mu*(x0^2+y0^2)/2               if L=mu.

Then D>0 and A0>0. All logarithms below are natural. The refinement is

    t_T = (3/2)*log(T) - log(log(T))
          + (1/2)*log(8*A0/(27*D)) + o(1).                 (R)

Constants and convergence rates may depend on the fixed instance, including
the positive gap L/mu-1 when L>mu. There is no uniform-in-kappa claim.

## 1. A common window for all minimizers

The approved C001 v1 proves t_T/log(T)->3/2 for every minimizing sequence,
and eventually every minimizer is interior and eta_T<1/L. Therefore eventually
ALL minimizers belong to

    I_T = [(7/5)*log(T), (8/5)*log(T)]

in the t coordinate. Otherwise selecting one outside this interval on an
infinite subsequence would contradict C001. This uses its all-minimizer
statement, not uniqueness. For a fixed capped interval, eta_T->0 makes the
upper cap inactive eventually.

## 2. Exact differentiated decomposition

Index the two coordinates separately even when their curvatures agree.
For a coordinate h in {mu,L}, define k_h=h/mu, a_h=1-k_h*t/T,
r_h=a_h^(2T), A_h=h*u_h^2/2. On I_T, eventually 0<a_h<1. Set

    B_h(eta)=(h/2)*eta^2*V_h(eta)/(1-(1-h*eta)^(2n)).

The denominator has a simple zero at eta=0, while V_h is a polynomial
with a double zero there. Its canceled expression extends analytically
through eta=0. By the finite polynomial expansion already used in C001,

    B_h(eta)=C_h*eta^3+O(eta^4),
    B_h'(eta)=3*C_h*eta^2+O(eta^3),
    C_h=s_h*h^2*n*(n+1)/48.

Differentiation is valid because of this analytic extension. It does not
differentiate an unspecified asymptotic remainder. If s_h=0, B_h and both
displayed terms are identically zero. Also sum_h C_h=mu^3*D.

With a dot denoting differentiation in t at fixed T, the exact objective is

    Q_T(t)=sum_h [A_h*r_h+B_h(t/(mu*T))*(1-r_h)],
    dot r_h=-2*k_h*a_h^(2T-1),
    Q_T'(t)=sum_h [A_h*dot r_h+dot B_h*(1-r_h)-B_h*dot r_h].  (1)

No division by r_h or zero variance is needed.

## 3. Uniform variance-derivative estimate

All estimates in this section hold uniformly for t in I_T. Since t=O(log T),
eta=t/(mu*T)->0 uniformly. The analytic expansions give

    sum_h dot B_h = 3*D*t^2/T^3 + O(t^3/T^4),
    sum_h |dot B_h| = O(t^2/T^3),
    sum_h |B_h| = O(t^3/T^3).

Indeed dot B_h=B_h'(eta)/(mu*T), including the chain-rule factor.
For large T, a_h>=1/2, and log(1-z)<=-z gives

    0<r_h<=exp(-2*k_h*t)<=exp(-2*t),
    |dot r_h|=2*k_h*r_h/a_h<=4*k_h*exp(-2*t).

The two corrective sums in the variance derivative from (1) therefore have
absolute magnitude at most

    C*(t^2+t^3)*exp(-2*t)/T^3.

Since D>0, division by 3*D*t^2/T^3 is legitimate on I_T. Thus

    sum_h [dot B_h*(1-r_h)-B_h*dot r_h]
      = 3*D*t^2/T^3 * (1+epsilon_2(T,t)),
    sup_{t in I_T}|epsilon_2(T,t)|
      <= C*[log(T)/T+(1+log(T))*T^(-14/5)] -> 0.          (2)

The exponent 14/5 is twice the lower window endpoint 7/5. Zero noise
in either coordinate is permitted: only the sum D must be positive.

## 4. Uniform deterministic-derivative estimate

For fixed k_h>=1, the Taylor estimate of log(1-k_h*t/T) yields

    (2T-1)*log(a_h)=-2*k_h*t+O((t+t^2)/T).

The remainder tends to zero uniformly on I_T. Hence

    A_h*dot r_h=-2*k_h*A_h*exp(-2*k_h*t)
                *[1+O((t+t^2)/T)].

When L=mu, both terms have k_h=1 and combine into amplitude A0.
When L>mu, the flat term has A_mu=A0>0 and the stiff term divided
by 2*A0*exp(-2*t) is bounded in magnitude by

    C*exp(-2*(L/mu-1)*t)
      <= C*T^(-(14/5)*(L/mu-1)) -> 0.

If y0=0 this term vanishes identically. Consequently in both cases

    sum_h A_h*dot r_h=-2*A0*exp(-2*t)*(1+epsilon_1(T,t)),
    sup_{t in I_T}|epsilon_1(T,t)| -> 0.                  (3)

The equal-curvature case cannot be handled by discarding the stiff
initial displacement; that is why A0 is defined piecewise.

## 5. Stationarity and the constant

Every minimizer is eventually interior. Equations (1)-(3), evaluated there,
give

    2*A0*exp(-2*t_T)*(1+epsilon_1)
       = 3*D*t_T^2/T^3*(1+epsilon_2).

Both error factors are positive for large T. Taking logarithms is valid,
and uniform smallness makes log(1+epsilon_j)=o(1). Therefore

    2*t_T=3*log(T)-2*log(t_T)+log(2*A0/(3*D))+o(1).

C001 gives log(t_T)=log(log(T))+log(3/2)+o(1). Substitution yields (R),
because

    (1/2)*log(2*A0/(3*D))-log(3/2)
      = (1/2)*log(8*A0/(27*D)).

All log arguments are positive. The constant combines a derivative factor
3 with the squared leading step factor (3/2)^2; balancing function values
instead of derivatives would give a different, unjustified log-log term.

## Checks and limits

The 48 Decimal cases in logs/second_order_numerics.json test stationary
derivatives and slow convergence, not global minimality or asymptotic proof.
The finite exact derivative-identity checks are recorded separately.
Formal arithmetic checking, if available, concerns only the displayed
rational factor identity; it does not certify this analytic proof.
The least-trusted step for independent review is the uniform differentiation
and relative scaling in (2)-(3). [Lemma lem:parity of the hitting time of arXiv:2607.19658, 'Hitting time mixing for random $k$-cycles'] Suppose that \(k\) is even and \(2\leq k=o(n/(\log n)^4)\). Then 
$$ 
\mathbf P(\tau \text{ is even})=\frac12+O\left(\epsilon_n\right),
\qquad
\mathbf P(\tau \text{ is odd})=\frac12+O\left(\epsilon_n\right),
$$
where $\epsilon_n = \exp\left(-(\log \log n)^{1/2+o(1)}\right).$
In particular,
$$
d_{\mathrm{TV}}\left(
\mathbf P(\tau \text{ is even})U_{\mathfrak A_n}+\mathbf P(\tau \text{ is odd})U_{\mathfrak A_n^c},
U_{\mathfrak S_n}\right)=\exp\left(-(\log \log n)^{1/2+o(1)}\right).
$$

body:
[Lemma Euclidean spherical condenser of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] Let
\(0 < \varepsilon < R\), and let \(u\) be the capacitary
potential of the spherical condenser
\(\left( \overline{B(0,\varepsilon)},\,\mathbb{R}^{d}\backslash B(0,R) \right)\),
that is, the harmonic function on
\(B(0,R)\backslash\overline{B(0,\varepsilon)}\) with \(u = 1\)
on \(\partial B(0,\varepsilon)\) and \(u = 0\) on
\(\partial B(0,R)\). Then

\[\int_{B(0,R)\backslash B(0,\varepsilon)}^{}|\nabla u|^{2}\, dx = \left\{ \begin{matrix}
\frac{2\pi}{\log(R/\varepsilon)}, & d = 2, \\
\frac{(d - 2)\,\omega_{d - 1}}{\varepsilon^{2 - d} - R^{2 - d}}, & d \geq 3.
\end{matrix} \right.\ \]

In particular, for \(d \geq 3\) the Newtonian capacity of a
ball is
\(cap\left( B(0,\varepsilon) \right) = (d - 2)\,\omega_{d - 1}\,\varepsilon^{d - 2}\),
and for every fixed \(R > 0\) one has, as
\(\varepsilon \rightarrow 0\),
\(\int|\nabla u|^{2}\, dx = (d - 2)\,\omega_{d - 1}\,\varepsilon^{d - 2}\left( 1 + O\left( (\varepsilon/R)^{d - 2} \right) \right)\)
for \(d \geq 3\) and
\(2\pi/\log(1/\varepsilon)\,\left( 1 + O\left( 1/\log(1/\varepsilon) \right) \right)\)
for \(d = 2\).

[Proposition prop:diffusion_mixed_tail of arXiv:2609.01576, '\normalfont Pointwise Majorization for sub-Weibull and Mixed Tail Processes with Applicati'] Under Assumptions (ass:diffusion_coefficients of the paper) and
(ass:diffusion_index_class of the paper), $d_1$ and $d_2$ are finite-valued
pseudo-metrics and $(\cF,d_1+d_2)$ is separable. The map
$(\omega,f)\mapsto Z_\tau(f)(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, its sample
paths are almost surely $(d_1+d_2)$-continuous, and $Z_\tau(0)=0$ almost
surely. Moreover, for every $f,h\in\cF$ and $u\ge0$,
\begin{align}
\PP_\pi\cbr{
|Z_\tau(f)-Z_\tau(h)|
>
u\,d_1(f,h)+\sqrt u\,d_2(f,h)
}
\le2e^{-u}.

\end{align}
Consequently, $\cbr{Z_\tau(f)}_{f\in\cF}$ is an anchored two-metric
mixed-tail process of orders $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(1,2)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Mixed-tail property of the occupation process

Join (k,f(k)) to (k+1,f(k)) horizontally and then move vertically at column k+1 to f(k+1). Its two end directions are +e1 and -e1 because f(k)/abs(k) tends to zero, but neither tail lies eventually in any finite horizontal strip because f is unbounded at both ends. [Thm 5 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] Fix $0< \delta< \frac{1}{2}$. Let $\{X_n, n\ge 1\}$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with a common nonuniform distribution $\{p_i, i\ge 1\}$ satisfying $\ee|\ln p(X_1)|^{2+\delta} < \infty$. Assume that there exists an integer valued function $K(n)$ such that,
\beq
K(n)\le n^{\frac{1}{2}-\delta},\ \ n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\ln n\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i \leq C
\ \ \text{and}\ \ -n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i\ln p_i\leq C,
\deq
then we have
\beq
\sup\limits_x\left|\pp\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}(\hat H_n-H)}{\sigma}<x\right)-\Phi(x)\right|
 \leq Cn^{-\frac{\delta}{2}},
\deq
where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function and $\sigma^2=\Var(\ln p(X_1))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Cor cornegbin of arXiv:2605.01878, '\Large Random trade timing and power-law tails in realized prices'] Maintain the assumptions on $X$ and the type distribution, and Assumption (asshol of the paper), in Proposition (propmain of the paper), but replace the conditional geometric law of $T$ by the negative-binomial law (equation eqnbinom of the paper). Suppose that there exists $\alpha>0$ such that $r_D(A(-\alpha))=-\log(1-p_1)$. Then $\alpha$ is unique, and there exist constants $0<C_1\le C_2<\infty$ such that, for all sufficiently large $y$,
\[
\widetilde M_n C_1 \le (\log y)^{-(n-1)}y^\alpha \mathbb{P}(P_T>y) \le \widetilde M_n C_2,
\]
where $\widetilde M_n>0$ is given by
\[
\widetilde M_n = q_1\left(\frac{p_1}{1-p_1}\right)^{n}\bigl(-\,y_{p}' B^{(1)}(-\alpha)x_{p}\bigr)^{-n}(y_p'x_p)^{n-1}(w_0'x_p)(y_p'1_N),
\]
with $B(s) = e^{\log(1-p_{1})I+A(s)}$, $B^{(1)}(s) = \frac{d}{ds}B(s)$, and $x_p$, $y_p$ right and left eigenvectors of $B(-\alpha)$ associated with the unit eigenvalue. In particular, the negative-binomial IIM has the same Pareto exponent as the geometric IIM, but for $n\ge 2$ the tail carries a logarithmic correction of order $n-1$.

body: The heat (diffusion) equation is the parabolic PDE u_t = k Laplacian(u) with diffusivity k > 0, modelling the diffusion of heat or concentration. On all of R^n, initial data f evolves by convolution with the heat kernel (4 pi k t)^(-n/2) exp(-|x|^2 / (4kt)), the Gaussian fundamental solution; the equation smooths arbitrary initial data at once (infinite propagation speed) and satisfies the maximum principle: on a space-time cylinder a solution attains its maximum and minimum on the parabolic boundary (the initial time or the lateral boundary).

[Lemma lem:itoformula of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] If $\mathrm{d} X=b\,\mathrm{d} t+U\#\mathrm{d} S$ with $X$ self-adjoint and $b,U$ adapted, then for

\[
  \mathrm{d}(X^{n})=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}X^{k}(\mathrm{d} X)X^{n-1-k}
  +\sum_{0\le k<l\le n-1}X^{k}(\mathrm{d} X)X^{\,l-k-1}(\mathrm{d} X)X^{\,n-l-1},
\]
where the second sum is evaluated using Lemma~(lem:itorules of the paper).

[Thm algebraic_local_sewing of arXiv:2606.21049, '\textsc{Locality of rough path lifts}'] \begin{enumerate*}[label=(\roman*)]
\item  There exists a linear map \(\Lambda \colon E[0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^{\triangle}\)
such that $\delta_2\Lambda=\mathbbm 1$ and $\Lambda$ is strongly local (cf.\ (rem:timeloc of the paper)) in the sense that, for all \(\tau\geq 0\) and $(s,t) \in \triangle$ such that \(t+\tau\leq 1\) and \(\Xi,\Xi'\in E [0,1] \) such that $\Xi_{a,b,c} = \Xi'_{a+\tau,b+\tau,c+\tau}$ for all $(a,b,c)\in\triangle^3[s,t]$,
one has
\(
(\Lambda\Xi)_{s,t}=(\Lambda\Xi')_{s+\tau,t+\tau}
\).
\medskip
\\

\item  There exists a linear map \(\Lambda \colon F[0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^{\triangle}
\)
such that $\delta_2\Lambda =\mathbbm 1$ 
and which is local in the sense that, for all $(s,t) \in \triangle$ and \(\Xi,\Xi'\in F [0,1] \) such that $\Xi|_{\triangle^3[s,t]}= \Xi'|_{\triangle^3[s,t]}$,
one has
\(
(\Lambda\Xi)_{s,t}=(\Lambda\Xi')_{s,t}
\).
\medskip
\\

\item  There does not exist a map
\(
\Lambda \colon F[0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^{\triangle}
\)
such that 
\(
\delta_2\Lambda=\mathbbm 1
\)
and which is time translation--invariant in the sense of (def:weak_sewing of the paper)(pt:time_translation_def of the paper).

In fact, there exists \(\Xi\in F[0,1]\) which is translation-invariant in the sense that $\Xi_{s,u,t} = \Xi_{s+\tau,u+\tau,t+\tau}$ for all $(s,u,t),(s+\tau,u+\tau,t+\tau)\in\triangle^3$
and for which there exists no \(A\in \mathbb{R}^{\triangle}\) with $\delta_2A=\Xi$ and which is translation-invariant in the sense that \(A_{s,t} = A_{s+\tau,t+\tau}\) for all $(s,t),(s+\tau,t+\tau)\in\triangle$.
\end{enumerate*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm algebraic_local_sewing of arXiv:2606.21049
