Let C and D be projective plane curves over an algebraically closed field k, defined by homogeneous polynomials F, G in k[X, Y, Z] of degrees m and n with no common factor (the curves share no component). Then C and D meet in exactly mn points of the projective plane P^2(k) when each intersection point P is counted with its intersection multiplicity I_P(C, D) = dim_k O_P / (F, G) (the local ring at P modulo the ideal of the two curves); in particular they meet in at least one and at most mn distinct points. The multiplicity is at least m_P(C) m_P(D), the product of the multiplicities of the two curves at P, with equality exactly when the curves have no common tangent at P. Over a non-closed field, or in the affine plane, the count mn is only an upper bound on the number of points (missing points are at infinity, in a field extension, or hidden in multiplicities). The affine-line special case says a polynomial of degree n has n roots with multiplicity; the case of a line and a conic gives the two intersection points behind the quadratic formula.
k algebraically closed; the curves are projective and have no common component
intersection multiplicity is the local-ring dimension (equivalently Fulton's axiomatic multiplicity)
over non-closed fields or in affine coordinates only the upper bound mn on the number of points holds

[Lemme 29 of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] The matrix entry $\big( M_{\bs{\sg}_{N-1}}^{\, \vsg} \big)_{ j+\sigma_j, j }$ can be evaluated in closed form

$$\big( M_{\bs{\sg}_{N-1}}^{\, \vsg} \big)_{ j+\sigma_j, j } \,  =  \,

\ln\left|\Phi\left(\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta_j}{\delta_{j+\sigma_j}}\right)\right| \qquad \text{for} \qquad j \in \intn{1}{N-1} \;. $$

Here, we introduced $\Phi(x) := 2x+1+2\sqrt{x(1+x)}$, and have set

\beq

\delta_j \, =  \, |\lambda_j^+ - \lambda_j^-|  \qquad and \qquad  \Delta_j \, = \,  \lambda_{j+1}^{\ups_j}  \, - \,  \lambda_{j}^{\ups_j} \, .

\enq

body:
Let K be a compact metric space and let F be a family of real- or complex-valued continuous functions on K. Suppose F is (i) uniformly bounded: there is M with |f(x)| <= M for all f in F and all x in K, and (ii) equicontinuous: for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(x, y) < delta implies |f(x) - f(y)| < epsilon for every f in F simultaneously. Then every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on K (to a continuous limit); equivalently, F is relatively compact in C(K) with the supremum norm. Conversely, a relatively compact subset of C(K) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. (Pointwise boundedness plus equicontinuity already implies uniform boundedness on compact K; the classical statement on K = [a,b] is the special case.)
K is a compact metric space
F is a uniformly bounded family in C(K)
F is equicontinuous on K

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The asymptotic moments of a block-modified Wishart matrix 
$$\widetilde{W}=(id\otimes\varphi)W$$
with parameters $d,m,n\in\mathbb N$, as above, are given by the formula
$$\lim_{d\to\infty}M_e\left(\frac{\widetilde{W}}{d}\right)=\sum_{\sigma\in NC_p}(mn)^{|\sigma|}(M^\sigma_e\otimes M^\gamma_e)(\Lambda)$$
where $\Lambda\in M_n(\mathbb C)\otimes M_n(\mathbb C)$ is the square matrix associated to $\varphi:M_n(\mathbb C)\to M_n(\mathbb C)$.

[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2608.02319, 'Averaging Principle for Ordinary Differential Equations in a Multiscale Random Environment'] Let $(\mathbf X,\mathbf I)$ be a stochastic process with values in $E \times I$, and let $\tau_1$ be a stopping time such that $(\mathbf X,\mathbf I)$ satisfies the strong Markov property at time $\tau_1$. Let $\mathbf Z$ be defined as the solution to
\[
\frac{\mathrm d\mathbf Z_t}{\mathrm dt} = F_{\mathbf I_t}(\mathbf Z_t,\mathbf X_t), \quad \mathbf Z_0 = z,
\]
where $(F_i)_{i \in I}$ is a family of measurable functions from $Z \times E$ to $Z$, and assume that this equation admits a unique adapted solution. Then the process $(\mathbf Z,\mathbf X)$ satisfies the strong Markov property at time $\tau_1$.

[Lemma lem:time-change-general of arXiv:2604.05941, 'Banach spaces of continuous paths with finite $p$-th variation'] Let $\pi=(\pi^n)_{n\ge0}$ be a partition sequence on $[0,1]$, and let $\phi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ be an increasing homeomorphism. Define
    \[
        \pi^n(\phi):=\phi^{-1}(\pi^n)
        =\{\phi^{-1}(t_i^n):\, i=0,\dots,N(\pi^n)\},\qquad n\ge0.
    \]
    If $x\in V_\pi^p$, then $x\circ\phi\in V_{\pi(\phi)}^p$ and $[x\circ\phi]_{\pi(\phi)}^{(p)}(t)=[x]_\pi^{(p)}(\phi(t))$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Moreover, if $x\in C^\alpha([0,1])$ and $\phi\in C^\beta([0,1])$ for some $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1]$, then $x\circ\phi\in C^{\alpha\beta}([0,1])$.

[Lemma nsm of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] [TVuniversality] 
Let $1\leq k \leq n$, and let $A'$ be  a $k \times n$ matrix of rank $k$ with singular values $s_1(A') \geq \cdots \geq s_{k}(A') \geq 0$ and rows $R_1,\cdots, R_{k}$. For each $i \leq k$, let $W_i$ be the subspace generated by the $k-1$ rows $R_1, \cdots, R_{i-1}, R_{i+1}, \cdots, R_{k}$. Then we have
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k} s_{i}^{-2}(A') = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mbox{\rm dist}^{-2}(R_i, W_i).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Continuous curves in the Poisson-coloring frontier structural attempt Result: The established dimension lower bound already rules out a countable union of rectifiable curves: every rectifiable curve has Hausdorff dimension at most1, and the dimension of a countable union is the supremum of the component dimensions. Thus any affirmative construction must use nonrectifiable curves. Compact connectedness alone also cannot supply path connectedness, as shown by the topologist sine-curve closure. Check: The sine-curve closure of{(x,sin(1/x)):0<x<=1} together with the limiting vertical segment is compact and connected but not path connected. This does not by itself refute a countable-curve covering; it specifically blocks the inference from connectedness to a single continuous parametrization. Obstruction: A scale-uniform crossing/tightness estimate is needed to construct continuous interface paths. The source lacks the correlation inequality used to establish such estimates in standard planar models.

[Corollary 17 (The rational comparison determinant is nonzero) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(S\) be an irreducible algebraic stratum of degree-\(m\) polynomials
satisfying the isolated-leading-part hypothesis and on which fixed monomials

matrix

 B_{\mathrm{Jac}}(P,t)

\end{equation}

\[
 \det B_{\mathrm{Jac}}\not\equiv0.
\]
Different division data, monomial bases, or resolved charts change
\(B_{\mathrm{Jac}}\) only by invertible rational gauge transformations.

\[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{\mathcal{C}^0_{x}} \leq K 2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
    Then for any $y \in \T^d$, $\delta>0$,
    \[G_{y,\delta} := \begin{cases} \Big\{x \in \T^d : |x-y| < 1/8,\, U(y) \cdot (x-y) > 0, \text{ and } \frac{U(y)}{|U(y)|} \cdot U(x) >  2\delta\Big\} & U(y) \ne 0,\\ \emptyset & U(y) =0,\end{cases}\]

    \begin{equation}

    \end{equation}
and any $T \in (0,1]$, if for all $t \in [0,T], X^i_t \in G_{y,\delta}$, we have that
    \[\sup_{t \in [0,T]} |X^1_t - X^2_t| \leq M_{y,\delta}|X^1_0 - X^2_0|.\]

[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2608.19832, 'Sharp Convex Concentration for Symmetric Random Tensors with Subgaussian Coordinates'] Let \(Q\ll \Pp\), and assume \(H=D(Q\Vert \Pp)<\infty\). There is a coupling \((X,Y)\)

\begin{align}
 \sum_{i=1}^n
 \E\left[\E(\abs{X_i-Y_i}\mid X)^2\right]

 \\
 \sum_{i=1}^n
 \E\left[\E(\abs{X_i-Y_i}\mid Y)^2\right]
 &\le C K^2\Psi_n(H),
 \\
 \E\norm{X-Y}^2
 &\le C K^2(\sqrt{nH}+H).
 
\end{align}

body:
[Lemma of arXiv:2607.18011, 'From local giants to locality in long-range percolation'] \thlabel{lem:non_integrable_limits}
    Let $G$ be a transitive graph of polynomial growth with $d \geq 2$, and let $J : V \times V \to \mathbf{R}_+$ be the transitive kernel given by $J(x,y) = d_G(x,y)^{-d \alpha}$ for $\alpha > 0$.
    
    Let $(G_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ be a sequence of transitive graphs and let $(J_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ be the sequence of transitive kernels given by $J_n(x,y) = d_G(x,y)^{-\dim(G_n) \alpha_n}$ with $\alpha_n > 1$.
    
    If the sequence $(G_n,J_n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}$ converges locally to $(G,J)$, then $\alpha = \lim_{n \to \infty} \alpha_n\dim(G_n)/ d$.
    
    In particular, if $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \dim(G_n)<d$ and $\limsup_{n\to \infty} \alpha_n< d/\limsup_{n \to \infty} \dim(G_n)$ then $\alpha<1$ and the pairs $(G_n,J_n)$ are integrable for all $n$, but not uniformly integrable, and the pair $(G,J)$ is not integrable.

body:
[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Consider $(A_p)_p$ in  Case \caseS or Case \caseR.
There exist constants $c, C>0$ such that for any finite set of primes $B$, and for any  $\{\phi_p\}_p \subset \C$ in Case \caseS or $\{\phi_p\}_p \subset \R$ in Case \caseR, there exists a coupling of $\langle\phi A\rangle_B$ with a  Gaussian $Z_{B}$ such that 
\[
  \mathrm{Cov}(Z_B) = \mathrm{Cov}\langle\phi A\rangle_B\,,
\]
and, letting $\Delta_{B} \coloneqq |\langle\phi A\rangle_B - Z_{B}|$, we have the first moment bound
\begin{align} 
  \E \Delta_{B} \leq C \min\bigg( V_{B}^{1/2} \,,\, \frac{T_{B}}{V_{B}} \bigg)
\end{align}
and the tail bound
\begin{align}
  \P(\Delta_{B} > u ) \leq Ce^{-c u^2/V_B}
\end{align}
for all $u\geq 0$, where we use the interpretation that $1/V_B \coloneqq 0$ if $V_B = 0$.

\begin{proof}
Since the case $V_B = 0$ is trivial, we assume throughout the proof $V_B>0$. Moreover, it is quick to show $\E\Delta_B \leq C V_B^{1/2}$: we simply take the independent coupling between $\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B$ and $Z_B$ (they are realized as independent random variables on the same probability space). Then $\E\Delta_B \leq \E|\langle\phi A\rangle_B| + \E|Z_B| \leq C V_B^{1/2}$ by Jensen's inequality.

To prove \eqref{eq:block-coupling-expectation}, it  remains to show $\mathbb{E}\Delta_B \le CT_B/V_B$. 
The proofs are identical in Case \caseS and Case \caseR, so for concreteness we take $A_p = \alpha_p$ iid Steinhaus.
We  apply \cref{lem:berry-esseen} in dimension $k=2$, identifying $\C$ with $\R^2$.  Observe 
$\Cov \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B = \tfrac12 V_B \id$. 
Letting $X_p \coloneq \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \phi_p \alpha_p$, we then have 
\[
\sum_{p \in B} \Cov(X_p) = \id \qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{p\in B} \E |X_p|^3 = \big(\tfrac{2}{V_B}\big)^{3/2} \,T_B\,. 
\]
The third-moment condition of \cref{lem:berry-esseen} then becomes, for some constant $c>0$,
\begin{equation}
T_B/V_B^{3/2}\leq c
\end{equation}

Suppose first that \eqref{eq:third-mom-condition-proof} is satisfied.  Then \cref{lem:berry-esseen} yields a Gaussian vector $Z\sim \cN(0,\id)$ with
\begin{align}
  \Big|\P\Big( \Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big|  \leq r \Big) - \P (|Z| \leq r )\Big|\ll \frac{1}{(1+r)^3} \frac{T_B}{V_B^{3/2}}
\end{align}
for all $r\geq 0$.
Observe that the $W_1$ distance between two rotationally-symmetric random variables is bounded by the $W_1$ distance between their norms: the same uniform random variable can be used for both angles, taken independently of the norms. 
We may then use the formula \eqref{eq:vallender}
to compute
\begin{align*}
  W_1\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B, Z\Big) \le W_1\Big(\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big|, |Z| \Big) = \int_0^{\infty} \Big| \P\Big(\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big| \leq r\Big) - \P(|Z| \leq r) \Big| \ll \frac{T_B}{V_B^{3/2}}\,.
\end{align*}
Scaling each random variable by $\sqrt{V_B/2}$ yields $W_1(\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B, Z_B) \ll T_B/V_B$, where $Z_B = \sqrt{V_B/2} Z$ and therefore $\Cov \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B = \Cov Z_B$. This completes the proof of \eqref{eq:block-coupling-expectation} when \eqref{eq:third-mom-condition-proof} holds.

If \eqref{eq:third-mom-condition-proof} does not hold, i.e.,
$T_B/V_B^{3/2} > c$,
then the independent coupling of $\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B$ and $Z_B$ yields 
\[
  \E\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}}(\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B - Z_B)\Big| \leq  \E\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}}\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big| + \E |Z| \leq C'
\]
for some constant $C'>0$. Choose $C$ such that $C' < cC < T_B/V_B^{3/2}$. It follows that 
\[
  E\Delta_B \leq C V_B^{1/2} \frac{T_B}{V_B^{3/2}} = C \frac{T_B}{V_B}\,.
\]

The tail bound \eqref{eq:block-coupling-tail} follows from the triangle inequality and Hoeffding's inequality. Choose any coupling such that \eqref{eq:block-coupling-expectation} holds, and write
\[
\P(\Delta_B >u) \leq \P(|\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B| > u/2) + \P(|Z_B|> u/2)\,.
\]

[Definition Maximal e-families and minimal non e-families of arXiv:2412.08400, '\vspace{-1.0cm} Characterization of Exponential Families of \\ Lumpable Stochastic Matrice'] We consider the partial order on non-vacuous lumpable and irreducible families induced from their edge sets ordered by inclusion. We call $\mathcal{W}_\kappa(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E})$ a maximal e-family, if $\mathcal{W}_\kappa(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E})$ forms an e-family, and any non-vacuous lumpable family $\mathcal{W}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E}')$ such that $\mathcal{E} \subsetneq \mathcal{E}'$ does not form an e-family.
    Similarly, we call $\mathcal{W}_\kappa(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E}')$ a minimal non e-family, if $\mathcal{W}_\kappa(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E}')$ does not form an e-family, and any non-vacuous lumpable family $\mathcal{W}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{E})$ such that $\mathcal{E} \subsetneq \mathcal{E}'$ forms an e-family.

[Prop MOP-as-colim of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The cocone $\sigma$ expresses $\textbf{\textup{MOP}}$ as the colimit of the global functor ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak J}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}\colon\ul\textup{VRep}\to{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}$, i.e.\ as a left adjoint object with respect to $\textup{const}\colon{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\textup{gl}\to{\textup{Fun}}(\ul\textup{VRep},{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl})$.
    \begin{proof}
        As ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak T\kern-1pt\mathfrak h}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}$ is a global left adjoint, it suffices to prove that the terminal object of $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}[\textbf{\textup{BOP}}]$ is equivalent to the global colimit of $\bar y_{\textup{top}}$ (in a necessarily unique way). This on the other hand may be checked after postcomposing with the equivalence $\Psi^{-1}\colon\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}[\textbf{\textup{BOP}}]\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\ul\Spc_{\textup{Glo}/\ul\textup{VRep}^{\oplus}}$. We claim that the resulting composite $\ul\textup{VRep}^{\oplus}\to\ul\Spc_{\textup{Glo}/\ul\textup{VRep}^{\oplus}}^\otimes$ is equivalent, even as a \emph{symmetric monoidal} global functor, to the parametrized Yoneda embedding; the proposition will then follow since the colimit of the latter is indeed terminal by [martiniwolf2021limits]*{Proposition 6.1.3}.
        To prove the claim, we may again restrict to $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus$, i.e.~it will suffice to identify $(\psi^\otimes)^{-1}\circ y_{\textup{top}}^\otimes$ with the Yoneda embedding of $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus$. This however holds by construction of $\psi^\otimes$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition P:ordered metrics of arXiv:2507.01236, 'Disintegration theorem for multifunctions, \\ with applications to empirical Wasserstein d'] Consider two metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$ on a metric space $\mathfrak{X}$ which induce the same topology and hence the same Borel $\sigma$-algebra.  Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on 
$\mathfrak{X}$.  Fix $n \geq 1$ and let~$\nu$ be a probability measure on $[n]$.  Given $x \in \mathfrak{X}$ and $r > 0$, write $B^{(k)}(x, r)$ for the closed $d_k$-ball of radius~$r$ centered at~$x$ for $k = 1,2$.   

Now fix $r > 0$, let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d.\ with distribution~$\mu$ on a probability space $(\Psi, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, let 
$\mathcal{B}^{(k)}_n := (B^{(k)}(X_1, r(n)), \ldots, B^{(k)}(X_n, r(n)))$ and let $F^{(k)}$ denote the corresponding multifunction defined as in (equation eq:Fn of the paper), for $k = 1, 2$ . Assume that $d_1(x, y) \leq d_2(x, y)$ for $(\mu \times \mu)$-almost every $x, y \in \mathfrak{X}$.  Then 
\begin{align*}
\{& \text{$\mathcal{B}^{(2)}$ covers $\mathfrak{X}$ and $(\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_n)$ is a disintegration of $\mu$ along $F^{(2)}$ with respect to $\nu$} \} \\
&\subseteq \{ \text{$\mathcal{B}^{(1)}$ covers $\mathfrak{X}$ and $(\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_n)$ is a disintegration of $\mu$ along $F^{(1)}$ with respect to $\nu$} \}.
\end{align*}

Transient labels Z plus distinct cemetery state; bounded jump and killing rates

metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:fb4d817f6c0790e0f1cd7906c2e5d2c480117050a03b4c527ad2a8dcd9a5e0ea","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/fb/fb4d817f6c0790e0f1cd7906c2e5d2c480117050a03b4c527ad2a8dcd9a5e0ea.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:91acd56335975a932539f4073e0edfa8458a1eb6dee249a431112ed253e3e53b","bundle_entry_key":"two-end-rank-two","bundle_id":"population.probability-critical-moments-two-end-kernels-and-dependence-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.markov:candidate-pollett-lambda-transient-polynomial-kernel-rank-two","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0288: a rank-two polynomial transition asymptotic for a killed chain

Status: full author-checked counterexample candidate to Pollett's Section 2 conjecture (ii). No independent review or novelty certificate is claimed. The chain has a countably infinite irreducible transient class and bounded rates. This does not contradict the rank-one theorem in the lambda-positive recurrent setting.

## Primary source and precise target

Phil Pollett, *Quasi-stationary distributions for queueing and other models*, Queueing Systems 100 (2022), 241-243; arXiv:2202.05428, Section 2, PDF page 2. Primary source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.05428 . The complete three-page preprint was read, including the discussion distinguishing lambda-null recurrence from lambda-transience.

The source assumes a conservative, stable and regular continuous-time chain on an absorbing state and an irreducible countable transient class, with absorption almost surely. Conjecture (ii) says that if the polynomially corrected transition probabilities have finite strictly positive limits, their limit is always of the form $A x_i m_j$, allowing invariant or subinvariant vectors and measures. We refute this factorization. The other numbered asymptotic claims are not separately asserted false.

## Construction and source hypotheses

Use transient labels $C=\mathbb Z$ and a cemetery label $\partial$. From every $i\in\mathbb Z$ jump to each nearest neighbor at rate one. Kill at rate $\kappa>0$ everywhere, and at an additional rate $v>0$ when $i=0$. Thus the generator on the transient class is

$$
 Q=\Delta-\kappa I-v|0\rangle\langle0|,
 \qquad (\Delta f)(i)=f(i+1)+f(i-1)-2f(i).
$$

Give the cemetery state rate zero. The full rate matrix is conservative: its killing rate is an actual transition to the cemetery state. Exit rates are at most $2+\kappa+v$, so the chain is stable and nonexplosive, and its transition function is unique. Its transient class is irreducible because every finite nearest-neighbor path has positive probability of being followed before killing. Independent rate-$\kappa$ killing implies absorption almost surely from every transient state.

To use the source's literal labels, map $\partial$ to its absorbing label $0$, lattice $0$ to $1$, positive lattice $k$ to $2k$, and negative lattice $-k$ to $2k+1$. Thus $C$ is exactly countably infinite as required. The distinguished lattice site is not the absorbing state.

Put $K=-\Delta+v|0\rangle\langle0|$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$ and

$$
 H_t(i,j)=\langle\delta_i,e^{-tK}\delta_j\rangle,
 \qquad p_t(i,j)=e^{-\kappa t}H_t(i,j).
$$

The operator $K$ is bounded, nonnegative and self-adjoint. Its semigroup is the nearest-neighbor walk killed at the additional rate $v$ at lattice zero, by the elementary killed-generator construction.

## Exact resolvent

For real $s>0$, define

$$
 D(s)=\sqrt{s(s+4)},\qquad
 r(s)=\frac{s+2-D(s)}2\in(0,1).
$$

The free resolvent is

$$
 R_s^0(i,j)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}e^{t\Delta}(i,j)\,dt
 =\frac{r(s)^{|i-j|}}{D(s)}.
$$

Indeed $r+r^{-1}=s+2$ solves the homogeneous nearest-neighbor resolvent recurrence, and the jump of its first difference at $i=j$ is $D(s)$. Decay as $|i-j|\to\infty$ selects the displayed root. The rank-one resolvent identity then gives

$$
 R_s(i,j):=\langle\delta_i,(s+K)^{-1}\delta_j\rangle
 =\frac{r^{|i-j|}}D-\frac{v r^{|i|+|j|}}{D(D+v)}.                 \tag{1}
$$

This formula can also be checked directly by substituting it in the recurrence with the extra diagonal term $v$ at zero.

## The lower spectral edge and the time asymptotic

Write $a=|i-j|$, $b=|i|+|j|$ and $q=\sqrt{s}$ on the principal branch. As $q\to0$,

$$
 D=2q+\tfrac14q^3+O(q^5),\qquad
 \log r=-q+\tfrac1{24}q^3+O(q^5).
$$

Consequently

$$
 \frac{r^a}{D}
 =\frac1{2q}-\frac a2+\left(\frac{a^2}4-\frac1{16}\right)q+O(q^2),
 \qquad
 \frac v{D+v}=1-\frac{2q}v+\frac{4q^2}{v^2}+O(q^3).
$$

Subtracting the two terms of (1) cancels the pole and yields

$$
 R_s(i,j)=\frac{b-a}{2}+\frac1v-L_{ij}\sqrt{s}+O(s),
 \qquad
 L_{ij}=\frac{b^2-a^2}{4}+\frac bv+\frac2{v^2}.                 \tag{2}
$$

A bare Laplace-transform expansion is not, by itself, a pointwise Tauberian theorem for an off-diagonal transition probability. Here the explicit resolvent supplies the stronger spectral information that is needed.

For $0<E<4$, set $s=-E+i0$. Then

$$
 D=i\sqrt{E(4-E)},\qquad r=1-E/2-i\sqrt{E(4-E)}/2.
$$

In a sufficiently small interval $0<E<\varepsilon$, formula (1) has smooth boundary values and no denominator zero. Stieltjes inversion for the finite spectral measures therefore gives an absolutely continuous density there. The coefficients of its convergent expansion in $q$ are real, so the $O(s)$ term of (2) is real on this interval and its first possible further imaginary contribution is $O(E^{3/2})$. Hence

$$
 \frac{d\mu_{ij}}{dE}(E)
 =-\frac1\pi\operatorname{Im} R_{-E+i0}(i,j)
 =\frac{L_{ij}}\pi E^{1/2}+O(E^{3/2}).                         \tag{3}
$$

There is no atom at zero: $sR_s(i,j)\to0$, or equivalently the nonnegative quadratic form of $K$ has no nonzero square-summable null vector. Any spectral mass outside $[0,\varepsilon)$ contributes $O(e^{-\varepsilon t})$ to $H_t(i,j)$; the total variation of an off-diagonal spectral measure is finite by Cauchy-Schwarz for spectral projections. Possible high-energy atoms are consequently harmless.

Integrating (3) against $e^{-tE}$, substituting $u=tE$ and bounding the stated remainder gives

$$
 H_t(i,j)=\frac{L_{ij}}{2\sqrt\pi}t^{-3/2}+O(t^{-5/2}),
$$

since $\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt\pi/2$. Using
$b^2-a^2=2(|i||j|+ij)$, the leading kernel is

$$
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \lim_{t\to\infty}t^{3/2}e^{\kappa t}p_t(i,j)
 = C_{ij}
 =\frac{(|i|+2/v)(|j|+2/v)+ij}{4\sqrt\pi}.}                  \tag{4}
$$

Every $C_{ij}$ is finite and strictly positive, including opposite signs, because $(|i|+2/v)(|j|+2/v)>|ij|$. Thus the source decay parameter is exactly $\lambda=\kappa$.

## Lambda-transience and failure of factorization

Monotone convergence in the nonnegative integral defining the resolvent, followed by (2), gives

$$
 \int_0^\infty e^{\lambda t}p_t(i,j)\,dt
 =\lim_{s\downarrow0}R_s(i,j)
 =\frac{|i|+|j|-|i-j|}{2}+\frac1v<\infty.
$$

The transient class is therefore lambda-transient in exactly the source definition. The power $3/2$ is the unique exponent yielding a finite strictly positive limit for each fixed pair, so it also satisfies the source's smallest-exponent wording.

Take $v=2$ and transient lattice labels $i,j\in\{0,1\}$. Equation (4) yields

$$
 (C_{ij})_{i,j\in\{0,1\}}
 =\frac1{4\sqrt\pi}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det(C_{ij})=\frac1{16\pi}>0.
$$

Every matrix of the form $A x_i m_j$ has all its two-by-two minors equal to zero. Allowing subinvariant vectors cannot alter this algebraic necessity. Thus conjecture (ii), under the stated general lambda-transient hypotheses, fails for this chain.

## A second check from reflection and the odd sector

Reflection about lattice zero commutes with $K$. On odd functions the killing potential vanishes. For positive integers $i,j$, cancellation of the defect terms in (1), or the killed-walk reflection principle, gives the exact identity

$$
 H_t(i,j)-H_t(i,-j)=k_t(i-j)-k_t(i+j),
$$

where the free kernel has Fourier representation

$$
 k_t(n)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
 e^{-2t(1-\cos\theta)}\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta.
$$

The difference of cosines is $2\sin(i\theta)\sin(j\theta)=2ij\theta^2+O(\theta^4)$. Gaussian scaling around zero, with exponential suppression away from zero, therefore gives

$$
 \lim_{t\to\infty}t^{3/2}[H_t(i,j)-H_t(i,-j)]
 =\frac{ij}{2\sqrt\pi}.
$$

This matches (4). It also supplies a separate structural obstruction: a strictly positive symmetric rank-one kernel invariant under simultaneous reflection has an even positive factor, so it would satisfy $C_{ij}=C_{i,-j}$. The nonzero odd-sector limit rules that out independently of the displayed minor calculation.

## What this does and does not settle

The source's common-exponent conjecture has an elementary conditional observation: if finite strictly positive pure-power limits already exist for every pair, irreducibility and the Chapman-Kolmogorov lower bound compare any two entries at times differing by a fixed constant. Comparison in both directions forces their exponents equal. This does not prove existence of all pairwise limits from a single pair and is not counted as another new solution.

This packet addresses the rank-one assertion (ii). It makes no claim to characterize all limiting conditional distributions or to refute the separate survival-exponent assertion (iii). Rank-one perturbations, killed nearest-neighbor kernels and two-end harmonic functions are classical tools. A later theorem, earlier example or prior formulation may already contain this counterexample. Initial searches of the title, author page and conjecture wording found no verified disposition; that is not a novelty or current-openness certificate. A full independent source and spectral-argument review remains required before promotion.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:fa4eb0186ec9e6a4a54c5d0dce5c1c32bd0f2b21885951bb5ed32afb6346b693","revision_digest":"sha256:96df55fe2cb158bbc7977869b1fa4b3b3f5e32427aaafa369db2192f887664fa","source_id":"owner-authored-probability-notes-20260907:two-end-rank-two","source_revision":"private-author-checked-2026-09-07T00:56:03Z","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem:least-action of arXiv:2608.23545, 'Eulerian walkers on $\Z^2$ have range exponent $2/3$'] Let $\xi_0,\ldots,\xi_n$ and
		$\widehat\xi_0,\ldots,\widehat\xi_m$ be legal routings with
		$\widehat\xi_0=\xi_0$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
			\item If $\xi_n$ is stable, then $m\leq n$, and each vertex is actuated no
			more often in the second routing than in the first.
			\item If $\xi_n$ and $\widehat\xi_m$ are both stable, then $m=n$, their
			final states agree, and each vertex is actuated equally often in the two
			routings.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let D be a real diagonal d-by-d matrix,d>=1,and m>=0 an integer. For U uniform on the unit sphere,put S_0=1 and S_j=(1/(2j))*sum_(i=1)^j trace(D^i)*S_(j-i). Then E[(U^T D U)^m]=m!*S_m/(d/2)_m,where (d/2)_m is the rising factorial and the m=0 ratio is1. In the exact real-arithmetic model these moments through degree m are computable using polynomially many operations in m,d. This is an arithmetic-operation count,not a bit-complexity bound. [Defn 24 of arXiv:2608.26068, 'All once-extended 3D TQFTs are Reshetikhin--Turaev theories'] Let $K$ be a ribbon-colouring of $\Gamma = (V,E,L)$, and $v\in V$. We may assign a vector space to this as follows: let $X_1,\ldots,X_a$ be the colours of the source edges of $v$, $Y_1,\ldots,Y_b$ the colours of the target edges, which both ordered according to the orderings on $E_s(v),E_t(v)$. Define $\epsilon_i \in \set{\pm1}$ for each $1\le i\le a$ to be $+1$ if the $i^\text{th}$ source edge is incoming, and $-1$ otherwise. Define $\varepsilon_j \in \set{\pm1}$ for each $1\le j \le b$ to be $+1$ if the $j^\text{th}$ target edge is outgoing and $-1$ otherwise. Then, define the \emph{space of labels of $v$} to be
    $$\mathcal{V}_K(\Gamma,v) := \Hom_\mathcal{C}\pa{\bigotimes_{i=1}^a X_i^{\epsilon_i}, \bigotimes_{j=1}^b Y_j^{\varepsilon_j}}$$ 
    where each $X^{+1}$ is taken to be $X$ and $X^{-1}$ is taken to be the dual $X^*$.

    The \emph{space of labels} of $\Gamma$ is the vector space $$\mathcal{V}_K(\Gamma) := \bigotimes_{v\in V} \mathcal{V}_K(\Gamma,v).$$

\[

\]
and
\[
    G(p,q)=p+q+2\sqrt{pq}\cosh u_{p,q}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
    \mathsf P_{p,q}'(u)
    =
    \frac{4pq\sinh^2u}{p+q+2\sqrt{pq}\cosh u}>0
    \qquad(u>0).
\]

[Proposition p.growth of arXiv:2505.07145, 'Nonamenable Poisson zoo'] Consider a Poisson zoo on an infinite transitive graph $G$ with intensity $\lambda>0$ and a lattice animal measure $\nu_o$ that has unbounded support. Assume further that there exist constants $0 < c_1(G,\lambda), c_2(G), C(R) < \infty$ and a function $\vartheta \, : \, \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ with $\lim_{R \to \infty} \vartheta(R) = \infty$ such that for any $R \in \mathbb{N}$ and for any finite connected subset $A \subset \subset V(G)$ of vertices and any subset $B \subseteq \partial_{\mathrm{ext}} A$ of its exterior boundary for the restricted process of Definition~(def:point_measure_restricted_to_hit_B_but_not_the_closure_of_A of the paper), we have
\begin{equation}
	
	\mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \mathrm{Tr} \left( \check{ \mathcal{X} }_{A,B}^R \right) \right| \right] \geq 
	c_1(G,\lambda)  \cdot \vartheta(R) \cdot \big[ c_2(G) \cdot |A| - \left( | \partial_{\mathrm{ext}} A | - |B|  \right) \big]
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}
	
	\mathrm{Var} \left( \left| \mathrm{Tr} \left( \check{ \mathcal{X} }_{A,B}^R \right) \right| \right) \leq
	C(R) \cdot \mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \mathrm{Tr} \left( \check{ \mathcal{X} }_{A,B}^R \right) \right| \right].
\end{equation}

Then the exploration process defined in (equation def:exploration_process_general_step of the paper) survives forever with positive probability:
\[
	\mathbb{P} \big( |E_n|>0 \text{ for all }n\ge 0 \big) > 0.
\]

body:
[Lemma lem:prop_adm_classes of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Fix \(A,\sigma_0>0\), and \(R\in(0,\infty]\). Let \(\omega,\omega'>0\) and \(\ell\in\mathbb N\).
  All classes below are taken with respect to the same domain \( \mathcal D_{A, \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},
  \sigma_0}\) or \( \mathcal D_{R,A, \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0}\). The following stability
  properties hold.

  \vspace*{-10pt}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item 
    The classes \(\mathfrak B_\ell\), \(\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), \(\mathfrak P_\ell\) and
    \(\mathfrak G_\ell\) are vector spaces. Moreover, \(\omega\geqslant\omega'\) entails that
    \(\mathfrak E_\ell^{\omega}\subset\mathfrak E_\ell^{\omega'}\subset \mathfrak B_\ell\).

    \item 
    Let \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\), \(E\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), \(P\in\mathfrak P_\ell\) and
    \(G\in\mathfrak G_\ell\). Then the product functions \(BE,BP\) and \(BG\) satisfy
    \begin{equation*}
      BE\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega, \qquad BP\in\mathfrak P_\ell, \qquad BG\in\mathfrak G_\ell.
    \end{equation*}
    If, in addition, for \(i=1,2\), \(E_i\in\mathfrak E_\ell^{\omega_i}\), \(P_i\in\mathfrak P_\ell\),
    \(G_i\in\mathfrak G_\ell\), then, with \(\bar\omega=\min\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}\),
    \begin{equation*}
      E_1E_2 \in\mathfrak E_\ell^{\bar\omega}, \quad P_1P_2 \in\mathfrak P_\ell,
      \quad P_1G_2\in\mathfrak G_\ell, \quad G_1G_2\in\mathfrak G_\ell.
    \end{equation*}

    \item 
    If \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\) then \(B^{-1}\in\mathfrak B_\ell\) provided that
    \begin{equation*}
      \inf_{\|a\|\leqslant A,\ x\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\ 0<\sigma\leqslant\sigma_0} |B(a,x,\sigma)|>0.
    \end{equation*}
    \item 
    If \(P\in\mathfrak P_\ell\), then, for every \(c_0>0\), \(\Gamma_{c_0}P \in\mathfrak G_\ell\).

    \item 
    If \(R=\infty\), \(G\in\mathfrak G_\ell\) and \(B(a,x,\sigma) = \int_{\mathbb
    H_c^m}G(\zeta;a,x,\sigma)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta\), then \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\).

    \item 
    Let \(q\ge1\), let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^q\) be open, and let \(\psi\in C^\infty(\Omega)\).
    \begin{enumerate}
      \item[(a)] If \(B=(B_1,\dots,B_q)\),  with \(B_i\in
      \mathfrak B_\ell\), and the range of \(B\) on \(\mathcal D_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0}\) is
      contained in a compact set \(K_\psi \Subset\Omega\), then \(\psi\circ B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\).

      \item[(b)] If \( P=(P_1,\dots,P_q)\) with \(P_i\in
      \mathfrak P_\ell\), and the range of \(P\) on \(\mathcal D_{R,A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}\)
      is contained in a compact set \(K_\psi\Subset\Omega\), then \(\psi\circ P\in\mathfrak
      P_\ell\).
    \end{enumerate}
    The same conclusions hold without the compact-range assumption if \(\psi\) and all of its
    derivatives up to order \(\ell\) are globally bounded on \(\Omega\).

    \item
    
    Let \(B\in\mathfrak B_\ell\), \(E\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), \(P\in\mathfrak P_\ell\) and
    \(G\in\mathfrak G_\ell\). If \(q\in\mathbb N\), then
    \begin{equation*}
      \sigma^qB\in\mathfrak B_\ell, \qquad \sigma^qE\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega,
      \qquad \sigma^qP\in\mathfrak P_\ell, \qquad \sigma^qG\in\mathfrak G_\ell.
    \end{equation*}
    If \(M\in\mathbb N\) and \(E\in\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\), then \(\sigma^{-M}E \in \mathfrak
    E_\ell^\omega\).
  \end{enumerate}
title: Basic calculus of the admissible classes

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.07290, 'Boundary behaviour of the Volterra square-root process'] Let $0 \neq K \in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\R_+)$ is completely monotone. Let $L$ be the corresponding resolvent of the first kind. The following assertions hold.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] Suppose that $K$ is regularly varying of the form \eqref{eq: regularly varying} with $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $\ell$ slowly varying at zero. Then 
        \[
            L_0(t) \sim \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\frac{t^{-\alpha}}{\ell(t)}, \qquad t \searrow 0.
        \]
        \item[(b)] Suppose that $K(0^+) < \infty$ and $-K'(t) \sim t^{\alpha - 1}\ell(t)$ for $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and a slowly varying function~$\ell$. Then 
        \[
            L_0(t) \sim \frac{|K'(t)|}{K(0^+)^2}, \qquad t \searrow 0.
        \]
        \item[(c)] Suppose that $K(0^+) < \infty$ and $|K'(0^+)| < \infty$. Then 
        \[
            L_0(0^+) = \frac{|K'(0^+)|}{K(0^+)^2}.
        \]
        \item[(d)] One has
        \[
            L_0(\infty) = \left( \int_0^{\infty}K(t)\, \mathrm{d}t \right)^{-1}.
        \]
    \end{enumerate}

body:
[Definition 44 (Typed Peter--Weyl fusion tree) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] A typed Peter--Weyl fusion tree $\mathscr D$ consists of the following data.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A finite connected acyclic graph whose vertex set is the disjoint union
\[
 V(\mathscr D)=V_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathscr D)
 \sqcup\{b_1,\ldots,b_N\},
\]
with a distinguished root in $V_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathscr D)$; every boundary
vertex $b_j$ has degree one.
\item At every local vertex $v$, a block family
$\mathbf v_{\boldsymbol\lambda_v}$ as in
Definition~\ref{def:peter-weyl-block-family}.  Each tensor leg is either
paired with exactly one graph edge or is designated external, and the paired
legs at $v$ are in bijection with the graph half-edges incident to $v$.  Every
external negative leg contributes to the global factor
$\conj{\cC_{\mathscr D}}$, and every external positive leg contributes to
$\cE_{\mathscr D}$, through fixed unitary identifications and a fixed order.
\item At $b_j$, fix an integer $m_j\ge0$ and a coefficient-kernel
configuration
\[
 \cH_{j,1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\cH_{j,m_j}
 \otimes\conj{\cC_j}\otimes\cE_j.
\]
Exactly one of its two deterministic coefficient legs is paired with the
incident edge; the other is external.  Its stochastic legs are all external.
The factor $\conj{\cC_j}$ is a negative deterministic leg and $\cE_j$ is a
positive deterministic leg; the attached one is regarded as a
singleton-labelled boundary leg.  Only the compressed local-vertex legs,
not an arbitrary boundary coefficient space, are required to be
finite-dimensional.
The external deterministic factors over all vertices are identified,
in fixed order, with
$\conj{\cC_{\mathscr D}}\otimes\cE_{\mathscr D}$.  With
$q:=\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j$, the stochastic legs are identified with $[q]$ by
concatenating $b_1,\ldots,b_N$ and retaining their internal slot orders.
Writing $\cE_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathscr D)$ for the ordered tensor product of
all surviving factors, the data include a fixed unitary
\begin{equation}

 J_{\mathrm{ext}}:
 \cE_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathscr D)
 \longrightarrow
 \left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^N\bigotimes_{k=1}^{m_j}\cH_{j,k}\right)
 \otimes\conj{\cC_{\mathscr D}}\otimes\cE_{\mathscr D}
\end{equation}
that implements these identifications and orders.  More precisely,
$J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the tensor product of the specified legwise unitaries,
followed by the specified permutation of tensor factors.  In particular,
for every global cut it induces unitaries separately on the input and output
sides of the associated flattening.
\item Every edge $e$ pairs one positive leg
$Z_{e,+}(\rho)$ with one negative leg
$\conj{Z_{e,-}(\lambda)}$.  As part of the edge data, fix a relation
\[
 \mathscr R_e\subset
 \mathscr L_{e,-}\times\mathscr L_{e,+}
\]
of allowed endpoint-label pairs, where $\mathscr L_{e,\pm}$ are the label
sets of the two endpoint legs.  For every
$(\lambda,\rho)\in\mathscr R_e$ the edge
carries a bounded connector block
\[
 U_{e;\lambda,\rho}:
 Z_{e,+}(\rho)\longrightarrow Z_{e,-}(\lambda)
\]
and the contraction on that edge is the complex-linear functional
\begin{equation}

 \operatorname{ev}_{e;\lambda,\rho}
   (\conj y\otimes x)
 :=\ip{U_{e;\lambda,\rho}x}{y}_{Z_{e,-}(\lambda)}.
\end{equation}
If the two factors occur in the reverse tensor order, the canonical flip is
used first.  When an edge comes from a global bounded map $U_e$ between
spectrally decomposed Hilbert spaces, its connector block is, by definition,
$P_\lambda^-U_eP_\rho^+$ viewed as a map from $Z_{e,+}(\rho)$ to
$Z_{e,-}(\lambda)$; thus cross-scale blocks are not discarded.
\item Labels on external legs and on boundary attachments are fixed.
Labels on the remaining internal half-edges vary over the countable set
$\Lambda_{\mathrm{int}}(\mathscr D)$ of assignments satisfying
$(\lambda_{e,-},\lambda_{e,+})\in\mathscr R_e$ on every edge.  Fusion and
other vertex restrictions may be encoded by declaring the corresponding
local tensor to be zero.  For
$\boldsymbol\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{int}}(\mathscr D)$,
$\boldsymbol\lambda_v$ denotes the tuple incident to $v$.
\en

[Proposition 37 of arXiv:2606.22611, 'Upper and Lower Bounds on Expected Soft Maxima\\of Gaussian Processes'] If $f:[0,1] \to [0,\infty)$ is non-increasing
  and $g:[0,1]\to [0,\infty)$ is affine and non-decreasing, for $r \ge 2$,
  \begin{align}
  
  \frac{1}{r}\sum_{k\ge 1} r^{-k} (f(r^{-k}) \wedge g(r^{-k})) 
  \le \int_0^1 (f(\epsilon)\wedge g(\epsilon)) \dif \epsilon 
  \le r^2 \sum_{k \ge 1} r^{-k} (f(r^{-k}) \wedge g(r^{-k})) 
  \end{align}

[Prop 2.1 of arXiv:2412.00708, 'Stochastic PDE approach to fluctuating interfaces'] Suppose $d=1$ and $\sup_{K\ge 1} \|\Psi^K(0)\|_{L^2({\mathbb{T}})}<\infty$.  Then,
the solution $\Psi^K$ of the SPDE (equation eq:6.2-Q of the paper) has a decomposition
$\Psi^K=\Psi_1^K + \Psi_2^K$ with $\Psi_1^K(t) \in\mathcal{D}'({\mathbb{T}})$ 
and $\Psi_2^K(t) \in C({\mathbb{T}})$ a.s.   As $K\to\infty$, $\Psi_1^K(t)$ converges to $0$
in the sense that $\langle \Psi_1^K(t),\varphi\rangle \to 0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ for
any test function $\varphi\in C^1({\mathbb{T}})$ and $t>0$, while  $\Psi_2^K(t,x)$ 
converges to $\Psi_2(t,x)$ in law for $t>0$ and $x\in {\mathbb{T}}$.
For each $t>0$ and $x\in {\mathbb{T}}$, the limit $\Psi(t,x)$ is an ${\mathbb{R}}$-valued 
Gaussian random variable with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2$ given by
\begin{align}    
\sigma^2 = \frac{c_2^2}{\sqrt{8\pi}}
\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-2cu}}{\sqrt{u}}du.
\end{align}
Furthermore, if $t_1\not= t_2$ or $x_1\not= x_2$,
$\Psi(t_1,x_1)$ and $\Psi(t_2,x_2)$ are independent. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 2.1 of arXiv:2412.00708

body:
[Lem 14 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
there exists a closed $\cD_\mu$-polytope $P$ such that
    \beq
       K_1 \equiv S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon']
        \subseteq P
        \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        	\frac\epsilon5,\frac\epsilon2\bigg) 
	\equiv K_2\,,
    \eeq
where $K_1,K_2$ are both
 $\cD_\mu$-convex bodies.

\begin{proof}
Note that $\Cost(\YY;\lambda)$, $(\|\BBb\|_2)^2$, and $-\Budget(\YY;\mu)$ are all convex functions of $\YY\in\cD_\mu$. (This uses the fact that for $\YY \in \cD_\mu$, the input to the $(\cdot)_+$ in $\Cost(\YY;\lambda)$ is always nonnegative.) This immediately implies that $K_2$ is a $\cD_\mu$-convex body. It also implies that $S_\star(\lambda,\mu)$ is a $\cD_\mu$-convex body, and therefore so is its $\epsilon'$-neighborhood $K_1$.

We now turn to the construction of the polytope $P$. Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.nbd.in.S.star.eps} gives
    \beq 
        K_1 \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        		\frac\epsilon5,\frac{\epsilon}{3}
		\bigg)
        \subseteq (K_2)^\circ\,,
    \eeq
    where $(K_2)^\circ$ denotes the interior of $K_2$ relative to the topology of $\cD_\mu$. We let $C$ denote the boundary of $K_2$ relative to the topology of $\cD_\mu$, that is,
	\[
	C\equiv \partial K_2
	\equiv K_2 \setminus (K_2)^\circ\,.
	\]
Note that $C$ is a compact set in the topology of $\cD_\mu$. It follows from \eqref{e:S.star.nbd.in.S.star.eps.consequence} that $K_1$ and $C$ are disjoint.

Recall from \eqref{e:D.mu.affine.closure} that we use $\mathcal{F}_\mu$ to denote the affine closure of $\cD_\mu$.
For each $\YY\in C$, by the (strict) hyperplane separating theorem, there exists an open half-space $U_\YY$ of $\mathcal{F}_\mu$ such that $\YY\in U_\YY$ and $U_\YY\cap K_1=\emptyset$. Then $V_\YY\equiv \cD_\mu \cap U_\YY$ is open in the $\cD_\mu$-topology, and we have an open cover
	\[
	C\subseteq
	\bigcup_{\YY\in C} V_\YY\,.
	\]
Since $C$ is compact, this must admit a finite subcover, so there exists finite $S\subseteq C$ such that
	\[
	C\subseteq
	\bigcup_{\YY\in S} V_\YY\,.
	\]
Let $A_\YY \equiv \mathcal{F}_\mu\setminus U_\YY$, a closed half-space of $\mathcal{F}_\mu$. It follows that we can express $A_\YY = \mathcal{F}_\mu \cap H_\YY$ where $H_\YY$ is a closed half-space of the full space $\R^{3r+s}$. We then define the closed $\cD_\mu$-polytope 
	\[
	P\equiv
	\cD_\mu\cap
	\bigg( \bigcap_{\YY\in S} H_\YY
	\bigg)\,.
	\]
Since each $U_\YY$ is disjoint from $K_1$, each $H_\YY$ must contain $K_1$, so we have $K_1\subseteq P$.
On the other hand, since 
	\[
	\cD_\mu \setminus P
	= \cD_\mu \cap 
	\bigg( \bigcup_{\YY\in S} U_\YY
	\bigg)
	\supseteq C\,,
	\]
we see that $P$ does not intersect $C$. Since $P$ is convex, it must be fully contained in either $(K_2)^\circ$ or
$(\cD_\mu\setminus K_2)^\circ$.
Since we already saw that $K_1\subseteq P$, the former must hold, so $P\subseteq K_2$ as claimed.\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 14 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Theorem thm:rigidity-equivalence of arXiv:2605.17082, 'Spectral Purification in Reversible Markov Chains: Hidden Parameters, Observable Equivalen'] Let $g_k = P^k g_0$ with $g_0 \perp \mathbf{1}$. The following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item There exists $\rho \in (0,1)$ such that $E_k = \rho^{2k} E_0$ for all $k \ge 0$.
    \item The initial condition lies in a single eigenspace: $g_0 = c \, \phi_i$ for some $i \ge 2$.
    \item There exists $\eta > 0$ such that $E_k - E_{k+1} = \eta E_k$ for all $k \ge 0$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, in this case $\rho = |\lambda_i|$ and $\eta = 1 - \lambda_i^2$.

body: [Definition spheresimplicial of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] The \emph{sphere complex} $S(M)$ of $M$ is a simplicial complex whose vertices are isotopy classes of embedded 2-spheres in $M$ that do not bound 3-balls---such spheres are called \emph{essential}. A collection of such isotopy classes $[S_0],\dots,[S_n]$ spans an $n$-simplex if and only if they are pairwise distinct and have pairwise disjoint representatives. In this case we call the set of embedded representatives $\Sigma\subseteq M$ a \emph{sphere system} representing the simplex.
title: Definition spheresimplicial of arXiv:2609.00233

body:
Every loopless planar graph is 4-colorable: its vertices can be assigned colors from a set of four so that the two endpoints of every edge receive different colors. Equivalently, the regions of any planar map in which regions are contiguous can be colored with four colors so that regions sharing a boundary segment of positive length receive different colors. The bound four is sharp (K_4 is planar and needs four colors). The only known proofs are computer-assisted (Appel-Haken 1976; Robertson-Sanders-Seymour-Thomas 1996; formally verified by Gonthier 2005).
graph planar and without loops
map regions contiguous; adjacency means a common boundary arc, not a single point

[Corollary C:-infty-case of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] There is a unique (in law) random continuous function $\mathcal{L}^{-\infty}:\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow \to \mathbb{R}$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $\rho \in\mathbb{R}$, $\mathcal{L}^{-\infty}$ is stochastically dominated by $\mathcal{L}^\rho$,  the half-space directed landscape with parameter $\rho$.
    \item For each $u = (x, s; y, s + t) \in \mathbb{Q}^4\cap \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$, we have
    $\mathcal{L}^{-\infty}(u) \stackrel{d}{=} \mathfrak{h}^{-\infty}_t\delta_x(y)$,
    where $\mathfrak{h}^{-\infty}_t$ is the half-space KPZ fixed point of parameter $-\infty$, and $\delta_x\in \operatorname{UC}_+$ such that $\delta_x(x)=0$ and $\delta_x(z)=-\infty$ for each $z\neq x$.
\end{enumerate}
We call $\mathcal{L}^{-\infty}$ the \textbf{half-space directed landscape} with parameter $-\infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary C:-infty-case of arXiv:2604.10020

[Definition 8 of arXiv:2609.01965, 'A logarithmic Bogomolov--Sommese vanishing theorem on compact K\"ahler manifolds'] A function $\varphi:X\rightarrow [-\infty,+\infty)$ is
    said to be quasi-plurisubharmonic (quasi-psh for short) if $\varphi$ is locally the sum of a plurisubharmonic function and a smooth function 
    (or equivalently, if $\ddbar\varphi$ is locally bounded from below). 

    If $\varphi$ is a quasi-psh function on $X$, the multiplier ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}(\varphi)$ is the ideal subsheaf of $\mathcal{O}_X$ defined by
    $$\mathcal{I}(\varphi)_x=\{f\in\mathcal{O}_{X,x}~|~\exists\ U\ni x\  \text{such that}\ \int_U|f|^2e^{-\varphi}d\lambda<+\infty  \},$$
    where $U$ is an open coordinate neighborhood of $x$ and $d\lambda$ is the standard Lebesgue measure in $\mathbb{C}^n.$
    
    It is easy to see that associated to a singular Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ satisfying
    $\image\Theta_{L,h}\geq\gamma$ 
    for some smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma$ in the sense of currents, 
    there is a well-defined multiplier ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}(h)$ on $X$ and $\mathcal{I}(h)$ is coherent (\cite{Nad90}).
title: Definition 8 of arXiv:2609.01965

PROOF (UNAUDITED). For normalized tanh features u_q (q in [0,1], u_0(z)=z), the angular Jacobian J(q,r,c)=E[u_q'(X)u_r'(Y)] satisfies exp(-1224(q^2+r^2))<=J<=exp(8(q^2+r^2)) for every c in [-1,1]. For the deterministic zero-bias critical tanh chain with equal initial marginal variance s_0 in (0,1], its normalized gap Dbar_l obeys exp(-14688s_0)Dbar_0<=Dbar_l<=exp(96s_0)Dbar_0 for all depths. Consequently positive moments normalized by Dbar_l can equivalently be normalized by the fixed nonzero Dbar_0, with depth-independent constants; a random empirical-angle denominator is not necessary for the next joint-moment route.
Gaussian pairs; q,r in [0,1] with normalized q=0 extension
For depth statement: fresh-weight deterministic GP recursion s_next=F(s), c_next=H(s,s,c), zero bias and critical weight variance 1/n; equal initial marginal variances
Dbar_0>0 only for quotient comparisons

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e4303b34e0a30622fdf1b76a8ed76f1f819fb7543aeb392cfea9148cc2e40856","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e4/e4303b34e0a30622fdf1b76a8ed76f1f819fb7543aeb392cfea9148cc2e40856.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:b72b841ffbded80cc0b3c2ed85e3e2b85b62e9dcef50b06b80b59745dcbbcfaa","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_noncollapsing_gp_gap","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c012-noncollapsing-gp-gap","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Gaussian-process limits and empirical Gram matrices","draft":"w712/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:critical-tanh-noncollapsing-gp-gap-two-sided-angular-jacobian","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C012 v1: critical tanh GP gaps do not collapse

Kind: moved. Target: 1, the two-input relative-gap propagation component.
Status: proof (unaudited). Literature novelty unverified. This is a
deterministic-reference reduction, not a stochastic multi-layer rate.

## Statement

For q in [0,1] let h_q(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(q) for q>0,
h_0(z)=z, a(q)=||h_q||_2, and u_q=h_q/a(q). Let
H(q,r,c)=E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)] for standard Gaussians of correlation c.
Define J(q,r,c)=E[u'_q(X)u'_r(Y)], with prime denoting input derivative.
Then uniformly on q,r in [0,1], c in [-1,1], with S=q^2+r^2,

    exp(-1224 S) <= J(q,r,c) <= exp(8 S).              (1)

Consequently, writing d(q,r,c)=1-H(q,r,c) and
b(q,r)=(1/2)||u_q-u_r||_2^2, one has

    exp(-1224 S)(1-c) <= d(q,r,c)-b(q,r)
                        <= exp(8 S)(1-c).            (2)

Fix s_0 in (0,1], cbar_0 in [-1,1], and define the equal-marginal
deterministic critical tanh GP chain by

    s_(l+1)=F(s_l), F(s)=E tanh(sqrt(s)Z)^2,
    cbar_(l+1)=H(s_l,s_l,cbar_l), Dbar_l=1-cbar_l.

For every integer l>=0,

    exp(-14688 s_0) Dbar_0 <= Dbar_l
                              <= exp(96 s_0) Dbar_0. (3)

Thus a positive initial normalized gap stays positive at every depth
and even has a positive depth-uniform lower bound. The constants are
deliberately loose. This assertion concerns this zero-bias, critical,
decaying-variance tanh chain. It is not asserted for ReLU or a positive
variance fixed point. At cbar_0=1 every Dbar_l is zero and the multiplicative
inequalities still hold, but no relative-error quotient is defined.

For Dbar_0>0, the random-denominator quantity (Q_l-R_l)^2/(1-c_l)
need not be the next object to bound. To control the error terms of C011
relative to the deterministic reference, it suffices instead to control
moments of (Q_l-R_l)^2/Dbar_0, together with the positive gap moments
and common-variance error terms. This replacement of the denominator is
exactly justified below; it does not itself supply these joint moments.

## 1. The first Gaussian coefficient is quadratic-close to one

Audited C002 v2 gives 1/2<=a(q)<=1 on [0,1]. For real t,
|t-tanh(t)|<=|t|^3/3 by integrating tanh(t)^2<=t^2. Hence

    ||h_q-Z||_2 <= q sqrt(15)/3,
    |a(q)-1| <= ||h_q-Z||_2,
    ||u_q-Z||_2 <= 4q sqrt(15)/3.                     (4)

Here Z denotes the identity function on Gaussian space and E Z^6=15.
Let beta(q)=E[Zu_q(Z)]. Since ||u_q||_2=||Z||_2=1,

    1-beta(q)=(1/2)||u_q-Z||_2^2 <= (40/3)q^2.        (5)

Also 0<=beta(q)<=1: the integrand Zu_q(Z) is nonnegative, and the upper
bound is Cauchy-Schwarz. Gaussian integration by parts gives
E[u'_q(Z)]=beta(q). Its boundary term vanishes because |u_q(z)|<=2|z|
and the Gaussian density decays faster than any polynomial. At q=0
the same assertions hold with u_0(z)=z, beta(0)=1.

## 2. A quadratic bound on derivative fluctuations

Write w_q(z)=u'_q(z)=sech(sqrt(q)z)^2/a(q), w_0(z)=1.
As in C011 section 1, this can also be verified directly:

    |partial_q h_q(z)|<=|z|^3/3,
    |a'(q)|<=sqrt(15)/3<2,
    |partial_q w_q(z)|<=2z^2+8.                       (6)

The first inequality follows by integrating
tanh(t)-t sech(t)^2=integral_0^t 2v sech(v)^2 tanh(v)dv<=2t^3/3.
For the last inequality, differentiate sech(sqrt(q)z)^2, whose derivative
has absolute value at most z^2, divide by a>=1/2, and bound the derivative
of a^(-1) by 8. At zero the numerator derivative tends to -z^2.
These polynomial envelopes justify differentiation and endpoint continuity
in Gaussian L2 by dominated convergence. Integrating (6) in q yields

    Var(w_q(Z)) <= E[(w_q(Z)-1)^2]
      <= q^2 E[(2Z^2+8)^2] = 108 q^2.                (7)

This is a variance bound, not an independence assertion. For ANY paired
standard Gaussians (including correlations +/-1), Cauchy-Schwarz bounds
the covariance of w_q(X) and w_r(Y) from below by -108 qr. Using
Ew=beta and beta(q)beta(r)>=1-(1-beta(q))-(1-beta(r)), (5) gives

    J(q,r,c) >= 1-(40/3)(q^2+r^2)-108qr
              >= 1-(202/3)(q^2+r^2)
              >= 1-68 S.                            (8)

The middle step uses 2qr<=q^2+r^2 for q,r>=0. No decorrelation of
features or rows is used here.

## 3. A positive global floor and the exponential lower bound

On the event |X|<=2 and |Y|<=2, q,r<=1 and a(q),a(r)<=1 imply
w_q(X)>=sech(2)^2>=exp(-4), and similarly for w_r(Y).
Markov's inequality at each marginal, followed by the union bound, gives

    P(|X|<=2, |Y|<=2) >= 1-1/4-1/4 = 1/2.

Therefore J>=exp(-8)/2>=exp(-9); this uses exp(1)>=2. This floor holds
uniformly even for the degenerate paired distributions at c=+/-1.

If 0<=S<=1/136, then x=68S lies in [0,1/2]. The elementary inequality
log(1-x)>=-2x holds on that interval: the derivative of log(1-x)+2x
is (1-2x)/(1-x)>=0 and the value at zero is zero. Consequently (8) gives

    J>=1-68S>=exp(-136S)>=exp(-1224S).

If S>=1/136, then 1224S>=9 and the global floor gives
J>=exp(-9)>=exp(-1224S). The two cases cover all S in [0,2], including
their common boundary and S=0. This proves the lower half of (1).
Audited C004 v1 gives J<=1+8(q^2+r^2); using 1+x<=exp(x) proves
the upper half. No change to audited C004 is made.

## 4. Integrate Price's identity and iterate the equal-state chain

Price's identity (Voigtlaender, arXiv:1710.03576, Theorem 1 and
Corollary 2) gives partial_c H=J in the interior. The features grow at
most linearly, and 0<w_q<=2. Coupling Y=cX+sqrt(1-c^2)Z for independent
standard X,Z justifies continuity at both endpoints by Gaussian domination.
Thus, for every c in [-1,1],

    1-H(q,r,c)
      = (1/2)||u_q-u_r||_2^2 + integral_c^1 J(q,r,t)dt.

Integrate (1) over an interval of length 1-c>=0 to get (2). When q=r=s_l,
the shape term vanishes and S=2s_l^2. Thus

    exp(-2448s_l^2)Dbar_l <= Dbar_(l+1)
                                <= exp(16s_l^2)Dbar_l.

For l>=1 multiply exactly the l inequalities with indices k=0,...,l-1;
this introduces the finite sum sum_(k=0)^(l-1) s_k^2. Audited C002 v2
implies s_(k+1)<=s_k-s_k^2/6. Telescoping therefore gives

    sum_(k=0)^(l-1) s_k^2 <=6(s_0-s_l)<=6s_0.

Since the lower exponential is decreasing in this sum, substituting its
upper bound preserves the LOWER bound exp(-2448*6s_0)Dbar_0.
For the upper exponential, substitution preserves the upper bound
exp(16*6s_0)Dbar_0. This proves (3), with 2448*6=14688 and 16*6=96.
At l=0 the empty product is one and the two inequalities are immediate.
All s_l remain in (0,1], so the normalized features used at every finite
depth are defined. The q=0 extension above is used for uniform estimates,
not to divide by a zero physical variance.

## 5. Exact deterministic-denominator reduction

Assume Dbar_0>0. Let p>=1 be finite, and let W_l>=0 be ANY random
variable (with possibly infinite pth moment). Since both denominators
below are deterministic, (3) gives pointwise

    exp(-96s_0) W_l/Dbar_0 <= W_l/Dbar_l
                       <= exp(14688s_0) W_l/Dbar_0.   (9)

Taking pth powers and expectations gives the corresponding moment
comparisons with these constants raised to p. Apply this first with
W_l=(Q_l-R_l)^2, then with positive population or empirical gap errors
when those are the quantities being estimated. This uses no independence
and no negative moment of an empirical angle.

For example, C011 yields for actual fresh-row states Q_l,R_l,c_l,
with D_l=1-c_l,

    E[(Q_(l+1)-R_(l+1))^2/Dbar_0 | past]
      <= [(1-(Q_l+R_l)/12)^2+3/n]
            (Q_l-R_l)^2/Dbar_0
          + 8 Q_l R_l D_l/(n Dbar_0).

This illustrates the new remaining object: positive JOINT moments such as
E[Q_l R_l D_l/Dbar_0] and E[(Q_l-R_l)^4/Dbar_0^2]. It does not bound
them by products of separate expectations. One must also control the
common-variance term in C011 and accumulated conditional gap noise in C010.
The full C003-type relative recursion, finite-width rate for transpose
programs, and non-Lipschitz target remain open.

## Audit and verification boundary

The new lower Jacobian bound and its fixed-reference consequence await
independent review. Constants and finite polynomial identities can be
checked separately, but these checks do not certify Gaussian integration,
Price's identity, the domination arguments, or the full target. Existing
C002/C004 PASS is used only for their exact stated scalar/upper-Jacobian
facts. [Lemma 48 of arXiv:2512.07202, 'Hitting Probabilities for Hypoelliptic Differential Equations Driven by Fractional Brownia'] Let $I,J \in \mathcal{A}_1(l)$ with $|I|\leqslant |J|$. Then there is no $(\varepsilon,x)$-dependence in $\beta^{J,\varepsilon}_I$ and more specifically, one has
\[
\beta^{J,\varepsilon}_I(t,x)=
\begin{cases}
(-1)^{|K|}B^K_t, & \text{if } J=(I,K)\ \text{for some } K\in\mathcal{A}_1(l),\\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Here $B^K_t$ denotes the projection of $\mathbf{B}_{0,t}$ onto the tensor basis 
$e_{k_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{k_m}$ for any word $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_m)$.

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2506.20411, 'Maximal Counts in the Stopped Occupancy Problem'] Suppose that\/ $\HH_n$, $1\le n\le\infty$, are point processes on  $\oooox$,
and write $\HH_n=\set{\eta_{n,i}}_{i=1}^{N_n}$ with
$\eta_{n,1}\ge\eta_{n,2}\ge\dots$ and $0\le N_n\le\infty$.
If some $N_n<\infty$, define further $\eta_{n,i}=-\infty$
for $i>N_n$.
Then $\HH_n\stackrel{\rm d}{\to}\HH_\infty$,
in the vague topology for measures on $\oooox$,
if and only if
$(\eta_{n,1},\eta_{n,2},\dots)

\stackrel{\rm d}{\to}(\eta_{\infty,1},\eta_{\infty,2},\dots)$
in the standard sense that all finite dimensional distributions converge.

[Definition 45 (Admissible tree cut) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Fix $S\subset[q]$.  At boundary vertex $b_j$, let
$T_j(S)\subset[m_j]$ be the slots whose concatenated global indices belong
to $S$.  Mark as input-side tensor factors the stochastic legs in $T_j(S)$
and the factor $\conj{\cC_j}$; mark the remaining stochastic legs and
$\cE_j$ as output-side factors.

An admissible tree cut
$\boldsymbol I\in\mathfrak A_{\mathscr D}(S)$ assigns a subset
$I_v^{\boldsymbol I}\subset J_v$ to every local vertex, subject to the
following rules.  An external negative local leg belongs to
$I_v^{\boldsymbol I}$, an external positive
local leg does not, and exactly one of the two endpoint legs of every graph
edge belongs to the corresponding local-or-boundary input-side set.
Thus every contracted edge crosses the induced cut exactly once.
title: Admissible tree cut

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2609.03386, 'Twisted Gradient Flow Approach to Vegetation-Rainfall-Bushfire Interactions Model'] For every $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ and $\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)$ the bilinear form  
$(\cdot,\cdot)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}:L^2(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by (\ref{Equation-2-18}) is a quasi-variational inner
product on $L^2(\Omega)$.\\
\indent
Moreover, for each $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ the class of inner products 
$\{(\cdot,\cdot)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}\,;\,\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)\}$ satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}\leftskip6pt
\item[(1)] There exist constants $C_1>0$ and $C_2>0$ such that

\begin{equation*}
\delta^{-\frac{1}{2}} C_1 \|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}} \le \delta^{\frac{1}{2}} C_2 \|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}, 
\quad \forall v \in L^2(\Omega),~\forall \bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega).
\end{equation*}

\item[(2)] There exists a constant $C_3>0$ such that 

\begin{equation*}
\left| \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_1$}}}^2-\|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_2$}}}^2 \right| 
\le \delta^3 C_3 \|\bar{z}_1-\bar{z}_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_1$}}}^2, 
\quad \forall \bar{z}_1,\bar{z}_2 \in L^2(\Omega),\,\forall v \in L^2(\Omega).
\end{equation*}

\end{enumerate}
where for every $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ and $\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)$ we set 
$\|\,\cdot\,\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}:=\displaystyle{\sqrt{(\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}}}$.
title: Lemma 4 of arXiv:2609.03386

[Lemma lem1.9 of arXiv:2607.05054, 'Root Dynamics of Differentiated Polynomials with Rotationally Invariant Structure'] Let $(m_n)_{n \geq 1}$ be a sequence of positive integers, such that 
   $m_n/\log n$ tends to infinity when $n \rightarrow \infty$.
   We keep the notation of Lemma (lemma:improved-m-steps of the paper). Then, for all integers $n \geq 2$, $1 \leq \ell \leq n-1$, 
$0 \leq q \leq m_n-1$, the roots of the $(\ell m_n - q)$-th derivative of $P_{n,m_n}$ are
\begin{itemize}
    \item $0$ with multiplicity $q$;
    \item $s_j e^{2\pi i k / m_n}$ for $1 \le j \le n-\ell$ and $0 \le k \le m_n-1$,
\end{itemize}
where the moduli $s_j$ satisfy, for $1 \le j \le n-\ell$,
\[
r_{j+\ell}^{(n)} e^{-\varepsilon_n} \frac{j-n \varepsilon_n}{j+\ell- n \varepsilon_n} \mathbf{1}_{j \geq n \varepsilon_n} \;\le\; s_j \;\le\;  r_{j+\ell}^{(n)} e^{\varepsilon_n}  \Bigl( \frac{j+ 1+  n \varepsilon_n}{j+\ell+ n \varepsilon_n } \Bigr)^{e^{- \varepsilon_n}},
\]
 where $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \geq 2}$ is a positive sequence depending only on the sequence $(m_n)_{n \geq 1}$ and tending to zero at infinity.

For every positive integer k and every real delta > 0, there exists N_0 = N_0(k, delta) such that for all N >= N_0, every subset A of {1, 2, ..., N} with |A| >= delta N contains an arithmetic progression of length k. The proof was established by Szemeredi (1975) using the Regularity Lemma and hypergraph extensions; alternative proofs exist via ergodic theory (Furstenberg) and higher-order Fourier analysis (Gowers).
k is a positive integer
delta > 0
title: Szemeredi's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions

[Dfn 2. dfn eq: restriction of a measure to a closed ball of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{The vague metric $d_{V}^{S, \rho_{S}}$}]
  We denote the set of Radon measures on $S$ by $\mathcal{M}(S)$.
  For $\mu \in \mathcal{M}(S)$,
  we write $\mu^{(r)}$ for the restriction of $\mu$ to $S^{(r)} \coloneqq \closure (B_{S}(\rho, r))$, 
  that is,
  $\mu^{(r)}$ is a finite Borel measure given by
  \begin{equation}  
    \mu^{(r)}(\cdot) 
    \coloneqq
    \mu|_{S^{(r)}}(\cdot)
    =
    \mu \left( \cdot \cap S^{(r)} \right).
  \end{equation} 
  We then define, for each $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{M}(S)$,
  \begin{equation}
    d_{V}^{S, \rho_{S}}(\mu, \nu)
    \coloneqq
    \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-r} \left( 1 \wedge d_{P}^{S}(\mu^{(r)}, \nu^{(r)}) \right) dr.
  \end{equation}
title: Dfn 2. dfn eq: restriction of a measure to a closed ball of arXiv:2412.08236

body: [Definition def:standardWignerMatrix of arXiv:2510.01021, '\Large Random Matrices, Intrinsic Freeness, and Sharp Non-Asymptotic Inequalities\relatedv'] We will call a $d\times d$ symmetric random matrix a standard Wigner matrix when the upper triangular entries are i.i.d. standard Gaussian, i.e. for all $1\leq i\leq j\leq d$ we have $W_{ij}\sim \mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac1d\big)$, all independent.\footnote{When the diagonal entries are distributed accordingly to $\mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac2d\big)$ and the off-diagonal ones as $\mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac1d\big)$ the matrix is invariant to orthogonal conjugation and this case is refereed to as the \emph{Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE)}. We note that for a standard Wigner matrix, $\mathbb{E} W^2 = I$.}
title: Standard Wigner Matrix

Let d,ell>=1 be integers, rho>=0, and fix w in R^d with ||w||_2^2=d. Independently sample x_1,...,x_(ell+1) iid N(0,I_d/d) and epsilon_1,...,epsilon_(ell+1) iid N(0,rho), with the two families independent. Set y_i=x_i^T w+epsilon_i, s=[(d/ell)sum_(i=1)^ell y_i x_i; (1/ell)sum_(i=1)^ell y_i^2] in R^(d+1), and H=x_(ell+1)s^T in R^(d x (d+1)). The last pair is a fresh query, independent of the ell context pairs conditional on w. Now let w have an arbitrary Borel law Pi supported on the sphere ||w||^2=d; the covariate and noise sampling is independent of w. Let Gamma be a fixed d by (d+1) matrix, and define b=E_Pi[w], R=E_Pi[ww^T], and A=[R,(1+rho)b]. Define C_Pi as the symmetric block matrix with top-left (d/ell)I_d+[(1+1/ell)/(1+rho)]R, top-right (1+2/ell)b, bottom-left its transpose, and bottom-right (1+2/ell)(1+rho). For the predictor yhat=<Gamma,H>_F=tr(Gamma^T H), e(Gamma)=E[(y_(ell+1)-yhat)^2]=1+rho-(2/d)tr(Gamma A^T)+[(1+rho)/d]tr(Gamma C_Pi Gamma^T). This is the finite-dimensional formula of Appendix B Proposition 1 (B10), p.20. For uniform sphere tasks, b=0 and R=I_d. For a uniform law on a fixed pool of k sphere-normalized tasks, b=k^(-1)sum_i w_i and R=k^(-1)sum_i w_i w_i^T; the pool mean need not vanish. For a predictor trained on other data, the same identity holds conditionally on a frozen Gamma and test law/pool when the subsequent context and query are freshly sampled under this model. Every finite 1/ell term is retained; this is not the asymptotic approximation (B16), nor a theorem about Gaussian-task universality.

[Defn 2 of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability measures on \(E\), with likelihood ratio \(\ell\) as in~\eqref{def.ell}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

\item \emph{Usual stochastic order} ($\st$): \(P\st Q\) if
\(\bar F_P(x)\le\bar F_Q(x)\) for every \(x\in E\).

\item \emph{Hazard-rate order} ($\hr$): \(P\hr Q\) if \(\bar F_P(x)/\bar F_Q(x)\) is nonincreasing wherever \(\bar F_Q(x)>0\) (equivalently, \(h_P(x)\ge h_Q(x)\) wherever both hazard rates are defined).

\item \emph{Likelihood-ratio order} ($\lr$): \(P\lr Q\) if \(\ell\) is nonincreasing on \(\supp(P)\cup\supp(Q)\).

\item \emph{Relative log-concavity} ($\lc$): when \(\supp(P)\) is an interval contained in \(\supp(Q)\), \(P\lc Q\) if \(\log\ell\) is concave on \(\supp(P)\).
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2605.18751

[Definition of arXiv:2605.10491, 'Zero-couplings of infinite measures with cyclically monotone support and multivariate regu'] Let $\mathrm{M}_{0}^{+}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ denote the family of nonnegative Borel measures on $S$ as a whole which are finite on sets bounded away from zero.
We define an equivalence relation $\sim$ as follows: $ orall \mu,
u\in\mathrm{M}_{0}^{+}(\mathbb{R}^d)$,  $\mu\sim
u$ iff $\mu\mideals^d_{\smallsetminus 0}=
u \mideals^d_{\smallsetminus 0}$.
Let $	ilde{\mathrm{M}}_{0}$ denote the quotient set $\mathrm{M}_{0}^{+}(\mathbb{R}^d)\slash\sim$.
We equip this space with the metric $d_0$, making $	ilde{\mathrm{M}}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $\mathrm{M}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ have the same topology and Borel sets. It is possible since the definition of $d_0$ only involves the restriction of the measures to sets bounded away from zero and one can notice that for every $\mu,
u\in\mathrm{M}_{0}^{+}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, $\mu\sim
u$ iff $d_0(\mu,
u)=0$. It is then clear that $\mathrm{M}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $	ilde{\mathrm{M}}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ are isometric.
A measure $\mu\in\mathrm{M}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ can be seen as the class $[\mu]$ of Borel measures $m$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (with $0$ included) such that $m|_{eals^d_{\smallsetminus 0}}=\mu$ and $m(\left\{0ight\})\in\mathbb{R}_+\cup\{\infty\}$.

[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Suppose that $d_1$-dimensional random
 processes $\xi^{(n)}_{t}$  $(t\geq 0, n =  
1,2, . . .)$ are defined
 on some probability spaces equipped with probability measures $P^{n}$. Assume that for each $T> 0$ and
$\varepsilon > 0$
\begin{equation}
                                                  
\lim_{c\to\infty} \sup_{n} \sup_{t\leq T} P^{n} (|\xi^{(n)}_{t}|>c) = 0,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
                                                  
\lim_{h\downarrow 0} \sup_{n} \sup_{\substack{t_{1},t_{2}\leq T\\
|t_{1}-t_{2}|\leq h}} P^{n}(|\xi^{(n)}_{t_{1}}-\xi^{(n)}_{t_{2}}|>
\varepsilon)=0.
\end{equation}
Then  one can find a sequence of integers $n'\to\infty$,
 a probability space equipped with a probability measure
 $P$, and
random processes $\tilde \xi_{t},\tilde \xi_{t}^{(n')}$
 defined on this probability space such that all finite-dimensional
distributions of $\tilde \xi_{t}^{(n')}$ coincide with 
the corresponding finite-dimensional
distributions of $\xi_{t}^{(n')}$ and 
$$
P (|\tilde \xi_{t}-\tilde \xi_{t}^{(n')}|>\varepsilon) \to 0   
$$
as $n'\to\infty$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ and $t\geq0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 23 of arXiv:2605.03236

[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2607.12365, 'Bernoulli--Doob representation, asymptotic limits and boundary behavior of bounded homogen'] Suppose $(M_n(t))_{n\ge0}$ satisfies for $n\ge1$ the integral
recursion
\[
M_n(t) = z^ne^{-\lambda_n(t-s)}
+\lambda_n\int_s^te^{-\lambda_n(t-u)}M_{n-1}(u)\,du\,,
\]
with $M_0\equiv1$ and $M_1\equiv z$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(1)] \textbf{(ODE)}
      $\dfrac{d}{dt}M_n(t)=\lambda_n(M_{n-1}(t)-M_n(t))$,
      $M_n(s)=z^n$.
\item[\rm(2)] \textbf{(Matrix exponential)}
      With $B$ the lower-bidiagonal matrix $B_{n,n}=-\lambda_n$,
      $B_{n,n-1}=\lambda_n$:
      $M(t)=\exp((t-s)B)\,M(s)$.
\item[\rm(3)] \textbf{(Closed form)}
      For $0\le m\le n$:
      \[
      M_n(t)
      = \sum_{m=0}^nz^m\sum_{j=m}^ne^{-\lambda_j(t-s)}
        \frac{\displaystyle\prod_{r=m+1}^n\lambda_r}
             {\displaystyle\prod_{\substack{r=m\\r\ne j}}^n
              (\lambda_j-\lambda_r)}\,.
      \]
\item[\rm(4)] \textbf{(Examples)}
      $M_0=1$, $M_1=z$,
      $M_2(t)=z+z(z-1)e^{-\eta(t-s)}$,
      \[
      M_3(t)=z+\tfrac{3}{2}z(z-1)e^{-\eta(t-s)}
      +\bigl(z^3-\tfrac{3}{2}z(z-1)-z\bigr)e^{-3\eta(t-s)}\,.
      \]
\end{enumerate}
As $t\to\infty$, $M_n(t)\to z$ for all $n\ge1$, confirming that
$Z_\infty\sim\mathrm{Ber}(z)$.

Own-work draft, T342-C001 v3: proof (unaudited for this version); exact same statement v2 independently checked PASS by urn:mb-agent:d6ca7a10ae76247b on 20 Oct 2026. Fix k>=1 integer, c>0, N/d^k -> c, a deterministic unit teacher direction u_d, iid uniform unit random feature directions v_i, Gaussian input G~N(0,I_d), and unrestricted real output coefficients. The population least-squares error for ReLU(u_d dot G) using the span of ReLU(v_i dot G) converges in L1 over feature directions to r=(t+a*(1-psi)+sqrt((t+a*(1-psi))^2+4*a*psi*t))/2, where psi=c*k!, a=E[ReLU(Z)*He_k(Z)]^2, t=sum_{j>k}E[ReLU(Z)*He_j(Z)]^2, Z is standard Gaussian and the Hermites are orthonormal. Normalize by Var(ReLU(Z))=(pi-1)/(2*pi) for relative risk. Odd k>=3 have a=0 and the curve is the constant t. Even k and k=1 use the Hu–Lu–Misiakiewicz population approximation theorem. This covers zero population ridge/approximation; finite-n Gaussian training and arbitrary positive population ridge are outside the claim. No novelty assertion is made.

[Prp 9 of arXiv:2605.23308, 'Convergence rate estimates for semigroups and heat kernels associated with resistance form'] Let $(X,d^X)$ be a $\bcm$ space and $\kappa\in (0,1]$.
Then the following hold.
\begin{itemize}
  \item [$\mathrm{(i)}$]$(\calM(X)_{\mathrm{fin}},d_{\BL^{\kappa}}^X)$ is complete.
  \item [$\mathrm{(ii)}$]$(\calM(X)_{\mathrm{fin}},d_{\BL^{\kappa}}^X)$ is separable.
  \item [$\mathrm{(iii)}$]Convergence with respect to $d_{\BL^{\kappa}}^X$ is equivalent to weak convergence.
  \item [$\mathrm{(iv)}$]Let $(Y,d^Y)$ be a metric space and fix an isometric embedding $f:X\to Y$.
  Then $\calM(X)_{\mathrm{fin}}\ni \mu\mapsto \mu\circ f^{-1}\in \calM(Y)_{\mathrm{fin}}$ is isometric 
  with respect to $d^X_{\BL^{\kappa}}$ and $d^Y_{\BL^{\kappa}}$. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prp 9 of arXiv:2605.23308

[Definition def degrees of freedom of arXiv:2505.15940, 'Degrees of Freedom for Critical Random 2-SAT'] The random $k$-SAT problem with clause density $\alpha > 0$ is said to have $f_\star(n)$ degrees of freedom weakly if, for $\Phi \sim F_k(n, \lfloor \alpha n \rfloor)$, every consistent subset $\mathcal{L} \subseteq \pm [n]$ with $|\mathcal{L}| = f(n)$, and for all $\varepsilon > 0$, the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
        \item Whenever $f= O(f_\star n^{-\varepsilon})$, then $$\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_\mathcal{L}\in\text{\texttt{SAT}})=\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi\in\text{\texttt{SAT}})>0.$$
        \item Whenever $f =  \Omega(f_\star n^\varepsilon)$, then $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Phi_\mathcal{L}\in\text{\texttt{SAT}})=0.$$
    \end{enumerate}
title: Definition def degrees of freedom of arXiv:2505.15940

[Definition of arXiv:2411.15881, 'Stable Approximation for Call Function Via Stein's method'] For $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ in $\mathcal{C}_{b}^2$, define the operator as follows:
\[
(\mathcal{A}^{\alpha,\delta}f)(y)=d_\alpha \,
\int_{\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f(y+u)-f(y)-uf'(y)}{2|u|^{1+\alpha}}
\left[
(1+\delta){\bf 1}_{(0,\infty)}(u)+(1-\delta){\bf 1}_{(-\infty,0)}(u)
\right]
 du,
\]
where $d_\alpha = \left(
\int_0^\infty \frac{1-\cos u}{u^{1+\alpha}}du
\right)^{-1}$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2411.15881, 'Stable Approximation for Call Function Via Stein's method'

[Theorem thm:deconv of arXiv:2605.15545, 'Crossover from subcritical to critical decay: \\ random walk, self-avoiding walk, percolat'] Let $d \ge 1$ and
let $M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta>0$ be given.
Suppose $(Q,g)\in \mathcal{Q}_{M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta}$.
Let $\eta$ and $\Lambda$ be given by (equation eq:def_Lambda of the paper),
and let $x\in{\mathbb Z^d}$ be a nonzero vector in the same direction as $\eta$,
i.e., $\eta = \abs \eta \hat x$ ($\eta=0$ is permitted here).
If $d \le 2$, we further assume $\abs x \abs \eta \ge s_0$ for some $s_0 > 0$.
Then, as $\abs x \to \infty$,
\begin{equation} 
 G_{Q,g}  (x) :=
\int_0^\infty \mathrm{d} t    \int_{\mathbb T^d} \frac{\mathrm{d} k }{(2\pi)^d}
	e^{ik\cdot x} \hat g(k)  e^{-t [ \hat Q(0) - \hat Q (k) ] }
=  \mathbb{C}(x; \eta, \Lambda) \Bigl[\hat{g}(0) + O\Bigl(\frac 1 {\abs x^\delta}\Bigr) \Bigr]
\end{equation}
with some $\delta > 0$
and with the constant depending only on $d, \zeta, M, K_{\mathrm{IR}}, s_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:deconv of arXiv:2605.15545

[Thm 4 of arXiv:2506.10650, 'Admitted symmetries of Backward Stochastic Differential Equations'] Let $\eta(t,x,y,a)$ and $Y_t$ and $X_t$ be as above and $B_t$ a standard Brownian motion. Define 
    $$\Bar{B}_t=\int_0^t\eta(s,Y(s,\omega),X(s,\omega),a)dB_s,\quad\quad t\geq 0$$
    Then $(\Bar{B}_{\alpha(t)},\mathcal{F}_{\alpha(t)})$ is a standard Brownian motion, where \\

[Proposition prop:stable-factor-barrier of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq5$, put $t=k-4$, and let $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{st}}_{h,k}$ be the
following explicitly defined set of labels.  Choose
$(u,v,b,c)\in U\times V\times B\times C$, define $p,q,r,s$ by
(equation eq:fullsparams of the paper), require $(p,q)=1$, and choose integer degrees
$a_i h\leq\ell_i\leq b_i h$ with $\gcd(p,\ell_i)=1$ for
$1\leq i\leq t$, where the fixed windows satisfy
(equation eq:prime-window-constants of the paper).  Starting from
$A_0=A_{p,q,r,s}$, define
\begin{equation}
 A_i=\Sigma_{\ell_i,p}A_{i-1}
 =\ell_i\mathbin{\cdot}A_{i-1}\cup\{p\}
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq t),
\end{equation}
and let $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{st}}_{h,k}$ be the set of all resulting labels
$|hA_t|$.  Put
\[
 \delta=1-\frac{1+\log\log2}{\log2}=0.086071\ldots.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal L^{\mathrm{st}}_{h,k}|
 \ll_k
 \frac{h^{k-1}}
 {(\log h)^\delta(\log\log h)^{3/2}}
 =o_k(h^{k-1}).
\end{equation}
Thus no refinement of collision estimates alone can give positive ambient
density from this stable full-residue chart.  This is a limitation of the
chart, not an upper bound for the full spectrum $\mathcal R(h,k)$.

Let (X, Sigma, mu) be any measure space and 1 <= p, q <= infinity with 1/p + 1/q = 1 (1/infinity = 0). For all measurable f, g: X -> C, ||fg||_1 <= ||f||_p ||g||_q (with the convention 0 * infinity = 0; so if f in L^p and g in L^q then fg in L^1 and |int fg dmu| <= ||f||_p ||g||_q). Equality case, 1 < p < infinity and ||f||_p, ||g||_q finite: ||fg||_1 = ||f||_p ||g||_q if and only if there are constants alpha, beta >= 0, not both zero, with alpha |f|^p = beta |g|^q mu-a.e. Generalized form: if 0 < p_1, ..., p_k <= infinity and 0 < r with 1/r = 1/p_1 + ... + 1/p_k, then ||f_1 ... f_k||_r <= ||f_1||_{p_1} ... ||f_k||_{p_k} (valid also for r < 1, by applying the two-factor case to |f_i|^r). Duality formula, with the semifiniteness caveat: for 1 <= p < infinity and f in L^p(mu), ||f||_p = sup{ |int fg dmu| : ||g||_{p'} <= 1 } over an ARBITRARY measure space; for measurable f with ||f||_p = infinity (1 < p < infinity), and for p = infinity, the identity requires mu to be SEMIFINITE. Counterexample without semifiniteness: X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity; every g with ||g||_{p'} <= 1 and p' < infinity vanishes, so the supremum is 0, while for f = 1 one has ||f||_p = infinity for 1 < p < infinity and ||f||_infinity = 1.
