body:
[Lemma HS-kernel of arXiv:2608.21805, 'Logarithmic derivatives of variational and singular stochastic partial differential equati'] Suppose that $\Phi$ belongs to $\mathbb{D}^{1,p}(L^2([0,t]; L_2(U,H)))$ for some exponent $p \geq 2$. Then the following four statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For each deterministic $z \in H$, $\Phi^* z \in \mathbb{D}^{1,p}(H_W) \subset \operatorname{Dom}(\delta_U)$, with
\[
  \lVert \Phi^* z \rVert_{\mathbb{D}^{1,p}(H_W)} \leq \lVert z \rVert_H\,\lVert \Phi \rVert_{\mathbb{D}^{1,p}(L^2([0,t];L_2(U,H)))}.
\]
\item The linear map $\phi_\Phi: H \ni z \mapsto \delta_U(\Phi^* z) \in L^2(\Omega; \mathbb{R})$ is Hilbert--Schmidt from $H$ to $L^2(\Omega; \mathbb{R})$, with
\[
  \lVert \phi_\Phi \rVert_{\mathrm{HS}(H,\,L^2(\Omega))} \;\leq\; C_{\mathrm{Meyer}}\,\lVert \Phi \rVert_{\mathbb{D}^{1,2}(L^2([0,t]; L_2(U,H)))},
\]
for an absolute constant $C_{\mathrm{Meyer}} > 0$ from the Meyer inequality~[nualart2006malliavin].
\item By the canonical isomorphism $\mathrm{HS}(H, L^2(\Omega)) \cong L^2(\Omega; H)$, there exists a unique \emph{kernel} $\mathcal{K}_\Phi \in L^2(\Omega; H)$, denoted symbolically $\mathcal{K}_\Phi = \int_0^t\Phi_r\,\delta W_r$ (the $H$-valued Skorokhod integral), such that
\begin{equation}
  \delta_U(\Phi^* z) \;=\; \ip{z}{\mathcal{K}_\Phi}_H \qquad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s., for every deterministic } z \in H.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\mathcal{K}_\Phi \in L^p(\Omega; H)$ with
\[
  \norm{\mathcal{K}_\Phi}_{L^p(\Omega; H)} \leq C_{p,\mathrm{Meyer}}\,\lVert \Phi \rVert_{\mathbb{D}^{1,p}(L^2([0,t]; L_2(U,H)))}.
\]
\item For every jointly $\mathcal{F}_t \otimes \mathcal{B}(H)$-measurable $Z: \Omega \to H$, the pointwise-in-$\omega$ evaluation of the linear functional $z \mapsto \delta_U(\Phi^* z)$ at $z = Z(\omega)$ is given by
\begin{equation}
  \bigl[\delta_U(w^{\mathrm{lin}}(\cdot)(z))\bigr]_{z = Z}(\omega) \;:=\; \ip{Z(\omega)}{\mathcal{K}_\Phi(\omega)}_H \qquad \text{for }\mathbb{P}\text{-a.e.\ } \omega,
\end{equation}
where $w^{\mathrm{lin}}_r(z) := \Phi_r^* z$ denotes the linear random field. The right-hand side of~(equation eq:HS-kernel-random of the paper) is the substitution value appearing in the linear-field identity of Theorem~(thm:linear-sub-D12 of the paper), and differs from $\delta_U(w^{\mathrm{lin}}(\cdot)(Z)) = \delta_U(\Phi^* Z)$ (the Skorokhod integral of the composed, genuinely anticipating process) by the classical Nualart trace correction $\int_0^t\operatorname{Tr}_U[\Phi_r^*\,\mathcal{D}_r Z]\,\mathrm{d}r$ whenever $Z \in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}(H)$.
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition prop:regularity of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Let $(V^1,V^2)$ be the limit process of Theorem~(thm:main-final of the paper), set
$H_i:=\alpha_i-\tfrac12\in(0,\tfrac12)$, and write
\[
V^1=b_1+\mathcal S^1,
\qquad
V^2=b_2+\mathcal Z+\mathcal S^2,
\]
where
$\mathcal S^i_t=\nu_i\int_0^tK_i(t-u)\sqrt{V^i_u}\,d\beta^i_u$ are the
self parts and
$\mathcal Z_t=\gamma_{12}\nu_1\int_0^tL_{12}(t-u)\sqrt{V^1_u}\,d\beta^1_u$
is the inherited part.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(a)}] Almost surely, $V^i$ is H\"older continuous on $[0,1]$
of every order $\gamma<H_i$, for $i=1,2$.
\item[\textup{(b)}] Almost surely, the inherited part $\mathcal Z$ is
H\"older continuous of every order
$\gamma<\bigl(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\tfrac12\bigr)\wedge1$; since
$\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\tfrac12>\alpha_2-\tfrac12$, the roughness of $V^2$ is
carried entirely by its self part $\mathcal S^2$.
\item[\textup{(c)}] The exponents are sharp in the mean-square sense: for
every $s_0\in(0,1)$ there are constants $0<c\le C<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
c\,(t-s)^{2H_i}
\ \le\
\mathbb{E}\bigl[(V^i_t-V^i_s)^2\bigr]
\ \le\
C\,(t-s)^{2H_i},
\qquad
s_0\le s<t\le1,
\end{equation}
where the upper bound holds for all $0\le s<t\le1$.  In particular, for
every $\gamma>H_i$,
$\sup_{s_0\le s<t\le1}\mathbb{E}[(V^i_t-V^i_s)^2]/(t-s)^{2\gamma}=\infty$, so the
regularity in~\textup{(a)} cannot be improved: $H_i$ is the exact
mean-square H\"older exponent of $V^i$.
\end{enumerate}

Let $\tilde q_* = q_0$, so that condition~\ref{it:8.2} is satisfied, and $(\tilde p,\tilde \zeta,\tilde \zeta^\Ising) = (p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$. We will couple $\tilde{X}(q_0)=X(q_*)$ and 
$\tilde{Y}(q_0)=Y(q_*)$.

[Lemma lem:BBG-lem5 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:Wass of the paper) hold. Then, for every $N\ge2$ and every initial
configuration $(x^N_1(0),\ldots,x^N_N(0))\in(\mathbb R^d)^N$, the
$N$-particle SVGD system~(equation eq:svgd-continuous of the paper) associated with the kernel (equation eq:bilinear-matern-kernel of the paper)
has a unique global classical solution. Moreover, there exists
$C\in(0,\infty)$ such that, for all $T>0$,
\[
        \int_0^T \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \|x^N_i(t)\|^2\,dt
        \le
        CT+\frac{C}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N V(x^N_i(0)).
\]
Further, under the initialization in Assumption~(ass:Wass of the paper),
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{N\ge2}
        \mathbb E\left[\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N V(x^N_i(0))\right]
        <\infty .
\end{equation}
The corresponding mean-field equation (equation eq:mf-svgd of the paper)
is globally defined in the weak continuity-equation sense and satisfies, for all
$T>0$,
\[
        \int_0^T \int_{\mathbb R^d}\|x\|^2\,\mu_t(dx)\,dt
        \le
        CT+ C\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)\,\mu_0(dx) < \infty.

[Lemma lem:delta1-delta2-reduction of arXiv:2604.07711, 'Central Limit Theorem for Random Partial\\ Sphere Coverings in High Dimensions'] Let $U_1,U_2$ be independent random points on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with distribution $\sigma$, and define
\[
    p_N := \mathbb{P}\big(C_N(U_1)\cap C_N(U_2)\neq\varnothing\big).
\]
Then
\[
    \delta_1\le \frac{4}{N^4}\,p_N
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \delta_2\le \frac{16}{N^4}\,p_N^2.
\]

body:
[Lemma lma:realformsign of arXiv:2608.26564, 'Real ideal points, Conway spheres, and left-orderable Dehn fillings'] Let $R_\theta = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item If $A = G(\varepsilon \left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&s\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right))G^{-1}$ with $\varepsilon = \pm 1$, $s \neq 0$, and $G = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} g_{11} & g_{12} \\ g_{21} & g_{22} \end{smallmatrix}\right) \in GL_2(\mathbb{R})$, then $\mathfrak{d}(A) = \varepsilon s(g_{11}^2 + g_{21}^2)/\det G$. In particular, $\mathfrak{d} \neq 0$ on noncentral parabolic matrices, and two noncentral parabolic matrices of the same trace are $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$-conjugate if and only if their $\mathfrak{d}$-signs agree.
	\item If $A = GR_\theta G^{-1}$ with $0 < \theta < \pi$, then $\mathfrak{d}(A) = -\sin\theta\,(g_{11}^2 + g_{12}^2 + g_{21}^2 + g_{22}^2)/\det G$. In particular $\mathfrak{d} \neq 0$ on elliptic matrices, and two elliptic matrices of the same trace are $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$-conjugate if and only if their $\mathfrak{d}$-signs agree.
	\item The sign of $\mathfrak{d}$ on an elliptic matrix depends only on its rotation direction: if $\operatorname{tr} A = 2\cos\theta_A$ with $0 < \theta_A < \pi$, then $\mathfrak{d}(A) < 0$ if and only if the projective action of $A$ has rotation number $\theta_A/\pi$, and $\mathfrak{d}(A) > 0$ if and only if it has rotation number $-\theta_A/\pi$.
	\item For $\Omega = \mathrm{Ad}_{\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)}$, we have $\mathfrak{d}(\Omega(A)) = -\mathfrak{d}(A)$.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition prop:tailrl-closed-form-weights of arXiv:2609.02987, 'Tail Likelihood Reinforcement Learning'] For every $i=1,\ldots,N$,
\begin{equation}
\omega\bigl(r_{(i)}\bigr)
=
\sum_{k=1}^{i}
\frac{r_{(k)}-r_{(k-1)}}{N-k+1}.

\end{equation}
Equivalently, all weights follow the recurrence
\begin{equation}
\omega\bigl(r_{(i)}\bigr)
=
\omega\bigl(r_{(i-1)}\bigr)
+
\frac{r_{(i)}-r_{(i-1)}}{N-i+1},
\qquad
\omega\bigl(r_{(0)}\bigr)=0.

\end{equation}
title: Closed-form empirical weights

body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable map $T: X \to X$ is measure-preserving if $\mu(T^{-1} A) = \mu(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{B}$ (preimages, not images: $T$ need not be injective, and for non-invertible $T$ the condition $\mu(TA) = \mu(A)$ is neither implied nor required). The system is a probability-preserving system when $\mu(X) = 1$. A set $A$ is (strictly) invariant if $T^{-1}A = A$, and invariant mod $\mu$ if $\mu(T^{-1}A \,\triangle\, A) = 0$; every set invariant mod $\mu$ differs from a strictly invariant set by a null set. $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure; equivalently (for a probability measure) every measurable $f$ with $f \circ T = f$ a.e. is a.e. constant; equivalently every set $A$ with $T^{-1}A \subset A$ mod $\mu$ (or $T^{-1}A \supset A$ mod $\mu$) has measure 0 or 1. The invariant $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{I} = \{A : T^{-1}A = A\}$ is what the ergodic averages converge to conditional expectations onto. Ergodicity is not the same as mixing (mixing implies ergodic, not conversely: an irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing), and it is not preserved by passing to powers ($T^2$ may fail to be ergodic when $T$ is, e.g. the rotation by $1/2$ on two points).
T is measurable
invariance is expressed through preimages T^{-1}A
title: Measure-preserving transformation; ergodicity

[Corollary cor:1d_case of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be scalar random variables satisfying assumptions of Theorem~(thm:martingale of the paper) with
    \[
    \sigma^2_i \coloneqq \E [X^2_i | \mathscr{F}_{i-1}],
    \quad
    U_i \coloneqq \norm*{(X_i)_{+} | \mathscr{F}_{i-1}}_{\psi_{\alpha}}.
    \]
    Fix $\sigma > 0$, $U \ge K > 0$ and define the event
    \begin{equation}
    
        E \coloneqq \lrc{\sum^n_{i = 1} \sigma_i^2 \le \sigma^2, \quad
        \sum^n_{i = 1} U^{2}_i \le U^2, \quad
        \max_{i \in [n]} U_i \le K}.
    \end{equation}
    Then, with probability at least $1 - \mathbb{P}(E) - e^{-\mathrm{x}}$,
    \begin{equation}
        \max_{k \in [n]} \sum^k_{i=1} X_i \le \sigma \sqrt{2 \mathrm{x}} + \frac{4 Kz \mathrm{x}}{\min\left\{2 \alpha z^{\alpha},\, \hspace{0.2em}\underline{\log}\hspace{0.2em} \left(\left( \frac{Kz}{\sigma}\right)^2 \mathrm{x} \right)  \right\}}.
    \end{equation}
   The same holds for (equation res:ber of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.15874, '2608.15874'] Let $(M_n,\cF_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a martingale in $\cH$ with $M_0=0$ and increments
\[
  X_n=M_n-M_{n-1},
  \qquad
  \E[X_n\mid\cF_{n-1}]=0,
  \qquad
  \norm{X_n}\le1\quad\text{a.s.}
\]
Write
\[
  V_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X_i\otimes X_i\mid\cF_{i-1}],
  \qquad n\ge0.
\]
Then, for every $\rho>0$,
\[
  \roundb{U_\rho^h(M_n,V_n)}_{n\ge0}
\]
is a nonnegative supermartingale with initial value one. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\[
V'_i=V_i+aV_k
\]
and, for $\ell\neq i$, $V'_\ell=V_\ell$. Then $V'$ is upper unitriangular and dimension preserving, and
\[
DV'=R.
\]
Thus, $(R,V')$ has exactly the same reduced matrix and the same persistence pairs as $(R,V)$.

Suppose further that the interval $u$ has birth index $i$, dies at $t$, and that the interval $v$ with birth index $k$ survives beyond $t$. If $w_{ur}$ and $w'_{ur}$ denote the transition coefficients before and after the change, then
\[
w'_{uv}=w_{uv}+a
\]
and, for $r\neq v$, $w'_{ur}=w_{ur}$.

body:
On paths 0,...,n, put conductance c_n=1 for odd n and 2 for even n, normalized counting measure, and spatial scale 1/n. Graph metric-measure spaces converge and resistance is between half and all of graph distance. The stationary variable-speed walks accelerated by n^2 have no common limit of finite-dimensional laws: their cosine two-time covariance tends for t>0 to (1/2)exp(-pi^2*t) along odd n and (1/2)exp(-2*pi^2*t) along even n. This weighted-path example diagnoses the need for actual scaled resistance convergence; it is not a counterexample to an IIC scaling limit.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. This weighted-path example diagnoses a reduction, not the unweighted IIC itself.

For each n>=2 take the path with vertices 0,...,n, normalized counting measure and distance |i-j|/n. Put conductance c_n on every edge, with c_n=1 for odd n and c_n=2 for even n. These metric-measure spaces converge to the interval with uniform measure. Effective resistance is |i-j|/c_n, so it is uniformly between half and all of graph distance, yet the resistance distance divided by n has no single limit.

Let the continuous-time variable-speed walk have generator L_n h(i)=c_n*sum_{j adjacent i}(h(j)-h(i)), start in its uniform stationary law, and accelerate time by n^2. Its process laws do not have a single scaling limit along all n.

Proof: the nonconstant eigenfunction u_n(i)=cos(pi*(i+1/2)/(n+1)) has eigenvalue -lambda_n, where lambda_n=2*c_n*(1-cos(pi/(n+1))). Its uniform mean is zero and its uniform second moment is 1/2. Thus

    E[u_n(X_0)*u_n(X_(n^2*t))]=(1/2)*exp(-n^2*lambda_n*t).

u_n is uniformly close to the fixed spatial observable cos(pi*i/n). For any fixed t>0, the displayed bounded two-time expectation tends to (1/2)*exp(-pi^2*t) along odd n and (1/2)*exp(-2*pi^2*t) along even n. A common limit of finite-dimensional laws would force the same bounded continuous expectation, a contradiction. Also the endpoint hitting mean from 0 is n(n+1)/(2*c_n), independently confirming the two time constants.

Every graph here is a tree; both volume and resistance orders are controlled. To use a resistance-form convergence theorem for the IIC one must establish actual scaled resistance and measure convergence, matching embedding and time normalization, rather than replace convergence by constant-factor estimates. The example does not assert that the IIC has this alternation, or that its scaling limit fails.

Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: Compositions of coordinatewise isotone primitive maps remain isotone: if x<=y, first F(x)<=F(y), then G(F(x))<=G(F(y)). Consequently, a policy using an exogenously fixed sequence of the same monotone primitives inherits the comparison. An adaptive scheduler instead selects F_{a(x)} at state x and F_{a(y)} at y; isotonicity of each separate F_a gives no comparison between those two values. In one dimension, F0(x)=x and F1(x)=x+10 are both increasing, but selecting F1 below threshold one and F0 above it makes the chosen map decrease at the threshold. Check: The scalar pair x=0.9,y=1.1 yields outputs 10.9 and 1.1. This disproves the proposed generic inference from branchwise isotonicity, not monotonicity of any named queue discipline. Obstruction: No new non-FCFS discipline is proved monotone. A queue-specific comparison requires controlling policy switches and the admissible arrival order.

body:
[Thm robust of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Suppose $\mathcal{M}$ (resp. $\mathcal{M}_0$) decomposes as $\Theta \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ (resp. $\Theta \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}_0}$), where $\Theta$ is a compact metric space such that $\{\theta\} \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ is an invariant set ((inv-set of the paper)) for every $\theta \in \Theta$.
    
    Fix some $\theta_0 \in \Theta$. Suppose (as1 of the paper)--(as-compact of the paper) hold, except (as-V of the paper)(as-alpha of the paper) is replaced with: ``$\mathcal{L} V$ extends to a continuous function $H: \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}$ and there is a constant $\Lambda < 0$ such that $\sup_{\mu \in P_{inv}(\{\theta_0\} \times \mathcal{M}_0)} \mu H \leq \Lambda < 0$." Then for all $\theta$ sufficiently close to $\theta_0$, the results of (main of the paper) hold on $\{\theta\} \times \mathcal{M}$. To be more specific, let $\{Y_t^x\}_{t \geq 0, x \in \tilde{\mathcal{M}}}$ be the Markov process on $\tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ such that $(\theta, Y_t^x) = X_t^{(\theta,x)}$ (this is well-defined because $\{\theta\} \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ is an invariant set). Then we have:

    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item For all $x \in \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+ \coloneqq \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_0^c$ we have that, almost surely, all limit points $\mu$ of $\tilde{\mu}_t^x \coloneqq (1/t)\int_0^t \delta_{Y_s^x(\omega)}ds$ as $t \to \infty$ satisfy $\mu(\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+) = 1$.
        \item $Y_t$ is stochastically persistent, meaning for all $\epsilon > 0$ there exists a compact set $\mathcal{K}_\epsilon \subset \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+$ such that for all $x \in \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+$ $$\mathbb{P}(\liminf_{t \to \infty} \tilde{\mu}_t^x(\mathcal{K}_\epsilon) \geq 1 - \epsilon) = 1 \,.$$
        \item $P_{inv}(\{\theta\} \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+)$ is nonempty.
    \end{enumerate}

body:
[Conj 8 (\cite{HallEak2025}) of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $b_0$ be an invertible operator in a $W^\ast$-probability space $(\A,\tau)$.  Define
\[ \tilde{p}_0(z) = \tau[|b_0-z|^{-2}] \qquad \& \qquad \tilde{p}_2(z) = \tau[b_0^\ast b_0|b_0-z|^{-2}] \]
where, as usual, for any operator $a\in\A$, $|a|^2:=a^\ast a$.  Define $T(b_0,\cdot)\colon\C\to\R_+$ by
\begin{equation}  T(b_0,z) = \frac{\log(\tilde{p}_2(z))-\log(|z|^2\tilde{p}_0(z))}{\tilde{p}_2(z)-|z|^2\tilde{p}_0(z)}.
\end{equation}
For each $t>0$, define the open precompact set $\Sigma(b_0,t)$ by
\begin{equation}  \Sigma(b_0,t) = \{z\in\C\colon T(b_0,z)<t\}. \end{equation}
Let $b(t,\zeta)$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion (see Notation \ref{notat.ovweparam}) freely independent from $b_0$.  Then the support of the Brown measure of $b_0b(t,\zeta)$ is equal to the image $\overline{\Sigma(b_0,t,\zeta)}$ of $\overline{\Sigma(b_0,t)}$ under the map $\Psi^{b_0}_{t,\zeta}$ of \eqref{eq.Psi}. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: \cite{HallEak2025}

[Defn D: UB-offspring of arXiv:2606.10165, 'The frog model with death and drift on free products of complete graphs'] For $u \in \mathbb{D}_{m,d}$ and $v\in B_{n}(u)$, let $u_0=u < u_1 < \cdots < u_{n-1} < u_{n}=v$, be the unique geodesic connecting $u$ and $v$.
For each $\ell=1, 2, \dots, n-1$, we denote by $\{\m{u_0}{u_{\ell}}\}$ the event that $\{\s{u_0}{u_{\ell}}\} \cap \{\ns{u_0}{u_{\ell+1}}\}$.
We define $\{\cam{u_0}{u_{n}}\}$ inductively as follows
\[\{\cam{u_0}{u_{n}}\}:=\{\s{u_0}{u_{n}}\}\cup\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{n-1}\{\m{u_0}{u_{\ell}}, \cam{u_{\ell}}{u_{n}}\}, \text{for } n \geq 2,\]
with the initial condition $\{\cam{u_0}{u_1}\}:=\{\s{u_0}{u_1}\}$.
In addition, we denote the complement of $\{\cam{u_0}{u_n}\}$ by $\{\ncam{u_0}{u_n}\}$.

Let $\nu_1$ denote the number of offspring of individual 1 (arbitrarily

reproduction for a haploid population  of constant population size
$N$. If 
\be

   \lim_{N\to \infty} \frac{ N\ensuremath{\mathds{E}\left[ (\nu_1)_3 \right]} }{(N)_3 c_N } = 0
\ee
then $\lim_{N\to \infty} c_N = 0$ and  we have convergence to the Kingman
coalescent. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.23887, '2607.23887'] Let $X,Y$ be independent standard real Gaussian random variables and let
$P\in\C[X,Y]$ satisfy $\E(P^m)=0$ for every $m\ge1$. Write $P$ in the
coordinates \eqref{eq:coords}. Then either every monomial occurring in $P$ has
weight at least $1$, or every monomial occurring in $P$ has weight at most
$-1$. Consequently, for every $Q\in\C[X,Y]$,
\[
  \E\bigl(QP^m\bigr)=0 \qquad\text{whenever } m>\deg Q .
\]
In particular $\GMC(2)$ holds, with the explicit threshold $m\ge\deg Q+1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Outer vertex-isoperimetry of regular plane tessellations (18 September 2026) proves that for an infinite (d,f)-regular plane tessellation G with finite d, f >= 3, 1/d + 1/f <= 1/2 and face degree f >= 5, the outer vertex-isoperimetric constant equals the edge-isoperimetric constant: h_V(G) = h_E(G) = (d-2) sqrt(1 - 4/((d-2)(f-2))); in particular h_V(H_{5,5}) = sqrt(5). Together with the triangular and quadrangular cases of Haslegrave and Panagiotis, this answers the finite-faced regular/co-regular part of Question 6.20 of R. Lyons and Y. Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks; arbitrary transitive plane graphs, the further class in the question, are not covered. The proof rests on a general principle: an infinite simple graph of maximum degree Delta has equal edge and outer vertex-isoperimetric constants whenever its edge constant is at least Delta - 3, and the constant 3 is optimal uniformly in the degree. Paper (PDF): https://github.com/yspennstate/outer-vertex-isoperimetry (commit 9dff9a1b89b3); ResearchGate record 414470838. Not refereed.
title: Lyons-Peres Question 6.20 answered for finite-faced regular tessellations: the outer vertex-isoperimetric constant of a (d,f)-regular plane tessellation with f >= 5 is (d-2) sqrt(1 - 4/((d-2)(f-2))) (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/outer-vertex-isoperimetry)

body: [Theo 59 of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] For the ferromagnetic (nearest-neighbor) Ising model in dimension $d \ge 2$, Gaussian concentration holds in the uniqueness regime. In the phase coexistence regime $\beta \ge \beta_c(d)$, it fails for every shift-invariant ergodic Gibbs measure. More precisely, for $\beta < \beta_c(d)$, the unique Gibbs measure $\nu_\beta$ satisfies Gaussian concentration, whereas for $\beta \ge \beta_c(d)$ no shift-invariant ergodic Gibbs measure satisfies Gaussian concentration.

body: For a family p_theta with differentiable log-likelihood, the score is the derivative of log p_theta(X) in theta; it has mean zero under regularity, and the Fisher information I(theta) is its variance, I(theta) = E[(d/dtheta log p_theta(X))^2], equal under further regularity to minus the expected second derivative. For n iid observations the information is n I(theta); information is additive over independent data and measures the local distinguishability of nearby parameters.
title: Fisher Information

When $\beta = 0$ (resp.\ $\beta \neq 0$), we speak of the \textit{untilted} (resp.\ \textit{tilted}) gap process.

X is a real random variable

[Definition 1 (Oriented flattening) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] For $K$ in \eqref{eq:kernel-space} and $S\subset[m]$, regroup the tensor
factors as
\[
 K\in
 \conj{\bigl(\conj{\cH_S}\otimes\cC\bigr)}
 \otimes\bigl(\cH_{S^c}\otimes\cE\bigr).
\]
The corresponding Hilbert--Schmidt operator is the oriented flattening
\begin{equation}

 \Flat_S(K):\conj{\cH_S}\otimes\cC
 \longrightarrow \cH_{S^c}\otimes\cE.
\end{equation}
For $1\le r\le\infty$, define
\begin{equation}

 \Prof_{m,r}(K)
 :=\max_{S\subset[m]}\norm{\Flat_S(K)}_{\Sch_r}.
\end{equation}
For $1\le r<2$, the right-hand side is understood as $+\infty$ if one of
the flattenings does not belong to $\Sch_r$; it is finite on
$\cK_m^{\mathrm{alg}}$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Let K be the wake-and-stabilize kernel on k-particle configurations, and delta=sup_{x,y}TV(K(x,.),K(y,.)). If nu is stationary, convexity gives TV(mu*K,nu)<=delta for every input law mu. Consequently TV(mu,nu)<=TV(mu,mu*K)+delta. Even a proof that delta tends to zero only settles the target once the free-chain law mu is shown nearly invariant under the additional full wake. Check: Write nu=nu*K and integrate TV(K(x,.),K(y,.)) against mu(dx)nu(dy) for the first inequality; apply the triangle inequality for the second. This does not silently replace mu with its one-step image. Obstruction: The approximate wake invariance of the free-chain law and a vanishing Dobrushin coefficient are both unproved here. The reduction identifies the extra distributional obligation.

body:
Let V have n elements and X a random subset. The law of X is invariant under all permutations of V if and only if q(A) = P(A subset of X) depends only on |A|, say q(A) = a_|A|. Then P(|X| = r) = p_r = binom(n, r) sum_{j=0}^{n-r} (-1)^j binom(n - r, j) a_{r+j}, and given |X| = r, X is uniform over the r-subsets. A real sequence a_0, ..., a_n is the profile of some exchangeable random subset if and only if a_0 = 1 and every p_r >= 0, and the law is then unique. Monotonicity is not enough: for n = 2, a = (1, 3/5, 1/10) is nonincreasing in [0, 1] but gives p_0 = -1/10.
V finite with n elements

[Corollary eq:subquadratic-local-cost of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:general-tail-obstruction}
Assume that the distinguished coordinate has law \(\mu\).  Suppose that
for some \(M<\infty\), \(\eta>0\), \(\delta>0\), and a sequence
\(a_k\to\infty\), (equation eq:conditional-remainder-cost of the paper) holds with
\(a=a_k\) for every sufficiently large \(k\), and
\begin{equation}
 \overline I_\mu(a_k,\eta)\le\left(\frac12-\delta\right)a_k^2
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large \(k\), then, for every sufficiently large
\(k\), setting \(B_k=[a_k-M,a_k+\eta+M]\),
\begin{align}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J(B_k)
 &>\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^G(B_k),\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B_k)
 &>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B_k).
 
\end{align}
If the joint coefficient array is invariant in law under global sign
reversal \(J\mapsto-J\), the analogous strict inequality holds for local
minima in \(-B_k\).

[Lem 1 (Lemma 4.7 \& 4.8 of \cite{JX20-a}) of arXiv:2608.30173, '2608.30173'] (i) For every $1\le p<\infty$, we can find a constant $C$ depending only on $n,\Omega,p$ and $u_\infty$ such that
\[
\|f\|_{L^p(\om)} \le C \Big \|\Delta f+\frac{n+2}{n-2} r_\infty u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} f \Big\|_{L^p(\om)}+C \sup_{1\le l\le L} \Big|\int_\om u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} \phi_l f \,\ud x\Big|
\]
for all $f\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$.

(ii) There exists a constant $C$ depending only on $n,\Omega$ and $u_\infty$ such that
\begin{itemize}
\item
\[
\|f\|_{L^{\frac{n+2}{n-2}}(\om)}\le C \Big \| \Pi(\Delta f+\frac{n+2}{n-2}r_\infty u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} f )\Big\|_{L^{\frac{n(n+2)}{n^2+4}}(\om)}+C \sup_{1\le l\le L} \Big|\int_\om u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} \phi_l f \,\ud x \Big|
\]
for all $f\in W^{2,\frac{n(n+2)}{n^2+4}}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,\frac{n(n+2)}{n^2+4}}_0(\Omega)$.
\item
\[
\|f\|_{L^{1}(\om)}\le C \Big \| \Pi(\Delta f+\frac{n+2}{n-2}r_\infty u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} f )\Big\|_{L^{1}(\om)}+C \sup_{1\le l\le L} \Big|\int_\om u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} \phi_l f \,\ud x \Big|
\]
for all $f\in W^{2,1}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,1}_0(\Omega)$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:eta-kappa of arXiv:2411.10419, 'Lower bounds on the top Lyapunov exponent for linear PDEs driven by the 2D stochastic Navi'] For any $ \mathbf{q} > 2$ and $ \kappa \in (0, 1] $, we set $\hat M_i = (M_0 - i) \vee \kappa^{-\mathbf{q}}$ and define the  time $ \eta$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item Set $ \tau_{0} =0 $ and then for every $ i \geqslant 0 $:
\begin{equs}[e:def-tau-sigma-i]
\sigma_{i} &= \inf \{ t \geqslant
\tau_{i}  \; \colon \; M^{(2)}_{t} \geqslant \hat M_i \}\wedge \{ 
\tau_{i} + t_{\star}^{\kappa, \delta} (\hat M_i)\} \;,\\
\tau_{i+1} &= \inf \{ t \geqslant  \tau_{i}  \;\colon \; M_{t} \leqslant \hat M_{i+1}\}  \;,
\end{equs}
where $ t_{\star}^{\kappa, \delta} (M)$ is defined in (equation e:tsd of the paper). 
\item Define $ L = \min \{i \geqslant 0\,:\, \hat M_{i} \leqslant \kappa^{- \mathbf{q}} \}$ and the ``final step'' $i_{\mathrm{fin}}= \min \{ i \geqslant 0  \; \colon \; \sigma_{i} < \tau_{i+1} \} \wedge L$.
\item Finally, we set
$\eta = \sigma_{i_{\mathrm{fin}}}$.
\end{itemize}
title: Definition def:eta-kappa of arXiv:2411.10419

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let $\alpha\in[0,1]$. We define
		\[
		\mathbb A^\alpha
		\triangleq
		\left\{
		\mathcal A:\
		\text{there exist }\mathcal L\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^\alpha
		\text{ and }\mathcal G\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^0\text{ such that }
		\mathcal A=\mathcal L+\mathcal G
		\text{ and }
		\mathcal L+\mathcal L^*\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^0
		\right\}.
		\]
		Such a pair $(\mathcal L,\mathcal G)$ is called an admissible decomposition
		of $\mathcal A$. A family $\mathscr N\subset\mathbb A^\alpha$ is called
		bounded if one can choose an admissible decomposition
		$\mathcal A=\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}+\mathcal G_{\mathcal A}$ for every
		$\mathcal A\in\mathscr N$ such that
		\[
		\{\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}:\mathcal A\in\mathscr N\}
		\text{ is bounded in }\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^\alpha,
		\]
		and both
		\[
		\{\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}+\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}^*:
		\mathcal A\in\mathscr N\},
		\quad
		\{\mathcal G_{\mathcal A}:\mathcal A\in\mathscr N\}
		\]
		are bounded in $\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^0$.

[Cor 4 of arXiv:2608.06576, 'The Resultant Distribution Method: Universality for $p$-adic Random Matrices and Polynomia'] Let $K/\Q_p$ be a quadratic extension. For every $n\geq 1$, let
$A_n\in\Mat_n(\Z_p)$ be a random matrix whose entries are independent
and $\epsilon$-balanced. Then, we have
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\E[Z_{\mc{O}_K^{\new}}(P_{A_n})]=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{(1-p^{-1})(1-p^{-k-1})(1+p^{-k^2-2k-3})
p^{-\frac{k^2+k}{2}}}{(1-p^{-k^2-2k-2})(1-p^{-k^2-2k-3})},
&K/\Q_p\text{ unramified},
\\
\left\lVert\Disc_{K/\Q_p}\right\rVert
\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{(1-p^{-1})(1-p^{-2k-2})p^{-k^2-k}}{(1-p^{-k^2-2k-2})(1-p^{-k^2-2k-3})},& K/\Q_p\text{ ramified}.
\end{cases}
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Defn def:isotopy of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $C^0$-foliation. A \textbf{$C^0$-isotopy} of $\mathcal{F}$ is a topological isotopy $h_t : M \rightarrow M$ such that $\mathcal{F}_t = h_t(\mathcal{F})$ is a continuous path of $C^0$-foliations. In particular, the plane fields $T \mathcal{F}_t$ exist and vary continuously with $t$. This $C^0$-isotopy is \textbf{$\varepsilon$-small}, if $d\big(h_t(x),x\big)<\varepsilon$ for all $x\in M$ and furthermore $T\mathcal{F}_t$ is $\varepsilon$-close to $T\mathcal{F}$.

[Lemma janson1 of arXiv:2606.09488, 'The temporal stochastic block model'] Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$, $(\lambda_i)_{i\in [r]} \in (\mathbb{R}^+)^r$ and $X_i \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_i)$ be independent random variables. Define
$$ \mu = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^r X_i \right] = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{1}{\lambda_i}, \quad \quad \lambda_* = \min_{i \in [r]} \lambda_i. $$
Then, for $\epsilon >0$, we have 
$$ \mathbb{P}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^r X_i \geq (1+\epsilon)\mu \right] \leq (1+\epsilon)^{-1} e^{-\lambda_* \mu (\epsilon-\log(1+\epsilon))}.$$

body: [Definition 242 (The characteristics for the compressible Euler system) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] A surface $S \subset \R\times\Sigma$ (or curve $\ell \subset \R\times\Sigma$) is a \emph{characteristic} if at every point $p \in S$ (or $p \in \ell$), the co-normal space to $S$ (or $\ell$) at $p$, defined to be $\{\bm{\upxi} \in T_p^*(\R\times\Sigma) \, | \, \bm{\upxi}(V) = 0 \text{ for all } V \in  T_pS \}$ (or  $\{\bm{\upxi} \in T_p^*(\R\times\Sigma) \, | \, \bm{\upxi}(V) = 0 \text{ for all } V \in  T_p\ell \}$), is a subset of $C_p^*$ (or $P_p^*$).

[Theorem of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Suppose that $f \in L_2(\mathbb R^d)$, and its Hermite expansion in $L_2(N(0,1))$ is
\[ f = \sum_{\alpha} a_{\alpha} h_{\alpha}. \]
For any $\Omega > 0$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $f \in PW_{\Omega}$.
    \item There exist $M > 0$ and $\Omega > 0$ such that $|a_{\alpha}|\le M\dfrac{\Omega^{|\alpha|}}{\sqrt{\alpha!}}$
for every $\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{d}$.
    \item For any $r$-strictly sub-exponential  distribution $\mu$ with scale parameter $K$, there exists $C > 0$ and a sequence of polynomials $(p_m)_{m = 1}^{\infty}$ such that
    \[ \|f - p_m\|_{L_2(\mu)} \le C \frac{(\Omega K (er)^{1/r})^m}{m^{m/r}}. \]
    Moreover, if $f \in PW_{\Omega}$ then we can take any $H = er^{1/r}K\Omega$.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{proof}
    The equivalence of the first two is Theorem~(thm:paley-weiner-bargmann-rd of the paper). Given the third condition, the first condition follows as in the proof of Theorem~(thm:pw-universality of the paper): we can prove the second condition for any $\Omega' > \Omega$ by applying the case $r = 2$ and $\mu = N(0,I)$ and using Parseval's theorem, and then by using the Paley-Wiener theorem we conclude $f \in PW_{\Omega}$.
    
    Assuming that $f \in PW_{\Omega}$, let $p_m$ be the $L_2(\mu)$ orthogonal projection of $f$ onto the space of degree $m$ polynomials and observe by Lemma~(lem:fourier-error-rep of the paper) that
    \[ \|f - p_m\|_{L_2}^2 =  \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n} \int \hat f(\xi) \varphi(\xi)\, d\xi,  \]
    and by Theorem~(thm:Rd-pw-strict of the paper) that provided $m > r (K\|\xi\|_2^2)$,
    \[ |\varphi(\xi)| \le  A \norm{f - p_m}_\mu \, \Big(\frac{er}{m}\Big)^{m/r} (K \|\xi\|_2)^{m}. \]
    So dividing by $\|f - p_m\|_{L_2}$, using that $f \in PW_{\Omega}$, and applying H\"older's inequality,
    \[ \|f - p_m\|_{L_2} \le \frac{A}{(2\pi)^{d}} \|\hat f\|_{L_1} \Big(\frac{er}{m}\Big)^{m/r} K^m \Omega^m \]
    which proves the result. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 5 (Aru-Sep\'ulveda-Werner \cite{ASW}) of arXiv:2509.01797, 'Relation between Wick powers and excursion clusters of the 2D GFF'] Let $b>v$ and $a<v$, such that $b-a\geq 2\lambda$.
Fix $z\in D$.
Then
\begin{displaymath}
\Big(\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log\Big(\dfrac{\CR(z,D)}{\CR(z,D\setminus A_{a,b})}\Big), \ell_{a,b}(z)\Big)
\end{displaymath}
has the same law as $(T_{a,b},W_{T_{a,b}})$ under $W_{0} = v$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Aru-Sep\'ulveda-Werner \cite{ASW}

body: [Definition def:history of arXiv:2412.00279, 'Optimal local storage policy based on stochastic intensities and its large scale behavior'] A filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ in $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ (i.e. an increasing family of $\sigma$-algebras contained in $\mathcal{F}$)  is \emph{a history} of the simple locally finite point process $\Phi$ if $\Phi((a,b])$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable for all $a<b\leqslant t$. The \emph{natural history} of $\Phi$ is $\mathcal{F}_t=\sigma\left(\Phi((a,b]):a<b\leqslant t\right)$ the smallest filtration satisfying this property.
title: Definition def:history of arXiv:2412.00279

Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), T326-w697-C07 v1; independent reviewer PASS pending. For the source augmented K^TQ model with v21 held zero and m21 trained, the scalar-value/factor flow from Q0=K0=alpha I_(d+1), v0=alpha sqrt(d), 0<alpha^3/sqrt(d)<2, is global and bounded for every nonzero finite pool with a nonzero target. The written proof gives matrix/scalar balance, exact input-nullspace retention and a uniform bound on the effective inherited-nullspace contribution. That contribution vanishes uniformly over all training times as alpha->0 at fixed pool/dimension; it also vanishes in fresh-task norm in probability for each fixed positive M as d->infinity with alpha=epsilon/sqrt(d), fixed epsilon in (0,1). Consequently any zero-loss accumulation point selects the minimum-effective-norm interpolant in these limits. IF zero-loss convergence holds, the fixed-M risk still tends to 1+1/M. Zero-loss convergence is explicitly not proved here. In raw coordinates C=E_pool[(Rz)(Rz)^T], T=d[I,0], P projects onto range C, N=I-P, and R=diag(I/d,1). The proof establishes BB^T-A^TA=alpha^2 ee^T, v^2=||A||_F^2 and BN=alpha N. With lambda the smallest positive eigenvalue of C, K0=||TP||_F+sqrt(2L0/lambda), and Zmax=max(2d alpha^2,(2d K0^2)^(1/3)), one has v^2<=Zmax globally. The inherited-nullspace term H=alpha v A N R has normalized fresh-task squared norm at most alpha^2 Zmax^2/d times [1/d^2+(eta-1/d^2)q], with q=e^TNe and eta=(1+rho)^2+2/d. For fixed M and alpha=epsilon/sqrt(d), this bound is O_P(1/d). Zero-loss convergence for M>=2 remains the missing hypothesis for the 1+1/M selector conclusion.
Augmented source block retained: Gamma=v A B diag(I_d/d,1), A=Q_:,1:d^T and B=K, v=v22; v21 fixed zero
All relevant key/query parameters trained by Euclidean population gradient flow; no ridge; exactly infinite context
Initialize A0=alpha[I_d,0], B0=alpha I_(d+1), v0=alpha sqrt(d); at least one nonzero task; target T=d[I_d,0]
Joint fixed-M claim uses iid standard Gaussian tasks, fixed rho>=0, fixed epsilon in (0,1), alpha=epsilon/sqrt(d), fresh isotropic Gaussian task/query
Selector and 1+1/M conclusion conditional on zero-loss accumulation/convergence; no global-minimum convergence theorem or growing-M limit claimed

body: [Theorem 1.7 of arXiv:2404.17260, 'The evolution of the permutahedron'] Let p = p(n) and let λ(n, p) = (n + 1)! (1 −p)n. Then lim n→∞P(Perm(n)p is connected) =    0 if λ(n, p) →∞; e−c if λ(n, p) →c ⩾0. Both the superexponential order of |Perm(n)| and the lack of explicit control of the number of subgraphs and their expansion properties make it hard to argue as in the proof of Theorem 1.4.
title: Theorem 1.7 of arXiv:2404.17260: The evolution of the permutahedron

[Theorem thm:msk_weakext of arXiv:2510.26960, 'Free energy fluctuations in SK and related spin glass models: \\ A literature survey'] {DeyWu23}}]
Consider a MSK model with Gaussian disorder. Assume that the external field is scaled as $h = \rho N^{-a}$ for some positive constants $\rho$ and $\alpha$. We have the following statements of convergence in distribution as $N \to \infty$.
\begin{enumerate}
     \item (Sub-critical) For $\alpha>1/4$ and $\beta<\beta_c$,
        \[
        N \left(F_N - F(\beta) \right) \to \mathcal{N}(-\frac12 V_1^2, V_1^2).
        \]
        \item (Critical) For $\alpha=1/4$ and $\beta<\beta_c$,
        \[
        N \left(F_N - F(\beta) \right) \to \mathcal{N}(-\frac12 \left(V_1^2 + \rho^4 V_2^2 \right), V_1^2+\rho^4 V_2^2).
        \]
        \item (Super-critical) There exists $\beta_0\leq \beta_c$ such that, for $\alpha<1/4$ and $\beta<\beta_0$, then 
        \[
        \frac{\sqrt{N}}{h^2}\left(F_N - \widehat{F}(\beta)\right) \to \mathcal{N}(0, V_2^2).
        \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:talagrand-parisi of arXiv:2602.12595, '\textbf{Michel Talagrand and the Rigorous Theory of Mean Field Spin Glasses}'] For the SK model (and, more generally, mean-field Gaussian spin glasses with covariance \(N\xi(R_{1,2})\)
under suitable convexity/regularity assumptions on \(\xi\)), the limiting free energy exists and equals the Parisi variational value:
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\,\mathbb{E}\log \sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma_N}
\exp\Bigl(-H_N(\sigma)+h\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_i\Bigr)
=
\mathcal{P}(\xi,h).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Parisi formula for SK and an even/convex class \cite{Talagrand2006Parisi}

[Ppn 246 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}  and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}, and assume that condition~\eqref{e:w2.coupling.assumption} holds. Then, for the stopping times defined by \eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time}--\eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time.ISING}, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\frac1M \sum_{a=1}^M
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\sigma(q_d,a)^2; \tau(a)<1
	\bigg]
	&\le O(\epsilon) + o_{\trK}(1)\,,\\
	\frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\Ising(q_d,i)^2; 
	\tau^\Ising(i)<1
	\bigg]
	&\le o_{\trK}(1)
	\end{align*}
uniformly over $N$. 

\begin{proof} 
Throughout this proof, we write $\bE_a$ for expectation over a uniformly random index $a\in[M]$, we write $\E$ for expectation over the gaussian disorder, and we write $\E'\equiv \bE_a\E$ for expectation over both. The assumption \eqref{e:w2.coupling.assumption} says that there exists a coupling of $X(1)$ with $Z\sim\mu$ such that
	\[
	\E'\Big[(X(1)-Z)^2\Big]
	\le \epsilon\,.
	\]
We can use this to bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\frac1M  \sum_{a=1}^M (\E X^\RomI(1,a))^2
	=\frac1M  \sum_{a=1}^M (\E X(1,a))^2
	\le
	\frac1M  \sum_{a=1}^M \E[ X(1,a)^2 ]
	=\E'[ X(1)^2 ] \\
	&\qquad\le 
	2 \E'\Big[ (X(1)-Z)^2  + Z^2\Big]
	\le 2\Big( \epsilon + \E'(Z^2)\Big)
	\le O(1)\,,
	
	\end{align}
where the $O(1)$ indicates a large constant depending only on $\mu$. 
Recall that the $X^{\RomII}$ and $X^{\RomIII}$ processes have mean zero, so $\E X^{\RomI}=\E X$. Next, a straightforward gaussian computation gives the identity
	\[
	\E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) = p(q_d) \E X^{\RomI}(1,a)\,.
	\]
It follows by combining with the result of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.I.minus.mean} that
	\begin{align*}
	&\frac{1}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M
	\E \bigg[\max_{0\le d\le\dmax} X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)^2\bigg]\\
	&\qquad\le\frac{2}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M
		\E \bigg[\max_{0\le d\le\dmax}
			\Big( X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) \Big)^2
			\bigg]
	+ \frac{2}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M \max_{0\le d\le\dmax} 
		(\E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a))^2 \\
	&\qquad
	\le L^{O(1)}
	+ \frac{1}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M 
		(\E X^{\RomI}(1,a))^2
	\le L^{O(1)} +O(1) \le L^{O(1)}\,.
	\end{align*}
As a consequence (recalling $L\ll \trK$) we conclude
	\[\frac1M\sum_{a=1}^M \P(\tau^{\RomI}(a) < 1)
	\le
	\frac{1}{M\trK^2} \sum_{a=1}^M 
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le \dmax} X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)^2
		\bigg] \le o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
uniformly in $N$. We also have from Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} that 
	\beq
	\bigg\{
	\max_{a\in[M]}
	\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\P(\tau^\sigma(a) < 1)\bigg\}
	+ \bigg\{
	\max_{i\in[N]}
	\P(\tau^\Ising(i) < 1) \bigg\}
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,,\eeq
so altogether we obtain
	\beq
	\frac1M\sum_{a=1}^M \P(\tau(a) < 1) 
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\eeq
uniformly in $N$. We can also estimate
	\begin{align*}
	(*)&\equiv \frac1M
	\sum_{a=1}^M
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}  X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)^2; \tau(a)<1
	\bigg]
	\le 2\textup{(A)} + 2\textup{(B)}\,,\\
	\textup{(A)}
	&\equiv \frac1M \sum_{a=1}^M
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\Big( X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E  X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) \Big)^2;
		\tau(a)<1
	\bigg]\,,\\
	\textup{(B)}
	&\equiv  \frac1M \sum_{a=1}^M
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	(\E  X^{\RomI}(q_d,a))^2 \P(\tau(a)<1)
	= \frac1M \sum_{a=1}^M
	(\E  X^{\RomI}(1,a))^2 \P(\tau(a)<1)\,.
	\end{align*}
We then use Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.I.minus.mean} to bound
	\begin{align*}\textup{(A)}

	o_{\trK}(1)\,.

Independent derivation pending w440 review. On the infinite 3-regular tree, iid Bernoulli bond percolation has p_c=1/2 and almost surely no infinite cluster at p_c, but E_{p_c}|C(o)| is infinite. At distance k>=1 there are 3*2^(k-1) vertices, each connected with probability 2^(-k), giving expected connected shell size 3/2. Below p_c, chi(p)=1+3p/(1-2p), which diverges as p increases to p_c. Thus finiteness of susceptibility for every p<p_c cannot be transferred to p=p_c without a further uniform integrability or domination argument; it cannot be assumed as a bridge to critical extinction.

critical p=1/2 for the endpoint claim

title: DRAFT: Critical extinction can coexist with infinite susceptibility

[Lemma lem:greedy of arXiv:2507.09120, 'Chemical distance in graphs of polynomial growth'] Let $G$ be a transitive graph which has polynomial growth of degree $d$.
   Given $N \in \mathbb{N}$, let $I_{e,N}$ be a collection of Bernoulli random variables indexed by
   edges $e$ of $G$ such that for every $2N$-separated subset $S$ of $E$,
   the family $\{I_{e,N}\}_{e \in S}$ is independent.
   Define
   \[
      \Gamma_{L,N} := \max \left\{ \sum_{e \in \pi} I_{e,N} : \pi \mbox{ a path from } o \mbox{ of length at most } L \right\},
   \]
   \[
      q_N := \sup_{e \in E} \mathbb{E}[ I_{e,N} ].
   \]
   Then there exists a positive constant $C$ depending on $G$ such that for all $L \in \mathbb{N}$,
   \[
      \mathbb{E}[ \Gamma_{L,N} ] \le CLN^d q_N^{1/d}.
   \]

[Lemma lem:transfer-minors-master of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $1\leq s\leq k$, and let
$z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(s)}\in\mathbb Z^k$ have coordinate sum zero.  Delete
the same $k-s$ coordinates from every row.  If $Q$ is the resulting
$s\times s$ matrix, then
\begin{equation}
 |\det Q|\leq\prod_{i=1}^s\rho(z^{(i)}).
\end{equation}
In particular, if every $z^{(i)}\in\mathcal D_{h,k}$, then
$|\det Q|\leq h^s$.

[Lemma 29 of arXiv:2608.12804, 'Scaling Limits for Ising Models on Inhomogeneous Random Graphs and Applications'] For all $\bs, \bt \in \{-1,+1\}^N$, as long as $\theta_N = \Omega(N^{-2/3})$, we have:
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        &&\E T\left(\bs\right) T\left(\bt\right)\\ &=&
        \exp\Bigg(-\frac{\beta^2}{2N^2\theta_N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{i}{N}\right)
        -\frac{\beta^2}{N^2}\sum_{i> j}W^2\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)-\frac{\beta^4}{6 N^4\theta_N^3}\sum_{i> j} W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right) + o\left(\frac 1{N\theta_N}\right)\\
        &+& \frac{\beta}{N}\sum_{i> j}W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)(\sigma_i \sigma_j + \tau_i\tau_j)+\frac{\beta^2}{\theta_N N^2} \sum_{i>j}W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)\left(1-\theta_N W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)\right)\sigma_i\sigma_j\tau_i\tau_j\\
        &+& O\left(\frac{1}{N^3 \theta_N^2}\sum_{i>j}W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)\sigma_i \sigma_j \right) + O\left(\frac{1}{N^3 \theta_N^2}\sum_{i>j}W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)\tau_i \tau_j\right)\\&+&O\left(\frac{1}{\theta_N^3 N^4}\sum_{i>j}W\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)\sigma_i\sigma_j\tau_i\tau_j\right).
    \end{eqnarray*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 35 of arXiv:2604.13454, 'Invariant and periodic measures in classical spin systems on infinite lattices with highly'] (H\"ormander probabilistic setting, Ichihara - Kunita). Assume $X(t)$ is the strong unique  solution to the Stratonovich SDE
		$$
		dX_i(t) = b_i(t,X(t))dt + \sum_{j=1}^{d}\sigma_{i,j}(t,X(t))\circ dW_j(t),\quad t\geq 0,\quad i=1,\cdots, n
		$$
		where $b_i,\sigma_{i,j}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^+\times\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}), 1\leq i,j \leq n,$. Suppose that following (H\"ormander) condition is satisfied
		$$
		dim(Lie\{A_0,A_1...,A_n\})=n+1, \ \forall x\in \mathbb{R}^n,
		$$
        where $A_0(t,x)=(1,b_1(t,x),\cdots,b_n(t,x))^T$ and $A_j(t,x)=(0,\sigma_{1,j},\cdots,\sigma_{n,j})^T$ for $1\leq j\leq n$.
		Then the transition probability kernel $\mathcal{P}_t(x,\cdot)$ associated with $X(t)$ admits a density function $p_t(x, y)$ such that 
        \begin{equation*}
            p_t(x, y)\in C^\infty (\mathbb{R}^+\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}).
        \end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Lemma (campaign status: audited-pass): Batching: at step s pick a still-present matching pair P_t, pick a witness row E_s containing it, and remove B_s = {u : P_u still present and P_u cap E_s nonempty}, a_s = |B_s| (tag 10). With V_s the union of pair endpoints in B_s and U_s = E_s cap V_s: the U_s are pairwise disjoint, E_s contains at least a_s+1 coordinates of U_s, and E_t cap U_s = empty for t < s. Conditioning on coordinates outside the union of U_s and peeling U_k,...,U_1 in reverse gives Pr(h_s.X in {+-1} | earlier) <= psi(a_s+1) (tag 11), hence 2^{-ell} <= prod_s psi(a_s+1) (tag 13). Notes: S7 confirms this is a triangular CONDITIONAL-EXPECTATION product, not an independence claim, and requires the proof be rewritten with the disjoint U_s and an explicit reverse conditional expectation. Rows E_s may still involve variables in earlier U_t; those are held as arbitrary parameters, which is why target uniformity is needed.

[Corollary 3 (Scalar dyadic formula) of arXiv:2606.08703, '2606.08703'] For the usual scalar dyadic Mandelbrot cascade, let \(W_0,W_1\) be independent
copies of \(W\), and set
\[
        X_i=\frac{W_i}{2},\qquad i=0,1.
\]
Then
\[
        \rho(q)=2^{1-q}\E W^q .
\]
Under the scalar Kahane--Peyri\`ere assumptions \eqref{eq:KP}, almost surely on
\(\{\mu\ne0\}\),
\begin{equation}
        \dimF(\mu)=\dimE(\mu)=\dimtwo(\mu)=D^+(W),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
D^+(W)=
\sup_{1<q<2}
\left[
2-\frac2q\bigl(1+\log_2\E W^q\bigr)
\right]_+,
\end{equation}
with the convention that the corresponding term is \(0\) when
\(\E W^q=\infty\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Scalar dyadic formula

[Lemma lem:canonical-conditioning of arXiv:2607.04264, 'Macroscopic Feynman Cycles and Poisson--Kingman Universality in Bose Condensation'] For every \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that \(Z_{L,N}>0\),
\[
        \Xi_{L,N}
        \stackrel{d}{=}
        \Pi_L^{(\kappa)}
        \,|\,
        \{S_L^{(\kappa)}=N\}.
        \]
\iffalse
Equivalently, for every bounded measurable functional \(\Phi\),
\[
        \mathbb E_{L,N}^{\mathrm{can}}[\Phi(\Xi_{L,N})]
        =
        \mathbf E_L^{(\kappa)}
        \left[
            \Phi(\Pi_L^{(\kappa)})
            \,|\,
            S_L^{(\kappa)}=N
        \right].
\]\fi
The conditional law does not depend on the chosen value of \(\kappa>0\). In particular,
\[
        \mathbf P_L^{(\kappa)}(S_L^{(\kappa)}=N)
        =
        \exp\{-\Lambda_L^{(\kappa)}\}
        e^{-\kappa N/V_L}
        Z_{L,N}.
\]
title: The conditional PPP representation

[Defn 10 (Broadcasting process) of arXiv:2606.22960, '2606.22960'] Let \((T_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the tree growth model above. Each vertex carries one of two colours, which we identify with the values \(-1\) and \(1\). The root vertex \(1\) is assigned a random bit \(B_1\in\{-1,1\}\), chosen uniformly at random. For each \(n\geq 1\), once the new vertex \(n+1\) has chosen its parent \(p_{n+1}\), it inherits the bit of its parent with probability \(1-q\) and flips it with probability \(q\), independently of the tree growth and all previous broadcasting steps. Equivalently,
	\[
	B_{n+1}=B_{p_{n+1}}Z_{n+1},
	\]
	where \((Z_n)_{n\geq 2}\) are independent \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variables satisfying
	\[
	\mathbb P(Z_n=-1)=q,
	\qquad
	\mathbb P(Z_n=1)=1-q.
	\]
	The parameter \(q\in[0,1]\) is called the bit-flip probability.
title: Broadcasting process

[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2608.30089, 'On the Coefficients of Hurwitz-Type Matrix Polynomials'] Let \(\mathbf f_n\) be a \(q\times q\) HTM polynomial.
\begin{enumerate}\item[\textnormal{(a)}]
For every HTM polynomial of degree at most \(3\), all its coefficient
matrices have strictly positive determinants.
\item[\textnormal{(b)}]
The assertion in \textnormal{(a)} fails for degree \(4\). More
precisely, there exists an HTM polynomial of degree \(4\) having a
coefficient matrix with negative determinant.
\end{enumerate}

body: [Lemma 1 of arXiv:2511.05218, 'On the Color Discrepancy of Spanning Trees in Random and Randomly Perturbed Graphs'] Fix $\delta>0$. [Lemma tensoring-natural of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let ${\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}}$ be pointed $S$-cocomplete $T$-$\infty$-categories, and let $X$ be a global section of $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*}$. Then the two $T$-functors
    \[
        \ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$S$-cc}(X\otimes{-},{\mathcal{D}}),
        \ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$S$-cc}({\mathcal{C}},X\otimes{-})\colon\ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$S$-cc}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})\rightrightarrows\ul{\textup{Fun}}^\textup{$S$-cc}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})
    \]
    are naturally equivalent. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, status proof (unaudited); novelty unestablished. Fix lambda>0 and alpha>0 independently of N. Let M=ceil(exp(alpha*N)) and X_1,...,X_M be independent N(0,I_N) vectors. Put v_i=||X_i||^2/N, F_i=log(sum_{j!=i}exp(lambda*X_i.X_j))/(lambda*N), and T(x)=sum_i a_i(x)X_i with a_i(x)=exp(lambda*x.X_i)/sum_j exp(lambda*x.X_j). Let J(v)=(v-1-log(v))/2, b=lambda*(1-lambda/2) if lambda<1 and b=1/2 otherwise, and let u_b be the unique solution in (0,1) of J(u_b)=b*u_b. Set a_G=min(b*u_b,log(2)/4). If alpha<a_G, there are constants d,rho,c>0 such that with probability tending to one, v_i-F_i>=d for every i, and T contracts every closed ball B(X_i,rho*sqrt(N)) into itself, with its fixed point at distance at most exp(-c*N)*sqrt(N) from X_i for all sufficiently large N. If alpha>a_G, with probability tending to one some row has own softmax weight a_i(X_i)<=exp(-c*N) for a constant c>0. Thus a_G is a strict uniform self-weight dominance threshold and a retrieval capacity lower bound; no equality case or Gaussian nearby-fixed-point capacity upper bound is claimed. The paper derives the same a_G as alpha_c^lb; its partially non-rigorous argument is not used as an independent audit.
Independent centered standard Gaussian pattern vectors in R^N.
Fixed strictly positive alpha and lambda, M=ceil(exp(alpha*N)), N tends to infinity.
Unconstrained full-space softmax update as explicitly defined; convergence in probability over the patterns.
Strict inequalities alpha<a_G or alpha>a_G; no assertion at alpha=a_G.
Author proof draft, independently unaudited; no fixed-point capacity converse or novelty claim.

[Lem productBoundary of arXiv:2606.30517, '\textsc{Convergence towards Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations with a focus on Diestel--'] Let $E''=E\times E'$ as above.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item  Under the $L^1$ metric, one has $\overline{E''}\equiv \overline{E}\times\overline{E'}$, and hence, $\partial E''\equiv (\partial E\times\partial E')\sqcup (E\times\partial E')\sqcup (\partial E\times E')$. More precisely, $\partial E''$ consists of the following functions: $(x,x')\mapsto d_{x_0}(x)+d_{x'_0}(x')$, where $(x_0,x'_0)\in (\overline{E}\times\overline{E'})\setminus (E\times E')$.
			
			\item  Under the $L^{\infty}$ metric, one can write $\partial E''\equiv (\partial E\times \partial E' \times I) \sqcup \partial E\sqcup \partial E'$, where $I=\mathbb Z$ if both $E$ and $E'$ are graphs, and $I=\mathbb R$ otherwise. More precisely, $\partial E''$ consists of the following functions: $(x,x')\mapsto \max\{d_{\theta}(x), d_{\theta'}(x')+ c\}$, $(x,x')\mapsto d_{\theta}(x)$ and $(x,x')\mapsto d_{\theta'}(x')$, where $\theta\in\partial E$, $\theta'\in\partial E'$ and $c\in I$.
		\end{enumerate}

[Definition 23 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Recall \eqref{Equation: Gaussian Kernel}.
Let $Z$ and $Z_1,Z_2$ be stochastic processes taking values in $\mbb R^2$.
For every $\eps>0$ and bounded Borel measurable set $A\subset[0,\infty)^2$, define
the approximate self-intersection local time (SILT) of $Z$ on $A$ as
\[\be^\eps_A(Z)=\int_Ap_\eps\big(Z(r_1)-Z(r_2)\big)\d r,\]
and the approximate mutual intersection local time (MILT) of $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ on $A$ as
\[\al^\eps_A(Z_1,Z_2)=\int_{A}p_\eps\big(Z_1(r_1)-Z_2(r_2)\big)\d r.\]
title: Definition 23 of arXiv:2507.06186

body: [Lemma 6 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $A$ and $B$ be sets such that $A\cap B = \varnothing$. Let $\fm{\mb A}{I}$ and $\fm{\mb B}{J}$ be partitions of $A$ and $B$ respectively. Let $\fm{\mb C}{I\sqcup J}$ be such that $\mb C(1,i) = \mb A(i)$ for every $i\in I$ and $\mb C(2,j) = \mb B(j)$ for every $j\in J$. Then $\mb C$ is a partition of $A\cup B$.

body: Every $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ is $\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat f(S)\chi_S$ with $\chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i$; Parseval gives $\sum_S\hat f(S)^2=E f^2$, and for Boolean $f$ the spectral sample is the law $P(\mathcal S=S)=\hat f(S)^2$.

[Prop 60 ({\cite[Propositions 4.3-4.7) of arXiv:2608.26068, 'All once-extended 3D TQFTs are Reshetikhin--Turaev theories'] {BDSV4}}] 
    The symmetric monoidal functor $Z_\mathcal{C}:\mathbf{F}(\mathcal{P}) \rightarrow \KV$ sends the generating 2-morphisms $\gamma$ of $\mathcal{R}$ to the following matrices of linear maps:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For each of $\gamma=\alpha,\rho,\lambda,\phi_1,\phi_2$, upon contracting along the unique internal edge, the source and target ribbon graphs may be identified with each other. Then, $Z_\mathcal{C}(\gamma)$ act as matrices of identity linear maps on the spaces of labels.
        \item For $\gamma=\theta$, the only nonzero entries are given by the linear maps $$Z_\mathcal{C}(\theta)_i^i: \Hom(X_i,X_i) \rightarrow \Hom(X_i,X_i)$$ sending $\id_{X_i}$ to the twist $\theta_{X_i}$.
        \item For $\gamma=\beta$, each $$Z_\mathcal{C}(\beta)_{i_1i_2}^j: \Hom(X_{i_1}\otimes X_{i_2}, X_j) \rightarrow \Hom(X_{i_2}\otimes X_{i_1}, X_j)$$ is the linear map given by sending $f \mapsto f\circ\beta_{X_{i_2}\otimes X_{i_1}}^{-1}$.
        \item For $\gamma=\nu$, upon contracting the target ribbon graph along its one edge we are left with defining a linear map $k \rightarrow \Hom(\mathbbm{1},\mathbbm{1})$; $\nu$ is sent to the linear map sending $1$ to $\id_{\mathbbm{1}}$.
        \item For $\gamma=\mu$, the only nonzero entry is $$Z_\mathcal{C}(\mu)_1^1: \Hom(\mathbbm{1},\mathbbm{1})\otimes\Hom(\mathbbm{1},\mathbbm{1}) \rightarrow k$$ which sends $\id_{\mathbbm{1}}\otimes \id_{\mathbbm{1}}$ to $1$.
        \item For $\gamma=\epsilon$, the only nonzero entries are the linear maps $$Z_\mathcal{C}(\epsilon)_i^i: \bigoplus_{k_1,k_2}\Hom(X_i,X_{k_1}\otimes X_{k_2})\otimes\Hom(X_{k_1}\otimes X_{k_2},X_i) \rightarrow k$$ given by composition and identifying $\id_{X_i}$ with $1$.
        \item For $\gamma=\eta$, contract the target ribbon graph along its one internal edge. The only nonzero entries are the linear maps $Z_\mathcal{C}(\eta)_{ij}^{ij}: k \rightarrow \Hom(X_{i}\otimes X_{j}, X_{i}\otimes X_{j})$ sending $1$ to the identity morphism $\id_{X_{i}\otimes X_{j}}$.
    \end{itemize}
    For the unspecified entries, either the source or the target ribbon graph will have the zero vector space as its space of labels, and thus the linear map in this entry has to be the zero linear map. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 188 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] For any $i,s=1,2,...$, $t>0$, and 
$$
f(t_{1},...,t_{i})=\{
f^{k_{1},...,k_{i}}(
t_{1},...,t_{i}),k_{j}=1,...,d_{1}\},  
$$
 given
on $\Gamma_{i}(t_{0})$ and square integrable there
we have
\begin{equation}
                         
E\Big(\int_{\Gamma_{i}(t_{0})}f(
t_{1},...,t_{i})\,dw_{t_{i}}\cdot...\cdot dw_{t_{1}}\Big)^{2s}
\leq N \|f\|_{L_{2}(\Gamma_{i}(t_{0}))}^{2s},
\end{equation}
where $N\, (<\infty)$ depends only $i,s,d_{1}$, and by the repeated stochastic
integral above we mean
\begin{equation}
                         
\sum_{k_{1},...,k_{i}}
\int_{\Gamma_{i}(t_{0})}f^{k_{1},...,k_{i}}(
t_{1},...,t_{i})\,dw^{k_{i}}_{t_{i}}\cdot...\cdot dw^{k_{1}}_{t_{1}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 188 of arXiv:2605.03236

$\mathbf{Cyl}:=[\min(f),\max(f)]\times \mathbb{S}^1$

 \tilde{A}:=\sum_{n\geqslant 0} \left(\int_0^r\sqrt{\sigma(s,\theta)}\xi_n^{\mathfrak{g}}(s)ds\right)   e_n(\theta) \mathrm{d} \theta = \partial_\theta \left\langle \xi,1_{\square(r,\theta)} \right\rangle  d\theta

body: [Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(X\) be a compact space and \(\mu\) a Borel measure on \(X\). We say that \(\mu\) is locally positive if \(\mu(U) > 0\) for every \(U \subset X\) open. We say that \(\mu\) is non-atomic if \(\mu(\{x\}) = 0\) for every \(x \in X\).

[Theorem Wallis 4 of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We have the following integration formula over the complex sphere $S^{N-1}_\mathbb C\subset\mathbb C^N$, with respect to the uniform mass $1$ measure, 
$$\int_{S^{N-1}_\mathbb C}|z_1|^{2k_1}\ldots|z_N|^{2k_N}\,dz=\frac{(N-1)!k_1!\ldots k_n!}{(N+\sum k_i-1)!}$$
valid for any exponents $k_i\in\mathbb N$. As for the other polynomial integrals in $z_1,\ldots,z_N$ and their conjugates $\bar{z}_1,\ldots,\bar{z}_N$, these all vanish.

        for all $n \geq n_0.$

Method: Optimal edge-fluctuation scales for arbitrary random-matrix polynomials structural calculation Result: The nondegeneracy qualifier is necessary even for a one-variable quadratic polynomial. For a standard GUE matrix G_N let P(x)=20-(x-2)^2. With probability tending to1 its spectrum lies in a fixed neighborhood of[-2,2] where P is positive. Then norm(P(G_N))=20-min_i(lambda_i-2)^2. Since the largest GUE eigenvalue is2+O_p(N^-2/3), one has0<=20-norm(P(G_N))<=O_p(N^-4/3). Check: The upper bound uses the largest eigenvalue as one candidate in the minimum. Spectral mapping and positivity give the norm identity. Consequently N^(2/3)*(norm(P(G_N))-20) tends to0, rather than a nondegenerate Tracy-Widom variable. Obstruction: The example is deliberately degenerate and does not contradict the stated research direction. A correct general theorem must identify regularity of the polynomial edge before asserting the universal scale.

[Proposition P:arc-fixed-cutoff-package of arXiv:2607.15966, 'Canonical Mandelbrot Cascades on Curves Are Rajchman'] For every integer \(j\geq1\) and every
\(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\),
\[
        \Psi_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{safe}}
        +
        \sum_{d\in \mathfrak D_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{osc}}}\chi_{\xi,d}
        =
        1
        \qquad\text{on }[0,1].
\]

For every fixed integer \(h\geq0\), almost surely on non-extinction, and for every \(j\geq1\),
\[
        \limsup_{n\to\infty}
        \sup_{2^n\leq|\xi|<2^{n+1}}
        \mu_{n+h}
        \bigl(\operatorname{spt}\Psi_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{safe}}\bigr)
        \leq
        C_\gamma\Delta_{C_\gamma2^{-j}}(\mu).
\]
Moreover, this upper bound tends to zero as \(j\to\infty\) on non-extinction.

Suppose that \(n\geq1\) and \(2^n\leq|\xi|<2^{n+1}\).  
Then
\[
        \#\mathfrak D_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{osc}}
        \leq
        C_{\gamma,j},
        \qquad
        |m_{\xi,d}-n|
        \leq
        C_{\gamma,j}
        \quad
        \bigl(d\in \mathfrak D_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{osc}}\bigr).
\]
For every \(d\in \mathfrak D_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{osc}}\), every \(\ell\geq0\),
and every \(J\in\mathcal{D}_{\ell+1}([0,1])\),
\[
        |c_J(\xi,d,\ell)|
        \leq
        C_\gamma\min\{1,2^{\ell-m_{\xi,d}}\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
        \sum_{d\in \mathfrak D_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{osc}}}
        \left|
        \int_0^1
        \mathrm{e}^{i\phi_\xi(t)}
        \chi_{\xi,d}(t)
        \,\mathrm{d}t
        \right|
        \leq
        C_{\gamma,j}2^{-n}.
\]

Finally, let \(d\in \mathfrak D_{\xi,j}^{\mathrm{osc}}\), \(k\geq1\), 
and \(J\in\mathcal{D}_k([0,1])\), and set
\[
        \Gamma_J(\xi,d)
        =
        A_{J^-}c_J(\xi,d,k-1).
\]
Then \(\Gamma_J(\xi,d)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{k-1}\)-measurable and satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
        |\Gamma_J(\xi,d)|
        &\leq
        C_\gamma A_{J^-}
        \min\{1,2^{k-m_{\xi,d}}\},
\\
        |\Gamma_J(\xi,d)|W_J
        &\leq
        C_\gamma A_J
        \min\{1,2^{k-m_{\xi,d}}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

    \]

For l>=1 and s in Cplus, define zprev(s,z)=(z_-1+(1-b^2)/s,z_0,...,z_(l-2),z_(l-1)+b^2/s), with the middle coordinates omitted when l=1. Let v_l=(1-b^2,0,...,0,b^2), a vector of length l+1. Define s_l(z) as the Cplus solution of s=1/z_l+gamma_l*t_(l-1)(zprev(s,z),v_l). Then set wprev=(w_-1,...,w_(l-1))-(w_l/z_l)*(z_-1,...,z_(l-1)) and t_l(z,w)=w_l/z_l+t_(l-1)(zprev(s_l(z),z),wprev). For each l=1,...,L and every z in D_l, the displayed fixed-point equation has exactly one solution s_l(z) in Cplus. Thus it defines s_l and t_l recursively from t_0 on the stated domains. This specifies the admissible branch; it is not a claim that the equation has only one complex root in the whole plane.
Fixed integer depth L>=1; n,d_0,...,d_L tend to infinity; n/d_l->gamma_l in (0,infinity) for l=1,...,L.
All weights W_l in R^(d_l by d_(l-1)) and w in R^d_L have independent N(0,1) entries, independent of the input matrices.
sigma:R->R is twice differentiable with globally bounded first and second derivatives. For Z~N(0,1), E sigma(Z)=0 and E sigma(Z)^2=1.
X_0 is (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal as in the companion definition for constant B, epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0; the ESD of X_0^T X_0 converges to a deterministic probability measure mu_0.
X_l=d_l^(-1/2)*sigma(W_l X_(l-1)); scalar output f_theta(X_0)=w^T X_L; theta contains all hidden and readout weights; K_NTK=(grad_theta f)^T grad_theta f at random initialization.
b=E sigma'(Z) is nonzero, Z~N(0,1).
Explicit input condition: for every column x_alpha, | ||x_alpha||^2-1 |<=epsilon_n; for alpha!=beta, |x_alpha^T*x_beta|<=epsilon_n; ||X_0||_op<=B; sum_alpha (||x_alpha||^2-1)^2<=B^2. B is constant and epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0.

\begin{align*}

{{\mathbb P}_{\rm Gibbs}(\mathcal{A})  \over \sum_{\mathcal{B}\in \mathcal{E}_{\rm far}}  {\mathbb P}_{\rm Gibbs}(\mathcal{B}) },

\begin{align*}
{\mathbb P}\left(0.22 \ge \exp(c_3 n)\right) \ge 1-\exp(-c_4 n),
\end{align*}
where the probability is with respect to the random choices of the MCMC.

title: FPP chi=1/3 campaign, 2026-08-15 fires 9-15: (L2') HOLDS at laptop sizes - the per-block conditional kurtosis SATURATES - and the earlier growth claim was a moving baseline. DECOMPOSITION (elementary, known in kind - cf. Dembin-Elboim-Peled arXiv 2307.01162 on edge influence): resampling block L leaves every path AVOIDING L untouched, so X = min(A,C) and X^L = min(A',C) with the SAME C; on the touching event the geodesic is in the through class so X = A <= C, giving Delta = min(A',C) - A and the exact cap 0 <= (Delta)^+ <= min{(Delta_0)^+, G_L} with G_L = C - A the gap to the best avoiding path. This matters because CRUX 6d.1 (D7) says the engine consumes ONLY the positive part. MEASURED (U[1,2] on Z^2, exact Dijkstra, axis blocks, four occupation points, pre-registered read): A4/(A2^+)^2 = 5.7339 [5.642,5.838], 6.1143 [6.010,6.223], 6.2345 [6.022,6.439], 6.2290 [5.962,6.509] at occupation 3.95 / 6.04 / 10.08 / 14.05, while the reroute fraction goes 0.167 / 0.384 / 0.606 / 0.740. Increments +0.3804, +0.1202, -0.0055: rise, decelerate, flat. A log fit to the first step predicts +0.46 and +0.30 for the next two, so growth is far slower than logarithmic. The two-sided kurtosis - (L2')'s literal statement - is flatter still at 2.9590 / 3.0564 / 3.0854 / 3.1219. THAT IS WHAT (L2') HOLDING LOOKS LIKE. MECHANISM (hypothesis): (Delta)^+ is a mixture under a RANDOM ceiling G, so its level sits elevated (~6.2) against a null of ~3.1-5.1, but once nearly every resample reroutes the mixture stops changing composition and kappa4 saturates as the reroute fraction does - a one-off elevation the engine absorbs into its constant, not a divergence. METHOD CORRECTION THIS SUPERSEDES: the earlier claim that rerouting fattens the engine's functional and grows was an artifact of reporting a DIFFERENCE against a falling null. With four points: the excess grows 4.8x (+0.655 -> +3.135) while the quantity moves 9 percent (5.7339 -> 6.2290) and is flat over the last two, because the null fell 5.0787 -> 3.0944. LIMITS: occupation 4-14 edges against an engine whose hypotheses start near l_0 ~ 1e18; square blocks not the engine's tall thin W ~ sqrt(nQ); one weight law; widest CI at the last point. Saturation over a measured range is evidence for boundedness, never proof. And all of this is (L2'), which is NOT the wall - (L1') is, and nothing here touches it. chi = 1/3 UNMOVED.

Fix one iid sparse critical law on Z^4 with P(eta=1)=P(eta=-1)=p, P(eta=0)=1-2p, 0<p<1/2. Use synchronous discrete-time nearest-neighbor SRW, stationary capacity-one holes, and graph distance. Write H_t(x) for an unfilled-hole indicator and h_t=E H_t(0). Assume the source properties h_t tends to zero and h_t>=c0/(t+1) eventually for some c0>0. If for some fixed a>0 and finite C, sum_{0<|z|<=floor(a h_t^(-1/4))} P(H_t(0)=H_t(z)=1) <= C h_t eventually, then limsup_{t->infinity} P(origin strictly nearer an unfilled hole than an active particle)>0. The Palm clustering assumption remains unproved for parking; this is a conditional reduction, not a solution of I0005. Novelty: UNCHECKED (limited primary/source and brain search). Status: independently checked proof.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:8c6e80e635200bb5367f1f9af3cc58b0b5b376e7efb39bf24994618a849425fe","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/8c/8c6e80e635200bb5367f1f9af3cc58b0b5b376e7efb39bf24994618a849425fe.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:a31d174696b39217c23e18b76d86886c8a46b0b980c4086414d1bd398b3b5ce2","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c9","bundle_id":"population.i0005-palm-reductions-and-comparisons-004","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"interacting particle systems and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:four-dimensional-parking-finite-palm-clustering-reduction-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C9 v1: bounded Palm clustering suffices for a fixed-law counterexample

Novelty: UNCHECKED. A new-to-this-round reduction using local-priority thinning, finite-time hitting, and hole-loss mass transport. It was compared with the source's proof of Theorem 1.6 and prior own reductions; no assertion of priority. It does not establish its Palm-clustering hypothesis in d4.

Fix one sparse critical law on Z^4 with P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p and P(η=0)=1−2p, where 0<p<1/2 is fixed. Write h_t=P(H_t(0)=1), and F_t for the event that the origin is strictly nearer an unfilled hole than an active particle in graph distance.

Suppose there are fixed a>0 and C<∞ such that for every sufficiently large integer t,

sum_{0<|z|_1≤floor(a h_t^−1/4)} P(H_t(0)=H_t(z)=1) ≤ C h_t.       (PC)

Then limsup_{t→∞}P(F_t)>0. In particular the affirmative limit-to-zero statement is false for that fixed law. The criterion permits any finite C, unlike C2's small Palm neighbor-count condition. It proves a positive limsup, which is enough to contradict convergence to zero; it does not assert a positive liminf.

More precisely, constants κ≥2 and D<∞ depending only on the Z^4 walk can be fixed as below. Let c0>0 be any constant for which h_t≥c0/(t+1) eventually (source Lemma 5.1 permits a universal choice), set A=2/c0, and choose b>0 satisfying

2κb≤a, and b^4≤1/[4AD(1+C)].

Then the lower limit along a sequence of times is at least b^4/[48(1+C)].

## 1. A finite-time one-target hitting estimate

There are κ≥2, c_hit>0 and R0 such that for every integer R≥R0 and every y with |y|_1≤R, a free walk from y hits zero within n=2R² steps before exiting B_{κR}, with probability at least c_hit/R².

To prove this, use the periodic local CLT established in C1. For R²≤j≤2R² on the allowed parity, |y|_2≤R gives p_j(y)≥cR^−4 for all large R, uniformly in y. There are at least cR² allowed times. Hence sum_{j=0}^{2R²}p_j(y)≥c1/R². By the strong Markov property at T0, the expected number of visits after the first hit is at most G(0)=g<∞, so P_y(T0≤2R²)≥c1/(gR²).

The Green-function bound G(z)≤C2/|z|_1² for z≠0 follows from Lawler–Limic, Theorem 4.3.1, or the standard Gaussian heat-kernel sum. Let τ be the first exit from B_{κR}. Conditional on τ<T0, the probability of any subsequent hit is G(X_τ)/g≤C2/(gκ²R²). Strong Markov at τ bounds the probability of hitting by 2R² after an earlier exit by the same number. Choose an integer κ sufficiently large that C2/κ²≤c1/2. Subtracting gives the asserted estimate with c_hit=c1/(2g). All constants are uniform for R≥R0. Put D=1/c_hit.

## 2. Select well-separated holes without requiring isolation in the original field

At time t, attach iid continuous uniform priorities to every lattice site, independently of the process and its future. For a deterministic integer R≥R0, select an unfilled hole x if its priority is the smallest among all unfilled holes within distance 2κR of x. Distinct selected centers have distance greater than 2κR, so their closed balls of radius κR are disjoint. The construction is translation-covariant.

Let i_t be the selected-hole intensity. Conditional on the hole field and H_t(0)=1, selection probability is 1/(1+N), where N counts other holes within 2κR. Therefore Jensen's inequality gives

i_t=h_t E[1/(1+N) | H_t(0)=1]≥h_t/[1+E(N|H_t(0)=1)].

Under (PC), for R=floor(bh_t^−1/4) and 2κb≤a, this is at least h_t/(1+C). These selected centers are not necessarily isolated among all holes; the remaining holes will be helpful for the hole-loss argument.

## 3. A nearby active particle forces some hole loss in its selected ball

Let j_t be the intensity of selected centers with at least one active particle within distance R. Conditional on the complete time-t history and the priorities, choose one such active particle by a translation-covariant rule. For example, order its current displacement and initial-origin displacement relative to the center lexicographically; the set of eligible labels is finite. Its unused future increments remain independent simple-walk steps under the particle-walk construction.

On the event in Step 1 for this particle's free future path relative to the center, at least one hole that was unfilled at time t inside B_{κR}(center) fills by time t+n. Indeed, if the particle settles before reaching the center, its settlement is at a hole inside that ball. If the center's hole has already filled by its arrival, that is already a hole loss in the ball. Otherwise its arrival, possibly in a tie with other particles, fills the center's hole. The free path has not exited the ball before that arrival. Other surviving holes can stop the particle earlier but cannot invalidate the assertion that some hole in the ball fills.

Thus each eligible center has conditional probability at least c_hit/R² of a hole loss in its ball during the window. Independence between different centers is neither required nor asserted.

For each eligible center with such a loss, choose one lost hole in its ball and send one unit of mass from that hole to the center. The balls are disjoint, so a lost hole sends at most one unit. Translation invariance and nonnegative mass transport give

(c_hit/R²)j_t ≤ density of eligible centers witnessing a loss
≤P(H_t(0)=1,H_{t+n}(0)=0)=h_t−h_{t+n}.

Hence j_t≤D R²(h_t−h_{t+2R²}). Capacity one and permanent filling justify the final equality. This bound uses a time-window hole loss, not a hole–active decorrelation estimate.

## 4. Cover sites near the selected centers with no nearby active particle

The good selected centers, those with no active particle within R, have density at least (i_t−j_t)_+. Every site within floor(R/2) of a good center is strictly nearer its hole than every active particle: for such a site w and active site z,

|z−w|_1≥|z−center|_1−|w−center|_1>R−floor(R/2)≥|w−center|_1.

These small balls are disjoint because the selected centers are more than 2κR apart. Sending unit mass from each good center to each site of its small ball therefore yields

P(F_t)≥|B_floor(R/2)|[i_t−D R²(h_t−h_{t+2R²})]_+.

This finite-scale inequality is valid for any deterministic R≥R0 and any translation-covariant separated-hole selection as above.

## 5. There are arbitrarily late windows with controlled inverse-density growth

For the sparse critical law, h_t↓0 and h_t≥c0/(t+1) eventually, by source Corollary 1.3 and Lemma 5.1. Set g_t=1/h_t; it is nondecreasing and g_t≤(t+1)/c0 for all sufficiently large t. For R_t=floor(bg_t^{1/4}) set n_t=2R_t². Eventually R_t≥R0 and n_t≥1.

There are arbitrarily large t with

g_{t+n_t}−g_t≤A n_t, where A=2/c0.

Otherwise, beyond some T the reverse strict inequality would hold at every integer time. Starting at t0=T and iterating t_{k+1}=t_k+n_{t_k} gives t_k→∞ and, by telescoping,

g_{t_k}−g_T>A(t_k−T).

But g_{t_k}≤(t_k+1)/c0. Dividing by t_k and letting k→∞ forces A≤1/c0, a contradiction. No differentiability, smooth density asymptotic or fixed-window independence is used.

At the resulting sequence of times,

h_t−h_{t+n_t}=h_t h_{t+n_t}(g_{t+n_t}−g_t)≤A n_t h_t².

Consequently

j_t≤D R_t² A n_t h_t²=2AD R_t^4 h_t²≤2AD b^4 h_t≤h_t/[2(1+C)].

Since i_t≥h_t/(1+C), good selected-hole density is at least h_t/[2(1+C)] along this sequence. Finally,

h_t|B_floor(R_t/2)|→(2^4/4!)b^4/16=b^4/24.

Step 4 gives the asserted positive subsequential lower bound b^4/[48(1+C)].

## Exact unresolved piece

Proving (PC) for one fixed sparse d4 law would now refute the limit-to-zero statement. It is enough to bound the Palm expected count of other holes in one fixed fraction of the mean-spacing ball by an arbitrary finite constant. No small pair-sum constant, mixed-moment bound, or positive-liminf density estimate beyond the universal inverse-time lower bound is required. C5/C8 supply initial-p estimates that grow like p/h_t on this scale, so they do not prove (PC).

Sources used: arXiv:2609.02820v1, Lemma 5.1/Corollary 1.3, and comparison with Theorem 1.6 proof; Lawler–Limic, author PDF, Theorem 4.3.1; own audited C1 periodic local CLT. body:
The identification of the dual of L^p has two genuine exceptions. (1) p = infinity fails in general: apart from the degenerate case of finitely many atoms all of finite measure (where L^1 = L^infinity is finite-dimensional and the duality is trivially true), L^1 is a proper closed subspace of (L^infinity)*. On [0,1] with Lebesgue measure, C[0,1] embeds isometrically in L^infinity (for continuous functions the sup norm equals the essential sup norm); extend the evaluation functional h -> h(0) from C[0,1] to a norm-one functional Lambda on L^infinity by Hahn-Banach. If Lambda were integration against some g in L^1, then taking continuous h_n with h_n(0) = 1, 0 <= h_n <= 1, supported in [0, 1/n], dominated convergence would give int h_n g -> 0 while Lambda(h_n) = 1. (Concretely, (L^infinity)* is the space of finitely additive bounded measures absolutely continuous with respect to mu.) (2) p = 1 without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) fails: let X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity. Then L^1(mu) = {0}, so (L^1)* = {0}, while L^infinity(mu) is one-dimensional; the canonical map L^infinity -> (L^1)* is not injective, let alone onto. (3) For 0 < p < 1 and mu nonatomic (e.g. Lebesgue on [0,1]) the dual is trivial: (L^p[0,1])* = {0}, so no duality/Hahn-Banach argument survives below p = 1. Only the range 1 < p < infinity is safe for an arbitrary measure space: there L^p is reflexive and (L^p)* = L^{p'} for every measure, whereas L^1 and L^infinity are reflexive only in degenerate finite-dimensional cases.
examples use Lebesgue measure on [0,1] and a one-point space of infinite measure
statements about (L^infinity)* use the axiom of choice via Hahn-Banach
the degenerate exception in (1) is a measure that is a finite sum of atoms of finite measure
title: Pitfall: (L^1)* = L^infinity needs sigma-finiteness, and (L^infinity)* is strictly larger than L^1
