ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Even agreement of every one- and two-site marginal need not identify a measure. On Z, partition into triples with a uniformly random phase and use iid uniform even-parity bit triples (000,011,101,110). Every pair of distinct bits is independent Bernoulli(1/2), including pairs across triples. The measure is translation invariant. For three consecutive sites, however, the all-ones probability is (1/3)*0+(2/3)*(1/8)=1/12, whereas iid Bernoulli(1/2) gives 1/8. Thus the pair-correlation experiments cannot distinguish all possible candidate laws. Check: For an aligned triple, 111 is forbidden. In each nonaligned phase the triple crosses a block boundary; two bits from one block are independent and the third is independent of them, giving 1/8. Averaging the three phases gives 1/12. Obstruction: Need a coupling or a characterization using all cylinder events. This auxiliary counterexample refutes only the proposed inference from pair data, not equality of the actual ARW limits.

body:
[Prop 36 of arXiv:2608.28355, 'About the contractibility of the walking coinductive equivalence'] Let $0\leq t\leq d-2$.
Let $A$ be a complicial set, and $\tau$ a $d$-simplex of $A$ whose restriction to the first copy of $\Delta[t]$ is degenerate at a vertex, which is represented by a map $\tau\colon\Delta[d]/\Delta[t]\to A$. Then there exists a $(d+1)$-simplex in $A$, represented by a map \[\widetilde\tau\colon\Delta[d+1]\to A\]
such that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\widetilde\tau$ defines a map of marked simplicial sets
\[
\widetilde\tau\colon\Delta^{t+1}[d+1]\amalg_{\Delta[d+1]}\Delta^{t+2}[d+1]\to A;
\]
    \item $\tau$ is the $(t+1)$-st face of $\widetilde\tau$; that is, the diagram of simplicial sets commutes
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\Delta[d]\arrow[d,"\tau"swap]\arrow[r,"d^{t+1}"]&\Delta[d+1]\arrow[d,"\widetilde\tau"]\\
A\arrow[r,equal]&A; 
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\item
  the restriction of the $(t+2)$-nd face of $\widetilde\tau$ to the first copy of $\Delta[t+1]$ is degenerate at a vertex; that is, it is represented by a map of simplicial sets
\[
d^{t+2}\widetilde\tau\colon\Delta[d]/\Delta[t+1]\to A.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In particular, there is a commutative diagram of marked simplicial sets
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\Delta[d]\arrow[r,"d^{t+1}"]\arrow[d]\arrow[rd,"\tau"swap]&\Delta^{t+1}[d+1]\amalg_{\Delta[d+1]}\Delta^{t+2}[d+1]\arrow[d,"\widetilde\tau"]&\arrow[l,"d^{t+2}"swap]\arrow[d]\Delta[d]\arrow[ld,"d^{t+2}\widetilde\tau"]\\
\Delta[d]/\Delta[t]\arrow[r]&A&\Delta[d]/\Delta[t+1]\arrow[l]
\end{tikzcd}
\]

[Theorem thm:d23-critical-level-percolation of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Fix $d\in\{2,3\}$, $\nu_{0}>0$, $\theta_{0}>0$, and $K_{0}<\infty$. There are
$c=c(d,\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})>0$ and
$t_0=t_0(d,\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})<\infty$ such that, for every mean-zero i.i.d.\
field $(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ satisfying
\[
    \Var(\zeta(0))\geq\nu_{0}^2\, ,\qquad \mathbb{E} e^{\theta_{0}|\zeta(0)|}\leq K_{0}\, ,
\]
and every $t\geq t_0$, the planar set
\[
    \{x:u_t(x)>c t^{(4-d)/4}\}
\]
contains an infinite nearest-neighbor component almost surely, where $x$ ranges
over $\mathbb{Z}^2$ if $d=2$, and over $\mathbb{Z}^2\times\{0\}$ if $d=3$.

[Theorem thm:GS of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] There are positive constants $\mathsf c_0,\mathsf c_1,\mathsf c_2$, depending only on $d$, such that the following holds.
Tessellate as in (sec:tessellation of the paper) with $\beta/L^2<\mathsf c_0$, and let $E(i,\tau)$ be an
increasing event restricted to the super-cell $\scell{i}{\tau}$. Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and fix
$w$ such that
\[
  w\ \ge\ \sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{o}\beta}{\mathsf c_2L^2}\,\log\Big(\frac{8\mathsf c_1}{\varepsilon}\Big)} .
\]
Then there is $\alpha_0>0$, depending on $\varepsilon$, $\mathfrak{o}$, $w$ and the ratio $\beta/L^2$ but
not on $L$ nor on the intensity, such that if
\begin{equation}

  \min\Big\{\varepsilon^2\eta L^d,\
  \log\frac1{1-\nu_E\big((1-\varepsilon)\eta,\,Q_{(2\mathfrak{o}+1)L},\,Q_{wL},\,\beta\big)}\Big\}
  \ \ge\ \alpha_0 ,
\end{equation}
then almost surely a two-sided Lipschitz surface $F$ exists on which $E(i,\tau)$ holds for every
$(i,\tau)\in F$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Existence of the surface

[Satz th:BBLM of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] If $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are independent random variables and $f = f(X) \in L^\infty({\mathbb P})$, with the constant $\kappa = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2\,(\sqrt{e} - 1)}$, we have for any $r \ge 2$,
	\begin{equation*} 
		\lVert (f - \mathbb{E}f)_+ \rVert_r \le (2\kappa r)^{1/2}\, \lVert \mathfrak{h}^+f \rVert_r \quad \text{and} \quad
		
		
		\lVert (f - \mathbb{E}f)_- \rVert_r \le (2\kappa r)^{1/2}\, \lVert \mathfrak{h}^-f \rVert_r.
	\end{equation*}
	Consequently, this leads to 
	\[
	\norm{f - \IE f}_r \le (8\kappa r)^{1/2} \norm{\mathfrak{h}f}_r.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition def:h-i-constrained-walk of arXiv:2605.06511, 'Logarithmic Mixing of Random Walks on Dynamical Random Cluster Models'] Let $h, i \in \mathbb{N}$. An \textit{$(h, i)$-constrained walk} on a rooted tree is a walk of length $h + 2i$ starting at the root of the tree, with exactly $h + i$ transitions increasing the depth by $+1$ and $i$ transitions decreasing the depth by~$-1$. By $\omega_{h, i}$ we denote the number of $(h,i)$-constrained walks on the rooted infinite $d$-regular tree, while by $\widetilde{\omega}_{h, i}$ we denote the number of $(h,i)$-constrained walks on the rooted infinite $(d - 1)$-ary tree.
title: $(h, i)$-constrained walk

body: In combinatorics, a matroid is a structure that abstracts and generalizes the notion of linear independence in vector spaces. There are many equivalent ways to define a matroid axiomatically, the most significant being in terms of: independent sets; bases or circuits; rank functions; closure operators; and closed sets or flats. In the language of partially ordered sets, a finite simple matroid is equivalent to a geometric lattice.

Suppose the limiting boundary decomposes into invariant measurable sets A1,...,Ak of positive intensity, nuclei in every Ai produce nonempty cells, and the associated boundary label can be reconstructed measurably from each cell and its diagram. Then selecting cells whose label is Ai is an equivariant rule, so these classes are distinguishable. Independent restrictions of the boundary Poisson process preserve all k label populations, but geometric visibility of those nuclei remains an additional requirement. Check: Equivariance of the recovered label implies invariance of each selection rule. Positive intensity alone is not enough: nuclei with empty cells would not provide a cell type, which is why nonemptiness was explicitly assumed. body:
Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y) a bounded linear operator. T is a Fredholm operator if (a) its kernel ker T is finite-dimensional and (b) its range ran T has finite codimension, i.e. the quotient vector space Y / ran T is finite-dimensional. The index of a Fredholm operator is the integer ind T = dim ker T - dim(Y / ran T). The range of a Fredholm operator is automatically closed (a bounded operator between Banach spaces whose range has finite algebraic codimension has closed range), so texts that add 'ran T is closed' to the definition define the same class. For Fredholm T one has dim(Y / ran T) = dim ker T', where T': Y' -> X' is the Banach-space adjoint, so ind T = dim ker T - dim ker T'. Examples on l^2: an invertible operator has index 0; the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is injective with range of codimension 1, so ind S = -1, and its adjoint (the backward shift) has index +1; I + K with K compact has index 0. The set of Fredholm operators X -> Y is written Phi(X,Y).
X and Y are Banach spaces over the same field
T is a bounded linear operator from X to Y
title: Fredholm Operator and Fredholm Index

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2609.00867, '2609.00867'] Let \(g=g_{d,s}^{(m)}\), where \(m=0\) when \(s=0\), and let
\((\kappa_j)_{j\ge1}\) be the nonincreasing eigenvalue sequence used in
\eqref{eq:kernel-spectral-decomposition}.
Assume that \(\rho\) is bounded below by a positive constant almost everywhere
on a ball \(D\subset\mathbb R^d\).  Then
\begin{equation*}
 \kappa_j\ge c_{d,s,m,\rho,D}j^{-(d-s)/d},
 \qquad j\ge1.
\end{equation*}
In particular, \(A_{g,\rho}\) has infinitely many positive eigenvalues.

body:
[Theorem 24 of arXiv:2608.19976, 'Random valuations'] Let $\Phi$ be a non-trivial stationary $\sigma$-continuous non-negative ID
  valuation with independent increments and vanishing deterministic
  part. If $\Phi$ is $\alpha$-stable in argument, then 
  $\alpha\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, and its L\'evy measure has representation
  \begin{equation}
    
    \nu(\sC_L\times A)=\int_A
    \int_{G(d,d-\alpha)} V_{\alpha}(\Pi_{E^\perp}L)
    G_{d-\alpha,r}(dE)\mu(dr)
  \end{equation}
  for all compact sets $L$ in $\R^d$ and Borel
  $A\subset(0,\infty)$. Furthermore, in the corresponding Poisson
  point process $\{(F_i,r_i), i\geq1\}$ all sets $F_i$ are affine subspaces
  of dimension $d-\alpha$. Conversely, for each
  $\alpha\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, representation
  \eqref{eq:stable-stationary} implies that $\Phi$ is
  $\alpha$-stable in argument.

[Corollary thm_diffusive of arXiv:2608.07236, 'Negative association of Busemann functions \\in exponential last-passage percolation'] Fix $\varepsilon >0$. 
For any $\rho_1,\rho_2, \dots,\rho_n \in [\varepsilon,1 -\varepsilon]$, any down-right path $\mathcal{Y}= (\mathbf y_i)_{i\in \mathbb{Z}}$, and any $t\ge 0$, we have
\begin{subequations}
\begin{align} 
\mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n B^{\rho_{i}}_{\mathbf y_i, \mathbf y_{i+1}} - \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^n B^{\rho_{i}}_{\mathbf y_i, \mathbf y_{i+1}} \Big]\geq t \sqrt n \Big) 
&\leq e^{-\min\{\varepsilon^2t^2, \varepsilon t\sqrt n\}/4}\\
\text{and} \quad 
\mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n B^{\rho_{i}}_{\mathbf y_i, \mathbf y_{i+1}} - \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^n B^{\rho_{i}}_{\mathbf y_i, \mathbf y_{i+1}} \Big]\leq -t \sqrt n \Big) 
&\leq e^{-\min\{\varepsilon^2t^2, \varepsilon t\sqrt n\}/4}.
\end{align}
\end{subequations} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Concentration of sums

body:
A ring R (associative, with 1) is semisimple - every left R-module is a direct sum of simple modules, equivalently R is a finite direct sum of simple left modules, equivalently R is left Artinian with zero Jacobson radical - if and only if R is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings over division rings: R = M_{n_1}(D_1) x ... x M_{n_r}(D_r). The integers r and n_i and the division rings D_i (up to isomorphism) are determined by R: r is the number of isomorphism classes of simple left R-modules, and the simple module S_i = D_i^{n_i} has End_R(S_i) = D_i (opposite conventions aside). A simple left Artinian ring is a single matrix ring M_n(D). Consequences: for a finite group G and a field k of characteristic not dividing |G| (Maschke), the group algebra k[G] is semisimple, so k[G] = prod M_{n_i}(D_i); over an algebraically closed field the D_i are k itself, the n_i are the degrees of the irreducible representations, r is the number of conjugacy classes, and |G| = sum n_i^2. A commutative semisimple ring is a finite product of fields. Wedderburn's little theorem (finite division rings are fields) then gives: a finite semisimple ring is a product of matrix rings over finite fields.
R associative with identity; 'semisimple' means semisimple as a left module over itself (equivalent to the right-module version)
the division rings need not be commutative (the real quaternions H occur, e.g. in R[Q_8])

(3) Every ring is anti-isomorphic to its endomorphism ring as a left module over itself, R^{op} = End_R(R), via r -> right multiplication by r. (4) Hom_R(S_i^{n_i}, S_j^{n_j}) = 0 for i != j (Schur), so End_R(R) = prod_i End_R(S_i^{n_i}) = prod_i M_{n_i}(End_R(S_i)) = prod_i M_{n_i}(D_i), the middle step being the description of endomorphisms of a direct sum of n copies of a module by n x n matrices over its endomorphism ring. (5) Hence R = (prod M_{n_i}(D_i))^{op} = prod M_{n_i}(D_i^{op}), and D_i^{op} is again a division ring; renaming gives the theorem. body:
[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2606.11389, 'Instability of a nonlinear oscillator with small friction and small additive noise'] (i)  Suppose $g: \R^2 \to \R$ is in $L^1(\mu)$.  Then for all $\e > 0$ and all $(x_0,y_0) \in \R^2$
   $$
  \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} g(x_n,y_n) \to 0 \quad \mbox{almost surely}.
   $$

(ii) Suppose the process $\{X_t: t \ge 0\}$ satisfies $|X_t| \le g(x_t,y_t)$ where $g: \R^2 \to [0,\infty)$ is in $L^1(\mu)$.  Then for all $\e > 0$ and all $(x_0,y_0,v_0)$ with $v_0 \neq 0$
 $$
   \limsup_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t}\left|  \int_0^t X_s ds \right| \le  \limsup_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t} \int_0^t g(x_s,y_s) ds  =  \int_{\R^2} g(x,y)d\mu(x,y) <\infty
   $$    
almost surely.

(iii)  Suppose the process $\{X_t: t \ge 0\}$ is non-anticipating and satisfies $|X_t| \le g(x_t,y_t)$ where $g: \R^2 \to [0,\infty)$ is in $L^2(\mu)$.  Then for all $\e > 0$ and all $(x_0,y_0,v_0)$ with $v_0 \neq 0$
   $$
      \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t} \int_0^t X_s dW_s = 0
      $$
 almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 11 of arXiv:2606.11389

There exists a constant $C_W$ such that for any diagrammatic graph ${\bf G}=(G,S,\ell)$ with an edge adjacent to $0$ (i.e.~$\ell(x)=0$ for some $\{x,y\} \in E(G)$), we have

\]

[Lem div of arXiv:2412.09535, 'Local limit theorem for joint subgraph counts'] If $H'$ and $H$ are graphs with $v(H) \geq v(H')$, then
\[\frac{\aut H' \cdot X_{H'}(H) \cdot (v(H)-v(H'))!}{\aut H} \in \setz.\]
In particular, for $H \in \mathcal{C}_2\cup\mathcal{C}_3\cup\mathcal{C}_4\cup\mathcal{C}_5$,
\[\frac{v(H)!}{\aut H}, \quad \frac{2(v(H)-2)! e(H)}{\aut H},\quad \frac{4X_{K_2\sqcup P_2}(H)}{\aut H}\in \setz\]
(the above statement applied for $H' = \emptyset, K_2, K_2 \sqcup P_2$).

body: [Lemma of arXiv:2411.07125, 'Mixing on the cycle with constant size perturbation'] For any $ 0<\delta_4<1$ as exception probability, there exists $\alpha_4>0$ such that with probability at least $1-\delta_4$, for all $Y_m \in \mathcal{Y}_m$ and for all $y \in Y_m$, there exist another two points $y',y''\in Y_m$ such that $0< f(y)-f(y')< \alpha_4 s$ and $0< f(y'') - f(y) < \alpha_4 s$. In other word, for all possible $Y_m$ and any $y\in Y_m$, there exist two "neighbors" $y'$ and $y''$ such that their mapped positions $f(y')$ and $f(y'')$ fall on the two sides of $f(y)$, and their distance to $f(y)$ is of the order of the standard distance $s$.
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2411.07125, 'Mixing on the cycle with constant size perturbation'

[Lemma lem:double_flow_lines_interior of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Fix $p \in (0,1)$, $a'>0$. Let~$h$ be a GFF on~$\mathbf{D}$ with boundary values so that its flow line $\eta$ is an ${\rm SLE}_{\kappa}${} from $-i$ to $i$. Let $X^0_{0,1}$ be as defined in~(equation eq:fl_annulus of the paper). Let $I_\epsilon$ be the event that there exist two strands $\eta_{w_1}$, $\eta_{w_2}$ of $X^0_{0,1}$ so that the following hold.
\begin{itemize}
 \item The continuations of $\eta_{w_i}$, $i=1,2$, hit $B(0,\epsilon)$ before exiting $B(0,3/4)$ and without merging.
 \item The conditional probability given $X^0_{0,1}$ and the values of $h$ on $X^0_{0,1}$ that $\eta$ merges into $\eta_{w_1}$ before entering $B(0,1/4)$ and then into $\eta_{w_2}$ before entering $B(0,1/4)$ again is at least $p$.
\end{itemize}
Then there exists $\epsilon_0 > 0$ so that
\[
 \mathbf{P}[I_\epsilon] \leq \epsilon^{\alpha_{4,\kappa}-a'}  \quad\text{for}\quad \epsilon \in (0,\epsilon_0).
\]
title: Lemma lem:double_flow_lines_interior of arXiv:2507.15589

For every d>=2, 0<epsilon<=1/96 and 0<delta<=1/4, any randomized or improper learner learning all sign(a^T U b), U in O(d), under independent standard Gaussian a,b with error <=epsilon at confidence 1-delta requires n>=log(1/delta)/(96epsilon). Paired block rotations yield disagreement between t/6 and t for every d. This standard-testing supplement remains proof (unaudited), with no novelty claim; it supplies the confidence term, not the separate d^2 term.
d>=2; independent Gaussian input blocks; noiseless labels; n IID labeled observations.

metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:45ac823e855903243d2b234b934e93c0b867d02662863dbabef7fd7cd064141d","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/45/45ac823e855903243d2b234b934e93c0b867d02662863dbabef7fd7cd064141d.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:eb398ae394ea335b46c99e6906b8a563306617a87f7bdad65e7646ed9f727bd3","bundle_entry_key":"bilinear-confidence-full-rank-rotation","bundle_id":"population.t407-draft-gaussian-bilinear-confidence-supplement","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning theory","draft":"w693/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.sample_complexity:draft-gaussian-bilinear-orbit-two-point-confidence-lower","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Confidence supplement for the Gaussian bilinear orbit

Status: proof (unaudited). Standard two-point testing, not a novelty claim.
Target 2; supplements LOW-003 v2 without changing that proof or its audit status.

For every d>=2, 0<epsilon<=1/96, and 0<delta<=1/4, any possibly randomized, improper learner achieving population disagreement at most epsilon with probability at least 1-delta for every h_U(a,b)=sign(a^T U b), U in O(d), under independent standard Gaussian a,b, requires

    n >= log(1/delta)/(96 epsilon).

## A pair with dimension-independent disagreement

Let r=floor(d/2), q=2r, P project onto the first q coordinates, and J consist of r standard 2x2 skew rotation blocks and a zero last coordinate if d is odd. Then J^T=-J, J^2=-P. For 0<t<=1/4 put

    U_+(t)=I-P+cos(t)P+sin(t)J,
    U_-(t)=I-P+cos(t)P-sin(t)J.

Both matrices are orthogonal. Conditional on a nonzero b, the normals U_+b and U_-b have equal length ||b|| and distance 2 sin(t)||Pb||. Their angle is therefore

    theta(b)=2 arcsin(sin(t)||Pb||/||b||).

A standard Gaussian a has uniform angular projection onto the span of these normals, so its two sign labels disagree with probability theta(b)/pi. This also holds for coincident normals by continuity. Write u=b/||b||, uniform on the unit sphere. Consequently

    rho_d(t)=(2/pi) E arcsin(sin(t)||Pu||).

When d is even this is exactly 2t/pi. In all dimensions, 0<=||Pu||<=1 and E||Pu||>=E||Pu||^2=q/d>=2/3. Using arcsin(x)>=x, sin(t)>=t/2 and pi<=4 gives

    rho_d(t) >= 2t/(3pi) >= t/6.

Since arcsin(sin(t)||Pu||)<=t, also rho_d(t)<=2t/pi<=t. These are analytic inequalities, uniform in d. Set t=24 epsilon. Then

    4 epsilon <= rho_d(t) <=24 epsilon <=1/4.

## Exact testing overlap, including randomized learners

Let Q_+ and Q_- be the distributions of one labeled observation under these targets, with the same Gaussian input marginal. On their disagreement region D, the two observation distributions have disjoint label support. On D's complement they coincide. For n independent samples their common mass (the integral of the minimum of their densities with respect to a common dominating measure) is exactly

    overlap(Q_+^n,Q_-^n)=(1-rho_d(t))^n.

Indeed, shared labeled samples occur precisely when every input avoids D; that event has marginal probability (1-rho_d(t))^n. Equal-prior optimal testing error is half this mass: pointwise, the cheaper error contribution is half the minimum of the two densities. Adding independent random coins cannot reduce this optimum.

Decode the learner's output by choosing the closer of the two target classifiers in population disagreement, breaking ties arbitrarily. The triangle inequality and separation >=4epsilon imply this decoder is correct whenever the learner's error is <=epsilon. Uniform confidence thus gives testing error <=delta. Hence

    (1-rho_d(t))^n / 2 <=delta,
    n >= log(1/(2delta))/[-log(1-rho_d(t))].

For 0<=rho<=1/4, -log(1-rho)<=rho/(1-rho)<=2rho<=48epsilon. Also delta<=1/4 implies log(1/(2delta))>=log(1/delta)/2. The stated bound follows.

## Relation to the remaining frontier claim

This proves only the confidence contribution. If LOW-003 v2's separately unaudited dimension lower is correct, then for delta<=1/4 and epsilon below a universal constant the two necessary bounds combine as

    n=Omega((d^2+log(1/delta))/epsilon),

because max(A,B)>=(A+B)/2. This would match the independently accepted UP-002 v2 upper order. The combined conclusion remains a candidate until the dimension lower passes independent audit. The hardest outstanding piece remains the source matrix-packing use and conditional-entropy/Fano argument in LOW-003 v2, not this two-point argument.

Primary context: Li-Zhang-Arora, arXiv:2010.08515v2, Lemmas D.2 and D.4. The confidence proof above is self-contained and extends the two-dimensional testing step already in LOW-003 v2 section 5. body: Spread hub (bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture). Let U = <c, X_H> for a set H of hub coordinates with c_h^2 <= |c|^2/2 for every h, and Q = 2 U (L + beta) + sum_{h in H} phi_h(X_h) + lambda V^2 + 2 L <q, X'> + sum_i phi_i(X_i) with the light part as in the single-hub normal form. Then |phi_Q(eta)| <= 8 pi^{3/2} |c|^{-1} |lambda|^{-1/2} |eta|^{-3/2} and ||p_Q||_inf <= 12 (|c|^2 |lambda|)^{-1/3} for all laws and every cross term q. Proof: the hub factor prod_h psi_h(2 eta t c_h + eta b_h) has int dt <= 2 pi/(|eta| |c|) by Hoelder with p_h = |c|^2/c_h^2 (one-dimensional Brascamp-Lieb, shift-invariant), and pairs with the slice bound 2 (4 pi/|eta lambda|)^{1/2}. Roughness of the hub law is an obstruction only when the hub is one coordinate.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked, no independent read.] This is an exactly solved adjacent case of Open Problem 14.12 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). For n>=3 let C_n be the simple cycle on n vertices. Start a particle at every vertex. Each particle independently jumps at rate one to a uniformly chosen neighbor, and particles merge on meeting. Let T_coal be the first time only one particle remains. Then E[T_coal]=(n^2-1)/6. If P is the cycle's discrete-time simple-walk matrix, define its mean spectral hitting-time quantity K=sum_{j=2}^n 1/(1-lambda_j(P)); then K=(n^2-1)/6 also. Thus E[T_coal]=K exactly. Its relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-cos(2pi/n)) satisfies tau_2/K -> 3/pi^2, so this family has the equality conclusion even though the small-relaxation-time hypothesis in the source problem fails. In the extracted optional-stopping proof, EC in a stopping-time subscript denotes the random coalescence time; the final displayed EC denotes its expectation. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Continuous-time rate-one simple walks; one initial particle per vertex.
n>=3 and coalescence occurs on occupying the same vertex.

neighbour, and particles at the same vertex merge.

Label the $k$ particles round the cycle and let $g_1,\dots,g_k \ge 1$ be the gaps between consecutive
particles, so $\sum_i g_i = n$. Put
$$M \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^k g_i^3 .$$

Take a particle with gap $a$ on its left and $b$ on its right. It steps right at rate $1/2$, sending
$(a,b) \mapsto (a+1,b-1)$, and left at rate $1/2$, sending $(a,b) \mapsto (a-1,b+1)$. The two
increments of $M$ are
$$(3a^2+3a+1) + (-3b^2+3b-1) = 3(a^2-b^2) + 3(a+b),$$
$$(-3a^2+3a-1) + (3b^2+3b+1) = -3(a^2-b^2) + 3(a+b),$$
and the quadratic parts cancel in the average, leaving $3(a+b)$. Each particle jumps at rate one, so
summing over the particles,
$$\mathcal L M \;=\; \sum_{i} 3\,(g_{i-1} + g_i) \;=\; 3\,(n+n) \;=\; 6n,$$
independent of the configuration and of the number of particles. That last point is what makes the
argument work: the drift does not care how far along the coalescence is.

When two particles merge, the gap between them has just become zero and is deleted. Since $0^3 = 0$,
$M$ does not jump at a coalescence, so it is continuous through the whole process.

Hence $M_t - 6nt$ is a martingale. $M$ is bounded by $n^3$ and $EC$ has finite mean, so optional
stopping applies. At time zero all $n$ gaps equal one and $M_0 = n$; at time $EC$ there is one particle
and one gap of size $n$, so $M_{EC} = n^3$. Therefore
$$n^3 - n \;=\; 6n\cdot EC, \qquad EC \;=\; \frac{n^2-1}{6}. \qquad\square$$

That $\tau_0(C_n) = \sum_{m=1}^{n-1} 1/(1-\cos(2\pi m/n)) = (n^2-1)/6$ is classical, and is checked

[Proposition 6 (Equivariant flows on the quotient) of arXiv:2608.26961, 'Gromov--Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation'] Let \(v:I\times\R^D\to\R^D\) be \(G\)-equivariant and assume that
\eqref{flow-ode} admits a unique flow \(\gamma_t\). Then \(\gamma_t\) induces
the well-defined quotient flow
\[
\bar\gamma_t([x])\coloneqq[\gamma_t(x)].
\]
For every \(\eta\in\mP_2(\R^D)\) and \(t\in I\),
\[
\mathfrak q_\sharp\gamma_{t,\sharp}\eta
=
\bar\gamma_{t,\sharp}\mathfrak q_\sharp\eta.
\]
In particular, if
\(\mathfrak q_\sharp\eta=\mathfrak q_\sharp\widetilde\eta\), then
\[
\mathfrak q_\sharp\gamma_{t,\sharp}\eta
=
\mathfrak q_\sharp\gamma_{t,\sharp}\widetilde\eta,
\]
so the projected curve is independent of the representative lift at time
\(0\).

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); D0007-C008 v1; audits pending. If F=p Uniform[a,b]+(1-p)G with 0<p<1, a<b finite and G bounded-support, then F is n-completely mixable for every sufficiently large integer n. Symmetry is unnecessary and the uniform interval need not contain mean(F). Put ell=b-a, c=(a+b)/2, m=E_G[X], R=B-A for an interval [A,B] supporting G, C=|c-m|+R, and K0=ceil(max(2,6C/ell,2+2C/ell)). Every n>=ceil(K0/p) works. Cyclic quantile strata couple residual coordinates with sum discrepancy at most R. Rounded uniform counts K and conditional affine density tilts absorb the remaining discrepancy; E[delta]=0 restores the exact full marginal. Finite rounding of delta followed by a weak limit at fixed n handles conditional-coupling selection. Therefore a bounded law with a positive density lower bound on just one subinterval is eventually n-CM. This does not cover densities with essential infimum zero on every interval; general D0007 remains unresolved. The established Wang-Wang monotone density criterion is used as stated in Wang arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(b), equation (6), p.9; novelty not asserted.

Status: proof (unaudited). Uses the established monotone-density CM criterion and fixed-order weak compactness. Novelty not asserted.

Statement. Let 0<p<1, a<b finite, and let G be any bounded-support probability law, possibly discrete. Then

    F=p Uniform[a,b]+(1-p)G

is n-CM for all sufficiently large integer n. The uniform interval can be anywhere, not necessarily centered at mean(F). Thus any bounded absolutely continuous law whose density is bounded below by a positive constant on even one nondegenerate subinterval is eventually n-CM. No density floor is required elsewhere; symmetry is unnecessary.

An explicit threshold: put ell=b-a, c=(a+b)/2, m=E_G[X], R=B-A for any finite interval [A,B] supporting G, and C=|c-m|+R. Choose the integer

    K0=ceil(max(2,6C/ell,2+2C/ell)).

Every n>=ceil(K0/p) works. The p=1 uniform law is directly CM for all n>=2.

Known theorem used: If a probability law has a monotone density on essential [a,b], it is K-CM iff a+ell/K<=its mean<=b-ell/K. Source: Wang-Wang (2011), doi:10.1016/j.jmva.2011.05.002, stated by Ruodu Wang in arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(b), equation (6), p.9. We cite this established theorem rather than reprove it.

1. Bounded-discrepancy coupling for G. For every L>=1, let Q be a quantile of G, with endpoint bounds Q(0)=A and Q(1)=B (values at the endpoints do not affect the law). Draw U uniform on [0,1/L] and form Q(U+(i-1)/L), i=1,...,L. Apply an independent uniform coordinate permutation. Each marginal is G, since the uniformly selected stratum has a uniform quantile argument in [0,1]. The sum S_L does not change under permutation and satisfies

    |S_L-Lm|<=R almost surely.

Indeed monotonicity traps S_L between the lower and upper endpoint sums for the L quantile intervals; Lm lies between the same sums, and their difference telescopes to Q(1)-Q(0)=R. For L=0 take the empty vector and S_0=0. This construction applies to atoms without change.

2. Uniform label counts. Choose K from floor(np) and ceil(np), with expectation np; if np is integer use that fixed count. Set L=n-K. The threshold ensures K>=K0 in every state. Conditional on K draw the G coupling of Step 1, and define

    delta=n*mu-K*c-S_L,
    mu=p*c+(1-p)*m.

Algebra gives delta=(np-K)(c-m)+(Lm-S_L), so |delta|<=C. Also E delta=0 because E K=np and E[S_L|K]=Lm.

3. Monotone uniform tilts absorb the discrepancy. For any K>=K0 and d in [-C,C] define

    t=6d/(K*ell),
    q_{K,d}(x)=(1/ell)[1+t*2(x-c)/ell] on [a,b].

Since |t|<=1 this is a probability density with full essential support [a,b]. It is monotone (increasing for d>0, decreasing for d<0), and its mean is c+t ell/6=c+d/K. Because K>=2+2C/ell,

    |d|<=(K/2-1)ell.

Thus the mean belongs to [a+ell/K,b-ell/K]. The cited theorem supplies a K-CM coupling of q_{K,d}, with sum K*c+d.

4. Avoid any unproved measurable selection. For each mesh eta>0, choose a finite grid in [-C,C] and a measurable rounding function d_eta(delta) with |d_eta(delta)-delta|<=eta and |d_eta(delta)|<=C. If C=0 use the singleton grid {0}. Only finitely many K and rounded d occur. Choose one of the couplings from Step 3 for each pair. Conditional on the G-vector and K use the coupling for d=d_eta(delta), combine its K coordinates with the L G coordinates, and uniformly permute all n coordinates. This is a well-defined Borel probability coupling because there are only finitely many selected kernels.

Its total sum is

    S_L+K*c+d_eta(delta)=n*mu+d_eta(delta)-delta,

so its deviation from n*mu is at most eta.

5. The identical marginals converge exactly to F. A fixed permuted coordinate has G-contribution (1-p)G, since E L/n=1-p and conditional on K every G-coordinate has marginal G. Its uniform-reserve contribution is E[(K/n)q_{K,d_eta(delta)}]. The constant density part is p/ell. The linear part is proportional to

    E[K*t]/n=6 E[d_eta(delta)]/(n*ell).

Since E delta=0, |E d_eta(delta)|<=eta. The L1 norm of this signed linear perturbation is at most 3 eta/(n*ell). Hence the full marginals converge in total variation to F as eta goes to zero. No independence between K and the discrepancy is assumed.

6. Take a fixed-n weak limit. All coordinates are supported on the fixed compact interval spanning [A,B] and [a,b]. Therefore the sequence of n-dimensional couplings as eta decreases to zero has a weakly convergent subsequence. Coordinate projections are continuous, so every limiting marginal is F by Step 5. The continuous sum map and the uniform sum error bound in Step 4 force the limit to have sum n*mu almost surely. Equivalently the expectation of the bounded continuous squared sum error tends to zero. This gives an exact n-complete mix.

7. Local density-floor corollary. If an absolutely continuous bounded-support F has f(x)>=c0>0 almost everywhere on [a,b], set p=c0*(b-a). The global mean need not be the uniform interval center.

\end{equation}

(2) The space (X, d) is called δ-hyperbolic (or Gromov-hyperbolic) if every geodesic triangle in Xis δ-slim.

\[
 \left(\prod_e c_1(L_e)\right)
 \left(\prod_vc_{\rk F_v}(F_v)^{r_v}\right)
 =
 \ctop\!\left(\bigoplus_vF_v^{\oplus b_v}\right),

[Definition def:G_mu of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Fix a smooth, increasing function $\chi:\R\rightarrow[0,1]$ 
such that $\chi|_{(-\infty,1]}=0$ and $\chi|_{[2,\infty)}=1$.
For any $\mu\in[0,1]$ and $t\geqslant0$, 
we define the regularized kernel $G_\mu$, which is given by
   \begin{equs}
       G_\mu(t)\eqdef \chi(t/\mu) \,, \end{equs} 
with the convention that $G_0=G$. 
Finally, we write $\dot G_\mu(t)\eqdef\d_\mu G_\mu(t)$.

body:
[Cor 170 (quenched second moment bounds for $Y^{\RomI}$ and $Y^{\RomI,\frozen}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $N$ large enough, we have
	\beq
	\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0 \le d\le \dmax-1
	\bigg\}
    \le L^{O(1)} \delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2
    \,,
    \eeq
with $\MAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}. The same bound holds with $\vY^\frozen$ in place of $\vY$. 

\begin{proof} It follows using
Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} that
	\[\bE\Big(
	\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big)
	\le \bE\Big( \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))^2\Big)
	+ O(\eta)\bigg\{ \bE\Big| \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	+ \eta\bigg\}\,.\]
From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from $[M]$, even if we condition on the gaussian disorder. Thus we can apply Proposition~\ref{p:X.second.mmt.quenched} with $a(q_{d+1})$ in place of $\hat{a}$. Together with Jensen's inequality and \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound}, it implies
	\[
	\bE\Big[\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big]
    \le L^{O(1)}\Big\{ \delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2
    + \eta^2\Big\}
    \le L^{O(1)}\delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
using that $\MAX_N\ge1$ and $\eta\ll\delta$ from Assumption~\ref{a:params}. This proves \eqref{e:Y.I.second.quenched}, and the analogous bound for $Y^{\frozen,\RomI}$ follows by the same argument.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: quenched second moment bounds for $Y^{\RomI}$ and $Y^{\RomI,\frozen}$

body:
[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $V$ be a $G$-representation. Then $\ev_V\colon{\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}\to\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl},*}({\mathbb B{G}\times{-}})$ admits a left adjoint $\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\otimes_G{-}$.
    \begin{proof}
        As ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}$ is globally cocomplete, the functor ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}\to{\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}(\mathbb B{G}\times-)$ equipping an $H$-global spectrum with the trivial $G$-action admits a left adjoint. Thus, it will suffice to show that the functor ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}(\mathbb B{G}\times-)\to\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl},*}(\mathbb B{G}\times-)$ induced by the functor $\ev_V\colon\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}\rightarrow\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}$ sending $X$ to $X(V)$ with the diagonal $G$-action admits a left adjoint. For every compact Lie group $H$, the induced functor $\ev_V\colon\cat{$\bm{(G\times H)}$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}\to\cat{$\bm{(G\times H)}$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}_*$ is right Quillen by Lemmas~(lemma:ev-RA of the paper) and~(lemma:restr-right-Quillen of the paper), and its left adjoint $\textbf{\textup{O}}(V,-)\smashp{-}$ sends $(G\times H)$-global weak equivalences between well-based $(G\times H)$-orthogonal spaces to $(G\times H)$-global level weak equivalences by Corollary~(cor:global-smash-well-based of the paper). The same argument as in the proof Lemma~(lemma:omega-oo-both-adjoints of the paper) (which considered the special case $G=1$ and $V=0$) therefore shows that the individual left adjoints ${{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\text{$(G\times H)$-gl},*}\to{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\text{$(G\times H)$-gl}$ satisfy the Beck--Chevalley condition and hence assemble into the desired global left adjoint.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'

[Lemma 24 (Shifted distance recursion) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Let $E_{\mathrm{weak}}$, $E_{\mathrm{strong}}$, and $\Gamma$ denote the weak-error,
strong-error, and coupling-increment functions of
Propositions~\ref{prop:weak-error-app}, \ref{prop:strong-error-app},
and~\ref{prop:coupling-increment-app}, and set
\[
  a_0(x):=E_{\mathrm{strong}}(x),
  \qquad
  a_1(x,y):=E_{\mathrm{weak}}(x)+\Gamma(x,y,\lambda)\,E_{\mathrm{strong}}(x).
\]
For $0\le n\le N-1$, let $\eta_n\in[0,1]$,
$\widetilde Y_n:=(1-\eta_n)Y_n'+\eta_n\widehat X_n$, and
$d_n^2:=\E\|\widehat X_n-Y_n'\|^2$, and put
\[
  \overline a_0
  :=\sup_{0\le k<N}\|a_0(\widehat X_k)\|_{L^2},
  \qquad
  \overline a_1
  :=\sup_{0\le k<N}\|a_1(\widehat X_k,\widetilde Y_k)\|_{L^2}.
\]
Then, with $L:=e^{K'\lambda}$, for every $0\le n\le N-2$,
\[
  d_{n+1}^2
  \le
  L^2(1-\eta_n)^2\,d_n^2
  +2(1-\eta_n)\,\overline a_1\,d_n
  +\overline a_0^{\,2}.
\]

body:
[Theorem 6 (Configuration-space factorization of the Palm-cell volume) of arXiv:2607.20680, 'Exact Scale--Shape Factorization of the Typical Poisson--Voronoi Cell Volume in Arbitrary '] Let \(K=N(C_0)\). Then the quantities defined in \eqref{eq:p-def} are the facet-number probabilities:
\begin{equation*}
  \mathbb P(K=k)=p_{d,k},
  \qquad k\geq d+1.
\end{equation*}

For every \(k\) with \(p_{d,k}>0\), let \(\bfx\) have distribution \(\mathsf P_{d,k,\lambda}\), and define
\begin{equation*}
  T_k=Q(\bfx),
  \qquad
  U_k=Q(\bfx)^{-1/d}\bfx\in\Sigma_{d,k}.
\end{equation*}
Then their joint distribution is the product measure
\begin{equation}
  
  \mathsf P_{d,k,\lambda}
  \{T_k\in\dd t,U_k\in\dd\bfu\}
  =
  \frac{\lambda^k}{\Gamma(k)}
  t^{k-1}e^{-\lambda t}\,\dd t\,
  \nu_{d,k}(\dd\bfu).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation*}
  T_k\sim
  \operatorname{Gamma}\bigl(k,\operatorname{rate}=\lambda\bigr),
  \qquad
  U_k\sim\nu_{d,k},
  \qquad
  T_k\perp U_k.
\end{equation*}

Writing
\[
A_k=\alpha(U_k)=\frac{G(U_k)}{Q(U_k)}=G(U_k),
\]
the conditional Palm-cell volume satisfies
\begin{equation}
  
  V_{d,\lambda}\mid\{K=k\}
  \overset{\mathrm d}=T_kA_k,
\end{equation}
where
\[
A_k\sim\eta_{d,k},
\qquad
T_k\perp A_k.
\]

Equivalently, for the intensity-normalized cell volume
\[
Y_d=\lambda V_{d,\lambda},
\]
one may construct \(K\) with \(\mathbb P(K=k)=p_{d,k}\) and, conditionally on \(K=k\), independent random variables
\[
A_k\sim\eta_{d,k},
\qquad
Z_k\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(k,\operatorname{rate}=1),
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
  
  Y_d\overset{\mathrm d}=A_KZ_K.
\end{equation}
Values assigned on strata with \(p_{d,k}=0\) are immaterial.
title: Configuration-space factorization of the Palm-cell volume

[Proposition prop:cesaro of arXiv:2607.19844, 'Binomial probabilities at a fixed distance from the mode:\\ size-biasing and the complete '] Let $0<p<1$ and $h_N=\lceil Np\rceil-Np$.
	\begin{itemize}
	\item[(i)] If $p$ is irrational, then $(h_N)_{N\ge1}$ is equidistributed in $[0,1)$ and, for
		every $n$ and every fixed $r\in\mathbb Z$,
		\[
			\lim_{M\to\infty}\frac1M\sum_{N=1}^{M}c_n(h_N+r;p)=\gamma_{n,0}(r;p)
			=\int_0^1 c_n(h+r;p)\,dh .
		\]
	\item[(ii)] If $p=a/b$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$, then $h_N$ is periodic in $N$ with period $b$ and
		takes each of the values $0,\tfrac1b,\dots,\tfrac{b-1}b$ exactly once per period.  The
		mean of $c_n$ over a period is obtained from (equation eq:cn-basis of the paper) by the substitution
		\[
			B_j(h)\;\longmapsto\;b^{-j}B_j\qquad(j\ge0),
		\]
		where $B_j=B_j(0)$, so that in particular $B_1=-\tfrac12$.
	\end{itemize}

[Lemm l:quenched-weak-convergence of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] Almost surely, the un-normalized measures $M_{\beta,n}^\xi$ converge weakly to a finite measure $M_{\beta}^\xi$.
    The limiting annealed un-normalized measure is $\mathbb{E}[M_\beta^\xi] = \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{BB}}$.

title: Quenched weak convergence of GMC measures

[Lemma lem:Qlimit of arXiv:2511.01058, 'Limit profiles and cutoff for the Burnside process on Sylow double cosets'] Let \(p=p_m\) and \(k=k_m\) be two sequences with \(p_m \to \infty\). Then,

              \[

[Definition 97 (Measurable fixed-point domain) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] For a data pair $(\Upsilon,z)$ on $[0,T_0]$, set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal C_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z):=
 \left\{
 M_{T_0}^{\mathrm{bd}}(\Upsilon,z)\le k+1,
 \quad
 \mu_T(\Upsilon,z)P_{R_k}\le\frac18
 \right\},
 \qquad k\in\mathbb N,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal A_T(\Upsilon,z):=
 \bigcup_{k\ge1}\mathcal C_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z).
\end{equation}
On $\mathcal C_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z)$, let $Z_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z)$ denote the
radius-$R_k$ fixed point, extended by zero off this event, and define
\[
 D_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z)
 :=\mathcal C_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z)\setminus
   \bigcup_{\ell<k}\mathcal C_{\ell,T}(\Upsilon,z).
\]
The associated partial solution map, extended by zero outside
$\mathcal A_T(\Upsilon,z)$, is
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr S_T(\Upsilon,z)
 :=\sum_{k\ge1}
 \mathbf1_{D_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z)}Z_{k,T}(\Upsilon,z).
\end{equation}
title: Measurable fixed-point domain

[Lemma 26 (Persistence of the retained fibration on a large block) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix \(\delta_0>0\), \(0<\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}<\delta_0/10\), and
\(\theta_{\max}>0\).  Let
\[
 \theta,\quad \beta_{\mathrm{fib}},\quad \eps_{\mathrm{fib}}
\]
be any fixed choice of constants for which
Lemma~\ref{lem:pointwise-fixed-fiber} holds with these parameters.

Let \(p(\tau)\), \(1\leq\tau\leq100\), be a parabolically rescaled
\(\delta_0\)-large block, and let \(q(\tau)=\Psi_\tau^*p(\tau)\) for a smooth
family of diffeomorphisms.  Let \(r(\tau)\) be a smooth family of invariant metrics for one fixed fibration
\(\pi:M\to S^1\).  Suppose
\begin{equation}
 d_{\TT^2}(r(1))<\theta
\end{equation}
and, for every \(\tau\in[1,100]\),
\begin{equation}
 \|q(\tau)-r(\tau)\|_{C^1(M,r(\tau))}<\beta_{\mathrm{fib}}.
\end{equation}
Suppose also that at every such \(\tau\) there exist an invariant metric \(h_B(\tau)\) and a torus fibration
\(\pi_B(\tau):M\to S_B^1(\tau)\) such that, for every
\(\pi_B(\tau)\)-fiber \(F_B\),
\begin{equation}
 \|h_B(\tau)-q(\tau)\|_{C^1(M,q(\tau))}<\eps_{\mathrm{fib}},
 \qquad
 \diam_{q(\tau)}F_B\leq\eps_{\mathrm{fib}}.
\end{equation}
Then, throughout the block,
\begin{align}
 d_{\TT^2}(r(\tau))&<\theta,                                    \\
 L(S^1,r_{S^1}(\tau))&\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}.                     
\end{align}
Moreover, every \(\pi_B(\tau)\) is fiber-equivalent to \(\pi\).

[Corollary theo:diffeo of arXiv:2411.10235, '\textbf{Smooth transport map via diffusion process}'] Let $p,q:\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be probability density functions of the form $$p(x)=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|\Sigma_p^{-1/2}(x-\mu_p)\|^2+a(x)\right) \quad \text{ and } \quad q(x)=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|\Sigma_q^{-1/2}(x-\mu_q)\|^2+b(x)\right),$$
with $\mu_p,\mu_q\in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\Sigma_p,\Sigma_q$ symmetric  matrices satisfying $K^{-1}\text{Id}\preceq \Sigma_i\preceq K\text{Id}$ for $i\in \{p,q\}$.
Suppose that $a,b \in \mathcal{H}^{\beta,\theta}_K(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R})$ with $\beta\geq 0$, $\theta>1$ and $K>0$. Then, there exists a map $T\in C^{\lfloor \beta \rfloor+1}(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^d)$ satisfying $\nabla T,\nabla T^{-1}\in  \mathcal{H}^{\beta}_C  (\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $T_{\# }p=q$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In the mathematical field of graph theory, Kirchhoff's theorem or Kirchhoff's matrix tree theorem is a theorem about the number of spanning trees in a graph. It states that this number can be computed as any cofactor of the graph's Laplacian matrix. This shows in particular that the number of spanning trees can be computed from the graph data in polynomial time. Kirchhoff's theorem is a generalization of Cayley's formula which provides the number of spanning trees in a complete graph. The theorem is named after the German mathematician Gustav Kirchhoff, who published it in 1847. An English translation of Kirchhoff's paper was published in 1958.
title: Kirchhoff's theorem

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Low-density genealogical limit of branching coalescing walks structural calculation Result: Immediate parent-daughter returns renormalize the branching clock. For two independent simple walks started at neighboring sites in Z^3, their relative walk is a time change of simple walk. The probability they never meet is q=1-G(e,0)/G(0,0)=1/G(0,0), using G(0,0)=1+G(e,0) by the first-step identity and lattice symmetry. Thus a rare branch at rate beta produces a macroscopically surviving split at leading rate beta*q, rather than beta. Check: The equality of the two Green-function expressions follows from translation and reflection symmetry of all six neighbors. It concerns an isolated pair; the chance of interference by other particles has not been set to zero without justification. Obstruction: A thinning heuristic suggests time scaling1/(beta*q), but a proof needs control of third-particle encounters, dependent return episodes and joint Palm genealogies. Stationary balance of split and merge counts does not imply independent Poisson clocks.

body: [Proposition 46 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mf A$ be an HTM, $\mathcal Q$ be a $\sigma$-ring, and $\mf B$ be a sequentially closed topological submonoid of $\mf A$. Then $\ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf B)$ is a submonoid of $\ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf A)$. If $\mf A$ and $\mf B$ are topological groups, then $\ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf B)$ is a subgroup of $\ms M(\mathcal Q,\mf A)$.

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The sequence of cumulants $k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4,\ldots$ is as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $\mu=\delta_c$ the cumulants are $c,0,0,0,\ldots$

\item For $\mu=g_t$ the cumulants are $0,t,0,0,\ldots$

\item For $\mu=p_t$ the cumulants are $t,t,t,t,\ldots$

\item For $\mu=b_t^2$ the cumulants are $0,t,0,t,\ldots$
\end{enumerate}
Also, for the compound Poisson laws the cumulants are $k_n(p_\nu)=M_n(\nu)$.

[Corollary 67 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let $X$ be a Noetherian scheme such that every closed point of $X$ is contained in the closed fiber $X_{\F_p}$.
Assume that $X$ is globally $+$-regular. 
Then \(X_{\F_p}\) is HT-split.

In particular, if $X$ is smooth and projective over $W(k)$ for a perfect field $k$ of characteristic $p$, then for every ample line bundle $L$ on $X$, we have
\[
H^i_{(p)}(X,\Omega^j_{X/W(k)} \otimes L^{-1})=0 \quad (i+j<\dim X).
\]

body: [Definition of arXiv:2609.02123, 'Groups of Transverse Stratifications and the Hierarchy of Configuration Spaces'] The stratification $\mathcal{S}$ is called \emph{transversely nice} if for every stratum $C \in \mathcal{S}^{(2)}$ and for every stratum $V \in \mathcal{S}^{(1)}$ such that $C \subset \overline{V}$, the stratum $V$ occurs exactly twice in a small neighbourhood of $C$, and the two occurrences are from opposite sides.

[Proposition 19 (Relation between velocity error and score matching loss) of arXiv:2607.25685, 'Mimicking diffusion processes with differential equations'] Let
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal {E}_\theta^2:=\int_\delta^T\!\!\int_{\R^d}p_t(x)\,\big|s_\theta(x,t)-\nabla\log p_t(x)\big|^2\,\dd x\,\dd t 
\end{equation}
be the  denoising score-matching loss function. If the conversion factor
\[
\kappa_{\delta,R}:=\int_\delta^T\!\!\int_{B_R}\frac{\dd x\,\dd s}{p_s(x)} <\infty
\]
\[{\rm is\  finite, \ then}\qquad
  \mathcal E_v\;=\;\tfrac12\big\|\sigma^2\big(\nabla\log p-s_\theta\big)\big\|_{L^1([\delta,T]\times B_R)}
  \;\le\;\frac{\|\sigma\|_{L^\infty}^2}{2}\mathcal{E}_\theta\;\sqrt{\kappa_{\delta,R}}.
\]

[Thm 4 of arXiv:2605.21638, 'Markov renewal theory for transfer operators and point processes on the line'] Let $\mu_{n,\beta}^x, \Phi$ be defined as above.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item [(a)] For every local bounded measurable function $F\colon\mathbf N\to \R$, 
            	\[
            	   \lim_{x_0\to -\infty} \lim_{n\to \infty} \int_{\R^n} F(\delta_{x_1}+\cdots +\delta_{x_n}\bigr) \dd \mu_{n,\beta}^{x_0}(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \E\bigl[F(\Phi)]. 
                \] 
        \item [(b)] For all bounded intervals $A,B\subset \R$ and some $\eps>0$,
        	\begin{equation*}
        		\E\bigl[ \Phi(A) \Phi(B+t)\bigr] - \E\bigl[ \Phi(A) \bigr]\E\bigl[ \Phi(B) \bigr] = \Or(\e^{-\epsilon t})  \quad \textrm{as } t\to\infty.
            \end{equation*}
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:hitandblock of arXiv:2607.08914, 'Linear spreading speed in non-monotone population models'] Under Assumptions~(ass:flow of the paper)--(ass:irreducibility of the paper)
  there are constants $\Cl{c:liverbig}, \Cl{c:liversmall}\in (0,\infty)$, and
  $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ such that for every $\eta_0$ which is non-zero only at
  the origin, every $x>0$, and every $\rho < \varepsilon \sqrt x$,
  \begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{P}_{\eta_0}\big( D_\rho(x, \eta_{\tau_\mathrm{hit}(x)})> \rho^2,
      \tau_\mathrm{hit}(x)<\infty\big)
    < \Cr{c:liverbig}\big(e^{-\Cr{c:liversmall} \sqrt x}
      + e^{-\Cr{c:liversmall} \rho + 2\log x}\big).
  \end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:hitandblock of arXiv:2607.08914

body:
[Lemma lem_3a of arXiv:2607.11469, 'Breuer-Major-Donsker invariance principle'] Fix an integer $q\geq 2$ and $r\in\{0,1,..., q-1\}$. Define
\[
\Theta_n :=
\#\{1\le k\le n:\ k = r \, ({\rm mod}\, q)\}.
\]
For all $n \geq q$ {\rm(}i.e., $\Theta_n>0${\rm)}, define
\[
\theta_{n}(t)
:=
\frac{
\#\{1\le k\le\lfloor nt\rfloor:\ k = r \, ({\rm mod}\, q)\}}{\Theta_n
},
\,\,   t\in[0, 1].
\]
Then
$
\tfrac{\Theta_n}{n}
\xrightarrow{n\to+\infty}
\tfrac1q.
$

Moreover, for all  $n\geq q$, the map
$
\theta_n:[0,1]\to[0,1]
$
is nondecreasing with
$
\big(\theta_n(0),\theta_n(1)\big)=(0,1)
$
such that
$
\sup\big\{  
\left|
\theta_n(t)-t
\right|:  t\in[0,1]  \big\}
\xrightarrow{n\to+\infty}
0.
$

body: Vitali covering lemma: from finitely many balls in R^d one can select a pairwise disjoint subfamily whose 5-times dilations cover the union of all the original balls; for infinite families with uniformly bounded radii a countable disjoint subfamily with the same 5x-dilation property exists. It is the standard step toward the Vitali covering THEOREM, which covers a set up to Lebesgue-null error by disjoint balls drawn from any Vitali cover.
title: Vitali covering lemma

[Lemma foster-lyapunov of arXiv:2608.09589, 'On stochastic stability of systems\\ driven by red noise\thanks{The authors gratefully ack'] Let $\mathcal{G}_{n}$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ be an arbitrary
filtration such that, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, 
$\sigma(X_{j},Y_{j},0\leq j\leq n)\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{n}$ and $\varepsilon_{n+1}$ is independent of $\mathcal{G}_{n}$.

    Under Assumptions (mju of the paper) and (equation of the paper) there exist $h_1>0$, $B\geq 1$ so that for $h\leq h_1$ 
    \[
    V(x,y) = |x|+B|y|
    \]
    serves as a proper Lyapunov function. That is, there exist $C_2>0, \delta_2\in(0,1)$ so that
    \begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}[V(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})\mid\mathcal{G}_{n}]\leq \delta_2 V(X_{n},Y_{n})+C_2.
    \end{equation}
        Furthermore, there are $C_{3}>0$ and $\delta_2<\delta_3<1$ such that on the event
$\{|X_n|+B|Y_n|>C_3\}$
\begin{equation}
    
    
    \mathbb{E}_n[V(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})\mid\mathcal{G}_{n}]\leq \delta_3 [V(X_{n},Y_{n})],
\end{equation}
that is, we have a strict contraction in expectation.
title: Lemma foster-lyapunov of arXiv:2608.09589

body:
[Corollary of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] Let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_d) \in_R \{\pm1\}^d$ with asymmetric coordinates $X_i$. 
Let $Y = (Y_1, \dots, Y_d) \in \Sym(X)$ with independent coordinates $Y_1, \dots Y_d$. 
Then, $H(Y) \ge H(X)$, with equality if and only if the following conditions are both satisfied: 

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For all $i \in [d]$, $f_{Y_i} = f_{-X_i}$,
\item the random variables $X_i$ are mutually independent. 
\end{enumerate}

Also, if $X_1 = \pm X_2 = \dots = \pm X_d$ (with any choice of signs), then $H(Y) \ge dH(X)$ with equality if and only if (i) is satisfied. 
\begin{proof}
Clearly 
\[ H(Y) 

= \sum_{i \in [d]} H(Y_i)
\ge \sum_{i \in [d]} H(X_i)
\ge \sum_{i \in [d]} H(X_i \mid X_1, \dots X_{i-1})
= H(X). \]

Equality conditions are clear from the analysis in the proof of (thm:hypercube_entropy of the paper). 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered corollary of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'

[Theorem 37 of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] (Local structure of $x_\tau)$
The $\tau$-interval $(-\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3})$ can be decomposed into  finitely many intervals such that on each interval, $x_\tau$ is locally represented in the form $x_\tau =\frac{a}{b+c\tau} + \frac{d\tau}{b+c\tau} + e$ for $a,b,c,d,e \in \mathbb{R}$ and denominators not identically $0$.

\begin{equation}

[Definition def:lack-of-memory of arXiv:2606.24881, 'Queues with Correlated Service Times --- the $M/M_D/c$ Model'] Random vector $(X_1,\ldots,X_c)$ is said to satisfy the (multivariate) lack-of-memory property in weak sense if, for every nonempty subset
$A=\{i_1,\ldots,i_\ell\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,c\}$,
\[
P(X_{i_j}>x_{i_j}+t,\ j=1,\ldots,\ell
\mid
X_{i_j}>x_{i_j},\ j=1,\ldots,\ell)
=
P(X_{i_j}>t,\ j=1,\ldots,\ell)
\]
for all $t\ge0$ and $x_{i_j}\ge0$, $j=1,\ldots,\ell$.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The logarithmic factor in the tuned constant-step rate of random reshuffling (November 2026), shows that for strongly convex finite sums the logarithmic factor in the last-iterate upper bounds for random reshuffling with a constant step tuned to the number of epochs cannot be removed. On a one-dimensional instance with mu = L n1/n, gradient size G at the minimiser, T = nK steps, initial distance D and Lambda = ln(mu T D/G), every constant step gamma <= 1/L leaves E F(x_K) - F* >= G^2 (Lambda - ln Lambda)^2/(512 mu T^2) once K >= n1(Lambda - ln Lambda)/2, while the step Lambda/(mu T) gives at most G^2 Lambda^2 (1 + o(1))/(8 mu T^2), so the tuned constant-step error is Theta(G^2 ln^2(mu T D/G)/(mu T^2)). The proof computes one epoch exactly; the epoch variance reduces to the variance of a Mann-Whitney statistic. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/rr-constant-step-log-factor (commit 4bc93e1799af). Not refereed.
title: The logarithmic factor in the tuned constant-step rate of random reshuffling cannot be removed (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/rr-constant-step-log-factor)

[Definition 6 (Finite $R$-transform and finite free cumulants) of arXiv:2605.02093, 'An analytic approach to the finite $R$-transform'] Let $p\in\calP_N(\C)$.
  The finite $R$-transform of $p$ is defined by
  \[
    R_p^{(N)}(s)
    := -\frac{1}{N}\frac{d}{ds}C_p^{(N)}(Ns)
    = -\frac{1}{N}\frac{d}{ds}\log \widehat{p}(Ns) = - \frac{\widehat{p}'(Ns)}{\widehat{p}(Ns)}
  \]
We also define the finite free cumulants of $p$ as the coefficients of the expansion
\[
  R_p^{(N)}(s)
  = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \kappa_{n+1}^{(N)}(p)s^n.
\]
title: Finite $R$-transform and finite free cumulants

\[
\mu_{i,0}=\mu_0,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.
\]

\[
\mu_i(t)=\mu(t),
\qquad
\beta_i(t)=\beta(t),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
for every \(t\geq0\). Consequently, every representative neuron receives total
input intensity
\[
a(t)=2\beta(t).
\]

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2608.19832, 'Sharp Convex Concentration for Symmetric Random Tensors with Subgaussian Coordinates'] Under the assumptions of \Cref{thm:main}, let $M$ be a median of $Z$.
There are constants $\eta_K,c_K,C_K>0$ such that the following statements hold.

If $1\le u\le \eta_Kn$, put
\[
 w_u=C_K(\sqrt{nu}+u),
 \qquad
 R_u=\sqrt{n+w_u}.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 \Pp\Big\{
 \abs{Z-M}>C_KL\big[
 &\sqrt d\,R_u^{d-1}h_n(u)
 \notag\\
 &+dR_u^{d-2}(\sqrt{nu}+u)
 \big]\Big\}
 \le C e^{-c_Ku}.
 
\end{align}
If $u\ge\max\{1,\eta_Kn\}$, put
\[
 \widetilde R_u=\sqrt n+C_K\sqrt u.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \Pp\left\{
 \abs{Z-M}>C_KLd\widetilde R_u^{d-1}\sqrt u
 \right\}
 \le C e^{-c_Ku}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem 236 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1\le \fq < \fp$ and $C > 0$, the spaces $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ and $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric,
are compact.

\begin{proof}
	We will show compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$, as compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$ is proved analogously.
	It suffices to show that every sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ has a subsequence converging in $\bbW_\fq$ to a measure in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$.
	Consider any such sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$.
	The set of measures $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ is clearly tight, so by Prohorov's theorem there exists a weakly convergent subsequence $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$. 
Let $\mu$ be its weak limit. By Skorokhod's theorem, we can find a coupling of random variables $X_j\sim\mu_{n_j}$ and $X\sim\mu$ such that
$X_j\to X$ almost surely. Then, by Fatou's lemma, we have
	\[
		\|\mu\|_{L^\fp}^\fp 
	=\E[|X|^p]^{1/p}
		\le
		\liminf_j \E[|X_j|^p]^{1/p}
		= \liminf_{j\to\infty} \|\mu_{n_j}\|_{L^\fp}^\fp
		 \le C\,,
	\]
	so $\mu \in \cP_\fp(\R,C)$. 
	It remains to show $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ converges to $\mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
	 Note that for any $\nu \in \cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, Markov's inequality implies
	\[
	\nu(|x|>K) 
	\le \frac{1}{K^\fp}\int
		|x|^\fp \,d\nu
		 \le \frac{C}{K^\fp}\,.
	\]
Combining this with H\"older's inequality gives
	\beq
		\int_{|x|>K} |x|^\fq \,d\nu
		\le \nu(|x|>K)^{1 - \fq/\fp} \bigg(
			\int |x|^\fp \,d\nu
		\bigg)^{\fq/\fp}
		\le \frac{C}{K^{\fp - \fq}}\,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq.tail} and the weak convergence $\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$,
	\begin{align*}
		\limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\bigg|
		&\le \limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			\,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			 \,d\mu
		\bigg|\\
		&\qquad + \limsup_{j\to\infty} \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		+ \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\le \frac{2C}{K^{\fp-\fq}}\,.
	\end{align*}
	Since $K$ was arbitrary, we infer the convergence of $\fq$-th moments
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\E[|X_j|^p]
		=\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		= \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		= \E[|X|^p]\,.\]
This implies that the random variables $\{X_j\}$ are uniformly integrable, so
	\begin{align*}
	&\bbW_\fq(\mu_{n_j}, \mu)^\fq
	\le \E[|X_j-X|^\fq]\\
	&\le\E\Big[
	\max\{|X_j-X|,2K\}^\fq\Big]
	+\E\Big[|X_j| ; |X_j|\ge K\Big]
	+ \E\Big[|X| ; |X|\ge K\Big]
	\\
	&\le o_j(1) + o_K(1)+ o_K(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
Since the left-hand side does not depend on $K$, we conclude that
$\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 236 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Theorem thm:joint_invm_class of arXiv:2605.22787, 'Invariant measures for half-space geometric LPP: classification and the one force--one sol'] Let $c \in [0,q^{-1})$. If $m \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\nu$ is an extremal $m$-invariant measure for $\operatorname{GLPP}_c$, then there exist $s_1,\ldots,s_m \in [r_c,q^{-1})$ such that 
     \[
      \nu = \mu_{c,s_1,\ldots,s_m}.
     \]
     Furthermore, for any $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m \in (0,\xi_{\max}^c]$,
\[
\Bigl(W^c_{\xi_1}\bigl((0,0),(k,0)\bigr),\ldots,W^c_{\xi_m}\bigl((0,0),(k,0)\bigr)\Bigr)_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \sim \mu_{c,s_1,\ldots,s_m},
\]
where, for $i \in \llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$,
\[
s_i = \begin{cases}
    (X_c \circ T_c)^{-1}(\xi_i) &\xi_i < \xi_{\max}^c \\
    r_c &\xi_i = \xi_{\max}^c.
\end{cases}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:joint_invm_class of arXiv:2605.22787

[Proposition cond:subcrit of arXiv:2606.01866, 'Phase Transition of a Semiflexible Membrane in Two Dimensions'] \label[proposition]{thm:massiveanalysis}
    For a fixed $M>0$, let $0<m\le M$ be a mass parameter. Suppose $x\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ satisfies $\|x\|\to\infty$. Let $G^m$ be the massive Green function with mass $m$. Then we have the following estimates:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=(\alph*)]
        \item 
        If $m\|x\|\to\infty$, then there exists $c,C>0$, depending only on $M$, such that
        \[G^m(x,0)\le C (m\|x\|)^{-1/2}e^{-cm\|x\|}.\]
        
        \item 
        If $m\|x\|\to s>0$ with $\|x\|\to\infty$, then for any multiindex $\alpha$ including $\alpha=0$,
        \[|\nabla^\alpha G^m(x,0)|\lesssim \|x\|^{-|\alpha|}.\]
        
        \item 
        If $m\|x\|\to 0$, then 
        \[|G^m(x,0)-G^m(0,0)-\mathfrak{a}(x)|=o(1).\]
        Moreover, the asymptotic (cond:supercrit of the paper) remains valid without the assumption $\|x\|\to\infty$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform estimate for massive Green functions

[Lemma 25 (Contracted response kernels) of arXiv:2608.29726, '\LARGE A Priori Estimates for Singular Fractional Stochastic Burgers Equations'] Let \(G_{\tau,3}^\eps\) and \(G_{\tau,1}^\eps\) denote the symmetric
kernels obtained from all one-pair and two-pair Wick contractions of
\eqref{eq:fifth-chaos-tree-kernels}.  In the regime
\eqref{eq:sbe-tree-response-regime}, uniformly in \(\eps\),
\[
 \mathcal C_{G_{\tau,3}^\eps}(\zeta)
 \lesssim
 \begin{cases}
  \langle\zeta\rangle_\gamma^{
   -(\gamma+1)-2(5q-\delta)+},
  &\tau\in\{\XoneFourB,\XtwoThree\},\\
  \langle\zeta\rangle_\gamma^{-(\gamma+1)-4q+},
  &\tau=\XoneFourC,
 \end{cases}
\]
and, for all three coordinates,
\[
 \mathcal C_{G_{\tau,1}^\eps}(\zeta)
 \lesssim
 \langle\zeta\rangle_\gamma^{
  -(\gamma+1)-2(5q-\delta)+}.
\]
title: Contracted response kernels

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2604.04267, 'On Sharpest Tail Bounds for Functions \\ of Tail Bounded Random Variables'] Let $m_1,m_2$ be measures on $\Omega$ with $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcalorig{F}$. The following are also measures on $\Omega$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $m_1+m_2$ given by pointwise addition (of sets).
\item For $\alpha \geq 0$, $\alpha m_1$ given by $(\alpha m_1)(A) = \alpha m_1(A)$.
\item For $m_1,m_2$ finite and $\forall U \in \mathcalorig{F}$, $m_1(U) \geq m_2(U)$, $m_1 - m_2$ given by pointwise subtraction.
\item For $U \in \mathcalorig{F}$, the restriction of $m_k$ to $U$. That is, $m_k\big|_U(A) := m_k(A \cap U), \forall A \in \mathcalorig{F}$.
\end{enumerate}

$$T=U^*M_fU$$
with $U:H\to L^2(X)$ being a unitary operator from $H$ to a certain $L^2$ space associated to $T$, with $f:X\to\mathbb R$ being a certain function, once again associated to $T$, and with
$$M_f(g)=fg$$
being the usual multiplication operator by $f$, on the Hilbert space $L^2(X)$.

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] \textbf{(Rooted ordered trees, subtrees, forests)}
$(\textbf{a})\, $ A \textit{rooted ordered tree} is a subset $ \fftree\! \subset \! \bbU$ satisfying the following conditions: 
\begin{compactenum}
\item[] \textbf{(1):} $\varnothing \ino \fftree$. \textbf{(2):} If $u\ino  \fftree\backslash \{ \varnothing\}$ 
then $\overleftarrow{u}\ino  \fftree$. \textbf{(3):} For all $u\ino  \fftree$, there exists $k_u ( \fftree)\ino \bbN\cup \! \{ \infty\}$ such that: $u \! \ast \!  (j)\ino  \fftree$  if and only if  $1\! \leq \! j \! \leq \! k_u ( \fftree)$. 
\end{compactenum}
Here, $k_u ( \fftree)$ is interpreted as the \textit{number of children of $u$} and if 
$1\! \leq \! j \! \leq \! k_u ( \fftree)$, then $u\ast (j) $ is the \emph{$j$-th child of $u$.}
We denote by $\bbT$ the set of rooted ordered trees.

\smallskip

\noindent
$(\textbf{b})\, $
Let $ \fftree\ino \bbT$ and $u\ino t$. Then 
$\theta_u  \fftree\!  = \! \{ v\ino \bbU: u\ast v\ino  \fftree \}$ is the \emph{subtree of $ \fftree$ stemming from $u$}. 
Note that $\theta_u t\ino \bbT$. 

\smallskip

\noindent
$(\textbf{c})\, $ A \emph{fores}t is a sequence of trees 
$(t^{_{(k)}}_{^{\,}} )_{k\in \bbN^*}$. It is sometimes convenient to view it as a single tree $t\ino \bbT$ with $k_\varnothing(t)\eqo\infty$ such that 
$t^{_{(k)}}_{^{\,}}$ is the subtree stemming from the $k$-th child of $t$: $t^{_{(k)}}_{^{\,}}\eqo \theta_{(k)}t$. \cq

Let U subset R^n be open, bounded, with Lipschitz boundary, n>=1, and H^1(U)=W^{1,2}(U). Then: (i) if n=1, H^1(U) embeds continuously into C^{0,1/2}(closure(U)); (ii) if n=2, H^1(U) embeds continuously into L^q(U) for every finite q in [1,infinity), but not into L^infinity(U) or C^0(closure(U)) in general; (iii) if n>=3, H^1(U) embeds continuously into L^{2*}(U), 2*=2n/(n-2), i.e. there is C=C(n,U) with ||u||_{L^{2*}(U)} <= C||u||_{H^1(U)} for all u in H^1(U). In every dimension the embedding of H^1(U) into L^q(U) is compact for every q strictly below the borderline exponent (q<2* for n>=3, any finite q for n<=2), by the Rellich-Kondrachov theorem.
U is open, bounded, with Lipschitz boundary
n = dimension >= 1

Let G = (X, Y, E) be a finite bipartite graph and, for S a subset of X, let N(S) be the set of vertices of Y adjacent to some vertex of S. There is a matching saturating every vertex of X if and only if |N(S)| >= |S| for every subset S of X. Equivalently, a finite family of finite sets (A_1, ..., A_m) has a system of distinct representatives (distinct a_i with a_i in A_i) if and only if every k of the sets have a union with at least k elements.

body:
Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. For 0 <= t <= n let H_t be the average of Var(E[f | X_T]) over the t-element sets T. Then H_t = sum_{k=1}^t [binom(t, k)/binom(n, k)] W_k, so H_0 = 0, H_n = Var(f) and H_t is nondecreasing in t; and for 1 <= k <= n, W_k = binom(n, k) sum_{t=0}^k (-1)^(k - t) binom(k, t) H_t = binom(n, k) Delta^k H_0 >= 0. The n + 1 averages determine the variance at every interaction order, though not the individual w_S.

[Theorem thm:massive_limit of arXiv:2605.15545, 'Crossover from subcritical to critical decay: \\ random walk, self-avoiding walk, percolat'] Let $d \ge 1$. Suppose $D(x)$ has finite support $\mathcal{U}$.
Let $x \in {\mathbb R^d}$ be on the boundary of $\mathrm{Conv}(\mathcal{U})$.
Then as $z \to 0$, we have
\begin{equation}
\abs x_{z} = \mathrm{rad}(\mathcal{U}) + O(m_z^{-1}) .
\end{equation}
In particular, $\lim_{z\to 0} | \cdot |_z$ defines a norm on ${\mathbb R^d}$, with its unit ball being $\mathrm{Conv}(\mathcal{U}) / \mathrm{rad}(\mathcal{U})$.
title: Theorem thm:massive_limit of arXiv:2605.15545

[Corollary 33 (Fixed reset probability) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] Assume $\rho_n\equiv\rho\in(0,1)$ and put $q=1-\rho$.  Then
\[
        s_n
        \sim
        \sqrt{2\pi\rho n}\left(q\rho^{\rho/q}\right)^n.
\]
Consequently
\[
        \rho\sqrt{2\pi\rho n}\left(q\rho^{\rho/q}\right)^nT_n
        \Rightarrow \Exp(1),
\]
and for every fixed integer $r\ge1$,
\[
        \Ebb\left[\rho\sqrt{2\pi\rho n}\left(q\rho^{\rho/q}\right)^nT_n\right]^r
        \longrightarrow r!.
\]
In particular,
\[
        \Ebb T_n
        \sim
        \frac{1}{\rho\sqrt{2\pi\rho n}}
        \left(q\rho^{\rho/q}\right)^{-n}.
\]

For $(\phi, \eta) \sim M_W$, conditioned on $\phi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$, we have $\phi|_A \stackrel d= h + \mathfrak h + (\frac\beta2 - Q)G_A(\cdot, \infty)$, where $\mathfrak h$ is the harmonic extension of $\phi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$ to $A$ which has normal derivative zero on $\partial A \cap \partial \mathbb{H}$,

[Theorem thmFi of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Let $\phi \in C^1((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^n)$, $b^{jk}=b^{kj}\in
C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $j,k=1,2,\cdots,n$, 
and $\ell,\Psi \in C^2((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^n)$. 
Let $u$ be an $H^2(G)$-valued, $\mathbf{F}$-adapted process such that $u_t$ is an $L^2(G)$-valued It\^o process. 
Set $\theta = e^\ell$ and $w=\theta u$. 
Then, for a.e.     $x\in G$ and ${\mathbb{P}}$-a.s. $\omega \in \Omega$,

\begin{align}
    \notag
      
    &   \theta \Big ( -2\phi\ell_t w_t + 2\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_{x_j} w_{x_k} + \Psi w \Big )
    \Big[ \phi du_t - \sum_{j,k=1}^n (b^{jk}u_{x_j})_{x_k} dt \Big]  
    \\ \notag
    & \quad+\sum_{j,k=1}^n \Big[ \sum_{j',k'=1}^n \Big (
    2b^{jk}b^{j'k'}\ell_{x_{j'}}w_{x_j}w_{x_{k'}} -
    b^{jk}b^{j'k'}\ell_{x_j} w_{x_{j'}}w_{x_{k'}}
    \Big )   
    \\ \notag
    &\quad  - 2 \phi b^{jk}\ell_t w_{x_j} w_t + \phi b^{jk}\ell_{x_j} w_t^2  +
    \Psi b^{jk}w_{x_j} w - \Big({\cal A}\ell_{x_j} +
    \frac{\Psi_{x_j}}{2}\Big)b^{jk}w^2 \Big]_{x_k} dt
    \\ \notag
    &\quad +d\Big\{ \phi\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_t w_{x_j} w_{x_k}-
    2\phi\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_{x_j}w_{x_k}w_t  + \phi^2\ell_t w_t^2
    - \phi\Psi w_t w 
    \\ \notag 
    & \quad \quad \quad 
    + \Big[ \phi {\cal A}\ell_t +
    \frac{1}{2}(\phi\Psi)_t\Big]w^2 \Big\}   
    \\ \notag
    &   =  \bigg\{ \Big[(\phi^2\ell_{t})_t + \sum_{j,k =1}^n (\phi
    b^{jk}\ell_{x_j})_{x_k} - \phi\Psi \Big]w_t^2   d t
    \\ \notag
    & \quad - 2\sum_{j,k=1}^n \big[(\phi
    b^{jk}\ell_{x_k})_t +
    b^{jk}(\phi\ell_{t})_{x_k}\big]w_{x_j}w_t   d t   
    +\sum_{j,k=1}^n c^{jk}w_{x_j}w_{x_k} d t + Bw^2 d t
    \\
    & \quad 
    + \Big(   -2\phi\ell_tv_t 
    + 2\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_{x_j}w_{x_k} + \Psi w
    \Big)^2\bigg\} dt + \phi^2\theta^2 \ell_t(du_t)^2,  
\end{align}

where 
\begin{align} \notag
    & {\cal A}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=}\phi (\ell_t^2-\ell_{tt})-\sum_{j,k=1}^n
    (b^{jk}\ell_{x_j}\ell_{x_k}-b^{jk}_{x_k}\ell_{x_j}
    -b^{jk}\ell_{x_jx_k})-\Psi,\\ \notag
       & {\cal B}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=}{\cal A}\Psi+(\phi {\cal A}\ell_t)_t\!-\! \sum_{j,k=1}^n\!({\cal A}
    b^{jk}\ell_{x_j})_{x_k}\! +\!\dfrac 12
    \Big[\big(\phi\Psi\big)_{tt}\!-\!\sum_{j,k=1}^n\!
    \big(b^{jk}\Psi_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}\Big],\\  
      & c^{jk}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=} \big(\phi b^{jk}\ell_t\big)_t\! +\!
    \sum_{j',k'=1}^n\! \Big[2b^{jk'}(b^{j'k}\ell_{x_{j'}})_{x_{k'}}
    \!-\!\big(b^{jk}b^{j'k'}\ell_{x_{j'}}\big)_{x_{k'}}\Big] \!+\! \Psi
    b^{jk}.
\end{align}

[Theorem 43 (Convergence under a strictly positive density after finitely many steps) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Assume \hyp{A}{A} and \hyp{E}{E}. Then
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\ \sup_{A \in \XXA} \bigl| (T^{n}\circ\mu)(A) - \pi(A) \bigr| = 0
  \qquad\text{for every } \mu \in \Prob,
\]
and $\pi$ is the unique invariant probability measure of $T$. More precisely, the
singular mass is bounded by the mass that has not yet entered the good sets:
\[
  \sing\bigl( T^{n}\circ\mu \bigm| \pi\bigr) \;\le\; 1 - \mu(\XX_{n})
  \qquad (\mu \in \Prob,\ n \in \N) ,
\]

Let D be an abelian (v, k, lambda)-difference set in group G. Let p be a prime divisor of k - lambda such that p is coprime to v and p > lambda. Then the map x -> x^p is a multiplier of D: there exists an element g in G such that D^p = {d^p : d in D} = g D.
G is abelian
p divides k - lambda
gcd(p, v) = 1
p > lambda

Fix $k, n  \in \N$. Let $(X_i)_{i\in \N}$ denote a sequence of  independent random variables taking values in $\R^k$ such that
\[
  \E X_j = 0 \,,\, 1 \leq j \leq n\qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{j=1}^n \Cov(X_j) = \mathrm{Id}\,.
\]
Let $Z$ denote a standard Gaussian in $\R^k$. There exist constants $c,C>0$  such that if 
\[
   \sum_{j=1}^n \E|X_j|^3 \leq c\,,
\]
then for all $n\in \N$ and $r\geq 0$, 
\[
  \bigg|\P\bigg( \bigg|\sum_{j=1}^n X_j\bigg|  \leq r \bigg) - \P (|Z| \leq r )\bigg|\leq \frac{C}{(1+r)^3} \sum_{j=1}^n \E|X_j|^3\,.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:grafting0 of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Given $\ell \in\N$ and a labelled tree $\underline{\sigma}\in\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$, we define a new labelled tree ${\underline{\sigma}}+\ell \in\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$ to be the labeled tree with node set ${N}(\underline{\sigma}+\ell) \eqdef \{ j + \ell : j \in N(\underline{\sigma})\}$ and such that the \textit{shift by $\ell$} defined as $ N(\underline{\sigma})\ni j \mapsto j+ \ell \in{N}(\underline{\sigma}+\ell)$ belongs to $\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\sigma},\underline{\sigma}+\ell)$ -- in particular, we have $ r(\underline{\sigma}+\ell)= r(\underline{\sigma})+\ell$. 
Note that $\underline{\sigma} + 0 = \underline{\sigma}$. 

Finally, given two labelled trees $\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}\in\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$, we set 
\[
\ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}}
\eqdef 
 \begin{cases}  
    \max N(\underline{\tau}) + 1& \text{if} \;N(\underline{\tau}) \cap N(\underline{\sigma}) \not = \emptyset\,, \\
    0 & \text{otherwise} \,. \\
\end{cases}
\]
We overload notation, identifying $\ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}}$ with the shift-isomorphism and write $\ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}} \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\sigma}, \underline{\sigma} + \ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}})$.
title: Definition def:grafting0 of arXiv:2411.07157

Let (X,d) be a metric space, A a nonempty subset, and 0<kappa<=1. Let f:A->R have finite M_inf=sup_(a in A)|f(a)| and finite Holder seminorm L=sup_(a!=b in A)|f(a)-f(b)|/d(a,b)^kappa, with the seminorm set to zero for a singleton. Then there is F:X->R with F|A=f, sup_X|F|=M_inf and [F]_(kappa,X)=L. Consequently the sum norm ||F||_(BL^kappa(X))=||F||_infinity+[F]_(kappa,X) equals ||f||_(BL^kappa(A)). A construction is g_sup(x)=sup_(a in A)(f(a)-L d(x,a)^kappa), followed by clipping to [inf_A f,sup_A f]. Equivalently, clipping g_inf(x)=inf_(a in A)(f(a)+L d(x,a)^kappa) gives such an extension. In particular kappa=1 gives a globally Lipschitz real-valued extension with the same bound. No closedness of A, completeness of X, compactness, or attainment of the extrema is required.
Arbitrary metric space with finite real-valued distances and a nonempty subset A
Real-valued f bounded on A with finite kappa-Holder seminorm
Exponent 0<kappa<=1, as fixed in primary Definition2.1
Classical real supremum and infimum; singleton seminorm convention zero
For preserving the supremum norm, clip the cone extension to the bounded range interval

Let mu be a positive Radon measure near x with finite positive local mass exponent a. The centered disk potential T(R)=(1/pi) integral_{B_E(x,R)} log(R/|x-y|) mu(dy) is finite and positive for sufficiently small R, and lim_{R->0} log(T(R))/log R=a. This is a Euclidean potential exponent, not a metric Hausdorff dimension or sample-path exit-time theorem.
mu positive Radon near x
mu(B_E(x,r))>0 eventually
finite local exponent a>0

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The following happen:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The Dirac masses are infinitely divisible.

\item The measures supported by $2\leq n<\infty$ points are not infinitely divisible.

\item In particular, the binomial laws are not infinitely divisible.

\item The negative binomial laws, including the geometric ones, are infinitely divisible.

\item The Poisson laws are infinitely divisible, and so are their compound versions.

\item The uniform laws are not infinitely divisible, while the exponential laws are.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 36 (Gram-reduced Hilbert--Stein extraction) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Start from $\bm M^{[0]}=0$.  At every active step, use the reduced
promotion \eqref{bridge:eq:reduced-promotion}, enlarge
$M_{q_*}$ by the orthogonal sum with $V_{q_*}^{\mathrm{red}}$, and
recompute $A,r,\Lambda_q,\mathcal N_q$.  Use one common trajectory and,
for $J\ge2$, stop its level $J$ as soon as
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak H_Q(A,r)
 \le\delta_J,
 \qquad
 \delta_J=\frac{dQa_QR^4}{J}.
 
\end{equation}
Then the terminal modules are nested and satisfy
\begin{align}
 \dim M_q^{[J]}&\le d(J-1),
 \\
 \mathfrak H_Q(A^{[J]},r^{[J]})
 &\le\frac{dQa_QR^4}{J},
 \\
 \Delta_{\mathrm{res}}(r^{[J]})
 +\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}(A^{[J]},r^{[J]})
 &\le\frac{dQ\mu_Qa_QR^4}{J}.
 
\end{align}
At every promotion made before the end of level $J$, the synthesis map
in \eqref{bridge:eq:reduced-promotion} has smallest singular value strictly
larger than
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\delta_J}{dQR}
 =\frac{a_QR^3}{J}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus no Gram mode which vanishes along a fixed level can be promoted after
renormalization.

Own-work draft; independently checked proof; D0010-C002 v1; audits w667:PASS, w668:PASS. On [0,1], f(x)=846x/37 for x<=1/6, (264-738x)/37 for 1/6<=x<=1/3, and 18/37 for x>=1/3 is continuous and unimodal with mean 1/3. It satisfies 3P(X>x)<=ceil(1/x)-1 for every x>0, but violates 2P(X>1-t)<=P(X<t) whenever 0<t<4/47 and is not 3-CM. Thus integer tail tests plus unimodality and boundary mean are insufficient.
As stated in the linked proof

Status: proof (unaudited). Explicit special counterexample; novelty not asserted.

Define f on [0,1] by

    f(x)=846x/37                 for 0<=x<=1/6,
    f(x)=(264-738x)/37           for 1/6<=x<=1/3,
    f(x)=18/37                  for 1/3<=x<=1.

It is continuous: both first formulas give 141/37 at 1/6 and the second gives 18/37 at 1/3. It is strictly increasing up to 1/6, strictly decreasing until 1/3, then constant. Thus it is unimodal, nonnegative, with essential support [0,1].

An easy integration check uses f=H T+c R with H=123/37,c=18/37. The triangle T is 6x on [0,1/6], 2-6x on [1/6,1/3], and zero thereafter. The ramp R is 6x on [0,1/6] and one thereafter. Their masses are 1/6 and 11/12; first moments are 1/36 and 107/216. Thus integral f=123/(37*6)+18*11/(37*12)=1 and integral x f=123/(37*36)+18*107/(37*216)=1/3.

For every x>0 the earlier necessary integer tail bound

    3 P(X>x) <= ceil(1/x)-1

holds (for x>1 both sides are zero). For 0<x<1/3 the right side is at least 3 and the inequality is automatic. At x=1/3, P(X>x)=12/37<2/3. For 1/3<x<1/2, the right side is 2 and the tail is <=12/37<2/3. At x=1/2 the right side is 1 and the tail is 9/37<1/3. For 1/2<x<=1 the right side is 1 for x<1, the tail <=9/37<1/3, and at x=1 both sides are zero.

Nevertheless the law is not 3-CM. For 0<t<=1/6, P(X<t)=423 t^2/37 and P(X>1-t)=18t/37. The endpoint-balance inequality from D0010-C001 would require 423t^2>=36t, which fails for 0<t<4/47. For example t=1/100 gives left side 423/370000 and required right side 36/3700. This is a strict rational contradiction.
