If there exists a positive weight $p$ and $M<\infty$ such that
\[
\sup_{\lambda}\frac1{p(\lambda)}\int |k(\lambda,\mu)|p(\mu)\dd\mu\le M,
\qquad
\sup_{\mu}\frac1{p(\mu)}\int |k(\lambda,\mu)|p(\lambda)\dd\lambda\le M,
\]
then $\norm{K}_{\op}\le M$.

body: [Corollary of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Assume that \(S\) is an embedded surface which is transverse to the almost pseudo-Anosov flow \(\varphi\). If \(S\) is not a fiber of \(M\), then \(\partial \Theta(\widetilde{S})\neq \emptyset\) and any infinite leaf ray \(L\) in \(\mathcal{F}_{S}^{\pm}\) must limit to a closed leaf and spiral toward it.

[Corollary cor:false-twin-stability of arXiv:2609.02845, 'Degeneracy bounds, stability, and a sharp gap for $B$-colorings'] Let $d$, $\Delta$, and $s$ be integers satisfying $1\le d\le\Delta$ and $0\le s<d$.  Let $G$ be a finite simple
$d$-degenerate graph with $\Delta(G)\le\Delta$ and $q_B(G)\ge d\Delta-s$.  Then some vertex $v$ has distinct neighbors
$u_1,\ldots,u_d$ such that $d_G(u_1)=\Delta$ and
\[
  \sum_{j=2}^{d}|N_G(u_1)\setminus N_G(u_j)|\le s,
  \qquad
  \sum_{j=2}^{d}|N_G(u_1)\oplus N_G(u_j)|\le2s.
\]
Consequently, at least $d-s$ of $u_1,\ldots,u_d$ have degree $\Delta$ and the same open neighborhood.  In particular, $G$
contains copies of $K_{d-s,\Delta}$ and $K_{d,\Delta-s}$.

PROOF (UNAUDITED). For normalized tanh features u_q, extended by u_0(z)=z, define delta(q,r,c)=1-E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)] for standard Gaussians of correlation c. Uniformly for q,r,s in [0,1] and c in [-1,1], |delta(q,r,c)-delta(s,s,c)| <= (121/2)(q-r)^2+20(1-c)(|q-s|+|r-s|). For c<1 its relative version has coefficients 242 and 80, dividing the contrast term by 1-c. For n independent fresh paired rows, E[(Qnew-Rnew)^2 | past] <= [(1-(q+r)/12)^2+3/n](q-r)^2+8qr(1-c)/n. These remove the absolute-Lipschitz loss in the deterministic gap comparison and expose the weighted radial-contrast term still needed for a multi-layer recursion.
q,r,s in [0,1]; c in [-1,1]; relative comparison only for c<1
Fresh paired Gaussian rows, independent across rows and conditional on completed past; integer n>=1
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:7076d4393689293319a7309eaf3c96e6c5b82dcaf126753efdf511edf8798e81","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/70/7076d4393689293319a7309eaf3c96e6c5b82dcaf126753efdf511edf8798e81.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:945ca18bb0a98db18e19c44e0797808647334210146f2f927f040de71041804d","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_gap_radial_comparison","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c011-gap-radial-comparison","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Gaussian-process limits and empirical Gram matrices","draft":"w712/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:tanh-population-gap-angular-factor-and-radial-contrast-recursion","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C011 v1: angular-factor comparison and radial-contrast recursion

Kind: moved. Target: 1, the reviewer's two-input relative-gap rung.
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified. This is a component lemma,
not the claimed multi-layer relative rate.

## Statement

Let F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2 for a standard Gaussian Z. On [0,1] define
h_q(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(q), h_0(z)=z, a(q)=||h_q||_2,
u_q=h_q/a(q). For a standard Gaussian pair (X,Y) with correlation c set
H(q,r,c)=E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)] and delta(q,r,c)=1-H(q,r,c).
For all q,r,s in [0,1] and c in [-1,1],

    |delta(q,r,c)-delta(s,s,c)|
      <= (121/2)(q-r)^2 + 20(1-c)(|q-s|+|r-s|).       (1)

For c<1 this gives the scale-free comparison

    |delta(q,r,c)/delta(s,s,c)-1|
      <= 242 (q-r)^2/(1-c) + 80(|q-s|+|r-s|).         (2)

For c=1 the reference gap is zero and (2) is NOT asserted; (1) still holds.

For a fresh independent collection of n standard Gaussian pairs of
correlation c, let

    Q'=mean tanh(sqrt(q)X_i)^2,
    R'=mean tanh(sqrt(r)Y_i)^2, e=q-r.

For every integer n>=1,

    E[(Q'-R')^2]
      <= [(1-(q+r)/12)^2+3/n] e^2
           + 8qr(1-c)/n.                             (3)

If q,r,c are measurable with respect to the completed network past and
the paired rows are fresh conditional on that past, (3) holds conditionally.
No future state, gradient, or sensitivity is conditioned on. In particular
at a state with equal q=r, the new contrast has zero conditional mean and
second moment at most 8q^2(1-c)/n. Equal marginal variances are not preserved
pathwise.

## 1. Uniform feature estimates

Audited C002 v2, steps 1-2, gives q/4<=F(q)<=q for 0<=q<=1,
and increasing concave F with F(0)=0 and F(q)<=q-q^2/6.
Hence 1/2<=a(q)<=1, including q=0, and |h_q(z)|<=|z|.
For t>=0,

    tanh(t)-t sech(t)^2
      = integral_0^t 2v sech(v)^2 tanh(v) dv <= 2t^3/3.

Differentiation yields |partial_q h_q(z)|<=|z|^3/3 for q>0;
at zero its continuous extension is -z^3/3. This polynomial envelope
justifies differentiation and continuity in Gaussian L2 by dominated
convergence. Thus |a'(q)|<=sqrt(15)/3<2 and

    |partial_q u_q(z)| <= (2/3)|z|^3+8|z|,
    ||partial_q u_q||_2 <= (2/3)sqrt(15)+8 <= 11.      (4)

Here E Z^6=15 and E Z^2=1. The last inequality follows from
sqrt(15)<=9/2. These are uniform bounds; endpoint derivatives are
one-sided and all parameter integrals are over [0,1]. In particular

    ||u_q-u_r||_2 <= 11|q-r|.                        (5)

The derivative in the input variable is

    w_q(z):=partial_z u_q(z)=sech(sqrt(q)z)^2/a(q),
    w_0(z)=1, 0<w_q(z)<=2.

For q>0, the derivative of the numerator in q has absolute value
|z tanh(sqrt(q)z) sech(sqrt(q)z)^2/sqrt(q)|<=z^2.
Its limit at zero is -z^2. Using a>=1/2 and |a'|<2 gives

    |partial_q w_q(z)| <= 2z^2+8,
    ||w_q-w_s||_1 <= 10|q-s|.                       (6)

The L1 norms refer to a standard Gaussian marginal, independent of the
joint correlation used below.

## 2. The gap separates into shape and angular parts

Price's identity, as in Voigtlaender, arXiv:1710.03576, Theorem 1 and
Corollary 2, gives for -1<c<1

    partial_c H(q,r,c)=J(q,r,c):=E[w_q(X)w_r(Y)].

The features have at most linear growth; their input derivatives are
bounded. Thus the identity applies at interior correlations. Coupling
Y=cX+sqrt(1-c^2)Z with independent X,Z, polynomial domination gives
continuity of H and J at both endpoints. Since |J|<=4, integration and
passage to either endpoint are justified. In particular

    delta(q,r,c)
      = (1/2)||u_q-u_r||_2^2 + integral_c^1 J(q,r,t)dt. (7)

No centered sample covariance is involved in this population identity.
At q=r=s the shape term is zero. For the same correlation t, subtract
the products w_q(X)w_r(Y) and w_s(X)w_s(Y). The triangle inequality,
the bound |w|<=2, and (6), without any independence of X,Y, give

    |J(q,r,t)-J(s,s,t)|
      <=20(|q-s|+|r-s|).                             (8)

Subtract (7) for the two states, integrate (8) over an interval of length
1-c, and use (5). This proves (1), including c=-1 and c=1.

## 3. A nonzero reference gap and relative comparison

Let b=E[Zu_s(Z)] and v(z)=u_s(z)-bz. Then E[Zv(Z)]=0 and
||v||_2^2=1-b^2. Gaussian conditional expectation E[X|Y]=cY gives
E[Xv(Y)]=E[Yv(X)]=0, including both degenerate endpoint pairs.
Cauchy-Schwarz therefore implies

    H(s,s,c)=b^2 c+E[v(X)v(Y)] <= b^2 c+1-b^2,
    delta(s,s,c)>=b^2(1-c).                          (9)

For s>0, the elementary inequality tanh(t)>=t/sqrt(1+t^2) for t>=0,
oddness, and F(s)<=s yield

    b >= E[Z^2/sqrt(1+sZ^2)]
      >= 1/sqrt(1+3s) >= 1/2.

The middle step is Jensen for the convex function x->(1+sx)^(-1/2)
under the probability measure with density Z^2, whose Z^2 mean is 3.
For s=0, b=1 directly. Consequently delta(s,s,c)>0 for c<1 and
delta(s,s,c)>=(1-c)/4. Dividing (1) by this lower bound proves (2):
(121/2)*4=242 and 20*4=80. No division by a zero endpoint gap is made.

## 4. Conditional contrast recursion

The scalar function f(t)=tanh(sqrt(t))^2 is 1-Lipschitz on [0,infinity):
for t>0 its derivative is [tanh(sqrt(t))/sqrt(t)]sech(sqrt(t))^2 in [0,1],
and its continuous derivative at zero is 1. Hence for A=sqrt(q)X,
B=sqrt(r)Y,

    |tanh(A)^2-tanh(B)^2| <= |A^2-B^2|.

Gaussian fourth moments give

    E[(A^2-B^2)^2]
      =3q^2+3r^2-2qr(1+2c^2)
      =3(q-r)^2+4qr(1-c^2)
      <=3(q-r)^2+8qr(1-c).                          (10)

The last step uses 1+c<=2 and 1-c>=0; it holds also for c=-1.
For independent paired rows, the variance of their mean difference is
the single-row variance divided by n. Bounding that variance by its
second moment and using (10) gives

    Var(Q'-R') <= [3e^2+8qr(1-c)]/n.               (11)

The mean is F(q)-F(r). For t>0, concavity and F(0)=0 imply
0<=F'(t)<=F(t)/t<=1-t/6. Differentiation is justified, for example,
by the derivative bound Z^2 for tanh(sqrt(t)Z)^2. At zero the derivative
is 1 by dominated convergence. Integrating this derivative bound between
q and r, in either order, gives

    |F(q)-F(r)| <= |q-r|[1-(q+r)/12].             (12)

The bracket is at least 5/6 because q+r<=2, so squaring preserves (12).
Add the square of this mean to (11) to obtain (3). The conditional
version uses precisely the same calculation after fixing the past;
only the fresh paired rows are independent.

## What remains open

C010 controls empirical gap noise relative to delta(Q_l,R_l,c_l).
Equation (1) removes the inappropriate absolute-Lipschitz comparison
with the GP state: its common-variance error carries the angular gap.
Equation (3) exhibits how fresh sampling creates radial contrast.
Neither is a closed relative multi-layer recursion. To iterate (2), one
must control the weighted term (Q_l-R_l)^2/(1-c_l) jointly with the
angle and the marginal errors, and compare the angle to the deterministic
angle. Replacing random denominators by their expectations or multiplying
unconditional moment bounds is not justified. No such step is asserted.

## Source and verification scope

Prior inputs: reviewer-PASS C002 v2 scalar facts; Voigtlaender's primary
Price identity at the locator above. C010 motivated this lemma but its
inverse-Lipschitz constant and unaudited moment theorem are not needed
in this proof. The new comparison and recursion await independent audit;
literature novelty has not been established. Any finite arithmetic checks
verify only their stated polynomial or rational identities, not the
analytic proof or the full target.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:518f766b67426759f30e8af49671a3b9d8d16c68f200bc9351ef0e8fa9d8db47","revision_digest":"sha256:ad83a72ff6e090c157d65d37c37ef544d8a8f16bcecdcf5091c33640dfc49344","source_id":"own-work:T250-w712-C011-v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T19:28:50.001126+00:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Thm of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[thm]{need at least rlogr}
    Let $0< \underline{\lambda} \le \overline{\lambda} < \infty$.
    Then there
    exists $q(\underline{\lambda},\overline{\lambda}, d) > 0$
    such that,
    if $\underline{\lambda} \le nr^d \le \overline{\lambda}$, then
    \[
        \mathbb{P}(
        \exists z \in \ker(Z_1(G_M(n;r)) \to H_1(M)) \setminus Z_1^{q r|\log r|}(G_M(n;r)))
        \to 1
    \]
    as $r \to 0$.
    Moreover,
    if $\underline{\lambda} >\lambda_c$,
    $z$ above can be chosen
    to lie in the largest component $\mathring{G}_M(n;r)$ of $G_M(n;r)$.
    In particular, in this case we have
    \[
        \mathbb{P}\left(\begin{array}{c} Z_1(G_M(n;r))/Z_1^{qr|\log r|}(G_M(n;r))
        \not \cong H_1(M) \mbox{ and } \\ Z_1(\mathring{G}_M(n;r))/Z_1^{qr|\log r|}(\mathring{G}_M(n;r))
        \not \cong H_1(M)
        \end{array}\right)
        \to 1
    \]
    as $r \to 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 35 of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] For any $a, b \in (0, \infty)$, the law of the boundary length process $(L, R)$ of $\MD(a, b)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:MD} is $C_\gamma B_{a, bi}^{\gamma, \bR^2_+}$ for some $C_\gamma >0$ depending only on $\gamma$. Moreover, the curve-decorated LQG surface $(\cD,\eta'){/}{\sim_\gamma}$ can a.s.\  be recovered from $(L,R)$ through the map $F$ in Definition~\ref{def:Quantum-cell}.

body:
[Lem 22 of arXiv:2608.30763, 'Ultracontractivity of heat semigroups with non-local Robin boundary conditions via two-sid'] The auxiliary operator semigroup $\mathrm{e}^{-t\tilde{L}(A, B)}$ is dominated by the auxiliary operator semigroup
 $\mathrm{e}^{-t\tilde{L}(A,-C)}$, i.e.
$$
\left| \mathrm{e}^{-t\tilde{L}(A, B)}u \right| \ \leq \ \mathrm{e}^{-t\tilde{L}(A,-C)} \left| u \right|
$$ 
holds pointwise almost everywhere in $\Omega$ for every $u \in   \mathrm{L}^{2}( \Omega )$. 
Furthermore 
$$
\left| \mathrm{e}^{-tL(A, B)}u \right| \ \leq \ \mathrm{e}^{-tL(A,-C)} \left| u \right|
$$
is a direct implication where $\lambda$ is chosen as described in Remark \ref{choice_lambda}.

		\left| \HarmlessWave{[1,N]} \right|
		&

				\left| \comdersmall^{[1,N];\le 1} \controlvars \right| + \left| \tandersmall^{[1,N]}\badcontrolvars\right|.
	\end{align}

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a sequence of general complex Wishart matrices
$$W_N=Y_NY_N^*\in M_N(L^\infty(X))$$
with $Y_N$ being $N\times M$ complex Gaussian of parameter $1$, we have
$$\frac{W_N}{N}\sim\max(1-t,0)\delta_0+\frac{\sqrt{4t-(x-1-t)^2}}{2\pi x}\,dx$$
with $M=tN\to\infty$, with the limiting measure being the Marchenko-Pastur law $\pi_t$.
title: Unnumbered theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

body:
[Ppn 197 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any subsequential limit $\Q$ as obtained by Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}, let $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\Gamma,\Upsilon,\mathcal{E})\sim\mu$ (so $\mathcal{E}\equiv0$). Denote the limiting processes as 
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	\Gamma
	&\equiv \Big(
	D^{\RomI}=D=Y^{\RomI},
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},Q^{\RomIII},Q^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,,\\
	\Upsilon
	&\equiv\Big( 
	Z^{\RomII}=Y^{\RomII},
	Z^{\RomIII}=Y^{\RomIII},
	Z^{\Ising}=Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,.
	
	\end{align}
Then $\Gamma$ is a finite-variation process, while $\Upsilon$ is a martingale. For each $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, the covariation of $Z^\sigma$ with $Z^\tau$ is given by $Q^{\sigma,\tau}$, where
$Q^{\sigma,\Ising}\equiv0$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}$. 
 The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds. 

\begin{proof}
Suppose $\Q_N\to\Q$ along some subsequence of integers $N\to\infty$.
By Corollary~\ref{c:tightness}, this means there exists a Skorohod coupling of the disorder matrices $\bG^N$ for which, with probability one over $(\bG^N)_{N\ge1}$, we have
$\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}\Rightarrow \mu$ with $\mu\sim\bar{\Q}$. Let $\cG(s)$ be the filtration generated by the limiting process $(\Gamma,\Upsilon)$. It follows from \eqref{e:def.drift} that if 
$0\le s\le t\le 1$, then for all $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$ and $A\in\cG(s)$, we have 
	\beq
	\bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ \Big( Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)
		-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
		\ind\{A\}\bigg]
	=\bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ \Big( D^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)
		-D^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
		\ind\{A\}\bigg]\,,
	\eeq
where $\bE_{\bG^N}$ denotes expectation with respect to $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$.
Now fix an event $A\in\cG(s)$. Let $L_R,U_R$ be bounded continuous $\cG(s)$-measurable functions such that $L_R \le \ind\{A\} \le U_R$, and both $L_R,U_R$ converge to $\ind\{A\}$ in the limit $R\to\infty$. Moreover, we can arrange for the convergence to happen fast enough so that
	\beq
	\E_N\Big(U_R-L_R\Big) \le \frac{o_R(1)}{R}\,,
	\eeq
where we recall that $\E_N$ denotes the overall expectation.
Define also the function
	\[
	I_R(x) = \max\Big\{\min\{x,R\},-R\Big\} \in[-R,R]\,.
	\]
Let $\bE$ denote expectation with respect to $\mu$.
Since $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}\Rightarrow\mu$, for fixed $R$ we have
	\begin{align*}
	\lim_{N\to\infty}
	\bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ I_R\Big( Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)
		-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
	L_R \bigg]
	&=\bE\bigg[ I_R\Big(Y^\sigma(t)-Y^\sigma(s)\Big) L_R\bigg]\,,\\

[Definition regulated process of arXiv:2607.29548, 'Generalized reflected BSDEs with irregular obstacles driven by RCLL increasing processes o'] \begin{itemize}
			\item A process
			\[
			\mathcal{X}:\Omega\times[0,T]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
			\]
			is called a \emph{regulated process} if, for
			$\mathbb{P}$-almost every $\omega\in\Omega$, the mapping
			\[
			t\longmapsto\mathcal{X}_t(\omega)
			\]
			admits a finite right limit at every $t\in[0,T)$ and a finite
			left limit at every $t\in(0,T]$.
			
			\item Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a process with regulated trajectories.
			For $s\in(0,T]$, we define its left limit and left jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s-}
			:=
			\lim_{u\uparrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_s-\mathcal{X}_{s-},
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_0=0$.
			
			For $s\in[0,T)$, we define its right limit and right jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}
			:=
			\lim_{u\downarrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}-\mathcal{X}_s,
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_T=0$.
			
			The trajectories of a regulated process have at most countably
			many discontinuities; see
			[DudleyNorvaisa2011].
			
			\item Let
			\[
			\mathsf{K}:\Omega\times[0,T]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
			\]
			be a regulated process of finite variation. Then $\mathsf{K}$
			admits the decomposition
			\[
			\mathsf{K}
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d+\mathsf{K}^g,
			\]
			where $\mathsf{K}^c$ is continuous, the càdlàg pure-jump process
			$\mathsf{K}^d$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^d_t
			:=
			\sum_{0<s\leq t}\Delta_-\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			and the càglàd pure-jump process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^g_t
			:=
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T].
			\]
			The above sums converge absolutely along each trajectory since
			$\mathsf{K}$ has finite variation.
			
			In particular,
			\[
			\mathsf{K}_t
			=
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}_t
			+
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			where
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}
			:=
			\mathsf{K}-\mathsf{K}^g
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d
			\]
			is the càdlàg, or right-continuous, part of $\mathsf{K}$.
			The process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is the left-continuous pure-jump part
			of $\mathsf{K}$.
		\end{itemize}
title: Regulated processes

body: For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). Consequently the enclosing-ball (quadratic lower) curvature condition excess >= c d^2/r holds at the axis if and only if p <= 2: for p < 2 the excess is of larger order than quadratic (the condition holds with room), at p = 2 it is exactly quadratic with constant 2, and for every p > 2 the contact is quartic or flatter and the enclosing-ball constant is ZERO. The curvature hypothesis consumed by localization arguments is therefore genuinely restrictive - entire familiar norm families fail it at their axis directions - and cannot be discharged by convexity or symmetry alone. Numerically verified: measured excess/predicted ratios 0.9995-1.0000 across p in {1.5, 2, 3, 4} at two offsets, and the quadratic test excess/(d^2/r) converges to a constant for p <= 2 and to zero for p > 2.

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and $\mu_G$ be the RFIM measure on $G$. We say that $\mu_G$ satisfies $\operatorname{WSM}(C)$ for some $C>0$ if for all vertices $v\in V$ and $r\geq 1$, we have 
    $$
\mathbb{E}_h[d_{TV}(\mu_G(\sigma_v\in\cdot\mid \sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=+),\mu_G(\sigma_v\in\cdot\mid \sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=-))]\leq Ce^{-r/C}.
    $$Here $\partial B_r(v)$ is the boundary of $B_r(v)$ in $V$ and $B_r(v)$ is the ball of radius $r$ around $v$ with respect to the graph distance on $G$. We use $\sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=+$ (resp. $\sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=-$) to denote the all plus (resp. all minus) boundary condition.

body:
[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2604.14427, 'A criterion for proving entropy chaos on path space'] Let $\PP$ denote the law of a conservative diffusion on $E$ which is the weak solution to a isotropic Brownian SDE with drift $b=u+v$  and marginal density $\rho_t$ and let $\mathbb{W}$ denotes the Wiener law. Then we have that
  \begin{align*}
    H(\PP|\mathbb{W}) &= \int_0^T \int |b(x,t)|^2 \rho(x,t) \dd x \dd t\\
                &= \int_0^T \int_{\RR^d} \Big(u(x,t)^2 + v(x,t)^2\Big)\rho(x,t)\dd x\dd t + H(\rho(0)) - H(\rho(T)).
  \end{align*}
  where 
  $H$ denotes the Boltzmann entropy as given in Definition~\ref{def_boltzmann}.

body: Ergodic theory is a branch of mathematics that studies statistical properties of deterministic dynamical systems; it is the study of ergodicity. In this context, "statistical properties" refers to properties which are expressed through the behavior of time averages of various functions along trajectories of dynamical systems. The notion of deterministic dynamical systems assumes that the equations determining the dynamics do not contain any random perturbations, noise, etc. Thus, the statistics with which we are concerned are properties of the dynamics.
title: Ergodic theory

[Lemma lem:second_moment_recurrences of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] Let $B_\mathcal{P}$ and $B_\mathcal{T}$ be defined as in~(equation eq:defn_B_s of the paper). For all $x>(3a-b)/2$, it follows that
\begin{align}
B_{\mathcal{P}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a}B_{\mathcal{P}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x-\varsigma }B_{\mathcal{T}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + q_{\mathcal{P}}(x), \quad \text{ and } \\
B_{\mathcal{T}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_\delta^{x-a}B_{\mathcal{T}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_0^{x-\varsigma }B_{\mathcal{P}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + q_{\mathcal{T}}(x), 
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}
q_{\mathcal{P}}(x) 
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a} e_{\mathcal{P}}(t)e_{\mathcal{T}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x-\varsigma } e_{\mathcal{T}}(t)e_{\mathcal{P}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright),\quad \text{ and } \\
q_{\mathcal{T}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a-\delta} e_{\mathcal{T}}(t+\delta)e_{\mathcal{T}}(x-a-t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_0^{x-\varsigma }  e_{\mathcal{P}}(t)e_{\mathcal{P}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright). 
\end{align}

[Theorem 17 of arXiv:2606.29512, '2606.29512'] Let Assumptions \ref{assumption1}, 
\ref{assumption2}, \ref{assumption3}  and \ref{assumption2c} hold.  
Then every admissible solution admits an $\cH$-valued c\`adl\`ag modification. 
Moreover,  there exists a constant 
$N=N(d,r)>0$
such that if $u$ is an admissible solution 
to \eqref{SNS5}--\eqref{div5}--\eqref{bin5} satisfying 
$\hat u\leq \delta/N$, then 
$$
\E e^{-\psi_{t}}|u_t-v_t|^2_{\cH}
\leq \E |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}^2\quad\text{for $t\in[0,T]$} 
$$
for any admissible solution $v$ of \eqref{SNS5}--\eqref{div5}--\eqref{bin5} 
on $[0,T]$ with $\cH$-valued initial condition 
$v_t|_{t=0}=v_0$, where 
$$
\psi_t=N\int_0^t\beta_s\,ds,
\quad 
\beta_s
=\hat u^2+\bar u_s^2+\lambda^2_s+\tilde\lambda^2_s+\vartheta^2+\chi^2_s+\kappa_s
$$
with a constant  $N=N(d,r,\delta)$. In particular, if $u_0=v_0$ 
then the $\cH$-valued c\`adl\`ag modifications 
of $u$ and $v$ coincide almost surely on  $[0,T]$.

body:
[Prop geods-dust of arXiv:2604.12963, 'Shocks, instability, and the twenty networks\\ of infinite geodesics in the Directed Lands'] Let $\omega\in\Omega_0$, $\theta\in\Theta^\omega$, and  $(x,s)\in\IG\theta$. Suppose that $(x,s)$ is not on the boundary of any stability island. Then the following are the only three possible $\theta$-directed geodesic configurations out of $(x,s)$, and each of the three occurs on a set of starting points that is dense in $\IG\theta$. See the first three configurations on the second row of Figure (fig:geodesics of the paper).
    \begin{enumerate}[label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}] \itemsep=1pt
        \item $(x,s)\not\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}\cup{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}$. Then $(x,s)\in\IGpns\theta$.
        
        \item $(x,s)\in {\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}$. Then $(x,s)\not\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}$, there are no distinct middle geodesics out of $(x,s)$, and
        \[
        \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}\preceq \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}\prec\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)} = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)}.
        \]

        \item $(x,s)\in {\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}$. Then $(x,s)\not\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}$, there are no distinct middle geodesics out of $(x,s)$, and
        \[
        \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}= \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}\prec\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)} \preceq\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)}.
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop geods-dust of arXiv:2604.12963

body: [Corollary co-uncited-4 of arXiv:2411.12623, 'Random signed measures'] For any random signed measure $\xi$ on $S$ and any sub $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}$ of $\mathcal{F}$, there exist $\mathcal{G}$-measurable kernels $\eta_+ = \mathbb{E}[\xi_+|\mathcal{G}]$ and $\eta_- = \mathbb{E}[\xi_-|\mathcal{G}]$ and pre-kernel $\eta = \mathbb{E}[\xi|\mathcal{G}]$ from $\Omega$ to $S$, such that $\eta_+(B) = \mathbb{E}[\xi_+(B)|\mathcal{G}]$ a.s. for all $B\in\hat{\mathcal{S}}$ and similarly for $\eta_-$ and $\eta$. If $\mathbb{E}[|\xi|]$ is locally finite, then $\eta_+$ and $\eta_-$ are random measures on $S$ and $\eta=\eta_+-\eta_-= \mathbb{E}[\xi|\mathcal{G}]$ is a random signed measure on $S$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\[
 s(\theta)\succ s(\eta)
\]
and $s(\theta)$ is not a permutation of $s(\eta)$, then
\begin{equation}
 M_{p,n,t}(\theta)>M_{p,n,t}(\eta).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\theta)>
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\eta).
\]

\sup_{\abs{z}\leq\rho}u(z)
 \leq \sup_{\abs{z}=\rho}u(z).
\]

    \]

Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent p'. For g in L^{p'}(mu) define Lambda_g(f) = int_X f g dmu. (a) If 1 < p < infinity, then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^{p'}(mu) onto the dual space (L^p(mu))*, for an arbitrary measure space. (b) If p = 1 and mu is sigma-finite (more generally, localizable), then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^infinity(mu) onto (L^1(mu))*. In particular L^p is reflexive for 1 < p < infinity. For 1 < p < infinity the map is isometric over every measure space; for p = 1 it is isometric as soon as mu is semifinite, and without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) it need not be surjective. The case p = infinity is genuinely different and is NOT covered: the analogous map L^1(mu) -> (L^infinity(mu))* is isometric when mu is semifinite but in general not surjective, so (L^infinity)* is in general strictly larger than L^1 (see the pitfall).

body: A Riemannian metric g on a smooth manifold M is a smooth assignment to each point p in M of a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form g_p on the tangent space T_pM: g_p: T_pM x T_pM -> R is bilinear and symmetric, satisfies g_p(v,v) > 0 for every nonzero v in T_pM, and p |-> g_p(X(p),Y(p)) is a smooth function of p for any pair of smooth vector fields X, Y. The pair (M,g) is called a Riemannian manifold. The metric g determines lengths of tangent vectors, angles between them, and, by integration along curves, the length of any piecewise smooth curve and the induced distance function between points of M.
title: Riemannian Metric

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.25725, 'Gr\"obner Bases for Alexander Fitting Ideals of Links'] For \(k\ge0\), define
\[
\AG_k(G,\phi)
 :=\mathcal G_P\!\left(\PP(E_k(G,\phi))\right).
\]
We call this the \emph{\(k\)th Alexander--Gr\"obner invariant} of
\((G,\phi)\). The target \(\Z^\ell\) is understood with its fixed ordered
standard basis. The reduced Gr\"obner basis of the unit ideal is \(\{1\}\),
and that of the zero ideal is the empty set. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:CF-invariance} and uniqueness of reduced Gr\"obner bases,
\(\AG_k(G,\phi)\) depends only on \((G,\phi)\).

For $k\ge1$, let $H_k$ be the Hermite polynomial of degree $k$ normalized so that $\mathbb{E}[H_k(\xi)^2]=k!$. Define
\[
S_N(t) = \frac{1}{N^H} \sum_{n=1}^{[Nt]} H_k(\xi_n), \qquad t\ge 0.
\]
Then, as $N\to\infty$, the finite-dimensional distributions of $S_N(t)$ converge to those of the Hermite process $Z_H^k(t)$. Moreover, let $u^N$ be the mild solution of (equation eq:main of the paper) with $\dot{S}_N$ in place of $\dot{Z}_H^k$. Under the assumptions of Theorem~(thm:exist of the paper), we have
\[
u^N \xrightarrow{\text{law}} u \quad \text{in } C([0,T];\dot{H}^\nu),
\]
where $u$ is the mild solution of the original problem. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let (Omega, T) be a MINIMAL topological dynamical system, Omega a compact metric space and T a homeomorphism, and let V: Omega -> R be continuous. For each omega in Omega let H_omega be the discrete Schrodinger operator on l^2(Z) given by (H_omega u)(n) = u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega) u(n). By minimality the spectrum sigma(H_omega) is one and the same compact set Sigma contained in R for every omega. For an energy E in R define the Schrodinger cocycle (T, A^E) over (Omega,T), where A^E(omega) is the SL(2,R) matrix with rows (E - V(omega), -1) and (1, 0); its iterates are A^E_n(omega) = A^E(T^{n-1}omega) ... A^E(omega), and they transfer solutions of the difference equation u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega)u(n) = E u(n). The cocycle is UNIFORMLY HYPERBOLIC if there is a continuous T-invariant splitting R^2 = E^s(omega) + E^u(omega) and constants C > 0, lambda > 1 with ||A^E_n(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^s(omega) and ||A^E_{-n}(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^u(omega), for all n >= 0 and all omega; equivalently (for SL(2,R) cocycles over a compact base) ||A^E_n(omega)|| >= C lambda^n for all omega and all n >= 0. THEOREM (R. Johnson): E belongs to R \ Sigma if and only if the cocycle (T, A^E) is uniformly hyperbolic. Equivalently, Sigma is exactly the set of real energies at which the Schrodinger cocycle fails to be uniformly hyperbolic. The same statement holds in the continuum setting for Schrodinger operators -u'' + V(T_t omega)u on the line with a minimal flow, which is Johnson's original formulation, and it is the standard dictionary between spectral theory and the dynamics of the transfer-matrix cocycle. SHARP EDGES. (a) UNIFORM hyperbolicity is far stronger than a positive Lyapunov exponent, and this is the single most often misused point. In the supercritical almost Mathieu operator, and more generally in the localisation regime, the Lyapunov exponent L(E) is positive at EVERY energy of the spectrum; those energies are in Sigma, so the cocycle there is non-uniformly hyperbolic. 'Positive exponent' therefore does NOT imply 'in the resolvent set'; only uniformity does. (b) Minimality of the base is used twice: to make sigma(H_omega) independent of omega, and to propagate the exponential dichotomy from one orbit to all of Omega. For a non-minimal base the spectrum can genuinely depend on omega and the statement must be reformulated (typically with the union of the spectra over the support of an ergodic measure, or over the whole base), so do not apply the equivalence verbatim outside minimality. (c) The theorem characterises the RESOLVENT set, which is open; correspondingly uniform hyperbolicity is an open condition in E and in the cocycle, whereas positivity of the Lyapunov exponent is not open. (d) The statement is for real E; for non-real E the operator is invertible anyway and the associated cocycle is not an SL(2,R) cocycle.

(Omega, T) is minimal
V: Omega -> R is continuous
H_omega is the discrete Schrodinger operator with potential n -> V(T^n omega) on l^2(Z) (equivalently, the continuum Schrodinger operator over a minimal flow)
E is a real energy
uniform hyperbolicity is understood with constants uniform over all of Omega

(Uniform hyperbolicity implies E in the resolvent set.) The invariant splitting produces, for each omega, a solution of the difference equation that decays exponentially as n -> +infinity (the stable direction) and one that decays exponentially as n -> -infinity (the unstable direction). These two solutions are linearly independent, since a common solution would decay at both ends and would then be an l^2 eigenfunction forcing a contradiction with the uniform expansion estimate. From the two solutions one builds the Green kernel G_omega(m,n) of (H_omega - E)^{-1} in the standard way, and the exponential dichotomy bounds give |G_omega(m,n)| <= C' lambda^{-|m-n|} with constants independent of omega. A kernel with uniform exponential off-diagonal decay defines a bounded operator on l^2(Z), so H_omega - E is boundedly invertible for every omega, i.e. E is not in Sigma. (E in the resolvent set implies uniform hyperbolicity.) If E is not in Sigma then H_omega - E is invertible with an inverse bounded uniformly in omega, again by minimality and compactness. Bounded invertibility of the operator for all omega is equivalent, through Sacker-Sell exponential dichotomy theory applied to the first-order system defined by the transfer matrices, to the existence of an exponential dichotomy for the cocycle over the closure of the orbit; the dichotomy projections are then continuous in omega, and minimality makes them globally defined on Omega. That is exactly uniform hyperbolicity of (T, A^E). The only delicate ingredient is the dichotomy criterion, which is where the compactness of Omega and the continuity of V are used.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:b37e769019af9c3c806bc40c8bcd035f4ed3ab30f89685ef51d9f4cfa8dc0756","revision_digest":"sha256:ae02788a467b182215c0322bd89b1ed9531f9fb0c3a5dbf18d877ba74f12ef05","source_id":"wikipedia:Almost_Mathieu_operator","source_revision":"as-read-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
Let X be a topological space and f: X -> (-infinity, +infinity] an extended-real function. f is lower semicontinuous (lsc) at a point x0 if for every real a < f(x0) there is a neighbourhood U of x0 with f(x) > a for all x in U. f is lsc on X iff any one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (i) the superlevel set {x : f(x) > a} is open for every real a; (ii) the sublevel set {x : f(x) <= a} is closed for every real a; (iii) the epigraph {(x,t) in X x R : t >= f(x)} is closed in X x R. If X is first countable (in particular metric), lower semicontinuity at x0 is equivalent to liminf_{x -> x0} f(x) >= f(x0). f is upper semicontinuous iff -f is lsc, and f is continuous iff it is both. Standard facts, each of which is the reason lsc is worth naming: (1) the pointwise SUPREMUM of an arbitrary family of lsc functions is lsc; (2) a sum of finitely many lsc functions is lsc provided no (+infinity) + (-infinity) occurs, and a nonnegative multiple of an lsc function is lsc; (3) a nondecreasing pointwise limit of continuous functions is lsc, and conversely on a METRIC space every lsc function bounded below is the pointwise nondecreasing limit of a sequence of Lipschitz functions (Baire); (4) the indicator 1_A is lsc iff A is open; (5) WEIERSTRASS FORM: if X is compact and f is lsc then f attains its infimum on X, because the sublevel sets {f <= a} are closed and have the finite intersection property. This is the form in which lsc is used in the direct method of the calculus of variations: coercivity plus lsc on a compact (or weakly compact) set yields a minimiser. SHARP EDGES, i.e. what is NOT true. (a) lsc buys you MINIMA only, never maxima: on the compact space [0,1] the function f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 is lsc (every superlevel set {f > a} is (a,1) or [0,1] or empty), its supremum is 1 and it is not attained. (b) The supremum of lsc functions is lsc but the INFIMUM of infinitely many lsc functions need not be: on R the continuous functions f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n|x|) have pointwise infimum the indicator of {0}, whose superlevel set {f > 1/2} = {0} is not open. (c) 'lsc at every point' is genuinely weaker than continuity; an lsc function may be discontinuous on a dense set. (d) Statement (3) uses metrizability of X; on a general topological space an lsc function need not be a pointwise limit of continuous functions (it is a supremum of continuous functions on compact Hausdorff or, more generally, normal spaces, by Urysohn/Katetov-Tong, but for arbitrary X no such representation is available). (e) In integration theory the useful instance is Fatou's lemma, which says exactly that f -> integral f is lsc along pointwise convergence of nonnegative measurable functions; no upper semicontinuity holds there without a domination hypothesis.
X is a topological space
f takes values in the extended reals (-infinity, +infinity]
for the liminf characterisation, X is first countable (e.g. metric)
for the attainment-of-the-infimum statement, X is compact
for the approximation by Lipschitz functions, X is metric and f is bounded below

\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(1)] Let $\eta\in C^1(\R)$ be

\eqref{eq:2.3}. Suppose that $\eta$ has a bounded first derivative or $u$ is bounded on $E$. Then $\eta(u)\in D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}^{\diamond}$ and is $\mathscr{E}$-subharmonic in $D$ satisfying \eqref{eq:2.3}. If further $u\in D(\mathscr{E
})_{\loc}^{\diamond}$, then $\eta(u)\in D(\mathscr{E})_{\loc}^{\diamond}$.  
\item[\rm(2)] Let $\eta\in C^1(\R)$ be 
an increasing convex function and $u\in D(\mathscr{E
})_{e,\loc}^{\diamond}$ be an $\mathscr{E}$-subharmonic function in $D$ satisfying \eqref{eq:2.3}. Suppose that $\eta$ has a bounded first derivative or $u$ is bounded on $E$. Then the same conclusion of {\rm(1)} also holds.  
\item[\rm(3)] If $u\in D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}^{\diamond}$ {\rm(}resp.~$u\in D(\mathscr{E})_{\loc}^{\diamond}${\rm)} is an $\mathscr{E}$-harmonic function in $D$ satisfying \eqref{eq:2.3}, then  
$|u|\in  D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}^{\diamond}$ {\rm(}resp.~$|u|\in D(\mathscr{E})_{\loc}^{\diamond}${\rm)} 
satisfies \eqref{eq:2.3} and $|u|$ is $\mathscr{E}$-subharmonic in $D$. 
Let $p>1$ and $u\in D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}^{\diamond}$ be an $\mathscr{E}$-harmonic function in $D$ satisfying \eqref{eq:2.3}.  
Assume that \eqref{e:2.3} holds.
Suppose that $|u|^p\in  D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}^{\diamond}$ and it  
satisfies \eqref{eq:2.3}. 
Then $|u|^p$ is $\mathscr{E}$-subharmonic in $D$.
\item[\rm(4)]
Suppose that $u_1,u_2\in D(\mathscr{E})^{\diamond}_{e,\loc}$ satisfy 
\eqref{eq:2.3} and they are $\mathscr{E}$-subharmonic in $D$. 
Then $u_1\lor u_2\in D(\mathscr{E})^{\diamond}_{e,\loc}$ also satisfy \eqref{eq:2.3} and it is $\mathscr{E}$-subharmonic in $D$. 
The same assertion also holds for $u_1,u_2\in D(\mathscr{E})^{\diamond}_{\loc}$ satisfying \eqref{eq:2.3}. 
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:chain-of-price-inequalities of arXiv:2512.21026, 'Minimax Duality in Game-Theoretic Probability\thanks{Work in progress: mistakes are likely'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{Z})$ be a gamble space and $X:\Omega\to{\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}}$ a measurable variable.

body:
[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Suppose $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ is an NCP. 

Let $\{a_i\}$ be self-adjoint variables such that, $\varphi(a_i)=0, \varphi(a_i^2)=1$, and  $\sup_i|\varphi(a_i^m)| < \infty$ for every positive integer $m$. 
Then the following hold for $S_n:=a_1+\cdots +a_n$.\vskip5pt

\noindent (i) If $\{a_i\}$ are free, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} s$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (ii) If $\{a_i\}$ are independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} z$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (iii) If $\{a_i\}$ are half-independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}
\stackrel{*}{\to} r_S$.

\vskip3pt

\noindent In other words, $\varphi(S_n/\sqrt{n})^m$ in (i), (ii) and (iii) respectively, equal $\varphi(s^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(z^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(r_S^m)+o(1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop p.axioms of arXiv:2507.16056, 'Conditional GMC within the stochastic heat flow'] Take $q\in(0,\infty),\theta'\in\mathbb{R}$, and any probability space that houses random $M'_{[s,t]}\in\mathcal{M}_+(\Gamma_{[s,t]})$ for $s<t\in q\mathbb{D}$. Write $Z'_{s,t}:=M'_{[s,t]}\circ\margin{\{s,t\}}^{-1}$ for the time-$\{s,t\}$ marginal.
If for all $t_0<\cdots<t_{\ell}\inq\mathbb{D}$ we have that
\begin{enumerate}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item 
$M'_{[t_0,t_1]},\ldots,M'_{[t_{\ell-1},t_{\ell}]}$ are independent, 
\item 
$M'_{[t_0,t_\ell]}\circ\margin{\{t_0,\ldots,t_\ell\}}^{-1} = Z'_{t_0,t_1}\circ\cdots\opdotZ'_{t_{\ell-1},t_{\ell}}$\ , and
\item 
$
	\mathbf{E} Z'_{s,t} {}^{\otimes n}
	=
	\mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} x' \, \mathcal{Q}^{[\![n]\!],\theta'}(t-s,x,x')
$
for all $s<t \in q\mathbb{D}$ and $n=1,2,3,4$,
\end{enumerate}
then $M'_{[0,q ]}$ is equal in law to $M^{\theta'}_{[0,q ]}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop p.axioms of arXiv:2507.16056

body:
[Lemma 25 (Amplification via many macroscopic subtrees) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Fix $\theta>0$ and let $H_n$ denote the height of the Ewens tree $\mathcal T_n$.
Assume that there exist constants $p_0\in(0,1)$ and $m_0\ge 1$ such that
\begin{equation}
\inf_{m\ge m_0}\Pp\left(H_m\ge h(m)\right)\ \ge\ p_0,
\end{equation}
for some function $h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$.
Fix any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and set $m:=n-1$ and the macroscopic threshold
\[
t_n := \lceil m^{1-\delta}\rceil,
\qquad
h_{\min}(n):=\min(\{h(j):\ t_n\le j\le m\}).
\]
Then, for all $n$ large enough so that $t_n\ge m_0$,
\begin{equation}
\Pp\left(H_n \ge 1+h_{\min}(n)\right)
\ \ge\
1-\E\left[(1-p_0)^{N_0}\right].
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\E[(1-p_0)^{N_0}]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0
\qquad\text{and therefore}\qquad
\Pp\left(H_n \ge 1+h_{\min}(n)\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\end{equation}

    \item if $X, Y\in\mathcal{H}$, then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{H}$ \citep[][Proposition 3]{CHSZ25}.

    \item If $X, Y\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}^\ast$].
    \end{itemize}

  \item[{\rm (vii)}] If $X\in \mathcal{H}$, then $(X-c)_+\in\mathcal{H}$ for any $c\in\R_{++}$ \citep[][Proposition 5]{CHSZ25}. \\
       If $X\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $(X-c)_+\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$] for any $c\in\R_{++}$.

  \item[{\rm (viii)}] Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent such that $X\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$]. If $Y$ is non-negative, then $(X-Y)_+\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$].

  \item[{\rm (ix)}]  If $X\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $[X|X>c] \in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$] for any $c\in\R_{++}$. However, $[X|X>c]\notin \mathcal{G}$ for any $c\in\R_{++}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In graph theory, the Robertson–Seymour theorem (also called the graph minors theorem) states that the undirected graphs, partially ordered by the graph minor relationship, form a well-quasi-ordering. Equivalently, every family of graphs that is closed under taking minors can be defined by a finite set of forbidden minors, in the same way that Wagner's theorem characterizes the planar graphs as being the graphs that do not have the complete graph $K_{5}$ or the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$ as minors.

[Proposition prop:shadow3 of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \(l\) be a component of the frontier of \(\Theta(\widetilde{S})\) in \(P_{\varphi}\). Then,
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(l\) is a slice leaf of \(\mathcal{F}^{s/u}\). If it is a slice leaf \(l\) of \(\mathcal{F}^{s}\), then as a sequence of point \(\{p_{n}\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\) tends to a point in \(l\), the preimages \((\Theta|_{\widetilde{S}})^{-1}(p_{n})\) in \(\widetilde{S}\) escape in the positive direction.
Similar conclusion holds for unstable boundary slice leaves.
\item \(l\) is periodic, namely, there is an element \(g\in \pi_{1}(M)\) such that \(g\) fixes \(l\) and hence a unique point in \(l\).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:shadow3 of arXiv:2608.30973

[Proposition thm:ratefall of arXiv:2607.09946, 'Statistics on Yau's conjecture: Variance asymptotics'] For any sequence $\eta_\ell= \mathrm{o}(\ell)$, let $\varepsilon_\ell=\varepsilon(\phi_{[\ell-\eta_\ell,\ell]}^M)$. Under the assumption that the scaling limit  $\delta_\ell=\delta_{[\ell-\eta_\ell,\ell]}^M\to 0$ holds, there exists $r_0>0$ such that for all $r_0\le r_\ell\le \rho\ell$, we have
\begin{gather} 
{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}}\left( Y_M([\ell-\eta_\ell,\ell])\right)
\le

\frac{1}{\ell^n}\left(\frac\ell{\eta_\ell}\mathrm{O}( \varepsilon_\ell) 
+\mathrm{O}(r_\ell)\right)
\\
+ \mathrm{O}(1)\int_{\substack{x,y\in M,
\\
\frac{r_\ell}{\ell}
\le \mathrm{dist}(x,y)\le \rho}}\|(\ell^{n-1}\eta_\ell)^{-1}j^{1,1}_{x,y}E_{[\ell-\eta_\ell,\ell]}\|^4_{g^{\ell}} \dd x \dd y 
\\
\text{ setting $r_\ell=\mathrm{O}(1)$, we get:}
\\
{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}}\left( Y_M([\ell-\eta_\ell,\ell])\right)
\le
\frac{1}{\ell^{n}}
\left( 
\frac\ell{\eta_\ell}\mathrm{O}( \varepsilon_\ell+\delta_\ell^2) 
+a(\ell) \right),
\\
\text{ using that $\varepsilon_\ell\le \delta_\ell \le \mathrm{O}(\frac{\ell}{\eta_\ell}\delta^M_{[0,\ell]})$,}
\\
\le
\frac{1}{\ell^{n}}\mathrm{O}\left( 
\frac{\ell^2}{\eta_\ell^2}\delta_{[0,\ell]}^M
+a(\ell)
\right) 
\\
\text{ using the general bound $\delta^M_{[0,\ell]}=\mathrm{O}(\ell^{-1})$,}
\\
\le
\frac{1}{\ell^{n}}\mathrm{O}\left( 
\frac{\ell}{\eta_\ell^2}+a(\ell)
\right).
    \end{gather} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition thm:ratefall of arXiv:2607.09946

[Lemma BDSL of arXiv:2604.21591, '\bf Long-time dynamics of stochastic 2D hydrodynamic-type evolution equations driven by mu'] For any $p \geq 1$ and $\tau\in \mathbb{R}$, there exists a positive constant $C_p$ such that for any real-valued square-integrable c\`{a}dl\`{a}g martingale $M$ with $M(0)=0$, the following inequality holds:
	$$
	C_{p}^{-1} \mathbb{E}[M]_{T}^{\frac{p}{2}} \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{\tau \leq t \leq \tau+T}|M(t)|^{p}\right] \leq C_{p} \mathbb{E}[M]_{T}^{\frac{p}{2}},\quad \forall \, T > 0,
	$$
	where $[M]_{T}$ is called the quadratic variation of $M$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma BDSL of arXiv:2604.21591

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Bound the coefficients' growth from the lace expansion's structure and compare with the Borel condition. Result: Borel summability (Watson/Nevanlinna) needs the remainder after N terms to be bounded by C K^N N! (2d)^{-N} uniformly in a sector, and the coefficients to grow at most like K^N N!. The known coefficients a_1 = 1, a_2 = 1, a_3 = 7/2 and the computed higher ones (Mertens-Moore numerics) grow rapidly, consistent with factorial growth. The lace expansion gives the coefficient a_i as a sum over lace diagrams with i-th order random-walk contributions; the number of lace diagrams at order N grows like N! (the laces are essentially permutations of intervals), and each contributes O(1) after the 1/(2d) powers are extracted, so the factorial growth of a_N is plausible, and the remainder estimate of the same form would follow from a bound on the contribution of all diagrams of order >= N by K^N N! (2d)^{-N}. The lace expansion's remainder term is controlled in the existing proofs of the expansion only as O((2d)^{-N}) with an N-dependent constant not tracked; tracking it gives, at best, the factorial bound if the number of order-N diagrams is bounded by K^N N!, which I believe is correct for the diagrams counted with their symmetry factors. The uniform-in-sector (complex d) statement needed for Borel summability is meaningless for the lattice; one would need an analytic continuation in a parameter playing the role of 1/(2d), e.g. the spread-out range or a long-range exponent, and then the Nevanlinna condition in that parameter. So the honest reduction: Borel summability requires (i) K^N N! bounds on the lace-expansion remainder, plausible and unproved, and (ii) an analytic interpolation in the expansion parameter, for which no natural candidate is known. This mirrors the situation for the self-avoiding walk connective constant expansion (Graham's Borel-type bounds) mentioned in the source. Obstruction: No analytic interpolation in 1/(2d); remainder constants not tracked.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0080-borel-summability-of-the-1-d-expansion-of-the-percolation-threshold
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved
title: Attempt on Borel summability of the 1/d expansion of the percolation threshold

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a set $X$, which can be finite, countable, or even uncountable, a discrete probability measure on it is a linear combination as follows,
$$\mu=\sum_{x\in X}\lambda_x\delta_x$$
with the coefficients $\lambda_i\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $\lambda_i\geq0$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. For $f:X\to\mathbb R$ we set
$$\int_Xf(x)d\mu(x)=\sum_{x\in X}\lambda_xf(x)$$
with the convention that each Dirac mass integrates up to $1$.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.30178, '2608.30178'] Assume that the model \eqref{eq:noimm-system} is source-conservative, \(0\le\theta_2<1\), and
\beqnn
	b_{20}=0\ \text{or}\ r_{20}=1,
\qquad b_{21}=0\ \text{or}\ r_{21}=2,
\qquad b_{22}=0\ \text{or}\ r_{22}=\alpha_2.
\eeqnn 
 Let \(G_2\) be given by \eqref{eq:G2}. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every \(t<\tau_0\),
\begin{equation}
 Y_t=G_{2,t}\left[
 y^{1-\theta_2}-(1-\theta_2)a_2
 \int_0^tG_{2,u}^{\theta_2-1}X_u^{\kappa_2}\dd u\right]^{1/(1-\theta_2)}.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \tauY=\inf\left\{t\ge0:
 \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_0}G_{2,u}^{\theta_2-1}X_u^{\kappa_2}\dd u
 =\frac{y^{1-\theta_2}}{(1-\theta_2)a_2}\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \{\tauY=\infty\}
 \subseteq\left\{
 \int_0^{\tau_0}G_{2,u}^{\theta_2-1}X_u^{\kappa_2}\dd u
 \le\frac{y^{1-\theta_2}}{(1-\theta_2)a_2}\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
\item  Assume additionally that $b_{10}>0,$ $b_2>0$, and $r_1 \ge 0$. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item If \(r_1=0\) and $(1-\theta_2)b_2>\kappa_2b_1,$
then $\Pp_{x,y}(\tauY<\infty)=1$ for every $x,y>0$.
\item If {
\((1-\theta_2)b_2=\kappa_2b_1\)} and
\beqnn
 r_{10}=1,
 \qquad b_{11}=0\ \text{or}\ r_{11}=2,
 \qquad b_{12}=0\ \text{or}\ r_{12}=\alpha_1,
\eeqnn 
then $\Pp_{x,y}(\tauY<\infty)=1$ for every $x,y>0$.
\item If \(r_1>0\), then
{ \(\Pp_{x,y}(\tauY<\infty)=1\) for every \(x,y>0\).}
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.30178

[Corollary 2-l12 of arXiv:2412.04015, 'Linear fluctuation of interfaces in Glauber-Kawasaki dynamics'] Fix a function
$F\colon {\mathbb R}_+ \times (\sqrt{K} {\mathbb T} \times {\mathbb T}^{d-1}) \to {\mathbb R}$
and a cylinder function $f$. Then, there exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak c}({\boldsymbol u}^N)$, depending only on ${\boldsymbol u}^N$, $f$ and $d$, uniformly
bounded in $N$, such that
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\nu^N} \Big[\, \Big|\,
\int_0^t \, 
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_N} \widehat {F_{s}}(Ax) \,
(\Xi^{\rm c} _{{\boldsymbol u}^N (\cdot), x} f) (\eta (s))
\, ds \, \Big| \,\Big]
\\
&\quad \;\le \;
{\mathfrak c}({\boldsymbol u}^N) \, \Big\{ \frac{1}{K_N} \;+\;
K_N\,  \int_0^t (\, 1 + \Vert F(s)\Vert^2_\infty\,)\, \big[ \,
H_N(f^N_s)  + (N/\ell_N)^d \,\big] \, ds\; \Big\}
\\
& \quad \; + \;
\int_0^t \frac{1}{\gamma_s}  \big\{\, H_N(f^N_s) +
\log 2 \, \big\} \; ds
\;+\; {\mathfrak c} ({\boldsymbol u}^N) \,  K\, N^{d-2}\, \int_0^t   \gamma_s \,  {\mathfrak m}_K (F(s))^2\,
\, e^{c ({\boldsymbol u}^N) \, \gamma_s\,  {\mathfrak m}_K (F(s)) \, \epsilon_N }\; ds
\end{align*}
for all $t>0$, $\gamma\colon [0,t] \to (0,\infty)$.  In this equation,
$f^N_s$ is given by (equation 2-34c of the paper), $(\ell_N : N\ge 1)$ is the sequence
introduced in the statement of Theorem (mt1 of the paper), and
$\epsilon_N = K^{1/2}/N$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 2-l12 of arXiv:2412.04015
